Programme: AUDIT-7 (Drew directive, 2026-11-23 ~17:56 CST). Lane 7 of 7.
Umbrella: #13871

## Scope
Every PR and issue that did NOT come from a design or specific roadmap item — bug fixes, other work — plus, for the hygiene pass, everything open right now AND anything closed or with any activity since 2026-10-23, across:
- developing-today/code
- developing-today-forks/opencode
- developing-today-forks/openchamber
- dezren39/fleet

## Work
- Read each in-scope item in full, one by one, no sampling.
- Determine trends across stray work: what kinds of fixes keep recurring, what that says.
- Add appropriate labels; correct titles/descriptions only where actually wrong or empty, logging every correction.
- For each stray item, judge whether there is an appropriate parent it should have been added to — bug tracker, epic, specific design — and link it in.

code.title: AUDIT-7 Lane 6: DESIGN-GAPS — designs missing, demanded, or insufficient (tracking)
code.body:
## AUDIT-7 — Lane 6: DESIGN-GAPS

Umbrella: #13871
Directive: Drew, 2026-11-23 ~17:56 CST. Seven parallel audit lanes over developing-today/code, developing-today-forks/opencode, developing-today-forks/openchamber, dezren39/fleet — exhaustive, every item read in full, no sampling.

### This lane's scope
Find all designs AND all issues that demanded a design. Produce the list of designs yet to make, or poorly implemented / very simple, and add them all to the prioritised agent-next short list as queue packets (`fleet queue`, queue `repo-health-code-pilot`, kind `feature_slice` + `payload.slice`, never kind `design`) so `fleet agent next` can pick them up. Each packet states the sufficient-design standard in full and names its source issue.

### Sufficient-design standard (judge every design against this)
1. problem + context — what breaks today, with evidence
2. goals and explicit non-goals
3. alternatives considered with honest tradeoffs, including do-nothing
4. chosen approach — interfaces/contracts, data model, security and capability analysis where relevant
5. dependency-ordered build slices, each sized for one lane/session with its own acceptance criteria
6. rollout + rollback plan
7. verification plan — how we prove it works (tests, live proof)
8. open questions, each with a named decider
9. recorded as a dated design document in doc/ + a tracking issue + a queue item

A design that is only a paragraph, has no slices, no alternatives, and no acceptance criteria is INSUFFICIENT.

### Prioritisation
1. Designs blocking other work
2. Designs demanded by open issues
3. Deficient-design upgrades

### Coordination
Lane 5 (DESIGN-REVIEW) judges internal soundness; this lane judges existence + sufficiency and owns the queue packets. Claims by other lanes are a hard stop — check umbrella + issue comments first.

### Slices
- [ ] Slice A: code repo — design docs in doc/ + issues demanding design
- [ ] Slice B: opencode fork — same
- [ ] Slice C: openchamber fork — same
- [ ] Slice D: fleet — same
- [ ] Slice E: packetise prioritised gaps, file report doc, final summary

Progress will be posted at every slice boundary on this issue.

code.title: Audit programme: seven-lane review of PRs, issues and designs (2026-11-23)
code.body:
# Audit programme: seven-lane review of PRs, issues and designs (2026-11-23)

Drew's directive (2026-11-23 ~17:56 CST): seven parallel audit lanes over the four repos —
developing-today/code, developing-today-forks/opencode, developing-today-forks/openchamber,
dezren39/fleet. Exhaustive: every item in scope, one by one, read in full, no sampling.

This umbrella is the cross-lane coordination point. Each lane files its own tracking issue,
links it here, and posts progress at every slice boundary. **Dedupe rule:** check this
umbrella and an issue's comments before acting on it — if another lane has claimed it, the
lane whose primary scope it is owns the action; the other records a pointer comment here,
never a duplicate issue or PR.

## The seven lanes

1. **PR-SWEEP** — every open PR not currently being worked on, across the four repos.
   Why hasn't it merged? Merge it if possible; fix minor issues and merge; otherwise record
   the exact blocker with the unblocker named. Per-PR disposition ledger.
2. **CLOSED-ISSUES-REVIEW** — every issue closed since 2026-10-23. Gaps left behind,
   issues closed that shouldn't have been (reopen with reasons), follow-ups that never got
   issues (file them), missing links/tags/labels (add them). Per-issue ledger.
3. **OPEN-ISSUES-AUDIT** — every open issue, one by one. Missing labels, missing links,
   blockers not documented legibly for the fleet system. Judge whether each "blocker"
   actually is one; find and break mutual blocks; restructure parents that should be epics
   or aggregators; for anything marked decision-needed/parked/blocked, determine whether it
   really is, unblock what isn't, and state genuinely-needed decisions in plain words.
   Per-issue ledger.
4. **MERGED-PR-AUDIT** — every PR merged since 2026-10-23. Gaps, bugs, planned next steps
   that never got issues. Compare each PR against its spawning issue — especially PRs that
   closed an issue: fully implemented, or something left on the floor? If a later PR
   completed what an earlier one missed, record that instead of filing a gap. Outcome
   labels for later statistics. Per-PR ledger with comparison verdicts.
5. **DESIGN-REVIEW** — every design record in doc/ and its tracking issue. Gaps in the
   design itself; a dependency order that exists and makes sense; heads (first slices)
   prioritised appropriately. Findings on the design's tracking issue; follow-up issues
   for gaps. Per-design ledger.
6. **DESIGN-GAPS** — all designs and all issues that demanded a design. The list of
   designs yet to be made, or poorly/very simply implemented, each judged against the
   sufficient-design standard; all of them added as prioritised agent-next queue packets
   (kind feature_slice + payload.slice, queue repo-health-code-pilot) so the fleet can
   pick them up. Per-design deficiency list.
7. **STRAY-WORK** — one tracking issue for all PRs and issues not tied to a design or
   roadmap item, plus a hygiene pass over everything open now and anything closed or
   active in the past month. Trends, labels, linkage to the bug tracker/epic/design each
   item belongs under, links back to originating code, correct titles/descriptions, and
   parent-issue trees. Owns stray-work labelling; lanes 2–4 own theirs.

## Shared rules (all lanes)

- GitHub access via the fleet GitHub subcommand (`fleet gh api`) for reads and
  `~/tools/gh-post` (GitHub App identity) for writes. Never plain `gh` with the user
  token, never the GitHub connector.
- Work in laptop worktrees; never the sandbox for repo work.
- Merge authority applies: merge PRs when verified done (drafts/conflicted included, fix
  forward). Never force-push main. Never close issues for age. File-the-issue in the same
  pass for anything found.
- Flag doctrine: if a platform flag trips on a checkout, stop on that checkout, record
  it, vary the mechanic (worktree off the EXISTING clone, worktree at main then switch
  ref, vary transport) before stopping.
- Deliverables per lane: dated report + comprehensive log in doc/ under the dated-record
  convention, including the lane's own prompt verbatim; findings filed as they go; a
  repeatable-process skill where one exists to be made; a final summary comment on the
  lane's tracking issue.

## Lane tracking issues

_(each lane posts its link here as it lands)_

— AUDIT-7 coordinator, 2026-11-23

code.title: id(currency): issued conversion quotes are never evicted — expired quotes accumulate in the gateway verifier forever
code.body:
## Evidence

`pkgs/id/src/currency/conversion.rs` on `origin/main` (`1edf803aa5c79b8bbf4c14292ce2fe1d2861ffab`):

- `ConversionVerifier` holds `quotes: BTreeMap<u128, ConversionQuote>` (:594). The struct docs say one instance is the gateway's single consult point at submission time (:586-589) — i.e. this map lives as long as the gateway.
- The **only** mutation of that map anywhere in the `id` crate is `self.quotes.insert(quote_id, quote.clone())` in `issue_quote` (:845). Crate-wide grep for `quotes.remove / retain / clear / take` finds nothing.
- `verify_quoted` only `get`s (:874); an expired quote is refused with `QuoteExpired` (:877-881) but **left in the map**.
- Every quote dies 60 s after issuance (`QUOTE_LIFETIME_SECS = 60`, :457), yet nothing ever sweeps dead entries.

So each issuance permanently grows the verifier's map: after N quotes the gateway holds N entries, N-minus-live of them unusable expired weight. This is verification by code read — there is no removal path to exercise, so no runtime repro can show anything else.

Secondary observation for triage (same root cause, no lifecycle after issuance): `verify_quoted` takes `&self` and never consumes the quote, so one `quote_id` can back repeated executions for its whole 60 s lifetime. Issuance commits no usage and execution re-checks the cap, so the cap bounds the damage, but the docs ('a quote pays exactly the quoted computed_y and fee') read single-use. Triage should decide whether quotes are single-use (consume on execute) or intentionally multi-use within their lifetime.

## Why it matters

Unbounded state growth in a long-lived gateway singleton: memory grows linearly with cumulative quote volume, and every lookup/insert pays for a map full of dead entries. At gateway traffic this is a slow leak with no operator-visible signal until it hurts.

## Acceptance criteria

- Expired quotes do not accumulate: e.g. evict entries past `quote_expires_at` on `issue_quote`/`verify_quoted` (clock available via `submission.now`), or a bounded book with explicit eviction.
- Decide and document the single-use vs multi-use question above; if single-use, consume the quote on successful execution.
- Regression test: issue quotes, advance past expiry, show the book no longer retains them (and, if single-use, that a second execution under the same id is refused).

## Suggested fix shape

Sweep `self.quotes` against `submission.now` at the top of `issue_quote` and `verify_quoted` (both already take a `now`-carrying submission), and consider `remove`-on-successful-execute if triage lands on single-use. Keep it in the verifier — no new background task.

## Dedupe

Distinct from #13822 (overwrite on *reused* id — same map, opposite end: that one is about insert clobbering a live entry, this one is about entries never leaving), #13698 / PRs #13814 + #13820 (usage-book keying, not the quote book), and closed design #3802 (no eviction requirement stated there). No open PR touches the quote book.

code.title: Turso-to-D1 migration audit + programme
code.body:
Programme tracking for the Turso-to-D1 migration audit (2026-11-23). Full audit + design record lands as a dated doc record (linked from this issue once merged). Research/design only so far — no migrations have been made.

## What the audit found (measured, Turso API, current billing period)

- 50 Turso databases. Estate totals: ~65.8M rows written, ~7.47B rows read, ~10.0 GB storage this period.
- **fleet-platform is 87% of all writes** (57.4M rows written, 465 MB) — PM-stack/dashboard state owned end-to-end by Cloudflare Workers in pm-stack/.
- **fleet-queue is 81% of all reads** (6.08B) — broker/poller scanning; a query-shape problem, not a store-location problem.
- **atlas is 73% of storage** (7.28 GB) and is a native libSQL vector store (107,639 chunks + vec tables) across 33 sharded databases.
- The compile coordinator's tables (#13765: placement_owner_state / placement_claims / placement_budgets) live in the same single fleet-queue database as the rest of the broker store (not yet landed; build is queue task 21517).

## Groups

- **G1 MOVE-CLEAN — fleet-platform telemetry mirror & aggregates** (agent_mirror_*, agent_quota_records, agg_*). Derived/rebuildable data, Worker-only access. **Recommended first slice.**
- **G2 MOVE-CLEAN — fleet-platform ingest families** (ainventory/automation/research/engineering/finance/home *_sheet_rows + *_events + *_sources).
- **G3 MOVE-CLEAN — fleet-platform operational ledgers** (alerts_*, decision_set_events, ci_events, ideas_*, orch_*). Completes the fleet-platform evacuation: all 57.4M writes/month off Turso.
- **G4 STAY-TURSO — fleet-queue broker core** (tasks, events, leases, placement_*, coordinator tables, actions_exec_*). Rust broker on the laptop; transactional claim path; D1 has no local/embedded access path. Separate fix filed by the audit: index/cursor the pollers (the real read win).
- **G5 MOVE-WITH-BRIDGE — fleet-queue read-side mirrors** (github_mirror_*, agent_events_pg_history). D1-first reads, Turso fallback, watermark sync (pattern per #9134's D1 hot cache).
- **G6 MOVE-WITH-BRIDGE (low priority) — muse-meta coord_events** + small tables; coord_tasks/leases stay.
- **G7 STAY-TURSO — Atlas** (atlas + 32 shards). Vector search is libSQL-native; D1 has no vector index. Drew's sketch holds here: Turso remains the sharded embedding store.
- **G8 MOVE-CLEAN (opportunistic) — small stores** (notes-submissions, bedside-and-away, voice-line-ledger, fleet-dispatch-jobs). Exception: great-star-lord stays (standing keep + third-party app DB).

## Honest constraints

- Moving G1–G3 alone does NOT permit a Turso plan downgrade: remaining reads (~6.9B, queue-dominated) exceed Developer-plan inclusion, and remaining storage (~9.5 GB) sits at its line. Downgrade needs the G4 read-shape fix too.
- D1 walls respected in the design: 10 GB per database (one D1 DB per family), single-writer sequential processing (sync writers must batch), Workers/HTTP-API access only.
- Housekeeping decision needed: 8 frozen staging/recovery copies from the 2026-11-17/18 Supabase recovery (~480 MB) should be exported to object storage and deleted — never migrated.

## First slice (recommended)

G1: agent_mirror_* + agent_quota_records + agg_* from fleet-platform into one D1 database, dual-write cutover behind the pm-stack workers. Biggest write win (presumed majority of fleet-platform's 57.4M writes/month; per-table attribution is inference — the Turso API reports per-database only) at the lowest risk (derived data, rebuildable, Worker-only consumers). Side effect: fleet-mirror's duplicate copy of the same dataset can be retired after a parity check.

code.title: Route proxy: complimentary-token metering wall for openai-payg-free (per-group daily counting, wall at bucket, reset 00:00 UTC)
code.body:
## Problem

`openai-payg-free` (the data-sharing complimentary-token alias landed
for code#13677, PRs #13836 + #13838) draws on OpenAI's daily
complimentary-token buckets: large-model group 1M tokens/day (250K
for usage tiers 1-2), small-model group 10M/day (2.5M tiers 1-2),
reset 00:00 UTC.

Bucket exhaustion is **silent**: OpenAI returns no error — eligible
traffic simply starts billing at normal rates. Every wall mechanism
the estate has is failure-driven (fork quota walls, code#13693;
the route proxy's failure-run judging, PR #13735), so none of them
can ever fire for this alias. Today, once the day's bucket is spent,
the free legs keep serving and billing exactly like the paid tail,
bounded only by their seat weights.

## Smallest version

A **metering wall** in the layer that sees response usage (the
route proxy / route-attempt accounting):

1. Count tokens per complimentary group per UTC day from response
   usage payloads for seats under `openai-payg-free` (all three
   seated models are large-group; keep the group mapping in config
   next to the alias so a future small-group alias declares its
   own).
2. At bucket minus a safety margin, wall the alias's legs (the
   existing wall machinery + `wallScope: "account"` declaration on
   the alias) so routes fall through to the next legs; the
   `openai-payg` paid tail remains the final fallback.
3. Reset the wall at 00:00 UTC with the bucket. Persist the counter
   with the existing wall state so a proxy/server restart does not
   resurrect a spent bucket.

## Acceptance

- With the day's large-group count at the cap, a `systemone` /
  `luna-plan` turn no longer serves via `openai-payg-free` (route
  falls through; route_attempt shows the wall, not a billed free-leg
  success).
- After 00:00 UTC the free legs serve again without operator
  action.
- Counter survives a server restart mid-day.

## Context

Design + full evidence: code#13677 (OPENAI-FREE-SHAPE record,
2026-11-23). Related: code#13693 (wall scoping), code#13790 (fork
consumption of wallScope declarations).

code.title: pm-console: the laptop's console has not followed main since 2026-11-23 22:09Z
code.body:
**Seen.** On 2026-11-23 from 22:10Z to 22:52Z (and still, as this is filed) the laptop's console reports itself as running `91d1d63e2e76`, a commit from 19:26Z, while it reports to the edge every half minute as usual. In that time the console's code on main changed three times (`a0840e222f` at 22:09Z, `573067535905` at 22:38Z, `02218db96900` at 22:46Z), and the Worker deployed each of them. `pm-console-redeploy.timer` runs every minute, so the laptop should have followed each within a minute or two. Earlier the same day it did (17:42Z: Worker and laptop both on `3eb33d179b52`).

Read from outside, with no sign-in:

```
curl -s https://pm-console-edge.developing-today.workers.dev/console/health | jq '{version, hostVersion, hostSeen}'
```

**What it means.** Fixes that reach Cloudflare are not reaching what the laptop serves and does. The two sides still talk (the protocol has not changed), so nothing is failing loudly.

**Not known from outside, and where to look on the laptop.** `pm-stack/console/redeploy.sh` does nothing, quietly, in two cases, and fails in a third:

1. The checkout is not at main: `pm-git-sync` has stopped moving `~/git/code` (the checkout ahead and behind at once is #12520). `git -C ~/git/code status -sb` and `systemctl --user status pm-git-sync` say.
2. The checkout has changes under `pm-stack/console` or the console's units that match no commit (`redeploy.sh` leaves a checkout that looks part-way through an update for the next run, every run). `git -C ~/git/code diff --stat HEAD -- pm-stack/console pm-stack/systemd` says.
3. The new code did not pass its self-check there: `systemctl --user status pm-console-redeploy` shows the unit failed, and the state directory's `redeploy.log` has why.

**What done looks like.**

- The laptop's console is on main's code again, and the cause is written here.
- If it was case 2, `redeploy.sh` says so where someone will see it once it has skipped for more than a few minutes, and does not skip silently for hours.
- The edge can tell this by itself: both sides say which console code they run in a way that can be compared (the tree's hash, not the commit that happened to be at HEAD), and the Machines screen says when a machine has run other code than Cloudflare for longer than a few minutes.

Tracker: #13504.

code.title: pm-console edge: do what is held for a machine itself, once it can
code.body:
**Today.** When the edge is turned away while doing something the owner asked (GitHub's allowance used up, or its token refused for that kind of action), the action is handed to a machine: done at once if one is reporting, otherwise kept in the held list until one is. Held items are only ever done by a machine. With no machine, they wait, and after a day they are dropped and said to have been.

Since #13570 the edge keeps to the time GitHub gives for asking again, which can be most of an hour. So with the laptop away and the hour's allowance spent, a rank, a comment or a reply the owner makes is kept "for a machine" although the edge itself could do it a few minutes later.

**What done looks like.**

- When the edge can act again (GitHub's time has come, or the kind is no longer refused) it does what it holds that it could do itself, oldest first and in order by what each is about, with no machine involved. The owner sees the same outcome in "What you did" as for anything done late.
- Nothing is done twice. This is the hard part, and the rule already in force is that a name keeps to the side that first took it:
  - an item a machine may already have been handed (it was in a sync answer the machine has not reported back on) is not the edge's to do;
  - the edge takes an item out of the held list, and marks its name as its own, before it starts, so a machine that reports in the meantime is not handed it;
  - if the edge is turned away again, the item goes back as it was.
- Tests at the edge for each of those, including a machine reporting half-way through, and one in the real Worker runtime (`scripts/edge-smoke.ts`) with the stand-in GitHub turning calls away and then answering.

**Where.** `pm-stack/console/edge/src/edge.ts`: the held list (`keep`, `heldList`), `once()` and the `a:<id>` records (`running`, `done`, `given`), and the alarm. Related: #13398 (order between a held item and a newer one the edge does itself).

Design record: `doc/2026-11-23T06-50-00Z_architecture_pm_platform_cloudflare_core/` (sections of 2026-11-23T18:10Z and 22:40Z).

code.title: id(currency): issue_quote silently overwrites an in-flight quote under a reused quote_id
code.body:
## Summary

`ConversionVerifier::issue_quote` stores every issued quote with a bare
`BTreeMap::insert`, so a second issuance under an already-held `quote_id`
silently destroys the first quote. The record's own contract says the id is
`gateway-generated, unique in the book` — the code enforces neither half:
ids are caller-supplied and collisions overwrite with no error.

## Evidence

- `pkgs/id/src/currency/conversion.rs:470-471` — `quote_id`
  `(gateway-generated, unique in the gateway's store)`.
- `pkgs/id/src/currency/conversion.rs:791-793` — issuance stores the quote
  `under quote_id — a gateway-generated id, unique in the book, in the same
  caller-supplied-id shape as the pure layer's transfer ids`. Caller-chosen
  ids in a verifier-global namespace, with uniqueness only promised in prose.
- `pkgs/id/src/currency/conversion.rs:845` —
  `self.quotes.insert(quote_id, quote.clone())`. No `contains_key` check,
  no error arm; `BTreeMap::insert` overwrites and the old quote is gone.
- Readers (`:612-614` `quote()`, `:867-902` `verify_quoted`) give no
  hint a replacement happened: the first quoter's execution just starts
  failing with `QuoteMismatch` (different auth/amount pinned under its id),
  or silently inherits the second quote's `issued_at`/`quote_expires_at`
  window when auth and amount coincide.
- Design context: Phase 3 of #2290, #3802 (commit `dbf76598b86`).

## Repro

Temporary in-module test, reverted afterwards, on scratch at `origin/main`
`a77026ed`:

```rust
let mut verifier = ConversionVerifier::new();
let first = issue_valid_quote(&mut verifier, 77);   // x = 100
assert_eq!(first.x, 100);
let mut other = valid_submission();
other.amount = 200;
let second = verifier
    .issue_quote(&eligible_control(), &other, 77, 0, 0)
    .unwrap();                                       // Ok — no error
assert_eq!(second.x, 200);
assert_eq!(verifier.quote(77).unwrap().x, 200);      // first quote lost
```

`cargo test --lib currency::conversion::tests::repro_quote_id_silent_overwrite`
 run in `pkgs/id`: `test ... ok` — the overwrite is confirmed, not
hypothesized. Tree reverted to clean afterwards.

## Why it matters

Quote ids are caller-supplied into a verifier-global book with no ownership
or uniqueness enforcement. Any caller (or retry path) that reuses an id —
accidentally via collision, or maliciously — destroys someone else's
in-flight quote. The victim gets a confusing `QuoteMismatch` refusal at
execution time, inside its 60-second lifetime, for a quote that verified fine
at issuance. Same-auth/same-amount collisions are worse: execution succeeds
but under a different quote's expiry window, with no signal.

## Acceptance criteria

- Issuance under a `quote_id` that already holds an unexpired quote is
  refused with a typed pre-flight/store error (or an explicit, documented
  replace-with-acknowledgement path) — never a silent overwrite.
- Regression test: issue id 77 for x=100, re-issue id 77 for x=200 is
  refused; `quote(77).x` stays 100; the first quoter's `verify_quoted`
  still passes.
- Existing `currency::conversion::tests` (all quote tests:
  pinning, scale-aware `computed_y`, refusal propagation, expiry,
  since-revoked, superseded-version, unknown-quote, amount mismatch,
  exact-amount execution) keep passing.

## Suggested direction (not implemented)

Check `self.quotes` for a live entry before inserting and return a typed
error (e.g. `QuoteIdInUse`); document the caller-supplies-id collision
semantics and whether retry-with-same-id+same-content is idempotent. Expired
entries could be allowed to be replaced or reaped, but that is a deliberate
policy choice, not the current silent behavior.

code.title: id(serve): a failed blob-gate rebuild replaces the live gate with an empty fold, so every current member loses blob fetch until the next tick
code.body:
## Finding

The blob membership gate's periodic refresh task replaces the live gate with an empty one when a transient read fails. `build_blob_gate` (`pkgs/id/crates/id-cli/src/commands/serve/startup.rs`) substitutes fallback values on each error and returns them as if they were a complete fold:

- group log cannot be opened (`startup.rs:206-209`): `group_projection = None`
- group log does not fold (`startup.rs:201-204`): `group_projection = None`
- `document_references()` fails (`startup.rs:215-218`): `references = Vec::new()`
- end of function (`startup.rs:280-283`): `None` becomes `FoldedWorlds::new(Worlds::empty(), index)`, which has no members and an index built from the fallback references

The refresh loop in `commands/serve.rs:2399-2415` runs `build_blob_gate` every `GROUP_WARNING_INTERVAL` (60s) and calls `gate.refresh(folded)` unconditionally. `RefreshingWorlds::refresh` (`pkgs/id/crates/id-worlds/src/blob_gate.rs:227-231`) installs the new fold with no check that the previous one was valid.

Result: one failed read of the group log or the document references, which can be a transient I/O or lock error, makes every current member fail to fetch or observe blobs until the next successful tick. The only signal is a `warn!` line (`startup.rs:202, 207, 216`); no metric or state records that the gate is running on a degraded fold.

This is fail-closed for reads, so it is not a data leak. It is a silent availability regression, and the same fallback pattern is a plausible source of a hard-to-diagnose "blobs disappeared" report.

Related: #6979 covers the groups-fold gate in ingest (`event_store/resolve.rs`), not this blob-gate refresh path.

## Evidence

Checked on `origin/main` at `3be23e4943a`:

- `pkgs/id/crates/id-cli/src/commands/serve/startup.rs:193-283` (`build_blob_gate`): the three fallback branches above
- `pkgs/id/crates/id-cli/src/commands/serve.rs:2399-2415`: the refresh loop, with `gate.refresh(folded)` unconditional
- `pkgs/id/crates/id-worlds/src/blob_gate.rs:211-231`: `RefreshingWorlds::refresh` overwrites the fold without validation
- Existing refresh test (`id-worlds/src/blob_gate.rs` tests) covers only a legitimate membership removal, not a degraded read

## Why it matters

The gate's purpose is to keep blobs from peers who are not members. Dropping a live gate to empty on a read error makes it misbehave in the other direction for every legitimate member, and the failure only appears as a warning in the serve log. An operator has no way to tell a temporary read failure from a real membership change.

## Suggested fix shape

- Have `build_blob_gate` return `Result` (or an explicit `Degraded` variant), and have the refresh loop keep the last good fold when a rebuild fails, logging the failure at error level.
- Keep the fail-closed rule for a never-built gate: at startup, with no prior good fold, keep the empty gate.
- Add a test that a failed `GroupLog::open` or failed reference read keeps the previous membership in force, and that a later successful rebuild replaces it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A failed rebuild in the refresh loop does not replace the previous good `FoldedWorlds`; the previous fold stays in force.
- [ ] Each failed rebuild logs at error level with the failing step.
- [ ] A test covers: rebuild fails (log open error, fold error, reference read error) → previous membership still admits a current member's fetch; then a successful rebuild that removes the member revokes it.
- [ ] Startup with no prior good fold still refuses (no change to the fail-closed default).

code.title: feat(pm-aggregator): validate IdP access tokens + role-gate writes (first production consumer, #13416)
code.body:
Integration follow-on from #13416 (first consumer of the minimal IdP, story #13658), per the parent design #1253: the PM-stack aggregator is the first layer named for token validation, with Kaneo/Pad/Grist behind Cloudflare Access (#1182).

## Scope

- The aggregator validates access tokens from our IdP (`pkgs/idp-provider`) on its write paths, following the per-app integration pattern documented in the provider README (from #13416): discovery-driven configuration, JWKS verification **selecting the key by token `kid`** (rollover-safe), issuer + expiry + `token_use=access` checks.
- Writes require a write role from the token's `roles` claim (`owner` or `orchestrator` per the reference consumer's gate); reads accept any valid token. Enforcement is server-side in the aggregator; role data is never taken from request bodies or client-side state.
- Cloudflare Access continues to front the stack for reachability; the IdP token is the aggregator's own authorization input. The two compose — neither replaces the other. The #9608 break-glass owner token remains the outage path when the IdP itself is unreachable, exactly as designed there.

## Sequencing

- After the reference consumer from #13416 (pattern + proof exist), and most valuable once a federation door is live (#13411/#13412/#13414 registrations) so sign-in to the aggregator is a real door login rather than the local door alone. Not blocked on SAML (S3, #13795) — the aggregator consumes OIDC.

## Acceptance

- Aggregator write endpoint rejects a missing/invalid token (401), rejects a valid token without a write role (403), and accepts an owner/orchestrator token — demonstrated against the real provider, with the role-denial case covered by tests (the live provider's single account holds all roles, so the denial proof is test-level, as in the reference consumer).
- The integration is recorded on #13416 and #1253.

code.title: fork: consume wallScope declarations in the provider gate (WALL-SKIP follow-on from #13693)
code.body:
## Follow-on from #13693 (lane WALL-SKIP, slice C2)

PR #13784 landed `wallScope` declarations in `.opencode/opencode.jsonc` (`_commandcode` → provider; `_commandcode-free`, `groq`, the four free `google.*` aliases → per-model), validated by `bin/check-opencode-route-rules.mjs`. The declarations are currently **declarative only**: nothing in the fork consumes them yet, because the fork strips the field at decode — `packages/core/src/config/normalize.ts` (`migrateProviders`, `onExcessProperty: "ignore"`, no schema field for it), confirmed live in the decoded `/api/config` read-back after PR #13784 (slice C outcome, #13693 c.7114902291).

## Work

1. **Schema preservation**: carry `wallScope` through the fork's provider config schema/decode (values: `per-model` | `provider` | `account`).
2. **Reader**: expose it beside the existing membership readers — an `onWallScope`-style registered reader in `packages/core/src/config/plugin/model-routes.ts`, next to `onMembershipLimits` (the pattern `model-route.ts` already consumes).
3. **Consumption** in `packages/core/src/model-route.ts`: in `observeGatheredProviderWall` / `providerQuotaBlocked`, a provider declared `per-model` never receives a provider-scope gathered gate (its model-scope plants still apply); a provider declared `provider` or `account` is judged at that scope even when the reading's shape would infer a narrower one. Absent declaration = today's inference, unchanged.

## Acceptance

- Fork test: a provider declared `per-model` whose gathered reading is a single provider-wide known-full entry gets pair-scope plants only — `providerQuotaBlocked` does not block its other models.
- Fork test: no declaration → inference behaviour byte-identical to today (existing suites green).
- The #13693 design rule this completes: config declaration is the override when automatic scope inference gets a provider wrong; inference stays the default.

## Consideration

Drew (2026-11-23): "we should probably at least support it for compatibility layer — allow reading bsky in id natively, consider."

Scope: a **read-only** AT Protocol ingestion path for `pkgs/id` — resolve atproto identities, fetch their public repositories, **verify them cryptographically**, and surface the records inside id with provenance. No write support, no account creation, no Spaces/permissioned data, no AppView ambitions. Full research note: `~/workspace/p2panda-investigation/research/bluesky-atproto.md` (Part B); filed from the auth+transport investigation #13779, for the id epic #2056.

## What it decomposes into

1. **Handle → DID**: DNS TXT (`_atproto.<handle>`) or `/.well-known/atproto-did`, verified bidirectionally against the DID document.
2. **DID resolution**: `did:plc` via plc.directory (strong form: fetch and verify the audit-log operation chain — each op signed by the prior op's rotation keys, so the directory is trusted only for availability/fork choice); `did:web` via `/.well-known/did.json` (trust = DNS+TLS). From the document: the `#atproto` repo signing key and the `#atproto_pds` endpoint.
3. **Light record reads**: `com.atproto.repo.describeRepo` / `listRecords` / `getRecord` against the account's PDS, unauthenticated. Trusts the PDS for completeness — acceptable for display, not for verification claims.
4. **Verifiable repo ingest**: `com.atproto.sync.getRepo` → CAR v1 (signed commit + MST nodes + records). Verification: DAG-CBOR/CID discipline, MST reconstruction (SHA-256 key-depth, fanout 4, prefix-compressed nodes) with root equality against the commit's `data` CID, commit signature check (SHA-256 over the unsigned commit; secp256k1 or P-256 key from the DID document), `rev` monotonicity. This is the slice that makes "reads bsky natively" mean something more than "calls Bluesky's AppView".
5. **Optional live follow (later)**: relay `com.atproto.sync.subscribeRepos`; `#commit` diffs verify cheaply via op-inversion against `prevData` (per-repo state = rev + root CID). Full-network firehose is AppView-scale — a filtered/per-account shape is the realistic form.

## Where it would sit

Precedent: `pkgs/id/crates/id-import-notion` — importer-shaped work already lives in its own crate. Proposal: a new read-only importer crate (working name `id-import-atproto`): resolve → fetch → verify → emit foreign records with provenance (DID, collection, rkey, CID, commit rev) into id's existing store/events shapes. Explicitly **not** `id-core` (no core model change for a foreign protocol) and **not** `id-sync` (id's own log-sync/meta protocol — a different thing that happens to share a word).

Rust library state: **atrium** (MIT, actively released; `atrium-identity`, `atrium-repo` MST, codegen'd XRPC types — the default candidate, though its centre of gravity is client sessions); **jacquard** (MPL-2.0, `jacquard-repo` MST/CAR, zero-copy, but single-maintainer-shaped and pre-1.0 with frequent breaking releases); **atproto-crates** (MIT, separable primitives incl. CAR reading and identity, 0.14.x). Rolling our own MST/CAR verifier is bounded, spec-complete fallback work, not the plan.

## Costs, stated plainly

- MST/CAR/commit verification is real work — and is also the entire value over proxying an AppView.
- Unknown lexicons must ingest as opaque verbatim records; interpreting `app.bsky.*` is a separate opt-in layer.
- Deletion/takedown handling is a policy choice: repos are tombstone-free and mirrors are expected to honour deletions; verbatim retention must be a deliberate decision, not a default.
- Scale scoping: per-account ingest is tractable; "the network" is an indexing programme. This issue is about accounts.

## Open questions

1. PLC trust posture: (a) trust plc.directory HTTPS, (b) verify the audit-log chain per DID, (c) consume a PLC replica. Recommendation: (b).
2. Record modelling: verbatim DAG-CBOR with provenance index (recommended first slice) vs mapping into id's object model.
3. Which accounts/collections are in scope for a first slice — a named seed set, or any DID on demand?
4. Live follow: in scope at all, and if so filtered (per-account polling / Jetstream-shaped) vs relay subscription?
5. Blobs: reference-only, or fetch-and-store?
6. Does the importer emit into `id-events`/`id-store` directly, or land in a staging shape the atlas source-registry work (#3125 line) consumes?

## Links

- Epic: #2056 · Investigation: #13779 · AT Protocol repository spec: https://atproto.com/specs/repository · Sync spec: https://atproto.com/specs/sync · did:plc spec v0.3.0: https://github.com/did-method-plc/did-method-plc

- **p2panda** core + **p2panda-auth** + **p2panda-sync**
- **keyhive / subduction** (Ink & Switch lineage)
- **willow / meadowcap** (Earthstar lineage)
- **OCapN / CapTP / Endo / Spritely Goblins / Agoric** (object-capability networks)

- The wider field where it fits the estate: UCAN, Biscuit, Veilid, Holepunch/Hypercore, libp2p, Freenet, Holochain, and peers

code.title: fleet actions exec: live short-lived exec sessions inside Actions runners, coordinator-handed-off
code.body:
# fleet actions exec: live short-lived exec sessions inside Actions runners, coordinator-handed-off

Drew's order, 2026-11-23 15:17 CST: implement an alternate `fleet actions exec` mode that may become the primary — agents connect into GitHub Actions runners and exec commands themselves, temporary and short-lived like the commander/route subcommand family (#13717). The central coordinator (#13765) establishes the connection handoff; the fleet command background-watches the run after handoff.

## Premise (verified first-hand, 2026-11-23)

- **Coordinator (#13765)** has a complete design of record: broker verbs `/placement-claim|confirm|release|claim-status|load`, a coordinator sweep in the queue broker, client integration with a **singular fallback** that names itself via `placement_path`. Its build is routed separately; this mode composes with the design (claim a slot for the session's host surface when the verbs answer; proceed singular and record `placement_path` when they don't) and never forks it.
- **Fleet action constellation:** the generic fleet action lives in **dezren39/fleet** — composite action `.github/actions/fleet-command`, dispatch workflows `fleet-command.yml` (repo-queue dispatch runner) and `fleet-run.yml` (generic runner; developing-today/fleet fork adds runner choice + cache deltas that must survive syncs). Fixes land on dezren39/fleet main and sync to the forks.
- **Existing IO pattern (dispatch path):** command output lives in the Actions run log; reusable output chains via the `fleet-output` artifact (`previous_run_id` input downloads the prior run's artifact); caches via actions/cache and the R2 nix cache (`cache.push_nix` → signed `nix copy` to the R2 cache URL, skipping quietly when secrets are absent).
- **PM push surface exists:** `crates/fleet-queue/src/needs_drew.rs` (#8568) emits needs-drew alerts into the PM aggregator throat — `POST http://127.0.0.1:4870/api/alerts`, Bearer token resolved **by name** through fleet-secrets, body `{source, key, severity, title, body, needsDrew:{ledgerId, question, context, options[], links[]}}`, deduped by (source, key). The notification presents choices; this is the emergency-extension push path.
- **Rendezvous constraint (#10356):** the sandbox has no inbound path; every route names its rendezvous. Runners are on the public internet and the queue broker lives on the laptop — so this mode needs a public door in the commander/mcpx pattern (Worker gate + tunnel → laptop), path-scoped to the session verbs.
- **Route family shape (#13717):** timeout required by construction; the serving form is named in output.

## Method survey — direct runner access, filtered by the public-log leak

The hard filter: **most off-the-shelf runner-access methods print SSH/connection info into the run log, and in a public repo the log is world-readable.** Any method whose connection material can appear in logs is disqualified, however convenient.

| Method | Shape | Verdict |
| --- | --- | --- |
| tmate (mxschmitt/action-tmate et al.) | Runner opens tmate session; SSH string + web URL printed to log | **Rejected** — connection string in public logs is the exact leak |
| upterm (action-upterm) | SSH via upterm server; connection info printed to log; actor-limiting exists | **Rejected** — same leak; allowlists don't unpublish the log |
| tailscale/github-action | Runner joins the tailnet; reach it by tailnet name, nothing secret prints | Viable but not picked: couples runner access to tailnet enrolment/ACLs for every caller, and #13752 thread 1 is actively designing *away* from Tailscale-only reach |
| cloudflared + Access on the runner | Runner dials out to Cloudflare; requester authenticates via Access | Viable; the estate already runs this door pattern (commander/mcpx). Kept as the door technology, not the session protocol |
| iroh endpoint on the runner | NodeId is a public key — printing it leaks nothing; auth is the keypair (#13752 thread 2) | Right long-term transport for the fleet binary; not the v1 session protocol (pilot is scoped to seat→amd, and this mode needs the coordinator handoff semantics first). The session protocol below is transport-shaped so iroh can carry it later |
| **Runner-side agent dials OUT to the coordinator (chosen)** | The workflow starts a small agent (a mode of the fleet binary). The agent proves it is inside the run with the job's **GitHub OIDC token** (fetched from the Actions runtime, never logged), registers with the broker, and holds an outbound long-poll. Commands flow requester → broker → agent; IO flows back the same way | **Chosen** — no inbound path, nothing connection-shaped ever exists outside the two endpoints, the session handle is a public identifier (safe in logs), and the handoff *is* the coordinator's job in #13765's design |

Runner-side auth detail: the broker verifies the OIDC JWT against GitHub's JWKS and checks `repository`, `workflow`, `job_workflow_ref`, `run_id`, `run_attempt` claims against the session row the coordinator created at dispatch. Requester-side auth is the existing broker seat auth. Workflow inputs carry only the handle + non-secret parameters — never a token (inputs are visible on the run page; secrets would be masked but dispatch cannot receive them).

## Design

**Three pieces, one flow.**
1. **Action** — dezren39/fleet `.github/actions/fleet-exec-session` (composite, fleet-command conventions): sets up the pinned fleet binary, runs `fleet actions agent` for the session, ships the egress helper on PATH.
2. **Workflow** — dezren39/fleet `.github/workflows/fleet-exec.yml` (workflow_dispatch; inputs: handle, target repo/ref optional checkout, runner, lease/max seconds, hide-logs flag; `permissions: id-token: write`; job timeout = max lifespan + grace).
3. **Subcommand** — new `actions` domain in pkgs/fleet (fleet-registry + verbs.md in the same change): `fleet actions exec` group in the #13717 family shape — `--timeout` required by construction, serving form named in output.

**Flow:** requester runs `fleet actions exec start` → subcommand asks the coordinator to claim a slot for the host surface and create the session row (singular fallback per #13765 when the coordinator doesn't answer) → subcommand dispatches `fleet-exec.yml` with the handle → coordinator/subcommand binds run id + attempt (the **handoff**: handle, `OWNER/REPO#RUN_ID`, attempt) → runner agent registers via OIDC → requester execs via `fleet actions exec run <handle> -- cmd`, attaches/streams, renews, closes.

**Broker verbs** (new module `crates/fleet-queue/src/turso_queue/actions_exec.rs`, routed in `turso_queue::dispatch` beside the placement coordinator's; house conditional-UPDATE atomicity; DDL beside `placement_sessions`):
- `/actions-exec-open` (seat) — create session {handle, host_repo, seat, lease_until, max_until, hide_logs, state}.
- `/actions-exec-bind` (seat/coordinator) — record run_id + attempt.
- `/actions-exec-register` (agent, OIDC-verified) — bind agent to session, state `live`.
- `/actions-exec-poll` (agent) — long-poll for commands + lease state.
- `/actions-exec-command` (seat) — enqueue one command {cmd_id, text, timeout_s}.
- `/actions-exec-io` (agent) — append IO chunk {cmd_id, seq, stream, data}; `/actions-exec-result` (agent) — exit code, cmd terminal.
- `/actions-exec-stream` (seat) — IO chunks after a seq (attach + background watch read this).
- `/actions-exec-renew` (seat) — extend lease within max; past max → `extension-required`.
- `/actions-exec-extend-request` (seat) — past-max extension: creates the request **and emits the needs-drew alert** (source `fleet-actions-exec`, key `actions-exec-ext:<handle>`, options approve/deny, links to the run + this issue). Session enters `extension-pending` with a short decision grace so a live agent isn't killed mid-question.
- `/actions-exec-extend-decide` (seat acting on Drew's answer) — applies or denies. **Known gap:** the phone tap → broker write-back is the PM stack's next phase; v1's write-back is a seat running this verb on Drew's recorded answer. The alert is the push; the verb is the closest existing surface.
- `/actions-exec-close` (either side) — terminal; agent exits, workflow step ends.

**Disconnect tolerance:** requester disconnect is a non-event (broker holds commands, IO, lease). Agent network blips retry with backoff against the long-poll. Reconnect = re-attach with the same handle; the session and any running command survive a short grace window, mirroring the laptop attach pattern.

**Lease discipline:** lease = `--timeout` at start (required, no default). Hard cap = `--max-lifespan` (default 30 min, ceiling 120 min — the fleet-run leg cap). The agent enforces the lease locally as well as via the broker (dies at expiry even if partitioned, after a final IO/egress flush). Renewals move `lease_until` up to `max_until`; past that, only an approved emergency extension (push above) moves it, each approval bounded (+30 min).

**File egress:** the Action puts `fleet-exec-put <file>` on the session PATH: it copies the file into the session outbox (uploaded as the `fleet-exec-out` workflow artifact when the session step ends) **and** PUTs it to R2 (S3-compatible; credentials arrive as workflow secrets, are masked by GitHub, and are never echoed; absent credentials skip the R2 leg quietly, the fleet-run cache pattern).

**Log visibility + IO decision:** by default the agent echoes session IO to its own stdout, so commands and output land in the Actions run log (the dispatch path's existing visibility). `--hide-logs` on the subcommand turns the echo off. **Decision:** the transport is brokered in both modes (it is the handoff mechanism, not a visibility feature); the broker's IO chunk store is the cache of record either way — with logs visible it is the low-latency attach/watch source, with logs hidden it is the *only* IO path back to the requester. No second IO system is built.

**Background watch:** after handoff the subcommand can follow the run without holding the requester's terminal: `fleet actions exec watch <handle>` streams broker IO + run status (polled via the placement GitHub client) until terminal; `start --detach` returns after handoff and records the handle in the local session store so `watch`/`attach`/`run` resolve it from any seat (the portable `OWNER/REPO#RUN_ID` form works too).

## Slices

1. This issue: premise + survey + design.
2. Action + workflow in dezren39/fleet (agent bootstrap in proof mode: build the agent from a code ref in the runner; production pins the released fleet binary).
3. Broker verbs + DDL + tests (rusqlite fake-pipeline pattern from #13765's proof bar).
4. Runner agent (`fleet actions agent`): OIDC register, poll/exec/stream loop, lease enforcement, egress helper.
5. Subcommand (`fleet actions exec` group): start/run/attach/watch/renew/extend/close + coordinator composition + singular fallback naming.
6. PM push wiring for emergency extension (needs-drew throat emission + decide verb).
7. Live proof (below), runbook note in `doc/agents/remote-build-and-test.md`, verbs.md, PRs, merge on green.

## Proof bar

One live end-to-end run, recorded here: subcommand → coordinator handoff (handle + run id + attempt named) → exec a command on the runner → `fleet-exec-put` a file out to **both** the workflow artifact and R2 → requester disconnect/reconnect resumes the same session → renewal extends within the cap → a short-lease session dies at its cap unrenewed. Plus the leak acceptance test: **read the produced public workflow logs end to end and show no connection material** (no tokens, no OIDC material, no credential values — handles and run ids only).

Lane ACTIONS-EXEC. If the platform execution-risk check stops a build step, the stop is recorded here with the exact slice state for routing to a laptop session.

## Failing run
- Run: https://github.com/developing-today/code/actions/runs/45264370211 (workflow `mcpx worker publish`, event workflow_dispatch, ref main, head f98afcc9ea3f038ae15bc31583d7677a2fdd25c1, completed failure 2026-11-23T20:55:38Z)
- Failed job: `Upload mcpx Worker Version` (138007252746), step `Upload Worker Version and capture provenance`.

## Evidence (failed log)
- `GET .../workers/scripts/mcpx/deployments` returns 404, Cloudflare [10007] "This Worker does not exist on your account."
- `wrangler workers versions create --worker mcpx` returns "You cannot upload a new version of a Worker that does not yet exist. Please run the `deploy` command first."
- Workflow: `.github/workflows/mcpx-worker-publish.yml` on origin/main (runs `upload-version.mjs`).

## Diagnosis
The upload-only path assumes the Worker script already exists. It has never been created on the account, so the first publish needs a bootstrap `deploy`, which needs Cloudflare account access this fix path has not been given. Related: #13657.

## Owed
- Choose the bootstrap path (one-time `wrangler deploy` through the repo's cf flow, or have upload-version fall back to deploy when the script is absent), then re-run the workflow green.
- Do not change account state from this issue without the deploy path recorded.

code.title: fleet placement: central coordinator for compile dispatch — atomic slots, true load view, global budgets, cross-seat queueing
code.body:
# fleet placement: central coordinator for compile dispatch

Drew's order, 2026-11-23 15:09 CST: implement a central coordinator under the hood of the fleet compile/dispatch commands, using a worker, with the commands falling back to singular per-seat handling when the coordinator is unavailable. The four reasons below are from the 2026-11-23 09:03 CST placement analysis; each is a design requirement with a named proof.

## Premise (verified first-hand, 2026-11-23)

- The dispatch path is `fleet queue dispatch` → `decide()` → adapter dispatch in `crates/fleet-queue/src/placement.rs`. The local JSON store is, in the mirror module's own words, "the ONLY input to placement decisions" (`placement/remote.rs`); the queue backend's `placement_sessions` table (core.rs SCHEMA, #13146) is a best-effort visibility mirror only.
- Caps live in the embedded surface registry (`fleet-surfaces.json`): developing-today 20 concurrent jobs, developing-today-forks 20, dezren39 40 (macOS 5 each).
- Load view: `build_ctx` reads GitHub Actions run counts per runner-host repo with per-repo minted/user tokens. A repo the seat has no token for counts as **0 running** (coverage is reported via `owner_load_coverage`, and #13611 made the decision logic treat unread load as unknown — but the seat's view is still only its own).
- Blacksmith budget: registry surface `fleet-org-blacksmith` carries `budget.free_minutes_monthly = 3000`, `paid_cap_minutes = 0`. Used minutes are summed in `build_ctx` from the **local per-seat store's** `blacksmith_dispatches` — a per-seat honour system.
- No atomic claim exists anywhere in the dispatch path: `decide()` reads load, picks least-loaded, dispatches. The only lock is a per-seat file lock on the local store.
- The queue broker (`queue_broker.rs`) already hosts broker-side GitHub access (the #8276 dep probe) and spawns background threads; verb routing is `turso_queue::dispatch`; the house atomicity pattern is the single conditional UPDATE whose affected-row count decides the winner (task claim, `turso_queue/claim.rs`).

## The four reasons (requirements)

1. **Atomic slots.** Read-then-dispatch is racy: two seats see the same least-loaded pool and both pile in (observed: 62 active org jobs against a cap of 20 — caps steer, they don't gate). The coordinator claims slots atomically.
2. **One true load view.** A seat without token coverage for an owner reads that owner's load as zero and can pick wrong. The coordinator holds the true cross-owner load view and admission uses it, not the seat's.
3. **Global budgets.** The Blacksmith free-minute budget is per-seat honour system today. The coordinator enforces it fleet-wide, atomically (reserve at claim, settle at completion).
4. **Cross-seat visibility and queueing.** Sessions visible to every seat natively; when all pools saturate, jobs wait in a real queue with fairness (FIFO per owner) instead of every seat dispatching into the pile.

## Architecture

- **Home:** the queue broker's store (already the fleet's coordination point; `placement_sessions` already lives there).
- **Backend verbs** (new module `turso_queue/placement_coord.rs`): `/placement-claim` (atomic admission: conditional owner-counter UPDATE against cap using the coordinator's load rows + active claims; Blacksmith budget reservation in the same flow), `/placement-confirm`, `/placement-release` (with budget settle), `/placement-claim-status`, `/placement-load` (the true load view, readable by any seat).
- **Coordinator worker:** a background thread in the queue broker (the #12247 startup-thread pattern) that refreshes the true load view from GitHub on an interval (broker-side reads, same host-repo counts `build_ctx` makes, from the seat with full token coverage), expires stale claims/grants, settles confirmed claims whose runs finished, recomputes active-claim counters from the claims table (self-healing), and grants the waitlist fairly as capacity appears.
- **Client:** `fleet queue dispatch` asks the coordinator for a claim on the decided surface before dispatching (bounded roundtrip, same discipline as the #13146 mirror). Granted → dispatch as today, confirm with the run id. Saturated → the session is committed in state `queued` with its claim id and full job record (the shape the all-tiers-exhausted path already writes); `fleet queue session status` completes the dispatch when the claim is granted. Command surface (verbs/flags) unchanged.
- **Fallback contract:** when the coordinator is unreachable or times out, the command proceeds with today's singular per-seat dispatch and **says so in its output** (`placement_path` names `coordinator` vs `singular-fallback`, per the estate's route-visibility doctrine). A down coordinator never hard-fails a build.

Scope: the compile/dispatch path only (see `pkgs/fleet/doc/agents/remote-build-and-test.md`). The agent task queue is untouched; this coordinates with it through the shared broker store.

## Proof bar (one named test per reason, plus the fallback)

1. Concurrency: two simultaneous claims for the last slot — exactly one wins.
2. Load view: a seat with zero coverage for an owner is refused/queued when the coordinator's view shows the owner full, and admitted when it shows room; `/placement-load` returns the true counts to any seat.
3. Budget: reservations past the fleet-wide Blacksmith free-minute budget are refused; settle converts reservation to actual use.
4. Saturation: jobs queue, drain in fair (FIFO) order as slots free; a claim/session made on one seat resolves from another.
5. Fallback: coordinator down — dispatch still succeeds via singular handling and the output reports the fallback.

Lane: COMPILE-COORD. Progress posts at every slice boundary.

code.title: design: fleet transport & pooling — host selection without Tailscale, iroh for non-Muse agents, generic pool primitive
code.body:
## Direction

Drew, 2026-11-23 15:07 CST — the longer-term design threads that grow out of the laptop route codification (#13717, the route-form family; #13654 is its F1):

1. **Choosing hosts and access without Tailscale.**
2. **Direct iroh for non-Muse agents.**
3. **A generic pooling system.**

This issue tracks the design. The full design record lands as a dated doc (`doc/2026-11-23T21-10-36Z_design_fleet-transport-pooling/`); this issue carries the three threads as separable work items with the recommendation for each. Design only — every build item below needs its own slice issue when picked up.

## Premise check (read first, 2026-11-23)

- **#13717 already codifies the route forms** (3 methods × 2 shapes + the `fleet laptop` walker + the laptop-ssh F7 demotion). This design builds on it: thread 1 turns its laptop-specific matrix into per-host data; it does not redo it.
- **#10356 (2026-11-14) already designs explicit transport selection** — `fleet connect --method exec|ssh|job|auto`, sessions, drop semantics. Composition, not duplication: #10356 is *method choice on a known host*; thread 1 is *host choice + reach when no overlay exists*. #10356 also records the hard constraint: **the sandbox has no inbound path at all** — every connection is sandbox-initiated or rendezvoused. Any no-Tailscale design must name its rendezvous.
- **#2179 already specifies a machine registry as its target** ("a machine registry (identity, capabilities, …)") and a machine pool for placement. Thread 1 extends that registry with transport offers and identity bindings; it does not invent a second registry.
- **#1967 is closed with a recorded recommendation**: state the requirement (reach a daemon by cryptographic identity; NAT traversal with relay fallback; E2E + mutual auth from that identity), then pick the transport on merit — tsnet won *for mcpx, a Go binary*, because iroh is Rust and cgo/sidecar costs were priced in. Thread 2 does not reopen #1967: the fleet binary is Rust, so the embedding calculus that decided #1967 inverts for fleet-side components. For Go components #1967's answer stands.
- **opencode#2256 is closed** (fork PR #2598 landed the combined-signal wall). The live wall-scoping work is **#13693** (scope inference, alias providers, per-model free caps). Thread 3 aligns with #13693; it does not restart the wall debate.
- The fleet orchestration architecture record (`doc/2026-11-13T03-20-24Z_design_pm-stack-fleet-orchestration/architecture.md`) contains **no host-selection or transport design** (checked: no tailscale/iroh/placement material). The gap this design fills is real.

---

## Thread 1 — Host selection and access without Tailscale

**Problem.** Today "the laptop" is a hardcoded singleton, and two of its three route methods lean on the tailnet (laptop-agent legs hairpin the session proxy / DERP — #10356 measured warm ~0.4 s, cold CONNECT ~1.8 s; SSH rides a CONNECT proxy too). An agent with no tailnet — not enrolled, overlay down, or a non-Muse seat that never had one — has no route at all, even though the commander endpoint (#13404) already proves a non-Tailscale path: public HTTPS door (Cloudflare Worker gate) + tunnel to the host, OAuth/bearer auth, origin locked down.

**Shape.** A host is a registry record, not a name baked into scripts:

- **Static half** — the #2179 machine registry: host identity (one fleet identity per host, issued under the fleet CA program #9155 / the interim IdP CA), capabilities, and **transport offers**: for each transport the host serves — commander-style public door URL, laptop-agent endpoint, sshd, iroh NodeId — the offer carries its endpoint data and the credential *name* (never a value) that authenticates to it.
- **Live half** — the queue broker's seat records already track which seats are alive; the broker carries the live overlay (last-seen, load, health) on top of the static record. The broker is not the registry of record — it is a queue component, and its reachability is itself a bootstrap question.
- **Cold-start rendezvous** — DNS under our own zones publishes only the stable public doors (commander-style endpoints), so an agent with nothing but internet + DNS can find a first door. DNS carries offers, never secrets; liveness never comes from DNS.

**Selection.** Resolving a host yields candidate (host × transport-form) pairs — exactly the #13717 form matrix, as per-host data instead of a laptop table. Choosing among them is a pool decision (thread 3). `fleet laptop` is the N=1 special case of `fleet host <name>`.

**Access without Tailscale, per transport:**

| Transport | Reach without overlay | Auth at the door | Auth at the host |
|---|---|---|---|
| Commander-pattern public door (#13404) | Anywhere with internet | OAuth (agent/human identity) or machine bearer, by name from the secrets broker | The bridged service's own auth; origin lockdown (door is the only ingress) |
| iroh (thread 2) | Anywhere with internet; relay rendezvous, direct when punchable | NodeId allowlist (the key *is* the identity) | Application-layer authorization on top of the authenticated key (#1967's split: transport here, authorization separate) |
| Direct SSH/HTTP on public address | Only hosts with public reachability — not the general NAT case | sshd / daemon token | Same |
| Headscale (self-hosted tailnet control) | Removes the vendor, **not** the overlay — an agent with no overlay client still can't use it | Tailnet identity | Same as today's tailnet legs |

**Recommendation:** registry hybrid (static #2179 registry + broker live overlay + DNS cold-start doors), commander-pattern as the general no-overlay door, iroh as the peer-to-peer door (thread 2), Headscale recorded as "same shape, self-hosted" — not an answer to the no-overlay requirement. One host identity (fleet CA) binds all of a host's transport credentials, so adding a transport never mints a new identity.

**Work items (each its own slice when picked up):**
- 1a. Registry schema: extend #2179's record with transport offers + identity bindings (fleet cert, iroh NodeId, door URLs, credential names).
- 1b. Broker live overlay: last-seen/load/health keyed to the registry record.
- 1c. `fleet host` resolution + selection on top of the #13717 forms (the walker generalized from laptop to any host).
- 1d. DNS cold-start publication for public doors, with the offers-not-secrets rule written down.

## Thread 2 — Direct iroh for non-Muse agents

**Who this is for.** Fleet seats that are not Muse (opencode lanes, grok, felix, xaltha) ride routes built around Muse's session stack (session proxy, brokers, Muse enrollment). They deserve a transport that is theirs: direct, identity-addressed, no Muse session machinery in the path.

**What iroh is (from iroh's own docs, docs.rs `iroh` / `iroh-net`):**

- **Addressing/identity.** Every node has an ed25519 keypair; the public key is the **NodeId** and is the node's stable identity. QUIC's TLS handshake uses the node's secret key — there is no certificate chain; connecting to a NodeId *is* authenticating that node, and an accepting node learns the peer's authenticated NodeId. Authorization (which NodeIds may do what) is the application's job — an allowlist at accept time, per-ALPN protocol.
- **Connection shape.** A connection usually starts through the node's **home relay**, then upgrades to a direct path via hole punching (QUIC-native traversal in the current line); if no direct path exists, the relay path simply carries the connection. Relays forward **encrypted traffic addressed by NodeId only** — a relay cannot read payloads.
- **Discovery is composable** (the `Discovery` trait; multiple services run concurrently): DNS discovery backed by **pkarr** — signed DNS packets (key = NodeId) published via a pkarr relay and served by an `iroh-dns-server` (n0 runs a public instance; both server pieces are self-hostable); a pkarr resolver over HTTP; DHT discovery over the BitTorrent Mainline; and local-network (mDNS-style) swarm discovery. **Tickets** bundle NodeId + relay URL + direct addresses for out-of-band bootstrap with no lookup service at all.
- **Relay dependence, honestly:** a relay (or known direct addresses) is required to *start* most connections; it is a rendezvous + fallback, not a middleman for established direct traffic. Depending on n0's public relays is optional — `iroh-relay` is self-hostable with ACME TLS, per-client rate limits, and metrics.
- **Embedding.** iroh is a Rust crate (`Endpoint` builder, ALPN-based protocol router). In a Rust binary it is a library dependency — no FFI, no sidecar, no second process. (For Go, #1967's pricing stands: `iroh-ffi` via cgo, or a sidecar. A third-party Go port exists — unverified maturity; do not plan on it.)

**Replaces vs complements:**

- *Replaces*, for non-Muse seats: the rendezvous + traversal role the session proxy / DERP hairpin plays today, and the Cloudflare tunnel for point-to-point host traffic.
- *Complements*: the commander public door stays — hosted MCP clients (ChatGPT/Claude connectors) cannot run iroh and need an HTTPS door. tsnet stays where it already works (mcpx's Go daemon per #1967; the Muse session stack is untouched by this thread).

**Recommendation:** pilot iroh as one transport offer in the thread-1 registry for **one** non-Muse seat class — opencode-lane host reach (seat ↔ laptop without the session-proxy hairpin) — with the fleet binary (Rust) hosting the endpoint. Self-host one `iroh-relay` + pkarr/DNS under our own zones (n0's public relays only as bootstrap fallback), publish host NodeIds in the registry (1a), allowlist by NodeId bound to fleet identities. Measure against #10356's numbers: direct-path rate, p50/p99 setup + call latency vs the ~0.4 s warm hairpin. Pin the iroh version and hide it behind fleet's own transport trait — the crate is young and its API has moved before (iroh-net → iroh renames).

**Work items:**
- 2a. Pilot: fleet binary endpoint + one seat class; direct-path/latency record against the hairpin baseline.
- 2b. Self-hosted relay + pkarr/DNS under our zones; NodeId ↔ fleet identity binding in the registry.
- 2c. Accept-side allowlist + per-ALPN authorization shape (composes with the fleet CA / #9155 identity work).

## Thread 3 — A generic pooling system

**Problem.** The estate keeps reinventing the same machine: model pools (route tables, wall doctrine, failover — #13693, opencode#2256), the google-free round-robin (four projects, per-model-per-project caps), the route-form walker (#13717: ordered attempts, advance only on failure-to-serve, name the serving form), fleet placement (#2179 machine pool; #13611: unread load reads as *unknown*, never zero), and now host×transport selection (thread 1). Each re-implementation re-learns the same lessons — usually by hitting the same wall twice.

**The primitive owns** (domain-independent):

- **Member state machine** — serving / demoted / walled / probing, per member, with the wall keyed at the **narrowest true scope** the evidence supports (member, group, provider, account — the scope is data, with widening/narrowing rules: a sibling's success narrows a wide wall; repeated member failures at a shared scope widen it). This is #13693's doctrine stated once, generically.
- **Attempt semantics** — the #13717 distinction, generalized: advance to the next member on *failure to serve*; a served failure (the member answered and the answer was no) is recorded, classified, and only advances per the classifier's verdict.
- **Selection strategies as plug-ins** — ordered (tier walk), round-robin (google-free), weighted (route tables), free-first (an ordering by cost class), least-loaded where a load read exists — with #13611's rule built in: **an unread load is unknown, and unknown never sorts as zero**.
- **Recovery** — wall expiry at a recorded reset, probe-based re-admission (a bounded successful probe re-seats a member), and measured-increase rejoin (opencode#2256's path). One failed call never benches forever; a wall without a reset still gates (bounded inferred walls, per #13693 slice P / PR #13735).
- **Observability** — every selection decision records member, state, and reason. The form-visibility rule from #13717, generalized: a pool decision you cannot read back is a bug.

**The domain keeps** (not the primitive's business):

- What a member *is*: a model leg, a (host × transport-form) pair, a machine, a compile slot.
- Measurement: quota gatherers, latency probes, Actions-load reads — and the **classifiers** that turn a failure into a class (quota / transport / auth / served-refusal). The primitive consumes classified outcomes; it does not classify.
- Policy: weights, free-first ordering, reserve rules (OpenAI last), pace guards (#2732).

**Options:**
- (a) **A shared Rust crate in the fleet workspace** (working name `fleet-pool`): `Member` / `Classifier` / `Strategy` / `Probe` traits + the state machine. First consumers: the route-form walker (smallest, already specified in #13717) and host×transport selection (thread 1). Model routes consume it at the proxy/fork boundary through a recorded-outcome interface only — **not** a rewrite of #13693's in-flight work. Placement adopts last; its fairness/lease semantics (cf. id spill, #7572) stay domain-side.
- (b) Spec-only pattern, each domain re-implements: zero migration cost, and exactly the drift that produced this thread.
- (c) One central pool service: a single decision point — right for the compile coordinator's atomic cross-owner claims (a separate, already-directed build), wrong as the general shape: it makes every route decision a network hop and a shared failure point.

**Recommendation:** (a), adopted in the order walker → host×transport → model-route boundary → placement, each adoption its own slice with the domain's existing tests as the oracle.

**Work items:**
- 3a. `fleet-pool` crate: state machine + strategies + decision log, property-tested (wall scope invariants named as oracles).
- 3b. Walker adoption (#13717 composition becomes the crate's first consumer).
- 3c. Model-route boundary interface (recorded outcomes in, selection out) — sequenced after #13693 lands its scoping layer.
- 3d. Placement adoption review against #2179 (may legitimately conclude "not yet").

## Cross-links

#13654 (commander subcommand, form F1) · #13717 (route-form family) · #10356 (fleet connect: method selection, sessions) · #2179 (machine pool + registry) · #1967 (iroh and the Go-binding question — closed, recommendation stands for Go) · #13669 (mcpx→Rust pilot; tsnet is Go-only, iroh the Rust-side option) · #13693 (wall scoping) · opencode#2256 (wall doctrine — closed) · #13404 (commander endpoint, the non-Tailscale proof) · #9155 (fleet CA — the identity layer hosts bind to) · #8991 / #9399 (pool routing epics — thread 3 serves these, does not replace them)

code.title: id(phase-14): hosted worlds v2 Q4 — lifecycle automation + per-world limits
code.body:

code.title: id(phase-14): hosted worlds v2 Q3 — custody depth: incremental sets, pruning, replication
code.body:
Implementation packet Q3 from the hosted worlds v2 outline on #6284 (custody & lifecycle, part 3): `doc/2026-11-16_design_id6283_hosted_worlds_v1.md`, merged in PR #10692; refined outline + open questions posted on #6284 (2026-11-16, task 13294). Phase 14 core topic #6276; principles from #1240 govern.

## Scope
Custody depth beyond a local file set. The #806 signed stream is the landed input: incremental snapshot sets, retention/pruning of segment sets, and read-replica/backup replication if it earns its keep.

Must answer from the outline's open questions: transport for off-host sets — plain file copy of the signed segment set (v1 shape) vs a host-mediated export, and how a recipient verifies a set without trusting the sender. Read replicas — is a replica of a *world* (not just its segments) in scope, or does replication stay a backup mechanism only? Solo self-hoster rule: read replicas and replication-based backup are a deployment option, never a precondition — a solo self-hoster with a disk and a restore script keeps the full v1+custody story.

## Acceptance criteria
- Incremental snapshot sets defined over the #806 signed stream; retention/pruning policy for segment sets (whole-set removal, never journal edits).
- Off-host transport chosen and documented, with recipient-side verification that does not trust the sender.
- Replica-vs-backup decision recorded: either replicas are in scope with their consistency contract, or replication stays backup-only with the reason written down.
- No hosted-side backup API may become the only path: the export/import format stays the same signed segment set for local, p2p and hosted (per the #1240 p2p-identity tension named on #6284).

## Dependencies
Blocked by #10695 (P3 — snapshot/export shape, the primitive this extends). Builds on #806 (CLOSED 2026-11-14, signed stream landed). Does not depend on open #805 (F12.11).

code.title: id(phase-14): hosted worlds v2 Q2 — restore drills + drill record
code.body:
Implementation packet Q2 from the hosted worlds v2 outline on #6284 (custody & lifecycle, part 2): `doc/2026-11-16_design_id6283_hosted_worlds_v1.md`, merged in PR #10692; refined outline + open questions posted on #6284 (2026-11-16, task 13294). Phase 14 core topic #6276; principles from #1240 govern.

## Scope
Restore drills — the thing that makes a snapshot a backup. Drill cadence, and the drill check itself: restore into a **scratch world**, replay to the same journal head, and compare. Record each drill result so absence of a recent successful drill is visible (same posture as the #6045 attestation / #6058 ledger pattern: a missing record is the alarm). Restore-into-scratch is an explicit non-goal of v1 and belongs here. Reuses the P6 replay-equality harness (#10698) rather than reinventing it.

Must answer from the outline's open questions: drill cadence and evidence shape — how often must a restore drill succeed; does a failure of a scheduled drill block anything, or only surface for the operator? Operational ownership — does the drill harness live in `id-worlds` host mode, in `id-cli`, or as an external operator script? Where does the drill record live (issue comment, host file, ledger)? Local-record-first: the drill record must be readable locally, aggregation is convenience, not proof.

## Acceptance criteria
- Scheduled drills restore the latest snapshot set into a scratch world, replay to the same journal head, and compare against the live world; pass/fail is recorded per drill.
- A missing recent successful drill is visible as an alarm to the operator (no silent staleness).
- Cross-host import semantics for drill/verify flows are defined: importing a set for a world ID the target host already has — reject, fork to a new identity, or overwrite-under-operator-confirmation (v1 leaves this unaddressed).

## Dependencies
Blocked by #10695 (P3 — snapshot/export shape + manual restore procedure, the primitive drills exercise). Reuses #10698 (P6 — replay-equality conformance, the invariant a drill asserts). Uses restore/archive commands from #10696 (P4) where they exist.

code.title: id(phase-14): hosted worlds v2 Q1 — scheduled snapshots + retention
code.body:
Implementation packet Q1 from the hosted worlds v2 outline on #6284 (custody & lifecycle, part 1): `doc/2026-11-16_design_id6283_hosted_worlds_v1.md`, merged in PR #10692; refined outline + open questions posted on #6284 (2026-11-16, task 13294). Phase 14 core topic #6276; principles from #1240 govern.

## Scope
Scheduled snapshots + retention for hosted worlds. P3 (#10695) delivers the manual snapshot command producing a signed, self-describing journal segment set; Q1 adds the schedule and the policy on top: per-world (and per-host) cadence, retention count/age, where sets live (local data root vs off-host), and size accounting against per-state capacity (F3 counts capacity per state).

Must answer from the outline's open questions: snapshot cadence and retention — fixed interval, on-N-changes, or operator policy? How many sets and for how long, given storage growth is the #2 break-first risk in the v1 doc (§9)?

## Acceptance criteria
- A host takes snapshots on the defined schedule without operator intervention; cadence is configurable per world and per host.
- Retention is enforced: bounded set count + age safe on one node with one disk; pruning removes whole snapshot sets, never edits a journal (append-only invariant).
- Snapshot sizes are accounted against per-state capacity; the operator can see custody cost per world.
- Encryption at rest stays a deployment property — Q1 must not make the journal format crypto-aware (v1 §5 invariant).

## Dependencies
Blocked by #10695 (P3 — snapshot/export shape + manual restore): scheduling and pruning have nothing to operate on until P3 lands. Does not depend on open #805 (F12.11); records resync/export bytes so the #805 improvement stays measurable.

code.title: id(journal): durable per-world global position covering lease entries, surviving compaction (prerequisite for #7572 failover barrier)
code.body:
## Why

Spill v2 phase 1 (#7572, design #5787 §1 step 4 and §Q3) needs a **replay barrier**: a successor must prove it has replayed through the journal position of the `LeaseGranted` record before accepting writes. PR #13425 holds the tested pool/selection/fencing policy slice, but the actor cannot yet capture the grant position or enforce the barrier.

## Gap on current main

- `JournalEntry` lease records (`LeaseGranted`, `LeaseRenewed`, `LeaseHandedOff`, `LeaseRevoked`, `LeaseWriteRejected`) are not sequenced by a world-level counter. Only `Committed` events carry `sequence`.
- Compaction (`Journal::compact`) rewrites the file, so byte or entry ordinals reset and no position from before compaction names a stable record.
- `Checkpoint` records `sequence` (last event covered) and the `lease` state, but not the position of the last lease record.

## Requested

1. A durable, monotonic per-world global journal position assigned to every journal entry that changes lease state (and ideally all entries), persisted in the entry.
2. The position survives checkpoint compaction, so a checkpoint records the position of the last covered entry.
3. An accessor the actor can use to capture the grant position, and a replay API that reports the replayed-through position so a successor can enforce replay-before-resume.

## Acceptance

- Property test: positions are strictly increasing across appends, lease records, and compaction.
- Oracle: a successor replaying a journal with a grant at position P reports watermark >= P before it may accept writes.

## Unblocks

#7572 (task 21349). Trigger: none; this is a prerequisite, not gated on a person.

Refs #7572, #5787, #2819
