code.title: fix(quota-plane): reconcile.py fee_period vocabulary mismatch reports permanent drift
code.body:
## Problem

`pm-stack/provider-usage/reconcile.py` (#1270's reconciliation diff) compares the `fee_period` field across legs as a raw string, but the legs use different vocabularies for the same fact:

- Tracker leg (fenced plan-facts block, schema approved 2026-11-16): `month` / `year`.
- Plan-store leg: the store's Effect schema (`packages/core/src/model-plan.ts` in the opencode fork, `Period`) only admits `monthly` / `yearly` / `once`, and `ModelPlan.writeStore` validates against it — a store row written through the sanctioned edit path can never carry `month` / `year`.

Result: since #1270 slice 2 seeded the store (2026-11-23), every daily diff reports 9 `fee_period` findings (winner: plan-store) that are pure vocabulary noise, burying any real drift. The fixture in `test_reconcile.py` masks this because its hand-written store fixture uses `month` — a value the real store schema rejects.

## Fix shape

Normalise the period vocabulary on one side of the comparison in `reconcile.py` (e.g. map the store leg's `monthly`→`month`, `yearly`→`year` in `load_store`, or canonicalise both legs in `diff`), and extend the fixture tests: a store fixture carrying `monthly` against a tracker row carrying `month` must produce no `fee_period` finding, while a genuine period mismatch (monthly vs year) must still be caught with the winner named.

Evidence: the 2026-11-23 post-seed run recorded on #1270 (legs plan-store 9 / tracker 9 / measured 0; the only findings were the 9 `fee_period` vocabulary rows) and in the registry's RECONCILIATION FINDINGS — 2026-11-23 (post-seed run) section.

code.title: sccache daemon wedges specific in-flight Rust compiles on the laptop (clients park at 0% CPU; daemon stays responsive)
code.body:
## Evidence

On the laptop (`amd`), 2026-11-23 ~07:24–08:20 CST, cargo builds through the shared sccache daemon wedge on a small, reproducible set of crates: the `sccache rustc` client processes sleep at 0% CPU indefinitely (observed 31+ minutes) waiting on daemon sockets, while the daemon itself stays responsive — `sccache --show-stats` answers immediately (77,389 requests, 70.76% hit rate at the time) and standalone sccache compiles of unique content complete in ~0.2 s, both in a plain shell and inside `nix develop`.

Observed stuck sets, all with the same shape (cache-miss crates announced by cargo, then no progress, target-dir artifact count frozen):

- Lane XB run 1 (`cargo test --lib hosted`, pkgs/id, worktree target): `backon`, `axum`, `signature` clients parked 30:49–30:54 min; deps count frozen at 1098 for 15+ min.
- Lane XB run 4 (fresh cargo, same worktree): the identical front wave parked again — `axum`, `signature`, `backon`, `syn-mid`, `fixedbitset`, `cbor-core`, `rand_chacha`, all `Sl`, 0.0% CPU, 4:18 min and counting when killed.
- Same window, other lanes' processes showed the identical state at the same ages: a `cargo check -p id --all-targets` (lane WB worktree) and a clippy build (lane VZ, `/tmp/vz-clippy-target2`) both had ~31-min-old parked sccache rustc clients.

Daemon facts: PID started Mon Nov 23 03:12 (no restart at the freeze window ~07:24), 100+ open sockets when inspected, disk not full (`/home` 94%, 219G avail). `strace` attach is blocked by `kernel.yama.ptrace_scope=1`, so the exact wait channel inside the client is unconfirmed; `/proc/<pid>/wchan` reads `wait_woken`, fds show the daemon sockets open, no child rustc — the client is waiting for a daemon reply that never arrives for these requests.

## Workaround (verified)

Bypass the wrapper for the affected build: `RUSTC_WRAPPER= RUSTC_WORKSPACE_WRAPPER= cargo test …`. Lane XB's pkgs/id lib build then completed in ~5 minutes (deps 1098 → 2186 artifacts, tests green) after ~50 minutes wedged across three sccache attempts.

## Impact / ask

Every lane doing Rust work on the laptop can silently lose its build to this wedge; the failure mode looks like a slow compile, so it burns lane time before anyone suspects the cache layer. Please diagnose the daemon-side stall for these in-flight requests (daemon log at the freeze window, per-request state) and add a guard: a client-side or daemon-side timeout that fails a wedged request loudly instead of parking the build forever.

code.title: C4 design section 4: compound range form unimplemented and day form unreachable in the shared formatter
code.body:
Found while landing the C4.2 reset-duration builder (#13258, PR #13352), comparing the C4 design's §4 against the shipped shared formatter.

**Design** (`doc/2026-11-13T15-12-00Z_design_reporting-architecture-event-driven/c4-forecasting-design.md` §4):

- "mixed spans render compound: \"2 days 4 hours to up to 3 days 16 hours\"" — no landed code produces this form. `renderPredictionRange` in `pm-stack/aggregator/src/quota-downtime.ts` (the formatter C4.1 shipped and C4.2 now reuses) implements only the duration form, the decimal day form, and the calendar form.
- The day form ("2.5 to 3.7 days") is specified for "span ≥ 48h", but in the shipped formatter the cross-day calendar check runs **before** the span check, and any range ≥48h wide necessarily crosses a Chicago day boundary — so the day-form branch is unreachable as ordered. (It can only fire for a ≥48h-wide range whose bounds share a Chicago calendar day, which cannot exist.)

**Question for the design owner (#9572):** is §4's text or the shipped formatter the intended behaviour?

- If the formatter is right, §4's compound example and the day-form condition should be corrected in the design record so future C4 kinds don't re-derive them.
- If the design is right, the formatter needs a compound form and a check order that lets the day form fire — a methodology-visible change (records' stored `rendered` strings are what the scorer grades, design §1), so it should ride a methodology-log entry (§6), not a silent edit.

Neither blocks #13258: C4.2 reuses the one shared formatter per §4's "produced by one formatter" rule rather than forking a second interpretation.

code.title: Build: fleet kv phase 3 — authenticated blob offload and reference-safe GC
code.body:
# Phase 3 — blob offload only (threshold, streaming upload, capabilities, GC)

- Parent issue: https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/10359 (threshold/blob question; reference pattern from #9084).
- Parent design: [reviewed decision record](https://github.com/developing-today/code/blob/5ac3ddcec60017b05b655b8fe665b06c61369ec3/doc/2026-11-23T12-45-00Z_design_fleet_kv/2026-11-23T12-45-00Z_design_fleet_kv.md) (§8 threshold D009, §9 upload/read D011, §10 dedup/reference D010/D012). Stable decision IDs: D009, D010, D011, D012, D015 (envelope versions `kv:raw-v1`/`kv:ref-v1`; D013 reversed/superseded — no lists/tables in this phase).
- Prerequisite: design PR https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/13294 must merge before this phase starts. Depends on: Phase 2 https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/13316 (shared primary + CAS sweep + supported auth); its implementation PR must be merged before Phase 3 implementation begins. Phase 1 is https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/13314.
- Scope (blob-only): per-namespace threshold knob (default 256 KiB, subordinate to the shared partition policy — may only narrow, never widen past the partition ceiling/16 KiB conservative start); `--force-blob` one-directional override (forces blob at/below ceiling; no force-inline above ceiling); staged → verified → published upload through the trusted endpoint (streaming length + recomputed BLAKE3-256 over exact bytes in ≤ 64 KiB chunks, ≤ 1 MiB resident; multipart completion is not publication — publication is the CAS + ref-registration transaction); `KvBlobRefV1` rows (`profile raw-blake3-256`, digest, `bytes_len`, `partition {jurisdiction, tier}`, opaque adapter locator, `state=published`); hash-never-bearer reads via short-lived (5 min) object+operation-scoped capabilities minted from live reference state; component-F mark-and-sweep GC per `(jurisdiction, tier)` over the full root set (published rows, retained versions, conflict-proposed refs, unexpired archive/snapshot refs, dedup pins) sharing the central per-partition serialization point; the effective-threshold formula `effective = min(namespaceKnob, partitionCeiling)` resolves the nominal-vs-effective gap (256 KiB knob nominal, 16 KiB partition start effective where component E governs); the proposed `partition_fences` table (no code in this issue) lives on the SHARED primary and orders publish-CAS against the delete-fence sequence in one transaction serialization — group DBs never fence; cross-partition references refused (`partition_mismatch`). No lists/tables, no manifests: any future shape arrives as a new envelope version under D015.

## Acceptance

1. At/below effective threshold: inline `kv:raw-v1` row; above: `kv:ref-v1` row after staged→verified→published; promotion is a new version with identical read semantics; `--force-blob` forces blob treatment at/below ceiling; any attempt to place bytes inline above the ceiling refuses with a typed error.
2. Arbitrary-byte streaming: a value well above any threshold (test: ≥ 64 MiB random bytes — larger than the streaming buffer, with resident working set asserted ≤ 1 MiB, not larger than machine memory) pushes and pulls with bounded resident memory, and the pulled bytes hash to the identical BLAKE3-256 digest recomputed streaming on receipt.
3. Central never accepts an unpublished blob reference; staged/verified-but-un-CASed objects are invisible to reads and reaped by staging TTL under the staging pin; crash after publish-CAS leaves a retained ref root retired only by grace/GC; a "published"-marked object without its CAS is an orphan under grace/GC, never staging-TTL-reaped.
4. Read without a live authorized reference mints no capability; hash presentation alone serves nothing; capabilities expire at 5 min and are object+operation-scoped.
5. GC sweep: unreferenced content per partition passes candidate → grace → re-verify → fenced delete + audit over the full root set (published rows, retained versions, conflict-proposed refs, unexpired archive/snapshot refs, dedup pins); a reference created during grace clears candidacy via the shared serialization point; cross-partition resolution refuses.
6. The blob row's `(jurisdiction, tier)` is identified from the authenticated scope's placement policy, never from the session `partitionId`; a placement-policy lookup failure refuses the upload (no default partition).
7. Done check from repository root: `cargo test --manifest-path pkgs/fleet/Cargo.toml -p fleet-kv blob` runs the proposed `blob_*` property/model/integration suite with a nonzero test count. It must include threshold boundary cases, binary 64 MiB streaming with the documented buffer budget, corruption refusal, reference-authorized capability expiry, retained-history pins, and reference-create/delete-fence interleavings. Also run `cargo test --manifest-path pkgs/fleet/Cargo.toml -p fleet-kv` to preserve Phases 1–2. A zero-match filter is failure, not evidence. Reuse the existing component-F endpoint/GC conformance tests rather than creating a parallel object-plane protocol.

## Oracles

- Property: threshold placement — a value's placement (inline vs reference) is a pure function of (effective threshold, `--force-blob`), and reads are placement-indifferent. (PBT over sizes ±1 byte around the threshold; override only ever moves toward blob.)
- Property: publish-before-reference — no execution reaches a readable reference row without a prior publish-CAS (CAS + ref-registration transaction) for the same digest. (Trace property over upload/CAS interleavings.)
- Property: streaming hash integrity — pulled bytes always re-hash to the row digest; any mismatch refuses rather than serving. (PBT over sizes, chunk splits, truncation/corruption injection.)
- Property: GC safety — a delete event implies (no live reference at re-verify) AND (grace elapsed) AND (fence epoch recorded). (PBT over reference/GC interleavings; derived index drift may only delay, never cause, delete.)
- Model: blob lifecycle state machine (staged → verified → published → candidate → deleted) against the reference-row oracle; cross-partition attempts as typed refusals.

Stable decision IDs: D003, D004, D005, D006, D007, D008, D011, D014 (D002 reversed/superseded — do not implement row-scopes-only).
- Prerequisite: design PR https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/13294 must merge before this phase starts. Depends on: Phase 1 https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/13314 (local verbs + full-identity overlay + durable outbox); its implementation PR must be merged before Phase 2 implementation begins.
- Scope: shared Turso primary over the queue-style libSQL HTTP pipeline at configurable `FLEET_KV_URL` (no hardcoded or fake deployed hostname); proposed migrations/handler paths (no code in this issue): `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-kv/migrations/` for `kv_namespaces`, `kv_heads`, `kv_versions`, `kv_conflicts`, `idem_receipts`, `kv_grants`, and pipeline handlers beside the existing queue HTTP handlers. Central key derivation per write/read: from the explicitly selected scope — the shared `scope_id` of the namespace for authorized agents, or the private `scope_id` of the owning `(user, context)` — resolved via `kv_namespaces` + `kv_grants`; no implicit extra fallback scope exists.
- Scope: shared Turso primary over the queue-style libSQL HTTP pipeline; central key `(scope_id, registry_id, namespace, key)` with one shared scope per shared namespace (shared-scope tombstones affect all shared readers; private scopes separate); `kv_namespaces` with designation-only `global_flag`; `kv_grants` with explicit-grant group DBs under fail-closed admission/provisioning policy (no default per-session proliferation; group DBs inline-only — no blob refs, ceiling checked before any group-DB write, blob-needing group writes refuse with `blob_requires_shared_primary`); `--global` now serves central (authoritative bypass); local-first reads (ordinary cache ≤ 1 s; miss/expiry refreshes or typed `unavailable`/`stale`, `--allow-stale` opt-in with age; overlay reads immediate offline) with local-override + merged `list`; durable sweep keyed `(owner_user_id, context_id, session_id)` via outbox + per-key CAS (≤ 5 attempts, jittered exp backoff capped at 1 s), receipts keyed `(authenticated_writer, host_incarnation_UUID, outbox_UUID)` + immutable fingerprint; tombstones sweep through CAS; five-agent rule (single-writer-per-key CAS; KV CAS is not a queue lease — no leases/expiry/steal); 15-minute archive checkpoint TARGET (unbounded loss when offline/unarchived; archive carries inline payloads only up to the effective threshold — no Phase 3 upload here). Auth: RP/agent JWT or route-scoped service token to the trusted endpoint; secrets-broker fetch path is not request auth; per-user Turso data-plane tokens refused (`data_plane_credential_refused`). v1 operational integration ships here: migrations, credential wiring, grant-policy implementation, backup/restore runbook, health probes.

## Acceptance

1. `--global get/set` round-trips against central; plain `get` merges local + central with stated origin marks and never silently hides the shadowed row; `--global` bypasses the 1 s cache.
2. Sweep: session dirty set merges idempotently (re-run safe; retransmit with same key+fingerprint returns the stored result); two sessions racing one key produce one winner + one typed `conflict {expected, actual}` with both versions retrievable — never silent last-writer-wins, never Turso Sync last-push-wins; rebase after conflict is a new intent/new id, never silent overwrite. CAS-before-ack order: receipt written atomically with CAS, ack after; crash between CAS and ack replays the recorded result, never a spurious new conflict.
3. Archive carries inline payloads only (≤ effective threshold) via the archive owner command `fleet kv backup` (equivalently `fleet kv sync --archive` mode) plus the 15-minute online-checkpoint-target sweeper; over-threshold local-working bytes are reported `protection_unavailable_needs_phase3`, never uploaded — no blob upload exists before Phase 3. Over-ceiling bytes addressed to central before Phase 3 land typed `pending_needs_phase3` (queued intent, not a row), never silently buffered inline. Crash before ack re-sweeps fully.
4. Grants: a group DB exists iff a `kv_grants` row authorizes it; unknown group/namespace refuses fail-closed; with no grant, everything lands on the shared primary. No per-session DB is provisioned by default. Group DBs accept inline bytes only: over-ceiling bytes addressed to a group scope refuse with `blob_requires_shared_primary` (shared-primary placement required, no auto-move), so no unrestricted write bypasses the ceiling.
5. Data-plane credential presented to the endpoint is refused with the typed rule, not an incidental signature failure; central access reuses the hosted RP/agent JWT or route-scoped service token path only.
6. Load probe (REQUIRED, correctness-only fixture — not a latency/perf promise, and no billing claim): five writers × ~1–10 keys/min on a ~10k-key namespace all converge; `list` polling observes at most the documented 1 s staleness.
7. Done check from repository root: `cargo test --manifest-path pkgs/fleet/Cargo.toml -p fleet-kv central` runs the proposed `central_*` model/property/integration suite with a nonzero test count. It must include the five-agent fixture, scope isolation, clear-versus-sweep, same-ID/different-body refusal, duplicate delivery, archive restore, and expired-cache refusal. Also run `cargo test --manifest-path pkgs/fleet/Cargo.toml -p fleet-kv` to preserve Phase 1 behavior. A zero-match filter is failure, not evidence.

## Oracles

- Property: CAS linearity — concurrent same-key writers serialize; the central head always equals one writer's full intent, never a blend; losers get typed conflicts. (PBT over concurrent CAS attempts.)
- Property: sweep idempotence — sweeping the same outbox twice changes central once. (PBT over duplicate deliveries.)
- Property: tombstone sweep convergence — delete-vs-write races resolve to a retrievable conflict or a tombstoned head, never resurrection-by-replay.
- Model: central head machine (version, parent_version, writer) against a sequential CAS oracle; sweep as an outbox-draining refinement of it.

code.title: Build: fleet kv phase 1 — local verbs, scoped SQLite and backup
code.body:
# Phase 1 — local verbs (`fleet kv get/set/list/delete/clear-override/revert`, namespaces, tombstones)

- Parent issue: https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/10359 (`fleet kv` design owner; items 1–3: verb family, local store, namespaces).
- Parent design: [reviewed decision record](https://github.com/developing-today/code/blob/5ac3ddcec60017b05b655b8fe665b06c61369ec3/doc/2026-11-23T12-45-00Z_design_fleet_kv/2026-11-23T12-45-00Z_design_fleet_kv.md) (§1 local store + logical identity, §2 namespaces/registry, §3 verbs). Stable decision IDs: D001, D003, D004, D005, D015 (envelope versions `kv:raw-v1` accepted, `kv:ref-v1` refused as `unimplemented_central_in_phase1`).
- Prerequisite: design PR https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/13294 must merge before this phase starts. No dependency on other phases (this is the first).
- Scope: local-only. One SQLite file per host (WAL) with `kv_local` keyed by the full identity tuple `(owner_user_id, context_id, partition_id, namespace, key)`, cached `kv_namespaces` + `kv_grants`, durable `outbox`, backup manifest row. Local identity source (explicit, proposed): the existing `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet/src/session_state.rs` binds the session ID only (session-ID validation + liveness) — it carries no owner/context. Phase 1 therefore requires a new trusted launch-identity accessor that supplies `(owner_user_id, context_id)` at session start; offline identity comes from the validated persisted launch record, never from a client-supplied user override (fail closed when absent). Merged `list` shows local rows only; any central-origin mark is deferred to Phase 2 (this phase must not display or imply central state).
- Scope: local-only. One SQLite file per host (WAL) with `kv_local` keyed by the full identity tuple `(owner_user_id, context_id, partition_id, namespace, key)`, cached `kv_namespaces` + `kv_grants`, durable `outbox`, backup manifest row. Verbs `get/set/list/delete/clear-override/revert` + `--namespace`; `--global` flag parsed but refused as `unimplemented_central_in_phase1` (typed refusal, never silent local fallback). Strict CLI/registry/docs updates: multicall registration, `--help` text for every verb, registry entries, and the command reference updated in the same diff. Unknown arguments are a strict usage error before any I/O (argument contract: parse and validate the whole command line first; no subprocess, file write, or DB touch on unknown/malformed args). No central, no sweep, no blobs. LOCAL working bytes vs central inline distinguished: the threshold governs central rows only — locally, over-threshold bytes live as a streamed working file plus an atomic local DB ref (never fully buffered above the 1 MiB resident budget), so no local value is ever rejected for size.

## Acceptance

1. `fleet kv set/get/list/delete/clear-override/revert` round-trip locally; `list --include-tombstones` shows tombstones with `masked` origin. Merged `list` marks only local origins; central marks (`shadowed-by-central`) are deferred — assert they never appear in Phase 1 output.
2. `clear-override` drops the overlay row, advances the local generation fence (cancelling unsent intents; bounded-wait/`clear_busy_try_again` per the design), and reveals central-nothing (local-only). `delete` writes a masking tombstone that still sweeps later; `revert NS KEY --to V` appends a restoring version, where `--to V` is a positive monotone version ID (never a value). The three are never conflated in help text, errors, or reads.
3. `--namespace` selects scope; unknown namespace or malformed key is a typed refusal naming the registry/scope (`unknown_namespace`, `malformed_key`). No `(ns, key)`-only cross-identity read path exists: reads filter by the caller's full identity tuple.
4. `--global` on any verb fails closed with the typed refusal (documents Phase 2 ownership).
5. Crash recovery: killed mid-`set` leaves either the old row or the full new row + exactly one unacked outbox entry — never a half-row or half-file (re-run the verb sequence after `kill -9` in test).
6. File backup: snapshot of file + WAL + manifest row restores on a fresh host to the same reads; the manifest pins every live working file (content id + length + hash) and the snapshot includes them, so a restore re-links working bytes; 6 h snapshot cadence and WAL-replay RPO documented in the runbook entry this phase adds.
7. CLI/registry/docs: `fleet kv --help` documents every verb + `--namespace`/`--global`/`--force-blob` (refused where unimplemented); registry and command reference updated; unknown envelope versions refused, not ignored.
8. Proposed test home (no code in this design run): new crate `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-kv` with modules `overlay`, `outbox`, `backup`, `cli`. Done check from repository root: `cargo test --manifest-path pkgs/fleet/Cargo.toml -p fleet-kv` passes with a nonzero test count asserted in CI (fail if 0 tests ran); `fleet kv --help` output snapshot matches the registry doc; `kill -9` crash-recovery script exits 0. If implementation uses an existing crate instead, record the exact equivalent runnable command in this issue and preserve the named oracles/nonzero-count requirement.

## Oracles

- Property: tombstone convergence — interleaved set/delete/clear-override/revert sequences on one key always read as the last version's value-or-absent; deleted keys never resurrect except via `revert`, and `clear-override` revealing central state is not resurrection (it removes the overlay; the revealed value was never deleted).
- Property: outbox durability — every acknowledged local `set/delete` has exactly one unacked outbox row until Phase 2 consumes it or until terminal cancellation by `clear-override` (cancelled is a terminal state, not a leak and not "pending until Phase 2 forever"). (PBT over crash-point injection.)
- Model: verbs as a state machine against an in-memory map oracle (get/set/delete/clear-override/revert/list incl. tombstone flags).
- No F12.5 confusion: assert a 100 KiB local value succeeds (local working bytes + atomic ref, not a world-sandbox entry under #1062 caps; the 16 KiB partition ceiling governs central inline placement only, which is Phase 3's concern).

code.title: impl(deploy): the release verb — tag cutting, attestation, and the untagged-release refusal (#11177 implementation)
code.body:
# impl(deploy): the `release` verb — tag cutting, attestation, and the untagged-release refusal (#11177 implementation)

Implements the release workflow designed in
`doc/2026-11-23T13-09-25Z_design_release-workflow-per-app-tags/`
(#11177, follow-on to #5790 §5). Until this lands, no per-app
release tags are cut — that is the design's recorded gate decision
(§7).

## Scope

In `pkgs/deploy/deploy.py` (plus registry/tests as needed):

1. **`deploy release <app> [--version X.Y.Z] [--commit <sha>]`**
   per design §2: refuse unless the commit is reachable from
   `origin/main`, the attestation gate (§3 of the design) is green
   for that exact commit, and the version obeys the ratified
   discipline (short deploy-name prefix, first tag `0.1.0`, 0.x
   only, next minor/patch only). On success: create the annotated
   app tag carrying the `release-attestation:v1` block, create the
   annotated `repo/v<YYYYMMDD>.<minor>.<patch>` tag at a release
   point, push, and append the release record to the deploy
   ledger.
2. **Attestation judging** per design §3: the main-gate watched
   set (`.github/workflows/main-broken.yml`, in sync with
   `.github/scripts/release-gate.sh`) judged by the release-gate
   rules for the exact commit, plus the app's own evidence
   workflow when outside the watched set. Add the per-app
   evidence-workflow field to the deploy registry (fleet:
   `fleet-rust-tests`).
3. **The deploy-time refusal** per design §6: a deploy claiming
   release status (artifact self-reports a clean `X.Y.Z`) is
   refused unless an attested `<app>/vX.Y.Z` tag exists at the
   artifact's source commit with a verifiable attestation block.
   Prerelease (`-dev`) deploys are unaffected.
4. **`deploy status`** reads the release ledger (design §4):
   releases and their gate evidence beside the existing
   per-target deployed-version report; a ledger/tag disagreement
   is reported, with the tag winning.
5. A pointer line in `pkgs/fleet/README.md`'s "Tag and release
   procedure" naming the design record as the workflow of record.

## Acceptance

- The pkgs/deploy test suites cover: refusal on a red gate,
  refusal on a version-discipline violation, refusal of a
  release-claiming deploy without an attested tag, a successful
  release against a fixture remote producing both tags with a
  parseable attestation block, and the ledger record round-trip
  through `deploy status`.
- The first real release cut with the verb (expected:
  `fleet/v0.1.0` plus the repo tag) is recorded on #11177.

## Out of scope

- Changing the numbering scheme, derivation, or bump discipline
  (#5790, ratified).
- Migrating the mcpx pipeline (decision 0005); it already
  consumes tags compatibly. `mcpx/v0.1.0` is grandfathered.

code.title: Atlas CLI family consistency: exit codes, version strings, and the HOME fallback split (book survey, #13251)
code.body:
Found by the Atlas book survey (#13251, survey A). Cross-binary consistency gaps in the Atlas CLI family; the book documents each binary's actual behaviour because no family-wide rule can be stated.

1. **Exit-code philosophy is inconsistent across the family.** atlas-search: 1 = runtime, 2 = usage. atlas-stage: same split via different mechanics. atlas-classify and atlas-sweep: 2 for everything, including pure runtime failures. atlas-github-comments: 1 for everything, including pure argument errors. atlas-eval: 2 usage / 1 runtime. fleet search adds 3 (routing unavailable) and inherits fleet's 69. No two hand-rolled binaries agree.
2. **Version strings collide.** atlas-search --version and fleet search --version both print 0.1.0, but they are different packages' versions (fleet's derived build is `0.1.0-dev+gb8bbcc0` per `fleet version`). No atlas binary exposes a source revision.
3. **HOME-failure behaviour is split inside atlas-core.** atlas-search's home_dir() (and atlas-core path expansion, and fleet-search's copy) panic on missing/empty HOME per the #5640/#5762 contract. But JsonlTraceSink::default_dir() and JsonlFeedbackSink::default_dir() fall back to `PathBuf::from(".")` — traces/feedback land under the CWD in exactly the situation the contract forbids, and the CLI's search path constructs the trace sink from default_dir() on every run.

Book chapters: pkgs/atlas-search/book/reference/*.md exit-code tables; operations/troubleshooting.md.

**Commission (Drew, 2026-11-23): a full-investigation master prompt for the Fleet program, same pattern as the ID (#13240) and Atlas (#13241) programs.**

The full prompt is the first comment on this issue. It directs a program-scale investigation and build-out of Fleet — the `fleet` multicall binary and brokers (`pkgs/fleet/`), the queue/placement/dispatch machinery, agent lifecycle and multi-seat coordination, the secrets broker and credential distribution, the self-healing channel/broker stack, the repo constellation (dezren39/fleet, developing-today/fleet, 102-fork sync), the quota plane, observability, and the fleet↔Atlas↔ID integration surface.

Ground truth was researched first-hand on 2026-11-23 (research files in `~/workspace/fleet-investigation/`). Headlines the prompt is built on:

- The two big queue defects are **fixed on main and deployed nowhere**: #13091 (double-serve, PR #13143 merged) and #13191 (repair verb, PR #13218 merged) — the running broker is generation 5 (`b8bbcc0`, activated before both merges) and no deployed binary has `fleet queue repair` yet. The publish/pin/broker rollout is the program's first tranche, and #13146 criterion 1 (cross-seat session status) completes on it.
- The fleet book (55 chapters, 98,894 words, live at /code/fleet/) is already stale for main: no `repair` chapter, placement sessions still described as a local-JSON "STOPGAP". Extending it is a deliverable, under the DOC-01 contract.
- Census (Search API, 2026-11-23): **185 open issues** in the fleet label union (406 all-state); 98 of the 113 open `app/fleet` issues are `kind/design`, most of it the pm-orchestration DAG. dezren39/fleet has 7 open issues (five fleet-build leg failures, #88, #87). No fleet charter exists — producing one is a deliverable.
- Standing corrections the research established: the umbrella has **22 submodules** (not 12); the fleet nixpkgs pin is **`f9887a8a…`** (not `11dd50b`); there is **no `fleet-quota` crate** (live quota code is `pm-stack/aggregator/src/quota-*.ts`); the "~30 malformed packets" list exists on no single issue — the census itself is program work.

**Deliverables (per the prompt):** a fleet charter; the fleet book extended in place under /code/fleet/ (design series joins it, DOC-01 honoured); an issue-by-issue map of ALL fleet issues prioritized with blockers marked; landed designs in the `doc/` archive; merged implementation PRs wherever unblocked. The prompt states explicitly that it is a starting point, not a stopping point — expand, review, repeat.

**This issue stays open** — it is the program's tracking home, not a task to close. Flag-held items named in the prompt (#13159 family and the rest of the recorded hold set) are Drew's item-specific decisions: the program investigates and designs around them, never implements them.

**Commission (Drew, 2026-11-23): "make one of these for mcpx"** — a full-programme investigation master prompt for mcpx, mirroring the ID programme prompt (#13240) and the Atlas programme prompt (#13241). The full prompt is the first comment on this issue; it also lands in the repo as a dated design record under `doc/` by starter PR.

**Scope in one paragraph:** mcpx is the fleet's single MCP gateway — a Go daemon + CLI in `pkgs/mcpx/` that owns every MCP server process and serves every harness, with a 252-setting typed config registry, an effect-probe ratchet with an 8-setting exemption tail, transports over local socket/systemd, ssh, and tsnet, a live book at the repo Pages root, and live integrations (Atlas as a remote server; ID's capability-first MCP bridge; fleet integration at design stage). The prompt drives its executors to establish purpose, current + planned capabilities, and short/long-term roadmap; review and improve **all** existing designs and create new designs for the obvious next steps toward a fully featured MCP platform (not an MVP) — server onboarding and lifecycle (the supervisor design), per-client policy and capability ceilings tied to Atlas's sensitivity tiers and ID's capability discipline, remote/hosted servers as versioned deployments, config-system completion (the exemption tail to zero), observability, library/embedding use of mcpx's parts, and the mcpx↔fleet↔Atlas↔ID integration surface.

**Deliverables:** the mcpx book extended (starting from a mechanical book-vs-binary coverage audit), a dependency + blocker map, a prioritized issue map of **all** mcpx issues with blockers marked, landed designs, and merged implementation PRs wherever unblocked. code.title: C4.6 — Downtime-window demonstration against a known wall (Sunday-evening reopening set)
code.body:
Component of #9572 (C4 quota forecasting) — its acceptance item 3. Depends on C4.1 (downtime-window prediction, #13257).

Scope: demonstrate the downtime-window prediction against a known wall — the canonical case is a Sunday-evening reopening set (pools walled over the weekend reopening on reset). Replay the snapshot store through the C4.1 predictor as of a chosen known-wall moment, compare the predicted window against the realized reopening, and publish the error in the accuracy record.

Acceptance:
- [ ] A named historical complete-downtime episode is selected and its realized window established from the store.
- [ ] The predictor, run as-of before the episode, produces a downtime_window record for it.
- [ ] Predicted-vs-realized error (start/end/overlap) is published in the accuracy ledger and linked from #9572.

code.title: C4.5 — Forecast push alerts (downtime + wall predictions to push notifications)
code.body:
Component of #9572 (C4 quota forecasting), per its design record (doc/2026-11-13T15-12-00Z_design_reporting-architecture-event-driven/c4-forecasting-design.md).

code.body:
Component of #9572 (C4 quota forecasting), per its design record (doc/2026-11-13T15-12-00Z_design_reporting-architecture-event-driven/c4-forecasting-design.md).

code.title: C4.3 — Day-type and spike-day adjustments for quota forecasts (data-gated)
code.body:
Component of #9572 (C4 quota forecasting), per its design record (doc/2026-11-13T15-12-00Z_design_reporting-architecture-event-driven/c4-forecasting-design.md).

Scope: S2.6 day-type adjustments (same time-of-day on other days, other Fridays, other weekends) and S2.7 spike-day modeling (a week running ~10% light predicts a ~+20% spike day, stated explicitly by the model) as adjustments to the v1 pace forecast.

DATA GATE (from the Stage-3 design §2/§8, which deferred this): at 33 days of store history there were ~4–5 samples of each weekday per window — too thin. This issue first re-measures sample sufficiency per the design's threshold; cells below threshold keep the honesty state `adjustment_unavailable` and the unadjusted forecast stands. No tuned guesses on thin data.

Acceptance:
- [x] Sample-sufficiency measurement over the live snapshot store, per pool/window/day-type cell, recorded on this issue.
- [ ] Adjustments implemented for cells meeting the threshold, as a named methodology version (methodology-change log entry per the C4 design).
- [ ] Accuracy compared adjusted vs unadjusted in the S2 harness before any adjustment ships as the published forecast.

# Atlas program — full investigation, next-steps design & build-out (program tracking)

Drew's directive (2026-11-23): dig into the **full Atlas system** and design the next steps —
integrate all data sources with automatic ingest; improve query planning; integrate search for
fleet and for ID; MCP and programmatic access; more search characteristics on top of Snowflake;
reranking; a recommender; and everything else the investigation surfaces.

## Ground truth (verified 2026-11-23)

- Program epic #8983. Canonical store: laptop Turso/libSQL `~/atlas/turso-atlas/data/atlas.db`
  + 29 topic shards. Last verified census (2026-10-31, #3125): 18,325 sessions / 122,124
  messages / 107,639 chunks; the monolith has since grown to ~7.3 GB **without a verified
  recount** — consumer-facing counts are frozen at the October publish.
- #3125 phases 1–2 landed (12,092 CAS objects interned, ~2.6 GB, verify OK); phases 3–4 open.
- Production embedding model: `Snowflake/snowflake-arctic-embed-m-v2.0`, 768 dims; vectors are
  plain BLOBs — `vector_top_k` does not work on them; semantic search is an exact cosine scan
  (~4 s). Legacy BGE-small space coexists. Second-embedder evaluation open (#9092).
- Retrieval: hybrid FTS + vector, **RRF fusion only — no reranker in the serving path**.
  Query-planner flags (spell/query-class/rewritten) accepted but unimplemented
  (#9092/#5773/#5774). #12900 thread 1 landed; thread 2 (multi-client) is Drew's open question.
- Evaluation: golden-311 v3 + held-out 54, ablation harness (#5741), standing programme #8627.
  Feedback capture exists with no ranking consumer. Recommender: design only (#9140, #9109
  Part C); no candidate generation exists.
- Ingest is manual/script-driven (only schedule = daily backup); the target source list is
  #9097 Workstream E; sweep runner #7969 unbuilt.
- Sensitivity: corpus tiers public/internal/secret vs client ceilings
  shareable<personal<local-only<secret-bearing, enforced server-side. **#8479 is open: the 638
  secret-bearing chunks also live in the production monolith — the tier boundary does not
  currently hold outside the shard set** (purge-vs-reclassify is Drew's decision).
- Census: 57 open `epic/atlas-program` issues.

## Workstreams

A. Automatic ingest of all data sources (pipeline: CDC/hooks + reconciliation sweeps,
classification before promotion, tombstone purge across all stores).
B. Query planning (classifier → transforms → routed retrieval → fuse → rerank; planner flags
made real).
C. More search characteristics on top of Snowflake (MRL two-resolution index, learned sparse,
late interaction, metadata pre-filtering with tier as a security boundary, ANN path to replace
the 4 s scan, second-embedder decision).
D. Reranking (cross-encoder over fused top-50–200, golden-set-gated per corpus; BGE-Reranker-v2-m3
default candidate; feedback loop wired in).
E. Recommender (single-user signals: profile centroid, session co-occurrence, recency/frequency,
graph neighbours; more-like-this / related / resurface surfaces).
F. Fleet + ID search integration (freshness for `fleet search`; #6062 publication format +
projectors #11182–#11186 + #9109 Part C — ID's first live query path).
G. MCP + programmatic access (one retrieval core; MCP/REST/CLI surfaces; versioned API contract
from atlas-proto; #8625 cross-client acceptance; Worker cache TTL #6805).
H. Evaluation & quality programme (golden set from real traces, per-stage metrics, CI gates).
I. Book + issue map (below).

## Deliverables

1. An **Atlas book in bookwright form**, published on the existing code-repo Pages site under
   `/code/atlas/`, with a DOC-01-style docs-sync contract.
2. **An issue-by-issue map of ALL Atlas issues**, prioritized in best working order, with all
   blockers marked on the issues and in the list.
3. Designs landed by PR for every workstream; implementation PRs merged wherever unblocked.

## Operating rule

The prompt (posted as the first comment on this issue, and added to the repo by the starter PR)

repeat. Many parallel agents across analyze/research/design/document/implement workstreams.

code.title: id-caps: surface role definitions in world.toml (declarative [role_config] manifest section)
code.body:
PR #13234 (branch codex/agent-next-01-8299-role-config, commit b44c08e0b59) lands the #8299 acceptance: a new `id-caps` `role_config` module with validated, versioned `RoleDefinition`, audited grant/list/revoke events, editable starter roles, and `PolicyPoint::refresh_ceiling` next-frame refusal. It does not touch `world_manifest.rs`, so role definitions are not yet declarable in `world.toml`.

**Gap:** `id-caps::world_manifest` has no `[role_config]` section — a world cannot express its role set as data the way it expresses grants, ceiling, profile and schedules, and `id world diff` cannot reconcile role drift.

**Proposal (docs-first, then implement):**
- Add `WorldManifest.role_config: Option<RoleConfig>` — a present table is authoritative, an omitted field leaves live roles alone (the manifest's existing convention).
- `RoleConfig` carries `version = 1` (unknown versions refused at parse, per the #2876 strictness rule applied to roles), roles keyed by name, each definition with ceiling (known capabilities, no `*`), quota class, delegation-lifetime bounds within the v1 §9.2 range (15 min–4 h), and a review policy defaulting to `owner`.
- Validate definitions at parse time so a malformed manifest fails before any apply partially mutates a live world (#3015 rule).
- Reuse the `role_config` module's types from PR #13234 rather than redefining them, so manifest-surface and programmatic-surface stay one contract.

**Evidence a working slice exists:** branch `lane-any-n-8299` (commit 898f787cd54, worktree from this lane's task 21308 run) implements exactly this manifest surface with 41 green `world_manifest` tests — 254 id-caps unit tests total — but it was cut before PR #13234 appeared and duplicates `RoleDefinition`/validation instead of reusing the module, so it is a superseded prototype kept as reference, not a competing PR. Rebase the surface onto the merged module types.

**Docs-first:** `doc/2026-11-23T17-25-00Z_feature_world_role_manifest/2026-11-23T17-25-00Z_feature_world_role_manifest.md` on that branch records the slice design and test oracle (`cargo test -p id-caps world_manifest` from `pkgs/id`).

Follow-up to #8299 (parent #6301); intentionally not filed on the 21308 dedupe key — this is post-merge surface work, not a competing implementation.

code.title: fleet queue: add a repair verb for quarantined/malformed task packets (in-place payload fix)
code.body:
## Problem

Queue task 18533 (for #7709) was quarantined by the claim path: its `payload.dedupe` lacks `checked_at`/`basis` (validation #5444), so every claim re-quarantines it. `quarantine-recheck` diagnoses it (`still_quarantined`, with that `last_error`) but cannot fix it, and **no verb repairs a task payload in place**. The only disposition available was cancel-with-disposition (done 2026-11-23; full record on #13091). The blocked pool likely contains more rows in this class — rows that read as "blocked" but are actually quarantined malformed packets.

What exists today (verified against the b8bbcc0 binary's `fleet queue --help`): `unblock` (incl. `--drop-dep`), `quarantine-recheck` (diagnose only), `revive`, `cancel`, `verify-disposition`, `dep-recheck`. None of them mutates a payload to fix a validation defect.

## Ask: `fleet queue repair <task-id> [--dry-run]`

A broker-side verb, sibling to `unblock`:

- Loads the task by id in whatever non-terminal state it sits in (blocked/quarantined; cancelled stays `revive`'s job — repair composes with revive, it does not replace it).
- Runs the packet validators and lists every defect it finds.
- Applies deterministic, semantics-preserving repairs for known defect classes. First class, the #7709 shape: a dedupe payload missing `checked_at`/`basis` is repaired by **re-performing the dedupe check live** — verify no other live task carries the same (repo, issue, kind) work identity — and stamping `checked_at`/`basis` recording that the repair verb performed that check at that time. If a duplicate live task exists, stamping would be a false attestation: refuse and say so.
- Repairs never invent content: an unrepairable defect (a missing issue reference, a malformed prompt body, anything whose correct value cannot be re-derived by performing the check the field attests to) fails with a non-zero exit, lists the defects, and mutates nothing.
- `--dry-run` reports defects + planned repairs and writes nothing.
- On success: re-run validation; when clean, clear the quarantine and restore the task to claimable state — queued, or blocked with its recorded deps intact — and append a timeline entry naming the verb, the operator, the defects found, and the repairs applied.

## Also in scope

Audit `unblock` against a quarantined row: before repair it should refuse with a message naming the quarantine and pointing at `repair`, not silently no-op or misreport state. Fix in the same PR if it doesn't.

## Tests (fleet-queue crate, named oracles)

- The #7709 shape (dedupe payload missing `checked_at`/`basis`, no duplicate live task) repairs, re-validates clean, and becomes claimable.
- `--dry-run` on the same shape writes nothing (row byte-identical).
- A duplicate-identity dedupe defect is refused; the row is unchanged.
- An unrepairable defect fails non-zero; the row is unchanged.
- A repaired task's timeline carries the repair entry (verb, operator, defects, repairs).

## Acceptance

- The tests above green in CI on main.
- A live `repair --dry-run` against one currently-quarantined production row, reported on this issue (read-only — no production row is mutated by the acceptance check).
- Do not change task 18533's cancelled state; it stands as the worked example, revivable later by an operator decision.

code.title: fleet placement: session actor hardcoded, timeout_minutes never sent, registry budgets unenforced
code.body:
Found while surveying placement for the fleet book (#13165). Three behaviour gaps between the surface registry / workflow contract and the placement engine:

1. Session records hardcode the actor as `developing-today[bot] (GitHub App dispatch)` although fleet-org, fleet-forks, and Blacksmith surfaces dispatch as the user — records misattribute who dispatched.
2. Placement never sends the `timeout_minutes` input that `fleet-command.yml` accepts: every dispatch is capped at the workflow default (60 min) regardless of the job, and `dispatch_id` is a fresh correlation id rather than the placement session handle, which makes records harder to join.
3. Registry fields are declared but never enforced: `plan` / `private_minutes_monthly`, the Codespaces 180 core-hour budget, and `max_live: 3`.

Fix shape: record the real dispatching identity per surface auth route; thread an explicit timeout through placement (with a documented default); either enforce the registry budgets or mark the fields advisory in the registry schema so readers don't trust them.

code.title: impl(id): E6 remainder — run EventStoreBackend over the tenant row layer (#12801 follow-up)
code.body:
Follow-up to #12801 (E6 of #9083, design §11 item 6). The first E6 slice (branch `xaltha/12801-tenant-store-adapter`) lands the tenant DB store adapter's foundation in `id-store`:

- the Turso/SQLite-over-HTTP pipeline codec (`POST /v2/pipeline`, baton sessions, hrana value encoding) and an HTTPS transport carrying the tenant's scoped token (never stored, redacted from Debug);
- `TenantStore`: the native event store's 17 tables mirrored as SQL rows with redb's table semantics (byte-ordered keys, last write wins, multimap sets in value order, ordered range/prefix scans, explicit transactions over the baton session), with cross-backend row conformance tests against real redb tables.

## Remaining for #12801's acceptance

- [ ] `store_traits::EventStoreBackend` runs over the tenant row layer, so `SharedEventStore` over a Turso tenant DB behaves identically to the native store. The ingest semantics (verification, fork handling, waiting pool, resolution) live in `id-events`' `EventStore`, written directly against redb transactions; port them onto the row layer (or abstract the event store's table access onto it) **without forking the semantics into a second implementation** — one storage interface, backends differ only in storage (peer principle, design §0/§5.1).
- [ ] The `crates/id-store/tests/store_traits.rs` conformance suite runs against both backends (native redb and tenant Turso), not only the native one.
- [ ] No hosted-only special-casing in callers above `store_traits` (already true of the foundation slice; keep it true).

Sequencing: E3 (#12799) needs E1 + E6; this remainder is the part of E6 that E3's hosted sync ingress ultimately exercises.

code.title: perf(opencode-claimant): cut poll.py end-to-end latency (parallelize + bound its sequential external reads)
code.body:
## Problem

`pm-stack/opencode-claimant/poll.py` takes 43–100s wall with only ~2s CPU per run (measured 2026-11-23: 73.8s by the #13112 triage, 55–100s in the #13112 evidence, 74.2s / 43.5s in Lane OI's timed runs). The time is waits on sequential external reads: turso ledger SELECTs via the turso-exec helper, broker queue queries (claimed + handed_off per queue), and the OpenCode server session list over a 28k+ root-session store.

#13112 fixed the starvation symptom by raising claimant.py's gate timeout 30s -> 300s (PR #13134). That leaves the gate budget ~3x the observed worst case, but poll latency itself keeps growing with the session store, and every claimant fire pays it.

## Ask

Reduce poll.py's own end-to-end latency so the gate budget has durable margin:

- Parallelize the independent external reads (ledger bindings, per-queue claimed/handed_off rows, session list, active-id set) instead of running them strictly sequentially.
- Bound each external read with an explicit per-read timeout and a recorded slow-read note, so one slow backend degrades the poll visibly instead of silently eating the budget.
- Keep the output contract byte-compatible: claimant.py's cap counting delegates to poll.py's pinned functions (#6609), so the JSON shape and the pinned semantics (root = no parentID, activity = time.updated falling back to time.created, finished = time.idle or a top-level outcome) must not change.

## Acceptance

- poll.py timed over 10 runs on the laptop: p99 wall time < 30s (the pre-#13112 gate budget), with all runs exit 0.
- Hermetic suite (`run_hermetic_tests.py`, incl. test_poll.py / test_poll_transport.py) green with no new failures vs base.
- A live claimant fire using the sped-up poll passes the gate and the fire log shows the reduced poll duration.

## Context

- Parent symptom: #13112 (claimant starved, gate_unknown on every fire).
- Triage verdict on #13112 (oc-code-04): "preferable is parallelizing independent queue/status reads and bounding slow external reads."

Report from queue task 21097 (tracking issue #12776), diagnosed and verified 2026-11-23 ~02:37–02:50 CST by Lane NT (archer).

## Which link was broken

Link 1 — **pm-git-sync could not pull**: the laptop's primary checkout `~/git/code` carried a local, never-pushed commit, so every `git pull --ff-only` failed once origin/main moved past it. The checkout froze, so pm-console-redeploy had nothing new to deploy and the console kept serving the last deployed code (hostVersion `6226e4d93599`, main as of 2026-11-23T00:20Z) while staying up and reporting fresh `hostSeen`. This is the dispatch prompt's case 1 (a local commit that is not on origin stops the pull). It is **not** the flake.lock case, so nothing is owed on #12520.

## Evidence

- The local commit: `8e472164d4cfa15c5154c7d84585cf95c8898773` — "fix(opencode-claimant): raise poll timeout 30s -> 300s so live fires pass the gate", committed 2026-11-22 20:04:53 CST directly in the primary (touches `pm-stack/opencode-claimant/claimant.py` only).
- First sync failure, `journalctl --user -u pm-git-sync.service`, 2026-11-22 20:11:16 CST, repeating every ~30 s for ~5.5 hours:
  - `fatal: Not possible to fast-forward, aborting.`
  - `pm-git-sync: FAIL git pull --ff-only 8e472164d4cfa15c5154c7d84585cf95c8898773 -> 24be6fdd6f40b3ea13e89763a1c7de8ba6189ec0 in /home/user/git/code`
- Aggravator: at 2026-11-23 01:39:38 CST the checkout was moved to a detached HEAD (`e4968ed23ee`, "checkout: moving from main to FETCH_HEAD" in the HEAD reflog) during lane verification activity, which would have kept sync from advancing even had the divergence been cleared first.
- The redeploy and service links were never broken: once the checkout moved, pm-console-redeploy.service deployed within a minute and pm-console.service restarted (01:47:51 CST); its journal shows clean one-minute runs throughout.

## What fixed it

The checkout repair landed at 2026-11-23 01:46:57–01:47:00 CST (primary-seat fix, recorded in the HEAD reflog): checkout `main`, then `merge --ff-only origin/main` to `fe34e5cd9da`. `git pull --ff-only` fast-forwards resume in the reflog immediately after (01:49, 01:50, 01:52, 01:55, …) and continue to current main.

The unpushed claimant commit was **not** discarded: it is preserved on branch `parked/opencode-claimant-poll-timeout-20261122` in `~/git/code` (pointing at `8e472164d4cf`). Its change is not on main — current main's `claimant.py` still carries `timeout=30` in `run_poll` — so its owner still needs to land it properly (worktree + PR) if the 300 s gate is still wanted.

## Acceptance, verified 2026-11-23 ~02:50 CST

- `https://pm-console-edge.developing-today.workers.dev/console/health`: `hostVersion` = `fe34e5cd9da1`, `hostSeen` fresh, `ok: true`.
- Ancestry: compare `45191b4e2e14...fe34e5cd9da1` = ahead 384 / behind 0, so the running version contains `45191b4e2e14` as required.
- Nothing is queued behind it: compare `fe34e5cd9da1...d3bec26356c4` (current main) shows **zero** changed files under `pm-stack/console` or `pm-stack/systemd`, so the deployed console code is current with main.
- `~/git/code` is on `main` at origin/main; pm-git-sync.timer, pm-console-redeploy.timer and pm-console.service all active.

## What would have caught it sooner

pm-git-sync logged a clear FAIL every 30 seconds for ~5.5 hours and nothing surfaced it; the console's own health stayed green because the service was up — only the *age* of `hostVersion` showed the stall. Either signal would have caught this in minutes: (a) alert on pm-git-sync.service failure / repeated `FAIL git pull` lines, or (b) a staleness check on the console health `hostVersion` (alert when the running version is more than ~15 minutes behind origin/main while merges are landing). The stewardship cycle's fleet-feed staleness check (added 2026-11-23 under #2990) watches the aggregator feed, not the console hostVersion, so this class is still uninstrumented.

code.title: cold-store: atlas /dump download cut mid-transfer (curl 18) on every attempt; endpoint ignores Range so no resume is possible
code.body:
## Problem

The `atlas` Turso export can now fail one stage earlier than #12000's rebuild defect: the `/dump` download itself is cut mid-transfer, and the endpoint offers no way to resume.

First-hand evidence, 2026-11-23 01:57–02:23 CST (a standalone run of the atlas leg of `export-turso.sh` — token mint, `/dump` download, filters, rebuild — filing nothing):

- 4 download attempts (the script's initial try + `--retry 3 --retry-all-errors`): **all four ended `curl: (18) transfer closed with outstanding read data remaining`**, at varying offsets (the first reached ~1.28 GB; later attempts were cut far earlier).
- Range probe straight after: the endpoint answers a `Range:` request with **HTTP 200 and no `Content-Range`** — it ignores the header and streams from the start, so `curl -C -` resume cannot work against it.
- Throughput in the probe's last windows was ~3–6 KB/s (76–190 KB per 30 s), far below the ~3 MB/s the same download started at — the stream is being starved or stalled, then closed.

Circumstantial match: the 2026-11-22 nightly filed 50 databases (transfer ledger, 09:12–09:44 UTC) but **no atlas**, and `cold-store-nightly.service` exited FAILURE at 04:20 CST. Atlas is exported last, so a download that keeps getting cut fits — but it cannot be confirmed after the fact, because **no output from the unit survives**: `journalctl --user -u cold-store-nightly.service` returns no entries at all.

## Relation to #12000

Distinct stage. #12000's defect (rebuild dying on a duplicated `chunk_id` from a repeated table in the dump) is fixed — dedupe/vector-index filters on main — and its acceptance was met on 2026-11-19 and 2026-11-21 (atlas filed, 3,581,679,110 bytes gzipped each time; filing only happens after `integrity_check = ok` and the user-table check pass). This issue is the download stage that now fails first on bad nights.

## Ask

1. **Durable nightly output:** the nightly unit's per-step outcome and ERROR lines must survive the run (a log file under the cold-store home, or equivalent), so the next failure names its stage without a live probe.
2. **A download strategy that survives a cut, non-resumable stream:** e.g. spread the largest database's whole-download retries across the run's existing deadline budget instead of four attempts inside a few minutes, so a bad window can pass; or an alternate export path for `atlas`. Restarting a 10+ GB stream from zero on every attempt is the current shape and it is not working on bad nights.
3. **Acceptance:** three consecutive nightly runs file an `atlas` export, or one files it on a night when a probe shows the stream being cut.

Found by Lane LR while reconciling #12000.

Parent: #9128 (social app reference model design, §5 + §9). Program #9106, epic #9107. Builds on #9127 (append-list protocol) and #9130 (moderation/tombstones).

code.title: impl(id): freshness token + frontier check in id-core (per #9128 design)
code.body:
Parent: #9128 (social app reference model design, §6 + §9). Program #9106, epic #9107.

Implement the freshness token as pure logic in `pkgs/id` id-core, per the #9128 design record §6:

- `FreshnessToken` type: view_id (hash of canonical view definition), frontier, issued_at, server identity, signature; canonical encoding + sign/verify seam (key handling follows Part A conventions).
- Frontier type: per-input high-water marks — append-list accepted head sequence (#9127 §4) + tombstone-set revision (#9130) for list inputs, projection checkpoint (#9125) for relation inputs; component-wise equality/ordering.
- The check verdict as a pure function: given a presented token and the current frontier, return `nothing-new` | `delta` (with per-input after-seq positions) | `resync` (frontier unreachable). A token failing signature/view verification is treated as no token, never an error (§6.5).

Acceptance: unit + property tests — frontier comparison is reflexive/transitive-consistent; a token issued at the current frontier yields nothing-new; an advanced input yields delta naming exactly the advanced inputs; an unreachable frontier yields resync. Oracle: the §6.3 check table in the design record.

code.title: fix(heal): secrets-broker restart cadence starves its first refresh
code.body:
The laptop-channel heal loop can starve the secrets broker's refresh indefinitely.

Observed 2026-11-23 ~01:54-01:58 CST: the heal restarted `fleet serve secrets-broker` at 07:54:27Z, 07:54:32Z, 07:55:21Z and 07:56:24Z because health kept returning 503 with `refreshing:true, secrets:0`. But a full refresh shells out to one `bws secret get` per secret (~221 secrets) and takes longer than the heal's restart patience — every restart killed the in-flight refresh, so the broker never reached `serving:true`. Left alone, the 07:56 instance completed its refresh and health went green (221 secrets) with no other intervention.

Fix shape: the heal should not restart a secrets broker whose health reports `refreshing:true` with refresh progress underway (or whose bws children are active); give the first refresh a patience window sized to the secret count, and only restart when the process is absent, wedged with no bws activity, or still not serving after that window.

code.title: fleet-queue: chunked_list declares required-features=[client] but the crate does not compile with client alone
code.body:
## Problem

`pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-queue/Cargo.toml` declares the `chunked_list` integration test with `required-features = ["client"]`, but the crate does not compile with the `client` feature alone:

```
$ cargo test -p fleet-queue --features client --test chunked_list
error[E0433]: cannot find `turso_queue` in the crate root
   --> crates/fleet-queue/src/client/commands_lifecycle.rs:384:20
error[E0433]: cannot find `validate` in the crate root
   --> crates/fleet-queue/src/client/support.rs:682:12
error: could not compile `fleet-queue` (lib) due to 3 previous errors
```

Client code references `crate::turso_queue::BATCH_CLAIM_MAX` and `crate::validate::validate_not_before`, but both modules are configured out unless `queue-broker` is enabled (`lib.rs:48`, `lib.rs:52`). With `--features client,queue-broker` the same test builds and passes (2 passed, verified 2026-11-23 on main `ed65beca46e`).

So the declared feature contract for the test is wrong in one direction or the other: either `client` must stop referencing broker-gated modules (or pull in what it needs), or the test's `required-features` must name the set that actually builds.

## Acceptance

- `cargo test -p fleet-queue --features client --test chunked_list` (exactly the declared required-features) compiles and passes, OR the Cargo.toml declaration is corrected to the feature set the code genuinely requires and the client-only build of the lib target succeeds.
- No regression: `--features client,queue-broker` test suite stays green.

Found by: Lane LF (archer) during the #9001 done-check, 2026-11-23.

code.title: fleet-agent: registered_lane_worker has no mapping for oc-* lanes — oc-code-02 queue claims rejected (lane belongs to repo-worker-code)
code.body:
## Summary

`fleet agent next --agent oc-code-02 --lane oc-code-02 --repo developing-today/code --filter 'repo = code'` can never reach the queue rung: the front door claims with `--worker oc-code-02`, but the broker's lane registry binds lane `oc-code-02` to worker `repo-worker-code`, so every claim is refused with `claim_repo_task: lane oc-code-02 belongs to worker repo-worker-code, not oc-code-02`. The run then falls through shortlist/priority (both empty) and exits 5. The lane starves deterministically, not transiently.

## Reproduction

```
$ fleet agent next --agent oc-code-02 --lane oc-code-02 --repo developing-today/code --filter 'repo = code'
{
  "agent": "oc-code-02",
  "rung": "none",
  "task": null,
  "then": [],
  "tried": [
    {"rung": "push", "result": "empty", "why": "no command waiting"},
    {"rung": "queue", "result": "down", "why": "exit 6: repo-queue: primary queue store failed on /claim (exit 4): claim_repo_task: lane oc-code-02 belongs to worker repo-worker-code, not oc-code-02;          switching this work to the GitHub fallback"},
    {"rung": "shortlist", "result": "empty", "why": "nothing is listed, and it was filled or claimed for filling recently"},
    {"rung": "priority", "result": "empty", "why": "no open issue with a priority label is free"}
  ]
}
Exited with code 5
```

Observed on installed fleet rev `a732766` (`fleet version`: `0.1.0-dev.15194+ga732766`), 2026-11-23 ~07:38Z, twice in a row with a 60s wait between. Deterministic, not a transient broker outage (`fleet agent doctor` reports the queue leg ok).

## Root cause

`registered_lane_worker` in `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-agent/src/next.rs` maps lane families `code|any|not-code|opencode|openchamber|nix` with a single-letter suffix (plus three explicit `not-code-*` rows) to their shared `repo-worker-*`. It has no mapping for the `oc-*` scheduled-lane families (`oc-code-02`, etc.: after `rsplit_once('-')` the family is `oc-code` and the suffix `02` is not a single letter), so the worker falls back to the agent name (`oc-code-02`), which the broker rejects. Present at HEAD (`36f1f0a`), not just in the installed build — d1a67f8 ("claim known lanes as registered worker") covered the original families but not `oc-*`.

Evidence the broker binds `oc-*` lanes to the shared worker: sibling lane `oc-code-01` executed queue task 20424 as worker `repo-worker-code` (doc/2026-11-18T19-00-00Z_report_c5_efficiency-accounting.md), and lanes `oc-code-04`/`oc-code-07` landed work on 2026-11-22/23 (PR #12906, schedule-registry merge note).

## Suggested fix

Extend the mapping so `oc-<family>-<suffix>` resolves to the same worker as `<family>` (oc-code-* → repo-worker-code, oc-opencode-* → repo-worker-opencode, oc-openchamber-* → repo-worker-openchamber, oc-nix-* → repo-worker-nix, including the `not-code` variants), and extend the #6853-style oracle table in `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-agent/src/tests.rs` (`next_uses_the_registered_worker_for_a_known_lane`) with `oc-` rows.

## Acceptance

`fleet agent next --agent oc-code-02 --lane oc-code-02 ...` issues `fleet queue claim --worker repo-worker-code --lane oc-code-02 ...` (and the `then` completion commands carry `--worker repo-worker-code`), instead of the lane-ownership refusal.

## Filing note (deliberately not queued)

Filed by OpenChamber scheduled lane oc-code-02 outside a creator run. Per the filing rule this records why no triage packet was enqueued in the same pass: this lane operates through the Fleet front door exclusively and the front door cannot currently claim for this lane identity — the defect filed here. Queue coverage reconciliation remains the backstop for pickup.

code.title: fleet queue list: --status dep_blocked can never match — dep-blocked pool is unenumerable
code.body:
## Problem

`fleet queue list --status dep_blocked` returns `(no tasks)` at every limit, even when `fleet queue health` reports a large dep_blocked pool for the same queue.

Observed live 2026-11-23 ~07:44Z (laptop fleet, production broker):

- health, queue `repo-health-code-pilot`: blocked 402, **dep_blocked 177**.
- `fleet queue list --queue repo-health-code-pilot --status dep_blocked --limit 3|10|100|500` → `(no tasks)` every time.
- Same window, `--status claimed --limit 500`, `--status blocked --limit 500`, `--status parked --limit 500`, `--status done` all return rows normally.

## Root cause (source, current main)

Dep-blocked tasks are not stored with a distinct status: they are `status='blocked'` rows carrying a structured `blocked_deps` record (#8276). Health folds them into a separate `dep_blocked` count (`apply_dep_blocked` in `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-queue/src/turso_queue/admin.rs`), but the broker `/list` handler (`verb_list`, same file) filters literally on `status = ?` — no row ever carries `status='dep_blocked'`, so the filter can never match. The dep_blocked pool is therefore unenumerable from either seat (this already blocked a broker dep_blocked sweep: `fleet queue dep-recheck --limit 200` checked 0 and list returned no rows while health counted ~176).

## Acceptance

- `fleet queue list --status dep_blocked --limit 500` returns the dep-blocked rows health counts (blocked rows with a dep record), for any queue.
- A regression test covers listing dep_blocked rows through the broker /list path.
- `--status blocked` keeps its current meaning or the split is documented where the verb's help/status list is defined.

Found by: Lane LF (archer) during the #9001 production done-check, 2026-11-23.
Related: #9001 (same /list surface; its own acceptance is separately verified), #8276 (dep-block design).

code.title: [pkgs/id] GraphFrontier re-resolves the whole store on every gated message
code.body:
## Evidence

`GraphFrontier::is_authorized` runs on every inbound relay message (`pkgs/id/crates/id-sync/src/graph_frontier.rs:71-81`) via `RelayGate::decide` (`pkgs/id/crates/id-sync/src/relay_gate.rs:233-236`).

Each call runs `EventStore::roster` (`pkgs/id/crates/id-events/src/event_store/mod.rs:554-566`), which calls:

- `resolve::load` (`pkgs/id/crates/id-events/src/event_store/resolve.rs:568-611`) — iterates and decodes **every stored event** plus its action/device-op rows, plus all fork rows and proof headers;
- `resolve::resolve` — full causal fold over the loaded store;
- `resolve::roster_of` (`resolve.rs:676`) — projects one group's roster from the full resolution.

So per-message gate cost is O(store size): N stored events decoded + folded for every relay message, even when group membership has not changed. `SharedEventStore::read` (`id-store store_traits.rs`) is a plain lock with no memoization, so there is no caching layer underneath.

## Why this matters

The relay gate sits on the hot path for every message a relay receives. As the store grows (more groups, more history), each authorization check gets slower even for steady-state traffic in one small group. Membership changes are rare relative to message volume, so re-resolving the whole graph per message repeats work whose answer almost always hasn't changed.

## Acceptance

- Relay-gate authorization cost per message is bounded by group/roster size, not by total store size (e.g. per-group roster cache, ingest-generation invalidation, or an incremental membership projection).
- A regression test ingests N unrelated events and asserts `is_authorized` latency/message cost does not grow with N (or asserts roster reads hit the cache and miss only on ingest).
- Existing frontier tests still pass: `cargo test -p id-sync --lib graph_frontier`, including removal-takes-effect semantics (a removal in the store is refused at the gate as soon as ingested).

## Fix shape (suggestion, not prescription)

- Cache `group -> (roster, store generation)` inside `GraphFrontier` (or below `EventStore::roster`), bump the generation on ingest, and serve cache hits without `load`+`resolve`;
- or expose an incremental membership projection the frontier can read directly.

Scope is the caching follow-up only. The remaining end-to-end bridge re-check named on #3796 stays separate.

code.title: id: design pass — capability class assignments for the 16 post-#5999 registrations (kv/blob/notify/form/device.info/speech/client.*)
code.body:
Refs #5999 (§2.1–§2.2), #12982 (which landed the `class` field + shipped table), #12921, #5955.

## The gap

#12982 shipped the class table exactly as #5999's record wrote it. Sixteen registered provider names were registered *after* that record and have no designed class assignment, so their manifests carry `CLASS_UNKNOWN` — they always disclose, fail-closed (#5959 §1) — until a design pass assigns them classes:

- World storage: `kv.get`, `kv.set`, `kv.delete`, `blob.put`, `blob.get`, `blob.delete`
- User-facing effects: `notify`, `form.present`, `form.result`, `form.cancel`
- Device data: `device.info`, `speech.transcribe`, `speech.capture`, `speech.synthesize`
- Client-side providers: `client.file.read`, `client.notify`

A test in `cap_class.rs` (`names_without_a_designed_class_carry_unknown_until_assigned`) pins this exact list as a tripwire.

## What the pass must decide, per name or family

- The class id and its client-side sentence (the disclosure a person acts on, #5999 §2.1), or an assignment into an existing class where the consequence genuinely matches (e.g. is `kv.get` the same disclosure as `world.records`? is `speech.capture` a peer of `device.location`?).
- Subsumption edges against the existing lattice (#5999 §3) for any new class.
- Whether read/write splits matter (kv/blob have both; `records.read`'s class is read-only today).
- Client-side providers' classes are client-table questions too: `client.file.read` reads the *user's* files under a user-selected root — its disclosure is not `fs.read.arbitrary`'s ("any file this server can read").

## Landing shape

A design record in the #5999/#5959 shape (decision table per name), then a small implementation change: manifest `class:` values + the tripwire test list shrink in the same commit, and `CAP_CLASS_TABLE_VERSION` bumps if any class is added/split/merged. Until then the fail-closed state is correct behaviour, not a bug: these names prompt as `unknown` rather than slipping through silently.

code.title: fleet queue: live tasks table still defaults max_attempts to 4 — align with the code DDL (1000) or record acceptance
code.body:
## Gap (from the #12901 attempt-cap reconciliation, 2026-11-23)

The live fleet-queue Turso database's `tasks` table still carries the pre-#8973 column default:

```
max_attempts INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 4
```

(read live 2026-11-23 via `turso db shell fleet-queue` on the laptop: `SELECT sql FROM sqlite_master WHERE type='table' AND name='tasks'`).

Every current source of truth says 1000:

- Code DDL for a fresh store: `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-queue/src/turso_queue/core.rs` — `max_attempts INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 1000`.
- Enforced range at packet/client/broker: 1..=1000 (`MAX_ATTEMPTS_CEILING`, validate.rs, #9609).
- Creation default on every broker creation path: 1000 (`TASK_DEFAULT_MAX_ATTEMPTS`, #8973), written explicitly — which is why the stale column default has not bitten: live distribution is 17,921 rows at 1000 vs a small historical tail (75 @ 3, 72 @ 4, 19 @ 6, 14 @ 2, 1 @ 10, 1 @ 5, all explicit per-task values from their creation era).

The broker only runs `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS`, so the live table never picks up the new DDL, and SQLite/libsql cannot change a column default in place — alignment needs a table rebuild (create new table with DEFAULT 1000, copy, swap) against the production queue store, or an explicit operator decision to accept the divergence because all broker paths write the value explicitly and the default only fires for out-of-band raw inserts.

## Acceptance

- The live `tasks.max_attempts` column default reads 1000 (verified by the sqlite_master query above), OR the divergence is accepted by an explicit recorded operator decision naming the reason.
- Queue health stays green across the change (no at-cap or claim regression; `fleet queue health` before/after).

This is an operator/primary-seat action on the production queue store — not a code change. #12901 stays open on this item only.

code.title: supabase-exec live-broken: canonical management token sees zero projects (muse-dev2 out of scope)
code.body:
## Problem

`~/tools/supabase-exec.py` — the fleet-wide Supabase SQL helper — is correctly converted to the canonical Bitwarden pointers (found by the #2796 audit re-verification, 2026-11-23), but it **fails live against muse-dev2**:

- The ref pointer `supabase.muse-dev2.project-ref` resolves correctly to the muse-dev2 ref.
- The token it resolves, `supabase.muse-dev2.access-token-muse-cli`, authenticates against the Supabase Management API (GET /v1/projects → HTTP 200) but the project list is **empty** — the token sees zero projects.
- Consequently POST /v1/projects/{ref}/database/query returns **HTTP 404 "Resource has been removed"** (the API's response for a project outside the token's visibility).

So the helper is silently broken for every consumer (e.g. `pkgs/fleet/runtime-db-export/run_sql_pg.py` and `load_rows_pg.py` shell out to it) — not by a hardcode, but because the management token's scope/account no longer covers muse-dev2. This is the same failure shape the 2026-10-30 cutover exposed (scoped token vs. project mismatch), one layer up.

## Evidence (2026-11-23, Lane HB)

- File read: `supabase-exec.py` contains no project ref/URL at all; ref and token both resolve from BWS at runtime.
- BWS `supabase.muse-dev2.project-ref` → resolves to the muse-dev2 ref (verified equal, value not recorded here beyond what #2796 already names).
- Live run `supabase-exec.py <select 1>` → HTTP 404, `{"message":"Resource has been removed"}`.
- Same token, GET https://api.supabase.com/v1/projects → HTTP 200, `[]`.

## Fix (owner: Drew — Supabase account action)

Mint or re-scope a Supabase management token so it can see the muse-dev2 project in the account/org that owns it, and store it in BWS under the existing name `supabase.muse-dev2.access-token-muse-cli` (no code change needed — that is the point of the pointer design). Then re-run `supabase-exec.py` with a trivial read-only query and confirm HTTP 200 with result rows.

## Acceptance

- `supabase-exec.py` with `select 1` returns HTTP 200 and rows against muse-dev2.
- GET /v1/projects with the stored token lists the muse-dev2 project.

Found during: #2796 acceptance criterion 3 re-verification.
