code.title: fleet: sessions wedge on a walled or dead model door instead of failing over
code.body:
## Problem

When a model door stops answering, sessions routed to it stay wedged in a retry loop. They do not fail over to a door that works, and new waves keep being routed to the dead door. Five issues report the same failure, one per door, with 58 to 96 comments each and no code change:

| Issue | Door | Failure |
| --- | --- | --- |
| #9549 | `_claude` | OAuth renewal answers 429; every session dies at launch |
| #9856 | `_antigravity` | 403, account disabled for terms of service |
| #9859 | `_muse` | 429, weekly window at 100% |
| #9961 | `cline-pass` | 429, monthly limit reached |
| #10085 | `opencode-go` sub-accounts | 429; sessions freeze at retry attempt 2 |

Each was parked on the owner. None needs him: a quota wall resets by itself, and what the fleet controls is whether it keeps sending work into the wall.

## What to build

1. **Measure first.** For each of the five doors, record today's state: answering, walled until a known reset time, or dead.
2. **A walled door is skipped until its reset.** When a door answers with a quota wall that names a reset time, or with an auth failure, the route marks the door unusable until that time (or until a probe succeeds) and stops routing new sessions to it.
3. **A wedged session fails over.** A session whose door fails this way moves to the next door in its route within one retry, or ends with a clear error that the scheduler can re-launch elsewhere. It does not hold a lane while it retries.
4. **Door state is data, not an issue.** The quota record already carries the windows. The hourly "issue remains open and tracked" comments stop.

## Done when

- A test routes a session at a door that answers 429 with a reset an hour away: the session completes on the next door, and no new session is routed to the walled door before the reset.
- A test with a door answering 403 shows the same, with the door marked dead until a probe succeeds.
- For one week, no session sits in a provider retry for more than five minutes while another door in its route is answering.

## Decided

- The five reports are one defect and are closed into this issue. Undo: reopen one.
- `_antigravity` leaves the rotation until the account answers again. An appeal for that account is optional and blocks nothing.

code.title: Root scratch symlink points at missing doc/hardware/scratch
code.body:
## Finding

`scratch` at the repo root is a tracked symlink to `doc/hardware/scratch`, and that target does not exist. The hardware-device-research skill documents `scratch/` as a working directory that `git add -A` stages, so the link looks intended but never works.

## Evidence (verified in the current tree)

- `ls -la scratch` shows `scratch -> doc/hardware/scratch`, and `file scratch` reports "broken symbolic link".
- `git ls-files doc/hardware` returns one entry, and no `doc/hardware/scratch` exists in the tree.
- `.gitignore` has no `scratch` entry.
- `.agents/skills/hardware-device-research/SKILL.md:49` and `:60-61` describe `scratch/…` as the working tier and say that `scratch/` and `doc/scratch/` are the same repository.
- No tracked script or workflow creates the directory, so the link is never valid for a fresh clone.

## Why it matters

Anyone who follows the skill writes into a path that a clone does not have, and tools that walk the tree see a dangling link. It is a small cleanup, but it contradicts the documented workflow.

## Suggested fix shape

Pick one of two: create `doc/hardware/scratch/` with a `.gitkeep` (and add it to the ignore rules if its contents should stay untracked), or remove the root `scratch` link and point the skill at `doc/hardware/scratch` directly. Either way, the skill's path and the tree must agree.

code.body:
## Finding

The repo root holds about 29 tracked one-shot status documents from earlier slice-1 work, plus an 800 KB chat transcript committed as `session-ses_2b17.md`. Nothing outside the root refers to them, and they clutter the root listing, which makes the real top-level layout hard to read.

## Evidence (verified in the current tree)

- `git ls-files` lists these as tracked at the root: `FINAL_SLICE1_COMPLETION_REPORT.md`, `IMPLEMENTATION_COMPLETE.md`, `IMPLEMENTATION_COMPLETE_SLICE1.md`, `IMPLEMENTATION_COMPLETE.txt`, `IMPLEMENTATION_STATUS.md`, `IMPLEMENTATION_SUMMARY.md`, `OPENCODE_CLAIMANT_SLICE1_COMPLETE.md`, `OPENCODE_CLAIMANT_SLICE1_SUMMARY.md`, `OPENCODE_SLICE1_COMPLETE.md`, `README_SLICE1_COMPLETION.md`, `SLICE1_COMPLETE.txt`, `SLICE1_COMPLETION_CONFIRMATION.md`, `SLICE_1_COMPLETION_REPORT.md`, `SLICE1_COMPLETION_REPORT.md`, `SLICE1_COMPLETION_SUMMARY.md`, `SLICE1_COMPLETION_SUMMARY.txt`, `SLICE1_FINAL_SUMMARY.md`, `slice1_final_verification.md`, `SLICE1_IMPLEMENTATION_COMPLETE.md`, `SLICE1_IMPLEMENTATION_CONFIRMATION.md`, `SLICE1_IMPLEMENTATION_SUMMARY.md`, `SLICE1_IMPLEMENTATION_VERIFICATION.md`, `SLICE1_TASK_COMPLETION.txt`, `TASK_COMPLETE.md`, `TASK_COMPLETE.txt`, `TASK_COMPLETION_SUMMARY.md`, plus `test_slice1_implementation.sh` and `verify_slice1_implementation.sh`.
- `git grep` for these names finds references only in the root files themselves (`TASK_COMPLETE.txt:89` lists `slice1_final_verification.md`). No build, CI, justfile or nix file calls them. The only exception is the `pm-stack/opencode-claimant/` copies, which are separate files.
- `session-ses_2b17.md`: 796,021 bytes, tracked, last changed in commit `19597b5262` with the message "idk". Nothing references it. A scan for common credential patterns found no matches.
- The two `*_slice1_*.sh` scripts are covered in a separate issue (broken exit under `set -e`).

## Why it matters

Each file is a point-in-time claim ("implementation complete") that goes stale, and the transcript adds about 800 KB to every clone. Both make the root harder to navigate and make it unclear which document is current.

## Suggested fix shape

- Move anything worth keeping into `doc/` (for example a single archived note), then `git rm` the root copies. Do not keep several parallel status files.
- Remove `session-ses_2b17.md` from the tree. Before deleting, check whether the fleet keeps transcripts by some other route, and keep the content in the transcript store if so.
- Add a check that rejects new `*COMPLETE*` / `*SUMMARY*` files at the root.

code.title: Conductor census helper session-count.py pages /api/session at limit=1000; the API caps limit at 200 — exit-3 census has stopped all conductor dispatch since 15:23Z
code.body:
## Symptom

`python3 /home/user/tools/session-count.py` — the mandated conductor capacity census — exits 3 with `session enumeration FAILED: HTTPError: HTTP Error 400: Bad Request` on every run since 2026-11-20T15:23Z. The runbook treats a census enumeration failure as a global stop, so the conductor's DISPATCH phase has been fully stopped for 6 consecutive cycles (15:23Z, 15:40Z, 16:00Z, 16:20Z, 16:40Z, and the in-flight cycle) while queued work exists in the pilot queues. The queue lanes themselves are still claiming; only conductor dispatch is gated.

## Evidence (2026-11-20, laptop-local)

- Live repro: `curl 'http://localhost:3000/api/session?limit=1000'` → HTTP 400 `{"_tag":"InvalidRequestError","message":"Expected a value less than or equal to 200\n  at [\"limit\"]","kind":"Query"}`. `limit=200` → HTTP 200 with cursor pagination; `limit=201` → 400. The helper sends `PAGE = 1000` (`list_sessions()` builds `/api/session?limit=1000`), so its very first page now fails.
- The helper worked at 14:41Z and 15:05Z (conductor-log.md: census succeeded, `unfinished roots 15/30` then `3/30`) and first failed at 15:23Z — the OpenChamber server side began enforcing the OpenCode ceiling in that window (exact restart/trigger not pinned; the enforcement itself is confirmed live above).
- The ceiling is already known and documented inside OpenChamber: commit `b003844b3` (2026-11-17, "fix(sessions): list sessions at most 200 a page, OpenCode's ceiling") added `SESSION_LIST_MAX_LIMIT = 200` with the comment *"OpenCode rejects a session.list `limit` above this with a 400 ('Expected a value less than or equal to 200'), which fails the whole list."* OpenChamber's own callers were fixed; the conductor helper was not.
- Impact record: conductor-log.md entries for the six stopped cycles (lines ~4111 onward), each recording the exact exit-3 failure and `sessions dispatched: 0`.
- A naive fix is incomplete: the helper already implements cursor pagination, but with `PAGE = 200` and the current `MAX_PAGES = 20` it would silently truncate at 4,000 of ~29,000 history rows; activity-map sessions older than that would surface as `unlisted N > 0`, which the mandate also treats as a stop condition.

## Root cause (verified, not suspected)

The helper violates the API contract: it pages `/api/session` with `limit=1000` while the endpoint (OpenChamber proxying OpenCode's session.list) validates `limit ≤ 200`. Everything else in the helper (cursor handling, activity-map population, counting rule) is unaffected.

## Ask

1. Fix `~/tools/session-count.py`: set `PAGE = 200` and raise `MAX_PAGES` enough to cover full history (~29k rows today → ≥150 pages; 400 gives headroom). The script is untracked local tooling under `~/tools`, so this needs Drew's word or a direct laptop edit — two constants, no logic change.
2. Until then the conductor stays in census-failure global stop, recording `sessions dispatched: 0` each cycle; the runbook is being followed, not bypassed.

Searched open and closed issues across the four repos (`session-count`, `session enumeration`, `conductor census`, `limit 200` in openchamber): no existing report. Related but different: #11764 (control-API 4s timeouts that stop the lane overlap checks — same family of laptop-tooling faults, different endpoint and failure).

Queue: deliberately not queued, same rationale as #11764: the deliverable is a file outside every repo (`~/tools/session-count.py`, untracked), and modifying Drew's mandated measurement instrument needs his sanction; a repo-pilot worker has no compliant worktree for it. Filed by the fleet conductor cycle (ses_e5e062bb3c8ffeNiJumoJZvan1) whose dispatch gate this failure has closed.

code.title: id(event-store): frozen-rival arrival order can strand dependent events
code.body:
## Problem

The event-store's result for an `after` dependency can depend on arrival order when that dependency names an event above a later fork point. `ingest.rs` says applied state depends on the event set, and that stored-but-unapplied events remain present as voids (`pkgs/id/crates/id-events/src/event_store/ingest.rs:29-41`). But its “Known limit: a rival refused as frozen” section documents that a post-fork arrival is refused (not stored), while the same event arriving before the fork is retained voided (`:82-90`). Since an `after` hash is satisfied by a stored voided event (`:57-60`), the dependency is present in one order and absent in the other.

This can strand an otherwise identical dependent event: one replica can accept it after the event is retained as voided; another can keep it waiting after the post-fork event is refused. This is a source-traced consistency/availability gap, not a claim of a reported production incident.

Existing focused tests pin the two sides separately: `test_an_after_hash_naming_a_voided_event_is_applied` (`ingest.rs:2281-99`) and `test_an_event_released_into_a_frozen_chain_leaves_no_row` (`:3765-98`). The current batch property compares batch and per-event paths for one arrival order (`:86-90`), so it does not catch this cross-order difference.

## Expected improvement

Define one order-independent rule for the presence/availability of authenticated events above a fork point, then cover it with an order/API matrix. At minimum, compare these same events in both orders: a chain through sequence 2, a conflicting sequence-1 event, and a different author's event whose `after` names sequence 2. Assert the dependent event has the same final disposition and the same dependency-presence result whether the fork arrives before or after sequence 2; include batch and per-event ingestion where supported.

## Verification

On `e8da4a4ae111601dbca602fd6bacfd3ea17f8693`, `cargo test -p id-events test_an_after_hash_naming_a_voided_event_is_applied` and `cargo test -p id-events test_an_event_released_into_a_frozen_chain_leaves_no_row` both pass (1 test each). These tests verify the two existing behaviors; no full end-to-end order-matrix reproduction was added in this creator pass.

- **Cleanup** — dead code, duplicated logic, obsolete files or config,
  leftover scaffolding.
- **Performance** — hot paths doing avoidable work, missing caching or
  batching, inefficient data structures or queries.
- **Security** — unsafe input handling, secrets or credentials in code or
  config, over-broad permissions, missing validation at trust boundaries.
- **Code Health** — confusing structure, missing or misleading error
  handling, functions/modules that have grown hard to change safely.
- **Testing** — important behaviour with no coverage, tests that assert
  nothing, flaky or order-dependent tests.

## Verify before you file — no speculative filings

Every candidate finding MUST be verified against the actual code before
it becomes an issue:

- Read the code at the location you cite. Confirm the problem is real in
  the current tree, not an assumption from a filename, a comment, or a
  pattern you expected to find.
- Check the surrounding context (callers, tests, configuration) — a
  candidate that turns out to be intentional, already handled elsewhere,
  or not actually reachable is rejected, not filed.
- Search the repo's OPEN issues before filing. If an existing open issue
  already covers the finding, comment on that issue with your evidence
  instead of opening a duplicate.

## Filing

- Per real, verified finding, file ONE issue in this repo with
  `gh issue create` from the laptop checkout. Each issue must include:
  - the canonical component label for its area; use `app/pm-stack` for
    PM-stack / aggregator issues in this repo. `app/aggregator` is a legacy
    alias and must not be used for new filings.
  - a clear title naming the problem;
  - file/line evidence (the exact paths and lines you verified);
  - why it matters (impact, risk, or cost);
  - the suggested fix shape — the direction of the fix, not a full
    implementation.
- CAP: at most **5 filings per pass** (new issues plus evidence comments
  on existing issues). If you verify more than 5 findings, file the 5
  highest-impact ones and list the rest in your summary as
  verified-but-deferred.
- Do NOT dispatch further tasks for the findings, and do not fix them in
  this pass. The issues are the record; the fleet's normal lanes pick
  work up from them.

## Finish

End with a short summary — as your session output, and as a comment on
this run's tracking issue if you can identify it — covering:

- **Filed** — each issue you opened or commented on, with its number and
  one line on the finding.
- **Verified and rejected** — candidates you checked against the code and
  did not file, with the reason.
- **Needs a human decision** — findings that are real but whose fix is a
  judgement call (trade-offs, product direction, risk appetite), stated
  plainly so a human can rule on them.

If the pass finds nothing worth filing, say so in the summary instead of
opening low-value issues to fill the pass.

code.title: atlas(#6666 slice 3): persistent embedded replicas for internal/public (libsql local-copy, design 5.5)
code.body:
## Parent

Follow-on from #6666 (atlas shard consumer), its slice 3: persistent embedded replicas for internal/public. Split out by queue task 20005 (2026-11-17) when slice 1 (serve-mode ShardedBackend wiring + re-discovery) landed separately: slice 3 is a distinct dependency + verification effort, not a remainder that should block slice 1.

## What design 5.5 requires

From `doc/2026-11-04T21-27-34Z_design_atlas_scaler_revision` section 5.5: embedded replicas are libSQL's local-copy mode — the laptop holds persistent local replicas of all `internal` core scan stores + `public` stores, syncing page/WAL deltas in the background within the recorded sync budget. `secret` stores are NEVER replicated off their home node (a replica is a copy; copies defeat the tier's physical separation). Staging-tier replicas: none.

## Current state (verified 2026-11-17, task 20005)

- The workspace has NO `libsql` crate dependency anywhere. Shard transports are a hand-rolled HTTPS pipeline (`atlas-core/src/turso.rs`) for hosted shards and rusqlite local files (`atlas-core/src/shards/local.rs`, whose header names it "the seam for embedded replicas (design 5.5) later").
- Slice 1 (serve wiring + periodic re-discovery with atomic snapshot swap) makes a replica directory immediately consumable: a synced replica home can be served via the `dir:` spec and stays fresh through re-discovery.

## Scope for this issue

1. Decide and record the integration shape: add the `libsql` crate as the embedded-replica transport for internal/public scan shards (builder with remote URL + auth token, local path, background sync), behind the existing `ShardTransport` seam in `shards/local.rs` — or record a different shape with reasons if the crate's sync model does not fit the pipeline contract.
2. Enforce the tier rule in code: replica creation refuses the secret tier, mirroring the discovery ceiling's fail-closed posture.
3. Wire replica homes into discovery (a spec or config naming replica-backed shards) so serve mode (slice 1) can consume them.
4. Verify live: initial sync of one internal + one public shard on the laptop, a promoted row appearing after a background sync without restart, and the sync-budget figures from design 5.5 re-checked against the Turso counters.

## Acceptance

- Internal/public shard replicas persist on the laptop and serve reads locally through the existing transport seam.
- Secret-tier replica attempts fail closed with a named error.
- Live verification recorded on this issue (initial sync size/time, delta sync after a promotion, budget check).
- The standalone and hosted serve paths are regression-tested unchanged.

Filed by lane any-m triage of design issue #5790 (task 19901, 2026-11-17). #5790's §5 recommendation: ratify the interim hybrid (done — derivation landed in #8566 / PR #8630, Drew's five open questions answered 2026-11-06) and spend the full-design effort on two areas, of which the deploy-tool identity ledger was #5766 (CLOSED). ## Scope

Decide and document the release workflow for the per-app tag scheme #5790 ratified:

1. **Who/what cuts the tags.** Per-app `<app>/vX.Y.Z` tags on the exact tested commit, plus the repo tag `repo/v<YYYYMMDD>` (plus `.N`) at release points, per Drew's 2026-11-06 rulings (short app-name prefixes for all apps, names unique; repo prerelease tags on deploys allowed; main deploys are prereleases, releases are tag builds only; apps start at 0.1.0 and stay in 0.x). Name the actor (deploy tool, CI job, or a documented manual step) and the trigger.
2. **How "tested" is attested.** A tag claims its commit was tested together. Record what evidence backs that claim (CI run ids, the checks required, where the attestation is stored so `deploy status` / a later audit can read it).

- The derivation itself (#8566, merged PR #8630).
- The deploy tool's target registry / identity ledger (#5766, closed).

- Inventing a new numbering scheme — #5790 surveyed and rejected the alternatives; this issue implements its recommendation.

## Acceptance

Your journal is NOT a log - only add entries for CRITICAL learnings that will help you avoid mistakes or make better decisions.

⚠️ ONLY add journal entries when you discover:
- A performance bottleneck specific to this codebase's architecture
- An optimization that surprisingly DIDN'T work (and why)

- A codebase-specific performance pattern or anti-pattern
- A surprising edge case in how this app handles performance

❌ DO NOT journal routine work like:
- "Optimized component X today" (unless there's a learning)
- Generic React performance tips
- Successful optimizations without surprises

Format: `## YYYY-MM-DD - [Title]
**Learning:** [Insight]
**Action:** [How to apply next time]`

BOLT'S DAILY PROCESS:

1. 🔍 PROFILE - Hunt for performance opportunities:

  FRONTEND PERFORMANCE:
  - Unnecessary re-renders in React/Vue/Angular components
  - Missing memoization for expensive computations
  - Large bundle sizes (opportunities for code splitting)
  - Unoptimized images (missing lazy loading, wrong formats)
  - Missing virtualization for long lists
  - Synchronous operations blocking the main thread
  - Missing debouncing/throttling on frequent events
  - Unused CSS or JavaScript being loaded
  - Missing resource preloading for critical assets
  - Inefficient DOM manipulations

  BACKEND PERFORMANCE:
  - N+1 query problems in database calls
  - Missing database indexes on frequently queried fields
  - Expensive operations without caching
  - Synchronous operations that could be async
  - Missing pagination on large data sets
  - Inefficient algorithms (O(n²) that could be O(n))
  - Missing connection pooling
  - Repeated API calls that could be batched
  - Large payloads that could be compressed

  GENERAL OPTIMIZATIONS:
  - Missing caching for expensive operations
  - Redundant calculations in loops
  - Inefficient data structures for the use case
  - Missing early returns in conditional logic
  - Unnecessary deep cloning or copying
  - Missing lazy initialization
  - Inefficient string concatenation in loops
  - Missing request/response compression

2. ⚡ SELECT - Choose your daily boost:
  Pick the BEST opportunity that:
  - Has measurable performance impact (faster load, less memory, fewer requests)
  - Can be implemented cleanly in < 50 lines
  - Doesn't sacrifice code readability significantly
  - Has low risk of introducing bugs
  - Follows existing patterns

3. 🔧 OPTIMIZE - Implement with precision:
  - Write clean, understandable optimized code
  - Add comments explaining the optimization
  - Preserve existing functionality exactly
  - Consider edge cases
  - Ensure the optimization is safe
  - Add performance metrics in comments if possible

4. ✅ VERIFY - Measure the impact:
  - Run format and lint checks
  - Run the full test suite
  - Verify the optimization works as expected
  - Add benchmark comments if possible
  - Ensure no functionality is broken

5. 🎁 PRESENT - Share your speed boost:
  Create a PR with:
  - Title: "⚡ Bolt: [performance improvement]"
  - Description with:
    * 💡 What: The optimization implemented
    * 🎯 Why: The performance problem it solves
    * 📊 Impact: Expected performance improvement (e.g., "Reduces re-renders by ~50%")
    * 🔬 Measurement: How to verify the improvement
  - Reference any related performance issues

BOLT'S FAVORITE OPTIMIZATIONS:
⚡ Add React.memo() to prevent unnecessary re-renders
⚡ Add database index on frequently queried field
⚡ Cache expensive API call results
⚡ Add lazy loading to images below the fold
⚡ Debounce search input to reduce API calls
⚡ Replace O(n²) nested loop with O(n) hash map lookup
⚡ Add pagination to large data fetch
⚡ Memoize expensive calculation with useMemo/computed
⚡ Add early return to skip unnecessary processing
⚡ Batch multiple API calls into single request
⚡ Add virtualization to long list rendering
⚡ Move expensive operation outside of render loop
⚡ Add code splitting for large route components
⚡ Replace large library with smaller alternative

BOLT AVOIDS (not worth the complexity):
❌ Micro-optimizations with no measurable impact
❌ Premature optimization of cold paths
❌ Optimizations that make code unreadable
❌ Large architectural changes
❌ Optimizations that require extensive testing
❌ Changes to critical algorithms without thorough testing

Remember: You're Bolt, making things lightning fast. But speed without correctness is useless. Measure, optimize, verify. If you can't find a clear performance win today, wait for tomorrow's opportunity.

If no suitable performance optimization can be identified, stop and do not create a PR.---

code.title: quota-recorder: units still vanish mid-boot — #6148 restore block only heals at init, switch activations wipe the /etc copies with no mid-boot restore
code.body:
## Symptom
The quota-recorder systemd units (`quota-recorder.service` / `quota-recorder.timer`, installed as imperative copies in `/etc/systemd/system`) still vanish mid-boot and stay gone until a person or a sweep notices and hand-reinstalls them. Recording silently stops in the gap.

## Evidence
- #6148 (closed 2026-11-05 as COMPLETED) fixed the filed defect: a restore block in `~/tools/init.sh` plus `~/tools/quota-recorder/install.sh` (dezren39/hatch `3efce1255`). Verified 2026-11-17 audit: `init.sh` contains the restore block and the timer is currently active.
- But the restore only runs at init/boot. On 2026-11-16 the units were lost at least 3 times in ~14 hours (fleet run reports, `~/memory/2026-11-16.md`), including one sweep recording verbatim: "quota-recorder units had vanished from /etc again — reinstalled via ~/tools/quota-recorder/install.sh; timer active, tick landed". Each loss was healed by a manual reinstall, not by the #6148 mechanism.
- Working pattern: imperative `/etc` unit copies are wiped by NixOS switch activations mid-boot; nothing re-runs the installer until the next boot or a human notice.

## Scope
Give the quota-recorder units a restore path that fires mid-boot — e.g. declare the units in the Nix configuration so switch activations carry them, or add a switch/post-activation hook (or a watchdog timer in a durable unit family) that re-runs `~/tools/quota-recorder/install.sh` when the timer is missing. Sandbox side (the recorder runs on the sandbox); do not change the recorder itself.

## Acceptance check
After a NixOS switch activation on the sandbox, `systemctl is-active quota-recorder.timer` is active with no manual reinstall, and a recorder tick lands (file-first + Turso ack) within one timer interval of the activation.

## Refs
- #6148 (the original restore-block fix this follows up)
- Audit: closed-work validation pass for 2026-11-05/06, run 2026-11-17

Perform a comprehensive daily codebase review, innovation scan, and issue/PR maintenance pass across developing-today/code.

You are acting as an unrestricted principal architect and senior systems engineer. Do not hold back: generate bold ideas, surface hidden gaps, polish proposals, and solve immediate problems opportunistically.
Follow these directives and areas of focus:
### 1. COMPREHENSIVE REPOSITORY & ACTIVITY AUDIT - Inspect recent commits on `main` to understand the latest velocity and architectural direction. - Review open, recently closed, and merged issues and PRs (`gh issue list --state all --limit 50`, `gh pr list --state all --limit 30`). - Review each major package, tool, and subsystem in the repository:
  - **`pkgs/id`**: Distributed identity, cryptographic event log, p2panda synchronization, local event store, group encryption, discovery, and capability delegation.
  - **`pkgs/mcpx`**: Model Context Protocol daemon, multi-server multiplexing, protocol compliance, session leasing, JIT secret prompt vault, and Code Mode projection.
  - **`pkgs/fleet`**: The Rust multicall fleet tools and queue client — automated multi-agent coding workflows, issue triage, and parallel agent execution (the retired packages were removed by PR #5376; audit the fleet queue automation under `pkgs/fleet` and `.github/workflows`, the dispatch actions `.github/actions/pm-dispatch-start` and `.github/actions/pm-dispatch-task`, the scheduler `.github/workflows/pm-scheduled.yml` and its repo-specific scheduled callers, and the CI-breakage automation).
  - **NixOS System Infrastructure & Web Services**: Modules, cloud functions, background daemons, and system services.

### 2. UNRESTRICTED INNOVATION & NEW FEATURE GENERATION - You are NOT restricted by what currently exists. Brainstorm things that *should* exist, would be exceptionally useful, or incorporate frontier concepts:
  - Edge architectures using Cloudflare Workers, Durable Objects, KV, and Queues.
  - Distributed SQLite / libSQL / Turso primitives for offline-first, syncable state.
  - Advanced autonomous coding loops, speculative tool execution, and local verification loops.
  - Cross-platform bridges, native desktop integrations, and performance optimizations.
- **Bias Toward Capture**: It is far better to create an issue to triage later than to let a valuable opportunity or insight pass.
### 3. ACTIVE ISSUE & PR MAINTENANCE - **Scope Variety**: Create single large architectural vision issues for strategic direction, or narrow, highly focused issues for targeted improvements. - **Issue Decomposition**: If an existing issue is too broad, ambiguous, or monolithic (including issues created by others), break it apart into a series of clear, modular, linked sub-issues with explicit dependencies. - **Deduplication & Consolidation**: Identify overlapping or duplicate proposals/issues and consolidate them into unified, high-quality reference issues. - **Comments & Spec Refinement**: Leave comments or edit existing issues/PRs to provide missing technical specifications, edge-case analysis, data schemas, or suggested test cases. - **Zero-Context Hand-off Standard**: Every issue you author must be self-contained, citing exact file paths, interfaces, architectural rationale, and verifiable acceptance criteria so a new agent with zero prior context can execute it.

### 4. OPPORTUNISTIC IMPLEMENTATION (QUICK-WIN PRS) - If you identify straightforward bugs, unhandled edge cases, missing test coverage, or clean opportunities to refactor code to prevent future merge conflicts:
  - You are actively encouraged to open small, focused Pull Requests implementing the fix or feature directly.
  - Ensure all added code follows repository standards, includes tests, and passes formatting/linting hooks (`treefmt`, `conform`).
  - Never introduce breaking regressions to existing stable flows.
  - **One PR per coherent set**: batch every instance of the same problem — and all related dependency updates — into a single PR, or a few PRs split by coherent group. Never one PR per item or per dependency.
  - **Prefer tracked, higher-impact work**: before inventing a new micro-fix, check the open issues and implement the highest-impact one you can complete and verify, even when it spans several files.
  - **Merging is permitted, never required**: merge your PR only when checks pass and you are reasonably certain it is correct and low-risk. Otherwise leave it open and state your confidence and what a human should check in the description.

---

code.title: fleet binary: implement the laptop-agent domain — automatic transport fallback (CF → Tailscale → SSH) + CF Access credential from fleet secrets; retire the Python client's routing
code.body:
Drew's directive (2026-11-16, Reports chat): the transport fallback belongs in the fleet binary itself, not in the Python laptop-agent scripts.

## Current state (verified 2026-11-16)
- The binary's proxy transport already does Cloudflare-primary / Tailscale-fallback: PR #10577 merged 2026-11-16T00:56:57Z. Transport design home: #10356 (open).
- The laptop-agent CLIENT is still Python (~/tools/laptop-agent.py + laptop-agent-broker.py in dezren39/hatch): the binary's `fleet laptop-agent` domain is a registry stub (exit 69; epic #5412 closed with the domain left as a later step).
- The Python client currently carries behavior that belongs in the binary: (a) the automatic fallback ladder — broker/CF failure retries over SSH instead of blocking callers (patched into the Python client 2026-11-16 after the morning outage; the daemon dying at 07:35 CST blocked every route because the fallback lived client-side); (b) the Cloudflare Access credential, now fetched from fleet secrets (`cloudflare.access-laptop-agent`, migrated 2026-11-16; the loose file tools/laptop-agent-cf-access.json is deleted). Both landed in dezren39/hatch commit 84fbd0475 — that Python behavior is the spec to mirror.

## Build
Implement the `laptop-agent` domain in the fleet binary (exec / run / poll / kill / jobs against the laptop daemon) with:
1. Automatic, non-blocking transport fallback inside the binary: fleet-proxy Cloudflare leg → Tailscale leg → SSH leg, in that order, without callers having to know or retry manually. A dead daemon or a dead leg degrades to the next leg; it never wedges the caller.
2. The Cloudflare Access credential sourced from fleet secrets (`cloudflare.access-laptop-agent`) by the binary — no credential files on disk.
3. Parity proofs before the Python client is retired: round-trip exec on each leg, hash-checked file transfer both ways, a forced-leg-down test showing the fallback carries the call, and trip logging equivalent to the Python client's v2.
4. On parity: re-point ~/tools/laptop-agent.py (and laptop-ssh.sh's delegation) at the binary and retire the Python routing code, per the #5412 stub plan.

## Acceptance
- `fleet laptop-agent exec` works on all three legs with automatic fallback demonstrated under a forced failure.
- No Python socket/routing code remains in the call path; the Python files are thin delegates or gone.
- The CF Access credential is read from fleet secrets by the binary; no on-disk credential file exists for it anywhere.

code.title: laptop keyring stays locked after daemon restart — Secret Service consumers (agy) blocked until manual unlock
code.body:
## Symptom
After the laptop's 2026-11-16 ~05:35–05:39 CT outage and recovery, `gnome-keyring-daemon` restarted (05:38) outside a desktop login session and stayed **locked**. agy's login lives in that keyring (Secret Service, go-keyring scheme), so the Antigravity account switch ordered by Drew was blocked at the delete step — "Cannot delete a locked item" — until Drew physically unlocked the keyring at the laptop screen.

## Why it should not happen
The keyring normally unlocks via PAM at desktop login. A daemon restart during service recovery bypasses that, leaving every keyring consumer (agy today; anything else using Secret Service) silently unauthenticated until a human goes to the screen. Drew's position: "it should unlock itself."

## Scope
- Make keyring unlock survive daemon/service restarts on the laptop: e.g. tie the daemon to the desktop session so a recovery restart re-unlocks the way login does, or an equivalent mechanism that does not store the keyring password in plaintext.
- Verify agy (and other Secret Service consumers) can read their items after a daemon restart with no manual unlock.

## Acceptance check
Restart gnome-keyring-daemon out-of-session (simulating the recovery path), then confirm `agy --print` authenticates with no unlock prompt and no manual step.

## Refs
- Surfaced 2026-11-16 during the agy popesdrew switch (drewrypope account is ToS-disabled, see #9856).

code.title: id(phase-14): Discovery, registry & federation — v2 — design: the public registry endpoint
code.body:
# Discovery, registry & federation — v2 — design: the public registry endpoint

Part of the Phase 14 core topic #6277 (Discovery, registry & federation). Previous steps: v1 design #6287 (record `doc/2026-11-16_design_id6287_discovery_registry_federation_v1.md`, PR #10703) and the v2 outline #6288 (refined outline posted there 2026-11-16).

## Scope (from the #6288 outline)
Design the public registry as a presentation + query layer over the v1 signed-list registry protocol, operated first on the hosted instance's curated registry and hostable by anyone over their own registry list:
- Browsing and search/filters over a registry's own entries (name/description text; tag, occupancy, visibility filters) computed over the local copy of subscribed lists — no central index.
- Freshness/decay derived mechanically from announcement fields (expires_at ≤ 7 days, heartbeat republication at half lifetime, monotone seq): expired = void; any soft demotion before expiry is this step's decision.
- Quality signals restricted to verifiable, non-gameable ones (curator inclusion by named registries, tombstone-history transparency, republication continuity). Popularity metrics are out of scope unless a gaming-resistant design is produced — v1 §12 excluded ranking/recommendation deliberately; this step either reconciles with that exclusion or overturns it with reasons.

## Entry condition
The v1 implementation items this layer stands on have landed: the registry list format + reference publisher with mirror tooling, and the client registry-subscription setting (items 3 and 5 of the v1 record §11 breakdown, filed from #6287).

## Deliverable
A v2 design record (doc/ PR, the #6287 pattern): the query-layer design, the freshness/decay functions, the signal set with its gaming analysis, multi-registry disagreement semantics (union/intersection for search across subscribed registries), and the listing display rules that keep names-as-claims honest (key provenance surfaced). Open questions answered or explicitly deferred, and the implementation breakdown filed from the record.

Drew's Phase 14 principles (#1240) govern: local-first always; hostable by anyone at any scale; p2p behavior identical to hosted behavior; our hosted instance is the public backstop, never a requirement.

code.title: id(phase-14): hosted worlds v1 P6 — hosted/local parity conformance suite
code.body:
Implementation packet P6 from the hosted worlds v1 design for #6283: doc/2026-11-16_design_id6283_hosted_worlds_v1.md (§7, §9), merged in PR #10692. Phase 14 core topic #6276; principles from #1240 govern.

## Scope
The hosted/local parity checklist as an automated conformance suite. Identical journal in → identical results out, on a local host and on the hosted node: journal replay result, program ceilings, membership/authority evaluation (including lifecycle transitions), name resolution outcomes, and content addressing (`modules/<blake3>.wasm`). Backend-only differences (quotas/storage tiers per #1067, abuse controls, public-endpoint rate limits, jurisdiction partitioning, encryption-at-rest choices) are asserted to be invisible as world-behavior differences. The suite also measures full-resync bytes per wake on the hosted node, recording the baseline that open #805 (F12.11 delta/binary frames, resume tokens) will improve — #805 is not assumed or required.

## Acceptance criteria
- The conformance suite runs the same journal fixtures through a local host and a hosted node and diffs replay results, ceiling enforcement, authority outcomes, name resolution, and content addresses — zero unexplained diffs (oracle: byte-identical replayed state and identical authority verdicts per fixture).
- A deliberately introduced backend-only difference (e.g. a storage-tier setting) produces no world-visible behavior diff in the suite.
- Wake full-resync byte counts are measured and recorded on #6283, naming them as the pre-#805 baseline.

## Dependencies
Builds on packet P1 (issue #10693); lifecycle verdicts need packet P2. Does not depend on open #805 (F12.11); it measures the gap #805 closes.

code.title: id(phase-14): hosted worlds v1 P5 — basement-cluster deployment pack
code.body:
Implementation packet P5 from the hosted worlds v1 design for #6283: doc/2026-11-16_design_id6283_hosted_worlds_v1.md (§3, §9), merged in PR #10692. Phase 14 core topic #6276; principles from #1240 govern.

## Scope
Basement-cluster deployment pack for the single-node host: a service definition (systemd/NixOS) running the one `id` host process, the data-root layout, and Drew's topology split from #6276 — one public main endpoint reachable by clients, with deeper backend pieces as separate iroh/id servers behind private tunnels with limited trusted access. Includes the operator runbook: start/stop/inspect, host restart after power events (recovery per design §5), adding a world by copying its directory in while asleep, and reading the per-state census for capacity. Power/thermal is the cluster's real ceiling: asleep worlds cost no CPU, and power events are ordinary host restarts — no new machinery.

## Acceptance criteria
- A fresh basement-cluster node deploys from the pack alone: service up, host mode running over an empty data root, operator CLI answering.
- The public/private split is enforced by the deployment: backend pieces are reachable only through their private tunnels, verified by a connection attempt from outside the tunnel failing.
- A world directory copied in while asleep appears in `host list`, starts, serves, and stops using only the runbook's steps.
- A simulated power cut (host killed uncleanly) recovers per design §5 with the runbook's verification steps confirming the recovered state.

## Dependencies
Builds on packets P1 (issue #10693) and P4 (operator CLI). Does not depend on open #805 (F12.11). Public-server operation for others is v4 (#6286), not this packet.

code.title: id(phase-14): hosted worlds v1 P4 — operator CLI (list/start/stop/inspect)
code.body:
Implementation packet P4 from the hosted worlds v1 design for #6283: doc/2026-11-16_design_id6283_hosted_worlds_v1.md (§6), merged in PR #10692. Phase 14 core topic #6276; principles from #1240 govern.

## Scope
Operator basics as `id-cli` subcommands against the host's local control socket (no network listener; the socket is filesystem-permissioned to the operator): `host list`, `host start <world>`, `host stop <world>`, `host archive <world>`, `host restore <world>`, `host inspect <world>`. All output is derived from the host file + journal headers — facts, never guesses. `inspect` reports state and transition history, journal version + head entry, module count, data-root path, quota posture per #1067, always-live pin / wake-on-connect mode, and the last recovery result; it never opens the world for serving. `start` on an archived world refuses and names the restore step.

## Acceptance criteria
- Each subcommand performs exactly the §6 semantics against a running host, verified end-to-end against a two-world fixture (one live, one asleep, one archived across the test run).
- `host list` output is the per-state census (live/asleep/archived counts + bytes) the design's capacity accounting reads.
- The control socket has no network listener and is not accessible to non-operator filesystem users.
- Inspect output for a world recovered after a crash names the recovery result (entries replayed, torn tail discarded if any).

## Dependencies
Builds on packet P1 (issue #10693) and the transitions of packet P2. Does not depend on open #805 (F12.11).

code.title: id(phase-14): hosted worlds v1 P3 — restart/recovery hardening + snapshot/export
code.body:
Implementation packet P3 from the hosted worlds v1 design for #6283: doc/2026-11-16_design_id6283_hosted_worlds_v1.md (§5), merged in PR #10692. Phase 14 core topic #6276; principles from #1240 govern.

## Scope
Restart/recovery hardening for hosted worlds, plus the v1 snapshot/export shape. Recovery is `id-worlds`' existing journal replay operated as a discipline: host restart replays only worlds recorded live; a single world's restart replays only its directory. The journal's per-append fsync bounds loss to the single in-flight append; a torn final line is discarded, never partially applied. Snapshot/export = a signed, self-describing journal segment set building on F12.13 journal replication (#806, CLOSED — completed 2026-11-14; its signed stream is the landed input). Encryption at rest stays a deployment property, never a journal-format change. A documented manual restore procedure is delivered; scheduled snapshots and restore drills are v2 (#6284) scope, not this packet.

## Acceptance criteria
- Crash-case test matrix passes: host process killed mid-append, world process killed, and simulated power loss during append — each recovers to the last fsynced entry with no partial application, pinned by automated tests (oracle: replayed world state equals the state produced by exactly the fsynced prefix of the journal).
- A host refuses to open a world whose journal version it cannot replay, names the version, and never rewrites a journal it cannot read (per #227's compatibility discipline).
- Snapshot/export produces a signed, self-describing segment set; the documented manual restore procedure, followed literally, restores a working world from it into a scratch directory.

## Dependencies
Builds on packet P1 (issue #10693); may proceed in parallel with P2/P4 once P1's host file format is fixed. Builds on #806 (closed); does not depend on open #805.

code.title: id(phase-14): hosted worlds v1 P2 — lifecycle transitions as authority-frame actions
code.body:
Implementation packet P2 from the hosted worlds v1 design for #6283: doc/2026-11-16_design_id6283_hosted_worlds_v1.md (§4, §10), merged in PR #10692. Phase 14 core topic #6276; principles from #1240 govern.

## Scope
World lifecycle transitions — wake, pause (live → asleep), archive, restore (archived → asleep) — implemented as authority-frame actions under the Phase 10 roles / F12.3 authority model, evaluated exactly as a local host evaluates them. Wake-on-connect: a member's connect to an asleep world is a wake request; the supervisor starts the world and membership/authority is enforced by the world before it serves — wake is never an authorization bypass. Idle-window sleep: when a live world's last client disconnects, it pauses to asleep after the operator-configured idle window (default 15 minutes, never 0); an operator may pin a world always-live. Zero connected clients never archives or deletes. Per-world operator-start-only mode (wake-on-connect off) is supported and recorded in the host file.

## Acceptance criteria
- Owner/operator can wake, pause, archive, and restore; a role without the authority is refused, and the refusal is the same frame outcome a local host produces.
- A non-member connecting to an asleep world cannot use the world after wake; membership is checked before serving in all cases.
- Idle-window sleep fires after the configured window and not before; an always-live pin prevents it and shows in inspect output (packet P4).
- Every transition is recorded in the host file with time, actor (operator identity or wake-on-connect), and prior state.

## Dependencies
Builds on packet P1 (issue #10693). Does not depend on open #805 (F12.11); does not assume its outcome.

code.title: id(phase-14): hosted worlds v1 P1 — host mode in the id binary (supervisor + data root)
code.body:
Implementation packet P1 from the hosted worlds v1 design for #6283: doc/2026-11-16_design_id6283_hosted_worlds_v1.md (§3, §4, §5), merged in PR #10692. Phase 14 core topic #6276; principles from #1240 govern.

## Scope
Host mode in the existing `id` binary (`pkgs/id`): a supervisor over one data root of world directories (same local layout — `journal.jsonl` + `modules/<blake3>.wasm` per world). The supervisor keeps a small host file beside the data root recording each world's lifecycle state (live / asleep / archived), data-root path, and state-change history (time, actor, prior state); the host file is rebuildable from the directories it describes — journals remain the only authority on world contents. Start = journal replay then serve; stop = drain, final fsync, record transition. Quota accounting hooks per the #1067 design (storage tier + per-state byte counts) — hooks only, no new quota system.

## Acceptance criteria
- One `id` binary runs in host mode over a data root with at least two worlds in different lifecycle states simultaneously.
- Host restart returns live worlds to live (by replay), asleep to asleep, archived to archived, driven by the host file; deleting the host file and rebuilding it from the directories loses no world and no journal data.
- No new binary, database, scheduler, or queue is introduced; world internals (`id-worlds` FileJournal, replay, ceilings) are unchanged.
- Per-state census data (counts + bytes for live/asleep/archived) is produced for the operator surface (packet P4) and follows #1067's accounting shape.

## Dependencies
First packet of the #6283 breakdown — P2, P3, P4 build on it. Does not depend on open #805 (F12.11); does not assume its outcome.

code.title: [projector] transferred issues: delete the source-repo row (Phase 4 disposition D-1, #4303)
code.body:
## What

Implement audit disposition D-1 from #4303 (Phase 4 of #4302): when an `issues` webhook arrives with action `transferred` naming this repo as the source, delete the source-repo row via `store.deleteItem` instead of upserting it as a live item.

## Why

The Phase 4 audit (#4303) decided: **delete the source-repo row.** A `transferred` event proves the issue left the source repo; the projection contract ("a projection writes only what the event proves", #4302) means a live source-repo row renders an issue that no longer exists there. Today `applyEvent`'s issues branch falls through to `applyIssue` for `transferred`, upserting the row under the source repo.

## Blocker / first step

There is **no captured `transferred` payload anywhere in this repo**, and the payload's number semantics are unverified: whether `payload.issue.number` in the source repo's delivery is the source number or the new number decides which row key the delete targets. Deleting on an unverified key risks removing the wrong row.

The repository's GitHub App integration can list webhook delivery history but cannot read delivery payloads (`GET .../deliveries/{delivery_id}` returns 403, `Resource not accessible by integration`). Capture is therefore a hands step:

<!-- hands:v1 kind=interactive-login action="Create and transfer one throwaway issue from developing-today/code to developing-today-forks/openchamber in GitHub, then attach the raw issues/transferred delivery JSON to this issue." -->

After the payload is attached, pin whether `payload.issue.number` is the source or destination number, save it as a test fixture, and then wire the branch:

- in `applyEvent`'s `issues` case, route `payload.action === "transferred"` to `store.deleteItem(ref, iso(issue.updated_at) ?? iso(issue.created_at))` with the fixture-verified ref;
- the target repo's own events create the row under its new ref — no re-keying needed;
- test: the fixture event removes the source row, its links, and its live comments, and plants the absorbing deletion marker (decision 6 semantics).

## Pointers

- Contract + full writer inventory: `pm-stack/projector/README.md`, "Projection contract (#4302, audited in #4303)".
- Dispositions recorded on #4302 by the #4303 audit.

code.title: fleet(queue): preserve independent holds and lease identity during automated quarantine rechecks
code.body:
Follow-up to #10648 / #10652, not a rollback of authoritative row `max_attempts`. The [deploy receipt](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/10648#issuecomment-6912343034) records 15 automated releases; eight also had independent lane blockers. All eight were reclaimed per that receipt, but it provides an individual reblock receipt only for 2504. Do not infer the other seven blockers cleared or take a competing claim.

I checked the released implementation at the merge, the deployed source revision, and current main: the quarantine predicate still relies on historical `last_error` and the dependency snapshot, refresh/release still match only ID and blocked status, lease deletion is separate from release and unscoped to a prior lease, and sweep selection can repeatedly revisit the same oldest rows without progress. See [original review](https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/10652#issuecomment-6912140097).

Acceptance:
- Only release a row when the current block is positively known to come from quarantine and no independent hold remains; unknown or conflicting provenance stays blocked. Cover historical quarantine followed by a manual release and an unrelated new block.
- Revalidate the current block identity and dependency state as part of the transition; neither a recheck release nor a reason refresh may overwrite a replacement block. Ensure lease cleanup cannot affect a new owner, and emit audit events only for transitions that committed.
- Give later eligible rows a turn when a full batch stays invalid, including across repeated sweeps. Exercise both the manual recheck and automated path in isolated tests; no test against the live queue.
- Existing broker owner: reconcile the eight task IDs in the linked receipt against live state, latest blocker, binding and active-session/lease evidence before further release; record per-row verified outcomes or explicit unknowns. Do not force-release a task, relaunch a session, change live settings or deploy as part of read-only reconciliation.

code.title: opencode handover not in effect: socket unit disabled, same-build switch darkened port ~16s and cut drain at 40ms (2026-11-16)
code.body:
## Defect: OpenCode server handover is not in effect on the laptop — socket unit disabled, same-build switch darkened the port ~16s and cut the drain at 40ms

Drew's standing design: a server switch/restart passes the port and sessions over without dropping anything; a same-code switch needs no restart at all. Measured live during the 2026-11-16 agy 1.5.9 system switch (`nixos-rebuild switch`, SWITCH_EXIT=0, system generation 558 → 559):

### Evidence (all 2026-11-16, UTC)

- The opencode build did **not** change in this switch: `2.0.30+5b65c2a`, store path `bdkm7bd1gbx4i0cmk92zrzwc5x16ms00-opencode-2.0.30+5b65c2a` before and after. The service restarted anyway: pid 967757 → 3365330, new instance start 08:24:14Z.
- A 2-second-interval probe of `http://127.0.0.1:13420/api/config` across the switch recorded the port refused from **08:23:58Z through 08:24:12Z**, answering again at 08:24:14Z — ~16 seconds dark (479 healthy samples vs 8 refused in the run).
- Server log, old instance: `08:23:57.964Z draining running sessions and requests sessions=["ses_e5e1c9ad3c3ffeWx7ITHH5v49w","ses_e5e1c8eefd0ffehalIMX1R225d"] requests=0 grace=30000` — then 40ms later, `08:23:58.004Z shutdown ended with sessions or requests still running; interrupting them`. The announced 30s drain grace was not honored; something ended the drain almost immediately (the fork's drain ends early on a second termination signal — source of the second signal not yet identified).
- `opencode.socket`: `ActiveState=inactive`, `UnitFileState=disabled`; the 13420 listener is owned by the server process itself (`ss`: pid 3365330, fd 8). Socket activation is **not** in effect, which contradicts the 2026-11-11 follow-up on #8261 recording socket activation as adopted after the 2026-11-10 cascade. Either the adoption regressed or it never landed in the deployed unit set.

### Impact today: interruption, not loss

- Session store intact: `session_v2` held 22,937 ids before the switch; after: **0 lost**, 26 gained.
- Both interrupted sessions were re-warmed by the new instance (`scheduled session warming` 08:24:19Z) and produced successful route attempts from 08:24:20Z; the conductor's 08:25Z sweep lists both as progressing with 0 errors. No job permanently failed.
- But the guarantee Drew specified does not hold: the port went dark and in-flight turns were interrupted on a switch that changed nothing about the server.

### Fix asks

1. Enable `opencode.socket` so the port survives process swaps (or establish why the Nov 11 adoption did not stick and close that gap).
2. Find and remove the second-signal source that cuts the drain; the 30s grace must be honored.
3. Skip restarting the opencode service when the build/store path is unchanged across a switch.

Refs: #8261 (2026-11-10 cascade; adoption claim), #1822 (socket activation audit), #8255 (incumbent-defer cutover).

code.title: quota scrape resilience: stale-read detection, failure classification, and CDP wedge probe for console-scraped pools (Mistral first)
code.body:
## The gap

The 2026-11-13→16 Mistral outage (57h dark) had two halves. The first half is now closed: the CDP Helium browser carrying the Mistral console session died at a laptop reboot and nothing owned it. As of 2026-11-16 it runs under a supervised systemd user unit (`helium-cdp.service`, restart-on-failure, correct profile, kill/restart recovery proven live — see #6032 comment 6910076337).

The second half is still unbuilt, and it is the half that made the outage silent for 57 hours:

1. **No stale-read detection that leads anywhere.** When a console-scraped pool's read goes stale, the quota-check stale-source escalation exists on paper (it fired once, 2026-11-14, quota-check v71) but dedupe held it forever and no repair was ever dispatched. Detection must end in a repair action, not a note.
2. **No failure classification.** On 2026-11-15 a replacement browser with the wrong profile (no Mistral session) bounced admin.mistral.ai to a login page and the gatherer reported it as `cdp-unavailable`. The design's `session-expired` class exists; the gatherer must distinguish at minimum: CDP endpoint down, browser wedged, session expired / login page, page reachable but data fetch failing.
3. **No CDP-level liveness probe.** Process supervision (`Restart=always`) catches a dead browser. A browser that is alive and still listening on :19222 but wedged (renderer hung, page unresponsive) passes supervision and fails every tick silently.

## Scope

For console-scraped quota sources (Mistral first; the pattern should generalize to any CDP-scraped pool):

- **Wedge probe:** periodic CDP-level check (endpoint answers + target page responsive, not just port listening). On wedge: restart the browser unit and verify a fresh read lands; escalate if it does not.
- **Staleness detector with teeth:** when a scraped pool's last good read crosses the stale threshold, (a) record the failure with its correct class, (b) create exactly one fleet-queue repair task (dedupe by pool + failure class), (c) re-escalate if the read is still stale at the next threshold instead of deduping into silence, (d) auto-close the escalation when a fresh read lands.
- **Session-expiry path:** a `session-expired` classification surfaces as a named attention state (sign-in needed) immediately — it is a human/agent action, not a retry loop. Never script token exchange or credential handling as part of recovery.

## Acceptance

- Simulated wrong-profile / logged-out session: gatherer reports the `session-expired` class (not `cdp-unavailable`) and the attention state names the needed sign-in within one tick cycle.
- Simulated wedged browser (process alive, CDP unresponsive): probe catches it, unit restarts, fresh Mistral read lands, no human touch.
- Simulated dead scrape with repair task ignored: escalation re-fires at the second threshold — silence past the threshold is impossible without an open, visible escalation.
- Fresh read after any automated recovery is verified from `quota-current.json` (new `measuredAt`, no `retainedFromFailedTick`), not from process state alone.

## Record

- Design lineage: #6031 (design), #6032 (watchdog core — supervision slice landed 2026-11-16, this issue is its remaining scope), #6033 (escalation design).
- Incident record: #6033 comment 6909868442; watchdog verdict: #6032 comment 6909869155; supervision landing: #6032 comment 6910076337.
- Drew's standing rule from the Nov 4 design: the watchdog must self-repair, else trigger a task for a browser-enabled agent. This issue is that rule, finished.

code.title: Scheduled Bolt — developing-today/code
code.body:
You are "Bolt" ⚡ - a performance-obsessed agent who makes the codebase faster, one optimization at a time.

Your mission is to identify and implement ONE small performance improvement that makes the application measurably faster or more efficient.


## Boundaries

✅ **Always do:**
- Run commands like `pnpm lint` and `pnpm test` (or associated equivalents) before creating PR
- Add comments explaining the optimization
- Measure and document expected performance impact

⚠️ **Ask first:**
- Adding any new dependencies
- Making architectural changes

🚫 **Never do:**
- Modify package.json or tsconfig.json without instruction
- Make breaking changes
- Optimize prematurely without actual bottleneck
- Sacrifice code readability for micro-optimizations

BOLT'S PHILOSOPHY:
- Speed is a feature
- Every millisecond counts
- Measure first, optimize second
- Don't sacrifice readability for micro-optimizations

BOLT'S JOURNAL - CRITICAL LEARNINGS ONLY:
Before starting, read .jules/bolt.md (create if missing).

Your journal is NOT a log - only add entries for CRITICAL learnings that will help you avoid mistakes or make better decisions.

⚠️ ONLY add journal entries when you discover:
- A performance bottleneck specific to this codebase's architecture
- An optimization that surprisingly DIDN'T work (and why)
- A rejected change with a valuable lesson
- A codebase-specific performance pattern or anti-pattern
- A surprising edge case in how this app handles performance

❌ DO NOT journal routine work like:
- "Optimized component X today" (unless there's a learning)
- Generic React performance tips
- Successful optimizations without surprises

Format: `## YYYY-MM-DD - [Title]
**Learning:** [Insight]
**Action:** [How to apply next time]`

BOLT'S DAILY PROCESS:

1. 🔍 PROFILE - Hunt for performance opportunities:

  FRONTEND PERFORMANCE:
  - Unnecessary re-renders in React/Vue/Angular components
  - Missing memoization for expensive computations
  - Large bundle sizes (opportunities for code splitting)
  - Unoptimized images (missing lazy loading, wrong formats)
  - Missing virtualization for long lists
  - Synchronous operations blocking the main thread
  - Missing debouncing/throttling on frequent events
  - Unused CSS or JavaScript being loaded
  - Missing resource preloading for critical assets
  - Inefficient DOM manipulations

  BACKEND PERFORMANCE:
  - N+1 query problems in database calls
  - Missing database indexes on frequently queried fields
  - Expensive operations without caching
  - Synchronous operations that could be async
  - Missing pagination on large data sets
  - Inefficient algorithms (O(n²) that could be O(n))
  - Missing connection pooling
  - Repeated API calls that could be batched
  - Large payloads that could be compressed

  GENERAL OPTIMIZATIONS:
  - Missing caching for expensive operations
  - Redundant calculations in loops
  - Inefficient data structures for the use case
  - Missing early returns in conditional logic
  - Unnecessary deep cloning or copying
  - Missing lazy initialization
  - Inefficient string concatenation in loops
  - Missing request/response compression

2. ⚡ SELECT - Choose your daily boost:
  Pick the BEST opportunity that:
  - Has measurable performance impact (faster load, less memory, fewer requests)
  - Can be implemented cleanly in < 50 lines
  - Doesn't sacrifice code readability significantly
  - Has low risk of introducing bugs
  - Follows existing patterns

3. 🔧 OPTIMIZE - Implement with precision:
  - Write clean, understandable optimized code
  - Add comments explaining the optimization
  - Preserve existing functionality exactly
  - Consider edge cases
  - Ensure the optimization is safe
  - Add performance metrics in comments if possible

4. ✅ VERIFY - Measure the impact:
  - Run format and lint checks
  - Run the full test suite
  - Verify the optimization works as expected
  - Add benchmark comments if possible
  - Ensure no functionality is broken

5. 🎁 PRESENT - Share your speed boost:
  Create a PR with:
  - Title: "⚡ Bolt: [performance improvement]"
  - Description with:
    * 💡 What: The optimization implemented
    * 🎯 Why: The performance problem it solves
    * 📊 Impact: Expected performance improvement (e.g., "Reduces re-renders by ~50%")
    * 🔬 Measurement: How to verify the improvement
  - Reference any related performance issues

BOLT'S FAVORITE OPTIMIZATIONS:
⚡ Add React.memo() to prevent unnecessary re-renders
⚡ Add database index on frequently queried field
⚡ Cache expensive API call results
⚡ Add lazy loading to images below the fold
⚡ Debounce search input to reduce API calls
⚡ Replace O(n²) nested loop with O(n) hash map lookup
⚡ Add pagination to large data fetch
⚡ Memoize expensive calculation with useMemo/computed
⚡ Add early return to skip unnecessary processing
⚡ Batch multiple API calls into single request
⚡ Add virtualization to long list rendering
⚡ Move expensive operation outside of render loop
⚡ Add code splitting for large route components
⚡ Replace large library with smaller alternative

BOLT AVOIDS (not worth the complexity):
❌ Micro-optimizations with no measurable impact
❌ Premature optimization of cold paths
❌ Optimizations that make code unreadable
❌ Large architectural changes
❌ Optimizations that require extensive testing
❌ Changes to critical algorithms without thorough testing

Remember: You're Bolt, making things lightning fast. But speed without correctness is useless. Measure, optimize, verify. If you can't find a clear performance win today, wait for tomorrow's opportunity.

If no suitable performance optimization can be identified, stop and do not create a PR.---

code.title: fleet queue: duplicate-task suppression at filing time on the (repo, issue, kind) work identity
code.body:
## Measured waste this attacks

From the outcome-taxonomy measurement (2026-11-16,
`outcome-taxonomy-2026-11-16.md`; fleet-queue Turso, all-time
unless noted):

- **630 issues carry ≥2 non-triage tasks** — 1,810 tasks sit on
  multi-task issues (485 issues have exactly 2 tasks, 108 have 3,
  26 have 4, 5 have 5). One structural outlier, code#7297 (the
  batch-disposition shepherd hub, 355 tasks), is excluded from the
  pair statistics below.
- **282 of 1,172 already-family tasks (24.1%) share their issue
  with another non-triage task** — a quarter of the fleet's
  already-done dispositions had a sibling task on the same work.
- **155 completions in the trailing 7d (6.6% of non-triage
  completions) were sibling_done**: the work landed under another
  task while this one was running — duplicated effort that
  completed anyway.
- Among issues with 2–5 tasks there are 1,015 same-issue task
  pairs, **86 with overlapping claim windows** — simultaneous
  duplication, the hardest slice.
- The identity material already exists and is unused as a
  constraint: `tasks.dedupe_key` is populated on 100% of tasks,
  and sampled packets state the identity in `payload.dedupe.basis`
  ("Closed issue number is the work identity"). Nothing checks it
  at enqueue.

**Honest limit:** most multi-task issues are legitimate sequences
— re-queue after a terminal failure, a shepherd task after a fix
task, recurring CI investigations. The data separates as *clearly
duplicative* only the sibling_done completions (155/7d), the 86
overlapping-window pairs, and the already-family sibling share.
This proposal therefore targets **open-task collisions**, not
task counts: a second task for work that already has a live task
or a fresh terminal verdict.

## Proposed mechanism

At **enqueue** (the single filing path all packet generators and
manual filings pass through):

1. Compute the work identity: `(payload.repo, payload.issue.number,
   kind-family)` — kind-family groups kinds that work the same
   issue the same way (e.g. small_fix; triage is its own family;
   pr_shepherd its own).
2. **Open-collision rule**: if a task with the same identity
   exists in a non-terminal state (queued, claimed, parked,
   blocked), the enqueue returns that task's id and creates **no
   new row**. The filer gets a machine-readable refusal naming the
   existing task, so generators can route their follow-up onto it.
3. **Fresh-verdict rule**: if a task with the same identity
   completed within the last 24h with outcome landed or
   already_done, the enqueue is held for the pre-claim staleness
   check (see the companion draft) rather than queued blind.
4. **Override**: an explicit payload flag (e.g.
   `dedupe_override: "<reason>"`) files anyway and is written to
   the task's events, so deliberate parallels are possible and
   auditable.
5. **Exemptions**: kinds whose identity is recurring by design
   (batch-disposition / shepherd hubs such as code#7297's,
   recurring CI investigations) declare an exemption in the packet
   (`dedupe_exempt: true` with the design ref) instead of relying
   on the override per filing.

Out of scope: merging or rewriting existing queued duplicates
(one-time cleanup is a separate sweep), and any change to claim
semantics (code#9178) beyond consuming its identity definitions.

## Relation to existing issues

- **code#9178** (fleet queue: resume-by-session, claim-any-task,
  and manual-only items) — the work identity defined here should
  be the same identity #9178's claim-any-task and dedupe
  discussions use; file this as a sibling under the same queue
  epic so the identity is designed once.
- **code#5444** (packet-validation quarantine) — a hypothesis to
  check during implementation, *not* a measured fact: the
  quarantine repair flows (`cleanup_repacket`, 223 events) re-emit
  packets, and may be one source of duplicate filings. The fix
  here makes any such re-emission safe by construction, whichever
  generator produced it.

## Acceptance criteria

1. Filing a second task with the same (repo, issue, kind-family)
   while the first is open returns the existing task id and
   creates no row (queue test).
2. Filing after the first task reached a terminal state files
   normally (sequential re-queue after failure is unaffected).
3. The override flag files a parallel task and leaves an audit
   event carrying the stated reason; the exemption flag is honored
   for declared recurring kinds.
4. The refusal is machine-readable (existing task id + state), so
   packet generators can attach follow-ups to the surviving task
   instead of erroring or silently dropping work — misplaced work
   is relocated, never dropped.
5. Measured effect: over the 7 days after deployment, the daily
   work-failures recompute shows sibling_done completions and the
   count of issues with ≥2 simultaneously-open non-triage tasks
   trending down vs the 2026-11-16 baseline (155 sibling_done / 7d;
   86 overlapping pairs all-time among 2–5-task issues).

code.title: fleet queue: pre-claim staleness check — auto-complete tasks whose linked issue is already closed / PR already merged, without burning a session
code.body:
## Measured waste this attacks

From the outcome-taxonomy measurement (2026-11-16,
`outcome-taxonomy-2026-11-16.md`; trailing 7d, fleet-queue Turso +
GitHub closedAt/mergedAt vs first-claim times):

- **652 of 2,344 non-triage completions (27.8%) were pre-done**: the
  linked issue was already closed / the linked PR already merged
  *before the task was claimed*. No work remained when a lane picked
  the task up.
- **625 of the 652 were already done before the task was created.**
  Sampled packets carry `payload.issue.state_checked_at` of
  2026-10-25 — the filing pipeline emitted tasks from a ~3-week-old
  state snapshot and nothing re-checked issue state at enqueue or
  at claim. Median creation→claim wait is ~0h, so a claim-time
  check catches essentially the whole class regardless of which
  side (filing or queueing) introduced the staleness.
- Cost shape: median disposition is ~1 minute (a session still
  spawns, verifies, and closes the task), 85.9% close <5 min after
  claim — and **72 tasks burned ≥30 minutes** (max ~78h across park
  cycles) on work that no longer existed.
- A further 155 completions (6.6%) were sibling_done — the work
  landed while the task ran. A claim-time check cannot catch
  in-flight races, but re-checking at claim (not at filing) shrinks
  the exposure window to the run itself.

## Proposed mechanism

In the queue **claim path** (broker claim verb, before a task is
handed to a lane):

1. Resolve the task's linked work from its packet:
   `payload.issue` (repo + number) and `payload.prs[]` /
   `result.pr` where present.
2. One GitHub read for state: issue `state`/`closedAt`, PR
   `state`/`mergedAt`. (The work-failures recompute already
   maintains exactly this data in a landing-times cache —
   `landing-times-cache.json`, GraphQL batches of 50, terminal
   facts cached permanently, open items refreshed at 24h. Reuse
   the pattern; do not build a second fetcher.)
3. If the issue is closed or a linked PR is merged with a
   timestamp **at or before the task's creation time** (strongest
   signal) — and in a second, separately-flagged tier, at or
   before claim time — complete the task immediately:
   - outcome `already_done`, with evidence recorded on the result
     (closed_at / merged_at, source ref, checked_at);
   - a dedicated event (e.g. `staleness_autocomplete`) so the
     daily measurement can count interceptions;
   - **no session is bound, no lane slot is consumed.**
4. **Fail open, always**: any lookup error, timeout, rate limit, or
   missing linkage → the claim proceeds exactly as today. A failed
   or stale read never blocks or idles work (standing rule,
   2026-10-30). Bound the check with a short timeout and the cache
   so claim latency is unaffected in the common case.
5. Apply the same state re-check at **filing time** for packet
   generators: a packet whose `state_checked_at` is older than a
   small bound (proposal: 1h) must re-verify issue state at enqueue
   or be stamped so the claim path checks it first. (The claim-path
   check in step 3 is the safety net and ships first; this step
   stops the stale-snapshot class at its source.)

Out of scope: tasks with no linked issue/PR (nothing to check —
they claim as today), and any change to what counts as a valid
packet (that is #5444's territory; this check runs on packets that
already pass validation).

## Relation to existing issues

- **code#9178** (fleet queue: resume-by-session, claim-any-task,
  and manual-only items) — this is a claim-path behavior and
  belongs with its claim-semantics work: the staleness check is a
  pre-dispatch gate inside the same verb family, and its
  auto-complete outcome must compose with #9178's claim/override
  semantics (an owner override must be able to force-claim a
  staleness-completed task's successor deliberately).
- **code#5444** (packet-validation quarantine) — related only as
  the other large source of wasted claims (447 tasks currently
  frozen; 322 completions in 7d passed through a freeze). The two
  fixes are independent: #5444 rejects malformed packets, this
  check retires well-formed packets whose work is gone. Neither
  should be gated on the other.

## Acceptance criteria

1. A task filed for an issue that is already closed (or whose
   linked PR is already merged) completes via the staleness path:
   status done, outcome `already_done` with evidence fields, a
   `staleness_autocomplete` event, and **no `lane_session_bound`
   event and no session** attached to the task.
2. A task whose issue closes between filing and claim is caught at
   claim (tier-2), with the same evidence trail.
3. With GitHub unreachable or the lookup erroring, the same tasks
   claim and run normally (fail-open test).
4. A task on a live, open issue claims byte-for-byte as today.
5. Claim latency: p95 added latency < 2s with a warm cache; the
   check times out open rather than queueing behind GitHub.
6. Measured effect: within 7 days of deployment, the daily
   work-failures recompute shows pre_done completions for tasks
   *created after* the fix trending to ~0, replaced by
   `staleness_autocomplete` events that consumed no session.

code.title: Close authority: require a verified disposition when a linked draft still carries unfinished work
code.body:
Refs #10136 and #10105. This is the open-draft / queue disposition case, not a re-filing of the fixed Refs-only merge behavior in #7610.

**Observed:** #9155’s issue timeline records a bot close at 2026-11-13 01:45:20 UTC and a maintainer reopen at 02:02:34 UTC. It is currently open. A later lane used stale closure information and marked task 15345 done/triaged while draft #9245 was still open and unmerged. Readback found unfinished traceability and manifest work and no granular publication receipts; see [reconciliation](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/9155#issuecomment-6904439768). No evidence that the draft itself caused the historical close; trace the event source separately.

**Acceptance**
- At a terminal decision, re-read current issue state, PR state, and the task’s own delivery criteria. An open/draft PR, historical closed event, green check, or queue disposition alone is not proof of completed work. A later reopen supersedes a prior close event.
- Preserve the existing close-authority and epic guards. When an authorized, intentional disposition can close this issue while related work is still open, record why and link an existing or new follow-up that owns the remaining requirement or the reason the draft cannot merge. Keep child gates and precise receipts. If ownership or acceptance is ambiguous, keep the item actionable and report rather than close or mark it done.
- Cover the #9155 replay, unrelated or superseded draft with verified successor, partial delivery with a recorded linked follow-up, failed/missing readback, and explicit legitimate closure. Verify GitHub and queue terminal decisions independently; never launch, reopen, or auto-merge solely from this detector.

code.title: Scheduled Suggestions — developing-today/code
code.body:
You are a code-review agent running as a dispatched session in this
repository. Your job is a suggestions pass: survey the codebase for real,
actionable improvements and turn the verified ones into GitHub issues.

## Dispatch context — read this first

- You are running in this repository's LAPTOP CHECKOUT (the repo's primary
  checkout on the owner's laptop). Work there; do not clone the repo
  elsewhere.
- A tracking issue and a queue task were ALREADY created for this run by
