code.title: PM aggregator /program still stalls on a cold first request
code.body:
## Problem

The PM aggregator's `/program` surface still stalls on a cold first request — the residual boot-window shape left over after #9594 was fixed. Two recurrences since lane 3c closed (PR #9861):

- **Steward run 387 — 2026-11-14 ~09:17 CST:** `/program` returned 503 on pass 1 at 14.88s, then recovered 200 in 0.10s on pass 2. (Noted on #5082: https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5082#issuecomment-6879667486)
- **Steward run 393 — 2026-11-14 ~15:17 CST:** `/program` timed out on pass 1 (curl 000 at 25.001s, 0 bytes), then recovered on pass 2 with 200 but slow at 8.43s. (Noted on #5082: https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5082#issuecomment-6884406610)

## Background

Lane 3c (PR #9861, merged 2026-11-14 ~04:16 CST) documented the residual when it closed: in the first ~30–45s after a restart, a cold request can still 503 on empty last-good (the #9594 boot-window shape). Related closed work: #9594 (program cold start boot stall), #9781 (uncached brief comments fan out), PRs #9596 and #9835.

Tracking issue #5082 stays closed — this issue is the dedicated lane for the residual.

## Ask

Root-cause the remaining cold-path stall — the empty last-good window and/or the slow first build — so a cold `/program` request never 503s or times out: the first request after a restart should serve last-good or a fast build, not fail.

code.title: Design: fleet secrets scoping — prefix / vault / store selection, per-device profiles
code.body:
## Design: `fleet secrets` scoping — prefix / vault / store selection, per-device profiles

Origin: Drew, 2026-11-14. Companion to the secrets verb as shipped
(#5554, closed: broker-first via the laptop secrets-broker, Bitwarden
fallback inside the verb; `list` shows broker names only).

### Verified current state (2026-11-14)

- `fleet secrets get <name>` / `fleet secrets list` are the whole
  surface. No `--prefix`, `--vault`, `--store`, or profile selection
  exists.
- The broker caches the whole Bitwarden set (one store, one view:
  list = every name). 1Password is reached separately
  (`op` with its own env setup) and is not behind the verb at all —
  "we have multiple secret stores and we haven't implemented our
  proxy over all of them" (Drew).
- The `fleet-connect` build stubs the secrets capability entirely
  (exit 69); widening it was recorded as Drew's call (#5554), still
  open.

### Drew's prefix semantics (requirements, stated 2026-11-14)

A prefix is a **namespace view, not a security layer** — its purpose
is preventing accidents and keeping an agent's visible context clean:

1. **Unconfigured = today's behaviour, exactly.** No prefix set → list
   shows everything, get takes names as-is. Zero change for any
   existing user or script.
2. **Configured prefix filters and rewrites.** An agent configured
   with (say) store = sandbox vault, prefix = `42` sees, on `list`,
   only the secrets named `42.<...>` — displayed with the prefix
   applied transparently. `fleet secrets get "cloudflare api key"`
   resolves `42.cloudflare api key` automatically.
3. **Full names still work.** Asking for `42.cloudflare api key`
   explicitly resolves the same secret.
4. **The prefix is applied exactly once, by the caller-visible name.**
   A secret literally named `42.42.<...>` inside the `42` namespace
   is reached by asking for `42.<...>` *while prefixed* — i.e. once
   you pass a name that already carries the prefix, you are speaking
   in full names. (Drew's formulation: "if you put a `42`-prefixed
   item inside your `42`-prefixed namespace, it would only be able to
   be set and gotten by saying `42.42`.")

### Store / vault / profile selection

- `--store` / `--vault` flags (and env/config equivalents) override
  the default store per call: Bitwarden (broker) today; 1Password
  behind the same verb when the proxy covers it.
- **Per-device / per-instance profiles**: a device or agent instance
  carries config naming its store + prefix (e.g. "sandbox vault,
  prefix 42"), and can hold its own keys, so what a given running
  agent can see is bounded by its configuration without any extra
  work at call time. Profiles are configuration, set at provisioning
  — the call sites never change.
- The broker's cache and its `list` must respect the caller's scope:
  a scoped caller must not receive unscoped names even from cache.

### Questions for the design

- Where does profile config live per host (fleet host manifest?
  per-instance config file?), and who may change it?
- Does scoping apply to `set` as well (a scoped agent writes only
  inside its prefix) — Drew's semantics imply yes for symmetry.
- How do broker (laptop) and fallback (direct Bitwarden) stay
  consistent under scoping, given list deliberately has no vault
  fallback today?

### Acceptance (design phase)

- [ ] Decision record covering the prefix rules above as testable
      cases (list/get/set × prefixed/unprefixed × short/full name).
- [ ] Build issue(s) split out; the no-config regression case
      ("byte-identical behaviour when nothing is configured") is an
      explicit test.

code.title: Design: automatic context propagation — every fleet action carries its origin
code.body:
## Design: automatic context propagation — every fleet action carries its origin

Origin: Drew, 2026-11-14. The goal: any command, session, secret lookup,
queue action, or file transfer in the fleet can be traced back to what
launched it — **automatically**, with zero per-call effort from models.
"If models have to stop and think about this every time, it has failed."

### The context record (what travels with every call)

Captured once at the outermost point available, inherited by everything
downstream:

- Muse session id + the internal model name serving it
- Queue task id + task name (when launched from the fleet queue)
- OpenCode session id + parent session id; the OpenChamber scheduled
  job that originated the session, when it came from one
- The triggering message id (internal message id of the exact message
  that led to the call) where the surface exposes it
- PID + a compact ancestor summary (enough to reconstruct the chain:
  cron → Muse → OpenCode → tool call)
- git HEAD hashes: hatch + hatch-personal repos (and the working repo
  of the call, when different)
- Host + which user-context is acting (see below)

### Mechanisms to evaluate and combine

1. **Init sourcing.** Init scripts set the environment by being
   *sourced*, not executed (`init source`), so the context variables
   persist into everything the shell launches afterward. Apply the same
   pattern on the laptop, where one OS user (`user`) is shared by
   Drew-interactive shells, OpenCode, and Claude-driven work: the
   context must distinguish *which* of those is acting, plus systemd
   timers/services as origins in their own right.
2. **An env contract.** A small, fixed set of variables (working name
   `FLEET_CTX_*`) set by init / launchers / hooks and passed unchanged
   through: laptop-agent exec and jobs (the daemon records them in the
   job spool), SSH (AcceptEnv / explicit prefix), the queue broker and
   secrets broker (logged per trip — trip logs already exist), and the
   file-transfer verbs (sibling build issue).
3. **OpenCode / OpenChamber hooks in the fork.** On session start, the
   fork injects the context env into the session; on tool calls and
   session end it stamps the context id. Chained calls keep the chain:
   a Muse call that triggers an OpenCode call extends the record
   rather than starting a new one. This extends work already in flight:
   claimant identity is stamped on queue claims today, and the
   task↔session multi-stamp link build is still outstanding — this
   design is its general form and should absorb it.
4. **MCPX passthrough.** When OpenCode (or any MCP client) calls
   through MCPX, context headers/env pass through to the tool call, so
   the far side can attribute the call without the model doing
   anything. Where a protocol cannot carry headers, the env contract
   is the fallback.
5. **Attribution at the stores.** Secrets lookups, KV reads/writes
   (sibling design), and broker trips log the context id, joining the
   observability we already have (atlas session corpus via
   `fleet search`, broker trip logs) into one traceable web.

### Hard constraints

- **Zero model effort.** Set by init, launchers, and hooks — never by
  a model remembering to pass a flag. A flag exists only as an
  override for tests.
- **Cheap on the hot path.** Capture once per session/init; inherit
  after. No per-command lookups (a warm fleet call is ~0.4 s; the
  context may not add a round trip).
- **No secrets in context.** Ids and hashes only — the context record
  is logged widely by design, so nothing sensitive may ride in it.
- **Absence is representable.** Interactive Drew shells and old
  callers produce a partial record, not an error.

### Questions the design must answer

- Where does the canonical record live per session (env only? a
  spool file keyed by context id? both), and who sweeps it?
- How are related sessions from one origin found later ("show me
  everything this task spawned") — the brokers' trip logs, the job
  spools, and atlas need one join key; is the context id that key?
- What is the laptop story for systemd timers (their context is the
  unit + last invocation, presumably recorded by the unit itself)?

### Acceptance (design phase)

- [ ] Decision record: the context record's fields, the env contract,
      and the capture points (init, claimant, OpenCode hooks, MCPX).
- [ ] Build issues split out per capture point, each with a
      "prove it end-to-end" test (e.g. a queue task's id visible in
      the laptop job spool, the secrets-broker trip log, and the
      OpenCode session record — same id, no model involvement).

code.title: Design + build: fleet connect — explicit transport selection, sessions, and drop semantics
code.body:
## Design + build: `fleet connect` — explicit transport selection, sessions, and drop semantics

Origin: Drew's questions, 2026-11-14. Epic: #5412. Builds on #5343
(laptop-agent), #5697 (`fleet proxy ssh`), #5972 (fallback connection
mode), and the session semantics of the file-transfer build (sibling
issue filed the same day).

### Verified current state (2026-11-14) — what Drew asked to confirm

Three ways to reach the laptop exist today, chosen by *which tool you
invoke*, not by a flag:

1. **Agent exec** (`laptop-agent.py`, the day-to-day path; the Rust
   `fleet laptop-agent` domain is still a registry stub — exit 69,
   "implementation lands in a later step of epic #5412"). Commands run
   as argv directly on the laptop, **no shell** unless `--shell` is
   passed (then a login `bash -lc`). Environment is the daemon's
   systemd-user-service environment (plus the login profile under
   `--shell`) — nothing from the caller's environment crosses. **There
   is no stdin channel at all**: interactive input during a run is
   impossible on this path, which is exactly why stdin-carrying shapes
   fall back to SSH. Transport is HTTP over pooled CONNECT tunnels
   through the session proxy (warm call ~0.39–0.45 s; cold CONNECT
   ~1.8 s — all traffic hairpins the NYC DERP relay).
2. **Detached agent jobs** (`run` / `poll` / `kill` / `jobs` on the same
   daemon). Jobs persist server-side: spool files under
   `~/.local/state/laptop-agent/jobs/` on the laptop survive client
   death, disconnection, and sandbox restarts; `poll` resumes output by
   byte offset (client offsets in `~/.cache/laptop-agent/`). This is
   the one place a session/resume model already exists.
3. **Real SSH** (`laptop-ssh-real.sh`, or `fleet proxy ssh` in the
   binary since the 2026-11-11 refresh): full SSH over an HTTP CONNECT
   ProxyCommand, connection-multiplexed (ControlMaster, ControlPersist
   600 s; sshd MaxStartups raised to 200 after the 2026-10-25 root
   cause). Real shells, real PTY, real stdin/stdout/stderr streaming,
   port forwards, the laptop login environment. Drew's belief is
   correct: this is the only path with true interactive sessions today.
   The shim (`laptop-ssh.sh`) auto-routes: exec-shaped calls go to the
   agent; interactive / forwards / stdin-carrying calls go to real SSH.

Drop semantics today, per path:

- Agent **exec**: a client disconnect deliberately *reaps* the remote
  command (own process group, TERM→KILL; fixed 2026-11-10, #5343) —
  nothing is buffered for later pickup; a hiccup loses the run.
- Agent **jobs**: the job keeps running and its output spools to disk;
  reconnect and `poll` from the last offset. Buffer limit is effectively
  disk; no replay cap is specified.
- **SSH**: a drop kills nothing server-side (sshd owns the process) but
  there is no output replay — whatever printed while you were gone is
  gone unless the program itself logged it. `timeout` on the SSH path
  bounds only the local wait.
- The sandbox has **no inbound path at all**: no SSH in, no HTTP in.
  Every connection is initiated from the sandbox side or rendezvoused
  through the session proxy / brokers. (Confirmed 2026-11-14.)

### What to design and build

1. **One surface, explicit method.** `fleet connect` wraps all three
   paths with `--method exec|ssh|job|auto`. `auto` codifies the shim's
   current heuristics (stdin data or PTY or forwards → ssh; detached →
   job; else exec). Callers can always force a method — Drew: "is there
   a way to actually flag and choose the SSH connection method versus
   the other?"
2. **A session model across paths.** Generalize the daemon's job spool
   into named connect sessions: `fleet connect session <id>` attaches
   (replays output from offset, like `poll` does today), `fleet
   connect sessions` lists live/recent sessions with metadata (owning
   context id — see the context-propagation design filed the same day —
   command, host, started, state, bytes buffered). Define per-path
   buffering limits and what happens at the cap. Exec-path sessions
   should gain the job path's survive-the-client property *without*
   losing the 2026-11-10 guarantee that an abandoned run does not
   orphan forever: a bounded grace window, then reap.
3. **Stdin decision.** Either the daemon grows a stdin channel (making
   exec interactive-capable), or the routing rule "stdin ⇒ SSH" is
   made permanent and documented as the contract. Pick one on evidence;
   today it is an accident of implementation.
4. **tmux: settle it in writing.** For the SSH path, tmux on the laptop
   IS the attach/detach answer (SSH carries the terminal — there is no
   HTTP attach method and none is needed). For the agent path, jobs +
   spool already cover it. Decide whether a managed tmux pattern
   (named sessions per context id, listable, swept when stale) is
   documented, tooled, or deliberately left manual — and make sure
   anything started under tmux is cleaned up. On the sandbox, Muse's
   own exec sessions already provide the equivalent; do not build a
   second one.
5. **Inbound-less hosts (future, recorded — not ruled out, not a
   priority).** A queue task that instructs a host to open a *reverse*
   connection to a named endpoint, after which that endpoint can drive
   the host's environment. Design space only in this issue; spin out if
   it ever becomes real.
6. **Direct node-to-node (future shape).** Nodes with full network
   access may later SSH directly with per-node client certificates
   under a shared CA, every connection logged under the cert identity,
   with the proxy/coordinator pool as the universal fallback (routing
   by command, load, or session stickiness). The sandbox's network
   idiosyncrasies must keep working automatically underneath all of
   this — the fallback path is the compatibility floor, not a legacy
   mode.

### Acceptance (design phase)

- [ ] Decision record covering items 1–4 with the measured numbers
      (warm/cold per path, batch behaviour, throughput) in one table.
- [ ] Build issues split out for: the `fleet connect` surface, the
      session list/attach surface, and the stdin decision's winner.
- [ ] #5972's fallback-mode scope reconciled with this design (one
      answer, not two).

code.title: Build: fleet file transfer — get / put / copy verbs (SCP-class, any-to-any)
code.body:
## Build: fleet file transfer — get / put / copy verbs (SCP-class, any-to-any)

Origin: Drew, 2026-11-14 — "we should add it as its own build item." This is the
implementation issue for the design in #5759 (`fleet proxy get`/`put` over the
agent channel), with the read-path alternative in #5757 §3 and Drew's
2026-11-14 requirements folded in. Epic: #5412. Daemon: #5343.

### Verified current state (2026-11-14)

- No file-transfer verb exists anywhere in the fleet binary. Domains:
  queue, serve, proxy, dispatch, dispatch-test, secrets, gh, search,
  laptop-agent. Everything carried today is commands and small JSON.
- The laptop-agent daemon's routes are exec + jobs only; every body is JSON.
  Files cross today only as (a) base64 inside exec calls (manual, ~33% size
  tax, ~1 MiB/stream practical cap, no resume), (b) stdin pushes over the
  real-SSH fallback (`fetch-charge-inputs.py`, `atlas-backup.py` — the two
  scripts #5759 names as waiting on this channel), or (c) out-of-band staging
  (the rclone-crypt → R2 path built for the sandbox-home backup move,
  hatch-personal#50 — proven both directions 2026-11-14, but it is a backup
  pipeline, not a general verb).
- The "more performant HTTP version" in Drew's memory is the agent's *exec*
  transport (commands over HTTP through pooled CONNECT tunnels) — it has
  never carried files. Recorded already on #5759 (2026-11-04).

### Requirements (Drew, 2026-11-14)

1. **At least SCP-capable.** `fleet get`, `fleet put`, and a `fleet copy`
   that takes SCP-style addressing on BOTH sides:
   `fleet copy sandbox:/home/hatch/test.txt laptop:/home/user/test2.txt`.
   Either side may be a remote; a bare path means the local host.
2. **The target is a parameter, never a hardcoded "the laptop."** Every
   connect-family verb takes an explicit remote/endpoint name
   (`--remote NAME` or the `host:` prefix). Today everything silently
   defaults to the one laptop; the addressing must generalize to
   laptop1/laptop2/pool members without a redesign. (Coordinator/pool
   routing — a lookup that picks the endpoint by command, load, or
   stickiness — is future work; the addressing must not preclude it.)
3. **Integrity end-to-end.** Hash-verified transfer (the #5759
   begin/write/commit protocol already specifies sha256 + deterministic
   temp names + atomic commit — implement that; the #5757 §3 raw
   byte-range GET is the candidate read path if profiling wants it).
4. **Resumable + clean.** An interrupted transfer resumes the same temp
   file instead of restarting; partial transfers are never visible at the
   destination path; abandoned temps are swept.
5. **Delegated (direct-path) copy is designed in from the start.** When
   source and destination can reach each other directly, the controller
   should be able to authorize and instruct the copy instead of relaying
   every byte through itself: the source validates the instruction and
   pushes/pulls directly. The naive relay path is the fallback and may
   ship first — but if the delegated path is not in v1, it MUST be split
   out as its own follow-on issue before this one closes (Drew: "it is
   not a question of whether it's a thing — that should be a thing").
6. **Performance close-out.** Report measured throughput for a 100 MiB
   file sandbox↔laptop against: base64-over-exec (today), scp over the
   proxy SSH path, and the new verb. The bar: decisively beat base64-exec,
   at least match scp.

### Acceptance

- [ ] 100 MiB file sandbox→laptop and laptop→sandbox, sha256-identical.
- [ ] Transfer killed mid-flight resumes and completes; destination path
      never shows partial content.
- [ ] `fleet copy laptop:/path sandbox:/path` and the reverse both work
      with explicit host addressing.
- [ ] The two waiting scripts (`fetch-charge-inputs.py`,
      `atlas-backup.py`) migrated off SSH-stdin pushes, or a recorded
      reason they stay.
- [ ] Delegated copy: working, OR follow-on issue filed and linked here.
- [ ] Throughput numbers posted in the close-out comment.

Related: #5759 (design), #5757 (perf census), #5697 (`fleet proxy ssh`),
#5972 (fallback connection mode), #5345 / #1794 (the ID project's own
server-to-server transfer designs — coordinate so the fleet verb and the
ID protocol do not grow into two incompatible answers).

code.title: impl(id): build-time defaults.json — typed parse, pair-atomic cascade, provenance (#5916 follow-on)
code.body:
Implementation follow-on of the #5916 design pass. The design record (doc/2026-11-14T19-05-00Z_design_id_build_defaults) settles all six questions; this issue is its §8 brief.

## Scope
1. Replace `pkgs/id/crates/id-core/src/defaults.conf` + hand parser with `defaults.json` + typed serde parse (`deny_unknown_fields`); `Defaults` gains `relay`, `gossip`, `mode`; field-compatible otherwise.
2. Pair-atomic resolution in `resolve_config` per design §5 (one layer supplies the whole topic/secret pair; a single-half layer is an error naming layer + missing half) — closes audit defects D1 (mixed pair in the default path) and D2 (`--replace-defaults` leaking to consts).
3. Remove the runtime `--replace-defaults` flag (build-time `"mode"` in the file replaces it); keep `--no-default-bootstrap` / `--no-default-topic`.
4. Wire `relay` (RelayPolicy selector) and `gossip` build defaults; launch flags override.
5. Provenance: SHA-256 of the embedded file at first parse; serve startup log + version surface report `defaults: file sha256=… mode=…` or `defaults: consts`.
6. Tests: equivalence flag-matrix (empty file ≡ const build; const-valued file ≡ const build); replace-mode missing-half error; file-layer single-half pair error (D1 regression); unknown-field rejection; checked-in defaults.json parses.

## Acceptance
A binary built with a custom defaults.json reports its provenance, resolves the topic/secret pair atomically from one layer, and a `{}` build is indistinguishable from the const build across the serve-flag matrix.

Design: doc/2026-11-14T19-05-00Z_design_id_build_defaults (PR for #5916). Parent: #5916. Relates #4756.

code.title: claimant mode file: guard the silent-deletion single point of failure
code.body:
## Problem (five words: silent mode deletion shadows claimant)

The opencode claimant's mode file (`~/.local/state/opencode-claimant/mode` on the laptop) is an unguarded single point of failure: when the file is missing, the claimant silently defaults to shadow mode (discovery only, no launches) with no signal. This has now bitten twice:

- 2026-11-08: mode file missing, claimant never launched anything until set to `live` by hand.
- 2026-11-14: `fires.jsonl` shows reads flipping live -> shadow at 14:46Z; the file was deleted ~5.5h after working live fires (deleter unattributed from available logs). This blocked the #9106 summit dispatch (`mode_not_live`, task 15354) until restored under Drew's authorization.

## Acceptance

- Mode file deletion or unreadability produces a VISIBLE alert within one surfacing cycle (wire into the #10141 silent-failure surfacing, now live) instead of a silent shadow fallback.
- Claimant startup/heartbeat records the mode it read and where from, so a flip is attributable in the log after the fact.
- Consider making the mode part of managed config (repo/systemd state) rather than a bare file any process can delete.
- A missing file must never again present as 'summits just aren't launching' for hours.

Refs: #9106, #10141, #9103. Filed from the 2026-11-14 summit-pool investigation (Track B).

code.title: fleet gh: make the token rotation configurable without code changes
code.body:
Five-word summary: configure rotation without code changes.

Follow-on to #8887 (closed; the passthrough itself works and is proven live). Everything below is about the rotation's CONFIGURATION surface, verified from the source (`pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet/src/gh.rs`, main @ 2026-11-14) plus live probes on 2026-11-14.

## Where it stands today (facts, not asks)

- The three Apps are a compiled-in enum (`GhApp::{Fleet, DevToday, Backup}`, `GhApp::ALL`); each App's private-key secret name is a code constant, and two of the three App IDs also come from broker secrets (`kaneo.github-app-id`, `github-app.backup-app-id`). Adding a fourth App today requires a code change + redeploy.
- Order and owner sets are env-only: `FLEET_GH_ORDER` replaces the whole rotation for one process; `FLEET_GH_APP_OWNERS` / `FLEET_GH_DEVTODAY_OWNERS` / `FLEET_GH_BACKUP_OWNERS` replace per-App owner lists. Nothing persists between shells/machines.
- Default owner lists are compiled in and small: fleet App — developing-today, developing-today-forks, dezren39; developing.today App — developing-today, dezren39; backup App — developing-today only. Reality check (live `GET /app/installations` per App, 2026-11-14): **all three Apps are installed in exactly the same 103 accounts** (dezren39 + 102 orgs; sets diffed identical). The short lists are historical scoping in code, not installation facts.
- `fleet gh tiers` enumerates the configured rotation only (7 lines today). There is no `--all`.
- Org coverage gap (Q4 finding): installation lookup IS live (`GET /app/installations`, paginated) but runs only for owners already in the configured list; the call's owner hint only reorders existing entries, it never adds one. Probe (2026-11-14, org `layercloud`, where all three Apps are installed but no leg is configured): an admin-scoped read under a configured leg failed `403 Resource not accessible by integration`; the identical read with `app:layercloud` added to the order succeeded; `/installation/repositories` under the developing-today leg contains zero layercloud repos, under the layercloud leg it lists them. In the default rotation the personal token (tried first) masks this while it has headroom; public reads also pass under any leg. Scoped/private access in an unconfigured org fails once the personal token can't serve it.
- Portability (Q5 finding): with `gh` absent from PATH, `fleet gh api user` prints exactly `fleet gh: failed to run 'gh': No such file or directory (os error 2)` on stderr and exits 3 — clean, no panic, no hang, but it does not tell the operator the remedy. With no resolvable credentials, each source's provider error is printed (the same key error repeats once per owner leg), then `fleet gh: no token source could be resolved`, exit 3.

## Asks

- [ ] (a) Persistent, reorderable token-source config for `fleet gh` (order + enabled set) that survives shells and machines — a config file in the fleet config surface, with the existing env vars kept as per-process overrides.
- [ ] (b) Config-defined Apps: a new GitHub App joins the rotation by configuration alone (app id source + private-key secret name + default owners), no code change, no redeploy of the binary.
- [ ] (c) `fleet gh tiers --all`: list every installation of every configured App (all 103 accounts today), keeping the default `tiers` output at the configured rotation set.
- [ ] (d) Error polish: when the real `gh` binary is missing, say the remedy (install `gh`, or set `FLEET_GH_BIN`) in the error; when no credentials resolve, print each distinct provider error once, then the summary line. Keep exit code 3 and the value-free error rule.
- [ ] (e) Decide the unknown-org behavior explicitly: either (i) dynamic hint leg — when a call names an owner and a configured App has a live installation for it, add that leg (the paginated installations lookup needed already exists in `mint_installation_token`), or (ii) keep the configured-list gate and document that unconfigured orgs are personal-token-only with the failure mode above. Recommendation: (i) — it matches how Drew actually works across ~100 orgs, and the personal-first order still applies.

code.title: design: provider/model kind marking + input-modality capability marking for routing
code.body:
## Drew's question (2026-11-14) — two separate axes

Do we need a way to mark providers/models by **type**, and separately a way to mark **which inputs they accept** (text, image, video, PDF, audio, audio streams)? Drew flagged these as two different questions; this issue keeps them separate and hands both to the design mill (#9399) rather than hand-adding config fields ad hoc.

## Axis 1 — kind/type marking (NOT yet designed anywhere)

Today the router treats every seated model as a chat model. Live counterexamples already in the config:

- **System One / Jev** (`system1` route, PR #10288): a typed decision endpoint — chat calls to it return 400. It is currently faked as an ordinary route with warning comments; nothing structural stops a chat session from being routed to it.
- **gpt-live-1** (Zen, voice, per-minute billing): no seat exists because there is no kind for it.
- Embeddings / image-generation / transcription models would have the same problem the day they are seated.

Proposal for the design pass: a `kind` on providers and models (chat / decision / voice / embedding / image / transcription / …), pools declare the kind they accept, and the router refuses a wrong-kind request structurally instead of relying on comments.

## Axis 2 — input-modality capabilities (design STARTED — wire it up)

The mill's capabilities supplement (`docs/2026-11-13T09-26-00Z_design_pool_effort_system/brief-capabilities-supplement.md`, PR #9550) already sets the headline rule — failover is scoped per capability (§0), pools are capability-gated (§1). What's missing:

- **Modality data**: models.dev already publishes per-model input/output modalities and context limits; the fork partially consumes this (route rules carry per-target context limits). The design should lean on catalog data first and hand-mark only the gaps (stealth/free models: Beam's context is unknown; Nemotron Super VL is vision-capable but sits in text pools where vision input never reaches it).
- **Request-side gating**: a request carrying an image/PDF/audio input should skip legs that cannot accept it, per the supplement's capability-set eligibility — including at class-fallback boundaries.
- Interaction with the `limited` class (per-target context caps) and with Axis 1 kinds.

## Ask

Design pass under #9399 covering both axes: schema (where kind/capabilities live — provider, model, pool, inline wrapper), catalog-data ingestion from models.dev, router enforcement points, and migration of the existing seats (system1 first). No config changes until the design lands.

code.title: Projector reconcile runs take hours
code.body:
**Observed 2026-11-14 on the laptop (amd) — `pm-projector-reconcile.service` (user unit) sits in `activating` for most of the day. This is a different failure class from the pm-git-sync dirty-checkout failure repaired today (see #10022); filing separately per triage.**

The unit is a `Type=oneshot` with **no `TimeoutStartSec`**, triggered by `pm-projector-reconcile.timer` `OnCalendar=*:0/15`. Actual run durations today (journal, CST):

| Start | Finish | Duration | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| 01:30:17 | 02:14:16 | ~44 min | |
| 02:30:10 | 03:03:05 | ~33 min | |
| 03:03:05 | 04:19:43 | ~76 min | back-to-back retrigger |
| 04:30:12 | 05:28:17 | ~58 min | |
| 05:28:17 | 08:02:27 | ~154 min | one run wrote 66,766 items |
| 09:45:16 | 11:06:14 | ~81 min | this is the run seen "stuck in activating" in the 2026-11-14 redesign pass |
| 11:15:04 | 11:15:20 | 16 s | after catch-up; see 403s below |

So the 15-minute cadence is meaningless during backfill: a single run can span 10 timer ticks, and any health check that samples the unit mid-run sees a permanent `activating`.

Second, probably related: in the fast 11:15 run, the `issues` stream for every repo succeeded, but **every PR-derived stream failed with `github_api_403`** — `prs`, `issue_comments`, `review_comments`, `reviews` for `developing-today/code`, `developing-today/opencode`, `developing-today/openchamber`, and `dezren39/nix` (`written: 0, error: "github_api_403"`), while the run still reports `{"ok": true}`. Independently, a `gh api` call from the sandbox at 17:24 UTC today returned "API rate limit exceeded for user ID 11225574", which suggests the 403s are GitHub API rate limiting on the shared token — so PR/comment/review projection silently stalls while the reconcile reports success.

Asks:

1. Bound a single reconcile run (per-stream page/item budget or a unit timeout) so one run cannot occupy the service for hours; let the cursor resume on the next tick.
2. Surface per-stream 403/rate-limit failures in the run result (not `ok: true` when 16 of 20 streams failed), including the rate-limit reset time when GitHub provides it.
3. Consider splitting the backfill path from the steady-state 15-minute reconcile so health checks can distinguish "catching up" from "stuck".

Evidence host: laptop `amd`, `journalctl --user -u pm-projector-reconcile.service` 2026-11-14; unit definition from the Nix store (`pm-projector-reconcile.service` / `.timer`, linked into `~/.config/systemd/user/`).

code.title: audit(pm-stack): whole-stack backup / disaster-recovery verdict 2026-11-14 — brand-new-computer rebuild not yet possible
code.body:
# DR verdict — whole PM-stack backup audit, 2026-11-14

Ordered by Drew 2026-11-14: *"Are there any other obvious gaps to our backup routines? Is the rest of the PM stack backed up? If I start up a brand-new computer, could we use backups to get the entire PM stack running?"*

Method: read-only audit. Every claim below rests on **observed artifacts** (files, manifests, journals, R2 listings read back, hashes recomputed), each consequential fact checked with a second independent call. Scratch drills were done only in `/tmp` on the laptop and cleaned up. Links: design #1258, cutover tracker #3989, DB backup #1514 (closed), slices #6815 / #6816, observability #3869.

## Bottom line

**No — a brand-new computer could not rebuild the entire PM stack from backups + repos today.** The core databases (Kaneo / Grist / Pad) and part of the aggregator state *can* be rebuilt, and that leg is genuinely good: daily, sha256-manifested, copied to local + R2 + Google Drive with every leg verified, and per-store restore checks pass. But a full rebuild would stall or silently lose pieces at the secrets bootstrap, the SOPS decryption key, the claimant/dispatch state, the decisions ledger, the OpenCode session store, and the laptop-state backup that has not run in 12 days. And the whole-stack rebuild has **never been drilled** — the runbook is still marked DRAFT — so even the "can" parts are partly inference.

## Brand-new-computer rebuild walk

PROVEN = restore-tested with evidence. INFERRED = should work, never tested end-to-end.

1. **Hardware / OS** — Install NixOS and switch the `amd` host config from the `developing-today/code` flake. *INFERRED* for a new machine (the switch is routine on the current laptop; a cold install + first switch has no drill record). **Missing:** nothing in data terms — the flake is in git — but the laptop sudo password is a 1Password item (Drew-held root, see step 2).
2. **Secrets bootstrap** — *INFERRED, with a hard manual gate.* Order that works on paper: Drew logs into Bitwarden → mint a new Secrets Manager machine token (the old tokens are in **no** backup — #10301) → fetch by name: restic passwords, R2 backup keys, Supabase DB password, Kaneo/Grist/Pad secrets, tunnel token (`cloudflare.tunnel.amd-6-pm-stack-token` — verified present by name) → 1Password service tokens (they live in BWS) → fresh Google OAuth for rclone Drive (token not backed up — #10301). **Missing piece: the SOPS age private key for the laptop recipient exists nowhere off the laptop** — every laptop-recipient SOPS file is undecryptable on the new machine (#10295).
3. **Repos** — Clone the four repos from GitHub; alternatively restore laptop mirrors. *PROVEN* in effect (clones happen daily across worktrees; github-backup mirrors verified today).
4. **Services** — `nixos-rebuild switch` brings up the systemd units + Docker stacks from the flake. *INFERRED* as a cold path: the deployed tree `~/pm-stack/` is **not a git repo** and its rendered files (`tunnel.token`, `tunnel.env`, `dispatch/.env`) must be re-rendered from vault/SOPS — possible for the tunnel (vault name exists), unverified file-by-file for the rest (#10298). pm-git-sync was observed *failed* today on a dirty primary checkout (another lane's files) — on a clean new machine that specific failure vanishes, but it shows the deploy path assumes a clean checkout.
5. **Data restores** —
   - Kaneo: `pg_restore` the daily dump. *PROVEN* at TOC level (2026-10-27 full scratch restore; 2026-11-14 TOC parse). **RPO gap: daily dump vs the accepted 1h target.**
   - Grist: copy back home/sessions/docs from the bundle. *PROVEN* at integrity level (today, from the actual backup copy).
   - Pad: copy back pad.db + `encryption.key` (it rides the same bundle — good) + config. *PROVEN* at integrity level; app-open with key last proven 2026-10-27.
   - Aggregator: unpack the dashboard tar's allow-listed files. *PARTIAL* — `decisions.json` and friends aren't in the archive (#10293); decision events could be replayed from Turso (inferred).
   - Projector: start empty, reconcile from GitHub; `pmp_links` from the export. *INFERRED.*
   - Fleet queue: the queue itself lives in Supabase cloud — a new *laptop* doesn't need its restore at all; restoring *Supabase* from the R2 dump is documented but the dump is currently ~30h stale and the job is failing (#10296).
   - OpenCode sessions: **cannot be restored — no copy exists** (#10297). Claimant mode: recreate by hand, content today is `live` (#10298). Laptop state (SSH keys, SOPS files): restic restore works from a **2026-11-02** snapshot (#10294).
6. **Offsite copies** — Pull from R2 (works once BWS is bootstrapped) or Drive (works once rclone is re-authed). The dashboard bundle's R2 + Drive legs were sha-verified in today's run record — *PROVEN* that today's generation is really off-machine.
7. **Public entry** — Re-point / re-run the Cloudflare tunnel with the vault-held token; Access policy is Cloudflare-side. *INFERRED* (never moved in a drill).
8. **Verification / smoke** — Runbook smoke steps exist (`pm-stack/COLD-RESTORE-RUNBOOK.md`) but the runbook is **DRAFT**, `doc/pm-stack/restore-drills/` does not exist, and no full-stack drill has ever been recorded (#10300). *INFERRED.*

## The 7 design questions from #1258 — status, with recommendations

**Correction to the audit brief:** these are *not* still awaiting Drew. The #1258 comment thread records Drew ruling on **all seven on 2026-11-03** (posted through 2026-11-05): Q2/Q7 all-in-Supabase; Q1/Q4/Q5 accepted as proposed; Q3/Q6 retention decided — and #3989's triage recorded the cutover as ungated. They are surfaced here as instructed, each with the ruling, my recommendation, and the conformance gap this audit found:

1. **RTO/RPO targets** (4h core RTO; 15m aggregator; 1h Kaneo/usage/link; 24h Grist/Pad/Project). *Ruling: accepted.* **My recommendation: keep them — and publish actuals against them.** Conformance: Grist/Pad meet theirs; Kaneo's daily dump gives ~24h RPO vs the 1h target, and the aggregator JSON stores give ~24h vs 15m. Those two misses are the sharpest numbers in this audit.
2. **Canonical DB homes.** *Ruling: superseded — ALL PM-stack state to Supabase `muse-dev2`; no cluster Postgres/volumes as system of record; no laptop-local exceptions (Q7).* **My recommendation: keep the ruling; judge #6815/#6816 against it literally** — including an explicit mapping for file-shaped stores (Grist docs, Pad attachments) rather than silent exceptions, exactly as Drew's ruling itself instructed.
3. **Backup destinations + retention** (local + R2 + Drive; daily 30d + monthly 12mo off-machine). *Ruling: decided, as stated.* **My recommendation: keep — and implement the monthly tier**, which does not exist anywhere today (#10299).
4. **Failover posture.** *Ruling: tested cold restore ≤4h, no warm standby; GitHub is the degraded mode.* **My recommendation: keep.** Conformance: the "tested" half is unmet — no drill yet (#10300).
5. **Restore evidence** (`doc/pm-stack/restore-drills/YYYY-MM.md`; monthly rotating / quarterly full / annual laptop-off). *Ruling: approved.* **My recommendation: keep — start the rotation this month**; the directory doesn't exist and the first monthly restore is already overdue under the ruling.
6. **Project export retention** (#1218 exports kept off-machine 1 year). *Ruling: 1 year.* **My recommendation: keep.** Conformance: #1218 is closed but no off-machine export copy with that retention was found (#10299).
7. **Laptop-local exceptions.** *Ruling: none — nothing intentionally laptop-only.* **My recommendation: keep, and treat every "No" row in the table above as a ruling violation to close, not a preference:** decisions ledger (#10293), claimant/dispatch state (#10298), OpenCode sessions (#10297), SOPS age key (#10295) are all unique laptop-only records today.

## Gap issues filed by this audit

Also observed, left to their existing owners (not re-filed): atlas-backup timeout + unchanged atlas sha since 2026-10-31 (Atlas track); cold-store Turso leg timeout today (#1723 track); pm-git-sync failing on a dirty checkout (fleet hygiene track); supabase-backup's watchdog absence is folded into #10296.

code.title: Fleet queue backup failing silently
code.body:
Found by the 2026-11-14 whole-PM-stack backup/DR audit (verdict issue filed same day; routine #1723).

**Observed (2026-11-14, laptop amd):**
- `supabase-backup.service` (twice-daily pg_dump of Supabase project `muse-dev2` — which holds the fleet queue in the `agent` schema — to R2 bucket `supabase-backups`, prefix `pg/muse-dev2`) **failed today**: 2026-11-14 04:49 CST, `pg_dump: error: Dumping the contents of table "events" failed: PQgetCopyData() failed … SSL connection has been closed unexpectedly`, exit 1.
- The R2 manifest read back via `supabase_backup.py --list` shows the newest successful dump is **2026-11-13T10:55Z** (44,215,425 bytes, sha256 `dbdc07f7…`) — i.e. ~30h old at audit time against a 12h cadence; at least two scheduled runs produced nothing.
- journalctl shows only the 04:45 run on 2026-11-14 (no 16:42-equivalent success on 11-13 evening in the window checked), and **no watchdog covers this job**: `laptop-backups-watchdog` checks only dashboard + repo-archive, and the run's own `{"status":"error"}` JSON goes only to the journal. A stopped fleet-queue backup is currently silent.

Note the dump is full-database (pgdump transport ignores the schema list), so when it succeeds it does cover the fleet queue `agent` schema, plus every other fleet schema. RPO target for the queue/aggregator class is 15 min per Drew's 2026-11-03 #1258 ruling — a twice-daily dump never met that even when it worked; that tension belongs to #3989/#6815, this issue is about the failing + silent routine.

**Fix shape:** diagnose the pooler SSL drop on `agent.events` (retry/resume or transport change), and wire this job's last-success into a freshness check that names it (extend the laptop-backups watchdog or equivalent).

Acceptance: two consecutive scheduled runs succeed (manifest shows fresh entries ≤12h apart) and a simulated stall is named by the watchdog.

code.title: SOPS decryption key not recoverable
code.body:
Found by the 2026-11-14 whole-PM-stack backup/DR audit (verdict issue filed same day).

**Observed (2026-11-14, laptop amd):**
- The code repo's `.sops.yaml` names two age recipients: `laptop-framework` = `age125acas5y8hnwl5uhcp364xm8zlhtwsjqvxxpge8k04dzzr67acrq0ttc34` and `claude-sandbox`.
- `age-keygen -y ~/.config/sops/age/keys.txt` on the laptop returns exactly the `laptop-framework` public key — the laptop's SOPS private key lives only in that one file (75 bytes, dated 2024-10-14).
- That file is in **no** backup set: `laptop-state-backup` covers only `~/.local/state/opencode`, `~/secrets/*.sops.yaml`, `~/.ssh`; `agent-backup` is local-only and does not list it; no other routine names it.
- The fleet secrets list (Bitwarden Secrets Manager, names only) contains `sops.age-private-key-sandbox` — the **sandbox** key — and no laptop/framework age key at all.

**Consequence:** the SOPS ciphertext is backed up (`~/secrets/*.sops.yaml` rides laptop-state-backup, and the `.sops.yaml` files are in git), but if the laptop disk dies, nothing can decrypt the laptop-recipient files on a new machine. The encrypted backups are then dead weight for every secret that is encrypted to the laptop recipient only.

**Fix shape:** store the laptop age private key by name in Bitwarden Secrets Manager (value never in git/chat), and/or add `~/.config/sops/age/keys.txt` to the laptop-state restic set; verify by decrypting one laptop-recipient SOPS file in a scratch dir using only the vault-retrieved key.

Acceptance: a named vault entry (or an equivalent backed-up copy) exists and a scratch decrypt proof is recorded — key value never printed in the proof.

code.title: Decisions ledger missing from backups
code.body:
Found by the 2026-11-14 whole-PM-stack backup/DR audit (verdict issue filed same day; parent context #1258 / #3989 / #1514).

**Observed (2026-11-14, laptop amd):** `~/.local/state/pm-aggregator/` holds ~80 live files. The daily `pm-dashboard-backup` archive (verified: `~/backups/dashboard/2026-11-14/dashboard-2026-11-14.tar.zst`, sha256 `8d2bd705…`, legs local+R2+Drive all `ok` in `.last-run.json`) stages only an explicit allow-list. A `comm` of the live directory against the archive listing shows these canonical files are **not** in any backup:

- `decisions.json` (3.3 MB — the decisions ledger state)
- `decision-events.jsonl`, `decision-events-outbox.jsonl`, `decision-events-outbox.jsonl.sync-state.json`
- `board.json`, `attention-last-good.json`, `needs-drew.json`, `notifications.jsonl`, `digests/`, `prefix-program.json`, `issue_pr_links.json`, `stack-health.json`

Partial mitigation, verified live: `pm-decision-events-sync.service` syncs the decision-events outbox to Turso + the decision-events Worker every 5 min (2026-11-14 11:21 run: `pending=0`). That covers the event stream, not `decisions.json` itself or the other files above. The backup script also still lists the old names `events.json.outbox.jsonl` and `views.json` and logs WARN-missing for both — the allow-list has drifted from the renamed live files.

**Fix shape:** reconcile the aggregator backup allow-list with the live state directory (canonical vs derived per file, named explicitly), add `decisions.json` + decision-events files, and make a required-missing canonical file fail the run instead of WARN.

Acceptance: a daily archive whose manifest contains the decisions ledger + decision-events files, verified by extracting a fresh archive and listing them; drift between the allow-list and live canonical files is caught by the run or the watchdog.

code.title: Federated-search tampering threat model: omission/injection/reordering/staleness and completeness claims
code.body:
## Problem and goal
Federated-search tampering threat model: omission/injection/reordering/staleness and completeness claims as an independently reviewable contract and implementation increment.

## Version and design basis
Version: V4. Settled design: https://github.com/developing-today/code/blob/main/doc/2026-11-13T03-40-00Z_design_id-atlas-summit/part-b/versioned-design.md#component-dispositions-and-statement-coverage (section: **Component dispositions and statement coverage**).
Tier: **contingent**. Start trigger: Research slice deliverable remains scoped; any implementation/adoption is triggered only by the versioned-design evidence threshold or a demonstrated abuse/workload need, and may conclude adopt-none.
Statement IDs: S1.109, S1.110, S1.111, S1.112, S1.113
Enables: Defines what result tampering is detectable and where omission proof is absent.

## Scope and ownership
Parent: #9148 (native component/meta parent).
- `pkgs/id/crates/id-sync/src/federation/slices/b30_search_integrity.rs` (new; owner: B30)
- `pkgs/id/crates/id-sync/tests/federation_b30.rs` (new; owner: B30)
Hard dependencies (native blockers): 9110-02 — Minimum output from #9110-02: root federation/slices registry scaffolding and Cargo convention, with this exact module path recorded but not exported before it exists. Slice PRs do not edit shared roots/Cargo/lib.rs; #9110-09 wires versioned public exports after module outputs land.; B17 — Minimum output: Query/relay/response signature validation, end-to-end responder provenance and stable request identity; stable interface needed by B30.; B29 — Minimum output: Ack/recipient-list contradiction detection, evidence retention, collusion threshold and public-log integration; stable interface needed by B30.
Soft sequencing (not blockers): none

## Test / evidence first
Create or validate `pkgs/id/crates/id-sync/tests/federation_b30.rs` first. Proposed command: `cargo test -p id-sync --test federation_b30`
Oracle: **model** — expected `Invalid injection is rejected; omission is not asserted unless matching completeness claim and proof obligations exist.`; verifier: `Independent reference state machine or golden fixture in the dedicated integration test; cryptographic tests use independent vectors, not the implementation under test.`.

## Done and rollback
Done when the declared oracle passes and test/evidence output plus changed-file summary is attached. Research evidence: not applicable.
Rollback: Mark remote result completeness unknown and stop federated integrity claims; preserve local-only search.

code.body:
## Problem and goal
Allocate a durable projection-ledger sequence for each complete `(tenant, query, generation)` feed entry, while retaining each source authority/epoch/sequence and pinned frontier; cursor `last_projection_seq` drives latest/since/before pages.

## Version and design basis
Version: V3. Settled design: https://github.com/developing-today/code/blob/main/doc/2026-11-13T03-40-00Z_design_id-atlas-summit/part-a-graph/versioned-design.md#7-9128--social-object-graph (section: **7. #9128 — social object graph**).
Tier: **recommended**.
Statement IDs: S5.37, S5.38, S5.39
Enables: Clients check latest/since/before without a full forum rescan and expired cursors never claim no changes.

## Scope and ownership
Parent: #9128 (native component/meta parent).
- `pkgs/id/crates/id-core/src/graph/feed_cursor.rs` (new; owner: A-GRAPH-9128-02)
- `pkgs/id/crates/id-events/tests/feed_cursor_model.rs` (new; owner: A-GRAPH-9128-02)
Hard dependencies (native blockers): A-GRAPH-9127-02 — Accepted server epoch/sequence log.; A-GRAPH-9128-01 — Feed projection and query scope.
Soft sequencing (not blockers): none

## Test / evidence first
Create or validate `pkgs/id/crates/id-events/tests/feed_cursor_model.rs` first. Proposed command: `cargo test -p id-events --test feed_cursor_model`
Oracle: **model** — expected `Two source authorities with identical source epoch/sequence yield distinct, ordered projection entries; latest/since/before use stable projection sequence plus entry ID at a pinned frontier; access/moderation generation changes invalidate; reset, retention gap, bad MAC and query/tenant replay return typed expired/mismatch states.`; verifier: `Independent complete-feed projection-ledger model interleaving two source authorities, restart, deletion/moderation, generation changes and retention gaps.`.

## Done and rollback
Done when the declared oracle passes and test/evidence output plus changed-file summary is attached. Research evidence: not applicable.
Rollback: Invalidate the new cursor generation and require a full scoped refresh; do not change accepted event ordering or claim global replica freshness.

code.title: pm stack: close authority — automation must never close an issue
code.body:
# PM stack: close authority — automation must never close an issue

Program epic from Drew's 2026-11-14 order: "review this entire system end to end and make the best fix possible… make something coherent that doesn't break this way."

## Why this exists

Defect #7610 (CLOSED): Kaneo's GitHub integration closed issues seconds after Refs-only PR merges. Root causes were structural, not a single bad setting:

1. **Close authority was never assigned.** GitHub issue state, `status:*` labels, Kaneo columns, and queue rows are all mirrored state with multiple writers. Kaneo's status sync means *any* move of a linked task to the final column closes the GitHub issue — the close path was a side effect of a board column, owned by nobody.
2. **The dangerous config lived only in a vendor DB.** `integration.config.statusTransitions` is set by nothing in this repo. The connect flow recreates it with the upstream default `onPRMerge: "done"`, and deleting the rule in the UI also falls back to `"done"` (see `pm-stack/KANEO-GITHUB-SYNC.md`).
3. **Loose linking × keyword-blind automation.** PRs link to tasks via any `#n` in the title; the merge handler never checked for a closing keyword.
4. **Silent defaults.** A missing claimant mode file silently means "shadow" (dispatch not-live, no signal); `pm-git-sync` can fail silently, breaking repo→laptop deploys.
5. **The safety net had holes.** Watchdog #10105 v1: no `dezren39/nix` coverage, a 2-hour horizon with an advancing watermark (permanent misses), no pagination, the closing-keyword veto also vetoed the open-sub-issues rule, and `status:done` without a close was invisible.

Victims on record: #5866, #5767, openchamber #1831, #2381, #5772, #9060, #9078, #9106, #9568. **#9060 is still wrongfully closed today** (bot, 2026-11-12T22:48Z, all 12 sub-issues open) — its reopen belongs to the closure-audit pass; it is the standing proof of slice 3 below.

## Target design (decided 2026-11-14; full review + design doc in `doc/`)

- **Source of truth:** GitHub for code-work issue state (reaffirms the 2026-10-24 PM design). Kaneo is the execution board, the queue DB is execution state; projectors/aggregators never write back.
- **Close authority:** a GitHub issue closes ONLY via (i) a GitHub-native closing keyword on a merged PR, (ii) a human closing on GitHub, or (iii) a human deliberately moving the linked Kaneo task to Done. Automation may label and comment; it must never cause a close. (pm-dispatch's compensation close is grandfathered: it may close only issues it created itself, in the same request, on enqueue failure.)
- **Epic invariant:** an issue with open sub-issues is never done — enforced by the watchdog and a periodic sweeper, since GitHub cannot hard-block a close (#9060's own gate design reached the same conclusion).
- **Enforcement layers we own:** (1) repo-declared Kaneo sync guard — the transition config is asserted from the repo at deploy time and hourly, self-healing, drift is loud; (2) closure watchdog v2; (3) the invariant sweeper. Kaneo's loose linking is contained by construction: with no transition allowed to target a closing state, a stray link can at worst move a task to in-review/in-progress.
- **Fail-safe:** missing config must mean "no mutation + a visible health signal", never a silent behavior change.

## Relations

- Contains the watchdog hardening of #10105 (v1, live) — v2 lands under this epic.
- Deployment end-state (Kaneo single manager, flake services, backups) stays with #1752; this epic references it, does not duplicate it.
- #9568 (reporting architecture) C2 event pipeline and C3 health hooks are downstream consumers of this epic's event/invariant surface. The orchestration program is #9196 — this epic is filed as its sub-issue.
- Evidence: #7610 (defect, closed), `pm-stack/KANEO-GITHUB-SYNC.md` (today's config fix: `onPRMerge` → `in-review`, verified live).

## Slices

Filed as sub-issues of this epic; each independently landable.

code.title: watchdog: reopen issues the bot wrongly closes on merges
code.body:
## Problem in plain words

The developing-today[bot] status automation closes GitHub issues seconds after a PR merge that merely references them (Refs-only, no closing keyword) and labels them status:done — defect tracked in #7610. Until the integration rule is fixed at the source (ordered by Drew 2026-11-14), and as a permanent safety net afterwards, nothing watches for these wrongful closures: epic #9106 sat closed for ~14.75 hours (2026-11-12 21:04 CST to 2026-11-13 11:48 CST) before a person noticed, and epic #9078 had an elaboration task wrongly consumed as already_done because the epic looked done.

## What this builds

A closure watchdog polling recent issue-close events in developing-today/code (plus developing-today/opencode and developing-today/openchamber, covered by the same app installation) every 15 minutes. When an automation (in practice developing-today[bot]) closes an issue and either:

- (a) the issue has OPEN sub-issues (native sub-issues API), or
- (b) the closing PR referenced the issue WITHOUT a closing keyword (Closes/Fixes/Resolves #n) in its title/body — i.e. a Refs-only merge,

then the watchdog: reopens the issue, removes the status:done label, posts a short evidence comment (closing actor, close time, closing PR, which rule fired), and reports the reopen to the ID & Atlas Space owner chat.

Legitimate closes (closing keyword present, or a human close with no linked merged PR) are left untouched.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] Watchdog runs on a schedule of at most every 15-30 minutes and keeps a watermark so each close event is processed once.
- [x] Dry-run against the historical #9106 timeline (PR #9184 merged 2026-11-13T03:03:53Z, bot close 03:04:00Z, title reference only, open sub-issues) shows it would have fired both rules.
- [x] Dry-run against the #9078 closure pattern shows rule (a) firing (closed with open components).
- [ ] A live wrongful close (or the verification fixture from #7610) is reopened with status:done stripped and an evidence comment posted.
- [x] No legitimate Closes-keyword close is reopened in dry-run or live operation.

Filed 2026-11-14 under Drew's direct order to fix #7610 and implement this watchdog.

code.title: id: cargo-fmt-check nix derivation unbuildable locally — zig 0.16 OptimizeMode has no 'small' member in the check closure
code.body:
## Finding

The nix derivation for the pkgs/id `cargo-fmt-check` flake check cannot build in a local nix sandbox: it fails while building a zig component in the check's dependency closure, before the fmt recipe ever runs.

Evidence (2026-11-14, laptop, reproduced identically on clean main `bc42ebf2` and on an unrelated fix branch — so it is not diff-caused):

```
$ cd pkgs/id && nix build .#checks.x86_64-linux.cargo-fmt-check --no-link
build.zig:4:78: error: enum 'builtin.OptimizeMode' has no member named 'small'
    const optimize = b.standardOptimizeOption(.{ .preferred_optimize_mode = .small });
note: enum declared in /nix/store/…-zig-0.16.0/lib/zig/std/builtin.zig (OptimizeMode)
```

The check's zig toolchain resolves to zig 0.16.0, whose `OptimizeMode` has no `small` member, while some `build.zig` in the closure (a dependency of the check sandbox, not pkgs/id's own code — pkgs/id has no build.zig) calls `standardOptimizeOption(.{ .preferred_optimize_mode = .small })`.

## Impact

- Any check sharing this mkCheck sandbox shape may be unbuildable locally even when its recipe is green (`cargo fmt -- --check` passes on the same tree), which hides real fmt verdicts behind a toolchain failure and pushes verification to CI runners only.
- Found during #9928's breakage verification: prettier/shellcheck/shfmt/rustfmt check derivations all build locally; cargo-fmt-check's does not, on clean main.

## Acceptance

- `nix build .#checks.x86_64-linux.cargo-fmt-check` succeeds locally on a clean main checkout (the zig component in the closure builds, or the check sandbox no longer depends on it), and the check's verdict again reflects the fmt recipe alone.
- The zig version mismatch is resolved at its source (pin the closure's zig to a version whose OptimizeMode matches the build.zig, or update the build.zig call), not by dropping the check.

code.title: Daily codebase innovation & maintenance
code.body:
Perform a comprehensive daily codebase review, innovation scan, and issue/PR maintenance pass across developing-today/code.

You are acting as an unrestricted principal architect and senior systems engineer. Do not hold back: generate bold ideas, surface hidden gaps, polish proposals, and solve immediate problems opportunistically.
Follow these directives and areas of focus:
### 1. COMPREHENSIVE REPOSITORY & ACTIVITY AUDIT - Inspect recent commits on `main` to understand the latest velocity and architectural direction. - Review open, recently closed, and merged issues and PRs (`gh issue list --state all --limit 50`, `gh pr list --state all --limit 30`). - Review each major package, tool, and subsystem in the repository:
  - **`pkgs/id`**: Distributed identity, cryptographic event log, p2panda synchronization, local event store, group encryption, discovery, and capability delegation.
  - **`pkgs/mcpx`**: Model Context Protocol daemon, multi-server multiplexing, protocol compliance, session leasing, JIT secret prompt vault, and Code Mode projection.
  - **`pkgs/fleet`**: The Rust multicall fleet tools and queue client — automated multi-agent coding workflows, issue triage, and parallel agent execution (the retired packages were removed by PR #5376; audit the fleet queue automation under `pkgs/fleet` and `.github/workflows`, the dispatch actions `.github/actions/pm-dispatch-start` and `.github/actions/pm-dispatch-task`, the scheduler `.github/workflows/pm-scheduled.yml` and its repo-specific scheduled callers, and the CI-breakage automation).
  - **NixOS System Infrastructure & Web Services**: Modules, cloud functions, background daemons, and system services.

### 2. UNRESTRICTED INNOVATION & NEW FEATURE GENERATION - You are NOT restricted by what currently exists. Brainstorm things that *should* exist, would be exceptionally useful, or incorporate frontier concepts:
  - Edge architectures using Cloudflare Workers, Durable Objects, KV, and Queues.
  - Distributed SQLite / libSQL / Turso primitives for offline-first, syncable state.
  - Advanced autonomous coding loops, speculative tool execution, and local verification loops.
  - Cross-platform bridges, native desktop integrations, and performance optimizations.
- **Bias Toward Capture**: It is far better to create an issue to triage later than to let a valuable opportunity or insight pass.
### 3. ACTIVE ISSUE & PR MAINTENANCE - **Scope Variety**: Create single large architectural vision issues for strategic direction, or narrow, highly focused issues for targeted improvements. - **Issue Decomposition**: If an existing issue is too broad, ambiguous, or monolithic (including issues created by others), break it apart into a series of clear, modular, linked sub-issues with explicit dependencies. - **Deduplication & Consolidation**: Identify overlapping or duplicate proposals/issues and consolidate them into unified, high-quality reference issues. - **Comments & Spec Refinement**: Leave comments or edit existing issues/PRs to provide missing technical specifications, edge-case analysis, data schemas, or suggested test cases. - **Zero-Context Hand-off Standard**: Every issue you author must be self-contained, citing exact file paths, interfaces, architectural rationale, and verifiable acceptance criteria so a new agent with zero prior context can execute it.

### 4. OPPORTUNISTIC IMPLEMENTATION (QUICK-WIN PRS) - If you identify straightforward bugs, unhandled edge cases, missing test coverage, or clean opportunities to refactor code to prevent future merge conflicts:
  - You are actively encouraged to open small, focused Pull Requests implementing the fix or feature directly.
  - Ensure all added code follows repository standards, includes tests, and passes formatting/linting hooks (`treefmt`, `conform`).
  - Never introduce breaking regressions to existing stable flows.
  - **One PR per coherent set**: batch every instance of the same problem — and all related dependency updates — into a single PR, or a few PRs split by coherent group. Never one PR per item or per dependency.
  - **Prefer tracked, higher-impact work**: before inventing a new micro-fix, check the open issues and implement the highest-impact one you can complete and verify, even when it spans several files.
  - **Merging is permitted, never required**: merge your PR only when checks pass and you are reasonably certain it is correct and low-risk. Otherwise leave it open and state your confidence and what a human should check in the description.

---
Launched by pm-dispatch for developing-today/code. Queue task and OpenCode session ids follow in a comment below.

code.title: id(phase-14) v3 step 5: review and quota for shared surfaces (#6302)
code.body:
Step 5 of the v3 shared-agent-worlds breakdown (#6302; outline §2.3, §2.4, §6).

**Scope:** review and quota for shared surfaces. "What changed since I was last here" summaries over shared surfaces; above-ceiling requests on shared edits (one-shot approval queue per v2 §2.5, with the request — not a standing widening); refusal digests for shared surfaces ("agent was refused object.export 12 times"); quota attribution (acting agent charged; aggregate per-role spend remains first-class; optional task-carried budget); task-carried budgets if adopted.

**Acceptance:**
- A human visitor/owner sees a delta summary over shared surfaces derived from the audit log.
- An above-ceiling request on a shared edit is held, expires, and executes once on approval under the owner's authority, audited as such; it never edits the role.
- Refusal digests surface repeated refusal shapes for shared surfaces.
- Quota attribution: acting agent charged; per-role aggregate spend visible; no double-charging on handoff.
- Conformance: an approved above-ceiling action does not persist as a ceiling change.

Blocked by v3 step 3 (agent-to-agent task delegation protocol), v3 step 4 (agent-majority worlds and human visitors), and v2 step 4 (owner review tooling, #8302). Parent: #6302 · core topic #6280.

code.title: id(phase-14) v3 step 4: agent-majority worlds and human visitors (#6302)
code.body:
Step 4 of the v3 shared-agent-worlds breakdown (#6302; outline §2.4, §6).

**Scope:** agent-majority worlds and human visitors. World configuration declaring agent-majority status; visitor defaults (presence emphasis, summary cadence, review surface prominence); presence honesty (every agent labelled as an agent with its owner's name — v1 §6.3); visitor affordances (observe shared surfaces, post chat, claim/review tasks per role) without implicit override; "what changed since I was last here" summary for visitors.

**Acceptance:**
- A world can declare itself agent-majority; the declaration is world configuration, readable by any client, not a transport mode.
- A human visitor with a role has exactly that role's ceiling; no silent override of agent work; any override is an explicit, audited owner action.
- Presence honesty holds: no agent may present as a human; an agent's owner name is visible wherever a human's would be.
- Visitor summary renders the delta on shared surfaces since the visitor's last presence, from the audit log (the record of truth).
- Conformance: a visitor cannot perform an action outside their role's ceiling even in an agent-majority world.

Blocked by v3 step 1 (shared work-surface data model). Parent: #6302 · core topic #6280.

code.title: id(phase-14) v3 step 3: agent-to-agent task delegation protocol (#6302)
code.body:
Step 3 of the v3 shared-agent-worlds breakdown (#6302; outline §2.3, §6).

**Scope:** agent-to-agent task delegation protocol — handing work, not authority (v2 §2.4 authority ban stands). Task states (open → claimed → in-progress → review → done/blocked); create/assign/claim/transition operations; atomic claiming at the host (no two agents claim the same task); stale-claim release by owner or timeout; assignment interacts with roles (assignee acts under its own role/ceiling/quota) and quotas (acting agent is charged).

**Acceptance:**
- An agent can create a task on a shared board and assign it to a role (or "any agent holding role X"); assignment is a world state change, not a capability transfer.
- Claiming is atomic: concurrent claims resolve to one claimant; the other receives a refusal, audited.
- A parked/quota-exhausted claimant's task is releasable by owner or timeout; never silently.
- Conformance: no sequence of task operations widens any agent's ceiling (no authority delegation); quota is charged to the acting agent.
- Audit: every create/assign/claim/transition names both agents and the task.

Blocked by v3 step 1 (shared work-surface data model) and v2 step 1 (role configuration, #8299) and v2 step 3 (per-agent quota ledger, #8301). Parent: #6302 · core topic #6280.

code.title: id(phase-14) v3 step 2: concurrency and conflict handling on shared surfaces (#6302)
code.body:
Step 2 of the v3 shared-agent-worlds breakdown (#6302; outline §2.2, §6).

**Scope:** concurrency and conflict handling on shared surfaces. Single-writer-per-revision serialization at the world host; edits carry the revision they were decided against (stale-decision token, v1 §4.3); a conflict surfaces as a stale-decision rejection, never a silent merge; the retry/reconciliation contract agents follow (re-read diff, reconcile, retry).

**Acceptance:**
- Two agents editing the same surface concurrently: the second's stale input is rejected with the current diff; no silent merge or lost update.
- Rejection is an audited world event (v1 §7) and is recoverable by the agent without rejoining.
- Conformance: stale-decision rejection fires on revision mismatch; a host that cannot serialize still refuses rather than merging.
- A scripted scenario proves no lost update across N concurrent editors.

Blocked by v3 step 1 (shared work-surface data model). Parent: #6302 · core topic #6280.

code.title: id(phase-14) v3 step 1: shared work-surface data model — task boards and shared documents as world state (#6302)
code.body:
Step 1 of the v3 shared-agent-worlds breakdown (#6302; outline: `doc/2026-11-14_design_id6302_shared_agent_worlds_v3_outline.md` §2.2, §6).

**Scope:** task boards and shared documents as world-state objects — their schemas (task: title, description, status, assignee, priority, blocked-by, artifacts, history; document: content, per-edit attribution, version history, review state), how they are stored and versioned with the world, role-gated visibility, and how an in-flight session learns a surface changed (region subscriptions / semantic diffs per v1 §4.2).

**Acceptance:**
- Task-board and shared-document schemas recorded in the v3 design and implemented as world configuration/state.
- Surfaces are first-class world state: they survive agent rejoins, are visible to any role granted read access, and are audited on every mutation.
- An agent subscribes to a surface region and receives semantic diffs; a host without the revision still serves at reduced fidelity with identical authority (v1 §4.2).
- Conformance: role without read access cannot read a restricted surface; mutation by an ungranted role is refused and audited.

Extends v1 (#6300) surfaces: region subscriptions / semantic diffs (#7913), MCP bridge (#7914). Extends v2 (#6301): role configuration (#8299). Parent: #6302 · core topic #6280 · principles #1240.

## mcpx release channel 3 (GHCR container image) never published — registry push denied, then the tag trigger was disabled

Follow-up remainder from #1881 (queue task 3114). Everything else on #1881 is live: the `mcpx/v0.1.0` GitHub Release (2026-10-30) carries the three platform tarballs + SHA256SUMS, and the installer channel was exercised green in both the snapshot run (41054027744) and the tag run (41113366617).

**The gap:** channel 3, the container image `ghcr.io/developing-today/code/mcpx`, has never been published.

Evidence:
- Tag run 41113366617 (2026-10-30): build artifacts ✓, installer exercise ✓, publish ✓; the `release: container image` job built the image and died at the registry push — `error from registry: denied` (exit 1). The workflow already declares `packages: write` (top-level permissions in `.github/workflows/mcpx-release.yml`), so the denial is at the GHCR package/org level (first-push package creation / package access for the repo-linked image `ghcr.io/developing-today/code/mcpx`), not a missing workflow scope on its face — root-cause it against the actual package state.
- Since 2026-11-13 the workflow header reads "Automatic tag-push releases disabled by owner" (CI gating change #4636 and the Nov 13 trigger sweep): `on:` is now `workflow_dispatch` only, and the container job only pushes when `github.event_name == 'push'`. So even with the registry denial fixed, no current trigger path publishes the image. Any fix must work within the owner's dispatch-only CI policy (e.g. an explicit dispatch input that publishes the container channel for an existing tag), not silently restore the tag trigger.

**Acceptance:**
- Root cause of the 2026-10-30 GHCR `denied` push recorded on this issue (package existence/access state, not a guess).
- `ghcr.io/developing-today/code/mcpx:0.1.0` (and `:latest` if still the design's intent) pullable, and `docker run ghcr.io/developing-today/code/mcpx:0.1.0 --version` reports 0.1.0.
- The publish path used is compatible with the dispatch-only CI policy, or the policy conflict is escalated with options instead of worked around.
