code.title: Fleet CA, credentials & secrets — v0.3 design mill (Summit build-out)
code.body:
# Fleet CA, credentials & secrets — v0.3 design mill (Summit build-out)

**Program epic.** Design-mill run ordered by Drew 2026-11-12 19:28 CST: run the Fleet v0.3 credentials/secrets/CA package through the design mill — preserve every requirement, break it into reviewed component designs, and turn each design into linked, testable implementation issues. A completed design is NOT a completed implementation epic; implementation children stay open until their own acceptance gates pass.

**Intrinsic urgency: 450 (High)** — ahead of normal actionable work (PM charter bands). Dispatch directive: direct Summit session, launched and verified by the orchestrator (this issue's comments carry the launch receipt).

## Authoritative sources (read as ONE intake; precedence: Drew's current instructions → dated addendum refinements → v0.3 spec baseline → decision review proposals → historical inputs)

1. **Muse handoff — Fleet CA, Credentials & Secrets** (Google Doc, modified 2026-11-12): https://docs.google.com/document/d/1yeSWQvMIer92zQ4lj99TsTH2oXZem0WfH-WMYKYJpJ0
2. **Fleet v0.3 complete package** (`fleet_architecture_v0_3_complete.zip`, SHA-256 `d853a2bacf391856a863c292b21f5a224352a6681dd81fe55c422040b1fb5644`, internal SHA256SUMS all verified at intake): the governing 50-section spec (§§0–49 + Appendix A), `SECRETS_BACKEND_RESEARCH_2026-11-06.md`, `DECISION_REVIEW_AND_NEXT_STEPS.md`, `fleet_agent_handoff_prompt_v0_3.md`, `source_input_3_architectural_perspective.txt`. Drive: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1cdmoblf8yQM2NuXsR2i90N45dABU1EPo/view
3. **Secrets addendum** (architecture/performance/infrastructure follow-up, refines the package): https://docs.google.com/document/d/1QkQMPYGEHbjdyMBdrcSdo4i2GKxlJYK2S3PDrvCRfVw/edit
4. **Summit coordinator handoff** (execution contract for this run): https://docs.google.com/document/d/1AKDACXObRcUwmJIeCfLaGv6bxcWC00e3rYjOztk4qiY/edit
5. Companion PM charter (shared queue/dispatch conventions ONLY — the CA epic stays separate from PM implementation): https://docs.google.com/document/d/1_DQwNbuRmJnITDKKJJ7A3Q0FJa-q2rkzWlz-4PyA_iw/edit

All sources are merged into the repo design directory (see the docs PR linked in comments) and staged on the laptop at `~/.local/share/fleet/intake/fleet-ca-v03-20261112/` (zip hash re-verified after transfer). Repo pinned at intake: `6a7843cae59878e10071f27440b93489053dbc68` (2026-11-12).

## Binding constraints (Drew)

- **ML-DSA-44 is the baseline signature scheme** for the CA design.
- **The Merkle-tree experiment (Cloudflare MTC) is OPTIONAL** — a separate, non-blocking controlled-stack research track; never a v1 dependency. (Handoff doc carries the full MTC analysis: inclusion proofs vs whole certs, landmark/cosigner provisioning, PQ-only separation, byte/CPU/latency comparison against the shortest conventional ML-DSA chain.)

## Scope (from the handoff doc — the CA/credentials workstream, NOT the PM-stack redesign)

Unified secret records + BWS/op/bw adapters (three DIFFERENT provider products — never conflated); daily three-way reconciliation with recoverable `zz.delete` history and false-delete prevention; audit/event journal + provider performance benchmarks; fnox library evaluation (near-term priority); SOPS/age/NixOS integration; password, SSH and iroh generation; reusable Rust APIs + the existing Fleet multicall CLI (no competing tool); PKI root/issuer/leaf lifecycle, publication, packaging, client trust and verification; nonblocking OpenBao/federation/infrastructure research.

**Reference PKI (spec controls):** four independent roots (Ed25519, P-256, RSA, ML-DSA-44), nine asymmetric root cross-certificates (ML-DSA root never signs classical roots by default), Base + Internal Web issuer sets with independent A/B partitions and eligible direct issuer cross-signatures — **20 CA key pairs / 65 CA certificate variants before leaves**. Reference expiries: roots `2050-07-07T12:00:00Z`, both issuer sets `2032-07-07T12:00:00Z` (distinct from the normal 20y/5y/90d defaults). RSA-2048 is a policy-gated compatibility option, not the default long-lived root. Root signing always requires an explicitly authorized signer source — never silently discover/exercise root keys.

**Root custody (addendum refinement):** initial roots escrowed to exactly three approved destinations — encrypted laptop storage, the authorized BWS project, the authorized 1Password vault — with integrity checks and tested restoration; NOT auto-extended to every future provider. R2 is a researched additional destination, not automatic authorization. Offline/hardware root signing is the future path; three OpenBao containers on one host are a lab, not three failure domains.

## V1 — what exists today (intake census; the Summit verifies and deepens)

- `fleet` multicall (laptop build, source rev `743966553e`) domains: queue, serve, proxy, dispatch, secrets, gh, search, laptop-agent. **No `cert`/`pki` or `generate` domain exists yet.**
- `fleet secrets get|list`: broker-first resolution with BWS fallback; name-only references; values never printed. The secrets broker is in production (see #6767 for a known broker staleness defect). No `put`, no reconciliation, no 1Password adapter in the CLI yet.
- `pkgs/fleet/crates/`: fleet, fleet-config, fleet-dispatch, fleet-proxy, fleet-proxy-proto, fleet-queue, fleet-registry, fleet-search, fleet-secrets.
- No prior Fleet v0.3 / PKI / ML-DSA / fnox / zz.delete program issues exist (searched at intake) — this epic and its domain starters are the canonical home. The earlier submission was cancelled per the handoff; nothing was launched from it.

## Safety gates (hard)

Design and synthetic proof only in this program phase. **No production CA generation or signing, no root escrow/export, no live vault writes or reconciliation, no credential rotation, no DNS/trust changes, no live service deployment** is authorized by this handoff. Synthetic fixtures must never be confused with production credentials. Design, synthetic proof, code implementation, and production rollout are separately statused.

## Build-out (Summit owns; design-mill pattern)

Statement inventory (every requirement in the spec + addendum + handoffs, numbered, zero unmapped) → state-of-the-art expansion per component → versioned designs (V1 = exists today; V2+ layer) → ADRs/threat model → granular implementation/test/research issues with measurable acceptance, source IDs, boundaries, tests, rollback → batched questions recorded on THIS issue with chosen defaults (never stall). Domain starter issues are native sub-issues of this epic; the Summit files the granular children under them.

## Supervision

Orchestrator check-ins on the bound Summit session (status, questions, artifacts vs the statement inventory); stall = one nudge, then replacement, recorded here. Durable monitor: the fleet's session-minder coverage plus the supervision record in this issue's comments.

## P-384 ADR — merge remainder (lane oc-code-03, 2026-11-23)

Refs #13778 — the P-384 root-identity dated design-record PR is open (branch certprog/p384-adr, head da81369e67c005fc4ff1e6922470e9466b98a1f8; two files: the new record folder plus one doc/README.md index line). The evidence record on #9163 (comment 7114665610) states READY TO MERGE. The lane does not merge; Archer merges via the GitHub API from that record. Bridging by cross-signing stays behind the production gate.

code.title: research(id): takeover resistance + acknowledgment-based inconsistency detection
code.body:
Program #9106 (extensible primitives / federation / namespaces), Drew directive 2026-11-12 18:29 CST.
Parent: #9108.

§1. Threat design: a highly trusted server is taken over (or waits until trusted) and begins behaving inappropriately — including tampering with search results. Worked detection: acknowledgments make lying expensive — if A answers 'don't have it' while B produces the recipient list showing the data was sent to A, one of them is provably wrong; defeating detection requires collusion across servers. All transfers are signed and ALL signatures still validated, always. Specify what's logged, what's provable, and the response playbook when a contradiction is detected. Acceptance: evidence-backed research note merged under doc/ and linked from the parent epic, with a recommendation the sibling designs can build on; open questions recorded, not silently settled.

code.title: epic: ID/Atlas extensible primitives, federation, namespaces — major design iteration (2026-11-12 directive)
code.body:
# Program: ID/Atlas extensible primitives, federation, namespaces

**Source:** Drew directive, 2026-11-12 18:29 CST (clarifies and greatly extends the hosted-editions program #9078). Filed via design-mill intake; the summit elaboration is queued as a design-mill task pointing at this issue.

## What this program is

A new major design iteration for the ID substrate and its Atlas-facing surfaces, in three parts:

- **Part A — ID core** (namespaces, ID shapes, triples, user attributes): the addressing and data model everything else stands on.
- **Part B — federation & trust**: how peer servers exchange signed data, sync, fan out queries, and earn or lose trust.
- **Part C — Atlas-facing economics & discovery**: storage benchmarks/economics, ID search, recommendations.

Program-level items (§0 extensibility architecture, §7 modes/configuration, refine-and-prioritize) sit directly under this epic.

**Why three parts, not one flat list:** the directive itself splits this way — one part Atlas, one part ID, one part the federation layer both share. The parts have different design tempos (Part A is data model, Part B is protocol/trust, Part C is measurement-driven) and different nearest neighbors (#2056 ID designs; #9083 tenancy; #8983 Atlas). One program epic keeps the statement inventory whole: nothing in the directive belongs to only one audience, and the summit owns cohesion across the parts.

## Clarification of record (§0)

Extensibility IS the architecture goal. Primitives, adapters, and hooks are **designed** for the full matrix of stores / buckets / streams / transports from the start. What was de-prioritized in #9078/#9082's framing is **implementing** the long tail now — the earlier "plumbing, not a matrix" line stands as an implementation priority, NOT as an architecture limit. Both tier-1 editions (Rust binaries, Cloudflare/Turso hosted) are fully featured; neither is a reduced edition. Everything behavioral is configuration where it is behavior, primitives where it is mechanism (§7). Our system is not special: every capability is a config option anyone could replicate by investing the same effort.

## Inputs / feeds

- Feeds into and amends: #9078 (hosted editions), #9082 (store abstraction), #9083 (tenancy), #9084 (content plane), #9085 (TS transports), Atlas starter #9091 and VFS #9100, ID epic #2056 (parent).

- Statement inventory: numbered S0–S7 in the proto design; every statement maps to a component issue under this epic or to a named existing issue. Zero unmapped is the intake acceptance bar; the summit verifies it again (mill return-on-agreement).

## Acceptance

- [ ] Statement inventory verified complete by the summit + a fresh judge pass (zero unmapped).
- [ ] Versioned designs (V1 = what exists today; V2+ layer the vision) merged under `doc/` for each part, or the part explicitly folded into an existing design by amendment with the link recorded here.
- [ ] Granular implementation issues filed under the component issues for everything implementable.

code.title: design(atlas): virtual filesystem over the content-addressed store + aggregated file index (Basin/Parquet evaluation)
code.body:
## Workstream H — Virtual filesystem over the content-addressed store

Parent program: #8983 · Proto design §H · **References, does not restate:** #9084 (content plane: addressing, GC, sensitivity tiers — the store this filesystem sits on) and #3125 (Atlas provenance/occurrence registry — in-domain prior art; the occurrence registry is this design's closest ancestor).

### The model (Drew, 2026-11-12)

- Content lands **content-addressed and immutable**: bytes are uploaded once and never change.
- **Paths are a first-class abstraction over the bytes** — a rough virtual filesystem. "Find everything referencing `geordi.png`" returns every path/location naming those bytes, across hosts and stores.
- The same bytes in five places = **one upload + five metadata records**. Each location record carries its own metadata: the path, the host it came from, the date, the process that produced/placed it — attached as metadata on the embeds/records for that location.
- Locations are editable/addable without touching the bytes: adding a sixth place that references the same content adds a metadata record, nothing else.

### Aggregated index (the performance rule)

Byte-hash and filename lookups must **not** scan the whole Atlas corpus's metadata. The virtual-file index is **aggregated**: its own Turso database, or dedicated tables maintained beside the bucket (a sidecar manifest/index uploaded alongside the content-addressed data so the bucket works standalone), with lookups by hash, by filename, by path prefix, and by host.

### Big-data evaluation (required, not optional)

Evaluate whether the aggregated metadata belongs in a big-data system instead of / beside the Turso index:

- **Parquet** (file-format lake over R2),
- **Cloudflare Basin** (verified: GA 2026-10-01; the renamed Cloudflare Data Platform — Apache Iceberg over R2: Basin Pipelines for ingest, Basin Catalog for table maintenance, Basin SQL for serverless queries over Iceberg tables; an analytics/lakehouse fit, not a transactional store),
- or another system the research surfaces — judged on lookup latency for the VFS query shapes (hash, filename, prefix), update cost under constant ingestion (workstream E), and operational weight.

### Acceptance

- [ ] Design merged under `doc/`: the location-record schema (aligned with workstream C doctrine), the aggregated index shape, and the VFS query set (by hash, filename, path, host) with latency expectations.
- [ ] The big-data evaluation published with a verdict (Turso index / Parquet / Basin / hybrid) and its evidence.
- [ ] Worked example in the design: one image at five locations — records, lookups, and what a rename/move/deletion of one location does (and does not do) to the others.
- [ ] Granular implementation issues filed; #9084 and #3125 cross-linked from the design.

code.title: impl(atlas): query-as-data — query embeds, full tool/parameter provenance, permanent result archive, versioning
code.body:
## Workstream G — Query-as-data, permanent result archive, and versioning

Parent program: #8983 · Proto design §G · Foundations already filed: #8245 (query trace capture — query_id + atlas-query-trace/v1), #8246 (trace ingestion + retention), #7647 (per-candidate embedding_model provenance), #8247 (retrieval statistics), #6027 (the statistics/feedback/traces design), #6805 + #8312 (Worker cache policy + purge route).

### The rules (Drew, 2026-11-12)

1. **Every query is ingested into the corpus.** A query is not just executed: it becomes an **embed stored in Atlas itself**, and that embed is what attaches to its results. Query records carry, verbatim: **every flag, parameter, and the query text**; the **disclosure context** (workstream D) the search ran under; and the **hash + version of every tool involved** (search binary/service, embedder model revision, corpus snapshot/watermark, schema version per workstream C).
2. **Cache everything, maybe forever.** All results are cached (workstream A sets the serving semantics); this workstream owns the **archive**: investigate storing cache/result data **forever** so the same query's results can be compared across time (corpus changes, embedder changes, planner changes). Storage growth of the archive is modeled, not hand-waved — the archive is itself corpus (classified, per workstream D) and inside the backup mesh (workstream B).
3. **Versioning everywhere:** every Cloudflare Worker deploy is versioned and recorded; the Turso and D1 **schemas are versioned** (schema-version registry + migration discipline aligned with workstream C's additive doctrine where it applies to stored metadata).

### Acceptance

- [ ] Design merged under `doc/`: the query-record schema (extending atlas-query-trace/v1, not replacing it silently), the query-embed ingestion path, and the result-archive retention model with growth math.
- [ ] Tool-provenance capture specified: which tools, which hash (binary/source) and version strings, where recorded.
- [ ] Deploy + DB schema versioning specified: where the version registry lives and how a search answer can cite the versions that produced it.
- [ ] Granular implementation issues filed, cross-linked to #8245/#8246/#7647 rather than duplicating them.

code.title: bench(atlas): embed-storage economics — vectors+hash+metadata in Turso, raw content content-addressed (feeds #9084)
code.body:
## Workstream F — Embed-storage economics: vectors in Turso, raw content content-addressed

Parent program: #8983 · Proto design §F · **References, does not restate:** #9084 (content-addressed plane — its reference-vs-copy-vs-hybrid evaluation and GC design own the general question; this workstream is the Atlas-specific measurement feeding it) and #3125 (Atlas provenance registry / content-addressed extracts — prior art in-domain).

### The question (Drew, 2026-11-12)

Can Turso store **the embeddings + a content-addressed hash of the value + per-embed metadata**, while the **raw content lives in the R2 / RustFS / Drive content-addressed system** — saving Turso space without R2 costing more than the saving, and without unacceptable latency? This must be **tested and confirmed with measurements**, not argued.

### Context numbers (verified 2026-11-12)

- Turso Scaler storage: 11 GB of the 24 GB cap used, **overages OFF** — Turso space is a hard constraint, which is what makes offload valuable.
- Atlas monolith 7.3 GB; the Snowflake vector table for 107,639 chunks at F32_BLOB(768) is ~331 MB raw — the design must account for what fraction of the 7.3 GB is vectors vs raw content vs FTS before claiming savings.
- R2 Standard: $0.015/GB-month, egress free.
- Offload path shape: content in R2 → fallback laptop → later the lab RustFS store (#9087); a **hot cache in Turso/D1** for frequently-hit content is part of the design space.

### Scope

1. **Composition audit:** where the atlas DBs' bytes actually are (vectors / chunk text / messages / FTS / indexes), per store (monolith, 29 topic shards, secret tier).
2. **Prototype + measurement:** a representative corpus slice served both ways (content-in-Turso vs hash+reference to R2) — storage delta, $ delta both sides, and latency delta on hydration-heavy queries (get-chunk, expand, with-message), including the hot-cache variant.
3. **Consistency rules:** what an embed record may assume about its content reference (immutability, GC interplay — resolved WITH #9084's GC design, not independently), and the failure mode when content is unreachable (degraded result vs error).
4. **Verdict + migration shape:** adopt / adopt-for-cold-only / reject, with the numbers; if adopt, the migration is staged per shard class and never a flag day.

### Acceptance

- [ ] Research/bench doc merged under `doc/` with the composition audit and both-ways measurements (storage, cost, latency).
- [ ] A verdict recorded with evidence, and — if adopt — granular implementation issues filed; the verdict is commented onto #9084 as its Atlas input.
- [ ] No part of this issue settles #9084's general reference-vs-copy question; the cross-reference is explicit in the doc.

The staging tier exists in code with a promote gate; the aggregator/embedder and session-close hook slices are not built.

### Sources (Drew's list, 2026-11-12 — all internal-use only, never exposed directly to public)

1. Turso queue data (fleet-queue) and PM stack data (aggregator state, boards, reconcile).
2. **All GitHub issues / PRs / commits / files for all orgs and repos** in scope (developing-today, developing-today-forks, Clustered-Computing, personal) — extending #6023 beyond its first pass.

### Rules

- Delta-only where the source supports it (#6028); full re-ingest is the exception, and re-embeds follow the mixed-embedder support in workstream A/C (no flag-day re-embeds).

### Acceptance

code.title: design(atlas+pm): Metadata schema v1 + evolution doctrine — additive-only, extras, strict enums, breaking-change parking lot
code.body:
## Workstream C — Metadata schema v1 + evolution doctrine (Atlas corpus AND issue/PR Metadata)

Parent program: #8983 · Proto design §C (the doctrine's canonical text lives there) · Shared with the PM program: #9060 design §12, slices #9073 (fleet Metadata superset) and #9074 (metadata DB + query) — amendments recording this doctrine are filed against both.

### Why

Every Atlas item and every issue/PR carries Metadata. Classifications layered on later — by agents who will NOT hold permission to rewrite the schema — only work if the schema evolves without breaking old data. Drew's doctrine (2026-11-12): **old metadata is as valid as new metadata; older embeds must run under a newer system; no dual-schema support burden.**

### The doctrine (to be specified in full; proto design §C is the draft)

1. **Version always carried.** Every Metadata object — corpus item, embed, issue, PR — includes its schema version (`pm_meta` for issue/PR Metadata per #9060 §12; the Atlas metadata schema carries its own version field). Writers write the current version; **readers accept every prior version indefinitely**.
2. **Additive-only by default.** A version bump may add fields and add enum values (where the enum allows). It may **never remove a field** and **never make an optional field required**.
3. **Breaking changes are parked, then batched.** Required-ification and deprecations go to a single **breaking-changes parking lot** (a named doc/issue location). When the parked set justifies it, the set is applied as **one version event**, followed by a **reclassify-everything pass** over the corpus/items. Prudent, rare, no churn.
4. **Extras policy.** The schema accepts unlisted data: unlisted keys live in an **`extras`** dictionary attribute on the object (the design evaluates root-level extras as an alternative and records why the chosen shape wins). **Type-directed handling:** a value whose type mismatches the declared field type is treated as an extra (relocated to `extras`), never an error. **Coercion rules:** values that losslessly convert may coerce (int-array into a string-array field is allowed; the reverse only when each value actually converts). Non-converting values relocate to `extras` unchanged.
5. **Strict core enums.** `kind`, `area`, `group`, `sensitivity` (at minimum) are documented strict value sets in the schema. Each enum declares whether it is **closed** (no extra values) or **open** (extra values accepted and preserved). **Invalid value in a safety enum defaults to the most locked-down value** — e.g. a typo'd `sensitivity` becomes the schema's most restrictive value, never the most permissive.
6. **Optional means optional forever.** Optional attributes are knowingly hard to filter/sort on; that is accepted (workstream A/G index what's extracted, the rest rides along). Optionality + versioning is the backwards-compatibility mechanism; classifying agents may add extras and classifications within the current version without schema changes.

### Scope

- The Atlas corpus metadata schema v1 (per-item + per-embed: identity, content hash, source, chunking, embedder identity + model revision, classifications per workstream D, provenance, extras) — aligned with the staging schema `atlas_stage_v1` and manifest practice where they exist.
- The issue/PR Metadata alignment: #9060 §12's block gains the version doctrine (its `pm_meta: 1` becomes a governed version, with the same additive/parking-lot rules); #9073's required-field injection and #9074's extraction must implement "readers accept all versions".
- The parking lot itself: location, entry format, and the version-event + reclassify procedure.

### Acceptance

- [ ] Schema v1 document(s) merged under `doc/` for Atlas metadata; the doctrine text merged once, canonically, and referenced (not copied) by the PM-side amendment.
- [ ] Amendments/comments landed on #9073 and #9074 binding them to the doctrine; #9060 design cross-linked.
- [ ] Parking lot created with the entry format and the version-event procedure; seeded with any already-known candidate breaking changes (or explicitly empty).
- [ ] A conformance fixture set: metadata at every historical version parses and is usable by the current reader (extends #8525–#8528 fixture family practice).

code.title: research(atlas): OpenCode DB backup economics — copy vs zstd vs restic-delta cost + growth model
code.body:
## Research — OpenCode DB backup economics + growth model

Parent program: #8983 · Feeds workstream B (backup mesh) · Proto design §B.

### Known (measured 2026-11-12, laptop production)

- `/home/user/.local/share/opencode/opencode.db` = **21,368,037,376 B (19.9 GiB)**, ~448 MB internal freelist; **net allocated growth Nov 2 → Nov 12 = 0 bytes** (two dated full copies beside the DB are byte-identical in size); it was ~26 GB in the past and was pruned/vacuumed down. Drew: the DB stays large; do not propose shrinking it as the answer.
- Measured zstd sample ratio on raw pages: **23.8% (~4.2:1)** → full compressed copy ≈ **5.1 GB**.
- R2 Standard pricing $0.015/GB-month, egress free → at today's size: raw copy ≈ **$0.32/mo**, zstd copy ≈ **$0.08/mo**, restic compressed+dedupe retention set ≈ **$0.09–0.14/mo** (at an assumed 1–5% daily page churn — churn is UNMEASURED). Storage price is not the constraint; restore time and upload bandwidth are.
- Current backups: none scheduled/off-laptop. Manual `just opencode-db-backup` copies exist as a mechanism only.

### Research questions

1. **True churn rate:** measure daily changed-page volume (WAL/page deltas over ≥7 days) so the restic-delta size is evidence, not assumption.
2. **Growth model:** what drives growth (sessions/messages/parts/events/route tables), per-table sizes (dbstat timed out in the first pass — get it via a bounded method), and a 6–12 month projection under current fleet usage, including the freelist-absorption effect.
3. **Scheme comparison, costed monthly at projected sizes:** (a) periodic full copy, (b) periodic zstd full copy, (c) restic zstd-stream deltas — each to **Google Drive + the laptop archive location** (Drew's named targets for this DB), with restore-time measurements for each scheme, not just storage cost.
4. **Consistency:** the safe capture method for a live 21 GB SQLite DB (online backup API vs snapshot vs brief quiesce) and its cost in time/IO on the production laptop.

### Acceptance

- [ ] Research doc merged under `doc/` with: measured churn, per-table breakdown, growth projection, and a costed table (storage $/mo + restore time) for the three schemes × two targets.
- [ ] A recommendation stated with its evidence; the chosen scheme becomes an implementation issue under workstream B.

Downstream implementation gate: Refs #13462. The OpenCode session DB leg proceeds after this research records the selected backup scheme.

code.title: impl(atlas/fleet): backup mesh — all-Turso 14d restic-zstd to R2, R2/laptop/Drive mesh, D1+laptop DBs into Turso
code.body:
## Workstream B — Backup mesh (Turso / R2 / laptop / Google Drive)

Parent program: #8983 · Proto design: `doc/2026-11-12T23-59-00Z_design_atlas_v1_proto/note.md` §B · Starter: the Atlas v1 design-mill starter issue (sibling).

### Current state (verified 2026-11-12)

- 40 Turso databases (~9.4 GB summed; plan meter 11 GB), Scaler plan, overages OFF (24 GB storage is a hard wall). Turso PITR: any point within 30 days on Scaler — **but Delete Protection is OFF on every database checked** (`atlas`, `fleet-queue`, `fleet-platform`), and PITR cannot resurrect a deleted DB beyond the 5-day deleted-DB window.
- Existing pieces: `atlas-backup` daily (local canonical atlas DB → laptop + R2 `supabase-backups` + Drive, #1515); `repo-archive-backup` daily restic to three repos (local, R2, Drive) with check + retention; `supabase-backup` twice-daily; `cold-store-nightly` exports **every** Turso DB → Drive — **its 2026-11-12 run FAILED (30-min start timeout, killed; which step timed out is unconfirmed)**, so the Turso→Drive leg is currently at risk. Coverage audit gaps: #1516. A local restic repo `~/backups/restic/laptop-state/` exists with **no identified writer** (unconfirmed).
- The OpenCode DB has **no scheduled or off-laptop backup** (economics: sibling research issue).

### Scope — the mesh

Cadence: **every Turso database backed up on a 10–15 day cycle (~14 days)**; Turso's own 30-day PITR covers the window until a backup ages past 30 days, after which the restic chain is the protection.

1. **Turso → R2:** per-DB restic backup as compressed deltas (stream-zstd) into R2 — replacing/augmenting today's full-export leg with delta efficiency; restore-tested.
2. **R2 → laptop and R2 → Google Drive:** the mesh is R2↔laptop↔Drive↔R2 plus Turso into all three stores; every store can rebuild any other. Retention per leg specified.
3. **D1 + laptop DBs → Turso** where appropriate (D1 exports and laptop-local DBs land in the Turso side of the mesh as their backup home), with the appropriateness line drawn explicitly.
4. **Embeds backup:** the embedding stores (vector tables / shard DBs) are inside the same mesh — a restore must be able to rebuild search without a re-embed pass.
5. **Hardening findings folded in:** enable Turso Delete Protection fleet-wide (or record why not, per DB); fix or replace the failing cold-store-nightly Turso export leg; identify or retire the orphan `laptop-state` restic repo; keep the freshness watchdog (#1841) as the verification surface, with every mesh leg restore-verified on a schedule, not just backup-verified.
6. Sequencing with #9060/#9078 hosting work: the mesh must not depend on the hosted editions existing; it protects today's laptop+Turso shape and extends to per-user Turso DBs (#9083) when they arrive.

### Acceptance

- [ ] Design doc merged under `doc/`: mesh topology diagram/table (source → leg → store → retention), the 14-day cadence mechanics per DB class, and the PITR-vs-restic protection argument per age band (0–30d, >30d).
- [ ] Delete Protection disposition recorded per database.
- [ ] cold-store-nightly failure root-caused or the leg replaced by the mesh design; the interim risk is named on #1516.
- [ ] Granular implementation issues filed (per leg + per DB class), each with a restore-verification acceptance step.

code.title: impl(atlas-search): search v1 — build-out, Workers fan-out, shard benchmarks, cache policy, second embedder
code.body:
## Workstream A — Search subcommand build-out + Workers fan-out

Parent program: #8983 · Proto design: `doc/2026-11-12T23-59-00Z_design_atlas_v1_proto/note.md` §A · Starter: the Atlas v1 design-mill starter issue (sibling).

### Current state (verified 2026-11-12)

`atlas-search` / `fleet search`: one-stage hybrid (FTS5/BM25 + Snowflake cosine, RRF k=10) over a 7.3 GB Turso monolith (107,639 chunks) + 29 topic shards. The shard fan-out path is a hidden experimental flag (`--shards`, #5755); the production default is the monolith scan. Contract flags for the query planner, spell correction, query-class hint, and `rewritten|both` variants are **accepted but unimplemented**. The Cloudflare Worker cache (one Durable Object per query key) caches results **indefinitely — no TTL, eviction, or invalidation** (#6805 open; gated purge route #8312). No result caching in the standalone CLI (#5668). Query-understanding front-end and parameter surface are open designs #5773/#5774.

### Scope

1. **Search v1 build-out:** implement the dead contract surface or formally retire each flag — planner (query understanding per #5773), spell, query-class hint, rewritten/both variants; Jaccard third signal per #5733 where it earns its place. Every advertised flag either works or is removed from the contract.
2. **Workers fan-out:** make the hosted search path fan out across Workers/Durable Objects/shards as the default serving shape: parallel shard queries, connection fan-out, DO roles (coordination, hot shards, cache). Respect platform limits in the design (Paid: 1,000 subrequests/invocation; DO SQLite 10 GB/object) — wider fan-out chains via queues/multiple invocations.
3. **Shard-size benchmark programme (own deliverable):** benchmark latency vs shard size and shard count across Turso shards AND D1, on the production corpus shape. **Named oracle:** p50/p95 end-to-end query latency at fixed recall@10 against the standing eval sets (#8627) — a shard configuration wins only at equal-or-better recall. Output: a measured shard-size recommendation + the fan-out width curve (where more parallelism stops helping).
4. **Cache policy:** results cached until the corpus changes; on corpus change, cached results may serve for a short, specified staleness window UNLESS the caller passes a real-time requirement or a cache-disable flag (both become first-class search flags, in the CLI, the service protocol, and the Worker). Builds on #6805's eviction/invalidation policy and #8312's purge route; the corpus-change signal (ingest watermark) is defined with workstream E.
5. **Second embedder:** evaluate a second embedding approach alongside Snowflake arctic-embed-m-v2.0 (candidates to evaluate, not pre-picked: BGE-M3, Voyage, OpenAI text-embedding-3, Workers AI models — judged on quality vs the eval sets, cost, self-hostability, and mixed-embedder corpus support under the workstream C schema). Per-corpus model identity already exists as a concept (#8623); v1 must support mixed embedders in one corpus without a flag-day re-embed.

### Acceptance

- [ ] Design doc(s) merged under `doc/` covering items 1–5, with the benchmark programme's protocol (corpus snapshot, query set, oracle) specified before any benchmark runs.
- [ ] Benchmark results published in the design or a linked research doc: latency/recall table per shard size × count, Turso and D1, with the chosen configuration named.
- [ ] Cache semantics specified exactly: invalidation trigger, staleness window value, real-time + cache-disable flag names and behavior at every surface (CLI/service/Worker).
- [ ] Granular implementation issues filed for each build item; dead-flag disposition (implement vs retire) recorded per flag.

code.title: design(fleet): second version in TypeScript — scope, WASM evaluation, transports (REST/WebSocket), and direct-Turso prudence rules
code.body:
Component **G** of epic #9078 (hosted editions program). Design first (design mill, under #9078). This is the program's cross-cutting runtime/transport design; components A–C consume its verdicts.

## Premise (Drew, 2026-11-12)

Workers limitations mean the hosted editions are substantially **a second version written in TypeScript**. The design says so plainly and scopes exactly what 'second version' covers — PM service (A), ID service (B), fleet tool (C) — and what is NOT rewritten.

## Scope of the design

1. **Rewrite-vs-WASM per component**: client-side WASM is allowed in selected areas. For each piece of Rust logic (ID crypto and store logic are the named candidates), evaluate: compile to WASM and reuse / rewrite in TypeScript / keep server-side only. Criteria: correctness risk (crypto!), maintenance divergence between two implementations of the same semantics, bundle/runtime limits.
2. **Transports**: ALL base functions must work over REST or WebSocket transports (HTTP/2/3, QUIC where the platform provides it). Define the base-function inventory per component and the transport contract for each (request/response vs streaming vs realtime sync), including offline/reconnect behavior.
3. **Direct Turso access**: also allowed — to the user's OWN database and to the PUBLIC database — 'when prudent'. This design defines prudent: which operations may go direct (reads? writes? sync?), under what credential scoping/expiry (from component E), and which operations must NEVER bypass the service layer (anything needing stamping, authorization beyond the DB scope, or cross-tenant access).
4. **Shared-semantics discipline**: how the TS version and the Rust/native version keep one data model (Metadata, packets, store contracts) — shared schemas/fixtures/tests, and what happens when they diverge.

## Builds on / relations

- Components A, B, C, D, E under #9078 (D's WASM question feeds §1; E's credential model feeds §3).
- #5671 — ID transport fallback for UDP-denied networks (transport prior art inside the ID program).

## Acceptance

- [ ] Design merged under doc/ as part of #9078's build-out: per-component rewrite/WASM table, base-function transport inventory, direct-Turso prudence rules.
- [ ] Granular implementation issues filed under this issue or handed to the owning component issues with cross-links.

code.title: design(pm-stack): content-addressed media/data plane — R2 dedup, reference-based access, GC when the last reference drops
code.body:
Component **F** of epic #9078 (hosted editions program). Design first (design mill, under #9078). This carries the program's CENTRAL open question.

## Drew's sketch (posed, not decided — 2026-11-12)

Media is **content-addressed and deduped in R2**. Sensitivity tiers decide placement and access: R2 with access controls, CDN for public content, or inside the Turso DB where that fits.

Because everything is already Turso/Cloudflare, maybe data does NOT need to be copied into each database: **the DB holds IDs/references; the content lives once in R2** and can be garbage-collected only when ALL references drop. Access rule candidate: a user may access an object iff their DB holds a reference to it, OR the object is public-published in one or more DBs.

## Alternatives the design must evaluate against the sketch

1. Reference-only (Drew's sketch above).
2. Copy-into-each-DB (content replicated per tenant DB).
3. Hybrid (small content inline in DB, large content referenced in R2; or hot/cold split by sensitivity/size).

Evaluation axes: storage cost under dedup, access-control soundness (can a reference be forged or enumerated?), GC correctness (reference counting vs mark-and-sweep across many DBs; races with new references), deletion/privacy (a user deleting content others still reference; jurisdiction rules per #3401), latency (extra hop through R2 vs local rows), and what 'published public' means mechanically.

## Builds on / relations

- Tenancy: component E under #9078 (per-user DBs + public DB are where references live). Turso + Cloudflare epic: #8987 (R2, CDN).
- #3401 — isolate hosted blobs by jurisdiction and minimize shared directory (ID hosted blobs; the sensitivity/jurisdiction input).
- Atlas's content-addressed provenance work (#3125) is a DIFFERENT domain — prior art to consult, not a dependency.

## Acceptance

- [ ] Design merged under doc/ as part of #9078's build-out: the three models compared on the axes above; a recommendation recorded — decided in the mill or batched to Drew with options + recommendation.
- [ ] Sensitivity tier table: which content classes go R2-private / R2 + CDN / in-DB, and the access check for each.
- [ ] GC design: reference tracking home (tenancy DB? per-DB?), collection safety argument.
- [ ] Granular implementation issues filed under this issue.

code.title: epic: hosted editions — PM service, ID service, and fleet tool as workable Cloudflare Workers equivalents (multi-tenant Turso/R2 architecture)
code.body:
## Program (Drew's directive, 2026-11-12 16:58 CST)

The PM stack and pkgs/id cannot run on Cloudflare Workers today. Build **workable equivalents** of the PM service, the ID service, and the fleet tool for the Workers world, on a multi-tenant data architecture. This is a large multi-part design program: it runs through the **design mill** — this epic is the starter issue; the design is produced by a summit session owning the queue item for this epic, in the mill pattern (statement inventory → state-of-the-art expansion → versioned designs → granular implementation issues). Component issues A–H below carry the open design questions; the mill's designs answer them and spawn the granular implementation issues.

Drew's sketch, in substance:

- **Per-user ID databases in Turso** plus a **central tenancy database**, handled and served by Workers and Durable Objects. Hosted per-user instances connect and sync their data; everyone can also connect to a large **public database** we offer.
- **Media/content plane:** media content-addressed and deduped in **R2**, with sensitivity tiers deciding placement and access (R2 + access controls, CDN for public content, or inside the Turso DB where that fits). Central open question (posed, not decided): because everything is Turso/Cloudflare, maybe data is **not copied into each DB** — a DB holds IDs/references and the content lives once in R2, garbage-collectable only when **all** references drop; a user may access an object iff their DB holds a reference to it, or it is public-published in one or more DBs. Copy-into-each-DB and hybrid models are evaluated against this sketch.
- **Transports:** Workers limitations mean this is substantially a **second version in TypeScript** — the design says so plainly and scopes it. Client-side **WASM** is allowed in selected areas (evaluate per component what Rust logic — e.g. ID crypto/store logic — compiles to WASM vs must be rewritten). All base functions must work over **REST or WebSocket** transports (HTTP/2/3, QUIC where the platform provides it). **Direct Turso access** to the user's own DB and to the public DB is also allowed when prudent, under the tenancy/auth rules.
- **ID data stores:** ID gains **Turso/SQLite-over-HTTP as a database store in addition to redb**, and **IndexedDB** is evaluated for the browser client — one storage interface, pluggable backends.
- **Identity:** the hosted services are relying parties for #9077 (GitHub/Google/Microsoft login gated to Drew + devtoday OIDC provider with roles + account linking); the tenancy account model lines up with #9077/#1253's roles. Identity itself is NOT re-designed here.

## Components (each its own issue under this epic)

- **A.** PM service, Workers edition — TypeScript equivalent of aggregator/dashboard/reconcile as one hosted service.
- **B.** ID service, Workers edition — the missing pieces on top of the existing serverless line (#5524, #5681, #3811).
- **C.** Fleet tool, Workers/TypeScript equivalent — hosted Metadata stamping/query, session provenance, sync tools.
- **D.** ID store abstraction — Turso/SQLite-over-HTTP beside redb; IndexedDB evaluated.
- **E.** Tenancy architecture — per-user Turso DBs + central tenancy DB; Workers/DO serving; public DB.
- **F.** Content-addressed media/data plane — R2 dedup, reference-based access, GC on last reference.
- **G.** Second-version-in-TypeScript scoping + transports — REST/WebSocket everywhere, WASM where it fits, direct Turso when prudent.
- **H.** SSO relying-party integration — hosted services consume #9077; tenancy accounts ↔ #1253 roles.

## Lineage and relations

- Data model consumed, not re-invented: #9060's merged design (doc/2026-11-12T22-50-00Z_design_pm-board-hierarchy-genealogy) — board registry, hierarchy, Metadata. Children #9062 (collector registry), #9070 (genealogy read model), #9073/#9074 (fleet Metadata superset + metadata DB), #9076 (dual ingestion) are the laptop-world counterparts this program's hosted editions must stay model-compatible with.
- Turso + Cloudflare epic: #8987. PM data unification background: #3142, #1744. Fleet sync tools: #9016. SSO: #9077, #1253, #2852. ID program: #2056.

## Acceptance (program level)

- [ ] Design-mill build-out complete: statement inventory covering A–H with zero unmapped statements; versioned designs (V1 = what exists today) merged to main under doc/.
- [ ] Every component issue's named open questions answered in a merged design or explicitly batched to Drew as a ruling with options + recommendation.
- [ ] Granular implementation issues filed for everything implementable, parented under the component issues.
- [ ] The F-plane reference-vs-copy question decided with evidence (or batched to Drew with a recommendation).

code.title: SSO for fleet services: GitHub/Google/Microsoft login gated to Drew + devtoday OIDC provider with roles + account linking
code.body:
## Drew's ask (2026-11-12)

Do we have SSO for our own fleet services shaped like this — and if not, this issue is its home:

1. **Accept external login, gated to Drew (for now):** sign in with **GitHub**, **Google**, or **Microsoft** — allowlisted to Drew's accounts only.
2. **Our own OAuth/OIDC provider:** stand up a devtoday identity provider usable by ANY of our apps, with **basic roles**, offered to our apps as a **"devtoday SSO"** button — the same way apps offer "Sign in with Google".
3. **Account linking:** one account, every door. GitHub / Google / Microsoft / the devtoday provider are all linkable to the SAME account at the user's choice, so a single account accepts any of the options interchangeably.

## What already exists (evidence, 2026-11-12 search)

- **#1182** — dashboard behind Cloudflare Access, identity = Drew's Google SSO. Covers a slice of (1) for ONE app via Cloudflare Access (Google only), and is explicitly gated on Drew's go, not yet implemented.
- **#1253** — design: one identity across the PM stack, SSO propagation from the public entry into every layer, roles (owner / orchestrator / agent / read-only) replacing asserted authorship. Assumes an IdP at the entry (Cloudflare Access); does NOT stand up our own provider, name GitHub/Microsoft as login options, or specify account linking.
- **#2852 / spec #2258** (ID program, epic #2056) — hosted provisioning + **SSO→ID binding**: external SSO identities bound to pkgs/id accounts; slices 1–2 landed (PRs #4854, #4885), slices 3–4 open. This is linking INSIDE the id system; it does not make any fleet service accept those logins, and id is not (yet) cast as an OIDC issuer for other apps.
- pkgs/id itself (epic #2056) is Drew's identity system — capabilities (id-caps), directory, groups; production node on the laptop :3005; a Cloudflare Workers "serverless edition" is designed/implemented under #5524 / #5681. Related login-design line: #5684 (identity, login & delegation), #5885, #5889.
- No issue found (searches: oidc, oauth, sso, "identity provider", "login with", "relying party", "devtoday") that frames (1)+(2)+(3) together for fleet services, and none that offers a "devtoday SSO" button to our own apps.

## Open design question (for the owner — NOT decided here)

**Is pkgs/id the OIDC provider, or a separate minimal provider?**
- For id-as-provider: it already has accounts, binding ceremonies (#2852), capability/role machinery (id-caps, id-groups), a hosted/serverless edition path (#5524), and Drew's 2026-10-28 ID program directive behind it. Cost: id's key-custody model (see #5684) is more exotic than a conventional OIDC issuer; fleet services need boring, standard OIDC first.
- For a separate minimal provider: a small standard OIDC issuer (GitHub/Google/Microsoft as upstream federated logins + linking tables + roles) is faster to make every app consume, but then two identity systems exist and the relationship (does the minimal provider later fold into id? does id consume it?) must be designed, not drifted into.
Either way the deliverables above stand: external logins gated to Drew, account linking across all four doors, basic roles consumed by fleet services (the role model in #1253 is the consumer-side contract).

## Acceptance

- A design note (repo `doc/`) answering the provider question above with evidence, naming the issuer, the linking model (one account, N linked external identities), the role set, and the Drew-only gate mechanism.
- Implementation issues filed as children of this issue for: provider stand-up, GitHub login, Google login, Microsoft login, account linking UI/flow, first consumer integration (PM stack, per #1253).
- First consumer proves the full loop: Drew signs into a fleet service via each linked door against the same account, roles enforced server-side.

Parents/relatives: PM stack coherence epic #1184 (this issue's native parent), ID program epic #2056 (cross-linked — the provider question lives there too), design-register/turso-cloudflare programs unaffected. Relates: #1182, #1253, #2852, #2258, #5684, #5524.

code.title: impl(fleet): fleet gh Metadata superset — create-path stamping + DB insert (extends #9016)
code.body:
Design: doc/2026-11-12T22-50-00Z_design_pm-board-hierarchy-genealogy/note.md section 13; extends the step-2 scope of #9016 (cross-linked). fleet gh issue/PR create parses any pm-metadata block already in the caller's description, stamps what fleet knows (queue ID, scheduled start, current time, pwd, worktree, host, queue pickup time, work start time, issues worked by the same lane start, session id, model), ensures required fields (injecting defaults/what it knows), pushes the item, then inserts the full record incl. full Metadata into the fleet database.

Acceptance:
- Create via fleet gh with no block, a partial block, and a complete block: resulting bodies read back with correct stamps; caller-supplied values never overwritten.
- DB row for the created item verified by query, full Metadata JSON round-trips.
- A forced DB-insert failure leaves the GitHub item intact and the miss is picked up by the ingestion slice (cross-ref), demonstrated or reasoned with the sweeper test.
- Plain gh behavior is unchanged when fleet gh is not used.

code.title: pm stack: multi-board hierarchy + full task genealogy
code.body:
# pm stack: multi-board hierarchy + full task genealogy

Starter epic for Drew's directive of 2026-11-12 (~16:27 CST). This epic owns the
program end to end: design first (Phase 1), then data side (Phase 2), then
dashboard surfaces (Phase 3). Implementation slices are filed as native
sub-issues of this epic as the design lands.

## The requirement (Drew, in substance)

The PM stack must support **many boards**, with boards as **siblings or
parent/children** of each other, forming one navigable hierarchy:

- Overall high-level roadmap → per-project roadmaps → per-project designs and
  epic-level items → a granular current-implementation / WIP board.
- **Every task has parents up to the top**, relayed through epics, milestones,
  and labels. The canonical genealogy statement the stack must be able to
  produce for any item:

  > "We are working on bugfix X as part of epic Y, which was spawned by
  > design Z; epic Y is part of larger project roadmap item A, which exists
  > as part of the overall system's second active roadmap priority CC, which
  > was started after C closed with the release on \<date\>."

- **Milestones are release containers**: a milestone closes with a release and
  carries close-out accounting — the counts of issues, designs, and epics it
  covered (the shape Drew gave: a milestone that closed with a release
  covering 123 issues, 23 designs, and 4 epics).
- **Epics can carry over across milestones.** A carryover epic may be larger
  in scope than the closed child epics under the milestone it carried over
  from — it holds fixes from already-merged work plus the later phases of a
  large design.
- **Designs spawn designs.** A large design can spawn further designs (Drew's
  example: 5 spawned — 2 done, 2 in progress, 1 blocking the final design's
  start). The blocking relation must be representable and visible.
- **Close rules**: a larger epic and its project roadmap item close when
  (a) its designs are all done, AND (b) its medium/high-priority bugs and
  follow-ups are closed. Whatever is still unfinished at that point is
  **re-parented** — to the most-related epic, or to the project's general
  maintenance epic.
- **Primary parent**: moved issues keep all their labels, but the **most
  important parent must be marked** — an extra label or a metadata section in
  the issue/PR description (Drew's two candidate shapes). At minimum this
  must exist in the PM stack; in GitHub too if feasible. The design phase
  picks the canonical form.

## Substrate already in place (build on it, do not redo)

- Native sub-issue chains + epic/design label families in this repo; taxonomy
  and current lineage in `pm-stack/lineage-manifest-2026-11-12.md` (PR #8980,
  merged).
- Boards: developing-today Project #4 (1,229 items, Area/Status fields, view
  #22 "ID Program"), developing-today Project #5 (Idea Register),
  developing-today-forks Project #1, Clustered-Computing "Lab Cluster"
  Project #1.
- Design register machinery: epic #8805 + `pm-stack/design-tracking-manifest-2026-11-11.md`.
- `project-reconcile.sh` — the board's single-writer sync, now on `fleet gh`
  (token rotation), all count caps removed by Drew's 2026-11-12 ruling.
- The 2026-10-26 visualization design (#1122): native sub-issue edges +
  blockedBy via the collector's GraphQL, effective-Area inheritance.

## Phases

- **Phase 1 — design.** A design note under `doc/` (repo convention) defining:
  (a) the board registry model (boards as data: org, project number, role —
  overall/project/wip — parent board, sibling order) so the collector is
  multi-board by configuration; (b) hierarchy levels + edge types (native
  sub-issue parent, spawned-by design→epic, epic→roadmap-item,
  roadmap-item→roadmap-priority, blocked-by) and where each edge lives;
  (c) milestones as release containers with close-out accounting + carryover
  semantics; (d) the primary-parent convention — canonical form, exact
  format, re-parenting behavior on close, and a maintenance epic per project;
  (e) the genealogy read model — ancestor-chain computation + sentence
  rendering + the dashboard surfaces. Implementation slices filed as
  sub-issues with acceptance criteria.
- **Phase 2 — data side.** Collector multi-board by registry (all current
  boards), hierarchy edges ingested, primary-parent implemented in the
  collector + backfilled over today's epics/chains (worked example: the
  crate-split chain — steps → #3447 → #3195 → #2056, designs linked),
  milestone/release accounting computed from existing milestones. Aggregator
  redeployed; the projects API serves boards + chains; the canonical
  genealogy example verified end-to-end on real data.
- **Phase 3 — dashboard.** Overall roadmap view, per-project roadmap views,
  genealogy header (the sentence) on item pages, milestone close-out
  summaries.

## Acceptance (program level)

- [ ] Design note merged; implementation slices filed as sub-issues.
- [ ] Collector serves all current boards from a registry (no hardcoded
      single project), with hierarchy edges.
- [ ] The canonical genealogy sentence renders from real data for a real
      item, end to end.
- [ ] Milestone close-out accounting (issues/designs/epics counts) computed
      for existing milestones.
- [ ] Primary-parent marks exist on the backfilled chains (crate-split chain
      as worked example).
- [ ] Dashboard shows overall roadmap, per-project roadmap, and the
      genealogy header — or Phase 3 remains as filed issues with the design
      merged, reported exactly as such.

## Links

- Lineage manifest: `pm-stack/lineage-manifest-2026-11-12.md` (PR #8980)
- Design register epic: #8805
- Visualization design: #1122
- Board design origin: #910


## Phase status (2026-11-12)

- **Phase 0 — intake: DONE.** This epic is filed with labels epic, app/pm-stack, epic/pm-stack. Native parenting under the PM-stack coherence epic #1184 was attempted and is **blocked by GitHub's 100-sub-issue-per-parent cap** (#1184 is full — API 422). Cross-linked by comment instead; the design (§2) records the cap as a substrate constraint with the intermediate-grouping-epic rule.
- **Phase 1 — design: DONE.** Design note merged to main via PR #9064 (merge 673bb403a1): `doc/2026-11-12T22-50-00Z_design_pm-board-hierarchy-genealogy/note.md` (27,629 B), including the 16:45 amendment sections 11–16.
- **Phase 2/3 — implementation: FILED** as the 12 native sub-issues below. The collector multi-board + per-org identity slice is the pre-filed #9062 (this design is its specification).

## Amendment absorption (Drew, 2026-11-12 16:45 CST)

1. **Link semantics** → design §11 + slice #9066. Links are records (relation + status active/historical/removed + since/until/reason): one direct parent at a time; splits retain the old parent as historical; misclassifications are removed (auditable removal, never blurred with history). Level-agnostic; board→board links use the same record shape.
2. **Metadata section in every issue/PR** → design §12 + slices #9066/#9073. Delimited `<!-- pm-metadata:start/end -->` block containing a JSON dictionary (JSON chosen over YAML: strict parse, native in both fleet/Rust and the TS collector; arbitrary keys, nested values). Canonical home of direct_parent, links[], lineage fields, provenance. GitHub-native marks remain the GitHub-side representation; reconcile keeps them in agreement and reports divergence.
3. **fleet gh superset** → design §13 + slice #9073 (extends #9016). Create parses existing Metadata, stamps queue id / scheduled start / now / pwd / worktree / host / pickup + work-start times / lane-start issue set / session id / model, enforces required fields, pushes, then inserts the full record into the DB itself. Metadata query features → slice #9074.
4. **Session state** → design §14 + slice #9075. Session id assigned per fleet start; stored in env AND a pwd-file at every operated worktree's root; resolution order explicit arg > env > pwd-file.
5. **Database** → design §15 + slice #9074. Every issue/PR in scope; full Metadata as JSON + extracted key fields indexed; first-class query surface alongside GitHub; bodies win on content, divergence is a healing target.
6. **Dual ingestion / self-healing** → design §16 + slice #9076. Webhook listener + interval sweeper; missing Metadata ascertained/generated/stored (+ written back where fleet has access); insufficient cases forwarded to full triage; quickly-merged PRs completed retroactively.

## Slice map (native sub-issues of this epic)

- #9062 — collector: board registry + multi-board + per-org identity (pre-filed; design = its spec)
- #9065 — satellite board field-schema standardization (forks #1, Lab Cluster #1)
- #9066 — primary-parent convention + historical link semantics + crate-split backfill
- #9067 — release milestones: convention, ingestion, close-out accounting
- #9068 — design-spawn backfill + spawn rollup
- #9069 — per-project maintenance epics + closure gate + re-parent tooling
- #9070 — genealogy read model: ancestors, spawned-by, sentence renderer, API
- #9071 — dashboard surfaces: genealogy header, per-project roadmap, overall priorities, releases
- #9073 — fleet gh Metadata superset: create-path stamping + DB insert (extends #9016)
- #9074 — metadata database + fleet Metadata query surface
- #9075 — session state: session id in env + worktree pwd-file
- #9076 — dual ingestion: webhook listener + interval sweeper, backfill, retroactive completion

Cross-links: #9016 (step-2 sync tools — the fleet-superset slices extend its scope), #9062 (above), #8805 (design register), #1122 (visualization design), lineage manifest PR #8980.

code.title: fix(id/serve-proxy): bound credit grants to flow-control limits
code.body:
## Evidence

`pkgs/id/src/serve_proxy.rs:52-56` defines finite initial stream and connection credits, but `CreditWindow::grant` at lines 415-418 uses `saturating_add` with no upper bound or error result. Each decoded `WINDOW_UPDATE` can grant a `u32` amount (`window_update_amount`, lines 234-247); repeated valid updates can therefore grow available credit arbitrarily up to `u64::MAX`. Once the mux uses this primitive, the sender can be authorized to exceed the receiver's bounded in-flight buffers. Saturation only hides integer overflow; it does not enforce a finite credit ceiling.

The relay backpressure design explicitly requires hard finite per-stream and aggregate per-connection byte limits, and says credit returns only as bounded buffer space is released (`doc/2026-11-08T11-08-53Z_design_id5813_relay_proxy_protocol/2026-11-08T11-08-53Z_design_id5813_relay_proxy_protocol.md:85-100`). The serve-proxy issue #7569 is closed and #5792 remains the protocol design tracker, but neither specifically tracks a maximum-credit guard. All-state searches for `CreditWindow`, `WINDOW_UPDATE`, and bounded flow control found no matching implementation issue. The currently open #8951 concerns frame stream/sequence semantics, not credit accounting; no open PR implements this guard.

## Why it matters

A peer can repeatedly send valid credit updates and defeat the flow-control bound that is supposed to keep per-stream and per-connection buffering finite. This risks unbounded queued/in-flight data or inconsistent accounting rather than pausing at the receiver's actual capacity.

## Acceptance criteria

- Give each credit window an explicit finite ceiling tied to the effective per-stream/per-connection limits (do not invent a universal deployment limit where the design delegates it to configuration).
- Make a grant that would exceed the ceiling or overflow an explicit protocol/resource error; do not silently saturate or mutate the window.
- Ensure mux-level accounting enforces both per-stream and aggregate per-connection limits before accepting DATA or returning credit.
- Add tests for normal credit return, exact-ceiling grants, over-ceiling/repeated `WINDOW_UPDATE` grants, and unchanged state after refusal.

# pkgs/web-gen-api-axum crate split

Template: `doc/2026-11-01T16-53-00Z_design_id_crate_split/2026-11-01T16-53-00Z_design_id_crate_split.md` (design of record for the pkgs/id split, from #3195). Worked example: pkgs/id umbrella #3447, step issues #4403-#4411. Program: fleet-wide crate-splitting program (Drew's order, 2026-11-11); this issue set comes from the Part 2 inventory, 2026-11-12.

## Current shape (inventory 2026-11-12)

Single crate, no workspace: package `start-axum` (edition 2021), lib (`cdylib`+`rlib`) + bin, **731 LOC in `src`, 0 tests**. Leptos 0.8 starter-shape app (axum ssr / hydrate features, libsql). Files: `src/app.rs` 435, `src/dark_mode.rs` 109, `src/error_template.rs` 76, `src/fileserv.rs` 40, `src/lib.rs` 25, `src/main.rs` 46. No `package.nix` (only `shell.nix`); recent commits are dependency bumps only. Existing-issue check (2026-11-12): **no pre-existing crate-split design or issue for pkgs/web-gen-api-axum**.

## Import-scan evidence

Real scan of `pkgs/web-gen-api-axum/src` — `crate::` references counted per file, aggregated per top-level module (the id design's method):

- Module graph (4 internal edges total): `app` -> `dark_mode` (app.rs: `use crate::dark_mode::DarkModeToggle`), `app` -> `error_template` (app.rs: `use crate::error_template::{AppError, ErrorTemplate}`), `fileserv` -> `app` (fileserv.rs line 14: `use crate::app::App`, inside the ssr file handler), `lib` -> `app` (lib.rs hydrate(): `use crate::app::*`).
- Leaves: `error_template` (76 LOC: `AppError` enum + `ErrorTemplate` component) and `dark_mode` (109 LOC: `ToggleDarkMode` server fn + `DarkModeToggle` component) are each referenced only by `app` and reference nothing local — clean leaves.
- The one upward-flavored edge is `fileserv -> app`: file serving is server glue that must render the app on error. Per the id template's seam rule (composition/server code belongs to the top crate), `fileserv` stays in the facade with `main.rs` (axum server) rather than dragging `app` down or inverting the edge.
- `app.rs` internally mixes components (`App`, `HomePage`, `SimpleCounter`) with two libsql-backed server fns (`AddVisitorData`, `GetVisitorRows`, lines 312-325); the scan shows no internal boundary there, so app moves as one unit in this pass — a server-fn sub-split is explicitly out of scope.

## Step sequence

One PR per step, in order:

- Step 0: #8966 — step 0: workspace conversion + baselines (no code motion) (https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/8966)
- Step 1: #8967 — step 1: extract start-axum-error (leaf: error_template) (https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/8967)
- Step 2: #8968 — step 2: extract start-axum-ui (dark_mode + app) (https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/8968)
- Step 3: #8969 — step 3: facade slimming (fileserv + server stay in start-axum) (https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/8969)

## Proposed crate map

`pkgs/web-gen-api-axum` becomes a Cargo workspace; members under `crates/`, shared versions pinned in `[workspace.dependencies]` from step 0. The facade keeps the package/lib name `start-axum` and re-exports the pre-split paths (`start_axum::app`, `start_axum::dark_mode`, `start_axum::error_template`, `start_axum::fileserv`) that lib.rs and main.rs use today.

| crate | contents (today's code) | depends on |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `start-axum-error` | `error_template.rs` — `AppError`, `ErrorTemplate` (76 LOC) | leaf, no internal deps |
| `start-axum-ui` | `dark_mode.rs` (109) + `app.rs` (435: components + visitor server fns) | start-axum-error |
| `start-axum` (facade) | `lib.rs` (`hydrate()`), `fileserv.rs`, `main.rs` (axum server) + facade re-exports | start-axum-ui, start-axum-error |

Dependency rule: one-way, down the table; the facade's server glue (`fileserv`) depending on the ui crate is the correct direction — it is the consumer side of the relationship.

Scale note: 731 LOC — small, but it has a real 4-module graph with two clean leaves, so the extraction steps are mechanical and low-risk.

Acceptance discipline (from the id template; applies to every step):
- One PR per step; no step bundles another step's extraction.
- Full test suite green on that PR. Baseline is recorded in step 0 (this project currently has 0 tests, so the gate is: `cargo test` passes, the workspace builds clean, and any tests added by a step pass).
- Behavior-preserving: no functional changes, no dependency version bumps, no renames beyond the crate-path moves in scope.
- Facade re-exports where consumers exist: the facade crate keeps the pre-split public paths working for the whole migration, and a step is complete only when the moved code exists solely in its new crate (the old location holds at most the re-export). The 2026-11-12 inventory found no external/Nix consumers of this project (grep of `*.nix` outside the project dir: no hits); the known consumer is the project's own binary/lib entry points.
- Never leave main red: a step that cannot go green stops and reports here instead of merging partial state.

code.title: Daily flake sync & config optimization
code.body:
Perform the daily configuration review for developing-today/code. Do NOT update the `opencode` or `openchamber` flake inputs — the flake-inputs-update workflow owns them.
Follow these instructions and rules:
### 1. FLAKE INPUTS — OWNED ELSEWHERE, DO NOT BUMP - The `opencode` and `openchamber` flake inputs are owned by the deterministic
  `flake-inputs-update` workflow, which bumps, validates, and merges them daily.
  Do NOT run `nix flake update` for them, do NOT change their pins in `flake.lock`,
  and do NOT open PRs that bump them. If their pins look stale, leave them — the
  owning workflow handles them the same day.
- Do NOT casually bump root `nixpkgs` (root nixpkgs is pinned deliberately per system stability policies). - Clean up any stale input overrides or unused flake dependencies in `flake.nix` (e.g. warnings about non-existent input overrides like gitignore or devshell).
### 2. CONFIGURATION & INFRASTRUCTURE IMPROVEMENTS - Investigate potential configuration improvements in `nixos/`, `home/`, `lib/`, and package definitions under `pkgs/`. - Check for:
  - Deprecated NixOS or Home Manager options
  - Suboptimal build phases or missing binary wrappers
  - Systemd service resilience (e.g. restart policies, socket activation)
  - Modularity and decoupling to prevent merge conflicts
- Clean up any dead code, unused flags, or documentation drift in Nix configurations.
### 3. EVALUATION & VALIDATION - Verify that all system and host configurations evaluate cleanly without errors:
  `nix eval --raw .#nixosConfigurations.nixos.config.system.build.toplevel.drvPath`
- Ensure git hooks, commit messages, and treefmt formatting pass cleanly.

### 4. PULL REQUEST & MERGE - If updates or improvements are present:
  - Open a clear Pull Request documenting any configuration enhancements made. Keep every related change in this one PR — never split changes into one PR per item.
  - Merge into `main` only when you are reasonably certain it is correct: all Nix evaluations and checks succeed, the PR is conflict-free, and the changes are limited to the intended bumps and fixes. Merging is permitted, never required — when any of that is uncertain, leave the PR open and explain what a human should check.

## Finding (pool meta-review, 2026-11-12, window 2026-11-11T13:12Z–2026-11-12T13:12Z)

openai.alternate — held by doctrine as the fleet's final OpenAI reserve — burned **+16pp of its weekly window in ~1 hour** at steward run 316 (2026-11-11T16:26Z): 5h 1% → 100% (walled), weekly 81% → 97%. In the same interval the designated sole absorber, openai.main, was FLAT (weekly 39%), so the draw did not come from absorber overflow. The reserve has sat at weekly 97% (3% headroom to its Mon Nov 16 11:45 AM CST reset) ever since.

The steward ledger (pool-change-ledger.md, run 316) recorded this as "observation only (consumption, not a config imbalance)" and no issue was filed. The consumer is unattributed: queue telemetry attribution is null (model_hint non-null 0/260 rows; code#4919), so neither the steward nor this review can name what drew on the reserve.

## Why it matters
- Reserve doctrine ("OpenAI is the final reserve"; alternate "should draw nothing further" — the steward's own wording from run 316 onward) was breached in fact, whatever the cause.
- openai.main is drawing +24pp/day as sole absorber (weekly 37 → 61 across this window) and at that pace walls ~Nov 14, before its Nov 17 reset — at which point the OpenAI line has effectively no reserve (3%).
- An unattributed consumer that can burn a held reserve in an hour can recur.

## Asked
1. Identify the consumer (session/route) that drew on openai.alternate in the 2026-11-11 ~15:15–16:15Z hour, or confirm it was deliberate direct use.
2. If it was fleet routing, name the route and why it bypassed the designated absorber.
3. Until attribution exists (code#4919), any ≥5pp single-interval move on a held reserve gets an issue in the same pass, not an observation line.

code.title: Epic: fleet GitHub Apps — permission parity, org coverage, registry
code.body:
# Epic: fleet GitHub Apps — permission parity, org coverage, registry

Program home for the fleet's three GitHub Apps: `developing-today` (App 5454422, the posting App), `developing-today-fleet` (App 5612056), and `developing-today-backup` (App 5562183). This program grew out of the token audit under the design-register epic #8805.

## Drew's rulings (2026-11-12)

- **Permission parity (~01:40 CST):** "backup should have the exact same permissions as the other two" — all three fleet Apps carry one identical permission set, as a standing expectation.
- **Org coverage (~01:43 CST):** "don't forget to add/update permissions so all 3 are on all [the] orgs I'm admin of" — every org Drew admins (102, verified by full pagination; the first inventory's 28 was a page-1 undercount) holds all three Apps, with permission updates accepted.
- **Registry (~01:43 CST):** "keep a list of all orgs in hatch personal and the permissions and apps each that you can refer back to, or maybe a table in turso and wire a fleet subcommand to list whatever."
- **Never Vertex (~01:22 CST, applied throughout):** if a web flow asks for Vertex/Microsoft SSO, decline it — "there's never a time it's required and you shouldn't stop." The fleet never authenticates into Vertex for its tooling, and a Vertex prompt is never a stopping blocker; work routes around it. (In this program the only human gate was GitHub's own sudo "Confirm access," cleared by Drew's GitHub Mobile approvals.)

## The parity set (all three Apps)

actions / checks / contents / issues / pull_requests / statuses / workflows: **write** · metadata: **read** · organization_projects: **write**. Events for the two writer Apps: issues, issue_comment, pull_request, push. The backup App carries the same events **plus** `repository` (kept deliberately — its backup-worker webhook depends on it); permissions are exact parity, events a functional superset for backup only.

## State

- **Phase 1 — DONE + verified.** Backup App permissions raised to the parity set via its settings UI; API re-reads show it identical to `developing-today-fleet`. The developing-today org installation (177388707) accepted the same pass.
- **Coverage (JWT ground truth, 2026-11-12):** all three Apps are installed on the **same 102 orgs** — set differences zero in every direction, so no org installs were missing and none had to be created. No org blocked anywhere in the program.
- **Ground-truth rule:** coverage is read from each App's own JWT against `GET /app/installations`, fully paginated. `GET /orgs/<org>/installations` under OAuth produced false negatives and is not used for coverage claims.

## Linked work

- Turso-backed registry + `fleet orgs` subcommand (DRAFT design for Drew's ratification): #8884
- Stale-record fix — `infra/github-backup/config.json` now documents the live App state: PR #8885 (merged)
- Registry document in dezren39/hatch-personal: [PR #46](https://github.com/dezren39/hatch-personal/pull/46) (merged) — `library/github-orgs-apps-registry.md`, all 104 memberships with role, repo counts, and per-App install state.
- Grew out of: #8805 (design-register epic — its token audit)

## Closing tallies (verified 2026-11-12, fresh JWT listings after all UI work)

- **Backup acceptance sweep: 102 of 102 accepted** — 101 org installations plus the personal (dezren39) installation, driven through the laptop browser inside the sudo window; zero failures, zero sudo expiries, no Vertex surface touched. (The 102nd org, developing-today, had accepted in Phase 1.)
- **`developing-today-backup`: 102/102 org installations at the exact parity set.** Its personal installation holds the full account-level set (see the org-only key note below).
- **`developing-today-fleet`: 102/102 org installations at the exact parity set** — zero outliers at every read; no installs and no acceptances were ever needed.
- **`developing-today`: 102/102 org installations at the exact parity set.** No installs needed.
- **The org-only key note:** both personal (user-account) installations — backup 177385379 and developing-today 175747567 — show the parity set minus `organization_projects`. That key is an *organization* permission and cannot attach to a user installation; GitHub's own update page for 175747567 states the app is "already up to date." This is platform behavior, verified two ways (API listing + GitHub UI), not a pending acceptance.
- **Personal account:** `developing-today-fleet` has no installation on Drew's personal account (the other two do). The coverage order scoped to orgs; the registry records this plainly.
- **Program state: COMPLETE.** Remaining open thread is by design: the Turso/`fleet orgs` successor (#8884) stays open as a draft design for Drew's ratification.

code.body:
**DRAFT design — filed for Drew's ratification under the design-protection rule (2026-11-11): this stays open until Drew parks or abandons it. Wording below is a draft in the fleet's voice, not Drew's.**

## Drew's ask (2026-11-12 ~01:43 CST, main chat)

> "keep a list of all orgs in hatch personal and the permissions and apps each that you can refer back to, or maybe a table in turso and wire a fleet subcommand to list whatever"

Context: the fleet GitHub Apps parity + coverage program (epic to be linked below) put all three fleet Apps — `developing-today`, `developing-today-fleet`, `developing-today-backup` — at one identical nine-permission set across all 102 orgs Drew admins. The first deliverable is a committed registry document in dezren39/hatch-personal (seed data for this issue). This issue is the durable upgrade Drew sketched: the registry as queryable data, not a document that goes stale.

## Proposal

1. **Turso tables** for the registry: orgs (login, Drew's role, repo counts, verified-at), apps (slug, app id, owner, permission set, events), installations (app × account, installation id, repository selection, permissions as installed, verified-at).
2. **Sync path**: a fleet job that regenerates the tables from GitHub ground truth. Ground-truth rule learned 2026-11-12: each App's own JWT against `GET /app/installations` (fully paginated) is authoritative. `GET /orgs/<org>/installations` under an OAuth token produced false negatives (33 orgs wrongly reported as having no fleet Apps) and must not be used for coverage claims.
3. **`fleet orgs list` subcommand**: prints the registry (org → role → repos → per-App install state + permission set), with a `--drift` mode that re-reads GitHub and flags any installation whose permissions differ from the App's current set (the acceptance-pending state this program just swept).

## Acceptance criteria

- `fleet orgs list` prints all 104 memberships with role, repo counts, and per-App state matching the hatch-personal registry doc.
- Drift mode exits non-zero and names the installation when any App installation's permissions differ from that App's declared set.
- Sync runs from the App JWTs; no OAuth-token coverage claims anywhere in the path.
- The registry doc in hatch-personal links here as the living successor; this issue stays open until Drew ratifies, parks, or abandons the design.

Program home: the fleet GitHub Apps epic (linked in comments). Related: #8805 (design-register epic — this program grew out of its token audit).
