code.title: fleet-stalling: Drew's expedite set has no active worker
code.body:
## Problem

The queue's claim order is set entirely by fleet machinery — enqueue-time packet banding and the 2026-11-03 effectiveness re-tier — and none of it is Drew's order. Drew has never opened, edited, or connected to the queue store, and should never have to: his priorities exist as chat rulings and (since 2026-10-29) as the `expedite` / `next-up` issue labels, but nothing runs triage against them.

Worse, the one channel Drew did build is inverted. The 2026-10-29 label design maps `expedite` ⇒ priority 90 and `next-up` ⇒ priority 70, but the broker claims **lowest number first** (`ORDER BY priority ASC, created_at ASC`, fleet-queue `turso_queue.rs`; verified 2026-10-26, 2026-11-01, 2026-11-05, and again 2026-11-07). So the 15 issues Drew expedited on 2026-11-03 (the ID design tracks: #3447 + steps, #2898, #4000, #5047, #3789, #3792, #4837, and #3418) have their queue tasks sitting at priority 90 — the last band claimed — untouched since 2026-11-05. The inversion was flagged 2026-11-01 and never fixed; the label-honoring monitor duty was written against the old Supabase store and shows no action on the Turso store. The 2026-11-03 re-tier reused the same inverted reading (its "critical" band 70 claims after its "low" band 30).

Evidence snapshot (2026-11-07 ~19:20 CST): the next 20 tasks lanes will claim across the four pilot queues carry zero Drew-expressed priority; the plain-English top-of-queue is written up in `~/workspace/scratch/queue-top-plain-2026-11-07.md` (hatch-personal). A draft priorities brief — sourced entirely from Drew's goals and standing rulings — is at `~/workspace/scratch/drew-priorities-brief-draft-2026-11-07.md`, awaiting Drew's correction/ratification in chat.

## What to build

1. **Triage runs against the brief.** Once Drew ratifies the priorities brief, the hourly orchestration pass triages all four pilot queues against it: every band assignment or move cites the brief line that justifies it. Heuristic-only re-tiers (the 2026-11-03 pattern) are retired. Until ratification, no reprioritizing under this issue.
2. **Fix the label mapping.** `expedite` ⇒ ensure a live queue task and place it in the 10–20 band; `next-up` ⇒ ensure a task and place it in the 20–30 band (Drew's 2026-10-29 design, numbers flipped to the broker's real claim order). The honoring mechanism must run against the Turso fleet-queue store (the Supabase-era Duty 5 does not). The expedite/next-up set is Drew's: lanes never add or remove those labels on their own judgment.
3. **Plain-English top-of-queue, published on cadence.** The OpenCode & Muse Activity Space (or a successor view) shows the current top-of-queue in plain English — what each task is, which repo/issue, why it's at the top — refreshed on the orchestration pass cadence from the live store. Drew reads the order there; he never opens the queue table.
4. **Chat rulings become queue order in the same pass.** Any Drew ruling of the form "X matters" / "do X first" / "prioritize #N" is translated by the orchestrator into the labels + queue priority above in the same pass it is given, and time-boxed rulings record their window and expire on schedule.

## Acceptance

- [ ] Brief ratified by Drew (corrected version filed where the orchestration pass reads it).
- [ ] Label mapping flipped and verified by readback: an expedited issue's task reads in the 10–20 band in the Turso store; the current 15-issue expedite set is re-banded accordingly.
- [ ] One orchestration pass completes citing brief lines for its triage moves.
- [ ] The Activity Space (or successor) shows a plain-English top-of-queue stamped with its read time, refreshed by the pass.
- [ ] A Drew chat priority ruling given after ratification is reflected in labels + band within one orchestration pass, with no Drew clicks.

Refs: Drew's ruling 2026-11-07 19:12 CST (the queue's order is not his; make the system useful). Related: #7016 (standing issue↔queue reconciliation), #6853 (lane registry), #6423 (packet validation).

code.title: watch: model deprecations + stealth refreshes — design, seed list, and the announcement gap
code.body:
Execution issue for tracked goal **Model deprecations + stealth refreshes watch** (goal_e32f74415598). Filed 2026-11-07 on Drew's ruling that the census "dead" goals were dormant because the fleet never ran work against them. This issue carries the watch design (the first step, recorded at filing) and is the standing work order for building the watch.

## Why

Models the fleet depends on get deprecated — or worse, *refreshed*: a technically different model silently replaces the old one under the same name, the old version disappears, and the details hide in press-release fine print. Plan math (quota pools, burn plans, route proportions) rots silently if nobody tracks this. Findings feed the AI plans records so the numbers stay honest.

## Watch design (v1, recorded 2026-11-07)

**Seed list (from Drew, 2026-10-21):**
- Claude Haiku 4.5 — deprecation announced for everywhere except business/enterprise tiers and maybe some API providers
- Several ChatGPT models — same pattern: deprecated from consumer surfaces, surviving (for now) on business/enterprise and some API routes

**What is already covered elsewhere (do not duplicate):**
- The **weekly binary wire-check** diffs the actual provider binaries/builds weekly. A stealth refresh that ships inside a binary or client build shows up there as a diff — that half of the stealth-refresh problem has a mechanism already.
- The general release-watch / weekly software review catches headline version bumps for the fleet's tools.

**The gap this watch still owns:**
- **Provider announcements**: deprecation notices, sunset dates, and fine-print changes (credits, tier eligibility, API-vs-consumer differences) that never touch a binary — e.g. an API-credits change buried in a Haiku release announcement. No existing job reads provider announcement surfaces on a cadence.
- **Plan-math feed**: when a deprecation or refresh lands, the AI plans records (plan windows, pool composition, route proportions) need a deliberate update pass — today nothing connects an announcement to a plan-math review.
- **Name-vs-model identity**: refreshes that keep the display name but change the model underneath, where the only evidence is announcement wording or behavior drift, not a binary diff.

## Acceptance

- [ ] A recurring watch mechanism exists (cadence + sources: provider announcement/changelog surfaces for Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Meta, DeepSeek, Mistral at minimum)
- [ ] Each seed-list item has a tracked state: announced date, sunset date, surfaces affected, fleet exposure (which pools/routes/plans use it)
- [ ] A deprecation/refresh finding produces a linked plan-math review action, not just a note
- [ ] First sweep of the seed list completed and recorded on this issue

code.title: investigate: CPU/memory load over time + parallelism sweet spot on the sandbox VM
code.body:
Execution issue for tracked goal **CPU/memory load over time + parallelism efficiency** (goal_8c75ed164542). Filed 2026-11-07 on Drew's ruling that the census "dead" goals were dormant because the fleet never ran work against them.

## Question

What concurrency level makes the sandbox VM (and the laptop executors) finish the most work per credit? Drew's framing: CPU near 99% because it's performing at peak is the target — 95% while 35 things complete beats 8-vs-6 things grinding the whole box to a halt. Find the concurrency sweet spot **empirically**, then fold the answer into delegation/orchestration practice.

## Plan

- [ ] Baseline: load profile snapshot (done — first comment on this issue, 2026-11-07 18:49 CST)
- [ ] Sampled profile over time: load average, run-queue depth, CPU user/sys/idle/iowait/steal, memory + swap pressure, sampled across busy and quiet windows (not just one evening snapshot)
- [ ] Concurrency sweep: run controlled parallel work at several lane/agent concurrency levels and measure completed-work throughput + latency degradation per level
- [ ] Identify the noisy-neighbor cliff: the level where context-switch / iowait / steal growth eats the gains
- [ ] Write the delegation battle plan: who orchestrates, how work is tracked, concurrency defaults per machine, coordination-chatter budget
- [ ] Fold the defaults into the orchestration / lane runbooks so the finding changes behavior, not just this issue

## Acceptance

- [ ] A measured sweet-spot number (per machine class) with the data behind it
- [ ] Runbook/orchestration defaults updated to the measured number
- [ ] The swarm delegation battle plan recorded and linked from the goal

code.title: turso CLI: no rename and no libsql->TursoDB mode conversion — every fix is a full export/import data move
code.body:
Found during the 2026-11-07 fleet-wide DB audit + rename/mode-fix program (#6619).

Facts, all empirically verified on scratch DBs (CLI v1.0.33):
- `turso db list` TYPE column is the only mode evidence: `SQLite` = libsql mode, `Turso` = TursoDB mode.
- There is no `turso db rename`.
- A `--from-db` fork INHERITS the source database's type; `turso db create --from-db X --tursodb` fails with "tursodb flag contradicts the database derived type". A fork can never change mode.
- The only working conversion is: `turso db export <db>` -> copy the export files to the target basename -> `turso db import <file>.db --tursodb` (the new DB is named after the FILE basename), then repoint every producer, confirm, and delete the old DB.
- `turso db dump` does not exist in this CLI version (prints help).

Impact: converting the fleet's 8 libsql DBs on 2026-11-07 meant 8 full data moves (~7.7 GB total exports), per-DB token re-mints, and producer flips — for what should be a metadata operation. If Turso ever ships a mode-convert or rename verb, the fleet's remaining libsql holdouts (atlas monolith, great-star-lord — both deliberately untouched, see #6619) should use it. Until then, any new fleet DB must be created with --tursodb at birth; a libsql DB created by accident costs a full migration later.

- [ ] If/when Turso ships a rename or mode-convert verb, the holdouts are converted with it and this issue is closed citing that conversion; until then this issue stays as the tracking record, not active work.

code.title: Atlas search Worker cache: eviction & invalidation policy (follow-up to #6788)
code.body:
Part of the Atlas family (#5755); follows #6788 (the per-query Durable Object search cache Worker, shipped with **indefinite retention — no TTL, no eviction — per Drew's explicit order for v1**).

Indefinite retention is the v1 contract, not an oversight. Before it becomes load-bearing at scale, the eviction policy needs a design pass. Nothing here is urgent; this issue exists so the questions are on the record rather than discovered later.

## Questions to settle

1. **Corpus invalidation.** The cache key pins the embedding space (model revision + vector table) and ceiling, so a re-embedding of the corpus (new model/table) naturally orphans old entries — they simply stop being keyed. But a re-ingest under the *same* space (chunk content changes, shards added/renamed) leaves stale results served forever. Is that acceptable for a personal-corpus search surface, or do we need a corpus-generation component in the key (e.g. a registry epoch the service reports), accepting that a generation bump cold-starts the whole cache?
2. **Growth bound.** Entries hold an embedding (~12 KB JSON) + result envelope (observed ~17 KB at k=3; larger at k=50). At personal query volumes this is small for a long time; still, is there a count/size ceiling after which LRU-by-`searched_at`/`hit_count` eviction (both already recorded per entry) should engage?
3. **Manual purge.** A gated purge route (per-key delete; maybe per-prefix) is cheap to add to the Worker — worth having from the start of any policy, if only for "this result is wrong, drop it" operations.
4. **Interaction with fan-out cost.** A hit is ~free; a miss costs a full fan-out (~9 s observed). Eviction policy is therefore also a latency policy: aggressive eviction re-pays fan-outs.

## Non-goals

- No TTL by default — Drew's order stands until he changes it.
- No cross-ceiling or cross-space serving — the keying already forbids it; eviction design must not weaken that.

Defaults until ruled: retention stays indefinite; stale-after-re-ingest is accepted; purge is manual via DO storage tooling if ever needed.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Each numbered question in the issue body has a recorded decision (in a comment or a linked design note), including the corpus-generation/key question and the growth-bound question
- [ ] If a policy is adopted, a follow-up implementation issue is filed and linked; if the decision is to accept indefinite retention as-is, that is recorded explicitly with the scale trigger that reopens it

Implementation follow-up for the design in #5925 ("design: telemetry rollup — one stats pipeline under `fleet init`"). The design is complete in that issue's body: inventory of 11 components with keep/fold/adopt/delete/move verdicts, coverage analysis, two-purpose audit of init, explicit end state, and acceptance criteria. This issue is the implementation half of criterion 4 (follow-ups as separate issues); the design itself implements nothing.

## End state (from #5925)

`fleet init` (location-aware, #5687) ensures exactly: {proxy serve + pool prewarm; sysstat-collector; pidstat collector; tree-size cache writers} on the sandbox. Aggregation lives laptop-side. The boot-init job shrinks to: append one boot record, invoke `fleet init` prewarm, exit — and `~/tools/init.sh` is deleted outright once the #5770 generic restorer owns the shed installers/restores.

## Slices

- [x] **pidstat collector**: add a persistent pidstat loop in the sysstat unit family (`pidstat -urd` class), writing per-PID daily files beside `~/logs/sysstat/sa-<day>`; 14-day retention to match.
- [ ] **Boot record fold**: fold the init.sh telemetry block into the rollup boot record; promote `~/logs/init.jsonl` to the canonical boot/stats series (one record per boot: duration, store/profile counts, disk, latency samples). Retire `~/logs/init-status` as the read path — sweeps read the JSONL.
- [ ] **resource-sampler retirement**: once the pidstat history + a daemon-state event exist in the rollup, retire `~/logs/resource/resource-<day>.log`'s bespoke script/unit (historical logs stay).
- [x] **Tree-size cache writers**: generalize the detached `du` → `~/logs/.nix-persist-size` pattern: one throttled cache-writer per watched tree, value+timestamp, consumers tolerate staleness explicitly.
- [ ] **Dead-probe removal**: delete `conn-watch.py` remnants (already stopped per #5775) and remove the init.sh live verification probes (`services-verify` 900 s budget, toolchain presence checks, nix eval smoke) — health is read from the rollup/watchdog, never probed at boot.
- [ ] **Laptop-side aggregates**: per-hour trip aggregates from trips.jsonl (counts by status/failure class; per-leg p50/p95 once #5702's four timestamps land) and the per-lane proof table (tasks completed per lane per shift) computed laptop-side on a slow cadence; fleet-watchdog reads these outputs instead of live-joining agent.tasks.

## Explicitly out of scope (per the design)

- quota-recorder stays separate (#5775 owns its cadence ruling) — rollup consumers may read its outputs as a source only.
- The installers/restores init sheds land in the #5770 generic restorer, not here; the final `~/tools/init.sh` deletion waits on that landing.
- No stats DB unless query pain actually appears; files first.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] All six slices landed or explicitly deferred with a named owner/issue.
- [ ] A consumer (watchdog or sweep) reads at least one rollup output instead of a live probe/join, demonstrated in its code.
- [ ] #5925's acceptance criteria all checked, including this issue linked from #5925.

code.title: Design: validate it where you read it — one validated-and-bounded contract for the fleet proxy's frame and peer values
code.body:
# Design: validate it where you read it — one validated-and-bounded contract for the fleet proxy's frame and peer values

Design doc: `files/designs/code-fleet-proxy-validated-bounded.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace. Audit at origin/main `b0c472d94`. Filed by the design architect (pass 62, 2026-11-06), originating on the trigger recorded at pass 61: *a fifth fleet-proxy bound/validation surface files* — #6518 filed the same day, the `token_file` sibling of #6516 in the same function.

## Summary

The fleet proxy (`pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-proxy`) and its sibling client (`pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-dispatch`) read two kinds of values they do not control: request frames from local callers (`serve.rs parse_request`) and HTTP responses from laptop services (`http.rs`, `connect_udp.rs`, dispatch's `lib.rs`). The stated doctrine (#5579, `http.rs` module doc) is that peer-declared sizes are never trusted — and sizes are capped (`MAX_RESPONSE_BODY_BYTES`, `MAX_LINE_BYTES`, strict Content-Length). But the doctrine was never extended past sizes:

- `parse_request` (serve.rs:610, verified at audit HEAD) validates `method`/`path` strictly (#5750) and collapses every other field: a present-but-invalid `port` (70000, -1, 4801.5, `"4801"`) becomes `None` and is **silently rerouted to the default 4799 service** (#6516); a present-but-non-string `token_file` becomes `None` and the **default credential is silently substituted** for the named one (#6518). A present-but-invalid value is treated as an absent one.
- The response reader caps every unit but no repetition: the interim-1xx, header-line and trailer-line loops in `http.rs` consume peer-controlled units forever, pinning a pooled tunnel and thread indefinitely (#6509).
- fleet-dispatch's `dechunked_len` (lib.rs:303-312, verified at audit HEAD) does unchecked arithmetic on the peer-declared chunk size — panic in debug, wrap in release — while its sibling `dechunk` and the proxy's `read_chunked` both guard the same value (#6512).
- The fourth leg, #6511 (connect-udp head bound checked only after a whole line arrives), **landed** 2026-11-06 (during-the-read `take(remaining + 1)` fix, connect_udp.rs:264-276 at audit HEAD) and is this design's embodiment for rule 3 — cited, not a phase.

## The contract

**Every value the proxy acts on is validated where it is read — type, range, arithmetic, count — and a present-but-invalid value is refused in that surface's own error shape, never defaulted, substituted, wrapped, or consumed without bound.**

1. **Present is not absent (frame fields).** `parse_request` distinguishes absent (documented default) from present-but-invalid (refused with the standard `{status: 502, body: {error: "broker: …"}}` frame naming the field and bad shape; no connection opened, no token read) — #5750's strictness extended to every field the broker acts on.
2. **Counts are bounds too (peer readers).** Every repetition loop over peer-controlled units carries a named count bound; exceeding it fails like a size cap (`HttpError::Malformed`, connection non-reusable).
3. **Arithmetic is checked, during the read.** A declared size is checked and capped before it is added, indexed, or allocated from; bounds are enforced while accumulating, not after (#6511's landed fix is the embodiment).
4. **One statement.** The contract is written into the `http.rs` module doc's peer-trust paragraph, extended from sizes to all four dimensions (lands with Phase 2, where the doc is).

## Decisions recorded on this issue

- **Port 0 is refused at the frame boundary** — pinning #6516's either/or against the documented-dial-error alternative: 0 names no service in the closed routing table, and leaving one invalid shape to fail later at dial time recreates the inconsistency #6516 names. All invalid ports fail in one place, in one shape.
- **`token_file: null` is absent** — pinning #6518's open rule: JSON null is how the typed proto (`Option<String>`) and the Python express "no token_file", and `parse_request` already treats a null `body` as absent in the same function (serve.rs:635). Non-string *non-null* values are refused.
- **Repetition bound values stay with Phase 2's fixer** (named constants beside the `MAX_*` size constants, "generously above anything a legitimate laptop service sends" per #6509's acceptance) — no legitimate-count evidence exists in-tree to pin numbers against; the contract fixes the failure shape and naming.
- **Out of scope:** the queue/secrets brokers' transports (fleet-queue `uds_http`, tracker #6515 — their Content-Length leg #6527 already landed copying `http.rs`'s rule; Phase 4 cross-references, does not adopt), #4375 (mcpx response reads), #6448 (fleet-queue packet values) — the same stance at different boundaries, cited not merged.

## Phased breakdown (sub-issues of this issue)

- **Phase 1 — frame fields:** #6516 + #6518 (adopted as phases, linked as sub-issues). Lands first — the only phase whose failure mode is silent wrong-service delivery / credential substitution.
- **Phase 2 — repetition counts:** #6509 (adopted). Includes the rule-4 contract statement in the `http.rs` module doc.
- **Phase 3 — dispatch arithmetic:** #6512 (adopted). Independent of Phases 1–2.
- **Phase 4 — closing inventory:** NEW issue filed this pass (linked as sub-issue, gated on Phases 1–3): every read site in fleet-proxy + fleet-dispatch dispositioned, with required dispositions for (a) unadvertised-port routing, (b) the `body` field's shape rule, (c) the #6515 brokers cross-reference, (d) verification that the port-0 / null-token_file pins landed as recorded.

Phases with open questions stay in the design doc (hello-frame field treatment, a shared bound-constant home, refusal-count visibility) — they are not issues.

## Grounding

- `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-proxy/src/serve.rs:610-646` — `parse_request` at audit HEAD (strict method/path, lenient port/token_file/body).
- `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-proxy/src/http.rs:16-52` — the #5579 peer-trust doc + size constants; `:215/:282/:355` the unbounded repetition loops (#6509).
- `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-dispatch/src/lib.rs:303-312` — `dechunked_len` unchecked arithmetic at audit HEAD.
- `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-proxy/src/connect_udp.rs:264-276` — #6511's landed during-the-read bound (embodiment).
- Origins: #6516, #6518, #6509, #6512 (adopted); #6511 (landed, embodiment); #5579, #5750, #5921 (precedents).

*Agent note: this is a `kind/design` issue from the fleet design architect. Its phases are its sub-issues; triage of the phases should record the phase structure rather than re-filing or re-scoping the contract — the two pins above (port 0 refused; null token_file = absent) are decided here.*

Per-table log lives in that plan file; wave status is summarized here and on each design issue.

## Classification (audit §9, verified against the doc 2026-11-06)

- **KEEP on Postgres (21):** queue core (`agent.tasks/leases/workers/checkpoints/lanes/watermarks/repo_task_lane_ledger`, `finance.events`), ainventory relational core (models, measurement/price/policy/benchmark tables + `v_latest_import_batch` view), alerts. **Not migrated. Shadow snapshots may proceed after the audit |

code.title: opencode-claimant: handed-off tasks are never launched — executed_lane/session_id stay null across repeated claim→handed_off→park cycles
code.body:
## Observed

On 2026-11-06, queue-worker lanes repeatedly claimed tasks from `repo-health-code-pilot`, found `assigned_lane = opencode` on every one, checkpointed `handed_off`, and parked them for the opencode claimant — and no claimant session was ever launched. The lane-ledger rows keep `executed_lane = null` and `session_id = null` across every cycle.

Lane code-k shift 2026-11-06 15:13–15:30Z alone handed off five tasks this way:

- task 11066 (issue #6295, triage) — attempts 2/6; also handed off by earlier lanes today
- task 10832 (issue #6405, triage) — attempts 5/8, handed off repeatedly all day
- task 10950 (issue #6459, small_fix) — attempts 4/4 (at cap)
- task 11181 (issue #6282, triage) — attempts 1/6
- task 10751 (issue #4000, triage) — attempts 11/12, handed off repeatedly since 2026-11-05

The prior lane code-k shift (14:36Z handoff snapshot) recorded the same pattern for task 11174 (issue #6523): handed off twice (13:49Z and 14:35Z) with no launch in between. Its snapshot is at `hidden_files/lane-handoff-repo-health-code-pilot-k.json` in the goal workspace (overwritten each shift; the 15:30Z version carries this shift's five).

## Defect (suspected)

`opencode-claimant` polls every 10 minutes for claimed, opencode-assigned, unbound tasks and launches a session bound at launch time (worker instruction §1b). For these tasks the poll either never sees them (they sit `parked` with `work/assigned` between handoffs, and are only `claimed` for the brief handoff window), or sees them and fails to bind/launch without recording anything on the ledger row. Either way the cycle is claim → handed_off → park (20 min) → re-claim → handed_off, burning attempts (task 10751 is at 11/12, task 10950 at 4/4) with zero execution.

## Related, but distinct

- #5400 — `bind_repo_task_lane_session` guarded recovery mode dropped by migration-0023 (recovery rejects expired leases). Related: may block relaunch after a lease expires, but these tasks were never bound in the first place (`session_id` null from the start).
- #5508 — poll.py re-offers tasks whose `progress.session_id` was cleared while a ledger binding remains. Opposite shape: there a binding exists and should suppress re-offering; here no binding ever appears.

## Impact

- Every opencode-assigned task in the code pilot queue is effectively unworkable right now: workers can only hand off and park, per §1b they must not work or launch these tasks themselves.
- Attempt budgets drain on handoff cycles (task 10751 at 11/12, task 10950 at 4/4) — the same capped-at-max_attempts failure mode repaired on 2026-10-26 for tasks 1063/1111/1114/1115.

## Acceptance

- Root cause identified: claimant poll output/logs for one named task above (e.g. task 10751) show whether it was seen, skipped, or failed at bind/launch, and why.
- A handed-off task is launched by the claimant within one poll cycle of its handoff, or the handoff protocol is changed so workers stop cycling tasks the claimant cannot take (e.g. park with a claimant-visible state instead of a 20-minute timer).
- Attempt counting no longer charges a task for a handoff cycle in which no execution was attempted.

## Acceptance criteria
- Handed-off tasks (assigned_lane=opencode) are actually launched by the opencode claimant: the lane-ledger row for a handed-off task gains a non-null executed_lane and session_id, and the bound session posts its first checkpoint.
- A handed-off task that cannot be launched surfaces loudly (ledger row records the failure/reason, or the task is blocked with a named reason class) instead of silently cycling claim → handed_off → park → re-claim.
- Handoff cycles stop burning attempt budget for work never executed: a task handed off repeatedly with no launch does not advance toward max_attempts unclaimability (or the burn is explicitly surfaced in queue health).
- Regression evidence: at least one previously stuck handed-off task from the code pilot queue (e.g. task 10751 / issue #4000 or task 10950 / issue #6459) is observed launched end-to-end after the fix.

# Sign only what receipt would accept — one sign-time refusal contract for `pkgs/id`

Design-architect pass 60 (2026-11-06), audit at origin/main `252d43085`.
Full design doc: `files/designs/code-id-sign-time-refusal.md` in the
keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace.

## Problem

`pkgs/id` states its validity rules on the receipt side (fold, viewer,
verifier, accept) and most of its signing entry points never consult
them, so a caller can mint a properly signed, signature-valid object
that no consumer will ever count — creation reports success,
consumption silently ignores. The crate has been fixing this one
signer at a time (#5623 artifacts, landed; #6441 attestation outcome
domain, landed 2026-11-06 via PR #6442). Seven filings in five days
are the remaining signers: #6422 (currency `sign_authorisation` never
calls `validate`), #6424 (attestation signers never check the signer
is a player), #6434 (match_audit `sign_header`/`sign_footer` check
nothing `verify_integrity` enforces), #6443 (directory_auth
`sign_request` signs any nonce, infallibly), #6447 (`sign_move`:
blank world / empty input), #6451 (`sign_rotation`: routine
self-rotation the fold can never count), #6469
(`SignedReplicationEnvelope::sign`: eight envelope-local `accept`
rules unchecked).

## The contract

**Sign only what receipt would accept.**

1. Mirror at sign time every receipt rule decidable from the signer's
   own inputs (key, object, existing arguments).
2. The decidability line is part of the contract: (a) intrinsic —
   object alone; (b) signer-relative — key vs object; (c)
   seam-extended — decidable only with one more input the seam
   conceptually has: the public seam changes, it never silently
   skips; (d) receiver-state — stays receipt-only, named with its
   reason in the closing inventory.
3. Refusal speaks the module's own vocabulary, naming the rule;
   wire formats and receipt verdicts unchanged.
4. A test bypass, where needed, is crate-private and named
   `*_unchecked` (the artifact pattern) — never a second public
   unchecked signer.

## Pins the phases carry

- #6422: `sign_authorisation` calls `RateAuthorisation::validate`
  for the signing key's issuer; refusal via `SignError`.
  `sign_revoke` unchanged (no revoke validator exists — Phase 4
  disposition).
- #6443: `sign_request` becomes **fallible** (pin: not a validated
  nonce newtype — all callers are in-crate tests/helpers); the
  nonce-domain predicate is defined once, shared by `sign_request`
  and `verify_signed`.
- #6424: `sign_genesis` refuses a non-player signer
  (`SignError::NotAPlayer`). `sign_claim` is class (c): **pin the
  artifact pattern** — a public checked entry point taking the
  agreement/player set; bare `sign_claim` becomes crate-private
  `sign_claim_unchecked`. #6441's intrinsic outcome check applies
  in both.
- #6434: `sign_header` refuses wrong version, invalid roster,
  non-roster signer; `sign_footer` refuses non-roster signer and
  a `seed_reveal` not digesting to `header.seed_commitment` — with
  the `AuditErrorV0` reasons. Log-context checks stay in
  `verify_integrity`.
- #6447: `sign_move` refuses blank `world_id` (core.rs:291 rule)
  and empty `input` (core.rs:1938). Input length stays
  receipt-only (per-world limit unknown at the seam).
- #6451: `sign_rotation` refuses a Routine rotation whose
  `successor_key` equals the signing key's issuer id. Recovery
  analogue stays fold-only (inputs don't name the replaced key).
- #6469: `SignedReplicationEnvelope::sign` returns `None` for
  every envelope-local `accept` rule (the origin's eight rows);
  its doc comment states the full refusal contract. Receiver-state
  rules stay in `accept`.

## Phases (adopt the origins — no parallels)

- **Phase 1 — call the validator that exists:** #6422 + #6443.
- **Phase 2 — signer membership:** #6424 + #6434. Independent of Phase 1.
- **Phase 3 — world and rotation signers:** #6447 + #6451 + #6469.
  Independent of Phases 1–2.
- **Phase 4 — closing sign-surface inventory + contract statement**
  (new issue, gated on Phases 1–3): every public signing entry point
  in `pkgs/id` dispositioned enforced / deliberately receipt-only
  (class-(d) reason named) / gap-filed; required dispositions
  include `sign_revoke`, `directory::sign_up`/`sign_up_keyed`, the
  #3231 builder symmetry, and `sign_unchecked`; the contract
  statement lands in the crate's documentation.

Open questions stay in the design doc (revoke rule set vs #4071;
verify-side defense in depth for #6447/#4346; validate() author
rule; extension beyond `pkgs/id`).

🤖 Filed by the repo design architect (fleet) — origins verified
with laptop probes by their filers; audit and pins are this
pass's, against origin/main `252d43085`.

## Acceptance criteria
- Every public signing entry point in pkgs/id refuses at sign time exactly the objects the receipt side (fold, viewer, verifier, accept) would not count, under one shared refusal contract — no signer-local validity rules remain.
- Sign-time refusal errors name the violated receipt rule, so a caller can fix the object before signing.
- The closing sign-surface inventory (child issue #6488) shows every public signing entry point dispositioned against the contract, and property tests assert sign-accept ⇒ receipt-accept for generated objects.

code.title: fleet(queue): alert when the repo-queue broker transport is down — lanes currently starve silently at the Step 0 gate
code.body:
## Problem

When the repo-queue broker transport fails, every worker lane exits **silently** at its Step 0 gate — by design — so a total queue outage produces no alert and no visible signal; the fleet just starves until someone notices.

Evidence: incident #5708 (2026-11-04). Root cause recorded on #5708: the broker host (laptop amd-6) was down 16:58–18:17 CST (orderly shutdown per wtmp, 1h19m), spanning the whole 17:11–17:20 CST failure window Lane G observed (`proxy closed during CONNECT` to 100.99.113.103:4801). The only reason the outage is tracked at all is that Lane G manually filed #5708. No automated check surfaced it.

## Ask

Add earlier detection for repo-queue transport outages:

- A check that runs on a cadence independent of lane shifts (e.g. the hourly repo-fleet-monitor, or a small standalone probe) that exercises `fleet queue health` end-to-end from the sandbox.
- On repeated failure (e.g. 2 consecutive probes, or ~10 minutes), it surfaces an alert in the main chat and/or files ONE deduped incident issue (search open issues for an existing transport-incident issue first, like #5708 was filed by hand).
- Recovery is also surfaced once (transport back up), so a silent gap in lane reports is distinguishable from a healthy idle queue.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Simulated/observed broker-transport failure produces a visible alert within ~15 minutes, without any lane needing to file by hand.
- [ ] No duplicate incident issues for the same outage window (dedupe against open transport-incident issues).
- [ ] The check itself does not depend on the queue it monitors (it must be able to report the queue being down).

## Secondary observation (no separate ask)

At the 2026-11-04 18:17 CST boot, queue-broker.service failed twice with `cannot bind 100.99.113.103:4801: AddrNotAvailable` (Tailscale address not yet assigned) and was listening by the 3rd systemd restart at 18:18:11 CST — self-healing in ~16s, recorded here for context only.

code.title: id: Phase 14 — hosted, federated, local-first (plan of record)
code.body:
# Phase 14 — hosted, federated, local-first (plan of record)

This epic is the plan of record for Phase 14, converted from the next-horizons discussion #1240 by Drew's decision on 2026-11-05: **all seven themes are planned**, with first-iteration designs and v2/v3/v4 follow-up outlines filed for each. Drew agreed with the suggested first implementation items: **hosted worlds + discovery first, agents-in-worlds as the differentiating spike**.

## Drew's principles for everything in Phase 14 (from #1240, 2026-11-05)
- Local-first is always the goal, AND a hosted version is intended: central coordination supporting a large graph of broadly accessible objects.
- Anything built must be completely usable by others hosting a small or large server themselves. P2P-hosted worlds and data behave the same as a large hosted public server; differences live in backend scale elements and access controls.
- Users connect to each other and transfer/interact directly wherever possible, so hosted resources are an offloadable backstop, not a requirement. The app must not technically need us to function. Collaborative / shared / federated / local-first / p2p.
- Our hosted instance is essentially public; other operators open theirs only as much as they want. Publishing paths: share to a big server, publish on pkarr, or self-host. All comms through iroh on the backend; first-class clients.

## The map (7 core topics, each with a v1–v4 ladder)
- **Hosted worlds & always-on hosting** — core #6276 (v1–v4: #6283, #6284, #6285, #6286)
- **Discovery, registry & federation** — core #6277 (v1–v4: #6287, #6288, #6289, #6290)
- **Program ecosystem (share, fork, gallery)** — core #6278 (v1–v4: #6291, #6293, #6294, #6295)
- **More shells (mobile, native, hardware)** — core #6279 (v1–v4: #6296, #6297, #6298, #6299)
- **Agents in worlds (MCP bridge)** — core #6280 (v1–v4: #6300, #6301, #6302, #6303)
- **Scale & performance hardening** — core #6281 (v1–v4: #6304, #6305, #6306, #6307)
- **Creator tooling & insight** — core #6282 (v1–v4: #6308, #6309, #6310, #6311)

## How this runs
- Every core topic is research + design: broaden the idea, answer the research questions, produce design docs and implementation issue breakdowns. Designs precede implementation, as with #534 for Phase 12.
- Near-term design queue is unchanged: F12.4 (#1061) and F12.10 (#1067) designs land first; then Phase 14 v1 designs in the order hosted worlds → discovery → agents spike → ecosystem → shells → scale → creators. Implementation follows Phase 13.
- Running-low and milestone resurfaces for this program ride the same system as before: when Phase 14's lined-up design work drains, the orchestrator brings it back to Drew (rule pattern from #1295).
- Drop rule: any item that proves blocked, wrong, or superseded gets parked or closed with a note. The map shrinks honestly rather than stalling silently.

Dashboard: org Project #4, Area `id-train`. The discussion of record is #1240; Drew's direction comment there (2026-11-05) is quoted in substance in every core topic issue.

## Acceptance criteria
- All seven Phase 14 themes have their first-iteration design issues and v2/v3/v4 outline issues filed, and are linked from this epic as native sub-issues (a child list that exists only in prose does not count).
- The agreed first implementation items — hosted worlds + discovery first, and the agents-in-worlds spike — each have a filed implementation issue linked from this epic.
- Drew's Phase 14 principles (from #1240, recorded in this issue's body) are referenced by each child design issue.
- Progress is tracked on this epic: as each theme's v1 design lands, the epic records it and the theme's next step is linked.

# Creator tooling & insight — Phase 14 core topic (research + design)

Filed from the next-horizons discussion #1240, decided by Drew on 2026-11-05: **all themes are planned**. This issue is the core topic for **Creator tooling & insight**. Its job is research and design — broaden the idea beyond what is already understood, set up multiple next steps, and produce implementation plans. No implementation starts here; the output is design documents and implementation issues.

## Drew's principles for everything in Phase 14 (from #1240, 2026-11-05)
- Local-first is always the goal, AND a hosted version is intended: central coordination supporting a large graph of broadly accessible objects.
- Anything built must be completely usable by others hosting a small or large server themselves. P2P-hosted worlds and data behave the same as a large hosted public server; differences live in backend scale elements and access controls.
- Users connect to each other and transfer/interact directly wherever possible, so hosted resources are an offloadable backstop, not a requirement. The app must not technically need us to function. Collaborative / shared / federated / local-first / p2p.
- Our hosted instance is essentially public; other operators open theirs only as much as they want. Publishing paths: share to a big server, publish on pkarr, or self-host. All comms through iroh on the backend; first-class clients.

## The idea, broadened
Worlds need authors, and authors need feedback and control. Broaden beyond analytics: what a world owner should know (visits, joins, program runs, where people get stuck), what they should control (moderation that matches the role model, not a bolt-on), and what a public world owes its visitors (safety signals, reporting). Local-first applies to data too: a self-hosted world keeps its analytics; the public server aggregates only what operators choose to share.

## Research questions (first pass)
- Owner metrics with privacy: counts without surveillance — what is measurable from journal/presence without tracking people
- Moderation surface: existing roles (Phase 10) vs needed powers (mute, slow-mode, ban by key, quarantine a program) and their audit trail
- Reporting flow for public worlds: visitor report → registry/host queue → action, with appeals
- Creator feedback loops: where do joiners drop off a world's first screen; can the platform show that without creepy telemetry

## Dependencies and existing pieces
Builds on Phase 10 roles, F11.7 metrics (#553), F12.6 audit (#1063), and the discovery/hosting topics (public worlds create the moderation need).

- **v1 — first-iteration design** — its own issue, filed in the same pass and linked in the first comment below

- Registry trust model: curated list, operator-run registries, mirroring and disagreement between registries
- Privacy: relay/proxy options through iroh so joining a public world does not broadcast a home IP

code.title: id(phase-14): Hosted worlds & always-on hosting — core topic (research + design)
code.body:
# Hosted worlds & always-on hosting — Phase 14 core topic (research + design)

Filed from the next-horizons discussion #1240, decided by Drew on 2026-11-05: **all themes are planned**. This issue is the core topic for **Hosted worlds & always-on hosting**. Its job is research and design — broaden the idea beyond what is already understood, set up multiple next steps, and produce implementation plans. No implementation starts here; the output is design documents and implementation issues.

## Drew's principles for everything in Phase 14 (from #1240, 2026-11-05)
- Local-first is always the goal, AND a hosted version is intended: central coordination supporting a large graph of broadly accessible objects.
- Anything built must be completely usable by others hosting a small or large server themselves. P2P-hosted worlds and data behave the same as a large hosted public server; differences live in backend scale elements and access controls.
- Users connect to each other and transfer/interact directly wherever possible, so hosted resources are an offloadable backstop, not a requirement. The app must not technically need us to function. Collaborative / shared / federated / local-first / p2p.
- Our hosted instance is essentially public; other operators open theirs only as much as they want. Publishing paths: share to a big server, publish on pkarr, or self-host. All comms through iroh on the backend; first-class clients.

## The idea, broadened
A world today lives while a host process runs. Hosting asks: what is a world when nobody is connected? Broaden beyond 'run the same binary on a VPS': world persistence semantics, who may wake/pause a world, journal custody and backup, operator trust, and how a hosted world stays the *same object* as the local one (same journal, same programs, same ceilings) so moving a world between a laptop, a home server and a public host is a transfer, not a port. Include the split Drew named: a totally public main endpoint, with deeper backend pieces as separate iroh/id servers behind private tunnels with limited trusted access.

## Research questions (first pass)
- World lifecycle states (live, asleep, archived) and who can transition them under the role model (Phase 10 roles, F12.3 authority frames)
- Journal custody: encryption at rest, snapshot/export formats, restore drills — what 'backup' means for a journaled world
- Basement cluster as the first hosting target: capacity, power/egress limits, what breaks first
- Hosted vs local parity checklist: which behaviors must be identical, which are legitimately backend-only (quotas, abuse controls, storage tiers)

## Dependencies and existing pieces
Builds on F12.11 multi-node worlds (#805), F12.13 journal replication (#806), F12.10 quotas (#1067), #227 journal rollback compatibility (done). First Phase 14 implementation theme (with discovery).

## Next steps — the version ladder
- **v1 — first-iteration design** — its own issue, filed in the same pass and linked in the first comment below
- **v2 — outline: custody & lifecycle** — its own issue, filed in the same pass and linked in the first comment below
- **v3 — outline: many nodes** — its own issue, filed in the same pass and linked in the first comment below
- **v4 — outline: public-server operation** — its own issue, filed in the same pass and linked in the first comment below

Plus a standing rule for this topic: anything the research surfaces that doesn't fit v1–v4 gets its own issue (Drew's rule: every feature, concept, or idea gets an issue), and future investigations are listed as comments here rather than lost.

## Sequencing
Design queue order: F12.4 provider registry (#1061) and F12.10 scheduling/quotas (#1067) designs land first; Phase 14 v1 designs then run hosted worlds → discovery → agents spike → the rest. Implementation follows Phase 13. The drop rule applies throughout: anything that proves blocked, wrong, or superseded gets parked or closed with a note — never a silent stall.

code.title: feat(atlas): schema-driven filter surface — implementation programme (from design #5410)
code.body:
Implementation programme for the design note landed for #5410: `doc/2026-11-05T13-03-49Z_design_atlas_manifest_filter_surface/` (PR #6223, merged f86e532b77). Recommendation there: **GO, with phasing**. Design only was authorized for #5410; this issue tracks the build.

## Phases (design note §8)
- [ ] Phase 1 — #5375 escaping fix, implementing the note §5 `exact` semantics (JSON-encode the value, then LIKE-escape the encoded element text; invariant = decoded element equality). Already filed as #5375; lands first.
- [ ] Phase 2 — Manifest schema + loader in atlas-core; today's surface expressed as the built-in manifest; generic label store (`generic_list` shape, note §4) + its query construction. Oracle: parity fixtures byte-identical under the built-in manifest.
- [ ] Phase 3 — Generic dimensions end-to-end: atlas-proto `FilterSpec` dimension map (named fields as aliases for one release), CLI flags generated from the loaded surface, serve-mode validation against the effective surface.
- [ ] Phase 4 — Serve-mode `CacheKey` gains `(manifest_version, content_hash)` (note §7); surface identity in job metadata.
- [ ] Phase 5 — Manifest writer in the classification/publish pass (same transaction as the labels); acceptance gate: one new `generic_list` dimension (e.g. source-app) shipped by manifest only, no binary change.

## Invariants (note §6, non-negotiable)
Sensitivity/ceiling semantics stay code-defined; no sensitivity keys exist in the manifest schema; shapes/stores are code-allowlisted; unknown request dimensions are loud errors; manifest failure falls back to the built-in surface loudly, never silently widening.

## NO-GO trigger (note §10)
If the classification/publish pass cannot write the manifest in the same transaction as the labels in both modes (local publish file + Turso), stop and re-take the §3 home decision before loader work.

Filed by queue worker lane code-a (task 10475) so the #5410 design does not sit without a linked implementation path.

## Acceptance criteria
- The schema-driven filter surface renders filters generated from the schema for the programme's named collections.
- Filter state round-trips through the URL/query contract used by the rest of atlas.
- Tests cover at least one collection end-to-end: schema -> rendered filter -> filtered results.

code.title: OpenClaw: post-fix follow-ups — activation queue behind #6156, memory-wiki, channel completion menu, gateway-death alerting
code.body:
Umbrella for what the 2026-11-05 OpenClaw fix pass (gateway death + heartbeat root-cause; PRs #6142/#6151/#6162) deliberately left queued, with the evidence for each.

## 1. Activation queue (blocked by #6156 — main's HM generation doesn't evaluate since #6146)

Merged and waiting for ONE gateway restart once #6156 is fixed:
- PR #6151: nix-openclaw pin 4b261b08 → 26516d99 (app pin still 2026.10.7 — upstream nix-openclaw has not published a 2026.10.10 pin; their Unreleased changelog already carries .10 pin validation, so the pin bump should follow within days; bump the day it appears) + memory-lancedb `autoCapture: true`.
- PR #6162: memory-lancedb `hooks.allowConversationAccess = true` (without it autoRecall/autoCapture hooks are blocked — the memory DB is at 0 entries).
Post-activation proofs owed: gateway health + Slack connected, `openclaw ltm stats` > 0 after a real conversation, a memory_recall hit from an agent turn, 3 wake-triggered heartbeat runs ok, version string from the new unit's store path.

## 2. memory-wiki plugin (evaluate + likely enable)

Disabled today. Upstream documents it as the companion to memory-lancedb (only one plugin owns the memory SLOT; wiki runs alongside) and the 2026.10.10 release notes show active Memory Wiki work. It turns Shed's accumulated memories into a browsable wiki in the workspace — the inspectable surface for the memory system we just switched on. Enable in home/openclaw (runtimePlugins + entry) in the same activation batch as §1 if evaluation stays favorable.

## 3. Vendored summarize plugin is not loading

`home/openclaw/default.nix` wires the vendored summarize plugin via `customPlugins` (fetchTree pin), and the gateway PATH contains the summarize 0.21.14 CLI — but `openclaw plugins list` on the live gateway shows **no summarize plugin** in either the enabled or disabled list. (#1030, the bundled-plugin re-enable, is closed/superseded by the vendored approach.) Diagnose why the custom plugin doesn't register; the summarize capability was a Drew request from 2026-10-26.

## 4. Channel completion menu (each needs the named Drew act; nothing else blocks)

Current state: Slack LIVE (socket, DM allowlist = Drew). Plugins for discord/whatsapp/matrix/signal/telegram are packaged; no credentials for them exist in the vault (checked 2026-11-05: only `openclaw.slack-*` present).
- **WhatsApp**: Drew scans a QR with his phone (`openclaw channels login --channel whatsapp` on the laptop).
- **Telegram**: Drew talks to @BotFather under his Telegram account to mint a bot token (file as `openclaw.telegram-bot-token`); the telegram plugin also needs adding to `runtimePlugins` in home/openclaw.
- **Signal**: Drew links signal-cli (QR/device link with his phone).
- **Discord**: a bot application + token under Drew's Discord account (developer portal), filed as `openclaw.discord-token`; then a channels.discord block like Slack's.
- **Matrix**: an account on a homeserver for Shed (registration is the step), filed by name; then channels.matrix config.
Per Drew's 2026-11-05 latitude ("setup whatever for claw"), each of these is a standing go once the named act exists. Email is explicitly OUT: no email sending about any of this, and email is not to be wired as a notification/delivery path (the imap plugin stays disabled).

## 5. Gateway-death alerting gap

The 2026-11-04 death was silent for ~24h: when the gateway is down, nothing off-box notices (the heartbeat dies with it). Candidate: a fleet-side watch (stewardship visibility or the morning readout) that checks the gateway health endpoint / unit state from outside the laptop and surfaces a dead gateway in the main chat. Any watch must NOT live inside OpenClaw itself.

## 6. heartbeat.skipWhenBusy

Upstream-recommended for constrained hosts; the nix-openclaw generated schema (both the old pin and 26516d99) has no such option. Re-check after the 2026.10.10 pin lands; add when expressible. The config carries a NOTE comment marking the spot.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Activation batch (§1) lands after #6156 is fixed and ONE gateway restart: post-activation proofs recorded here — gateway health + Slack connected, `openclaw ltm stats` > 0 after a real conversation, a memory_recall hit from an agent turn, 3 wake-triggered heartbeat runs ok, version string from the new unit's store path.
- [x] memory-wiki (§2): evaluation verdict recorded; if favorable, enabled in home/openclaw in the activation batch.
- [x] Vendored summarize plugin (§3): diagnosed — it registers in `openclaw plugins list` and the summarize capability works, or the gap is dispositioned with a named cause.
- [ ] Channel menu (§4): each channel is either live or waiting on exactly the named Drew act listed in the body; no email wiring (explicitly out).
- [ ] Gateway-death alerting (§5): an off-box watch (outside OpenClaw) surfaces a dead gateway in the main chat — proven by one drill or a real detection.
- [ ] heartbeat.skipWhenBusy (§6): re-checked after the 2026.10.10 pin lands; added when the schema expresses it, or the blocker re-recorded.

code.title: design(pm-stack): browser-dependent quota watchdog — CDP scrape producers that self-repair, escalate to a browser-enabled agent
code.body:
## Directive

Drew, 2026-11-04 ~23:18 CST: for providers whose quota/plan data can only be obtained through a logged-in website (Mistral is the first case), a CDP-driven browser scrape path is accepted — "but we'll need a watchdog agent that knows how to work a browser and can fix it whenever it breaks." If the data relies on a cookie, use the cookie. If self-repair fails, the watchdog triggers a task for a browser-enabled agent to fix it.

## Design (landed with this issue)

Full design note: `~/workspace/scratch/mistral-quota-watchdog-2026-11-04/design.md` (sandbox workspace). Shape:

- **Three parts, all on the laptop:** per-provider **producer** (oneshot, 15-min timer, writes the code#1301 file-export documents `~/atlas/<provider>-export/latest.json` + `history.jsonl`, classifying its own failures), a generic **watchdog core** (oneshot offset after the gatherer tick; health state + repair ladder + escalation), and the **gatherer**, which ingests each source via its existing `FILE_EXPORTS` machinery (registry currently empty, ingestion code intact) with code#1268 last-known retention.
- **Health model per source:** last-success timestamp, consecutive-failure count, failure **class** — `session-expired` / `cookie-missing` / `endpoint-changed` / `browser-down` / `cdp-unreachable` / `rate-limited` / `unknown` — each mapped to a repair.
- **Repair ladder, cheapest first,** attempt-capped and logged: (0) retain + disk-persisted cooldown (rate-limited only); (1) retry next tick; (2) re-validate/re-extract the session via CDP — primary pattern is the retired Meta producer's **in-page fetch, where the cookie never leaves the browser**; value extraction is the fallback and lands only in fleet secrets by name; (3) re-login in the browser via the standing Google SSO session ("click in and reset it") — a human-only challenge (2FA / verify-it's-you / passkey) makes the incident **human-blocked** and surfaces to Drew immediately; (4) escalate to a browser-enabled agent (fleet queue task with the full failure context + one deduplicated GitHub incident issue; auto-close on recovery).
- **State on disk, always:** `~/.local/state/pm-aggregator/quota-watchdog-state.json`, atomic writes. This is the direct application of code#5928's lesson — the watchdog is a oneshot and must not repeat the in-process cooldown/cache mistake.
- **Cadence:** producers `*:0/15`, watchdog offset on the same 15-min rhythm as the gatherer. **Alerting:** silent while self-repair works; Drew hears only human-blocked (immediately) or an escalation unresolved >24 h.
- **Generality:** per-provider **adapter** files (origins allowlist, data paths in preference order, cookie names, login hints, class map, thresholds). Mistral is adapter #1; Claude console / Open Design (code#5060) are named later adopters.
- **History:** health observations feed the existing usage snapshot pipeline (code#4889) once its laptop path bug is fixed; interim is the producers' `history.jsonl` convention — no parallel store.

## Position vs existing work

- This is the **quota-source specialization of code#1260** (pm-stack SLOs + self-healing: remediation catalogue, attempt caps/cooldowns, escalate only when remediation fails). Its catalogue entries fold back into #1260; code#1283 drills should eventually exercise it.
- It **revives the retired v1 Meta producer pattern** (CDP scrape, code#1301) for the one case the 2026-11-03 "quota is gathered by asking OpenCode" ruling does not cover: no API path exists at the credential class held. Preference order per source stays API → usage-capable token → browser-under-watchdog.
- Division of labor with openchamber#1619: that issue adds the Mistral key-validity provider (presence/validity via API). This program adds the **plan usage** read #1619 proved the API cannot give. Both land; neither replaces the other.

## Open questions (named, per #1260's rule)

1. Escalation-unresolved threshold before a NEEDS DREW line: 24 h proposed. Not blocking.
2. Recovery of a human-blocked incident: stay silent (closed issue is the record) — proposed.
3. Producer source home: `pm-stack/exporters/` in this repo (proposed) vs beside the quota module in openchamber.

## Implementation split (linked issues)

- Watchdog core: filed as a sibling issue in this repo, linked below.
- Escalation mechanism: filed as a sibling issue in this repo, linked below.
- Mistral adapter #1: filed in developing-today-forks/openchamber, **blocked on the sign-in lane's data-path outcome** (Vibe token usage API vs console endpoint + cookie), linked below.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] This design is reviewed and its open questions answered or explicitly deferred.
- [ ] The implementation issues linked from this issue exist and carry their own acceptance criteria (this issue carries no implementation work itself).
- [ ] The design's remediation-catalogue entries are reflected in code#1260's catalogue (comment or sub-issue link there).

code.title: task(atlas): audit existing embeds for provenance/path correctness against the marking standard
code.body:
Parent: [#6018](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/6018) (Atlas ingestion program). Statement S34 of the 2026-11-04 brief. **This is a task to execute, not only a design.**

## Task (Drew, in substance)

**Scan all existing embeds and determine whether they use the appropriate path or details.** The current corpus (107,639 chunks across the production monolith and the restored shards) accumulated over multiple ingestion eras with different conventions. The program's provenance standard (extensions on [#3125](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/3125)) requires every embed to carry a correct origin mark — `repo@hash:path` for git content, or a source-system mark (system @ machine @ date) for the rest. This audit measures how much of the existing corpus meets that bar and produces the defect list a repair pass would work from.

## Scope

- Inventory the provenance/path metadata actually present per chunk source class: well-formed `repo@hash:path`? path without hash? hash without path? free-text source strings? nothing?
- Correctness, not just presence: does the recorded path exist at the recorded hash? Do source-system marks name the right machine/date (e.g. session chunks attributed to the wrong host store)? Sampled verification against the live sources (repos on the laptop, the OpenCode DBs, the canonical atlas content stores: internal 18,235 sessions / 70,987 messages + secret 90 / 564 per the restoration records).
- Duplicates and orphans: chunks whose provenance points at sources that no longer exist, and duplicate chunks carrying divergent provenance (same content, different claimed origins) — both are logged states per the standard, and the audit counts them.
- Tier split throughout: report internal and secret tiers separately; handle secret-tier findings under the classification task's sensitivity rules (sibling task under [#6018](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/6018) — counts and IDs, never content).

## Done looks like

A dated audit report: per-class counts (well-formed / defective-by-kind / missing), sampled-verification results, and a sized repair backlog (fixable by re-derivation from sources vs needs re-ingest vs unrecoverable-but-logged) filed as follow-ons. The audit itself changes no data.

code.body:
Parent: [#6018](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/6018) (Atlas ingestion program). Statement S15 of the 2026-11-04 brief.

## Task (Drew, in substance)

Once the ingestion design is somewhat in place, run a **first pass adding all these data points into Atlas**:

- **All the code repos** (the full estate: developing-today/code, the forks, darwin-nix, hatch-personal, hatch, zettel, and the rest) — current content, ingested **delta-safely** so later re-runs are cheap.
- **All the docs we can find** — including the untracked material enumerated by the docs-migration Atlas sweep ([#5981](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5981)): research notes, goal workspaces, memory topics, scratch findings that survived.
- **The cairn repo** (dezren39/cairn, 473 files — Drew's dictation says "the can repo"; interpretation recorded in the program inventory).
- Plus the outputs of the sibling pieces as they land: our-repos GitHub comments (sibling extraction task under [#6018](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/6018)) and the operational sources (session/chat logs, statistics, reports).

## Explicitly OUT of this pass

- **External-repo comments** — gated on the licensing research (sibling issue under [#6018](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/6018)); they join a later pass if the gate clears.
- Anything the classification revalidation (sibling task) flags as mis-tiered gets its tier fixed at ingest, not copied forward.

## Execution requirements

- **Provenance from the start**: every object lands with the program's provenance marks (`repo@hash:path` for git content; source-system @ machine @ date marks for the rest) and occurrences recorded per [#3125](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/3125) — the first pass must not create a second provenance-audit debt (cf. the existing-embed audit task).
- **Delta-safe**: the pass runs on the delta-only machinery (sibling design) or, if that design is not yet built, on content-hash skipping at minimum, so re-running the pass is idempotent and cheap (the 21 GB rule: 20.5 GB already present must not be re-landed or retagged).
- **Tier discipline**: secret-class sources route only to the secret tier; the pass reports per-source tier assignments for spot-check against the revalidation findings.
- **Cost/disk discipline**: the pass reports its storage delta and runtime against the plan ceiling and the disk/IO guardrails from the operations design; a pass that would breach either stops and reports instead.

## Done looks like

A completed, reported run: per-source counts (objects in, chunks landed, skipped-as-duplicates, tier split), storage delta vs plan headroom, and a defect list (unassociated/unprovenanced items logged per the provenance standard, not silently dropped). Follow-on passes become the recurring sweeps of the operations design.

code.title: research(licensing): may we ingest external GitHub comments/discussions into Atlas? — gate for the external corpus
code.body:
Parent: [#6018](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/6018) (Atlas ingestion program). Statements S13–S14 of the 2026-11-04 brief. Family: tonight's licensing program — [#5977](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5977) (taxonomy/classifier), [#5979](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5979) (SPDX tooling), [#5984](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5984) (policy/ToS), [#5986](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5986) (AGPL/GPL hosting research). This issue is the **ingestion-side** counterpart: copying OTHER people's words IN, where the licensing program mostly covers our code and user uploads.

## The gate (Drew, in substance)

Before Atlas ingests comments from **external** repos, determine whether we may: **can I copy a comment from a GitHub discussion? Is it Creative Commons?** Drew's sequencing: figure this out **before the external corpus is built, but after it is somewhat designed** — so this research runs parallel to design and **gates the build** of the external half of the GitHub-corpus extraction (sibling task under [#6018](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/6018)). Our own repos are not gated.

## Questions the research must answer

1. **What license, if any, covers a GitHub issue/PR comment or Discussion post?** Facts to establish from primary sources (GitHub Terms of Service, esp. the user-content sections): users retain copyright; users grant GitHub a broad license; what, exactly, do OTHER users/third parties get (viewing + forking rights inside GitHub are granted — what about copying OUT)? Is any of it Creative Commons (short answer expected: no — but establish it, don't assume; note the contrast with Stack Overflow's CC BY-SA).
2. **Distinctions that may change the answer**:
   - Our own comments on external repos vs third parties' comments.
   - Issues/PRs vs Discussions vs gists vs wiki pages.
   - Storing + embedding for a **private, personal search corpus** (never redistributed) vs **redistributing/publishing** the text — does private, non-distributive copying for personal retrieval sit differently (fair use / implied license / API terms) than republication?
   - GitHub **API Terms** constraints on storing API-served content, independent of copyright.
   - A repo whose project license is copyleft (GPL/AGPL) — does the project license reach comments filed in its tracker? (Generally no, but confirm and note the exceptions people assert.)
   - Attribution obligations if any use is permitted.
3. **Practical postures available**: e.g. ingest-own-comments-only externally; ingest-all-but-never-redistribute (internal tier, no hydration into shared contexts); ingest metadata + embeddings only, fetch text live from GitHub at resolution time (store-no-text pattern — cf. [#3125](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/3125)'s resolve-at-read design); exclude Discussions while allowing issues/PRs. For each: what it costs the corpus and what risk it retires.

## Done looks like

A sourced research note (primary sources linked, no vibes) ending in a **clear gate ruling recommendation per posture**, recorded on this issue and linked from the extraction task and [#5986](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5986). The extraction build does not start its external half until Drew accepts a posture.

code.title: atlas ingestion program: semi-automated updates, versioning, provenance, feedback — long-term design + tasks (2026-11-04 brief)
code.body:
## Program (Drew, 2026-11-04)

A long-term plan for **semi-automating updates to Atlas ingestion**: what gets ingested, how content is versioned, a standard provenance model, delta-only updates, retrieval statistics + result feedback, classification safety, and disk/IO + plan-spend discipline. Statement inventory (S1–S40, auditable, with per-statement dispositions): `~/workspace/scratch/atlas-ingestion-brief-2026-11-04/statement-inventory.md` in the sandbox workspace; this issue is the canonical tracker — children are linked in a comment below and closed into this issue as they complete.

## Where Atlas stands (2026-11-04, verified)

- Shard restoration complete: 31 TursoDB shards; **internal = 28 shards / 107,001 chunks; secret = exactly 1 shard / 638 chunks** (secret material only in the 2 secret DBs). Production monolith stays libSQL for now; TursoDB for all NEW databases. Cold tiers → rustfs (2026-11-04 storage ruling). Current spend anchor: **Turso scaler $24.92/mo yearly — the plan is the ceiling** (see also [#5468](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5468), mirror storage pressure).
- Search: fan-out over shards [#5755](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5755); query front-end [#5773](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5773); full parameter surface with per-run vector logging [#5774](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5774); Jaccard rescore + ingest dedup ≥0.9 recorded edge [#5733](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5733); staging tier with merge-on-close promotion [#5669](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5669).
- Provenance registry already designed: [#3125](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/3125) (chunk_occurrences, content-addressed extracts, `repo@commit:path` pinning). This program **extends** #3125 (source-system marks, version lineage) rather than replacing it.
- Scripts migration into code + fleet binary: [#5670](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5670). Untracked Atlas material enumeration: [#5981](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5981) — ingestion source enumeration overlaps it.

## Topic map (children filed under this tracker)

1. **Ingestion operations design** — semi-automated updates; automatic source set (reboots/boot records, session logs, chat logs, statistics, reports); usefulness filter; disk + I/O monitoring; plan-spend ceiling.
2. **Classification revalidation (task)** — verify nothing sensitive sits at the wrong tier.
3. **Agent notes placement design** — zettel vs repo vs publishing directly into the ID graph (ties to [#5545](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5545), [#5686](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5686)).
4. **GitHub corpus extraction (task)** — ALL issue/PR comments from ALL our repos; external repos we interact with or rely on (external half gated, see 5).
5. **External-content licensing gate (research)** — may we copy external GitHub comments/discussions into Atlas at all? In the [#5977](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5977)/[#5986](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5986) family. **Must be answered before external-repo ingestion is built; design may proceed.**
6. **First-pass corpus (task)** — all code repos, all findable docs, dezren39/cairn.
7. **Content versioning + retention design** — new versions, rename lineage, newest-resolution ("take the max"), cold rollout, deletion triggers (date / superseding increments / never accessed).
8. **Retrieval statistics + feedback + query trace design** — top-K shard survival, top-1/2/3/5 after merge+rescore, thumbs up/down minimum, optional comments/essays, result↔query trace (per-stage scores, shard, exact embed state, metadata).
9. **Provenance standard** — extensions filed as a comment on [#3125](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/3125): one standard for when/where; marks of the form `repo@hash:path` AND source-system marks (e.g. `opencode-db @ amd @ <date>`); segment search to associate unlineaged files; unassociated/duplicate as a logged state.
10. **Existing-embed provenance audit (task)** — scan all current embeds for correct path/provenance details.
11. **Delta-only ingestion + offset embeds design** — the 21 GB rule (20.5 GB already present → only new files + edits land; no mass retagging); span-anchored embeds (content at file offsets 17–241) with search-time joins that never double merged lines.
12. **Expansive v2–v4 design** — the larger design that pushes depth/scope beyond this brief wherever research leads.

## Horizons

- **v1** — first-pass corpus (own repos incl. GitHub comments, docs, cairn) + delta ingestion + provenance marking standard + embed audit + classification revalidation run.
- **v2** — file versioning/retention live (cold rollout + deletion policy) + retrieval statistics (shard survival, top-1/2/3/5).
- **v3** — feedback loop live (thumbs/comments/traces) feeding retention + ranking evolution; classification revalidation recurring/automated; offset-embed joins in production search.
- **v4** — expansive: feedback-trained ranking, provenance-complete resolution, cross-source lineage graph, ID-graph-native corpus objects, classification-aware retrieval.

## Gates

- External-repo comment ingestion is **build-gated** on topic 5's answer (Drew's sequencing: licensing figured out before the external build, after the design is somewhat done). Our own repos are not gated.
- Nothing in this program raises spend past the current plan without Drew's explicit call (S3).

code.title: id: design: semantic cell/tag presentation model — one tagged state, many renderers
code.body:
Part of the worlds design program: [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955). Wave-2 follow-up from the prior-art research (Lane B item 37); parent topic issue: [#5970](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5970). Research source: `workspace/scratch/worlds-capabilities-brief-2026-11-04/prior-art-research.md`.

## The Dwarf Fortress rule

DF's presentation history is the canonical capability-tier story: ASCII glyphs (CP437) → community tilesets replacing glyphs 1:1 → full graphical tiles — *the simulation never changed, only the presentation mapping*, and the ASCII tier remains a complete, playable representation. The design rule: **world state must be expressible as a grid of typed cells with semantic tags** (creature/material/state), and each client tier renders tags at its fidelity. Drew's "blue cape with sparkles → blue letter C / cape emoji" is exactly a tag→glyph fallback rule.

## Scope

- The tag vocabulary: what a cell carries (kind, owner-visible identity, state flags) such that ASCII, tiles, and rich renderers can all be complete.
- How this composes with presentation-is-data as already shipped (legacy UTF-8 text or the versioned Screen cell buffer; guests never supply escapes/HTML/CSS) and with the tiers in #786 and the asset/filter model in #5970.
- Who assigns tags: world code declares them; the fallback mapping per tier is a client/presentation-layer table, not world code.

## Done looks like

A tagged-state spec (cell fields, tag vocabulary v1, per-tier rendering obligations) that #5970's fallback chain can reference.

code.title: id: design: feature-object library attachment — runtime attach/detach of library behavior to entities without world recompilation
code.body:
Part of the worlds design program: [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955). Wave-2 follow-up from the prior-art research (Lane B item 20); parent topic issue: [#5964](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5964). Research source: `workspace/scratch/worlds-capabilities-brief-2026-11-04/prior-art-research.md`.

## Precedent

**LambdaMOO feature objects** are the library model Drew described, working since the '90s: create a feature object implementing reusable verbs, and any player object can attach it and gain those commands — libraries as *runtime-attached objects*, no recompilation of the consumer (https://www.moo.mud.org/moo-faq/lcore-getting-started.html).

## Scope

Distinct from the taxonomy child of #5955 (attachment as *classification*: genre/game/entity/none) and from the DLL design (#5964: per-user *functions*): this is runtime attach/detach of *library behavior* to entities inside a running world.

- Attach/detach semantics: who may attach (entity owner, world author), at what moment (tick boundary), what happens to in-flight invocations.
- The attached library's capability footprint composes with the entity's and the world's ceilings — checked how, at attach time?
- Detach and version change: state the library accumulated on the entity — kept, migrated, dropped?

## Done looks like

A design note stating whether feature-object attachment is a v-next mechanism for us, and if so its semantics; if not, the recorded reason.

code.title: Docs migration: hatch-personal/hatch/darwin-nix → code canonical home (tracking)
code.body:
Drew's directive, 2026-11-04: documentation and designs that are **not strictly about the sandbox environment** move their canonical home from dezren39/hatch-personal + dezren39/hatch into this repo; darwin-nix keeps only flake documentation. We're aggregating docs and productionizing the binaries — designs that led to built things live together here. **Plan + issues only in this step; no files have moved yet.**

Full plan + machine-readable inventory (sandbox workspace): `~/workspace/scratch/docs-migration-plan-2026-11-04/plan.md` + `inventory.json`.

## Classification standard

Every tracked item is exactly one of:

- **MOVE** — canonical home becomes code.
- **STAY** — sandbox-environment / system-baked (init script, quota script, prompts, AGENTS.md, avatars, TOOLS.md/TOOLS.d; in darwin-nix: flake mechanics + functional config/code).
- **STAY-UNTIL-REPLACED** — register below; each names the missing fleet feature that is its exit condition.

Test: *would this make sense to someone running the fleet/code without this sandbox?* darwin-nix specialisation: docs **about** a topic move; flake code/config that **uses** the topic stays.

**Copy, never delete.** Source repos keep historical copies permanently; living docs get a one-line `Canonical:` pointer header in the source after the copy lands.

## Counts (tracked files)

| Repo | Total | MOVE | STAY-UNTIL-REPLACED | STAY |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| hatch-personal (482) / hatch public mirror (475 = same set − 7 submodule entries) | 482 | 110 | 18 | 354 |
| darwin-nix | 474 | 32 | 0 | 442 |

## Batches

- #5976 — backup scripts & backup documentation (27 files: runtime-db-export, bws-backup-secrets, backup process docs)
- #5978 — Fleet designs, task-system schema & fleet machinery (42 files: 29 Supabase migrations, fleet-fetch, archer-slack design, mcpx-opencode plan; fleet-brokers already migrated via #5430)
- #5980 — architecture & how-it-works docs, DB/platform tooling (25 files: supabase-exec, turso-exec, Cloudflare tooling, toolchain docs, platform research)
