code.title: id: research: SPDX identifiers and license-detection tooling for the classifier
code.body:
Part of the worlds design program: [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955). Supports the license taxonomy/classifier design (statements S82–S89 of the 2026-11-04 brief); filed as dedicated research per Drew's rule for sub-parts needing their own documentation.

## Task

Survey the existing machinery for machine-readable license identification so the classifier design doesn't invent a private format:

- **SPDX License List**: identifiers for every license in the brief's set (MIT and variants incl. MIT-0, BSD family, MPL-2.0, BlueOak-1.0.0, Apache-2.0, GPL-2.0/GPL-3.0/AGPL-3.0 with only/or-later distinctions, CC0-1.0, CC-BY-4.0, CC-BY-SA-4.0, CC NC variants), plus SPDX expressions for combinations (`MIT OR Apache-2.0`, `AND`) — the dual-licensing case our own standard (MIT or Apache) needs.
- **Detection tooling**: licensee, ScanCode, `cargo-about` / `cargo-deny` license checks, REUSE spec compliance — what they detect, from what evidence (headers, manifests, full text matching), and their false-positive behavior on variants.
- **Public domain handling** in SPDX (`LicenseRef`? CC0 as the recommended route?) and how registries (crates.io, npm, PyPI) validate/classify license fields today — including how they treat unlicensed code.
- What a manifest field should look like in our KDL manifests ([#5753](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5753)) if it's SPDX-expression-shaped.

## Done looks like

A research doc: the SPDX identifier table for the brief's full license set, a tooling comparison, and a recommendation for the classifier's identifier + expression format.

code.title: id: research: image/video conversion tooling — kitty graphics protocol and video-to-ASCII
code.body:
Part of the worlds design program: [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955). Statements S73–S74 of the 2026-11-04 brief. Filed as dedicated research per Drew's rule for sub-parts needing their own documentation.

## Task (Drew, in substance)

We need **a basic system to convert images and videos into the kitty protocol**, and there are also **IDF video-to-ASCII tools** out there — some of those might be used as well. Survey what exists before building anything:

- **Kitty graphics protocol**: encoder/tooling landscape (library support, terminal support matrix), stills vs animation/video over the protocol, bandwidth and chunking behavior.
- **Adjacent terminal graphics**: sixel, iTerm2 inline images — only insofar as the fallback tiers need them.
- **Video-to-ASCII**: the IDF tools Drew names and the wider field (jp2a-style stills pipelines, `mpv` ASCII outputs, dedicated converters) — quality, speed, color fidelity, licensing (this feeds the licensing program too: a converter's license constrains bundling).
- Where conversion should live: upload-time (presentation-layer conversion tools, per the assets design child of [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955)), client-side at render time, or both for different tiers.

## Not this

[#787](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/787) is the kitty **keyboard** protocol on the raw input path — a different protocol that happens to share the terminal. This research is graphics/media only; don't merge the two.

## Done looks like

A research doc: tooling survey with licenses, a recommended converter pipeline per tier (kitty graphics / ASCII video / static ASCII), and the conversion-placement decision with reasons.

code.title: id: design: user presentation assets — shaders, sprites by ID, filters, per-world gating, graceful degradation
code.body:
Part of the worlds design program: [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955). Statements S66–S72 of the 2026-11-04 brief. Extends the presentation-tiers design in [#786](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/786) — that issue covers capability tiers with in-band terminal detection; this one covers user-supplied assets and filters living on top of the tiers.

## Requirement (Drew, in substance)

- In the future, users might provide **GPU shaders**, and **images or sprites that were uploaded already as a given ID**.
- A user will be able to **set their sprite to have a cape and apply the filter "sparkle" to the cape** — **without any of that being specifically coded by a given app**.
- This is an **imperfect system**, and the **app would have to enable such capabilities**.
- Over time there may become a **common interface for different formats** and **basic conversion tools at the presentation layer**, to allow this to work on a **variety of devices** and a **variety of worlds**, which may or may not support different capabilities.
- **Per-world gating:** one world might not support filters, because you could make yourself look like a different kind of creature, or make a filter that basically **makes you invisible** — so it's **just disabled in this world**.
- **Graceful fallback is authored, not improvised:** "when filters are disabled, put static sparkles on the GIF image of my sprite."
- **Terminal degradation:** another user viewing on a terminal that only supports ASCII drops down to **Dwarf Fortress-style sprites** or to **a specific character that represents that user** — instead of a blue cape with sparkles, it's a **blue letter C** or an emoji of a cape — even though in other worlds, or in this world with a sufficient client, it's practically **MapleStory**.

## Design points to settle

- The asset/filter model: assets by ID (uploaded once, referenced everywhere), filters as named composable transforms applied to asset parts (cape), each with declared capability needs.
- The fallback chain as a first-class declaration: rich → static-substitute → sprite-sheet tier → glyph/emoji. Who authors each rung (asset author, world author, client)?
- World policy: which asset/filter capabilities a world enables is a world-level declaration users can see before joining (composes with the permission/registry story).
- Abuse surface: filters as disguise/invisibility is a *gameplay* decision per world; shaders are *code* — do user shaders go through the same compile/trust pipeline as user functions (DLL child of [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955))?

## Related

- Presentation capability tiers: [#786](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/786)
- Graphical client & tooling surface: [#5782](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5782); Bevy incorporation: [#5781](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5781)
- Media conversion research child of [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955) (kitty protocol / video-to-ASCII tooling)

## Done looks like

A design doc: asset-by-ID model, filter capability declarations, the authored fallback chain, and per-world enablement policy — mapped onto the tiers in [#786](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/786).

code.title: id: design: dynamic user functions — server-compiled DLLs, hot-swap into running worlds without world recompile
code.body:
Part of the worlds design program: [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955). Statements S36–S38 and S45 of the 2026-11-04 brief. This is the V3 stage of the program.

## Requirement (Drew, in substance)

User-level code should be passable into a **running world without recompiling the whole world**:

- At least in one version of the compiler there is a way to make a **DLL**. The **server side compiles that DLL itself** — user code is never trusted pre-compiled.
- The platform then **places the DLL in the appropriate location** for the world-side code to call it.
- If a user changes what's running, the world-side code **picks it up as soon as it's compiled and available to be hot-swapped in**.
- **Trust chain:** the server can trust the code because it did the compilation itself; and the only non-pure things the user function can do are from the **server's own platform being passed to it by the world author** — and the world author can trust that chain too.

## Design points to settle

- Interface contract: what signature/shape a user DLL exposes, and how the world discovers and binds it (name, version, interface hash). Mismatch behavior: refuse, fall back to previous version, or run the user's prior published code (see the compile-economics child — "keep running what you'd already published" is the stated default).
- Swap semantics: swap at tick boundary only? In-flight calls finish on the old code — state handoff between versions (the function's state is the world's problem, the function's problem, or serialized through a defined state type?).
- Which Roc compiler line actually supports the DLL path Drew remembers, and what it costs us to build on it (pin vs track).
- Isolation: a user DLL crashing or hanging must not take the world down (budgets: server-invariants child; per-function enforcement: gas/timeout research child).
- Distinction from the *authoring* hot-swap loop (`id world dev`, [#558](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/558) / [#5541](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5541)): that swaps world code for its author during development; this swaps **per-user functions inside a live world for its players**. Reuse its mechanics where they fit, but the trust and budget models differ.

## Related

- Programming-model child of [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955) (functions passed by the world are the static case of this)
- Per-user function mapping child of [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955) (the consumer of this mechanism)
- Compile chain today: `pkgs/id/src/world_compile.rs`

## Done looks like

A design doc: DLL interface contract, server compile pipeline, placement/binding, swap semantics incl. failure fallbacks, and the trust argument written out end-to-end.

code.title: id: research: permission-prompt precedents — Play Store, Android/iOS runtime permissions, OAuth scopes, extension permissions, TCC/portals
code.body:
Part of the worlds design program: [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955). Supports the permission-UX design (statements S19–S23 of the 2026-11-04 brief); filed as its own research per Drew's rule that sub-parts with a lot of prior art get dedicated documentation even when not needed for V1.

## Task

Survey how existing platforms present and remember capability grants, and extract what works and what users actually understand:

- **Google Play** permission declarations and runtime permission groups (the brief's named model).
- **Android runtime permissions**: ask-on-first-use, per-permission memory, "ask every time," permission auto-reset for unused apps.
- **iOS** prompts and privacy nutrition labels.
- **Browser extension** permissions (Chrome/Firefox): install-time vs runtime host permissions, optional permissions.
- **OAuth scopes**: blanket vs incremental authorization, scope creep complaints.
- **OS sandbox prompts**: macOS TCC, Flatpak portals — per-resource, per-app remembered grants.
- Failure literature: permission fatigue, blanket-accept rates, why install-time-only lists failed on Android and were replaced.

## Deliverable

A research doc: per-system summary (what's shown, when, what's remembered, revocation), a comparison table, and a shortlist of patterns that fit a two-sided (client + server admin) grant model — feeding the permission-UX design child of [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955).

## Done looks like

Doc landed and linked from the permission-UX design issue; every pattern the design adopts (or rejects) cites this survey.

code.title: id: design: capability-change notices on reconnect — expansion and sideways changes
code.body:
Part of the worlds design program: [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955). Statements S17–S18 of the 2026-11-04 brief.

## Requirement (Drew, in substance)

Design the system for when a place a user has **already connected to before** changes its capabilities:

- The change may be an **expansion** (strict superset), or a **sideways modification** — not a strict reproduction of the previous capability set.
- **By default there is a warning or notice before the user connects** and has unexpected results. No silent upgrades of what a known world can do.

## Design points to settle

- What is compared: the registry's requested set, the discovered-used set (see the capability-model child of [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955)), or both? A change in *used* with no change in *requested* is exactly the sideways case that matters.
- Notice content: diff presented in plain language (new capabilities named), not a hash change.
- User choices on notice: proceed once, proceed and accept the new set as the baseline, refuse. Is there a "remember for capability decreases only" asymmetry (decreases are safe, increases warn)?
- Who else gets notified: server admins for server-side capabilities, world authors when a library they depend on changes its capability footprint.
- Interaction with invites ([#5751](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5751)): does accepting an invite pin the capability set the invite was issued under?

## Related

- Permission UX child of [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955) (the notice is a permission-surface moment)
- Invites: [#5751](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5751)

## Done looks like

A design specifying the comparison baseline, the diff presentation, the user's options, and the re-baselining rule — implementable against the registry schema from the capability-model design.

code.title: id: design program: worlds — advanced Roc libraries, capabilities, permissions, dynamic user functions, licensing (2026-11-04 brief)
code.body:
Tracking issue for Drew's 2026-11-04 mega-brief on worlds: advanced Roc libraries, the capability model, permission UX, dynamic user functions, presentation assets, world governance, self-hosting, and licensing. The full statement-by-statement inventory (113 statements, S1–S113, each mapped to a child issue or an existing issue) is the decomposition record for this program.

## Program framing (from the brief)

- Design and build out how we improve the **permissions, observability, and composability** of apps, and the ability for **developers to publish libraries of their own**. (S28, S29)
- Our side's cares are narrow and hard: ticks/sessions/gas stay below set amounts, the platform side is solid and can't be exploited beyond its intent, and users are aware of what could be done. Within those bounds (disk etc.), users can pull whatever libraries they want.
- Ideally everything in the ecosystem is MIT / Apache / Blue Oak / MPL. (S92)

## V1 / V2 / V3 staging

- **V1 — imports with ceilings as they exist today:** worlds import pure dependencies and platform-dependent dependencies against the existing compile-time capability catalog in `pkgs/id/crates/id-core/src/world_caps.rs`; the demo library + app with both negative tests lands and is verified (closes the loop with the Phase 9–10 Roc-library verification debt in [#796](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/796)).
- **V2 — registry + permissions:** requested-vs-discovered-used capability sets listed in the registry, custom-compiled platforms when none fits, Play Store-style permission prompts with admin grant modes, capability-change notices on reconnect, and the licensing classifier + policy layer for uploads.
- **V3 — dynamic user functions:** server-compiled DLLs hot-swapped into running worlds without recompiling the world, per-function gas/timeout budgets, strategy switching, premium gating for raw-code uploads and persistent caching.

code.title: design: telemetry rollup — one stats pipeline under fleet init (sysstat + extra stats); init reduced to stats + prewarm
code.body:
# design: telemetry rollup — one stats pipeline under `fleet init` (sysstat base + fleet extra stats); init reduced to stats + prewarm

## Framing — Drew's two-purpose test (2026-11-04 20:48 CST)

> "now that init runs as part of every job starting, having an init job at all maybe is only helpful for getting stats and prewarming fleet conns."

So the test this design must pass: **an init job earns its existence only by (a) stats collection and (b) prewarming fleet connections.** Anything in today's init beyond those two is a candidate for deletion or re-homing, and the end state must say explicitly what remains of the boot-init job. This follows WS-C's init fix (75 s → 9 s), whose core lesson was the anti-pattern this design retires permanently: **a live probe nobody consumes** (the 60 s `du` that read "unknown" 138 times).

## Inventory — what exists now (measured/read 2026-11-04)

| # | Component | Measures | Consumer | Cadence | Cost | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **sysstat-collector** (`sadc -S ALL`, looped 5×120 s runs → `~/logs/sysstat/sa-<day>`, 14-day prune; restored by init.sh) | CPU split (user/system/iowait/**steal**), memory, swap, per-device disk, network-interface aggregates | Incident forensics (#5701), WS-C attribution | 2 min samples | ~0.003% of a core (measured) | **KEEP — the base collector** |
| 2 | **resource-sampler** (`~/logs/resource/resource-<day>.log`) | Load 1/5/15, mem used/avail, top process by cumulative %CPU, **hatch daemon PID watch** (death post-mortems) | Incident forensics | 120 s lines | Negligible CPU; a bespoke script + unit forever | **FOLD** — its unique values are the daemon-PID *event* and a crude top-process proxy; both are done properly by the rollup (pidstat history + a daemon-state event). Retire the script once those exist; keep historical logs |
| 3 | **pidstat** (sysstat suite) | Per-process CPU/mem/IO — the "which PID ate the box" history | *Nobody — installed and working (verified live) but never run as a collector* | — | — | **ADOPT** as the per-process layer of the rollup (see coverage analysis) |
| 4 | **init.sh telemetry block** | cache.nixos.org latency (HEAD + 3 parallel samples), nix version, store-path count, profile-bin count, subscription/quota status line → `~/logs/init-status` (latest boot) + `~/logs/init.jsonl` (per-boot records) | Boot-init sweeps, metrics enumeration | Per boot | ~2–4 s of the 9 s init | **FOLD** into the rollup as the boot record (below) |
| 5 | **Detached `du` → `~/logs/.nix-persist-size` cache file** | nix-persist tree size, written detached post-WS-C; consumers read the cache | init.jsonl record | Per boot, detached | One background `du` per boot | **KEEP the pattern, generalize it** — tree-size is not a sysstat metric; one throttled cache-writer per watched tree, always consumed with its age attached |
| 6 | **trips.jsonl** (client + daemon sides) | Per fleet-proxy trip: path, total_ms, status / duration, exit, byte counts | #5701/#5702 latency work, WS-C derived stats | Per call (1,644 daemon lines at last read) | Append-only local writes | **KEEP raw; FOLD aggregates into the rollup** (per-hour counts by status/failure class; per-leg p50/p95 once #5702's four timestamps land) |
| 7 | **quota-recorder** (1-min timer, ~5 s/run, broker-shipped records + Supabase acks) | *Provider* quota snapshots → stewardship visibility JSONL | Stewardship, quota-check | 1 min | The box's most frequent timer (#5775 has the cadence ruling) | **KEEP SEPARATE** — it is a billing-evidence record about *external providers* with delivery/ack semantics, not host telemetry; coupling it to a host-stats pipeline buys nothing and risks the record. Rollup consumers may *read* its outputs as a source |
| 8 | **fleet-watchdog per-lane reads** | Lane consecutive-failure counts, last-good times | Watchdog alerts | ~10–15 min | Repeated live joins across cron runs × agent.tasks | **CONSUMER, not a collector** — the per-lane proof gauge (tasks completed per lane per shift; the join fields exist on both sides, nobody computes it) becomes a rollup **output** the watchdog reads |
| 9 | **conn-watch.py** | (was) connection watching | Nobody | — | A zombie holding a deleted-inode fd until WS-C killed it | **DELETE** remnants — already stopped (#5775 records it); remove the script so nothing resurrects it |
| 10 | **init.sh live verification probes** (`services-verify` 900 s budget, go/rust presence checks, nix eval smoke) | "Is it healthy?" — answered synchronously at boot | Nobody, since WS-C | Per boot | The synchronous-probe anti-pattern in its purest form | **DELETE from init** — health is read from the rollup/watchdog, never probed at boot |
| 11 | **init.sh restorers** (per-service `install.sh` unit installs incl. #1/#2 above; nix-ensure/wrapper/profile-sync; symlink-layer repair) | Not stats. Not prewarm. | The sandbox recycle cycle | Per boot | Most of init's remaining bulk | **MOVE OUT** — they don't die, they change owner: the generic restorer (#5770, deploy design) + platform boot. Init is the wrong home (see two-purpose audit) |

## Coverage analysis — what sysstat already covers, what it cannot

Measured against the actual collector invocation (`sadc -S ALL 120 5`, looped):

- **Covered fully**: system aggregates — CPU split including iowait and steal (the #5701 oversubscription signal), memory/swap, per-block-device throughput and utilization, per-interface network throughput/errors. `sar`/`sadf` read the daily files; 14 days of history already accumulate (~2 MB/day).
- **NOT covered by sadc, by design**: **per-process anything.** sadc has no per-PID activity; the sa files can never answer "which process." pidstat *is* in the same suite, installed, and verified working on this box — it is simply never run persistently. The rollup therefore adds a pidstat collector loop (same unit family, e.g. `pidstat -urd -p ALL` at the sadc cadence, daily files beside the sa files) and the resource-sampler retires. Open choice for the implementer: 120 s to match sadc, or 60 s for finer incident resolution — storage is trivial either way.
- **NOT a sysstat metric at all**: directory-tree usage (`du`). Handled by the generalized cache-writer pattern (#5): detached, throttled, value+timestamp, consumers tolerate staleness explicitly.
- **Filesystem fill**: present in the boot record only (`disk_home`). If `sar -F` on our sa files doesn't yield a fill series, add a one-line `df` sample to the rollup writer rather than a new probe job.

## The two-purpose audit of today's init

**init-ensure.sh** (runs in every job's prelude — the "init runs as part of every job starting" of Drew's framing):
- Session-proxy ensure (`fleet proxy serve`, `LAPTOP_AGENT_POOL=50`) → **PREWARM. Keep** — this becomes `fleet init`'s sandbox role per #5687 (spawn {proxy}, pool warm), so the first real trip never pays cold CONNECT costs (cold 1.2–1.8 s vs warm p50 369 ms, WS-C).
- Fleet symlink ensure (`~/tools/bin/fleet`, `repo-queue`) → neither purpose; provisioning residue. Keep as a cheap guard only until the deploy tool (#5766) owns links, then delete.

**init.sh** (the boot job): telemetry block → **STATS** (folds, item #4). Everything else — restorers (#11), verification probes (#10) → **neither purpose**: re-homed or deleted per the inventory.

## End state

`fleet init` (location-aware, #5687) ensures exactly: **{proxy serve + pool prewarm; sysstat-collector; pidstat collector; tree-size cache writers}** — on the sandbox. On the laptop it ensures its own serve roles as #5687 specifies; the *aggregation* lives laptop-side, where the cores are (sandbox-minimalism doctrine: the sandbox collects append-only and computes nothing).

Rollup outputs (files first — the status-quo formats are proven; a stats DB only if query pain actually appears):
- `~/logs/sysstat/sa-<day>` (unchanged) + per-PID daily files beside them; retention 14 days to match.
- The boot/stats series: `~/logs/init.jsonl` promoted to canonical — one record per boot (duration, store/profile counts, disk, latency samples), read by sweeps instead of re-probed.
- Trip aggregates + per-lane proof table: computed **laptop-side** on a slow cadence from trips.jsonl (via `fleet get`, #5759) and agent.tasks; consumed by the watchdog, metrics passes, and #5701-class forensics.
- Consumers read rollups; **nobody probes live**. A consumer that needs a number nobody collects files it as a rollup addition — never as a new probe in a job's prelude.

### What remains of the boot-init job — explicitly

1. Append **one boot record** to the stats series, from caches and collector state (sub-second; no live probes).
2. Invoke **`fleet init` prewarm**: proxy up, tunnel pool warm.
3. **Exit.**

The 900-second `services-verify`, the per-service installers, the nix/symlink restores, and the toolchain checks are gone from init — the installers/restores land in the #5770 generic restorer (whose M3 recycle-drill acceptance also absorbs the boot-init cron's quota-recorder reinstall side-role), and verification becomes a rollup read. When the restorer lands, `~/tools/init.sh` can be **deleted outright**: `fleet init` — stats append + prewarm — is the whole job, exactly the two purposes Drew named.

## Interplay with the metrics enumeration's absent-metrics list

- *Init-duration series*: the raw series already exists (`init.jsonl`); what was absent is a **consumer/rollup** — this design names it canonical (the enumeration's "only the latest boot is kept" is true of `init-status`, not of the JSONL).
- *Per-lane shift proof*: becomes a rollup output (item #8), retiring the watchdog's live joins.
- *Trip failure taxonomy*: the aggregates half lives here; the four-timestamp instrumentation itself is #5702.

Links: #5701 (incident that exposed the sampler gaps), #5702 (trip log v2 — its aggregates belong to this rollup), #5775 (standing-load rulings; quota-recorder cadence stays Drew's call there), #5687 (`fleet init` location semantics), #5770 (generic restorer — receives everything init sheds).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The design inventories what `fleet init` and the boot-init job do today, and classifies every duty as keep-stats, keep-prewarm, delete, or re-home (with the new home named).
- [ ] It states the end-state contents of the boot-init job explicitly, and shows the result passes Drew's two-purpose test (stats + prewarm only).
- [ ] The telemetry rollup design names one pipeline (sysstat base + fleet extra stats) with its outputs and consumers.
- [ ] Implementation follow-ups are identified as separate issues/tasks — the design itself implements nothing.
