code.title: design: versioning for a monorepo whose apps deploy individually — derived versions, per-app tags + repo date tag, survey of schemes (WS-H)
code.body:
# design: versioning for a monorepo whose apps deploy individually

**WS-H** · Design task (survey + interim policy), filed 2026-11-04. Related: epic #5765 (deployment architecture — services layer + deploy tool), #5766 (deploy tool v1), #5760 (fleet Nix-build state; the deployed-lag table that motivates this), PR #5764 (the services-layer design).

## Why

Under the NixOS system closure, "what version is running" was declarative: the system profile *was* the answer. The services-layer design (#5764) deliberately takes apps out of that closure so they can deploy individually — which buys deploy/rollback flexibility and sells the free identity answer. #5760 shows the failure mode already, before any of that lands: the deployed fleet binaries lag `pkgs/fleet` HEAD by five commits — including a proxy request-line validation hardening — and nothing noticed, because every one of those commits self-reports the same version string, `0.1.0`. A hand-maintained version constant does not move when code moves.

Drew's counter-measures (2026-11-04): every binary **self-reports** an embedded version (number + git hash) via `--version`/`--about` or its version verb; versions are **derived automatically** from tags + branch state so no two builds ever collide; monorepo releases use **per-app prefixed tags** for what was actually tested and shipped, **plus a whole-repo tag** for the commit; the numbers are **technically semver, loosely followed** — the constraint that matters is Rust consumer breakage, not ceremony.

This issue carries (1) an **interim policy** that operates from now until the full design lands, (2) a **survey** of the alternative schemes with opinions, (3) **embedding mechanics** per stack, and (4) the **recommendation + open questions** for the full design.

---

## 1. Interim policy — operating until the design lands

1. **Self-report.** Every deployable binary embeds: app semver, full git commit hash, branch class (`main` / `tag` / `feature`), and build date — readable via `--version` (or the app's version verb: `fleet version` already exists and is the model).
2. **Derivation = git-describe, per app.** Nearest `<app>/vX.Y.Z` tag on the history:
   - exactly on the tag → clean `X.Y.Z`;
   - on `main`, *N* commits after `X.Y.Z` → `X.Y.(Z+1)-dev.N+g<shorthash>`;
   - on a feature branch → the same, plus `+<branch-slug>` build metadata (e.g. `0.4.3-dev.7+g1a2b3c4+ws-h-versioning`).
   Prerelease sorts before its release; build metadata never affects precedence; **no two distinct commits ever share a version string** (the `g<hash>` guarantees it). Note the transformation matters: raw `git describe` output (`v0.4.2-7-g1a2b3c4`) pasted into a version field would sort *before* the tag it descends from — the patch-bump + `-dev.N` form is what makes describe output semver-honest.
3. **Tags.** Per-app `<app>/vX.Y.Z` on the exact tested commit being released — five apps changing means five tags. Repo tag `repo/v<YYYYMMDD>` (plus `.N` if twice in a day) at release points, naming "the repo as it stood, tested together."
4. **Bump discipline (loose semver).** In the 0.x era: minor for a feature, patch for a fix, major only if a consumer actually breaks. Past v0: same, with major also allowed for compiler-forced breaks. Staying on v0 indefinitely is acceptable and expected for most apps.
5. **Deploy truth.** The deploy tool records, per target, the version string **read from the deployed binary**, never from paperwork. `deploy <t> status` is the identity check (#5766). A deployed artifact whose binary cannot state its version is treated as unidentified, not as "probably current."

## 2. Current state — fleet is the furthest along, and still collides

Audited 2026-11-04 (`pkgs/fleet`):

- ✅ `fleet version` prints workspace version + capability list + source rev; `--version` works through the argv0 personalities. This is the estate's model surface.
- ✅ Rev channel exists: `crates/fleet/build.rs` resolves `$FLEET_SOURCE_REV` → `git rev-parse` (dev builds) → env `FLEET_SOURCE_REV` baked via `cargo:rustc-env`; the flake path passes it from `lib/default.nix` (`sourceRev = inputs.self.rev or "dirty"`).
- ❌ **The semver is a hardcoded literal** — `version = "0.1.0"` in `pkgs/fleet/default.nix`, with the Cargo workspace version as a second hand-maintained copy. Neither derives from any tag; no `<app>/v*` tags exist. Consequence (the #5760 lag): six distinct commits all self-report `0.1.0`; identity is split across two fields (`version` + a separate `Source rev:` line), and the field a human reads first is the one that collides.
- ❌ **Collision-by-default fallbacks.** A dirty-tree flake build embeds the literal string `dirty` (every dirty build, any commit, same rev). A build where the caller forgot `sourceRev` and git is unavailable embeds `unknown`. Both violate interim rule 2's no-collision guarantee. Fixes are small: use `self.dirtyRev` (`<rev>-dirty`, a real hash) on the flake path, and make a missing rev a **build error** for release builds instead of a silent `unknown`.
- ❌ **No branch class, no build date** anywhere yet (interim rule 1 fields).
- Elsewhere: the Go side (mcpx) embeds **nothing** — VCS stamping is disabled fleet-wide (`GOFLAGS=-buildvcs=false`, a deliberate purity fix for the symlinked store), and no `-ldflags -X` identity has replaced it. Embedding there must be explicit (see §4).

## 3. Survey — schemes, properties, opinions

Each scheme scored on: mechanics · ordering/collision · cargo/Rust fit · monorepo fit · human readability · tooling cost → **opinion**.

### 3.1 Strict SemVer (semver.org)
Hand-bumped MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH carrying the full compatibility contract. Ordering total and tool-native; collisions impossible *if* humans bump — which is exactly what doesn't happen (see `0.1.0` × 6 commits). As a **numbering source** it fails silently; as a **grammar** it's what cargo, tags, and every consumer already parse. **Opinion: adopt as the grammar, reject as the derivation.** Humans decide what a release *means* (that's the tag); machines derive what a build *is*.

### 3.2 Loose-v0 SemVer (Drew's rule; the named cousin is ZeroVer, 0ver.org)
Stay on `0.x` indefinitely; minor = feature (and, per cargo's actual 0.x semantics, the breaking slot), patch = fix, major = a consumer genuinely broke. This is not laziness — it's a catalogued convention (see the scheme survey at nesbitt.io, "From ZeroVer to SemVer"), and it matches how cargo already resolves 0.x dependencies (leftmost non-zero component is the compatible boundary). Loses the "1.0 = stable promise" signal, which for internal fleet binaries is a signal nobody consumes. **Opinion: adopt as the bump discipline** — it is interim rule 4, and the survey found no reason to displace it in the full design.

### 3.3 CalVer (calver.org)
Date segments (`YYYY.M.D`, `YY.0M`, `YYYY.0M.0D[.MICRO]` — Ubuntu, yt-dlp, JetBrains). Superb at answering "how old is this?" at a glance; monotonic by construction; meaningless about compatibility. Cargo constraint, sourced from the CalVer 26.0 revision notes: **zero-padded segments are not SemVer-legal** (leading zeros forbidden — Cargo rejects `26.04.0`, Go modules reject `v26.04.0`), so a date that must live in a cargo version field has to be unpadded `YYYY.M.D`. **Opinion: reject for app versions** (our apps need the compatibility signal, however loose); **adopt for the repo tag** — `repo/v<YYYYMMDD>` is a git tag, not a version field, so padding is free there and the date is the entire point.

### 3.4 git-describe derivation
`git describe --tags --match '<app>/v*' --long` → distance + commit, transformed per interim rule 2. Collision-free by construction (hash suffix); monotonic along a lineage (distance counter); branch builds distinguishable via build metadata; zero human effort — it is the only scheme in this survey that *cannot* be forgotten at 1 a.m. Weaknesses: needs the tag history present at build time (shallow clones and tarball builds must be handled — fail loud, per §2); distance resets at each tag, so versions from diverged branches aren't globally ordered (they don't need to be — precedence only matters within an app's release line). This is also the industry-standard machinery (vergen & friends exist to feed it into Rust builds). **Opinion: adopt — it is the derivation layer of the recommendation.**

### 3.5 Prime-product (Gödel) versioning — the scheme Drew cited
Assign each app a prime; the repo version is the product of `prime^(app's version counter)` over all apps — the Gödel-numbering construction. Its one real relative in the wild, *SemVer Prime* (p-avital.github.io/semver-prime, 2024), assigns primes per *dimension* of one package and its author calls it "a bit of madness." Evaluated honestly, on Drew's per-app variant with worked numbers:

- Apps fleet/id/mcpx/atlas/opencode → primes 2/3/5/7/11. Each app's X.Y.Z must first be **collapsed to a single counter** (the form has one exponent per prime) — the per-app semver Drew wants to keep is destroyed on entry.
- Modest state (release-count exponents 12/7/3/1/2): V = 2¹²·3⁷·5³·7·11² = **948,423,168,000** — a 12-digit "version" for an infant monorepo.
- One year of weekly fleet patches (exponent 12→64) multiplies V by 2⁵² ≈ 4.5×10¹⁵ → V ≈ 10²⁷. SemVer numeric segments are parsed as u64 by the `semver` crate (max ≈ 1.8×10¹⁹): **the number cannot legally ride in a version field at all.**
- Drew's two objections both confirm: it explodes, and decoding needs the prime registry plus factoring (easy for small primes, but the number tells a human *nothing* at a glance — "which app changed?" is a computation, not a read). Two more he didn't list: cross-branch ordering is meaningless (incomparable products — bigger ≠ later), and monotonicity, while real (any bump strictly grows V; adding an app multiplies it), is the only property that survives — and git-describe + a counter provide it without the bonfire.

**Opinion: reject.** Beautiful encoding, wrong slot. (Recorded in full because it was explicitly asked about; the worked example is the refutation, not a strawman.)

### 3.6 Monotonic global counter (build numbers as version)
One integer, incremented per build/release (CI run numbers, a repo-wide counter commit). Perfectly monotonic and dead simple; says nothing about *which app* or *what changed*; commit-count variants break under history rewriting (rebase/ squash changes the count for the same tree); per-app meaning is zero in a monorepo. **Opinion: reject as the version; adopt as a component** — it already lives inside the recommendation as describe's `-dev.N` distance.

### 3.7 Nix store path / content hash as identity
`/nix/store/<hash>-fleet-0.1.0` — exact, free, already true for every Nix build: two different inputs never share a path. But it is not ordered (a hash says "different", never "newer"), it changes when *any build input* changes (a comment in a build script = new identity, same source), and it doesn't exist for the artifact that needs identity most — the ≤2 MiB connect binary dropped onto a bare host with no store around it. **Opinion: adopt as a recorded field** (`deploy status` shows the store path / profile generation beside the version), **reject as the version.**

### 3.8 OCI digest (containers)
`sha256:…` image digests are the container world's content identity — same class as §3.7: exact, unorderable, unreadable. Container deploy targets should record digest + the image's embedded app version (the binary inside still self-reports per rule 1). **Opinion: adopt as the container identity field, reject as a version.** (Pairs with the container audit, #5771.)

### 3.9 The interim hybrid (per-app tags + describe + repo date tag)
Per-app semver tags (§3.1 grammar, §3.2 discipline) + describe derivation (§3.4) + a date repo tag (§3.3 in its proper slot) + content identities recorded where they exist (§3.7/§3.8). Every property Drew specified is carried by the layer that's actually good at it: compatibility by the tag, uniqueness by the hash, ordering by describe's distance, repo-level "what stood together" by the date tag, exactness by store path/digest in `deploy status`. Tooling cost is the honest downside: a derive script/bake step per stack (§4) and tag discipline in the release flow (five tags for five apps — scriptable, and the deploy tool can refuse an untagged release build). **Opinion: adopt — this is the recommendation; the interim policy *is* its spine, so the full design starts from a running system instead of a green field.**

## 4. Embedding mechanics (per stack)

- **Rust** — extend the channel fleet already built: `build.rs` emits `cargo:rustc-env` values (derived version string, full hash, branch class, build date), read via `env!`. (`vergen`/`vergen-git2` can generate these; hand-rolled, as fleet's rev bake already is, is equally fine and dependency-free.) Cargo.toml's `version` stays the release-line version; the derived string layers on top as prerelease/build metadata — cargo rejects leading-zero numeric segments and >u64 segments, which is why dates and products-of-primes never enter app version fields (§3.3, §3.5).
- **Go** — explicit `-ldflags "-X <pkg>.version=… -X <pkg>.commit=…"` (or a small version package read by `main`). **Never `buildvcs`**: it is disabled fleet-wide (`GOFLAGS=-buildvcs=false`) for symlinked-store purity, and module-proxy builds lack VCS data anyway. Anything relying on it reports nothing — the mcpx gap in §2.
- **Nix** — version + rev enter as flake build inputs, the way `sourceRev` already flows (`lib/default.nix` → `pkgs/fleet` → `env.FLEET_SOURCE_REV`). Use `self.rev` for clean trees, **`self.dirtyRev`** (`<rev>-dirty` — a real hash that says the tree was dirty) for dirty ones; the current literal `"dirty"` fallback is the §2 collision. A build with neither available is not a release build and should fail rather than embed `unknown`.

## 5. Recommendation & open questions

**Recommendation:** ratify the interim hybrid (§3.9) as the design's spine — per-app loose-semver tags, git-describe derivation, one self-report surface per binary, store-path/digest recorded in `deploy status` — and spend the full-design effort on the two genuinely undecided areas: the release *workflow* (who/what cuts the five tags, and how "tested" is attested) and the deploy tool's identity ledger (#5766), not on inventing a new numbering scheme. Every alternative surveyed is either a grammar (SemVer), a discipline (loose-v0), a component (counter, content hash), or a refutation (prime-product).

**Open questions only Drew settles:**
1. Tag prefixes: the short deployed name (`fleet/v0.4.2`, `id/v1.2.3`) or the crate/package name? (Recommendation: the name the deploy tool and `--version` use — one name per app, everywhere.)
2. Is the repo date tag worth keeping permanently? It costs one tag per release point and buys a single checkout-able name for "the repo as tested together." (Recommendation: keep — it's cheap, and it's the only repo-level identity that survives apps deploying on independent cadences.)
3. Is the repo tag cut at every app release (a release *train* of one) or only at deliberate repo-level release points?
4. May `-dev.N` builds from `main` be deployed to real targets, or are deploys restricted to tagged versions except by explicit override? (Interim assumes: allowed, because the version string *says* it's a dev build — that's the point of deriving it.)
5. First-tag versions: start each app at `0.1.0` (continuity with fleet's current string) or `1.0.0`?

---
*Interim policy (§1) is in force from filing. Implementation of derivation for fleet (fixing the §2 conflicts) is a follow-on to #5760, not part of this design issue.*

code.title: id: design: ESP32 hardware platform line — boards, provisioning, firmware lifecycle, OTA, power
code.body:
## Summary

Design the **ESP32 hardware platform line**: the device side of ID — reference boards, identity provisioning, firmware lifecycle and OTA, power behaviour, and field failure modes — as its own design, under the protocol and provider model that already exist.

## Motivation

The ESP32 currently lives inside two other designs, and its hardware questions are explicitly homeless in both. #2343 designs the `id.device.v1` MQTT bridge (topic schema, wire bounds, refusal semantics) and scopes OUT, in its own words: "Firmware for a specific board, OTA, ESPHome components, power profiling." #5686 designs the capability-provider model an ESP32 plugs into — provider abstractions, deliberately target-agnostic. What no issue owns is the ESP32 as a *platform*: which boards, how a device gets its identity, how its firmware is built, signed, updated and rolled back, and what it does when power, Wi-Fi, or time itself misbehaves. Drew's 2026-11-04 instruction — each thing gets its own design issue — applies here directly: the bridge spec can be perfect and the device line can still fail in the field for reasons no filed design covers.

## Sketch

- **Board posture**: one reference board vs a supported family; ESP32 variants' memory/radio/flash differences measured against the bridge's 64 KiB frame budget and the firmware's closed capability subset.
- **Identity provisioning**: device key generation and enrolment (the device-owned identity question posed in #5686, answered for hardware); factory reset and re-provisioning semantics; what a stolen device knows.
- **Firmware lifecycle**: builds in CI/the flake, signed images, OTA with rollback to last-good, and the device-side journaling decision inherited from #2343 — spelt out as a lifecycle, not a per-decision list.
- **Power**: sleep/wake posture against the bridge's minimum `time.tick` floor; battery budgets for the reference build; wake-storm avoidance as a fleet property, not a per-device hope.
- **Field behaviour**: no-RTC time (what does a device do before it learns the time, and whose time does it trust), broker absence, captive-portal-class Wi-Fi failures, brownout mid-write.

## Open questions

- Firmware language/stack: Rust (esp-hal / esp-idf) vs C — and what the crate-split workspace can share with it?
- ESPHome: interop target, migration source, or ignore?
- Hardware-in-the-loop testing: does a physical rig join the deterministic testing infrastructure, or is the fake-device PoC (#2343) the permanent test double?
- Who is the hardware line *for* in v1 — Drew's own bench, or a reproducible build others can flash?

## Relations

Parent: epic #2056. Relations: #2343 (MQTT bridge spec — the protocol this platform speaks; its out-of-scope list is this issue's scope), #5686 (capability providers — the model this platform instantiates), #5684 (identity/delegation — device identity custody), #5671 (transport fallback — constrained radios). Filed in the 2026-11-04 gap pass (WS-F) per Drew's order.

code.title: atlas search: query-time parameter surface — every retrieval knob as a CLI flag / raw-query field, no hardcoded constants (extends #5741, #5668)
code.body:
Extends #5741 (SPLADE investigation + eval harness) and #5668 (query-embed cache + flags). Design commitments from Drew's direction 2026-11-04.

## Principle

**Anything not baked into how data is stored must be settable per query** — from the fleet-binary CLI flags AND from the raw query format (the full-access path), with **identical parameter names** in both — so values can be benchmarked and better defaults found **without editing code**.

If a retrieval constant lives in code today, that's a bug against this principle.

## Knob inventory (v1, extensible)

- **Per-shard top-k** — how many results each shard returns into the fan-out.
- **Global fan-in top-k** — how many combined results survive the merge.
- **Per-signal weights** — dense, BM25, SPLADE (the #5741 adaptive-weighting defaults, overridable per query).
- **Per-signal multipliers** — score scaling per signal, distinct from the weights.
- **Jaccard rescore depth** — candidate count entering the #5733 rescore stage.
- **Jaccard boost threshold** — the overlap at which the rescore boost applies.
- **RRF constant k** — if reciprocal-rank fusion is used in the merge, its k is a knob, never a hardcoded 0.6.
- **Stage toggles** — planner and spell correction off / deprioritized / on (companion issue: query-understanding front-end, extends #5741).
- **Hint override** — force the query class (code / docs / error / concept) instead of the classifier's call.
- **Variant selection** — raw / rewritten / both.
- **Expand-N** — #5668's existing `--expand N` flag folds into this surface rather than living as a one-off.

## Escape hatches as first-class presets

Power users must not need to edit code or config to say "just run my query":

- **`--raw`** = planner off, spell off, query verbatim, no expansion.
- **Per-signal weight 0 via flag = signal removed for that query.** "No BM25" is one flag, not a config edit — distinct from #5741's adaptive-weighting rule (weights floored, never zeroed), because that rule binds the *automatic classifier*, not an explicit user instruction. An explicit 0 is the user's call and is honored.

## Defaults are data, not code

- The **shipped default vector** is whatever #5741's eval harness last measured best; it ships as a versioned default set, not as constants scattered through the binary.
- **Benchmarking = grid runs over the flag space**, with the **full parameter vector logged alongside the results** of every run, so any number is reproducible and attributable to its knobs.

## Provenance

Results carry **which signals and which variants produced them** (the companion issue's `raw-only` / `rewritten-only` / `both` tags, plus per-signal contribution), so a knob change's effect is diagnosable from the output, not guessed.

## Boundary (explicit)

- **Storage-side parameters are NOT query-time knobs**: index tuning (e.g. `max_neighbors`), postings construction, shard placement. Changing those is a rebuild/migration decision, governed by #5667/#5669, not a flag.
- **Sensitivity filtering is NOT a knob**: it is a safety filter applied before ranking (the #5675/#5732 rules), and **no flag may widen it**. A parameter surface that can widen visibility is a vulnerability, not a feature.

## Open questions

- **Preset naming/versioning**: how named presets (`--raw`, future ones) are versioned so a benchmark citing a preset stays reproducible.
- **Per-corpus default vectors**: the code corpus and the docs corpus may legitimately ship different defaults — one global vector vs per-corpus vectors.
- **Guard rails**: maximum fan-out caps so an absurd per-shard k can't melt the shards — where the caps live (client, daemon, per-shard) and what error a capped request returns.

Related: #5733 (Jaccard signals), #5667 (Scaler/shard design), #5669 (shard implementation).

code.title: atlas search: query-understanding front-end — spell correction + LLM query planner/rewriter as toggleable stages, dual submission with provenance (extends #5741)
code.body:
Extends #5741 (SPLADE investigation + eval harness + adaptive weighting). Design commitments from Drew's direction 2026-11-04.

## What this adds

Two NEW front-end stages in front of retrieval, each independently toggleable (**off / deprioritized / on**), in pipeline order:

**spell correction → query planner/rewriter → signal weighting (#5741) → fan-out**

## Stage 1 — spell correction

Neither BM25 nor SPLADE tolerates typos: both match on exact terms. The mechanism is classical, not learned:

- **Candidate generation** by Damerau–Levenshtein edit distance (a transposition — flipped letters — counts as 1 edit) plus **character-trigram similarity** (set overlap over character 3-grams; the Jaccard family already in the stack per #5733).
- Candidates are drawn from a **corpus-vocabulary dictionary with term frequencies**, so corrections prefer terms the corpus actually contains.
- Correction is **conservative — high-confidence only**. The original query is **always retained as a variant**; a correction is never silently substituted. The raw and corrected forms can both fan out and merge like any other variant (see dual submission below).

## Stage 2 — query planner / rewriter

A small, fast model rephrases/expands the query into a retrieval-shaped variant: vocabulary the corpus would use, expansions of abbreviations, decomposed compound questions.

- **Dual submission is the default shape**: raw and rewritten both fan out; results merge with **provenance tags** (`raw-only` / `rewritten-only` / `both`) and flow through the normal rescore (#5733).
- The planner may also emit the **class hint** that #5741's adaptive weighting consumes — but keep the roles distinct: the planner produces *text*, the classifier produces *weights*.
- **Budget discipline from #5741 holds ("sameish" query time)**: the rewrite is one small inference, **cached under #5668's discipline** (a rewrite is a pure function of (text, model), exactly like a query embedding), so repeat queries skip it entirely. The Snowflake dense embeddings already handle part of the vocabulary-mismatch problem; the planner is an addition to be justified by measurement, not an assumption.

## Hard exclusions

- **Error-pastes and code identifiers are never rewritten or spell-"corrected"** — the #5741 shape rules (stack trace → error-paste; identifiers/paths → code) gate both stages off for those query classes.
- **Exact-match intent wins**: a quoted string or a pasted error line goes through verbatim.

## Evaluation

Planner on/off and spell on/off are **ablation axes in #5741's eval harness**, alongside the signal ablations. A stage stays only if measured gains (recall@10 / MRR per query class) justify its latency. The harness's held-out real queries are the deciding vote, as with every signal in this stack.

## Open questions

- **Planner model choice**: a Jev-class small local model vs a hosted small model — latency, cost, and the query-embed cache hit rate decide.
- **Rewrite count**: a single variant vs N variants (and if N, how provenance tags and fan-out budget scale).
- **Provenance-aware rescore weighting**: should "found by both raw and rewritten" boost a result? Intuition says yes; measure it.
- Interaction with spell correction ordering: correct-then-rewrite vs rewrite-then-correct — the pipeline order above is the starting position, not a settled answer.

Related: #5733 (Jaccard signals + rescore), #5668 (query-embed cache + flags — the parameter surface for this issue's toggles is designed in the companion issue on query-time knobs), #5667 (shard design), #5669 (shard implementation).

code.title: VMs: declarative guest definitions (nixvirt / microvm.nix) + mutable carve-out list
code.body:
VM track of the deployment-architecture epic (design: PR #5764 §6).

Current state (2026-11-04 inventory): `virtualisation.libvirtd.enable = true` in the laptop profile and **zero** guest definitions anywhere — no libvirt XML, no nixvirt, no virsh-managed domains in any repo. Seeds present: `microvm.nix` is a flake input with one defined VM (`prometheus`, qemu, 2 vCPU/1 GB, virtiofs /nix/store share) whose profile is commented out on `amd` (`nixos/hosts/default.nix:30`); the flake has `lib.make-vm-configurations` machinery (per-host `vm_<host>` NixOS variants).

Work:
- Evaluate nixvirt (declarative libvirt domains/networks/pools as Nix) vs flake-generated libvirt XML as the renderer for libvirt guests; record the pick and why in this issue. microvm.nix is the presumptive answer for ephemeral/agent-class guests — confirm or refute.
- Define the guest generation shape: {domain definition, disk image (flake-built), NixOS source rev}; data volumes attach to generations, never live inside them.
- Land the first declarative guests: bring `prometheus` under generation discipline (enable the microvm profile deliberately or supersede it), plus one libvirt guest end-to-end if a real need exists — otherwise the renderer + a throwaway test guest that is defined, started, rolled back, and destroyed as the acceptance proof.
- Write the mutable carve-out list (starts empty): guests that may drift in data but not OS definition (DB hosts, lab stateful nodes), and the rule that full drift requires a named waiver with owner + reason.

Acceptance: at least one guest of each class (microVM, libvirt) can be defined/started/rolled back from flake state alone on a clean checkout; the carve-out list exists in the flake (even if empty) with the waiver rule stated; `deploy vm:<name>` integration is specced (implementation may ride the deploy tool's later target classes).

code.title: deploy tool: Cloudflare target class — generalize the <name>-deploy apps to all Workers
code.body:
Part of the deployment-architecture epic (design: PR #5764, `doc/2026-11-04_deployment-architecture-services-layer.md` §4.3, Track C).

Generalize the 2026-10-31 Cloudflare deploy standard (`doc/2026-10-31T23-00-00Z_design_cloudflare_worker_deployment_standard.md`) from its current 3 workers to the whole estate, behind the `deploy` CLI:

- Absorb the existing flake deploy apps (`id-mail-deploy`, `pkarr-deploy`, `developing-today-backup-deploy`) as target renderers — no behavior change for those three.
- New targets: lab-ops-hub (worker deploy + its container image push become one `deploy lab-ops-hub`), cf-container-hello, cold-store-rehydrator (today: manual REST PUT of a committed bundle — becomes a built artifact + versions flow), agent-inbox, webhook-gateway + sink.
- Worker bundles become flake packages (pinned deps from the lockfile; no deploy-time `npm install` against the network).
- id-mail gains `--deploy-version` rollback parity with pkarr/developing-today-backup (today it has no rollback path at all); rollback-to-version verifies required secret bindings first (the github-backup check, standardized).
- Secrets gathered impurely at deploy time by name (SOPS account id, Bitwarden token) exactly as the current standard does.

Acceptance: every Worker in the design doc's §0 table is a `deploy` target with working `status`; one full deploy + rollback cycle demonstrated on a low-risk worker (cf-container-hello) with the version/deployment ids recorded in the generation log; no Worker remains whose only deploy path is a raw `npm run deploy` in a README.

Out of scope: Workers Builds / GitHub-Actions deploys (the design keeps deploys operator/agent-invoked via the flake).

code.title: Epic: deployment architecture — services layer + deploy tool (tracking)
code.body:
Tracking epic for the deployment-architecture design (PR #5764, `doc/2026-11-04_deployment-architecture-services-layer.md`).

Problem in one line: we have Nix build definitions for almost everything and deployment definitions for almost nothing — services ride the system switch, run out of a live checkout, or live as hand-placed files that switches/recycles/redeploys strand.

Program:
- [x] deploy tool v1 (registry + systemd generations)
- [ ] deploy tool: Cloudflare target class
- [x] M1: route-proxy hand unit → target
- [ ] M2: fleet three (laptop-agent, secrets-broker, queue-broker) — one declaration
- [ ] M3: sandbox quota-recorder + generic restorer
- [ ] M4: pm-stack off the checkout (filed when M1–M3 land)
- [ ] Containers: Nix-build audit (mcpx, lab-ops duplicate Dockerfile, amd-crd)
- [ ] VMs: declarative guests (nixvirt/microvm)

Rules for the whole program: each migration independently reversible; no migration requires a system switch to land; the only system-flake change is additive (the `deploy` package + `deployTargets` output); secrets are consumed by name from the brokers, never embedded.

code.title: Fleet path Nix-build state: deployed fleet lags pkgs/fleet HEAD; remaining non-Nix pieces
code.body:
## Fleet path Nix-build state: deployed fleet lags `pkgs/fleet` HEAD; remaining non-Nix pieces (audit 2026-11-04)

Drew's rule: *any binaries we run should be built using Nix.* Audit of the sandbox↔laptop fleet path against that rule, 2026-11-04 evening.

### The fleet binary itself: Nix-built ✓, current ✗

- Package: `pkgs/fleet/default.nix` via the root flake (`fleet`, `fleet-serve`, `fleet-connect`, `fleet-connect-static`, `fleet-static`, `fleet-brokers`). Brokers on the laptop run **directly from the store**: `/nix/store/9cq1vqzarr3gbg52l07j9f9as4rfnaqx-fleet-0.1.0/bin/fleet serve queue-broker|secrets-broker`.
- User copies: laptop `~/.local/bin/fleet` (glibc full build) and sandbox `~/tools/fleet` (musl static-pie — the `fleet-static` output, per the package comment's flip pattern). Both self-report source rev **18f0aa1a68** (PR #5601 merge, 2026-11-04T17:41Z).
- **`pkgs/fleet` on main has moved 5 commits past the deployed rev** (main HEAD c2bf5fca29): help exit-code fix (#5628), `fleet help` arg rejection (#5653), search paging-cursor rejection (#5655), treefmt, and **fleet-proxy method/path request-line validation (#5752)** — a transport hardening fix that is *not* in the running binaries. A re-build + re-flip of both copies (and the broker store path) is owed; nothing about the flips is automated or drift-checked (see gap below).

### Not Nix-built on the fleet path (with their trackers)

| Piece | What/where | Tracker |
|---|---|---|
| laptop-agent daemon | Python, `~/laptop-agent/laptop_agent.py`, deployed by copy from hatch-personal; unit runs `/usr/bin/env python3 …` | #5343 phase 3 (Rust `fleet serve` role) |
| Sandbox agent client trio | `laptop-agent.py`, `laptop-agent-broker.py` (Python broker — superseded by `fleet proxy serve` but still the client's auto-start fallback), `laptop-proxy-connect.py` (ProxyCommand helper still referenced by the atlas-search wrapper) | #5343 (client domains exist; shim still calls the .py) |
| SSH path | `laptop-ssh.sh` shim + `laptop-ssh-real.sh` (bash) | #5697 (`fleet proxy ssh`) |
| atlas-search wrapper | `/bin/sh` wrapper around a Nix-built binary (`/nix/store/…-atlas-search-0.1.0` ✓); the wrapper's SSH-forward glue is the non-Nix part | #5604 (search serve-role rehome) |
| Laptop-side Python broker | `~/hatch/tools/laptop-agent-broker.py` still running on the laptop (proto-0 warm broker for local CLI callers) | #5343 |
| quota-recorder | Python, sandbox (adjacent to the fleet path) | #5703 (broker redesign) |

### The untracked gap: no provenance/drift check

Deployed fleet copies are manual flips of Nix outputs. Nothing anywhere compares the running binaries' self-reported source rev against `pkgs/fleet` at main HEAD — the 5-commit lag above was found by hand. Proposal: a cheap rev check in the repo-fleet-monitor's digest (read `fleet version` on both hosts via the agent, compare to the latest commit touching `pkgs/fleet` on main, flag drift) so "Nix-built but stale" becomes a visible state instead of a surprise.

Scope of this issue: (1) re-flip the deployed fleet artifacts to current main and note the new rev here; (2) land the drift check; (3) keep the table above current as the tracked pieces retire — the per-piece fixes stay in their own issues.

code.title: Design: fleet proxy get/put — file transfer over the agent channel
code.body:
## Design: `fleet proxy get` / `fleet proxy put` — file transfer over the agent channel

Drew (2026-11-04): *"Maybe we need a tool to make it easier to get and put files onto the laptop, like `fleet proxy get`, `fleet proxy put`, or something — basically SCP. I think you already built a more performant version of that using HTTP, and maybe this is just papering over that concept. Whatever you think is best."*

Extends #5343 (laptop-agent; the daemon's Rust port is phase 3 there). Epic: #5412. Sibling design: #5697 (`fleet proxy ssh` — same "give the proxy domain the laptop verbs users actually reach for" logic).

### Inventory: what file movement exists today (verified 2026-11-04)

**There is no file transfer. Anywhere.** The "more performant HTTP version" Drew remembers is the agent's *exec* transport — warm pooled CONNECT tunnels + the session broker (~0.4 s warm vs ~1.8 s cold SSH) — and it carries commands and JSON results only:

- Daemon (`~/laptop-agent/laptop_agent.py` on the laptop, 347 lines, `laptop-agent.service`): routes are exactly `GET /health`, `GET /jobs`, `GET /jobs/<id>`, `POST /exec`, `POST /jobs`, `POST /jobs/<id>/kill`. Every body is JSON (`_body()` parses JSON; `_send()` replies JSON). No file/blob route, no streaming body path.
- Rust fleet proxy: verbs are `serve`, `connect`, `init` only. The broker wire (fleet-proxy-proto) is 8-byte-BE-length-prefixed JSON frames, 64 MiB ceiling — a JSON channel end to end.
- How files actually move today:
  - **SSH stdin pushes, deliberately left on the shim's real-SSH fallback**: `fetch-charge-inputs.py` (`cat > file.tmp && mv …` over SSH stdin) and `turso-atlas/scripts/atlas-backup.py`. The daemon has no stdin channel, so these never migrated (shim inventory, #5343).
  - **Base64 re-expression through `/exec`** for anything binary that must cross as a command result/argument — manual, per-call, no integrity or atomicity story.
  - Ad-hoc `cat`/`mkdir -p` shell-outs over the agent for text.

So the get/put verbs are not papering over an existing file channel — they *create* the channel the two named scripts have been waiting for.

### Options

0. **Client-only verb over `/exec`** (chunked base64 appends via shell commands). Works against today's daemon with zero server changes. **Rejected**: it institutionalizes the hack inside the binary that is supposed to be the clean end state — a shell process per chunk on the laptop, quoting hazards on every path, no atomic commit, no resume except client bookkeeping, and it dies anyway when the daemon goes Rust.
1. **Daemon file RPC over the existing channel (recommended).** New daemon routes speaking the same framed-JSON/HTTP-JSON as `/exec`; the client chunks. Zero transport changes: rides the pooled broker tunnels, token auth, trip logging, and the proto-0 legacy path unchanged. The same routes are implemented by the Rust daemon role (`fleet serve laptop-agent`, #5343 phase 3) when it lands, so the protocol outlives the Python daemon.
2. **Raw octet-stream routes over a direct CONNECT tunnel** (true streaming, no base64). The tunnel code exists (fleet-proxy `tunnel.rs`/`stdio.rs`), but it bypasses the broker's pooling/framing and needs the daemon to accept non-JSON bodies. Deferred as a profiling-driven optimization for multi-GB transfers (atlas dumps); v1's ~33% base64 tax on a tailnet path is not the bottleneck that connection setup was.

### Protocol (v1, option 1)

All routes on the daemon (port 4799), token-authed like every route, JSON envelopes:

- `POST /files/stat` `{path, sha256?: bool}` → `{exists, type, size, mtime, sha256?}` — hashing is opt-in per call (hashing a 1.5 GB dump costs seconds; callers that need verification ask once).
- `POST /files/begin` `{path, size, sha256, mode?}` → opens a transfer temp sibling named deterministically from `(path, sha256)` — `.<name>.fleet-part-<sha256[..12]>` — so an interrupted client resumes the *same* transfer by re-issuing `begin`. Refuses when free space < `size` + margin.
- `POST /files/write` `{path, sha256, offset, data_b64}` → appends/verifies at `offset` in the temp; returns `{size}` (bytes durably written). Idempotent at a given offset (rewrite of the same offset with the same bytes is a no-op success) so client retries are safe.
- `POST /files/commit` `{path, sha256}` → daemon hashes the temp; on match: fsync, atomic `rename` over the target, apply declared mode; on mismatch: `{error: "sha256 mismatch", actual}` and the temp stays for inspection/resume. `POST /files/abort` removes the temp.
- `POST /files/read` `{path, offset, length}` → `{data_b64, eof, size, mtime}`. The get flow is `stat` (with `sha256: true`) → `read` chunks into a local temp → verify whole-file sha256 → rename locally. Symmetric failure semantics both directions.

Chunk size: **2 MiB raw** (≈2.67 MiB base64 — far under the 64 MiB frame ceiling, small enough that a lost chunk is cheap). File size is unbounded by the protocol. Offsets are byte counts; resume = `stat` the deterministic temp, continue from its size.

Path handling: daemon normalizes, rejects NUL and non-UTF8; no confinement beyond the daemon user's own permissions (the daemon already executes arbitrary commands as that user — file routes are not a privilege change, and the design says so rather than pretending a sandbox).

### Client verbs (Drew's naming, proxy domain)

```
fleet proxy put [--mode OCTAL] [--no-resume] <local-path | -> <laptop-path>
fleet proxy get [--mode OCTAL] [--no-resume] <laptop-path> <local-path | ->
fleet proxy put -r <local-dir> <laptop-dir>     # recursive: client-side walk,
fleet proxy get -r <laptop-dir> <local-dir>     # per-file transfers
```

- `-` = stdin/stdout streaming: no resume, no temp (streamed chunks in order), sha256 still computed and printed to stderr at completion.
- Progress and the final sha256 go to **stderr**; stdout carries data only for `get -`.
- Directory recursion is per-file (each file resumable/atomic independently); empty directories are not preserved in v1 (noted, not hidden); symlinks are not followed by default.
- Mode: `put` sends the local file's mode in `begin` unless `--mode` overrides; default 0644 when the source has no mode (stdin). Ownership is always the daemon user (the daemon is unprivileged — no chown exists to offer). Timestamps are not preserved in v1.
- Exit codes follow the workspace convention: 2 usage, 3 transport, 69 capability-unavailable.

### Registry / capability placement

- Subcommands `get`/`put` join the proxy domain in fleet-registry (registry data, like `serve/connect/init`).
- Capability: the verbs are proxy-client surface, so the natural home is `proxy-connect` — which is compiled into **every** variant, including the D7-size-gated connect builds (≤ 2 MiB). Chunking + sha256 in std-only Rust is small, but this must be *measured* at implementation: if the connect-static gate breaks, the verbs move behind a `proxy-files` feature present in `full` (and absent from connect), and connect builds answer the established exit-69 stub. Either outcome is a normal registry decision, not a redesign.
- Implementation home: the fleet-proxy crate's client half, beside `connect` — it already owns broker negotiation, the legacy proto-0 fallback, and tunnel construction. The daemon client types shared with the `laptop-agent` domain should be factored rather than duplicated when the second consumer appears.

### Daemon side: Python now, Rust by construction

The Python daemon is to-be-deleted surface (#5343), so the question is whether interim routes there are worth it. **Yes**: the patch is ~100 additive lines on a 347-line file, the *protocol* is the durable artifact (the Rust role implements the same routes), and the two scripts blocked on a file channel (`fetch-charge-inputs.py`, `atlas-backup.py`) are live production paths, not hypotheticals. Their re-pointing off SSH stdin is a follow-up under their own owners once the verbs ship.

### Testing / build

- Workspace unit tests: chunk math, offset idempotency, resume-from-temp, sha256 mismatch refusal, path normalization.
- smoke.sh: hermetic broker round-trip — put + get a multi-chunk file through a real broker against a fake daemon; byte-identical round trip; interrupted put resumed to completion.
- Ships in the existing `pkgs/fleet` Nix package (all variants) — no new build machinery; deployed copies flip by the established pattern.

### Non-goals (v1)

No delta/rsync algorithm, no compression, no directory sync semantics (no delete-mirroring), no multi-file archives, no timestamp preservation, no cross-host (non-laptop) targets — the verbs speak to the daemon the proxy already reaches.

code.title: Connection perf: coalesce queue claim flow to 1 round trip, cross-service batch, real file-transfer verb
code.body:
## Coalesce queue claim flow + add a real file-transfer verb (fewer round trips, WS-C census)

Part of epic #5412. Census evidence: WS-C comment on #5701 (2026-11-04). Every sandbox↔laptop round trip costs ~200–600 ms warm, so round-trip COUNT is the lever until/unless the multiplexed-tunnel work lands.

### Round-trip census today (code + logs)
| Operation | Transport round trips | Wall (measured) |
|---|---|---|
| Single trivial exec (`laptop-agent.py exec -- true`) | 1 (unix to session proxy + 1 pooled-tunnel HTTP request) | wall 346–719 ms; trip p50 369 ms |
| `fleet queue claim` (one claim) | 1 (`call("/claim")` → one `broker_roundtrip` → one `unix_roundtrip`; repo-queue crate `crates/repo-queue/src/main.rs` cmd_claim/call) | ~1 trip ≈ 0.3–0.6 s warm |
| Claimant launch flow (claim + lane + bind) | 3 separate CLI invocations = 3 round trips (cmd_lane, cmd_bind are separate `call()`s) | ~1–2 s warm, ×3 failure surfaces |
| Detached job to completion (`run` + `poll` loop) | 1 + N polls (poll sleeps 3 s client-side and re-requests per iteration, laptop-agent.py `poll`) | grows with job length |
| Small file fetch from laptop | NO file verb exists: fetch = 1 exec round trip with `base64 -w0` in a shell string (measured 301 ms wall for /etc/hostname), 1 MiB/stream cap, +33% base64 size, no resume/offsets | 1 trip + encoding overhead |

Also measured: `fleet queue health` took 2.1 s and 5.8 s in two live probes (vs 0.30 s in the #5701 stage-2 window) — it visibly resolves secrets ("resolved via bitwarden") plus queries, i.e. multiple internal round trips; health should be 1 lightweight trip.

### Proposal
1. **Batch endpoint for the claim flow**: queue-broker `POST /claim-flow` {queue, worker, lane, session, launched_by} performing claim+lane+bind server-side (laptop-local, Supabase calls stay on the laptop) and returning the bound row. Client `fleet queue claim --bind ...` uses it when session info is present; the 3 separate verbs remain for compatibility. 3 trips → 1.
2. **Generic batch already half-exists**: the daemon `/exec` accepts `cmds: [...]` (exec-batch measured: 10 trivial commands in ONE trip, 483 ms wall total vs ~400 ms EACH singly). Publish this pattern to queue/secrets clients: a `/batch` on the session-proxy protocol that carries several service requests (mixed ports) in one frame and fans out at the broker. Client libraries coalesce independent calls made in one invocation.
3. **File-transfer verb**: daemon `GET /file?path=&off=&len=` returning raw bytes (Content-Type application/octet-stream, byte-range via query — the jobs poll already proves the offset pattern) + client `laptop-agent.py fetch PATH OUT`. No base64, chunked by offset, resume = re-request from last offset. Binary framing arrives free if the multiplexed-tunnel work (sibling issue) lands; the verb is useful on today's HTTP path too.
4. **Poll backoff**: `poll` interval 3 s fixed → exponential 1 s → 10 s cap with server-side long-poll option (`?wait_s=N` holds the request until state change or N s), cutting poll trips for long jobs by ~10×.

### Acceptance
- Claim+lane+bind in 1 round trip (verify in trips/broker logs: exactly 1 trip id per flow).
- `laptop-agent.py fetch` of a 5 MiB file: byte-identical (md5), no base64, trips = ceil(size/chunk) with chunk ≥ 1 MiB.
- Long-job poll trips reduced ≥5× at equal completion-detection latency ≤10 s.

code.title: Connection perf: multiplexed persistent streams over one tunnel (replace HTTP-per-call + pool of 50)
code.body:
## Multiplexed persistent streams over ONE tunnel for the sandbox↔laptop path (WS-C design, from #5701)

Part of epic #5412. Design evidence: WS-C connection-performance comment on #5701 (2026-11-04).

### Measured problem (2026-11-04, trips.jsonl n=1149 + live probes)
- Warm single trivial call: client trip p50 369 ms (status-200, <2 s subset, n=800) while daemon work is 1–11 ms (daemon trips.jsonl; example trip aedc705d4294: client 445 ms vs daemon 1 ms). Transport ≈ 99% of cost.
- The path is HTTP/1.1-request-per-call over a pooled CONNECT tunnel (pool 50 in `fleet proxy serve`). Even warm, one request/response costs ~170–600 ms over the runtime-proxy (:3130) + DERP hairpin path. A warm RTT is the floor for EVERY operation, and every CLI operation is a separate call.
- Cold CONNECT measured 1,434 ms trip (same-minute warm trip: 212 ms) — CONNECT setup ≈ 1.2–1.8 s, and the ramp test on #5701 showed CONNECT setup serializes under concurrency (128 tunnels = 14.6 s wall, no failures).
- Failure amplification: during proxy wobble, trips cluster at 502 after ~16.3 s (p50, n=119) and no-status after ~26 s (p50, n=73) — retry chains multiply the herd.

### Proposal
Replace HTTP-per-call over N pooled tunnels with ONE (or two, for redundancy) persistent tunnel carrying multiplexed streams:

1. **Framed stream multiplexer on the tunnel** (the broker already speaks length-prefixed frames on its unix socket — extend that framing end-to-end): each request is a stream (id, port/service, method, path, body) over a single TCP/TLS-less CONNECT tunnel; responses interleave by stream id. Candidates: yamux-style custom framing in the existing Rust `fleet-proxy`, HTTP/2 over the tunnel (h2 gives streams + HPACK + PING keepalive for free), or QUIC if the runtime proxy path ever allows UDP (it does not today — CONNECT/TCP only, so QUIC is out until that changes).
2. **No per-call CONNECT, no pool checkout, no HTTP/1.1 head-of-line blocking** per request; pool of 50 tunnels collapses to 1–2 tunnels + stream concurrency (ramp proved the tunnel path itself survives 128 concurrent; streams remove the serialized CONNECT setup that made the ramp slow).
3. **Keepalive**: application-level PING on the tunnel (replaces per-pool-connection health keepalives; current Python-broker constants KEEPALIVE_S=180 / idle-exit 3600 s carry over as starting values, but the broker must not idle-exit while a tunnel with in-flight streams is healthy — exit only when the tunnel is dead AND no calls for 3600 s).
4. **Backpressure + bounded retry**: per-stream timeout with a hard ceiling well under the current 16–26 s failure cluster; one retry on a FRESH stream (not a fresh CONNECT) when the tunnel is alive; tunnel re-establishment is single-flight (one CONNECT at a time, queued streams wait on it) so a proxy wobble cannot stampede 50 CONNECTs.
5. **TCP_NODELAY** on tunnel sockets end-to-end (absent in the Python stack today: grep finds no TCP_NODELAY in laptop-agent.py / laptop-agent-broker.py / laptop-agent-daemon.py) and coalesce header+body into one write per frame to avoid Nagle/delayed-ACK stalls on small request/response pairs.

### Acceptance
- Warm trivial exec trip p50 ≤ 50 ms (from 369 ms) at comparable load, daemon duration unchanged.
- 128 concurrent requests over the single tunnel: 0 failures, wall ≤ ramp's 128-tunnel wall (14.6 s) by ≥5×.
- Failure injection (kill runtime proxy briefly): calls fail or recover in ≤2 s, no 16–26 s cluster in trips.jsonl.
- Trip logs on both sides keep the same trip id so the client/daemon split stays measurable.

Risks: single tunnel = single point of congestion/failure → mitigate with 2 tunnels + stream load-balancing and the single-flight reconnect above. HTTP/2 dependency in Rust (h2 crate) vs hand-rolled framing is an implementation choice for the builder; the wire contract (streamed frames, per-stream ids) is the requirement.

code.title: atlas core consumer wiring: fleet atlas-search fan-out over the TursoDB shard core (tier ceilings, merge, --expand hydration)
code.body:
Consumer wiring for the restored atlas core tier (restore record: #5669, 2026-11-04). The core now exists as 29 TursoDB scan shards + 2 TursoDB content stores; nothing reads them yet — production search still runs against the monolith `atlas` (libSQL). This issue wires the consumer side. (Serve-role home for the service itself: #5604. Cache + flags: #5668 — coordinate, don't duplicate.)

**Shard layout (authoritative map on #5669):** `atlas-core-<tier>-<topic>-<nn>` scan stores (chunks + `vec F32_BLOB(768)` + `atlas_manifest`), tier ∈ {internal (28 shards, 107,001 chunks), secret (1 shard, 638 chunks)}; content stores `atlas-core-internal-content` / `atlas-core-secret-content` (messages + sessions for --expand hydration). Public tier: no corpora yet.

**Scope:**
- Shard discovery: consumer resolves the shard set from a registry (each shard's `atlas_manifest` is the self-description; decide the registry of record — candidates: the #5669 registry DB, or manifest fan-out at startup). New shards must join without code changes.
- Query path: fan out an exact-cosine scan (`vector_distance_cos(vec, ?)`, top-k per shard) across the caller's shards **in parallel**, merge by distance. Scoped queries (one topic) touch only that topic's shards. Metric is cosine for this corpus; TursoDB also offers dot product, L2, and Jaccard for future corpora.
- **Tier ceiling is physical:** a client fans out only to tiers its credentials open. Secret is never in a default fan-out; it requires a secret-capable token, explicitly.
- `--expand` hydration from the caller's tier content store (message/session rows by chunk message_id).
- Result-cache snapshot id (§3.2 of #5667) must incorporate the shard set + per-shard counts so a re-shard invalidates correctly (with #5668).

**Known gaps / data:**
- **FTS:** TursoDB rejects virtual tables in MVCC mode — the shards have no `chunks_fts`. Keyword search needs an answer (keep serving FTS from the libSQL monolith until cutover, or a dedicated FTS store). Decide here or spin out.
- **Latency (measured at restore, sandbox → us-east-1 HTTPS, network-inclusive):** per-shard top-10 scan 1.1–1.9 s at 3.5–4.5k rows — above the §5.2 250 ms server-side budget assumption for libSQL. Re-measure from the laptop consumer path; §5.5 embedded replicas for internal/public stores are the standing lever (secret is never replicated).
- Cutover criteria: fan-out parity vs monolith exact scan is proven at restore time (7/7 held-out queries, exact top-10). Re-run the parity harness against the wired consumer before any default switch; monolith stays untouched until then.

code.title: id: research/design: fork a Rust KDL stack for ID — universal + multiple annotations, upstream archaeology, fork-base selection (extends #5688)
code.body:
## Summary

Research + design for **forking a Rust KDL stack for ID**, extending #5688
(KDL → JSON → atomic triples → SQL/PGQ). This issue runs Drew's KDL
thread to ground in three directions:

1. **Archaeology (laptop hunt):** the missing KDL material Drew
   remembered exists — it is `pkgs/mappy/migrations/limit.kdl`, his
   Dec-2023 scratchpad, and it is the concrete ancestor of #5688's
   triples design.
2. **Archaeology (upstream):** Drew's actual capability asks to the KDL
   project were found — two GitHub Discussions in `kdl-org/kdl`
   (**#344 Children Annotation**, **#362 Property Annotation**, both
   Dec-2023) that were **not adopted** into KDL 2.0. Together with his
   spec-era comments and his Go-ecosystem work (kdl-go, koanf), they
   define the fork's extension list.
3. **Fork base:** fork **`kdl-org/kdl-rs`** (the `kdl` crate, v6.7.1) —
   the only maintained, format-preserving, dual-version (1.0 + 2.0)
   Rust KDL document parser, with serde and KQL built in. The
   annotation generalization Drew wants is a contained AST change
   there, and a rebuild-everything proposition anywhere else.

Umbrella: epic #2056. Parent design: #5688 (this issue supplies its
parser/implementation substrate and its annotation model).

---

## 1. Laptop hunt — what was searched, what was found

Searched (2026-11-04, laptop online): every `*.kdl` file under the
laptop home (deduped across the many worktrees/clones), plus content
greps for "kdl" over the laptop's zettel corpus (`~/git/zettel`),
cairn (`~/git/cairn`), hatch-personal, and notes trees
(`~/hatch/notes`, `~/git/fleet/notes`, `~/queue-notes`).

**Not covered / honest gaps:** the dozens of repo worktrees are clones
of the same trees (deduplicated, not re-read); the Atlas local chunk
store was not mined for documents; no ChatGPT `conversations.json`
export exists on the laptop (the late-2023 prose brainstorming remains
unrecovered — the #5688 follow-on stands).

### 1.1 The find: `pkgs/mappy/migrations/limit.kdl` (106 lines, Drew, 2023-12-17)

A design scratchpad inside the `mappy` graph/triples experiment
(Python + SQL migrations; cf. `node.sql`, `crdb.sql` beside it).
Committed 2023-12-17 — **the same day** as upstream discussion #362
below. Its key positions, verbatim in spirit:

- **Triples modeled as annotations** — the direct ancestor of #5688 §2:

  ```kdl
  (subject)character "Brian" {
      (predicate)"writesBooks" (object)"Wish It, Want It, Do It" (object)"Faster Than the Speed of Love"
      (predicate)"travelsWith" (object)"Stewie" (object)"Peter"
  }
  ```

- **Parameterized / structured annotation payloads** — far beyond the
  spec's single bare identifier:

  ```kdl
  (predicate#NotVeryWell)"writesBooks" (object#book#author:BrianGriffin)"Wish It, Want It, Do It"
  (object::Baby:Lois'sBaby::Kind-Of-Annoying)"Stewie" (object:FamilyGuy)"Peter"
  (yes:yes:no:::bool)"=" "yes" "no" "yes"
  (document:object)rdf { ... }
  ```

- **Annotations on every part** — node names, argument values (and, in
  the commented-out variant, `(subject)character="Brian"` prop-style
  modeling), plus experiments that leave the grammar entirely
  (`` `=(predicate) ``, `:=(object)"examples"`, annotations embedded in
  comments `/*(result)*/`).
- **The triples store sketched in comments**, Dec-2023:

  ```
  // nodes: id, type, key, value
  // links: id, type, from, to
  // meta_links: id, type, from, to
  ```

- An RDF / Dublin-Core record re-expressed in KDL under
  `(document:object)rdf`, and a tail of deliberate lexical torture
  tests (quote/escape/emoji edge cases) — parser-robustness probing.

This file is why the fork's annotation design (§4b) treats the
annotation slot as *structured data*, not a bare tag.

### 1.2 Other real KDL material on the laptop (all in `developing-today/code`)

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| `pkgs/roc/out-in.kdl` (39 ln) | Roc syntax brainstorm in KDL form (known fragment; links kdl-play) |
| `pkgs/roc/platform.kdl` (14 ln) | Prose platform notes as KDL strings |
| `pkgs/identity/config.kdl` + `pkgs/identity/configuration/embed/config.kdl` | Production identity-service config written in KDL |
| `~/.config/zellij/config.kdl` | Tool config (zellij) — not Drew's design material |

### 1.3 Negative results

- No KDL documents or design notes in the laptop zettel / cairn /
  notes corpora (one `flake.lock` substring hit only).
- `developing-today/hygge` (GitHub, 2022) is Drew's builder-only Rust
  KDL crate ("knuffel or kdl-rs for deserialization :-)"); its
  `SPEC.md` is a vendored copy of the KDL 1.0 grammar. It is prior art
  for the *serializer* half of our stack, not a parser base.

---

## 2. Drew's KDL-ecosystem threads — the capability-ask catalogue

Method: GitHub search (`author:` / `commenter:` / `involves:`) across
the `kdl-org` org and globally for "kdl", plus a full pass over
`kdl-org/kdl` **Discussions** via GraphQL (search does not index
Discussions — that is where the headline asks were hiding). All
threads below verified by reading them.

### 2.1 The two declined capability asks (define the fork)

| Thread | Date | Ask | Maintainer response | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [kdl-org/kdl discussion #344 — Children Annotation](https://github.com/kdl-org/kdl/discussions/344) | 2023-11-29 | "Allow annotating the children block in the same way that values and identifiers can be annotated." | tabatkins (spec editor): unconvinced — a node has only one child list, so the information "can just be expressed with a property or attribute"; asked for a use case. | **Not adopted.** KDL 2.0 grammar has no children annotation. |
| [kdl-org/kdl discussion #362 — Property Annotation](https://github.com/kdl-org/kdl/discussions/362) | 2023-12-17 | "Allow annotating properties in the same way that values and identifiers can be annotated." Drew supplied precedents: Go's `lunjon/gokdl` already implements `Prop.TypeAnnot` (`(author)name="Jonathan"`); Elixir's Kuddle supports it too (with `annotations: []` — a *list*). | tabatkins: parseable, but questions the value — keys are unique per node, so "all necessary context is already baked into their name"; asked for a use case. | **Not adopted.** KDL 2.0 grammar: `prop := string '=' value` — no key annotation. |

The irony the design should record: the use cases the maintainers
asked for existed the same week in `limit.kdl` (§1.1) — repeated names
disambiguated by role (`(subject)` / `(predicate)` / `(object)`,
parameterized `(object#book#author:BrianGriffin)`) — exactly the
"same name, different role" rationale the spec itself accepts for
node annotations, extended to every part.

### 2.2 Spec-era participation (KDL 2.0 design batch, Nov-2023)

| Thread | Drew's position | Outcome in KDL 2.0 |
|---|---|---|
| [kdl-org/kdl #343 — prefix keywords with `#`](https://github.com/kdl-org/kdl/issues/343) | Came around to supporting; asked whether `#` would be banned from identifiers / first-char, noting quoted names as the escape. | **Adopted:** 2.0 keywords are `#true` / `#false` / `#null`. |
| [kdl-org/kdl #342 — multiline comments in more places](https://github.com/kdl-org/kdl/issues/342) | "i think this should be legal, i don't know what it should do." | Partially adopted: 2.0 relaxed comment placement (e.g. `//` immediately followed by newline; comments in more positions). |
| [kdl-org/kdljs #21 — KDL 2.0 compliance](https://github.com/kdl-org/kdljs/issues/21) | 2024-12-29: nudged for a 2.0 update post-release (playground dependency). | Closed. |

### 2.3 Implementation-era threads (Go ecosystem, Dec-2023 → Apr-2024)

Drew was simultaneously *building on* KDL — a KDL config provider for
koanf, via kdl-go — and pressing the permissiveness philosophy the
fork inherits:

| Thread | Ask / work | Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| [sblinch/kdl-go #3](https://github.com/sblinch/kdl-go/issues/3) (authored) | Marshal panic on lists in `map[string]any`; discovered the `key=val` prop-coercion; asked "is there a toggle somewhere?" and for an error instead of a panic. | Fixed upstream (kdl-go list-marshal fix; Drew pulled it via koanf #267). |
| [sblinch/kdl-go #4](https://github.com/sblinch/kdl-go/issues/4) (authored) | Data-model fidelity cluster: empty nodes unmarshal as `nil` vs empty map; duplicate node names with changing types should be last-wins, not an error; `{ "" 5 ; "" 6 ; }` children mishandled; quoted `"1"` / empty-string identifiers vs bare-identifier rules; **asked for behavior flags/toggles "to extend what is permissible past spec."** | Maintainer asked for isolated test cases; thread closed with "Fixed in 3d5e45f" (2024-04-09). Partially addressed. |
| [knadh/koanf #265 / #266](https://github.com/knadh/koanf/issues/266) (authored) + [developing-today-forks/koanf PR #1, PR #3](https://github.com/developing-today-forks/koanf/pull/1) | Contributed a KDL parser provider for koanf (Go config library); negotiated the `emptyIsNil` difference generically rather than special-casing KDL in tests. | PRs merged in his fork; koanf gained its KDL parser from this work. |
| [knadh/koanf #267](https://github.com/knadh/koanf/issues/267) (authored) | kdl-go dependency update carrying the #3 fix. | Closed. |
| typestreamio/typestream #77 | Commented (local-data joins for stream filtering; libsql-as-file/URL). Tangential to KDL design. | Open; listed for completeness. |

Coverage caveat: issue/PR search + both ends of the Discussions list
were covered; comments Drew may have left inside *other people's*
discussions were not exhaustively enumerated.

### 2.4 The spec baseline (verified against both grammars)

Type annotations in **KDL 1.0** (SPEC_v1: "a prefix to any Node Name
or Value"; `prop := identifier '=' value`; `type := '(' identifier ')'`)
and **KDL 2.0** (IETF-draft grammar: `value := type? …`,
`prop := string '=' value`, `type := '(' string ')'`):

- node names: **one** optional annotation ✔
- argument values & property values: **one** optional annotation ✔
- property keys: **none** ✘ (Drew's #362)
- children blocks: **none** ✘ (Drew's #344)
- multiple annotations anywhere: **none** — the grammar's `type?` is
  singular, everywhere. (Kuddle's `annotations: []` shows at least one
  implementation already models it as a list.)

---

## 3. Rust KDL landscape — fork candidates

Verified 2026-11-04 against crates.io + the repos' current sources.

| | `kdl` (kdl-org/kdl-rs) | `knuffel` (tailhook) | `kaydle` (Lucretiel) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Version / state | **6.7.1**, actively maintained (repo pushed 2026-10; ~2.96M downloads) | 3.2.0, last release **2023-04** (stale) | 0.2.0, last release **2022-07** (unmaintained) |
| Role | Document parser + API; formatting/whitespace/comment-**preserving** parse & modify | Derive-based config decoder (serde-like `Decode`) | Serde ser/de layer *on top of* the `kdl` crate |
| Spec versions | **2.0 default; 1.0 via `v1` feature** (sibling `kdlv1` crate); converts documents between versions | 1.0 only | Whatever the underlying `kdl` crate did in 2022 (1.0 era) |
| Serde | **Built in** (`serde` default feature; `de.rs`/`se.rs`) | Is itself a derive stack (not serde) | Is itself serde — superseded by kdl-rs's built-in serde |
| Search/query | **KQL built in** (`query.rs` — the KDL Query Language) | None | None |
| Annotation model | `KdlNode.ty: Option<KdlIdentifier>`; `KdlEntry.ty: Option<KdlIdentifier>` (value); prop key = bare `KdlIdentifier` (**no slot**); `KdlIdentifier` = value+repr only | Annotations not first-class (consumed as Rust types during decode); no document fidelity | Inherits kdl's AST of its era |
| Round-trip of unknown annotations | Preserved **where representable** (node/value `ty` + full format preservation); structurally impossible for prop keys / multiples — the parser cannot even hold them | N/A (decode discards) | N/A |
| License | Apache-2.0 | MIT/Apache-2.0 | MPL-2.0 |

Also noted: `kdlv1` (the split-out 1.0 implementation kdl 6.x wraps)
and Drew's own `hygge` (builder-only serializer; a candidate to revive
for the output side, §4d).

### Recommendation: fork `kdl-org/kdl-rs` (`kdl` crate)

- It is the **only** candidate that is simultaneously: maintained,
  dual-version, format-preserving, serde-complete, and query-equipped
  (KQL matters for #5688's "searches efficiently" goal).
- The fork's core change is **contained**: generalize
  `ty: Option<KdlIdentifier>` → annotation lists, and add annotation
  slots where the AST has none (prop keys, children blocks). Every
  other subsystem (dual parsers, fmt preservation, serde, KQL,
  miette spans) carries over.
- Starting from knuffel means rebuilding 2.0 support, document
  fidelity, and a serializer from zero; kaydle is a layer, not a
  parser, and is abandoned. Neither survives contact with §4a.
- Apache-2.0; track upstream (spec evolution, test suites — including
  the official KDL test suite the crate already runs) and upstream
  what is upstreamable.

---

## 4. Fork design commitments (Drew, 2026-11-04)

**(a) Compatibility is absolute.** Every valid KDL 1.0 document parses
with its spec meaning unchanged; KDL 2.0 likewise, and future spec
versions are tracked. Extensions are **additive**: they never change
the meaning of a spec-valid document. (A document using extensions is
a superset document — a strict parser may reject it, and that is
accepted; the spec-valid subset always round-trips as plain KDL.)

**(b) Universal, multiple, structured annotations.** Generalize the
spec's value-only type hint to **every part**: node name, each
argument, property **keys**, property values, and the **children
block** (the #344/#362 asks), with **multiple annotations per part**
(Kuddle's `annotations: []` precedent). Open design question, with
`limit.kdl` as the evidence base: annotation **payloads** — Drew's
practice packs structure into the annotation (`#`-/`:`-separated
parameters: `(object#book#author:BrianGriffin)`,
`(yes:yes:no:::bool)`). Decide whether the payload stays an opaque
string (spec-shaped, maximally compatible) or gains a structured
sub-grammar in our dialect, and how either form decomposes into
triples under #5688.

**(c) Performance and search efficiency are first-class.** The
triples pipeline (#5688 §2) parses at ingest scale: streaming /
zero-copy parse paths where they matter, no format-preservation tax
on the hot path (make preservation opt-in per parse), and the
query story (KQL today; the SQL/PGQ graph layer in #5688) designed
against parsed-structure indexes rather than re-parse-per-query.

**(d) Output beyond KDL text — the document-language direction.**
Long-term this stops claiming to be KDL: it is *our document
language* with KDL as its default text form. Required renderers, in
#5688 §1.2's conversion-contract terms: KDL text (default), **JSON**,
**YAML**, and an **LLM sentence rendering** (a document rendered as
prose a model — or a person skimming — can read). Files are produced
"with an option": the same underlying document emits the requested
form. `hygge` (§1.3) is the in-house precedent for the builder/output
half.

## 5. Follow-on questions for the design pass

1. Annotation payload grammar (§4b) — opaque vs structured; triple
   decomposition of parameterized annotations.
2. Extension marking: does a document declare itself extended (a
   header annotation? a version node?), so tooling can warn before a
   strict-KDL consumer chokes?
3. Serde shape for annotation lists (attribute-style in derives?) and
   how the kdl-rs serde layer exposes prop-key annotations.
4. Which pieces, if any, get proposed back upstream (the Discussions
   show the maintainers' objection was use-case-shaped, and we now
   have the use cases — but the fork does not block on upstream).
5. Benchmarks: upstream `kdl` vs fork on the ingest corpus; the
   acceptance bar for §4c.

— Filed by the KDL research pass, 2026-11-04. Sources: laptop
(`~/git/code` primary checkout), GitHub (issues/PRs/Discussions via
search + GraphQL), crates.io, spec grammars (SPEC_v1 + the KDL 2.0
IETF draft) — all read directly during the pass.

code.title: Daily codebase innovation & maintenance
code.body:
Perform a comprehensive daily codebase review, innovation scan, and issue/PR maintenance pass across developing-today/code.

You are acting as an unrestricted principal architect and senior systems engineer. Do not hold back: generate bold ideas, surface hidden gaps, polish proposals, and solve immediate problems opportunistically.
Follow these directives and areas of focus:
### 1. COMPREHENSIVE REPOSITORY & ACTIVITY AUDIT - Inspect recent commits on `main` to understand the latest velocity and architectural direction. - Review open, recently closed, and merged issues and PRs (`gh issue list --state all --limit 50`, `gh pr list --state all --limit 30`). - Review each major package, tool, and subsystem in the repository:
  - **`pkgs/id`**: Distributed identity, cryptographic event log, p2panda synchronization, local event store, group encryption, discovery, and capability delegation.
  - **`pkgs/mcpx`**: Model Context Protocol daemon, multi-server multiplexing, protocol compliance, session leasing, JIT secret prompt vault, and Code Mode projection.
  - **`pkgs/jules` / `pkgs/jules-fleet` / `pkgs/jules-merge`**: Automated multi-agent coding workflows, issue triage, and parallel agent execution.
  - **NixOS System Infrastructure & Web Services**: Modules, cloud functions, background daemons, and system services.

### 2. UNRESTRICTED INNOVATION & NEW FEATURE GENERATION - You are NOT restricted by what currently exists. Brainstorm things that *should* exist, would be exceptionally useful, or incorporate frontier concepts:
  - Edge architectures using Cloudflare Workers, Durable Objects, KV, and Queues.
  - Distributed SQLite / libSQL / Turso primitives for offline-first, syncable state.
  - Advanced autonomous coding loops, speculative tool execution, and local verification loops.
  - Cross-platform bridges, native desktop integrations, and performance optimizations.
- **Bias Toward Capture**: It is far better to create an issue to triage later than to let a valuable opportunity or insight pass.
### 3. ACTIVE ISSUE & PR MAINTENANCE - **Scope Variety**: Create single large architectural vision issues for strategic direction, or narrow, highly focused issues for targeted improvements. - **Issue Decomposition**: If an existing issue is too broad, ambiguous, or monolithic (including issues created by others), break it apart into a series of clear, modular, linked sub-issues with explicit dependencies. - **Deduplication & Consolidation**: Identify overlapping or duplicate proposals/issues and consolidate them into unified, high-quality reference issues. - **Comments & Spec Refinement**: Leave comments or edit existing issues/PRs to provide missing technical specifications, edge-case analysis, data schemas, or suggested test cases. - **Zero-Context Hand-off Standard**: Every issue you author must be self-contained, citing exact file paths, interfaces, architectural rationale, and verifiable acceptance criteria so a new agent with zero prior context can execute it.

### 4. OPPORTUNISTIC IMPLEMENTATION (QUICK-WIN PRS) - If you identify straightforward bugs, unhandled edge cases, missing test coverage, or clean opportunities to refactor code to prevent future merge conflicts:
  - You are actively encouraged to open small, focused Pull Requests implementing the fix or feature directly.
  - Ensure all added code follows repository standards, includes tests, and passes formatting/linting hooks (`treefmt`, `conform`).
  - Never introduce breaking regressions to existing stable flows.
  - **One PR per coherent set**: batch every instance of the same problem — and all related dependency updates — into a single PR, or a few PRs split by coherent group. Never one PR per item or per dependency.
  - **Prefer tracked, higher-impact work**: before inventing a new micro-fix, check the open issues and implement the highest-impact one you can complete and verify, even when it spans several files.
  - **Merging is permitted, never required**: merge your PR only when checks pass and you are reasonably certain it is correct and low-risk. Otherwise leave it open and state your confidence and what a human should check in the description.

---
Launched by pm-dispatch for developing-today/code. Queue task and OpenCode session ids follow in a comment below.

code.body:
## Context

Follow-up to #3977. The code-local freshness journal/publisher contract is being implemented there, but the `orchestration-pass` producer is owned by the external `keep-the-four-repos-healthy` goal/cron, not by this repository. Do not edit the external scheduler/configuration from `developing-today/code`.

The current owner/retirement track is #2155 (under #2136), which remains blocked on its own access/ownership gate. Keep that gate and any schedule registry requirements intact.

## Scope

After #3977's publisher contract lands, update the owner-managed `orchestration-pass` to publish a source invalidation only after it has durably committed its verified source changes. Use a stable run/source-generation idempotency key and the established envelope/publisher contract; do not include credentials, secrets, or raw webhook bodies. A failed durable commit must not emit; retries after commit must be idempotent.

Do not change production routes/secrets without the #1182 gate, do not alter #1184's child hierarchy, and do not retire or disable the pass as part of this work.

## Acceptance

- The owner-managed pass publishes only after durable commit, with stable source, scope, reason, timestamps, and idempotency key.
- Retries do not create duplicate invalidations; durable-write failure emits nothing and remains retryable.
- The implementation is tested in the repository that owns the pass, and the result is linked back to #3977 and #2155.

code.title: design: bake the SSH recovery path into the fleet binary — orchestrate system ssh now, native russh deferred
code.body:
design: bake the SSH recovery path into the fleet binary

Links: epic #5412 · laptop-agent design #5343
Drew's end state: **no shell scripts, no Python scripts — just the fleet
binary.** This issue covers the *recovery* SSH path only (the daemon-down
escape hatch). The everyday path's Python is the sibling item: the
`fleet laptop-agent` client domain (see Ordering, below).

## Context — the recovery path today (three of our files)

`~/tools/laptop-ssh.sh` (the shim) delegates exec-style calls to the
laptop-agent, but shapes the agent cannot express fall back to real SSH.
The fallback classes, from the shim's own header:

- `LAPTOP_SSH_REAL=1` (explicit escape hatch / daemon-down recovery)
- no arguments (interactive session) or a **leading ssh option**
  (`-L/-R/-W/-N/-t/-p/-l/-i/-o …` — forwards and TTY allocation)
- **stdin carrying data** for the remote command (sudo -S feeds,
  `cat > file` pushes) — the daemon has no stdin channel

The fallback is `~/tools/laptop-ssh-real.sh`, which `exec`s system ssh:

```sh
exec ssh \
  -o "ProxyCommand=python3 $HOME/tools/laptop-proxy-connect.py" \
  -o "StrictHostKeyChecking=yes" \
  -o "UserKnownHostsFile=$HOME/.ssh/known_hosts_laptop" \
  -o "IdentitiesOnly=yes" -i "$HOME/.ssh/id_ed25519" \
  -o "ConnectTimeout=60" -o "ConnectionAttempts=3" \
  -o "ServerAliveInterval=15" -o "ServerAliveCountMax=8" \
  -o "ControlMaster=auto" -o "ControlPath=$HOME/.ssh/cm-%r@%h:%p" \
  -o "ControlPersist=3600" \
  "user@100.99.113.103" "$@"
```

…and `~/tools/laptop-proxy-connect.py` is the HTTP CONNECT relay to the
runtime proxy (:3130), reading the proxy credential from `HTTPS_PROXY`
and sending it only inside the CONNECT request (the #948 fix; the pinned
host key in `~/.ssh/known_hosts_laptop` is a single line:
`100.99.113.103 ssh-ed25519 …`).

## Findings — most of this is already in the binary

1. **The ProxyCommand already exists as Rust.**
   `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-proxy/src/stdio.rs` is documented as
   *"`fleet proxy connect --stdio` — the ProxyCommand relay:
   laptop-proxy-connect.py's job, fleet-shaped"* — it opens the CONNECT
   tunnel (`tunnel.rs`: credential from `HTTPS_PROXY`, inside the
   request only, never argv, never logged) and splices stdin/stdout
   onto it. Defaults already line up with the SSH target:
   `client.rs` `run_connect` uses `config.target_host()` for `--host`
   (fleet-config `DEFAULT_TARGET_HOST = "100.99.113.103"`) and
   `args.port.unwrap_or(22)`. It is already SSH-tested the hard way:
   the hand-rolled pumps exist because `splice(2)` froze the SSH
   handshake mid-stream (#5431), and the no-join teardown is the #5518
   fix. So the Python file is replaceable **today** by
   `ProxyCommand=fleet proxy connect --stdio`.
2. **The codebase is deliberately synchronous and small.**
   `fleet-proxy`'s dependency list is `fleet-registry`, `fleet-config`,
   `fleet-proxy-proto`, `serde`, `serde_json`, `libc` — no async
   runtime, no crypto stack. The workspace release profile is a size
   contract (design note §2: connect variant target ≤1.5 MiB, hard
   budget ≤2 MiB, `opt-level = "z"`, LTO, stripped). Any SSH-in-Rust
   route is measured against that contract.
3. **System ssh is present and is an OS component**: `/usr/bin/ssh`,
   OpenSSH 9.6p1 on this sandbox; NixOS provides it on the laptop side
   of life too. It is platform — like the kernel and libc the binary
   already relies on — not one of *our* scripts.

## Route (i): native Rust SSH via russh — what "possible" honestly means
