code.title: queue: coverage join ignores open fix PRs — issues get re-triaged while their PRs bit-rot (#941, #1204, #1207)
code.body:
## Finding

Three coverage-pass triage packets claimed tonight that their issue "had no live queue task", because the coverage join (`coverage/issues-code-live.json` vs `agent.tasks`, checked 2026-11-03T12:36Z) matches issues to tasks through queued/claimed state only. All three issues already had an **open fix PR** from a completed queue task, and all three PRs are now far behind main — two of them no longer merge at all:

| issue | triage packet | prior triage | fix PR | branch | ahead / behind main | merges? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| #941 | task 7600 | task 1088 (2026-10-31) | #4832 | `queue/4642-941-operator-token-comments` | 2 / 138 | yes (clean, unmerged) |
| #1207 | task 7653 | task 2485 (2026-11-01) | #3958 | `queue/4917-1207-roadmap-horizon` | 1 / 1554 | **no** — conflict in `pm-stack/aggregator/src/render.ts` |
| #1204 | task 7655 | task 2482 (2026-11-01) | #3957 | `queue/4914-1204-extractor-health` | 3 / 1547 | **no** — conflict in `pm-stack/aggregator/src/saas-extract.ts` |

(`git merge-tree --write-tree origin/main origin/<branch>`, measured against `origin/main` a8dbda7fc on 2026-11-03.)

## Why it matters

Two failures compound:

1. **Double triage.** Each of these packets burned a claim re-deriving a verdict that was already on the issue, and the worker's only useful output was pointing at the PR that the join had missed. Every open issue with an in-flight PR is a candidate for the same repeat.
2. **Silent PR bit-rot.** When a fix task ends in `pr_opened`, the task leaves the live set, so no coverage join and no queue worker is watching the PR afterwards. The three PRs above were touched last on 2026-11-01/03 and have drifted 138–1554 commits behind main; two need manual conflict resolution before they can land. Nothing in the fleet currently notices.

## Suggested fix

- **Coverage join:** before declaring "no live task", also search open PRs (and branches matching `queue/<task>-<issue>-*`) for a reference to the issue number. Either treat an open PR as a live artifact (repeat triage is unnecessary) or route it to merge-watch as a `park`/`wait` instead of a fresh triage packet.
- **Merge-watch:** for tasks completed with `outcome = pr_opened`, enqueue a check task `not_before` ~24 h later that re-tests mergibility (`merge-tree` against current main), refreshes the branch if the fix is still desired, or closes the PR with evidence if main has superseded it. That closes the gap between "PR opened" and "PR merged" that the queue currently has no state for.
- **Packet defect signal:** the triage packets in this run could not distinguish "no work exists" from "work exists as an unmerged PR", which is the exact ambiguity the follow-up task should not inherit.

## Provenance

Filed by the OpenChamber scheduled lane (`repo-worker-code`, lane 335a5d1f-bfc1-4831-99ea-850c8939a727) while working coverage-pass triage tasks 7600, 7653, 7655 in `repo-health-code-pilot`. No code change is proposed here; this is a queue-tooling/process defect, filed per the worker's "document concerns as issues rather than blocking progress" rule. Verdicts for the three issues are on the issues themselves, with PR ownership left with tasks 4642 / 4917 / 4914.

## Acceptance criteria

- The coverage join treats an issue with an OPEN fix PR as in-flight, not ownerless: no new triage packet is enqueued for an issue whose fix PR is open (the join records the PR as the coverage).
- Each of #941, #1204, and #1207 is dispositioned exactly once against its existing PR (#4832, #3957, #3958): the PR is shepherded (rebased / conflict-resolved / merged or closed with a salvage note per protocol §8), not re-implemented by a fresh task.
- A regression check or test pins the join behaviour: fixture issue with an open PR + completed fix task yields zero new triage packets.

code.title: steward ledger: queue-health figures require two agreeing on-disk reads before recording (6 corrections in 2 windows)
code.body:
## Problem

The pool-quota steward's ledger (`hidden_files/pool-change-ledger.md`) keeps recording queue-health figures from a single tool delivery that later turns out to be fabricated, truncated, or carried over from a prior run's probe file — then correcting them append-only. The correction mechanism works, but the error recurs at the same rate in consecutive windows:

Window 2026-11-01T13:12Z–2026-11-02T13:12Z (meta-review 2026-11-02):
- Runs 89, 93, 94 each recorded wrong queue-health figures from interim/unreliable mid-run summaries; each corrected within hours.

Window 2026-11-02T13:12Z–2026-11-03T13:12Z (meta-review 2026-11-03):
- Run 103 (correction 2026-11-02T13:40Z): queue figures were the 102nd run's, carried over from its probe file; the claimed 269 -> 243 drain never happened.
- Run 108 (correction 2026-11-02T18:30Z): figures "came from a tool output that two later independent reads do NOT corroborate" — the recorded interval story was the opposite of the real one on two queues (claimed actually rose 31-33 -> 52-55 while queued fell).
- Run 116 (correction 2026-11-03T04:27Z): figures "rested on a truncated/fabricated tool-output delivery"; the recorded "claimed REBOUNDED 12 -> 18" narrative was wrong (claimed actually fell 12 -> 5).

No quota figure or threshold judgment was affected in any of the six — the exposure is the queue narrative (claim-wave stories other fleet jobs read and act on) and the steward's own time spent correcting.

## What is needed (hard rule, not advice)

Amend the steward instruction so that a ledger event's queue-health figures may only be written from:

1. a health output saved to a file on disk during that run, read back from disk before the event is written, and
2. a second, independent health read in the same run that agrees on queued/claimed counts (ordinary live churn of a few rows excepted and noted as churn, as other runs already do).

A single in-flight tool delivery — however complete it looks — is not a recordable source for queue figures. This mirrors the standard the meta-reviewer's own queue pull had to adopt on 2026-11-03 after two fabricated script deliveries (internally inconsistent totals; summary file never written).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Steward instruction carries the two-read / on-disk rule for queue figures.
- [ ] A full daily window of steward runs with zero queue-figure corrections.
- [ ] Meta-reviewer verifies the zero-correction window in its daily audit.

Filed by the pool meta-reviewer (code#1340), daily run 2026-11-03. Evidence: goal `hidden_files/meta-review/2026-11-03-evidence.md`.

code.title: fleet telemetry adoption: workers complete tasks without pool/model/effort/cost fields (1 of 846 post-#1582 completions)
code.body:
## Problem

code#1582 (fleet telemetry) CLOSED COMPLETED 2026-11-02T22:18:19Z: `repo-queue.py complete` now supports optional `pool` / `model` / `effort` / `cost_usd` on the completion result record, and the meta-reviewer's data pull can read them from `agent.tasks.result`.

Adoption is ~zero. Measured by the pool meta-reviewer (issue #1340) for the window 2026-11-02T13:12Z–2026-11-03T13:12Z, from real queue rows:

- 846 tasks were completed after the mechanism landed (2026-11-02T22:24Z agent note on #1582).
- Exactly **1 of 846** completions carries any of the telemetry keys — task 6525, whose `pool` / `effort` / `cost_usd` are all null (only `model: "Muse Wonder"` is set).
- Queue payloads still carry `model_hint` in only 7 rows of 5,743, non-null in 0.

So the per-pool / per-effort scorecard the meta-reviewer is charged with (model-up + effort-down vs model-down + effort-up; where max effort buys nothing over high) remains unrecordable for an eighth consecutive window — now because workers do not pass the fields, not because the fields do not exist.

## What is needed

- Lane / worker completion discipline: every `complete` call from a fleet session includes the telemetry fields from its own resolved route (pool, model, effort; cost_usd where the route exposes one, else null) — via `--telemetry` or the top level of `--result`. Recorded from the resolved session, never inferred from route names (meta-reviewer guideline 2026-10-27).
- The dispatcher record change from #1582 already landed in the dispatcher instruction; this issue is about the queue-completion side's adoption by the lane shifts / queue workers.
- Suggested check: the meta-reviewer's daily pull reports the share of completions carrying non-null pool+model+effort; adoption is real when that share is the large majority of fleet-session completions for a full window.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Worker/lane instructions (or the completion helper's defaults) make telemetry the default on `complete`, not an opt-in a worker must remember.
- [ ] A full daily window shows most fleet-session completions carrying non-null pool/model/effort in `agent.tasks.result`.
- [ ] Meta-reviewer can publish at least one per-pool or per-effort cell with n>=3 from real rows.

Filed by the pool meta-reviewer (code#1340), daily run 2026-11-03. Evidence: goal `hidden_files/meta-review/2026-11-03-evidence.md`.

code.title: impl(pm-stack): cost-anomaly detection to Needs-you via the alert throat (#1259 slice 4)
code.body:
Part of epic #1184; implementation follow-up of design issue #1259 (spend rollups). Design note: `doc/spend-rollups-design-1259.md`. Depends on the rollup-store slice of #1259.

## Scope
Detect cost anomalies from the spend rollups and surface them through the existing alert throat (`pm-stack/aggregator/src/alerts.ts`, #3676) into Needs-you (/attention) and the Today/brief summary — no new notification path.

## Anomaly classes (v1, thresholds are named constants with tests, per the design note)
- **Burn without progress:** an epic/project consumes spend in a window while closing zero child issues in the same window.
- **Single-session dominance:** one root session accounts for more than the threshold share of an epic's window spend.
- **Unattributed growth:** the unattributed share of total spend rises window-over-window beyond the threshold.
- **Charge without activity:** a matched PAYG charge for a service with no corresponding session/quota activity in its period.

## Rules
- Missing or partial data suppresses the anomaly, never fabricates it: an anomaly needs a complete window on both sides of its comparison.
- Each surfaced anomaly names its evidence: scope, window, the two compared values, and a link to the rollup/drill-down.
- Delivery class: page + ledger (warning) in v1; no push, per the alerts design (warnings never push in v1).

## Acceptance criteria
- One test per anomaly class: fires on the constructed pattern, silent on partial data, silent just below threshold.
- Dedupe: a continuing anomaly updates the existing incident (alert-throat dedupe), it does not re-post every tick.
- Anomaly constants live in one named place, so Drew's threshold rulings (open questions in the #1259 design note) change one file.

## Checks
- `bun test` and `bunx tsc --noEmit` in `pm-stack/aggregator` pass (CI on the PR).

code.title: Design: one name, one owner — a file's name is canonical, its archive namespace is reserved, and its archives belong to exactly one file (pkgs/id FileOps)
code.body:
## Design: one name, one owner — a file's name is canonical, its archive namespace is reserved, and its archives belong to exactly one file (pkgs/id FileOps)

Design doc: `files/designs/code-id-fileops-name-archive-ownership.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace. Grounded at origin/main `a8aa52dc`.

### Problem

A "file" in pkgs/id is a *name* (an iroh-blobs tag) plus metadata tags, and `FileOps` (`pkgs/id/src/fileops.rs`) is the single implementation every surface calls — built so the operations could not drift apart (module doc, fileops.rs:1-10). Inside that single implementation, three things about a name were never stated as one contract, on top of a five-fix history (#1612, #2462, #2856, #2862, #4574 — closed today) in which every archive defect was patched at the site that exposed it:

1. **What a name may be.** `validate_name` (fileops.rs:221) refuses empty/rooted/traversal names, but `put` stores a padded name verbatim while `validate_target` (:240) trims — padded twins that rename/copy can never target (#4102) — and the archive shape `<name>.archive.<digits>` that FileOps itself mints (`claim_archive_name`, :166) is not reserved, so a user file with that shape is classified as an archive, hard-deleted by deleting a *different* file, and can silently overwrite a genuine archive (#4720).
2. **What an archive reference is.** `archive.rename`/`archive.replace` values are ownership records: `delete` (:496) follows them and hard-deletes every archive they name. The codebase already knows they must not travel carelessly — `ARCHIVE_IDENTITY_TAG_KEYS` (:32-44) keeps them off an archive subject during `archive_existing`, because letting one travel "orphans every earlier archive from the live file's delete (#4574)".
3. **Who may own one.** That reasoning was never applied to `copy`: `FileOps::copy` (:443) duplicates *all* source metadata via `copy_all_tags` (:465) with no exclusions, so a copy becomes a second owner of the source's archives and deleting the copy hard-deletes the source's archived versions while the source still exists (#4761, probe-verified).

### The contract (recorded decisions)

- **Rule 1 — one canonical name.** Every entry point resolves names through the same validation, and a stored name is never padded: leading/trailing whitespace is **refused** with `InvalidName`, not trimmed (pinning #4102's open choice — trimming at the store silently renames a user's file; surfaces that want to be forgiving trim before calling, as the web handlers already do). `validate_target` stops trimming.
- **Rule 2 — the archive namespace is reserved at the writer.** `validate_name`/`validate_target` refuse any name where `is_archive_tag_name` (:155 — the readers' existing spelling, unsigned ASCII digits per #4329) is true, with a distinguishable error (pinning #4720's primary acceptance over its metadata-only alternative: the prefix scan and `classify_tag` are load-bearing readers, and reservation is one check at the one gate every surface funnels through). Non-numeric lookalikes (`a.archive.notes`) remain valid user files.
- **Rule 3 — archive references are ownership, and ownership moves only when the source name ceases to exist.** `archive_existing` keeps them off the archive and restores them to the live name (landed, #4574); `rename` moves them (source name gone — correct, unchanged); **`copy` excludes them** — the destination starts with no archive references except the `archive.replace` for a file the copy itself replaced (:480). The exclusion sits next to `ARCHIVE_IDENTITY_TAG_KEYS` so the next metadata-duplicating operation inherits the question, not the bug.

### Phases (adopted origins — no parallel issues filed)

- **Phase 1 = #4720** — reserved namespace at the writer.
- **Phase 2 = #4761** — copy owns nothing it did not archive (independent).
- **Phase 3 = #4102** — one canonical name: padding refused at FileOps, surface inventory for trim-at-the-surface (independent).
- **Phase 4 = closing audit (filed with this design)** — `classify_tag` spelling vs `is_archive_tag_name`; delete's two archive-collection paths agreeing; any other metadata-duplicating operation's disposition; the legacy archive-shaped user-file disposition; the contract statement in fileops.rs's module doc. Gated on Phases 1–3.

### Open questions (in the design doc, not phases)

Deleting an archive by its exact name (legitimate today, unfiled as misused); writer/reader agreement for archives of names containing `.archive.` in a non-numeric position (Phase 4 probes it); a first-class archive listing (feature, no consumer filed).

<!-- agent-note:v1 design-architect pass=42 -->

code.title: Design: read it bounded — one response-read contract for mcpx's outbound calls
code.body:
Design doc: `files/designs/code-mcpx-bounded-response-reads.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace. Audit at origin/main `f93e6dc5b` — every defect below re-verified present at the cited lines this pass (2026-11-02).

## Summary

mcpx reads responses from endpoints it does not control — third-party MCP servers, configured model providers, remote embeddings services — with no byte bound in four places. A client timeout bounds *duration*, never *bytes*: a fast endpoint can deliver gigabytes inside the timeout. Each filing re-derived the same missing rule in a different package:

- **Daemon chat-completions proxy** — `proxyToUpstream` (`internal/daemon/routes_proxy.go:244`) uses `http.DefaultClient` (no deadline at all) and streams the response through a `TeeReader` into an unbounded `bytes.Buffer` kept as the feedback record (#2114; implementation PR #3380 in flight).
- **MCP client non-JSON fallback** — `HTTPTransport.Send` (`internal/mcpclient/http.go:218`) does `io.ReadAll(resp.Body)` uncapped and pushes the result as one "message", while the non-2xx path in the same function caps at 4 KB (#4282).
- **Both OpenAI-compatible providers** — `internal/model/openai.go:123` and `internal/scripting/provider.go:121` buffer whole; on non-2xx the entire body is embedded in the error (#4354; probe: a 32 MiB error body produced a 33.5 MB error string). The `baseURL` is configuration (OpenAI, a company gateway, LiteLLM, Ollama, LM Studio).
- **A fifth instance is unfiled** — the remote embeddings client's error path (`internal/catalog/embeddings.go:101`) reads the body whole into its error. Phase 4 dispositions it.

The conforming embodiments already agree: error bodies are read via `io.LimitReader(resp.Body, defaults.HTTPErrorBodyLimit)` (4 KB, `upstream.errorBodyLimit`) in `mcpclient/http.go:167` and `sse.go:76,225,228`; the SSE reader has a max line size; every daemon *inbound* body is bounded by `http.MaxBytesReader` / named `defaults` limits. The inbound side has a contract; the outbound side has exceptions.

## The contract

> **Every byte mcpx reads from a peer it does not operate is bounded, and the bound's shape depends on what the bytes are for: an error body is an excerpt, a buffered success body is refused past its cap, a retained copy is truncated while the delivered stream is not, and every call carries a deadline as well as a byte bound — a timeout bounds duration, never bytes.**

Recorded decisions (full reasoning, alternatives and risks in the design doc):

1. **Error bodies are excerpts, everywhere, at the existing limit** — any non-2xx body embedded in an error/record/log is read at most `defaults.HTTPErrorBodyLimit` (4 KB). No new limit, no exceptions.
2. **A success body mcpx buffers whole is refused past its cap, never silently truncated** — read cap+1; over → error naming the surface and the cap (truncated JSON fails parsing with a misleading error). Caps are named `defaults.json` entries: model + scripting providers **16 MiB**; the mcpclient non-JSON fallback **1 MiB** (aligned with `http.bodyLimit`), pinning #4282's open choice to **refuse** — over the cap, `Send` errors and pushes nothing (a truncated non-JSON body would manufacture a partial "message" out of a body that is definitionally not a protocol message). Under the cap, hand-on-whole behaviour is unchanged.
3. **A retained copy is truncated; the delivered stream never is** — the proxy's feedback record is capped with the truncation visible in the record; the client receives the full response. PR #3380 (for #2114) already implements this shape and is adopted as the embodiment.
4. **Deadline and byte bound are both required** — providers, embeddings and mcpclient already carry client deadlines; the proxy's `proxy.timeout` (PR #3380) closes the exception. A future outbound site is conforming only when both are present.

## Phased breakdown

Phases adopt the three filed origins as sub-issues (no parallels); Phase 4 is a new closing-audit issue, gated on Phases 1–3.

- **Phase 1 — providers: success cap + error excerpt** (adopted: #4354). Lands the two provider implementations under decisions 1–2.
- **Phase 2 — mcpclient fallback: bounded, refuse past cap** (adopted: #4282). Independent of Phase 1.
- **Phase 3 — daemon proxy: deadline + retained-copy cap** (adopted: #2114). In flight as PR #3380; the phase completes when it merges or a superseding conforming change lands.
- **Phase 4 — closing inventory + contract statement** (new issue, gated on Phases 1–3): every `resp.Body` read / buffered copy in `pkgs/mcpx` dispositioned; required dispositions — the embeddings error read (`catalog/embeddings.go:101`, fix in audit if it stays one line), the `internal/cli/*` own-daemon reads (local-trust; name any whose endpoint is configurable beyond the local daemon), decoder-streamed success paths, and stdin/file reads (out of scope — not peer bytes). Contract statement lands in `internal/defaults/defaults.go` beside `HTTPErrorBodyLimit`.

## Open questions (in the design doc, not filed)

A per-message byte bound for the mcpclient JSON decoder path; the 16 MiB provider cap revisited on Phase 1's real completion sizes; a decoded-value (max-dimension) bound for embeddings — a schema contract, not a byte contract.

## Related

Design doc (full problem/evidence/alternatives/risks): `files/designs/code-mcpx-bounded-response-reads.md` (goal workspace). Origins: #2114, #4282, #4354. Neighbours, not this design: #2082 (closed — daemon *request* bodies), openchamber #1127 (the same contract stated for that repo's codebase), #3068 (parsed-shape validation — what a value's shape may be, not how many bytes may be read).

<!-- agent-note:v1 -->
Filed by the design architect (pass 38, 2026-11-02): design issue for the mcpx bounded response-read contract. The three origin issues are adopted as its phases — triage of each origin should record the phase structure and the decisions above rather than re-filing or re-scoping. Phase 4's closing audit is filed separately and gated on Phases 1–3.

## Acceptance criteria
- One bounded response-read contract for mcpx outbound calls is stated in the design and adopted: every byte read from a peer mcpx does not operate is bounded, with the bound's shape matched to the bytes' purpose.
- Each of the four named unbounded sites (daemon proxy `routes_proxy.go:244`, MCP client fallback `http.go:218`, both OpenAI-compatible providers, and the embeddings error path at `embeddings.go:101`) is dispositioned by a phase of this design — fixed under the contract or explicitly excepted with reasoning.
- The conforming embodiments (4 KB `HTTPErrorBodyLimit` error reads, SSE max line size, bounded inbound bodies) are named as the contract's reference implementations.
- Child/phase issues (including #4376 Phase 4) carry the implementation work; this design issue closes when the contract is adopted and all phases are filed/landed or excepted.

code.title: chore(deps): remove the awscli botocore/s3transfer pins once nixpkgs' awscli pairing is consistent again
code.body:
## Context

Found via #2715 (the 2026-10-30 nixpkgs update). `awscli` (home/common/default.nix, via the assigned pkgs from nixos/nixpkgs/default.nix) fails `pythonRuntimeDepsCheck` on the new pins:

```
Checking runtime dependencies for awscli-1.44.21-py3-none-any.whl
  - botocore==1.42.31 not satisfied by version 1.43.79
  - s3transfer<0.17.0,>=0.16.0 not satisfied by version 0.19.2
```

awscli 1.44.21 pins botocore exactly and s3transfer to the 0.16 line, but every current pin (master/unstable/stable/25 alike) ships botocore 1.43.79 and s3transfer 0.19.2 — the tree is mid-transition (libraries bumped, awscli not yet). The skew is in the raw sets too, not an artifact of this repo's overlays. awscli and botocore are developed in lockstep (awscli imports botocore internals), so relaxing awscli's pins (pythonRelaxDeps) risks shipping a subtly broken CLI; pinning the libraries back for awscli only is the conservative fix.

## The temporary fix

An overlay in `nixos/nixpkgs/default.nix` (next to the patchelf override) overrides `awscli` to use dedicated botocore 1.42.31 and s3transfer 0.16.0 derivations (the set's own expressions with version/source rolled back), leaving the set's botocore/s3transfer at their current versions for all other consumers (boto3 etc.).

## Removal condition

Remove once stock awscli passes `pythonRuntimeDepsCheck` on the assigned set's pin — i.e. upstream nixpkgs bumps awscli to a release whose botocore/s3transfer requirements match the tree (or restores the pairing some other way).

## Removal test

Delete the overlay; build `awscli` from the assigned pkgs plus `config.system.build.toplevel` for amd; both must succeed, and `aws --version` in the system profile should report the tree's awscli.

## Acceptance criteria

- The temporary awscli overlay in `nixos/nixpkgs/default.nix` (dedicated botocore 1.42.31 / s3transfer 0.16.0 derivations) is removed once stock awscli passes `pythonRuntimeDepsCheck` on the assigned set's pin.
- With the overlay deleted, `awscli` builds from the assigned pkgs and `config.system.build.toplevel` for amd builds successfully.
- `aws --version` in the system profile reports the tree's awscli version.

code.title: impl(pm-stack): move stateful services off the laptop and prove host failover
code.body:
## Why

The PM stack still depends on the laptop as the only runtime/data host. Backups reduce data-loss risk but do not make the dashboard available when that host is off. Implement the host-independent deployment and verified cold-failover shape from #1258. Preserve each service's canonical store and the one-writer rule; this is not a big-bang shared-database rewrite.

## Scope

- Move the aggregator, Kaneo/PostgreSQL, Grist, and Pad runtime to the approved cluster/alternate host as their canonical deployment; keep the laptop as an operator/development client.
- Keep aggregator-owned mutable data on the Supabase `muse-dev2` path defined by #3142/#941; retain service-owned Kaneo, Grist, and Pad stores in their approved persistent homes.
- Configure persistent storage, backup/restore integration, and health/freshness reporting so no unique record is held only in laptop-local JSON or Docker volumes. Coordinate with #1514 and #3869; do not duplicate their backup implementation.
- Keep the stable Cloudflare Access URL. Route it to the active host; store host credentials by name in Bitwarden/SOPS and do not commit plaintext secrets.
- Implement explicit single-writer fencing and a cold-restore runbook; do not add automatic multi-writer failover.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A documented deployment target and ownership map exists for aggregator, Kaneo, Grist, and Pad; each service has one named canonical data home and one active writer.
- [ ] The production runtime and persistent data are usable with the laptop powered off; no PM service depends on laptop-only local state to serve or accept durable writes.
- [ ] Moving the public route to the active host keeps the existing Cloudflare Access hostname and policy; the old writer is fenced before failover promotion.
- [ ] A cold restore from an off-machine verified backup succeeds for each service-owned store, and an isolated full-stack laptop-off drill exercises real reads and a safe test write.
- [ ] Measured RTO/RPO are recorded in `doc/pm-stack/restore-drills/YYYY-MM.md` and meet or explicitly revise the #1258 proposals (4h core RTO; 15m aggregator mutable state; 1h Kaneo/usage/link state; 24h Grist/Pad).
- [ ] Backup age, active host, restore point, and failed/empty generations are visible in the existing health/watchdog path; no empty directory is reported as a successful backup.
- [ ] Configuration keeps the development/test path working, and the deployment can be rolled back without losing writes or creating two active writers.

## Boundaries

- #3142 owns the phased aggregator schema migration; #941/#4642 own identity/provenance semantics. This issue consumes those contracts, not redesigns them.
- #1514 owns the application-database backup routine; #3869 owns silent empty-day/container-name failure handling.
- #1218 owns GitHub Project audit export. GitHub remains canonical for GitHub data.
- No secrets, copied production data, or raw private records in this repository or drill reports.

Parent: #1184. Design: #1258.

code.title: id: world lifecycle and migration — tombstone, verified export/import as new world (from #3397 Phase 4)
code.body:
World-specific implementation follow-on from the #3397 design (doc/2026-11-01_design_id3397.md, PR #3853), Phase 4 of its phased plan.

**Scope:** world lifecycle operations inside one partition and across partitions by lifecycle move only — durable idempotent tombstone/delete (fence world, revoke memberships/invites, remove name resolution; blob bytes reclaimed only by reference-safe partition-local GC); world migration as export under source authorization → import and verify as a **new world with a new ID** in the target partition → reissue memberships/invitations under target policy → switch explicit discovery → tombstone source. No live move, no dual-homing; source stays authoritative until verification succeeds; cleanup is a separate retention/reference step.

**Not this issue:** #3402 is verified account-store (user-store) transfer and cleanup — it does not implement world migration (per the #3397 doc, Phase 4/6 notes). Account migration's per-world guest/exit treatment is #3402/#3404 territory; this issue owns the world side.

**Authority boundary:** #3397 is design-only and is not an implementation authorization. Implementation ordering follows the doc: this phase depends on Phases 1–3 (#3399, the world routing/admission follow-on, and partition-local world blobs building on #3401).

**Acceptance:** negative tests from the #3397 doc's matrix pass for this slice — migration interrupted before verification leaves source authoritative, target non-serving, retry idempotent; stale writers fenced; deletion racing a live reference/import preserves the reference; name reuse after tombstone does not resurrect old IDs, memberships, invites, or blob references.

## Acceptance criteria

- Migration interrupted before verification leaves the source authoritative, the target non-serving, and a retry idempotent.
- Stale writers are fenced after tombstone/move; a deletion racing a live reference or import preserves the reference.
- Name reuse after tombstone does not resurrect old IDs, memberships, invites, or blob references.
- World migration is export → import-and-verify as a NEW world with a NEW ID → reissued memberships/invitations under target policy → discovery switch → source tombstone; no live move, no dual-homing.
- Dependencies hold: Phases 1–3 (code issues #3399, #3898, and partition-local world blobs on #3401) have landed.

code.title: id: partition-scoped world routing, names, and admission (from #3397 Phase 2)
code.body:
World-specific implementation follow-on from the #3397 design (doc/2026-11-01_design_id3397.md, PR #3853), Phase 2 of its phased plan.

**Scope:** partition-scoped world lookup `(jurisdiction, name)` with no cross-partition existence oracle; fail-closed admission guards for reads/writes/invites/WebSocket/background/admin operations against the world's stored jurisdiction; participant-list and membership-metadata authorization equal to world reads; shard/coordinator jurisdiction inheritance (creation rejects a different jurisdiction); the explicit guest-grant seam, **disabled** until Drew settles the guest-membership policy (open question 1 on #3397).

**Not this issue:** #3400 covers account/user-store routing and object entry guards — this issue is the world-specific routing/admission layer that #3400 does not fully represent (per the #3397 doc, Phase 2 note).

**Authority boundary:** #3397 is design-only and is not an implementation authorization. Implementation ordering follows the doc: this phase depends on Phase 0 (#3403 provisioning gate evidence via #2285) and Phase 1 (#3399 authoritative jurisdiction records), and on #3400's routing foundation.

**Acceptance:** negative tests from the #3397 doc's matrix pass for this slice — wrong-jurisdiction read/write/invite uniformly denied with no existence signal; foreign account with no/expired/revoked guest grant denied incl. participant metadata; same-name world in another partition indistinguishable from nonexistent; shard assignment naming a different jurisdiction rejected.

## Acceptance criteria

- Wrong-jurisdiction read/write/invite is uniformly denied with no existence signal (same-name world in another partition is indistinguishable from nonexistent).
- A foreign account with no, expired, or revoked guest grant is denied, including participant-list and membership metadata.
- Shard/coordinator creation naming a different jurisdiction than the world's stored jurisdiction is rejected.
- The guest-grant seam ships disabled until the guest-membership policy (open question 1 on code issue #3397) is settled.
- Dependencies hold: Phase 0 (#3403 via #2285) and Phase 1 (#3399) evidence has landed, and #3400's routing foundation is in place.

code.title: id: implement: journaled region-seam export/import
code.body:
Implements the accepted design from #2818. See the design note `doc/2026-11-01_design_id2818.md` and design PR #3875.

Build the journaled handoff for an application-owned entity crossing between spatial region shard-worlds. Use dedicated source/destination journal entries plus coordinator open/close records. The required local order is prepare/validate → persist typed record → apply in-memory state → acknowledge. Keep region journals independent; do not emulate a cross-region transaction or put entity payloads in the coordinator journal.

## Phased packets

1. **Journal/schema/checkpoint foundation** — typed handoff records, entity-addressed input, world journal version 3 bump/rollback compatibility, and compaction preservation for active handoffs, epochs, tombstones, and receipts.
2. **Program contract + source export/fence** — pure `prepare_entity_transfer` hook, region-sharded mode gate, complete bounded entity payload, persist-before-apply source record, and source-side stale-write rejection. No receipt until apply/replay succeeds.
3. **Destination import** — module/schema/digest validation, persist-before-apply import, idempotency by handoff ID, durable receipt only after apply/replay, and failure tests.
4. **Coordinator/recovery** — journal start and observed receipts, retry/reconcile after crashes, and region-map switch only after matching durable receipts and a durable completion record.
5. **Client/operations** — explicit transit/stuck status, fail-closed entity reads/writes while in transit, stale-route response, metrics/alerting, and feature-gated end-to-end acceptance.

Dependencies: 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5. Each packet is separately mergeable after its predecessor. Follow the design note's recommended defaults; the open questions for Drew are recorded there and do not block the protocol work.

## Acceptance

- No entity duplication or silent loss across any injected failure point.
- Source mutations are fenced at durable export; destination is routable only after completion.
- Exact retries are idempotent; conflicting imports fail closed.
- Actor crash between journal append and in-memory apply recovers by replay before returning a receipt.
- Coordinator and region restart/replay/compaction retain correct ownership and recovery state.
- No cross-region transaction, automatic rollback after export, or durable client write queue.

## Acceptance criteria

- All five phased packets land in dependency order (1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5), each separately merged after its predecessor — filed as code issues #3900 (phase 1), #3901 (phase 2), #3902 (phase 3), #3903 (phase 4), #3904 (phase 5).
- No entity duplication or silent loss across any injected failure point (crashes between prepare/persist/apply/acknowledge, coordinator restart, region-map switch).
- Source mutations are fenced at durable-record time; a receipt exists only after destination apply/replay succeeds.
- Region journals stay independent: no cross-region transaction emulation, no entity payloads in the coordinator journal.

code.title: supabase backups: staging uploads leak incomplete multipart uploads; staging never reconciled
code.body:
## Finding (R2 review, 2026-11-01)

The Supabase backup staging uploads (`supabase-backups` bucket, `pg/muse-dev/staging/` prefix, written by `supabase_backup.py` from the laptop) leak **incomplete multipart uploads** when an upload fails or is interrupted: the staging object is retried under a new key and the failed upload is never aborted.

Evidence: 6 orphaned multipart uploads found initiated 2026-10-26 → 2026-10-30 (2 with one 8 MiB part each uploaded, 4 with no parts — 16 MiB of stored parts total). All 6 were aborted during the 2026-11-01 review and the bucket verified back to 0 incomplete uploads. Separately, one *completed* staging object (`pg/muse-dev/staging/f4b085ed-….api.jsonl.zst`, 10.8 MB, 2026-10-27) was left behind in staging. It is **not** accounted for: its sha256 (`5d38249d…`, computed during the review) appears neither in `pg/muse-dev/manifest.json` nor as a final hash-named object, so it may be the only copy of that export — the review left it untouched. Staging is neither cleaned nor reconciled after a run.

The byte cost today is trivial; the defect is that failed runs accumulate invisible state in the bucket (multipart parts don't show in normal object listings) and the staging prefix silently diverges from "empty between runs".

## Ask

- In `supabase_backup.py`: abort the multipart upload on any failure path (S3 `AbortMultipartUpload`); on success, finalize the staging object (hash-name + manifest entry) or remove it — and reconcile the one already stranded (`f4b085ed-…`, sha256 `5d38249dd92d15b07beb039e4933125a1cee00b50bd4a1b0167e670555c154e1`): land it in the manifest if it is a real backup, since right now it is an unaccounted possible-only-copy.
- Independently, as a bucket-level backstop: add an R2 lifecycle rule on `supabase-backups` aborting incomplete multipart uploads after e.g. 7 days, so any writer's orphans self-clean.

## Acceptance criteria
- `supabase_backup.py` aborts its multipart upload (S3 `AbortMultipartUpload`) on every failure/interruption path, so a failed run leaves zero incomplete multipart uploads in `supabase-backups` (verified by listing incomplete uploads after a deliberately failed run).
- On success, the staging object is finalized (hash-named + manifest entry) or removed; the `pg/muse-dev/staging/` prefix is empty between runs.
- The stranded staging object `f4b085ed-…` (sha256 in the finding above) is reconciled: landed in the manifest if it is a real backup, or given a documented disposition — it is not deleted before that check, since it may be the only copy of that export.
- A bucket-level backstop exists: an R2 lifecycle rule on `supabase-backups` aborts incomplete multipart uploads after ~7 days, verified in the bucket configuration.

code.title: id: build: durable multiplayer note checkpoints and merges
code.body:
Parent: #2048 (ID Zettelkasten design). Phase 3 — depends on #3814 (stable note identity/revision graph) and Drew's explicit answer to Q2 on #2048 (shared-write authority).

Bridge the existing live ProseMirror session to durable note revisions. Key sessions by stable note ID rather than filename; keep live steps/cursors as transient transport; on save/checkpoint publish a signed immutable revision with the current note ID and parent head(s). A stale/offline edit must not overwrite another writer: retain concurrent heads and require an explicit merge revision. Do not make one web process's in-memory collaboration state the replicated source of truth.

Gate: before implementing any shared-write authorization, re-read #2048 Q2. Use the selected policy; if Drew has not answered, park without changing authorization behavior. Do not infer write permission from friendly-name resolution or the reader's writer-set projection. No cross-store resolver work (that remains #2259).

Acceptance:
- Reopening a note by stable ID recovers its latest known revision and history across server restart/replica sync.
- A normal live session can checkpoint to a signed revision; ephemeral steps/cursors are not emitted as permanent events.
- Concurrent/offline sessions create separate heads; an explicit merge names its parents; no last-writer-wins data loss.
- The chosen group/write policy is tested at the boundary and is separate from viewer-specific visibility.
- Existing filename-based document editing remains compatible during migration; tests cover old and new paths.

code.title: id(app): PoC — sticky notes + did-it tracker, the first ID app (Phase 3 of #2031)
code.body:
Phase 3 of the first ID app set tracked by issue #2031 — the proof of concept itself. Design record: the task 5727 triage comment on issue #2031.

Depends on (all three merged before dispatch; P0/P1/P2 are independent of each other and can land in parallel):

Dispatch note: the `pkgs/id/examples/` entries are Roc programs (`main.roc` + `build.sh` + `README.md`), and `pkgs/id/Cargo.toml` declares no `[[example]]` targets. Build, following the `pkgs/id/examples/` pattern:

Acceptance (the PoC bar from issue #2031):
- Integration test: identities A and B exchange notes and did-it events; A's view excludes third party C's claims; C's claims are retrievable on demand and render with author + not-counted status.
- The example README states it is a PoC and names the review-round gate: no permanent feature is built on this PoC without a review round.
- Does not gate on the still-open ID core design issue #2028.

code.title: id: implement fenced jurisdiction migration control plane
code.body:
Follow-up to #2283. Implement a resumable per-account jurisdiction migration state machine with pending target, durable migration ID, lease/fencing token, CAS routing epochs, maintenance, source freeze/drain and target activation. Never rely on directory state alone to fence stale writers.

Acceptance: all mutation paths including WebSockets, alarms, RPC and bridges honor the durable source fence; export waits for freeze acknowledgement; target is non-serving until switch; fault/concurrency tests cover ambiguous CAS, retries and stale epochs. Post-switch recovery is forward or a fresh reverse migration. Depends on directory, restricted routing and actual hosted write interfaces.

code.title: id: gate hosted jurisdiction provisioning on verified DO and R2 support
code.body:
Follow-up to #2283. Implement fail-closed hosted signup/deployment configuration validation for configured jurisdiction and its restricted Durable Object namespace and R2 bucket. Consume deployed-account evidence from #2285; do not duplicate that PoC or imply a probe proves vendor residency guarantees.

Acceptance: production cannot enable signup or migration with missing/unverified jurisdiction, unsupported runtime/types, or missing mismatched bucket; explicit diagnostics and configuration tests cover unavailable US and no unrestricted fallback. Coordinate with the design doc on the #2283 branch.

code.title: id: implement verified resumable user-store migration and safe cleanup
code.body:
Follow-up to #2283. Implement versioned export/import and migration orchestration after fenced control plane: preserve signed bytes and journal, manifest reachable blobs, copy across jurisdiction-specific buckets, verify content, hashes and signatures before CAS switch, then retain and clean source safely.

Acceptance: fault-injection tests cover interrupted copy/import, corruption, pre-switch abort, post-switch recovery and signature preservation; shared source blobs are never deleted without jurisdiction-local concurrency-safe reachability and retention proof; staging exercises one-account migration runbook. Depends on fenced migration and hosted storage interfaces; no cross-jurisdiction shared worlds (#2284).

code.title: id: isolate hosted blobs by jurisdiction and minimize shared directory
code.body:
Follow-up to #2283. Configure and validate a separate jurisdiction-bound R2 bucket per supported jurisdiction; choose from authoritative jurisdiction with no fallback. Keep content-addressed dedupe and garbage collection jurisdiction-local. Make shared D1 directory data-minimal and document its residency exception and limitations.

Acceptance: bucket routing/config tests reject missing or mismatched bindings and cross-jurisdiction use; directory schema allowlist excludes graph/private content; disclosure acknowledges pseudonymous data and other platform residency gaps. Depends on #2285 provisioning verification and hosted routing.

code.title: id: enforce restricted jurisdiction routing and object entry guards
code.body:
Follow-up to #2283. Implement the single jurisdiction-required user ID/stub routing module, confined raw binding, restricted namespace selection and fail-closed identity guard at all identity-touching entry points. Both unrestricted and legacy pre-2026-03-15 alarm undefined jurisdiction cases must be safe.

Acceptance: missing jurisdiction cannot create a second empty store; mismatch and missing context reject without side effects; tests cover all entry paths, alarms and raw binding bypass. Depends on directory signup and the hosted Durable Object interface; use #2285 for deployed PoC.

code.title: id: add immutable jurisdiction and migration metadata to hosted directory
code.body:
Follow-up to #2283. Implement jurisdiction-aware account directory/signup: atomic default policy creation before object derivation, unique subject mapping, validated jurisdiction, routing epoch and migration state, restricted mutation via guarded state transitions, and legacy inventory without silently relabelling existing stores.

Acceptance: duplicate signup preserves record; absent/invalid jurisdiction fails closed; profile updates cannot change jurisdiction; atomic transitions and concurrent signup have tests. Deployment depends on provisioning evidence #2285 and the #2283 design.

code.title: fleet infra: laptop /home at 100% (5.6M free) — cargo verification fails with os error 28
code.body:
**Fleet infra — laptop (amd-6) `/home` is 100% full; local build/test verification is broken.**

Evidence (2026-11-01 ~06:28Z, queue task 5073 shift, via `~/tools/laptop-ssh.sh`):
- `df -h /home/user`: `/dev/nvme0n1p2  3.3T  3.2T  5.6M  100% /home`
- `cargo test --lib petname` in a fleet worktree (`~/git/fleet/5073/pkgs/id`) failed across many crates with `No space left on device (os error 28)` writing to `target/debug/deps` — a disk failure, not a test failure. PR #3360 was merged on other verified evidence (Codex re-review clean); this issue is about the verification capability, not that PR.

Impact: every fleet lane that verifies on the laptop (the standing rule: builds/tests run on the laptop or CI, never the sandbox) can silently lose its local verification path; failures look like compile errors unless the os error 28 line is spotted.

Acceptance:
- Identify the top space consumers under /home (du report attached to this issue).

code.body:
Part of #1261, epic #1184. Extend #1739’s event contract for audit-grade integrity, provenance and recovery; do not duplicate its stream or writers. Coordinate identity with #1253 and session attribution with #2072; use #1258’s storage, backup and restore decisions rather than inventing a competing platform.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Versioned records include stable ID, actor and attribution confidence, action, object, event/ingest timestamps, source link and source identity; pre-SSO/unknown actors are explicitly marked, never asserted as authenticated.
- [ ] Audit records cannot be silently edited or deleted: authorized annotations/corrections are separate attributable records; integrity violations are detectable and tested.
- [ ] A durable retry/reconciliation path prevents silent loss when a nonblocking #1739 append fails; failures and gaps are visible. Retention/archive policy and limits are explicit and do not silently discard required audit history.
- [ ] Backup and restore of events and checkpoints is exercised against the storage and RPO/RTO decisions of #1258, with results and remaining loss visible.

code.title: Standard task: per-repo hygiene census + cleanup documentation (low priority)
code.body:
**Low priority — standing standard task + tracking.** Established 2026-10-31 from a measured fleet-wide repo hygiene census ordered by Drew.

## Source documents (sandbox workspace, `~/workspace/`)

- `repo-history-census-2026-10-31.md` — per-repo blob census of main-branch history: junk classes, packed/uncompressed sizes, fresh-clone simulations, rewrite verdicts
- `repo-inventory-2026-10-31.md` — full inventory: every repo across dezren39 + all member orgs, with commit counts and first/last commit dates

## Per-repo hygiene notes (filed 2026-10-31)

- dezren39/hatch-personal — https://github.com/dezren39/hatch-personal/issues/12
- dezren39/hatch — https://github.com/dezren39/hatch/issues/1
- developing-today/code — https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/3204
- developing-today/opencode — https://github.com/developing-today/opencode/issues/1101
- developing-today/openchamber — https://github.com/developing-today/openchamber/issues/1069
- dezren39/nix — https://github.com/dezren39/nix/issues/1265

## Fleet-wide findings

- **Scope:** 863 repos across 17 owners (dezren39 + 16 orgs); **825 repos have commits; 635 are forks.** Most fleet size is upstream history in forks, not our junk.
- **Fresh clones are already lean.** For the six repos deep-dived (blob-level census), fresh main-only clones run 10–449 MB, and GitHub's repo sizes track the measured main packs within ~±10% — there is no hidden server-side bloat. (An early reading suggesting ~1.9 GB of GitHub-side sprawl was a fabricated tool output, retracted in the census doc after two independent re-runs agreed with on-disk measurement.)
- **No history rewrites anywhere.** The best case in the fleet (hatch-personal) would save 55 MB packed; the costs — every clone/worktree invalidated (~150 sandbox worktrees plus laptop primaries), open PRs orphaned (code 53, opencode 15, openchamber 12, nix 6, re-measured 2026-10-31), all cited SHAs stale — exceed the saving everywhere. The two forks (opencode, openchamber) must **never** be rewritten: it would sever upstream sync permanently, and on public repos the old history survives in forks and PR refs regardless.
- **The only real saving is local-clone `git gc`** + stale-ref cleanup (e.g. hatch-personal local `.git` 1.6 GB vs a 183 MB repo; hatch local 1.5 GB vs 100 MB). **Deferred by Drew's choice** ("locally is fine for now", 2026-10-31) — no SHAs change when it eventually happens.
- **Tip hygiene beats history surgery.** hatch-personal PR #11 (2026-10-31) untracked 4,433 scratch entries and gitignored the scratch classes; code's tip is already clean except one 12.5 MB doc file. Keeping junk out going forward is the whole game.

## The recurring standard task

**Quarterly** (and ad hoc when triggered):

1. Re-run the repo inventory (all owners, commit counts + date ranges) and the blob census for the fleet's actively developed repos.
2. File or update a per-repo hygiene note (same title pattern: `Repo hygiene: history & tip cleanup notes (low priority, measured <date>)`) in any repo where:
   - the main-branch pack crosses **~250 MB**, or
   - junk classes (build outputs, binaries, logs, scratch/dump dirs, committed databases) appear **at the tip**, or
   - a repo's verdict changes (e.g. Roc artifacts in code confirmed accidental → untrack + gitignore at tip).
3. Update this issue with links to the new/updated per-repo notes and a one-line fleet summary.
4. **Never** rewrite history as part of this task — especially never on forks. Any proposed rewrite needs Drew's explicit per-repo approval with the blast radius spelled out.
5. Standing rules enforced by the census: gitignore scratch classes; no binaries/logs/build outputs at the tip; runtime state files live outside repos (`~/.local/state/`, pm-aggregator precedent) with summaries committed instead.

## Open items carried by the per-repo notes

- code: are `pkgs/roc` `libhost.a` / `.rh` / `dynhost` + `build` outputs intentional distribution artifacts? Is `doc/NanoPi` (12.5 MB, tip) a keeper?
- hatch-personal: relocate in-place state JSONs out of the repo? Optional local `git gc` (deferred by choice).
- nix: is `.lootbox/lootbox.db` (2.8 MB) intentional?
- opencode / openchamber / hatch: measured clean or upstream-owned; no open actions.

## Acceptance criteria

- The per-repo hygiene census is re-run on the stated cadence (quarterly, or sooner if a repo's main pack crosses ~250 MB or junk classes appear at the tip) and the census + inventory documents are refreshed.
- Every fleet repo's hygiene verdict (rewrite / never-rewrite / no action) stays on record in its per-repo notes issue, linked from this tracking issue.
- No history rewrite is performed under this task without a fresh measured case that beats the verdicts already recorded.

code.title: investigate(routing): uncensored fallback lane (Sable) for content-policy rejections — long-term topic
code.body:
Drew's directive (2026-10-31): long-term investigation topic — use "Sable uncensored" as the fallback when an API gives a rejection, instead of the request just failing.

This is an INVESTIGATION topic (long-term, staged), not an implementation order. Deliverable is findings + a recommendation; seating anything needs the findings first.

## Problem

Mainstream APIs reject some legitimate work on content-policy grounds — security research and reverse-engineering tooling are the standing fleet examples, alongside adult/creative and controversial-topic work. Today a rejected request simply fails (or worse, in some ecosystems, repeated edgy work puts the account itself at risk). The fleet has no sanctioned lane for work a provider refuses to touch.

## Candidate: "Sable uncensored" — identity UNVERIFIED at filing

First-pass check on 2026-10-31 found NO model or provider named "Sable" in the models.dev / OpenRouter / OpenCode catalogs, and no clear web hit for an uncensored model by that name. Possibilities: a brand-new or niche service, a model id on a specific aggregator, or a dictation artifact for a sound-alike name.

**Deliverable 1 is a positive identification**: provider, model id, endpoint, context window, pricing, tool-calling support, data/retention terms — or a documented finding that no such service exists, with the closest alternatives ranked instead. Alternatives in scope for that ranking (verify, don't assume): Venice AI uncensored models, Cognitive Computations Dolphin builds, hosted abliterated open-weight builds (e.g. UnboundModels' Qwen3.8-27B uncensored), other OpenAI-compatible low-refusal APIs, and self-hosting an abliterated/Dolphin build on fleet hardware.

## Questions the investigation must answer

1. Identity & viability: what is Sable, who runs it, is it still operating, what does it actually serve (weights/build, context window, max output)?
2. Agent fitness: tool calling, structured output, reasoning quality — can it finish real agent work mid-session, or only single-turn text? At what context size?
3. Trigger design: how does the router know a rejection was censorship (error-class shapes per provider)? The companion opencode issue (cross-linked below) covers the other half — censor rejections must never poison route health. This topic covers what the rejected REQUEST does next: fail over to the uncensored lane for that request only.
4. Scope discipline: the uncensored lane is a rejection-triggered special route, NOT a general pool member and never a default. Roles state requirements (Decision 008); this lane's requirement is "the seated models refused this request on content-policy grounds".
5. Privacy & trust: what work may be sent to a niche provider (data terms, retention, training)? Some censored work is censored precisely because it is sensitive.
6. Cost & limits: pricing, rate limits, and whether a free tier exists (relates to the 2026-10-31 free-models investigation: InferX / OpenCode free / alternatives).
7. Bounds: lawful work only; the lane exists for provider over-refusal on legitimate tasks, documented as such.

## Acceptance criteria

- Findings doc: Sable identified or ruled out with evidence; alternatives compared in a table (context, price, tool calls, data terms, quality notes).
- Recommendation: seat / decline / self-host, with reasons, difficulty, and performance considerations.
- If seat: a design sketch for the rejection-triggered route (trigger classification, per-request failover, telemetry) linked to the companion opencode issue — as a follow-up implementation issue, not built from this one.

Companion: developing-today/opencode issue "content-policy (censor) rejections must not count toward model removal, demotion, or disable in routes" (filed 2026-10-31).

code.title: Long-term: migrate the pm stack into Supabase — refactor component state into schemas for central management
code.body:
## Long-term tracker: migrate the pm stack into Supabase and refactor its parts into schemas for central management

Drew asked for this as the long-term tracking issue (2026-10-31). The pm stack (aggregator, fleet feed, dashboard, orchestration, dispatch, usage hub) grew up as local files and laptop-local stores. The direction, proven piece by piece on 2026-10-31, is: state lives in Supabase (muse-dev2) in domain-appropriate schemas, components read/write the database, and local files become caches or exports — never the only copy.

### Where things stand (verified 2026-10-31)
Already Supabase-backed:
- Repo-queue backend (recovered onto muse-dev2 in the 2026-10-30 cutover; see #2767/#2768).
- Session mirror (agent schema mirror tables).
- Usage snapshots / usage hub collectors (#1050, #1111).
- Domain event streams: ainventory, engineering, finance, research, automation, home — tasks append typed events; orchestration-pass began appending material changes to automation.events on 2026-10-31.

Still local-only:
- Orchestrator working state: orchestration.json / orchestrator-state.json / orchestrator-log.md (goal workspace hidden_files) — the dashboard reads these files.
- Aggregator actions store + comments store (laptop-local) — Drew's dashboard triage actions and comments.
- Fleet-feed JSON pipeline (collector -> scp -> laptop aggregator serving JSON files).
- Backlog markdown files the orchestrator reads (backlog-*.md in the goal workspace).

### Scope (phased, each phase its own implementation issue)
1. Orchestration state: move tier/classification state + run log to Supabase tables (automation schema or a dedicated pm schema); orchestration.json becomes a generated export for the dashboard contract (#898 shape preserved).
2. Aggregator stores: actions + comments into Supabase with the same apply/result semantics (#1152/#1154/#1156 contracts preserved); the laptop aggregator reads/writes the DB.
3. Feed pipeline: fleet-feed snapshots land as DB rows first; the served JSON is derived, not transported.
4. Backlogs/queues: backlog state derived from DB + GitHub instead of hand-maintained markdown (markdown becomes a view).
5. Central management: one schema map (pm-stack/SHARED-SCHEMA-MAP.md, with the migration plan at pm-stack/SHARED-SCHEMA-MIGRATION-PLAN.md), one place to inspect/pause/repair every component's state.

### Non-goals / constraints
- No big-bang rewrite: each phase keeps the current file-based path working until the DB path is verified, then flips.
- Dashboard contracts (#898 orchestration shape, actions/comments semantics) do not change shape — only their backing store.
- Single-writer rules stay: orchestrator is the only writer to the GitHub Project; the same discipline applies per table.
- Secrets by name only; muse-dev2 is canonical (old muse-dev is dead; pointer audit tracked in #2796).

Related: #2767, #2768, #2796, #898, #899, #910, #2155.

### Phase implementation issues (filed 2026-11-03, task 8438):
- Phase 1 (orchestration state): #5005
- Phase 2 (aggregator stores / shared tables): #1744 (pilot area #941)
- Phase 3 (feed pipeline DB-first): #5006
- Phase 4 (backlogs as a view): #5007
- Phase 5 (central management surface): #5008

code.title: atlas: provenance registry (chunk occurrences), content-addressed extracts, multi-DB vector resolution
code.body:
## Direction (Drew, 2026-10-31)

Atlas moves from a single canonical DB + one Turso publish to provenance-first, scalable infrastructure. Design doc: hatch-personal `workspace/turso-atlas/docs/atlas-provenance-and-scale-design-2026-10-31.md`.

Rules:
1. Keep ALL data — nothing stripped from atlas.db or publishes to save space; only byte-identical dupes are cleaned, backups kept.
2. Backups AND plain extracts for every corpus.
3. Every chunk records EVERY place it was found: `chunk_occurrences` (chunk → array of source locators with spans, observed_at). Today dedup silently drops occurrences (~127K at first ingest); 6,344 canonical sessions own zero chunks for exactly this reason and their occurrences are unrecorded.
4. Every import is interned content-addressed (laptop extracts CAS / R2, registry maps CA hash → normal paths) or pinned as `repo@commit:path`. Registry also holds line numbers / dates / spans for extracts.
5. Retrieval: vector/FTS search across multiple Turso shard DBs (collection × month) returns IDs; a catalog/registry resolves an ID to a file, a chunk, or a start–end section — including a member of a tar in R2 (sidecar index, range fetch) or a local file.

Verified state feeding this (2026-10-31): canonical 18,325 sessions / 122,124 messages / 107,639 chunks; local-only = 6,941 chunks of personal-client TEXT held back from Turso by policy (not missing embeddings); Turso atlas 1.0 GB / 100,698 chunks; laptop ~/atlas 12 GB contains NO consequential byte-identical duplicates (hash-verified) — it is distinct versions/working sets, so no cleanup windfall exists.

## Phases
1. Add `chunk_occurrences` + `cas_registry` to canonical atlas.db; ingest writes occurrences from now on (no re-embed, no republish).
2. Laptop extracts dir + CAS; atlas-backup covers it; backfill extracts for sources still on disk.
3. Occurrence backfill from CAS extracts; document the local-only publish predicate in the publish script.
4. Catalog DB + shard layout at next publish growth (or full message-archive ingest); resolution as MCP tools (search → ids → resolve → fetch span).

<!-- agent-note:v1 agent=muse state=filed source=main-chat-2026-10-31 -->

## Acceptance criteria

- A `chunk_occurrences` provenance registry exists: every chunk records every source locator it was found at (with spans and observed_at), including occurrences previously dropped by dedup.
- Backups AND plain extracts exist for every corpus; imports are interned content-addressed (CAS hash → path registry) or pinned as `repo@commit:path`, with line numbers / dates / spans recorded for extracts.
- Retrieval works across multiple Turso shard DBs (collection × month): vector/FTS search returns IDs and the catalog/registry resolves an ID to a file, chunk, or start–end section (including a tar member in R2 via sidecar index + range fetch, or a local file).
- No data is stripped to save space; only byte-identical duplicates are cleaned, with backups kept.

code.title: Design: reconstruction is admission — validate authority-bearing inputs where they are rebuilt (pkgs/id)
code.body:
**Design (design-architect pass 23): reconstruction is admission — validate authority-bearing inputs where they are rebuilt.**

Design doc: `files/designs/code-id-reconstruction-validation.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace. Audited against origin/main `206f4fd7`.

## Summary

Six issues filed independently in one evening are one defect with six addresses: in `pkgs/id`, data that carries authority is validated when it is created live, and trusted when it is reconstructed — a world journal being restored, an attestation being computed from decoded objects, a manifest being parsed, a schedule cap being checked. The live path enforces invariants (only issued, JOIN-holding participants act; claims answer the agreement they name; a manifest step means what it says); the reconstruction paths enforce almost none of them, so a crafted or corrupted artefact acquires authority the live path would never have granted.

**The recorded rule:** reconstruction is admission. Anywhere `pkgs/id` rebuilds authority-bearing state from stored or supplied data, the rebuilding code validates the same invariants the live path enforces at creation, and refuses (never partially applies, never silently repairs) data that violates them. Corollaries: validate against state you hold, not claims the input makes; unnamed means refused (scope bits, manifest keys, outcomes); the system shape (sequence 0 / participant 0) is not borrowable by authority-carrying entries.

## Evidence (origin/main 206f4fd7)

- `pkgs/id/src/world/core.rs` `restore`: the `Committed` arm's only check is sequence continuity, then `commit_prepared` spends by `event.participant_id` with no record lookup (#2894); the `Checkpoint` arm validates ordering/schedules but no author; the `Issued` arm validates digest/parent/expiry/uses but never scopes — unnamed bits and CHAT/INPUT without JOIN restore clean (#2890). The function's own doc comment promises "unknown participants" are refused.
- The live invariants exist: issuance requires JOIN (`core.rs` issuance path, `scopes.contains(WorldScopes::JOIN)`), delegation subsets keep JOIN (`world/mod.rs` `WorldScopes`), admission runs `authorize(token, required)` per act. Restore consults none of it.
- `pkgs/id/src/attestation.rs` `compute_state`: signatures (verified by `chain::decode`) prove who signed, not that the agreement is well-formed — `players = [A, A]` computes `Agreed` from one key (#2863), and a claim's free-form `winner` naming a third party computes `Agreed` (#2868).
- `check_schedule_replacing` trusts a caller-supplied `replacing: bool` for the pending-schedule cap restore enforces — a mismatched flag admits a 65th pending schedule and underflows on an empty map (#2882). The ground truth is in `self.schedules`.
- `pkgs/id/src/world_manifest.rs`: serde with defaults, no `deny_unknown_fields` — a typo'd grants/ceiling revocation parses clean, plans zero steps, diff says "no drift" (#2876).
- Safety of strictness: there are no `Revoked` journal entries in the enum yet, and every capability live code has issued satisfies JOIN + named bits — a strict restore cannot refuse a journal the live code actually wrote.

## Phases (adopted origins — no parallel issues filed)

- **Phase 1 — journal restore validates authors and scopes.** #2894 (Committed + Checkpoint author check: author issued, holding the scope its kind requires) + #2890 (Issued scope check: named bits only, JOIN required). One seam, the security core. Independent.
- **Phase 2 — attestation agreement validity.** #2863 (players must be distinct, else `Proposed`) + #2868 (claim outcome domain: winner is `None` or one of the two players; out-of-domain claims ignored under the existing non-player rule). Independent of Phase 1.
- **Phase 3 — derive-don't-trust + closing audit.** #2882 (schedule predicate derived from `self.schedules`; trusted parameter removed) + #2876 (`deny_unknown_fields` on the manifest's authority-bearing structs) + a closing inventory audit of the remaining reconstruction seams (sandbox snapshot restore, `world_store` restore_program, directory/petname persistence), each dispositioned already-validating / fixed / exempt-with-reason, and the rule written into the restore and attestation module docs.

## Alternatives considered

- Fix the six sites independently: each lands, the rule stays unstated, the next seam re-opens the hole — the six-in-one-evening pattern is the evidence this is a family.
- Validate at write time only: journals outlive and out-travel the writer (forks copy them, backups restore under newer binaries); restore is the only point where data, invariants and refusal coexist.
- Sanitise at consumers: many consumers, one state; a phantom capability record has no single consumer to patch.
- Version-gate strictness: the invariants are not new, so no legitimately-written old journal can violate them; a gate would only protect journals that were never valid.

## Risks / open questions

- Restore corpus (v1/v2 headers, delegate expiry, fork fixtures) must pass unchanged; if Phase 1 triage finds a legitimate historical scope/kind mismatch, the issued-author check stands and the mismatch is filed as evidence — the check is not silently dropped.
- Manifest strictness: Phase 3 greps the repo's own manifest writers/fixtures for extra keys before the attribute lands.
- Open questions stay in the design doc (Revoked-entry semantics when that feature arrives; payload-shape validation at replay is execution, not admission; outcome domains for non-duel agreements; sandbox snapshot integrity if the audit finds authority flowing through it).

Agent note: this issue is the design of record for #2894, #2890, #2863, #2868, #2882, #2876 — they are adopted as its phases and linked as sub-issues. Their triage should record the phase structure, not re-file or split them.

## Acceptance criteria

- Every authority-bearing reconstruction path in `pkgs/id` named by this design (journal restore, attestation computation, manifest parsing, schedule checks) validates the same invariants its live creation path enforces, and refuses — never partially applies, never silently repairs — violating input.
- Each of the six filed instances (#2894, #2890, and the siblings named in the design doc) is either fixed under this contract or explicitly dispositioned against it.
- Regression tests exist for at least the journal-restore and attestation paths proving crafted/corrupted artefacts are refused.
- The recorded rule ("reconstruction is admission") is documented where a future reconstruction path author will find it.

code.title: fleet: laptop SSH unreachable again 2026-10-30 — MaxStartups drops blocking conductor + lanes (recurrence of #1667)
openclaw: gateway home module applies to all hosts but sops secrets are amd-only — audit/scope the Intel host
code.body:
## Problem

`home/openclaw` is imported unconditionally for `user` on every host that includes `nixos/users/user` (`home/user/default.nix:21-22`), so the openclaw-gateway user service is defined on both Framework hosts. But the sops-nix provisioning for its tokens (`nixos/hosts/amd-openclaw-secrets.nix`, landed by the #1558 fix) is imported only on `amd`, and the wrapper paths now point at `/run/secrets/openclaw/*`.

Surfaced by: Codex review finding (P2) on PR #2871, dispositioned there with the evidence below.

## Why it can't be fixed by just importing the module on `nixos`

- `secrets/sops/common/bws.yaml` has exactly one age recipient (`age125ac…`, `.sops.yaml` anchor `&laptop-framework`). Host sops keys derive from each host's SSH host key (`nixos/sops/default.nix`), so the Intel host cannot decrypt the file; importing the module there would fail its activation.
- `.sops.yaml` already TODOs this: "separate keys for other hosts, don't share allow all hosts to decrypt certain secrets".

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Determine whether the `nixos` (Intel) host actually runs the OpenClaw gateway (service state, whether `~/.secrets/openclaw/*` was ever provisioned there).

code.title: id: design: native-spill write lease protocol for hot worlds (from #2059)
code.body:
## From the #2059 investigation (hot-world sharding)

The landed investigation doc for #2059 (`doc/2026-10-30T19-35-00Z_investigation_hot_world_sharding/`, §3 rung 3) designs native-node spill for an indivisible hot world: a native `id` node runs the world's program turns while the hosted Durable Object keeps the journal of record. The doc is explicit that **the journaled single-writer lease is the whole safety design** — split-brain (DO and native node both accepting writes) is the catastrophic failure. The lease protocol itself was not designed. This issue designs it, so the #2046 synthesis adopts a designed protocol instead of a placeholder.

## Design to produce

- **Lease object**: grant/revoke/handoff as journaled entries — who grants (DO? coordinator? operator?), lease term and renewal, and how the grant is recorded so both sides and any auditor can prove who held the write lease at any journal position.
- **Fencing**: how a partitioned or crashed ex-holder is fenced out (monotonic lease epoch checked on journal append is the obvious shape — verify or replace), and what happens to writes an ex-holder attempts after losing the lease.
- **Handoff both ways**: DO → native at spill start, native → DO at de-escalation (investigation §2: spill ends when the warning band clears for ~1 hour), including in-flight command treatment at the boundary.
- **Failure walkthroughs**: native node crashes holding the lease; DO and node partitioned while both alive; lease expires mid-turn; journal mirror lag at handoff.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Design recorded in a doc under `doc/` and linked from this issue
- [ ] Lease grant/revoke/handoff specified precisely enough to implement against `pkgs/id/src/world/`'s journaled-entry patterns
- [ ] Split-brain impossibility argued from the protocol mechanics, not asserted
- [ ] Anything buildable that falls out is filed as its own issue(s)

---
Program: ID platform expansion, epic #2056. Parent investigation: #2059. Consumer: #2046 (serverless edition v1 synthesis).

code.title: fleet(pools): enforce monthly pace guards at seating time — steward hard stops are currently advisory and were burned through (cline-pass + both Go monthlies walled)
code.body:
## Problem

The pool steward's monthly pace guards are advisory notes, and lane/dispatcher seatings can — and did — burn straight through them:

- **cline-pass**: steward issued a hard stop at monthly 97% (ledger 2026-10-29T13:22Z, after a 93%→97% jump). Lane seatings at 08:40 and 09:40 CDT landed *after* the stop, and the decisive 16:40 / 17:00 CDT seatings burned the last ~2pp — cline-pass monthly **walled at 100%** (ledger 2026-10-29T22:27Z), ~7 days before its Nov 5 reset. Daily-pass verdict (2026-10-30T05:24Z): "BACKFIRED for the guard, HELD for the wall."
- **opencode-go**: Flash finishing-only + a >1pp/h pace guard failed on both workspaces — Lab monthly 87.17%→100% and Personal →100% by 2026-10-30T07:24Z, days before the Nov 2 / Nov 6 resets. Daily-pass verdict: pace guard FAILED.
- By contrast, once a pool is at a **known 100%**, the closed-pool rule held perfectly: cline-pass exactly flat for 13 consecutive steward intervals, Go for 4 — because at 100% the rule is binary and seatings actually stop.

The asymmetry is the finding: a binary closed rule is enforced; a percentage/pace guard is not, because nothing checks it at seating time.

## Proposal

Enforce monthly guards at seating time, in the dispatcher and lane-shift paths (not in steward notes):

1. Before seating a session on a pool whose monthly window is ≥97% (or whose trailing pace is >1pp/h toward a wall before reset), the seating path reads the pool's current monthly % from the quota hub (`quota-current.json`, ≤60 min old per the existing measurement gate) and refuses / reroutes the seating, logging the refusal with the % read.
2. A steward hard-stop note for a pool is recorded in a machine-readable place the seating paths check (e.g. the dispatcher log note is not sufficient — it was issued and ignored twice in one day).
3. Refusals surface in the dispatcher log as their own line (pool, %, guard source) so the meta-reviewer can score guard compliance from data, not from quota archaeology after a wall.

## Acceptance

- A seating attempt against a ≥97%-monthly pool is refused or rerouted and logged, demonstrable on the next pool that approaches its monthly wall.
- Steward daily pass can cite refusal counts instead of reconstructing post-hoc seatings.
- No change to the POOL MAP itself: pools still run to 100% and close at a known 100%; this only gives the pre-wall guard the same enforcement the closed rule already has.

Filed by the pool meta-reviewer (issue #1340 daily run, 2026-10-30) per the reviewer-guidelines rule that a guideline which should become a hard rule is filed as an issue instead of silently hardening. Evidence: `hidden_files/pool-change-ledger.md` events 2026-10-29T13:22Z / 22:27Z, 2026-10-30T05:24Z (daily pass) / 07:24Z; meta-review `hidden_files/meta-review/2026-10-30-evidence.md`.

code.title: id: implement grant lifecycle per #2254 spec — registry, pending holds, attestations, clawback/debt, revocation policy
code.body:

1. **Fingerprint registry + registration flow (spec §2)** — canonicalisation + domain-separated SHA-256 fingerprint, `grant_keys` table (primary key enforces one grant per key), Presented → Rejected/PendingHold flow, publisher-revocation batch intake. Lands first with §1: together they close #2042 abuse case 1.
2. **PendingHold lifecycle (§1)** — TigerBeetle pending transfer at registration, window config per grant source snapshotted onto the grant record, idempotent post sweep, void flow, timeout re-issuance fail-safe.
3. **Attestation intake (§3)** — service-signed external-event records (refund / chargeback / publisher revocation), authenticated source intake, `(source, external_ref)` idempotency, transition dispatch.
