code.title: mcpx: e2e and settings suites cannot run in the nix build sandbox (checkPhase exclusions)
code.body:
On 2026-10-30, three NixOS switch attempts in a row died inside the mcpx derivation's checkPhase:

1. **internal/e2e burns its whole 30m timeout in the sandbox.** The suite spawns real script subprocess trees; the build sandbox has no init reaping them, so they pile up as zombies (~3,800 observed, process table degraded) and the package runs to the `go test -timeout 30m` cap: `FAIL github.com/dezren39/mcpx/internal/e2e 1800.385s`.
2. **internal/settings env tests fail in the builder environment.** `TestNoUndeclaredEnvRead` and `TestTheScriptEnvironmentIsWhatTheCodeSets` assert the process environment is exactly what the code sets; the stdenv builder env makes that untrue inside the sandbox.

Interim fix (the mechanism package.nix itself provides): both packages are in `checkExclude` in pkgs/mcpx/package.nix with the reasons recorded there. The full suite still runs in CI on main.

To restore sandbox checks:
- e2e: bound and reap spawned subprocess trees when running under a non-init supervisor, or split the process-spawning cases behind a sandbox capability check.
- settings: scope the environment assertions to the variables mcpx itself controls, ignoring builder-provided vars.

## Acceptance criteria

- mcpx `internal/e2e` and `internal/settings` are removed from `checkExclude` in `pkgs/mcpx/package.nix` (or any remaining exclusion is narrowed and re-justified in place).
- The e2e suite's spawned subprocess trees are bounded/reaped under a non-init supervisor, so the suite no longer burns its 30m timeout in the nix build sandbox.
- The settings env assertions scope to the variables mcpx itself controls, so they pass in the stdenv builder environment.
- The full suite still runs in CI on main (unchanged).

code.title: unify(quota-plane): one quota read path — server endpoint, CLI, and aggregator gatherer must share the direct credential-store read
code.body:
Leg of epic #1149 (quota-plane Stage 2). Filed at Drew's direction, 2026-10-29: *"there was supposed to be a unification in the 3 quota read methods."* There wasn't — three independent quota readers exist today, they resolve credentials three different ways, and they disagree. This issue is the unification leg of #1149; it cross-links the legs it absorbs or depends on rather than replacing them.

## The three readers

1. **OpenChamber web server `/api/quota/*`** — resolves credentials through the running OpenCode server's `GET /api/credential` projection (openchamber `server/index.js:1647`; projection `server/lib/opencode/auth.js:91, 203-230`, active rows only).
2. **`openchamber quota` CLI** — server-first, with a direct credential-store fallback (`openCodeLocalCredentialSource`, reading `opencode.db` read-only). Built 2026-10-27 under #1251, which deliberately switches to the store ONLY on transport failure and stamps each row `credentialSource: server|local`.
3. **PM-stack aggregator gatherer** (`pm-stack/aggregator/scripts/gather-quota.ts:10-19, 116-149`) — reads `opencode.db` **directly, by design**, because the server-API path is known to diverge (#1251), replicates the server's projection itself, and additionally ingests bespoke per-provider file exporters (Meta: `pm-stack/meta-exporter/meta-quota-export.mjs`). Writes `quota-current.json` on a ~15-minute systemd tick.

## Divergence evidence (2026-10-29, same evening, same pools)

- **Antigravity:** the hub (reader 3) reads the pool fine — state ok, Gemini weekly 4%, Claude weekly 57% @ 2026-10-30T00:15Z. Reader 1 returns `{"ok":false,"configured":false,"error":"Not configured"}`. Root cause, pinned in developing-today/openchamber#858: the server credential projection drops the refresh token that openchamber's antigravity resolver requires (`providers/antigravity/auth.js:69-94`), while the sibling google provider accepts the same entry with an access token alone — google answered `ok:true` on the same server in the same pull. Compounding: the resolver swallows credential-store errors (`providers/antigravity/index.js:36-38`), so a failed read is indistinguishable from "no login exists."
- **Meta:** the route is verified healthy (opencode#818 closed/completed), but reader 3's private exporter has failed every tick since its last ok tick at 2026-10-29T16:15Z with `subscription-quota: field windowReset not a finite number` — one null reset from an inactive window fail-closes the whole export (diagnosed on #1301). The hub's file-export entry reads "unparseable" and its openchamber meta entry carries null percentages on both windows: a primary pool unreadable for 8+ consecutive steward runs.
- **OpenDesign:** absent from the hub entirely until its provider deployed to the laptop instance (developing-today/openchamber#536; deploy landed 2026-10-29, credential import still owed).

Meanwhile #2135 unified only the **consumers** — the steward went snapshot-first onto `quota-current.json` — but the dispatcher still live-probes reader 1, so consumers still disagree about the same pool at the same moment.

## Why it matters

The fleet measurement gate forbids placement on a pool without a fresh read ≤60 min old. Every reader disagreement therefore closes a **primary** pool: Antigravity is the Gemini Flash pool's ONLY source and carries the Claude seats' clean read; Meta is a primary pool. The cost is burn-by-expiry — Antigravity's weekly (4% used on the Gemini tiers) resets Sat Oct 31 8:11 AM CDT largely unspent while OpenCode Go's monthly sits at ~96%. Three readers also means three places for the same bug family to recur (cf. the exporter's sibling defects #2460/#2461/#2470).

## Proposed target state

One canonical read module: the **direct credential-store read** (the semantics reader 3 already implements and reader 2 falls back to) plus the shared provider fetchers, consumed by:

- the OpenChamber server endpoint (no more server-projection-only resolution),
- the CLI (no server-first/store-fallback split — one path, one provenance),
- the gatherer, which keeps its 15-minute tick and file-export ingestion but imports the same read module instead of carrying its own projection logic.

Exception providers fold into the same path where their integration plans allow (#1167/#1301 for Meta, #1169 for Google/Antigravity — this issue absorbs #1169's read-path half; the login/token-capture half stays with #1169). Per-provider error states stay **distinct** end-to-end: `not-configured` vs `store-read-failure` vs `provider-error` are different facts and must never collapse into one another.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] All three surfaces (server endpoint, CLI, gatherer/hub) return identical windows for the same pool in the same tick, demonstrated on Antigravity, Meta, and one ordinary pool (e.g. ClinePass or OpenCode Go).
- [ ] No surface can report `not-configured` for a credential the direct store read resolves.
- [ ] Dispatcher, steward, babysitter, and the /quota UI consume one source with identical semantics (the #2135 snapshot-first rule extends to the dispatcher's gate).
- [ ] A credential-store read failure surfaces as its own error state on every surface, distinct from `not-configured` (the #858 resolver swallow is gone or subsumed).
- [ ] The Meta exporter path either folds into the shared module or its parser contract is enforced by the same validation the shared path uses — a single bad field can no longer poison a whole pool's export.

## Related

- Epic: #1149 (this issue is its read-path unification leg)
- #1251 — quota-plane resilience; origin of the known server-vs-store divergence and the CLI fallback
- #1169 — Google/Antigravity exception integration (read-path half absorbed here by reference; token capture stays there)
- #1167 + #1301 — Meta exception integration + exporter (fix expedited 2026-10-29 at priority 90; its parser fix is a down payment on the last acceptance criterion, not a substitute for this issue)
- #1331 — gatherer per-pool row split (the gatherer's row shape this unification must preserve)
- developing-today/openchamber#858 — the endpoint symptom (Antigravity "Not configured")
- developing-today/openchamber#536 — OpenDesign deploy/import state

code.title: id: guardian social recovery — threshold approvals + delayed, cancellable key rotation
code.body:
Follow-up from the key-recovery investigation on #2060 (doc: `investigations/key-recovery.md`, §5/§7). Parent epic: #2056. Depends on the keyset/authorization-log follow-up from #2060.

## Problem
Users who lose all devices and any backup still need a last-resort recovery that is not custodial. The investigation recommends threshold guardian *authorization* (not Shamir key-splitting — rejected in the doc: share-holders become custodians of key material).

## Proposal
- User names n guardians (existing ID contacts) + threshold m; the set is a keyset record.
- Recovery: a new keypair publishes a recovery request (directory layer); m guardians sign approvals; the assembled rotation record installs the new key after a **delay window** during which the old key can cancel with one signature and all devices/bindings are notified.
- Adding a guardian is instant; removing one is itself delayed (anti-evict-then-attack).

## Acceptance
- [ ] Guardian set record + approval/rotation record formats specified against the keyset log.
- [ ] Delay + cancel + notify flow implemented with tests, including the guardian-eviction attack case.
- [ ] Server role is relay/timestamp only; no approval can be forged or the delay shortened server-side.

code.title: id: keyset/authorization log — device keys, revocation, bindings as signed records (identity substrate)
code.body:
Follow-up from the key-recovery investigation on #2060 (doc: `investigations/key-recovery.md` in the ID program workspace, §1/§3/§7). Parent epic: #2056.

## Problem
`pkgs/id` identity is a single Iroh Ed25519 secret key (`src/local.rs`: `SecretKey::generate()` / `open_with_key`); the public key IS the account (invites name it directly, `src/invite.rs`). There is no indirection for device keys, revocation, IdP bindings, or rotations — so a lost key is a lost identity and a second device is a second account.

## Proposal
Design (then implement) a signed keyset/authorization log as the identity substrate: an identity identifier plus an append-only chain of signed records — device-key enrolment/revocation, hosted IdP claim bindings (#2044 §4.3 option 1), guardian sets (see social-recovery follow-up), and key rotations. Group membership and directory records bind to the identity, not to one key. Keyset-admin operations (add/revoke device, change guardians) are narrower-scoped than everyday signing.

## Acceptance
- [ ] Design doc section or ADR covering record formats, fold/verification rules, and the identity identifier derivation.
- [ ] Enrolment + revocation of a second device key via QR/invite-style pairing (`src/qr.rs`, `src/invite.rs` surfaces exist).
- [ ] Existing group-encryption per-device sessions (`src/encryption/`) consume device keys from the keyset.
- [ ] Old single-key accounts migrate via a genesis keyset record signed by the existing key.

code.title: review loop PoC (Stage A): pr-diff-review records shadow verdicts, report distribution (design #2025 §8)
code.body:
**PoC — explicitly labelled as such. No permanent feature is built here, and nothing in this issue changes any job's charter.**

Implements Stage A of the #2025 review-loop design (`files/review-loop-design-2025.md`, linked from #2025).

For ~2 weeks or 30 reviewed PRs, the standing pr-diff-review job records the verdict it *would* issue under the design's vocabulary (accept / accept-with-followups / second-pass / reject) — with ring 1–3 notes and, for would-be second-pass verdicts, a checkable gap list — in its existing review log and in the issues it already files, each marked `shadow verdict (PoC)`. No PR comments, no commissions, no merges: the job's current outputs gain one section.

**Exit criteria / deliverable**
- [ ] Verdict distribution over the run reported on #2025 (counts per verdict, per repo)
- [ ] If would-be second-pass fires on >~40% of PRs, the report says so plainly — that is vocabulary/producer inflation data and Stage B should not proceed on it without a fix
- [ ] At least 3 shadow second-pass gap lists spot-checked for checkability (design §3.1) by Muse or Drew, with the spot-check result in the report
- [ ] Report ends with a Stage B go/no-go recommendation in substance (options, ramifications, recommendation) for Drew's decision D1

Parent: #2025 · Design: review-loop-design-2025.md §8 Stage A

code.title: review loop: fleet-monitor checks for verdict/packet reconciliation (design #2025 §7.3)
code.body:
Implements §7.3 of the #2025 review-loop design (`files/review-loop-design-2025.md`, linked from #2025).

The fleet monitor already reconciles queue↔GitHub divergence hourly; the review loop adds three checks to that duty, all **report-only** at Stage B:

1. **Verdict without packet** — a verdict agent-note or `review/second-pass` label with no live second-pass (or interim-form) packet → protocol gap, handled like protocol §6.4(a).
2. **Count divergence** — label pass ≠ packet payload `review.pass` ≠ latest verdict footer → flag and repair from the payload (authoritative), noting the repair.
3. **Stale pass** — a commissioned pass unclaimed past normal claim latency, or a pass artifact unverdicted past its effort-class deadline → tracker flag in `assigned-tracker.md`, as for any assigned item.
Plus: a `review/*` label surviving issue closure is a finding (the artifact left the loop without a terminal verdict, design §7.4).

**Acceptance**
- [ ] All three checks run in the hourly monitor pass and appear in its run summary only when they fire
- [ ] A planted divergence (test issue with mismatched label/payload pass) is detected and repaired from the payload
- [ ] No check takes a non-report action at Stage B

Parent: #2025 · Design: review-loop-design-2025.md §7.3 · Depends on the schema follow-up (pass payload) and the label follow-up landing first.

code.title: id: build: grant vesting reconciler and control-plane↔ledger drift alarm
code.body:
Follow-up from the #2065 design (`doc/2026-10-29T12-10-00Z_design_refundable_grants_pending_transfers/`, PR #2293), §6.3.

## Why

The pending-transfer mechanism adds failure modes the posted design did not have: a service that dies between reserve and vest leaves the user's paid grant to expire on the TigerBeetle `timeout`, and a crash between writing intent and submitting the transfer leaves a row whose state disagrees with the ledger.

## Scope

- Sweeper: `state=pending AND window_ends_at < now` → post (retry with backoff), then mark `posted`; `Expired` is a reconcilable state, not a loss.
- Safety net: `timeout` = window + slack (design recommends +72h) so a dead service cannot hold a grant forever; the sweeper must post before that, and the slack is a last resort.
- Drift alarm: compare each grant's `pending_transfer_id` resolution in TigerBeetle against the row state; mismatch is an alert (never a silent fix).
- Late-refund fallback per §6.2: clawback attempt, on `exceeds_credits` mark the grant `debt` and expose it to the gateway's grant/redemption refusal.
- Metrics: pending count, oldest pending age, expired-then-reconciled count, drift count, debt total.

## Depends on

The grant service issue (creates the table and endpoints this reads).

## Done when

A test cluster with a killed service between reserve and vest self-heals via the sweeper, a seeded drift row raises an alarm, and an after-vest refund lands in `debt` rather than throwing.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Sweeper posts pending grants past window end (retry with backoff) and marks them posted; Expired is handled as reconcilable, never a silent loss
- [ ] Drift alarm fires on a seeded row whose TigerBeetle pending_transfer_id resolution disagrees with the row state; mismatches alert, never auto-fix silently
- [ ] After-vest refund path lands the grant in `debt` and exposes it to gateway refusal (no throw)
- [ ] Metrics exist: pending count, oldest pending age, expired-then-reconciled count, drift count, debt total
- [ ] Killed-service test: a service dying between reserve and vest self-heals via the sweeper

code.title: id: build: grant service — pending-transfer grants (register/vest/void) with control-plane grant records
code.body:
Follow-up from the #2065 design (`doc/2026-10-29T12-10-00Z_design_refundable_grants_pending_transfers/`, PR #2293). Buildable once the control-plane/gateway shape in #2062 is settled.

## Scope

- Control-plane `grant` table exactly as §2.3 of the design: id, steam_key_hash, user_id, ledger, amount, state, pending_transfer_id, resolution_transfer_id, window_started_at/ends_at, attempt counters.
- Endpoints (§2.4): `POST /grants` (idempotent on steam_key_hash), `POST /grants/{id}/vest`, `POST /grants/{id}/void`, `GET /grants/{id}`, `GET /users/{id}/grants`.
- TigerBeetle side: one `flags.pending` transfer per key from `issuer.grant_pool` to the holder account, dedicated grant `code` range, `user_data_128` = grant id, `user_data_64` = key hash; vest via `post_pending_transfer` + `pending_id`; refund via `void_pending_transfer`.
- Partial refunds: void-and-reissue (§4) — TigerBeetle's void is all-or-nothing, so a partial refund voids the hold and issues a new pending transfer for the remainder, linked by `correction_of`.
- Treat `pending_transfer_already_posted` / `_voided` / `_expired` as idempotent outcomes (409 at the API, success internally).

## Not in scope

Vesting automation and drift detection — that is the reconciler issue. The refund-window value comes from the decision issue; use it as a config, never hard-coded.

## Done when

Register → vest and register → void both work against a dev TigerBeetle cluster with targeted tests, double-resolution returns 409, and a partial refund leaves no posted credit behind.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Grant table matches design §2.3 exactly (fields incl. pending/resolution transfer ids, window bounds, attempt counters)
- [ ] Endpoints live: POST /grants (idempotent on steam_key_hash), vest, void, GET one, GET per-user
- [ ] Register → vest and register → void both pass against a dev TigerBeetle cluster with targeted tests
- [ ] Double-resolution returns 409; already-posted/voided/expired treated as idempotent outcomes internally
- [ ] Partial refund via void-and-reissue leaves no posted credit behind; refund-window value comes from config, never hard-coded

code.title: id: build: TigerBeetle cluster provisioning — RTT mesh gate, 6-replica format, dead-replica runbook + rehearsal
code.body:
Buildable follow-on from the #2064 topology investigation (doc PR #2291). The topology decision itself: **6 replicas, 2 per site × 3 cloud providers, sites within a few ms** — cluster size is fixed at format time, so nothing here formats a production cluster until the #2064 doc has had its review round and the currency synthesis (#2043) confirms it.

## Scope

1. **Site RTT measurement mesh (pre-format gate).** Stand up one throwaway VM per candidate site (3 providers, metro-clustered region picks per the #2064 doc §5), measure the full pairwise RTT mesh over ≥24h (p50/p95/p99), and record the results on this issue. Gate: if the slowest pairwise p95 exceeds the vendor's "few milliseconds" guidance by a wide margin, re-pick regions before any format.
2. **Cluster provisioning.** Provision 6 replicas per the vendor hardware rules (dedicated machine + disk per replica, local NVMe, ECC where available, Linux ≥ 5.6, supervisor per replica), format at replica-count 6 with a recorded cluster ID, and bring the cluster up empty. No real value, no production data — this proves the shape.
3. **Dead-replica replacement runbook + rehearsal.** Jepsen (via #2040) found replica replacement the sharp operational edge: write the replacement procedure as a runbook in doc/, then rehearse it — kill one replica, replace it per the runbook, verify the cluster returns to full availability with balances intact.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] RTT mesh results (p50/p95/p99, ≥24h window) recorded on this issue for the three candidate sites
- [ ] 6-replica cluster provisioned and healthy (all replicas up, cluster committing test transfers on a throwaway ledger)
- [ ] Replacement runbook in doc/ and one rehearsed replica replacement recorded here
- [ ] Production format remains gated on the #2064 review round / #2043 synthesis confirmation — this issue builds and rehearses, it does not commit the production decision by itself

Parent epic: #2056. Origin investigation: #2064. Source investigation: #2040.

code.title: id: design: RateAuthorisation as a signed ID-graph object — schema, signing, revocation
code.body:
From the conversion-engine design on #2063 §2 (feeds #2043; parent epic #2056; relates to the issuance-in-graph investigation #2041).

Define the **RateAuthorisation as a signed ID-graph object**:

- Schema for the fields in #2063 §2: id, version, issuer (LP) identity, source/dest ledgers, integer-rational rate (rate_num/rate_den, scale-aware), per-conversion min/max, total cap, authorised callers (any / allowlist / single counterparty), not_before + mandatory expires_at, one-direction-only (reverse is a separate object).
- Signing: the object is signed with the issuer's ID key; specify how the gateway (#2062) verifies the signature chains to the identity controlling both liquidity accounts.
- Revocation: representation + how the control plane's revocation set is checked at submission; revocation stops new conversions and never touches posted ones.
- Quote binding: how a short-lived single-conversion quote references an authorisation (authorisation_id + amounts + fee + expiry).

Acceptance criteria:
- [ ] A schema + worked example (ABC→123 at 0.8123, both directions as separate objects) recorded in a design doc or on this issue.
- [ ] Signature-verification and revocation-check flows specified precisely enough for the #2062 gateway to implement against.
- [ ] Anything buildable that falls out is filed as follow-ups linked here.

Schema/design work only in this issue; the gateway implementation belongs to #2062's follow-ons.

code.title: id: investigate global (Mainline DHT) content discovery for public worlds
code.body:
Parent: #2050 (investigation: BitTorrent-style chunk retrieval for graph objects), epic #2056. Follow-up D of the #2050 investigation. Investigation-sized; gated on follow-up A (in-network holder discovery) landing first.

## Question
Should `pkgs/id` add **global** holder discovery for public content, using the approach n0 demonstrates in the experimental `iroh-content-discovery` repo: announce `SHA-1(BLAKE3 hash)` on the BitTorrent Mainline DHT (`announce_peer`/`get_peers`), translate returned host:port pairs to EndpointIds via a small signed-record UDP address-index service, verify candidates with a size query, then hand off to the iroh-blobs downloader? (Write-up: iroh.computer blog, "Iroh global content discovery", 2026.)

## Why it needs its own investigation
- Privacy/trust: a Mainline announcement publicly states "an endpoint at this IP claims this hash". Right for public boards/files; wrong for membership-gated worlds. Needs a per-world opt-in model (default off) and a clear statement of what the address-index service learns and stores (in-memory, expiring records, signed by the endpoint key).
- Fit: `pkgs/id` already ships optional Mainline *address* lookup (`iroh-mainline-address-lookup`, Cargo feature `dht`) — this is Mainline *content* discovery, a different use of the same network; evaluate sharing the DHT node/socket machinery.
- The experiment is upstream-immature: assess what adopting it commits us to maintaining if n0's experiment stalls.

## Deliverable
An investigation doc (on this issue or linked, per repo convention) covering: the announce/lookup flow as it would work for id's public worlds; the privacy model and per-world opt-in design; address-index deployment options (run our own vs rely on discovered services); maintenance risk; and a recommendation (adopt / adapt / skip) with the follow-on implementation issue filed if the recommendation is adopt/adapt.

## Acceptance criteria
- Doc answers the three bullets above with evidence (code read of the experiment repo, not just the blog).
- Recommendation is explicit; if adopt/adapt, exactly one implementation issue is filed and linked; if skip, the in-network channels from #2050 follow-up A are stated to be sufficient and why.

code.title: id: partial-holder re-serving while downloading, under LIST 8 serving budgets
code.body:
Parent: #2050 (investigation: BitTorrent-style chunk retrieval for graph objects), epic #2056. Follow-up C of the #2050 investigation. Depends on follow-up A (holder discovery + wired blob gate).

## Problem
In the #2050 design every downloader becomes a useful partial holder the moment its first chunk group verifies — FsStore persists verified ranges, and bao verification makes a partial holder's ranges exactly as trustworthy as a complete holder's. Nothing in `pkgs/id` enables, announces, or budgets that re-serving today, and turning it on widens the serving surface: swarm range-serving must be covered by the LIST 8 abuse controls (per-IP / per-ID / per-world MB and message budgets, rate limits) before any public server serves swarm traffic.

## Scope
- A node serving a world re-serves the verified ranges it holds for that world's blobs, subject to the blob gate (members of a referencing world only).
- Announce partial holdings through follow-up A's provider table/announcements (held-ranges summary, not just complete/partial boolean).
- Wire serving budgets: per-world and per-peer caps on swarm range-serving (bytes/window), reusing the LIST 8 budget shapes; a node over budget declines new range requests cleanly (requester requeues elsewhere — the #2050 flow already tolerates this).
- Eviction policy: LRU under store pressure for fetched blobs; a node configured as a world's public server must not silently evict that world's only-known copy — surface it in config/status instead.

## Acceptance criteria
- A third node can complete a blob fetch where the middle node only ever held (and served) a partial range set it had itself just downloaded.
- Budget caps demonstrably stop range-serving when exceeded, and requesters recover by scheduling other holders.
- Tests cover gate behaviour for partial serving (non-member refused, indistinguishable refusal).

Not in scope: global discovery (follow-up D); permanent-feature status for the PoC scheduler (follow-up B's review round decides).

code.title: id: PoC — multi-provider chunk-range retrieval in the get path (swarm scheduler over iroh-blobs)
code.body:
Parent: #2050 (investigation: BitTorrent-style chunk retrieval for graph objects), epic #2056. Follow-up B of the #2050 investigation. Depends on the holder-discovery follow-up A (provider table) — a hand-fed provider list is acceptable for the PoC's benchmarks.

## Problem
Retrieval in `pkgs/id` is single-source: `src/commands/get.rs` does one `store.remote().fetch(conn, hash)` over one connection. iroh-blobs (0.103, in Cargo.toml) already supports the swarm-shaped pieces — `(hash, ChunkRanges)` requests per provider, bao verified streaming (each 16 KiB chunk group verified against the blob's BLAKE3 root hash as it arrives, from any source, in any order), partial-blob state in FsStore, and providers reporting the exact missing location when they close a stream for data they lack. What does not exist is the scheduling policy that uses several holders at once.

## Scope — PROOF OF CONCEPT (review-gated; do not build the permanent feature on it)
Implement the #2050 §5 retrieval flow as a PoC in the `get` path:
- Wanted-set = chunk-group ranges of the hash; assign ranges rarest-first across the provider set; disjoint ranges per holder; start with ≤4 concurrent sources.
- Verified groups persist to FsStore immediately (resume + become servable partial state). Bad group → discard, requeue range, deprioritise that holder for the hash. Missing-range stream close → shrink that holder's ranges, requeue elsewhere.
- Endgame: duplicate-request trailing in-flight ranges; first verified copy wins.
- Works in both discovery modes from #2050: observe-informed (held ranges known) and optimistic (observe off/refused — learn from missing-range reports).
- Nobody-home case surfaces distinctly ("0 holders for ranges X–Y", resumable from persisted partial state), never as a generic transfer failure.

## Benchmarks required (n0 notes multiprovider single-blob download efficiency is still maturing upstream — measure, don't assume)
- 1 vs 2 vs 4 holders, complete holders; a partial-holder mix (e.g. two 50% holders with disjoint ranges); one holder leaving mid-transfer; observe-off mode.
- Report wall time + bytes duplicated vs the single-source baseline on the same blob sizes.

## Acceptance criteria
- PoC branch/PR demonstrates a zero-local-copy fetch of a blob from ≥2 holders with per-range provenance logged.
- Benchmark table posted on this issue; failure/stall cases above behave as specified.
- The PR is explicitly a PoC: a review round decides what (if anything) becomes the permanent retrieval path. Nothing merges to main as "the feature" without that review (program rule from #2050 / Drew 2026-10-28).

code.title: impl: fleet content-creation throttle — shared ledger, pacing budgets, and verify-by-read filing
code.body:
Implementation for the design in [#2013](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/2013) — design record: [`doc/2026-10-29T10-08-00Z_design_github-content-creation-pacing/`](https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/2226) (PR #2226).

## Problem

Every fleet lane authenticates as one account, so GitHub's content-creation ceiling (documented: ~80/min, 500/hour) is a single shared budget no job can see. On 2026-10-28 `developing-today/code` alone produced 2 916 content-creating events (479 issues/PRs + 2 437 comments), peaking at 511 in the 22:00Z hour; creation then stopped for 31m48s after #1999. `gh issue create` exited 0 with empty output while creating nothing, so no caller noticed.

## Scope

Code lands with the fleet tooling (`~/hatch/tools`, `repo-queue.py`, producer/filing scripts), not in this repository. This issue is the tracking record and the spec pointer.

1. **Creation ledger** — `~/.local/state/fleet/content-ledger.sqlite`, one row per content-creating call (`ts_utc, actor, job, repo, kind, ref, outcome`), written as a reservation before the call and finalised after the verifying read; windows computed from the ledger (60 s, 3 600 s), atomic across processes via `BEGIN IMMEDIATE`.
2. **Throttle wrapper** — `reserve(job, kind)` before every create. Account-wide 45/min and 300/hour; ≥ 1 s between POSTs; ≤ 8 in flight; per-lane 50/hour sustained with idle share reclaimable; 75/hour reserve for priority-10 breakage work; bulk programs ≤ 20 issues per 30-minute window.
3. **Verify-by-read** — success only when a read confirms the object: require non-empty stdout with a number/URL, else search for the `<!-- fleet-nonce:… -->` marker in the body; record `created | verified_existing | failed`. Empty output is a failure, never a success.
4. **Circuit breaker** — honour `retry-after`; without it wait 60 s then exponential ×2 (5 attempts); after 5 failures stop content creation for 15 minutes, park the calling task with a resume brief, alert. Never spin (GitHub warns retrying while limited can ban the integration).
5. **Structural reduction** — one live agent note per task, edited in place, instead of one comment per checkpoint (comments are 5× the issue volume). Target ≤ 2 comments per task.
6. **Gap detector** — alert when queued filing work exists and no creation is seen for > 5 minutes (belongs in the fleet monitor).

## Acceptance

- A filing script run through the wrapper cannot exceed the throttle budgets, proven by a test that replays a 100-create batch and asserts the ledger shape.
- A simulated empty-output/403 create is recorded as `failed`, and the batch tally does not count it — regression test for the 2026-10-28 silent failure.
- A simulated 403 with `retry-after` and one without both back off per the rules, and five failures open the circuit.
- Warn-only run for one week: the throttle logs what it would have delayed without delaying, and the log is reviewed before enforcing.
- Success measure after enforcement: no creation 403 for 14 days, account-wide hourly total under 300, and queue throughput unchanged.

## Order

Ledger + verify-by-read first (additive, fixes the silent-success bug), then the throttle in warn-only mode, then enforcing, then the comment-reduction change in the note-writing path.

## Out of scope

- The 42-issue program's partial filing (unknown whether items were lost; the ledger makes it answerable next time).
- Multi-host coordination (open question in the design if a sandbox lane ever files).

## Acceptance criteria

- The creation ledger exists at the design's path and records every fleet content-creating call (issues, PRs, comments) with actor/job/repo/kind/ref/outcome, written as a reservation before the call.
- Pacing budgets from the design (#2013) are enforced at the shared choke point(s): a caller that would exceed the budget is delayed or visibly refused — never silently dropped — and the `gh issue create` exits-0-but-creates-nothing failure mode is detected and surfaced to the caller.
- A verify-by-read pass demonstrates the ledger's counts against GitHub's actual creation events for one busy hour (the 2026-10-28 22:00Z peak hour, 511 events, is the natural test case).

code.title: Machine pool: onboard additional machines as fleet job nodes and redesign placement around a pool
code.body:
## What this is

Drew, 2026-10-29: the fleet's job execution runs on effectively one machine (the laptop, amd-6 — OpenCode server, queue workers, OpenClaw gateway). He wants (1) additional machines set up so they can be used for jobs the same way the laptop is used now, and (2) the fleet structure redesigned to connect to a **pool of machines** instead of a single host.

## Work

1. **Machine onboarding standard.** Define what a machine needs to join the pool: NixOS config from the flake, SSH access pattern, OpenCode server (attach pattern), queue worker capability, health reporting, and the secrets it may hold (by name only). A machine joins by applying the standard, not by hand-crafting.
2. **Bring the additional machines online.** The hardware exists (the Threadripper fleet in the basement, Osseo WI) — the on-site evidence cluster (code#1095/#1097/#1099/#1101) is the inventory input and is Drew's physical step. As machines are inventoried and installed, onboard them one by one against the standard. Relationship to the lab-cluster goal (Talos/Cozystack): that program stands up the Kubernetes cluster; THIS issue is about machines as fleet job-execution nodes. Where a machine serves both, the standard says so explicitly — do not let the two programs silently diverge.
3. **Redesign the fleet structure for a pool.** Today: hardcoded laptop assumptions (the 12-session cap, SSH target, scheduler residency, watchdog locality). Target: a machine registry (identity, capabilities, capacity, health), placement that picks a machine per job/session (the route-pool idea, one level down: machine pools beside model pools), and schedulers (Muse cron, OpenChamber scheduled tasks #2174, OpenClaw automations #2177) placing work across the pool. Observability follows the same move: per-machine attribution joins the per-job/per-model attribution in #2072 and the Supabase mirror.
4. **Failure shape.** A machine leaving the pool (off, overloaded, network) drains cleanly: its sessions/jobs are visible as orphaned in one place, and no other machine's state is corrupted (the plaza-objects/shared-state lessons).

## Acceptance

- The onboarding standard written and applied to the first additional machine end-to-end: it runs a real queue job and an OpenCode session, reviewed like laptop work.
- The registry exists and the watchdog covers every pooled machine.
- A written placement design (which scheduler places what, on which signals) with the first placement rule live.

## Related

Hardware evidence cluster code#1095/#1097/#1099/#1101 (Drew, on-site) · lab-cluster goal · #2072 observability · #2174 OpenChamber scheduled tasks · #2177 OpenClaw scheduled tasks · #2173 quota utilization (pool quotas are the other half of the throughput ceiling).

code.title: OpenClaw scheduled tasks: use the native automations scheduler for watchdog-class and laptop-local work
code.body:
## What this is

Drew, 2026-10-29: find where OpenClaw's own scheduled tasks can replace Muse tasks, with management and monitoring of those tasks and outcomes. Study + live smoke test: ~/workspace/research_notes/openclaw-scheduled-tasks-20261029/findings.md. Companion to #2171 (setup + job passing + the OpenCode comparison review).

## Verdict: the scheduler is fleet-grade and idle

- Gateway live and healthy (user service since 2026-10-28 20:43 CDT, HTTP 200, OpenClaw 2026.10.7).
- `openclaw automations` (alias `cron`) is a full scheduler: cron/every/at/on-exit/stream schedules; agentTurn / command / script payloads; isolated or bound sessions; per-job model, fallbacks, thinking level; announce/webhook/no-deliver delivery; failure alerts after 2 consecutive failures; backoff, catch-up runs, restart reconciliation.
- Ledgers live in ~/.openclaw/state/openclaw.sqlite (cron_jobs, cron_run_receipts, task_runs) — status, duration, error, summary. **No token columns**: token review must join each run's session transcript/agentMeta, and OpenClaw usage never enters the runtime DB — migrated jobs leave the Supabase export's attribution unless the ledgers get bridged (that bridge is #2072 work).
- Today exactly two managed jobs exist (hourly heartbeat-main; Memory Dreaming Promotion). No fleet work has ever been scheduled through it. The heartbeat currently SKIPS hourly (`heartbeat skipped: no-route` — no channel binding for main) and inbound webhooks are disabled (POST /hooks/agent → 404).

## Smoke test (2026-10-29, first job ever passed — review row #1)

- Route: `openclaw agent --agent main --session-key smoke-20261029 --json`. One real blocker found and cleared: a bare SSH shell cannot resolve the gateway token SecretRef; the documented fix is exporting OPENCLAW_GATEWAY_TOKEN from ~/.secrets/openclaw/gateway-token (value through process env only).
- Result packet: outcome ok (runId a323dfd6…), **13,746 input / 237 output tokens, $0 recorded, 11.8s gateway time** (74s wall including CLI startup at laptop load ~20). Answer quality good with one honest gap (described fleet peers from workspace docs instead of enumerating the actual second gateway agent, `opencode`).
- **KEY CATCH: the agent's configured primary — commandcode/deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash — failed 401** (the still-pending Command Code sign-in) and the run succeeded only by falling back to design-code/deepseek-v4.1-flash. Gate: fix the Command Code sign-in or repoint the primary before relying on OpenClaw runs.
- Cost shape for the review: a watchdog-class periodic digest costs ~376K Claude input tokens per run on Muse; an equivalent OpenClaw isolated run costs ~14K pool tokens and **zero** Muse subscription tokens (different budget, not free — pool quota).

## Migration candidates

1. **Watchdog-class periodic digests** (read-only synthesis over local state) — the cost shape above.
2. **Laptop-local read-only monitors** — quota/pool reads, backup verification: the data is already on the laptop; a Muse cron pays subscription tokens to go read it remotely.
3. **Deterministic script checks as command payloads** with webhook delivery — no model tokens at all unless a check trips and escalates to an agentTurn.
4. **OpenClaw housekeeping** — already native; extend rather than rebuild.

Poor candidates: queue worker shifts and anything whose product is a GitHub write under Muse's review loop (see #2174 for the OpenCode side).

## Gates before scheduling fleet work here

1. Command Code 401 resolved or the agent primary repointed (config change rides the NixOS switch path).
2. Channel bindings or --no-deliver/webhook delivery chosen per job (heartbeat no-route skip is the symptom).
3. Token bridge: cron_run_receipts/task_runs joined to session usage and exported into Supabase, so the #2171 review (outcome/tokens/time vs OpenCode) covers scheduled runs too.
4. Inbound webhooks enabled if event-triggered OpenClaw jobs are wanted (ties to the repository_dispatch bridge in #2176).

## What #1728 + the switch do and do not do

Config today: ACP enabled with exactly one allowedAgent and one acpx agent (opencode). The merge + switch expands allowedAgents to [opencode, claude, codex, agy] with per-agent command overrides in both the embedded acpx config and ~/.acpx/config.json — that turns OpenClaw into a dispatcher that can hand coding work to ACP harnesses (and later the muse harness, #2012) instead of only running its own native turns. It does NOT fix the gateway-token env, hooks, channel bindings, or the Command Code 401.

## Acceptance

- Gates 1–3 closed; first two candidate classes running as OpenClaw scheduled jobs for a week, each run reviewed (outcome/tokens/time) against its Muse-cron baseline on #2171's comparison.

code.title: OpenCode scheduled tasks: migrate the Muse→OpenCode cron wrappers into OpenChamber scheduled tasks (waves, monitoring gates)
code.body:
## What this is

Drew, 2026-10-29: find where OpenCode-native scheduled tasks can replace the Muse cron jobs that currently launch OpenCode — to save Muse tokens or raise throughput — with proper management and monitoring of those tasks and their outcomes. Study: ~/workspace/research_notes/opencode-scheduled-tasks-20261029/findings.md.

## Verdict: PARTIAL — the trigger exists, in OpenChamber, not OpenCode

- **OpenCode core has no scheduler.** Zero cron/timer code in packages/core|server|cli; sessions are purely event-driven.
- **OpenChamber has a real scheduled-tasks subsystem** (packages/web/server/lib/scheduled-tasks/): cron/daily/weekly/once with timezones, per-project + chats scopes, new-session-per-run (model/agent pinning, permission auto-accept, goal mode with token budget, sessions stamped metadata.kind='scheduled') or prompt-into-existing-session, cross-instance occurrence claiming, loop files (.agents/loops/*.md), REST + UI + CLI + an agent tool (openchamber_schedule).
- But it is a **prompt scheduler, not a job system**: state holds only the last run, no token capture, no alerting, in-code defaults of 4 global / 2 per-project concurrent runs, and a 30-minute run cap (vs ~90-minute shift windows).

## Migration waves (Claude input tokens, trailing-24h, runtime-DB attribution)

**Wave 1 (~3.4B/day of the fleet's ~5.1B/day):**
1. **Repo-queue worker shifts — ~2.26B/day, save ~2.1–2.2B.** The Muse layer is claim/checkpoint/terminal-verbs via repo-queue.py plus implementation over laptop-ssh — the identical runbook an OpenCode session already executes when dispatcher-launched. Ports near-verbatim as per-queue scheduled tasks. Blockers: repo-queue.py must run laptop-side; sandbox lane-lock files replaced by the atomic DB claim; run cap raised.
2. **Issue creators — ~0.96B/day, save ~0.9B.** The runbook already is a self-contained prompt. One API-created scheduled task per repo-lane. Note: this reprices the 3.93M-Claude-tokens/filed-issue figure behind Drew's held creator-throttle decision into pool tokens.
3. **OpenChamber dispatcher + babysitter — ~390M/day, save ~350–370M.** The most rule-bound jobs in the fleet, currently spending Claude tokens operating the API of the system that would run the loop natively. Port as existing-session scheduled pokes into persistent sessions (cross-round state lives in session context instead of being re-read at ~1.4M/run).

**Wave 2 (~0.25B):** fleet-monitor, pr-diff pair, issue-sweep, pool-quota-steward (partial fits).

**Keep on Muse:** fleet-watchdog (it is the monitor — it must instead gain coverage of the OpenChamber tasks) and orchestration-pass (the consumer/escalation collector).

## The honest trade

The throughput ceiling moves from Claude-subscription/cron concurrency to **pool quotas + the laptop's 12-session cap**. At a known-100% pool the native fleet stalls where Muse lanes currently sail past. This makes the migration dependent on the full-quota utilization program (#2173) keeping pools fed and rotated.

## Gating monitoring gaps (fix before migrating anything)

1. **Per-run history** — scheduled-task state is last-run-only (laptop JSON). Consume the already-emitted `openchamber:scheduled-task-ran` SSE events into Supabase.
2. **Token accounting** — every OpenCode assistant message already carries cost + tokens (schema/session-message.ts), but nothing exports it; the mirror covers only the Muse runtime. Build an OpenCode-side exporter twin of runtime-db-export (this is #2072 work).
3. **Failure alerting / dead-man's switch** — fleet-watchdog polls GET /api/openchamber/scheduled-tasks/status + queue-claim staleness.
4. **Server residency** — the scheduler dies with the OpenChamber server process; confirm the laptop deployment is always-on (not socket-activated or idle-stopped).
5. **Shared-state locality** — fleet bookkeeping (backlogs, sweep.log, lane locks) is sandbox-resident; OpenCode sessions are laptop-resident. Move per-job state to Supabase, following the queue pattern.
6. Identity binding (task id / session id / queue task id in one place), the loop-file approval gate (silently pauses migrated jobs), escalation path for urgent classes.

## Acceptance

- Gaps 1–4 closed and demonstrated on one pilot: ONE queue lane running as an OpenChamber scheduled task for 48h with per-run history, token accounting, and watchdog coverage — reviewed against its Muse-cron baseline (outcome, tokens, time), then a go/no-go for the rest of wave 1.

## Acceptance criteria

- Each Muse cron wrapper that launches OpenCode is inventoried (in the linked study or a comment here) with a disposition: migrated to an OpenChamber scheduled task, kept on Muse cron with a named reason, or retired.
- Migrated tasks run in waves with monitoring gates between waves: a wave's runs are observed completing (run records + outcome checks) before the next wave migrates.
- For every migrated task, the Muse-token cost change is measured or explicitly estimated, and any throughput change is noted — the migration's stated purpose is token savings or throughput, so the result must say which it got.

code.title: Add OpenClaw to #alignment — decide one shared channel vs point-to-point
code.body:
## What this is

#alignment (C0CBYQR65LL) is the agent coordination channel. Aster is in it and proposed the channel contract on 2026-10-28 (verified senders; every dispatch carries ID/owner/scope/evidence; ACK/BLOCKED then RESULT in-thread; dedupe; no credentials). OpenClaw is not in it yet — its bot binding and delivery are unverified. Drew asked 2026-10-29 to add OpenClaw and to settle whether one channel for all agents is enough, or each pair needs its own point-to-point path.

## The topology question

**One shared channel** (recommended):
- Channels stay O(1) as agents are added; pairwise grows O(n^2).
- Every dispatch and result sits in one record — the OpenClaw/OpenCode review needs to see traffic it was not part of.
- Threads per dispatch keep it readable; the contract keeps it disciplined.

**Point-to-point per pair**:
- Wins only for high-volume pair traffic, or content that should not be visible to the other agents.
- Costs: fragmented record, hidden context, and N^2 channels to babysit as the roster grows (Muse, Aster, OpenClaw, OpenCode today; more coming).

Recommendation: one shared #alignment for all dispatch and results, one thread per dispatch ID, contract as Aster proposed. Add a point-to-point path only when a specific pair proves it needs one (volume or sensitivity), and record that exception here.

## Work

1. Bind the OpenClaw bot into #alignment; verify send and receive both ways with a harmless round-trip.
2. Publish the sender ID registry (Muse, Aster, OpenClaw) in the channel and on this issue.
3. Adopt the contract for all agents; the first OpenClaw dispatch follows it.

## Acceptance

- OpenClaw posts and replies in #alignment, verified both directions.
- Topology decision recorded (Drew) and the contract pinned/linked.

code.title: Fold orchestration-pass residue into stewardship-cycle + program-tending, then retire the hourly pass
code.body:
Implementation follow-on from the #2136 triage (queue task 3166, 2026-10-29). Parent: #2136 (residue-owner map + retirement gates recorded there); fleet epic: #2055; roles: #2131.

Fold orchestration-pass's residue into Tend and retire the hourly pass, in this order — retirement is the LAST step, gated, never first:

1. **Operational residue → `stewardship-cycle`.** Amend its body to own: (a) cross-queue priority calls across the four pilot queues (which queue/task class goes first when lanes contend), and (b) stuck-work escalation decisions (detectors stay where they are: fleet-watchdog alerts, repo-fleet-monitor's in-progress tracker escalates per protocol §6.3 — stewardship-cycle is the named decision/dispatch owner that acts on them, including carrying the needsDrew / needsOrchestrator lists orchestration-pass carries today).
2. **Macro residue → `program-tending`.** Amend its body to own: (a) the goal-measurement rollup, and (b) the GitHub Project reconcile orchestration-pass runs today. **Access gate:** program-tending's 2026-10-28 run reported the Projects board unreadable (gh token lacks read:project scope) while orchestration-pass reconciles successfully — verify program-tending can execute the reconcile through the same access path before this duty moves; if it cannot, the reconcile stays with orchestration-pass and retirement waits.
3. **Evidence runs.** One evidenced run of each receiving job carrying its new duties (log lines naming the residue outputs).
4. **Retire.** Only after steps 1–3: disable `orchestration-pass` (disable, never delete — rollback is re-enabling it), and update the fleet-watchdog roster in the same pass.
5. **Gap watch.** The two daily token check-ins following retirement confirm no triage gap: the needsDrew/needsOrchestrator carry lists still produced (by stewardship-cycle), project reconcile still applied, no duty from the #2136 map unowned. Report the result on #2136.

Acceptance:
- [ ] stewardship-cycle and program-tending bodies amended with the named residue duties; project-reconcile access gate verified
- [ ] One evidenced run per receiving job carrying the residue
- [ ] orchestration-pass disabled (not deleted); fleet-watchdog roster updated
- [ ] Two post-retirement check-ins show no triage gap; result posted on #2136; #2055 linked

code.title: Implement repo-fleet-monitor snapshot/SQL-first fetch (digest-judged runs, ≤3M input/run)
code.body:
Implementation follow-on from the #2134 triage (queue task 3164, 2026-10-29). Parent: #2134 (design recorded there); fleet epic: #2055.

The 2h cadence half of #2134 is already live. This issue is the remaining half: rebuild repo-fleet-monitor's state fetch to be snapshot/SQL-first so a run costs ≤3M input (from 7.2M at check-in #5) with **no duty dropped**.

Design (full text on #2134):
1. **Deterministic precompute, run-start fresh.** A script (extend the existing `hidden_files/monitor-fetch.py` / `monitor-query.py` prototypes in the goal workspace) runs at the start of every monitor run and emits ONE compact digest: live queue tasks across all four pilot queues (PostgREST, one query per queue, live statuses only) joined against a bounded GitHub pull (only issues carrying `queue/*` or `work/*` labels and PRs bound to live tasks). The digest pre-flags divergences mechanically: claimed-but-unlabelled, labelled-but-no-live-task, expired leases still claimed, expired parks, PR merged/closed but task open, issue closed but task open, dead-in-queue (max_attempts reached, still queued).
2. **The agent judges only the digest.** Full task/issue lists never enter the agent's context; a flagged divergence is investigated with a targeted single-item fetch. Intake enrichment stays bounded (newest-first sample, as today) but draws its candidate list from the digest.
3. **Freshness is binding:** the digest is generated in-run; judging from a snapshot older than the run is forbidden (the stale 2026-10-28 prototype snapshot JSONs in hidden_files are the anti-pattern — delete or overwrite them in-run, never read them as evidence).
4. **No duty dropped — each protocol duty maps to digest fields:** reconciliation + auto-repair (divergence flags), dead-in-queue alerts (attempts flag), intake enrichment (unenriched-issue list), in-progress tracker (claimed tasks + label join), protocol checks (work/* without a fresh agent note = flag).

Acceptance:
- [ ] Monitor instruction rewritten to the digest flow; precompute script committed in the goal workspace and invoked by the job body
- [ ] One full monitor run executed on the new flow with all five duties evidenced in its output
- [ ] Input per run ≤3M measured over the following three daily token check-ins, with divergence-repair counts not below the pre-rewrite run average
- [ ] #2134 closed or updated with the measurement; #2055 linked

code.title: Shift batching, creator-style: lane handoff snapshots + supervision mode for queue lanes
code.body:
Queue shifts already bundle up to 10 tasks; their cost (6–13M input/run at check-in #5; the 9-lane shift family was 52% of all cron spend) is per-start state re-derivation plus in-shift supervision context — the same overhead class the creator batching change attacked (3.93M → ~1.4M input per filed issue).

Do:
1. Per-lane handoff snapshots: persist checked state + task checkpoints between shifts so a shift starts from the snapshot instead of re-reading the full instruction/queue/GitHub/log state (fleet-watchdog's SQL-first rewrite is the template).
2. Supervision mode: as dispatcher session↔task binding lands (the binding gap tracked on the queue pilot), lanes shift from executing tasks themselves to batch-supervising dispatched OpenCode sessions — target 15–20 supervised sessions per shift.
3. Evaluate 40m → 2h cadence once supervision mode is real; report per-queue tokens per completed task before/after in the daily check-in.

code.title: Design + PoC: event-driven Slack collector (Socket Mode) to replace archer-slack-review polling
code.body:
archer-slack-review polls a watermark every 15 min (~100K input/run × ~96 runs/day ≈ 9.6M/day) and usually finds nothing. Replace the polling with an event-driven collector (Drew approved 2026-10-29):

- A small service using Slack Socket Mode (outbound WebSocket — no public endpoint needed; Cloudflare Worker + Events API is the off-box alternative) appends messages, replies, and reactions from the watched channels to a local store.
- The review job wakes ONLY when the store has new items (hook/signal), reads just the delta, and acts.
- Placement per the flake rule (developing-today/code flake if on the laptop; sandbox systemd if on the sandbox). The service is deterministic — no LLM in the collection path.

PoC scope: the #alignment channel end-to-end (collect → store → wake → review). Success: quiet-day agent cost ~0; no missed Aster replies over a 3-day parallel run against the existing poller. Afterwards, generalize the pattern to other watermark polls.

code.title: Fold orchestration-pass into Tend (stewardship-cycle + program-tending); retire the hourly pass
code.body:
orchestration-pass (hourly, 43M input per 15h, the largest job body in the fleet at 26KB) has been mostly absorbed: producers create, the dispatcher assigns, lanes self-claim, the fleet monitor reconciles, stewardship-cycle reviews and dispatches, program-tending runs the daily roadmap pass.

Assess what remains uniquely its own — cross-queue priority calls, stuck-work escalation, goal-measurement rollup — and fold that residue into the Tend role: operational residue to stewardship-cycle, macro/alignment residue to program-tending (which owns Tend's look-back: completed + queued work vs projects, roadmaps, priorities). Then retire the hourly orchestration-pass. Done when the residue has named owners, the pass is disabled, and two check-ins show no triage gap.

code.title: id: delete requests, server delete policies, federated delete replication (code#185 decision)
code.body:
Implements the policy + federation layers of the owner decision on #185 (comment 6486250456, Drew, 2026-10-28). Likely splits into smaller issues; filed whole so the design stays in one place. Depends on the marker + default-view work (tag.clear as a role-aware marker).

## Pieces
1. **Delete requests.** A first-class operation: anyone can request deletion of a tag, carrying a reason. The request is delivered to the relevant authority holders — the tag's author, group admins, or server owners — and their grant/decline is recorded.
2. **Server delete policies.** A server admin can set policies on their own server that actually delete based on clear markers (and/or granted delete requests). Conditions are the server's business; nothing here is protocol-mandated. Deletes are events (auditable), not silent state edits.
3. **Federated deletes (opt-in per server owner, never default).**
   - A server owner may replicate deletes from federated co-servers.
   - A server owner may accept delete events from ANY server provided the delete is signed by the author or admins and the full chain validates; an invalid or incomplete chain means the foreign delete is not honored.

## Acceptance
- Delete request round-trips: request with reason -> delivered to author/admins/server owners -> grant produces a delete under the server's policy, decline is recorded with no delete.
- A server with no delete policy never hard-deletes from clear markers alone.
- Foreign deletes are honored only under the owner's chosen mode (federated co-servers, or any-server-with-valid-signed-chain) and rejected when the chain does not validate.

Refs #185.

## Acceptance criteria
- Delete requests are a first-class operation carrying a reason, delivered to the tag's author, group admins, or server owners, with grant/decline recorded.
- Server admins can set delete policies on their own server that act on clear markers and/or granted delete requests; deletes are auditable events, never silent state edits.
- Federated delete replication is opt-in per server owner (never default); a foreign delete is honored only when signed by the author or admins and the full chain validates.
- Tests cover request grant/decline, policy-driven delete, and rejection of an invalid/incomplete foreign delete chain.

code.title: External-system observability: unified PM + queue + quota attribution (webhooks, hot list, session IDs, projections)
code.body:
## Problem (owner direction, 2026-10-28)

Work is steadily moving off the main agent onto other systems that spend their own tokens under direction — the OpenCode fleet, OpenClaw-originated sessions, Codex/ChatGPT, Jules and other external agents. Direction stays centralized (adjust cadences, add/remove scheduled tasks, tell a persistent agent what it is doing right or wrong and let it fix itself), which saves main-agent tokens. The cost: **the main agent no longer directly knows what those systems did.** Today the record is scattered across GitHub, the queue DB, session stores and quota files, with no single place to answer "what happened, who did it, what did it cost, and was it any good."

This issue is the design + build tracker for closing that gap.

## Requirements

### 1. The PM stack and the queue must be available TO the external systems
Not just readable by the owner: the delegated systems themselves need to read queue state and report outcomes into the PM stack, so their work lands in the shared record as it happens instead of being reconstructed later.

### 2. Detect what happened OUTSIDE the system
Anything a delegated system does that bypasses the queue/PM record is currently invisible. Close this with **webhooks**: for every system/repo that can emit them (GitHub first), deliver events into an ingestion point that maintains a **hot list of everything created or changed since the last check** — issues, PRs, comments, edits, commits. The checking/triage systems then sweep the hot list and flag anything that was not expected (not traceable to a queue item, a schedule, or a directed task).

### 3. PM stack + queue: one integrated view
Merge or closely integrate the two so the owner can see, in one place:
- what is queued, and in what order;
- what has been picked up, and by which system;
- stats, metrics, graphs and trends over token usage, model selection, plan quotas, and all scheduled jobs.

### 4. Per-job / per-model outcome attribution
For each job (and model) the system should be able to say: "this job with this model made 2 PRs, closed 1 issue, created 3 issues, commented on these issues" — counting at least: issues/PRs **created**, **commented on**, **descriptions edited**, **commits to branches** — with every aggregate linking back to the exact issues, PRs and comments behind it.

### 5. Universal session identity
Every unit of delegated work carries a traceable ID:
- **OpenCode** already has session + parent-session IDs — use them as-is (session uploads/digests already preserve child-session lists and model switches).
- **OpenClaw** origination of an OpenCode session needs a recorded mapping (which OpenClaw context started which session).
- Systems whose internals we do not control (ChatGPT/Codex and similar): pull actual IDs from a **weekly ChatGPT export**; where no native ID exists, workers get an **assigned ID when they pick up a queue job** and reuse it across subsequent items.
- The same applies to the main agent itself: when it takes an item from the system it is told its session ID (or presents one it already holds), so its work is attributed the same way.
Sessions tie to: exact model(s), the system of origin, token usage where measurable (exact where the platform records it, absent where it cannot), and the quota series (item 7) — so a change to a job can be followed to its effects on quotas and outcomes.

### 6. Quality linkage
- PRs can be marked **reverted** or **had to be redone**, with links to the redo.
- A bug can be tied to the **multiple PRs that contributed** to it existing.
Together with item 4, this is how we find out what is actually causing bugs — which jobs/models/systems produce work that sticks vs work that gets reverted — and the UI should make that analysis easy.

### 7. Quotas in the same picture, with projections
- The assistant's own subscription quota joins the PM pool list as a first-class entry: current percentage, total tokens per week, position in the window. (Data source exists: a 5-minute recorder landed 2026-10-28 — `~/tools/quota-recorder.py` + the runtime token DB's per-message records; the laptop quota-gatherer already records the other pools every 15 minutes.)
- For every quota: a few days of percentage history against its reset, and a **projection** — either "projected to end the window at X%" or "projected to hit quota on <day> at <time>".
- Projections are **stored**, and later compared with what actually happened, so modifiers/rules can be learned over time to make the predictions better.

### Persistence principle
Not everything has to land in the database immediately — but everything must be **written down somewhere persistent**, with a system that gets it into a central location where it can be queried regularly.

## Pieces that already exist (build on these)
- PM aggregator + projector (laptop) with per-source health, comments/actions stores, quota-current and the monthly usage-snapshot JSONL.
- The queue system (Supabase `agent.tasks`: packets, dedupe keys, lane claims, completions — completions currently record queue-level worker identity, not per-lane; see the 2026-10-28 token check-in findings).
- The runtime token DB (`agent.agent_message_token_usage` + spawn metadata) — exact per-message tokens with cron attribution for everything on this platform.
- OpenCode session digests (full session/child-session/model-switch records).
- The 5-minute Muse subscription quota recorder + the laptop's 15-minute pool gatherer.
- GitHub webhooks are available on all owned repos; the fleet-feed collector pattern is a working ingestion precedent.

## Shape of the work (to be refined in design)
1. Design note first: identity scheme (session/job/system), the attribution event model, webhook ingestion + hot-list store, and the integrated PM/queue/quota views. Record the design on this issue before building.
2. Then implementation issues, one per piece, linked here: webhook ingestion + hot list; queue↔PM integration views; attribution rollups (per job/model/session); session-ID assignment at queue pickup + OpenClaw/Codex mapping; projection engine + accuracy tracking; Muse pool on the PM list.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A design note is recorded on this issue covering: the identity scheme (session/job/system), the attribution event model, webhook ingestion + hot-list store, and the integrated PM/queue/quota views.
- [ ] Implementation issues are filed, one per piece, and linked here (webhook ingestion + hot list; queue↔PM integration views; attribution rollups; session-ID assignment at queue pickup + OpenClaw/Codex mapping; projection engine + accuracy tracking; Muse pool on the PM list).
- [ ] GitHub webhooks (first source) deliver issue/PR/comment/commit events into the ingestion point, and the hot list reflects everything created or changed since the last check.
- [ ] The integrated view can answer, for a given window: what happened, which system/agent did it, what it cost, and its outcome — without hand-reconciling GitHub, the queue DB, and quota files.
