Parent: #181

## Summary

opencode v2 wraps every MCP server in its own code mode unless the server is configured `codemode: false`, and this machine's v1 does the same because `OPENCODE_EXPERIMENTAL` is set. So mcpx's `/mcp` ends up as a tool called from a program the model wrote for opencode's interpreter, and nothing in mcpx's docs says to opt out. v2 also appends `?codemode=false` to remote MCP URLs so servers that bundle code mode can expose raw tools; mcpx ignores it. opencode runs permission checks and plugin hooks per child call, shows live status, and cancels on abort. The plugin's `mcpx_exec` makes one blocking POST and ignores the abort signal (the session and field bugs are #189).

Found while writing the comparison register (`pkgs/mcpx/docs/compare/`) and checked against the code at `05c78b2`. Each row below links its register entry, which carries the value, effort, risk, the specification text and every source.

## Register rows

| row | difference | mcpx @ 05c78b2 | effort |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [CODE-53](https://github.com/dezren39/nix/blob/main/pkgs/mcpx/docs/compare/register/code-mode.md#code-53-opencode-wraps-mcp-servers-in-code-mode-by-default) | opencode wraps MCP servers in code mode by default | ✗ — docs never tell users to opt out | S |
| [PLG-35](https://github.com/dezren39/nix/blob/main/pkgs/mcpx/docs/compare/register/plugin-apis.md#plg-35-codemodefalse-appended-to-remote-mcp-urls) | `?codemode=false` appended to remote MCP URLs | ✗ — neither sends nor honours it | M |
| [PLG-36](https://github.com/dezren39/nix/blob/main/pkgs/mcpx/docs/compare/register/plugin-apis.md#plg-36-hooks-and-permission-checks-per-child-call-in-code-mode) | Hooks and permission checks per child call in code mode | ✗ — script calls bypass opencode permissions | L |
| [PLG-37](https://github.com/dezren39/nix/blob/main/pkgs/mcpx/docs/compare/register/plugin-apis.md#plg-37-live-status-of-each-child-call-during-a-script) | Live status of each child call during a script | ✗ — plugin makes one blocking POST | S |
| [PLG-38](https://github.com/dezren39/nix/blob/main/pkgs/mcpx/docs/compare/register/plugin-apis.md#plg-38-cancelling-in-the-harness-stops-the-script) | Cancelling in the harness stops the script | ✗ — plugin ignores the abort signal | S |

## What to do

Document `codemode: false` for mcpx in opencode config; decide whether `?codemode=false` should expose upstream tools flat; plumb abort and live status through the plugin's `mcpx_exec`.

## Ease · Impact · Related

**Ease** M · **Impact** med · **Related**: #189, #47, #48

## Acceptance criteria

- mcpx documentation tells opencode users how mcpx interacts with opencode's default code-mode wrapping, including how to opt a server out (`codemode: false`) (CODE-53).
- mcpx honors `?codemode=false` on its `/mcp` URL: raw tools are exposed instead of the code-mode surface.
- The plugin's `mcpx_exec` respects the host abort signal — an aborted session cancels the in-flight call instead of blocking to completion.
- Tests cover the query-parameter handling and the abort path.

code.title: mcpx: administration by intent — finish the operation surface, then route a sentence to a declared operation
code.body:
Relocated from dezren39/nix#113 on 2026-10-28 (placement audit): mcpx's single source lives in developing-today/code (pkgs/mcpx); re-home tracked at #309. Original body below; issue references inside it are historical (dezren39/nix numbering).

Parent: #176

## Summary

"Tell mcpx to do a thing and it tries its best" — administration by intent rather than by remembering which of sixty operations does what.

Most of the specific operations listed in the note already exist, and the ones that do not should be built as **ordinary declared operations first**, because the ops table is the thing that makes them reachable from every surface at once. The prompt layer on top is then a router from a sentence to an operation, not an interpreter that invents behaviour — which also answers the note's own parenthetical, "(same interface for this and clients? plugins?)": mcpx already solved that, and the answer is the ops table.

The second bullet — provisioning arbitrary languages, tools and repositories — is a genuinely different and much larger problem, and is treated separately below.

## Original notes

> - mcp-owned opencode api support
>   - install any language/tool/framework/library, clone whatever repo.
>   - prompt-based served endpoints (tell mcpx to do a thing it tries its best, tell it to install/remove/reconfigure itself, add/remove/configure mcp, administrate, restart mcp servers, force-detach, kill sessions, resume dead sessions, get config, exec/runwhatever. (same interface for this and clients? plugins?) 

## Current state (what mcpx does today, with file refs)

The "same interface" question is already answered architecturally. One ops table (`internal/api/ops*.go`) generates HTTP routes, MCP tools and the OpenAPI document; `internal/settings` gives every setting a config key, an `MCPX_*` variable, a CLI flag, `/v1/settings` and an MCP tool; the repository has an automated parity check (`internal/api/parity_test.go`). The rule is CLI = `/v1` = MCP = plugin.

Against the note's list:

| asked for | exists today | where |
| --- | --- | --- |
| add/remove/configure an mcp | **yes** | `POST /v1/servers`, `DELETE /v1/servers/{name}`, `mcpx servers`, live add/remove |
| find an mcp that is not configured yet | **yes** | `GET /v1/registry/search`, `mcpx registry search\|show\|add` (`internal/cli/registry.go:15`; there is no `mcpx connect`) |
| get config | **yes** | `GET /v1/settings`, `GET /v1/settings/{path}`, `mcpx config`, `mcpx schema` |
| reconfigure | **yes** | `PUT /v1/settings/{path}` with `persist`, `DELETE /v1/settings/{path}` |
| restart mcp servers | **yes** | `POST /v1/refresh`, `POST /v1/restart`, `mcpx refresh`/`restart` |
| administrate / inspect | **yes** | `/v1/status`, `/v1/health`, `/v1/stats`, `/v1/log`, `/v1/events`, `mcpx doctor`, `mcpx daemons` |
| exec/run whatever | **yes** | `POST /v1/exec`, `mcpx exec`/`run`, `mcpx api`, CLI→MCP adapters |
| stop the daemon | **yes** | `POST /v1/shutdown`, `mcpx stop` |
| release a session's hold on an instance | **partly** | `POST /v1/session/release` — releases, does not kill |
| **kill a session** | **no** | there is no session-level operation beyond release |
| **force-detach** | **no** | `mcpserver.Detached()` is an internal notion of a connection with no client; there is no operation to force an instance off its holder |
| **resume dead sessions** | **no** | nothing persists or revives a session |
| **install/remove mcpx itself** | **no** | no `mcpx install`; the command list is `run exec scripts recipes prompt diagnose ls catalog types search call client status daemons refresh restart stop daemon config settings servers init schema elicit doctor prompts resources tui explore log stats help` (`internal/cli/manual.go`; the dispatch table at `cmd/mcpx/main.go` also has `registry`, `adapter`, `api`, `openapi`, `serve`, `man`, `completion` — none installs mcpx) |
| **prompt-driven administration** | **no** | `mcpx prompt` / `POST /v1/intent` exists but targets **scripts**, not operations: it matches a recipe or generates TypeScript (`docs/consumer.md` §4) |

Also relevant: #76 already tracks the operations that exist on `/v1` and MCP but have **no CLI command** (resolve, protocol, artifacts, tasks, ask) and proposes generating the CLI from the ops table so it cannot fall behind again. That is the same rule this issue depends on, from the other direction.

## Approaches

### Approach A — least recommended: a `POST /v1/admin` that takes a sentence and does its best

One endpoint, free-text in, a model with shell access behind it.

Why not:

- **It bypasses the one invariant the codebase enforces automatically.** Every capability in mcpx is declared once and appears on four surfaces. A prompt endpoint that "does its best" is a capability surface with no declaration, no schema, no OpenAPI entry, no parity test, and no way for `mcpx schema` to tell you what it can do. The parity test would pass while the actual surface area doubled invisibly.
- **It is strictly more powerful than the sum of the declared operations**, because "do a thing" includes things nobody decided to expose. Every bounded operation mcpx has — `settings_set` with its `persist` scope, `servers_remove` with its project/user scope — becomes bypassable.
- **Irreversibility.** "Tell it to remove itself" executed by a model that misread the request is not recoverable, and there is no dry-run, no confirmation and no audit trail unless each is built anyway — at which point the declared-operations approach was the cheaper route.
- **Undiagnosable failures.** When a declared operation fails you get a structured error. When "do your best" fails you get a paragraph.

### Approach B — middle: finish the deterministic surface, no prompt layer

Build the missing operations properly and stop:

1. **Session operations as a group.** `GET /v1/sessions` (what exists, what each holds, idle time, pid), `POST /v1/sessions/{id}/release` (generalising the existing endpoint), `DELETE /v1/sessions/{id}` (kill: release holds, cancel in-flight calls, drop state). The data is already there — the disambiguation elicitation from #41 renders exactly this per instance: "holders, calls, idle time, pid — because a choice without that is not a choice."
2. **Force-detach.** `POST /v1/servers/{name}/detach` with a scope key: take a pooled instance away from whatever holds it. The pool already knows which scope key a connection serves (`docs/protocol.md` §3.4). Needed for the case where a holder died without releasing, which today requires restarting the daemon.
3. **Resume a dead session.** Depends on what a session *is* that could survive: today it is a scope key plus pooled instances, and reviving it means re-establishing leases, not restoring state. Worth scoping honestly — "resume" may only ever mean "reattach a new caller to the same scope key and its still-warm instances", which is useful and achievable, versus "restore a session that ended", which needs the event store (#6) and possibly per-server state that servers do not expose.
4. **Self-management.** `mcpx install` / `uninstall` / `upgrade` — harness registration (writing mcpx into an agent's MCP config), service installation (launchd/systemd), and the reverse. `docs/proposals.md` §"Harness integration and installation" and §"Packaging and service management" already design this; `mcpx init` exists as the nearest thing. Note it is partly outside the daemon's reach: a daemon cannot cleanly uninstall the binary running it, so the CLI owns that half.
5. **#76's missing CLI commands**, generated from the ops table.

After that, "administrate mcpx" is fully expressible as declared operations on all four surfaces — which is most of the note's list, done deterministically, with schemas and errors and an audit trail.

### Approach C — recommended: B, then extend `mcpx prompt` to route to *operations* as well as scripts

Do B. Then make the prompt layer a **router over the declared operations**, not a general executor. Three things make this small, safe and mostly already built:

**1. mcpx already publishes a machine-readable description of every operation it has.** `GET /v1/openapi.json` is generated from the ops table with full parameter schemas and descriptions (`internal/cli/openapi.go` — "it cannot describe an endpoint that does not exist or omit a parameter that does"). So operation selection is a constrained choice from a known list with known arguments — the same problem shape as tool-calling, which models are good at, rather than open-ended generation, which they are not.

**2. It is the same code path `/v1/intent` already runs.** Today intent ranks recipes, then optionally generates a script. Add a third candidate class — operations — ranked by the same deterministic scorer over name, description and parameter names, with the same `recipes.matchMargin` refusal when the leader is not clearly ahead. `mcpx prompt "restart the github server"` should match `POST /v1/refresh` deterministically, with **no model at all**, exactly as recipe matching does today. That is most requests, for free.

**3. The existing gates apply unchanged.** `prompt.mode: script` becomes `prompt.mode: plan` for operations: return *what it would do* — operation, arguments, effect — and execute only on explicit confirmation or `mode: run`. Destructive operations route through `elicit.confirmDestructive`'s existing policy, and an unanswered confirmation **refuses**, because "there, doing nothing is safe" (`docs/consumer.md` §2). Every operation the router may reach must carry an explicit annotation in the ops table. **Corrected at 05c78b2:** most of that already exists — `Op` has `Admin`, `Mutating` and `Destructive` (`internal/api/ops.go:59-67`), and `Op.Annotations()` (`:654-667`) maps them to MCP `readOnlyHint`/`destructiveHint`/`idempotentHint`. Five operations are marked destructive (`restart`, `shutdown`, `servers_remove`, `artifact_delete`, `ask_abandon`). What the router needs is for its confirmation gate to read those flags, and an audit that the marks are complete; a separate `Irreversible` is only worth adding if some operation turns out to be one and not the other (`Destructive` is already documented as "cannot undo").

**#181 collisions 3 and 5:** `prompt.mode: plan` is one of three autonomy dials. #111 carries the one vocabulary, decided in a decision record SURFACES is writing under `pkgs/mcpx/docs/decisions/`; the mode names here are input to it, and this issue adopts what it decides. The daemon-set ceiling a caller may lower but not raise is #185.

So: **no new endpoint.** `POST /v1/intent` gains a `scope` parameter (`scripts | ops | any`), and `mcpx prompt` gains the same flag. That satisfies the note's requirement — a prompt-based way to administrate — while the actual capability surface stays exactly the set of declared operations. And it answers "(same interface for this and clients? plugins?)" with: yes, necessarily, because the router's entire vocabulary is the ops table, which is already the shared interface.

### The provisioning bullet is a different feature

"Install any language/tool/framework/library, clone whatever repo" is not administration of mcpx; it is arbitrary environment mutation on the daemon's host. It is also a real need — #112's motivating example is *"I added a bunch of dependencies please make sure they exist where the job runs"* — and today mcpx has nothing for it: exec runs in a content-addressed workdir with a runtime that is already installed.

What exists to build on: `script.runtime` (auto/deno/bun/node), and the installed toolchain here is Node v24.20.0, Deno 2.9.6, Bun 1.3.11, Python 3.14.7, uv 0.9.28. Deno and Bun both resolve `npm:` and `jsr:` specifiers at import time with no install step, and `uv run --with <pkg>` does the same for Python — so **for the two ecosystems mcpx scripts actually use, "make sure the dependencies exist" is already solved by the runtime**, and the honest first answer to the bullet is a documented convention plus a preflight check that the specifiers resolve, not an installer.

Beyond that, three levels, and they should be separate decisions:

| level | what it is | verdict |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **declared dependencies** | a script header declares `// @dep npm:zod@3`, `// @dep py:httpx`; mcpx verifies resolvability in preflight and reports precisely what is missing | do this; it is deterministic, matches the existing `@param` recipe-header convention, and makes the failure legible instead of a runtime import error |
| **managed provisioning** | mcpx materialises the declared dependencies into the run's workdir — a lockfile, a per-run cache keyed by the existing content-addressed workdir scheme, `uv`/`bun install` under the hood | plausible, scoped, cacheable; a real feature with real value, worth its own issue — #103/#104 under #175 are where it lands |
| **arbitrary install / clone by prompt** | a model decides what to install and runs a package manager or `git clone` | the only genuinely agentic operation in this whole theme. If it happens at all it should be a *recipe* — a saved, reviewable script exposed as an operation with its own confirmation — not an unnamed capability of the prompt router. And it should run somewhere disposable; the daemon's host is not that. |

Recommended split: declared dependencies now, managed provisioning in #103/#104, arbitrary provisioning deferred and reconsidered only after the confinement question has an answer.

## Open questions

- What is a session, precisely, such that it can be killed and resumed? This needs settling before the session operations can be specified; it touches #6 (event store) and #78 (daemon state correctness).
- Should force-detach notify the dispossessed holder? An MCP client that loses an instance mid-call will see a confusing error otherwise.
- ~~Do `Destructive`/`Irreversible` annotations on ops belong in this issue or in the ops-table work #76 is already doing? Probably #76 — flag it there.~~ They exist (`internal/api/ops.go:59-67`). What is open is whether every op is marked correctly — an audit that belongs with #76, which is regenerating the CLI from the same table.
- Should `intent --scope ops` be allowed to *chain* operations ("add this server then refresh")? Sequences multiply the blast radius; a plan-then-confirm flow handles it, but it needs a transaction story for partial failure.
- `mcpx install`: which harnesses, and does the plugin install itself? #47 owns the plugin half (#44 is closed, fixed in #53: the plugin needs no binary).
- Is the route to run a *deterministic* provisioning step better served by the CLI→MCP adapter mechanism (declare `uv`, `git` and `bun` as adapter servers) than by anything bespoke? That would make "clone whatever repo" a declared tool with declared parameters and no shell escape — `internal/adapter`'s stated design goal is exactly "not a general shell escape". Likely yes, and it is cheap.

## Ease · Impact · Related

**Ease** L overall; the session/detach operations are **M**, the prompt-routing layer is **M** given `/v1/intent` exists, `mcpx install` is **M**, and provisioning is **L–XL** and should be split out · **Impact** medium-high — mostly it makes an existing surface reachable by people who do not have the ops table memorised, which is the actual complaint.

**Depends on / related**: #76 (**hard prerequisite**, in flight with SURFACES: CLI parity for `/v1`-only ops — the same rule, and the table the op annotations live in), #111 (owns the autonomy dial `plan` must adopt — #181 collision 3), #185 (owns `ClampedBy` — collision 5), #41 (closed, fixed in #58: `/v1/intent`, recipe matching, elicitation defaults — this extends all three), #6 (event store, for session resume), #78 (daemon state/cache correctness), #5 (config chain, for `persist` scoping), #52 (closed, fixed in #182 with `stop --all` over the daemon info files and a 60 s idle exit — existing operations, so it no longer argues for the session operations here), #103/#104 (managed provisioning). Siblings: #110 (the router's model), #112 (the dependency-provisioning example), #115 (`intent --scope ops` is what acts on its feedback).

Security/auth deferred; see tracker.

code.title: mcpx: lifecycle hooks on exec — prePrompt/postPrompt/onError as one declared list, script or prompt, with a declared effect
code.body:
Relocated from dezren39/nix#112 on 2026-10-28 (placement audit): mcpx's single source lives in developing-today/code (pkgs/mcpx); re-home tracked at #309. Original body below; issue references inside it are historical (dezren39/nix numbering).

Parent: #176

## Summary

`mcpx exec` runs a script and returns what it produced. This asks for the caller to be able to attach natural-language instructions to the *edges* of that run — before it, after it, on failure, on success — so the deterministic script stays deterministic and the fuzzy parts sit outside it.

That is a better factoring than it first appears. The script is the part that must be reproducible; "make sure these dependencies exist wherever this runs" and "clean up the results and transform them" are the parts that legitimately vary by environment and by caller. Keeping them out of the script means the same script file works everywhere and the variation is in the *options*, which is exactly the shape `ExecOptions` was designed for (#40, step 7: "not a new method, an option").

## Original notes

> - mcp-owned opencode api support
>   - accept prompt/prePrompt/postPrompt/onErrorPrompt/onSuccessPrompt
>     - the script interface just runs the scripts, but you can provide a prePrompt saying hey i added a bunch of dependencies please make sure they exist where the job runs, postPrompt to clean up the results and transform, either prompt/pre/post could say to fix error thing but onError gets provided above or below the error and is first seen with the error if theres an error. prompts can use templatevars to put content where they want it or for prompt overall to be stopped/resumed maybe.

## Current state (what mcpx does today, with file refs)

- **`execsvc.Options`** (`internal/execsvc/execsvc.go:101`) is the designated growth point: "Deliberately one flat struct that grows rather than a new endpoint per capability." It carries `Runtime`, `Timeout`, `Permissions`, `Placeholders`, `Session`, `Cwd`, `Env`, `Stdin`, `Output`, `Capabilities`, `Artifacts`, `Task`, `NS`, `Args`, `Export`. There are no prompt fields.
- **Placeholders already exist and already have substitution semantics worth copying.** Recipes declare holes in a header comment (`// @param repo:string`) and reference them as `@repo`; values are substituted **as JSON, never as text**, because "a recipe runs with the user's credentials; raw substitution would make every placeholder an injection site" (`docs/consumer.md` §3). Launchers use the same `@placeholder` spelling (#7). A recipe with an unfilled required hole is an invalid script, which is the right way round.
- **`ScriptConfig.Prefix`** (`internal/config/config.go:236-248`) already layers *code* in front of a script from config, resolved across the config chain (`docs/proposals.md` §"Layered script prefixes"). It is the deterministic sibling of a prePrompt and the precedent for how layering should work.
- **Deterministic edge hooks already ship — for the CLI and config, not for `/v1/exec`.** (Added in the 2026-09-30 issues pass, at 05c78b2; this issue predated them being noticed.) Five settings — `script.before`, `script.prefix`, `script.onSuccess`, `script.onError`, `script.suffix` (`internal/settings/registry.go:212-242`), layered through `ScriptConfig` (`internal/config/config.go:236-257`) and rendered as `runner.Phases` (`internal/runner/runner.go:190-205`) — inject source into a file script's launcher: `onSuccess` sees `result.value`, `onError` sees `result.error` and **the error is rethrown** ("a hook, not a handler"), `suffix` runs in a `finally`. They run inside the script's own process, and they are deliberately **not** on the wire `Options`: `execsvc.RunWith` keeps phases CLI-only (`internal/execsvc/execsvc.go:358-366`). So Approach B below is partly built already, in a different shape; what is missing is per-call hooks over `/v1` and MCP, a typed context, and prompt hooks. The shipped names are one of the four hook vocabularies in #181 collision 2.
- **The exec stream has an ordering contract**: `start`, then `log`/`emit`/`stdout` interleaved, then `artifact`, then `result` or `error`, then `end`, with bodies strictly after `end` (`execsvc.Frame`, `docs/exec.md`). Any hook output has to find a place in that order, and that is a real design constraint, not a formality.
- **`internal/diagnose`** produces structured diagnostics that already sit next to an error.
- **Tasks** (`internal/tasks`) provide the pause/resume machinery the note's "stopped/resumed maybe" is reaching for, and `2026-07-28`'s MRTR pattern gives a caller-facing way to resume a request mid-flight.
- mcpx has no model; see #110. Every rung below degrades to a no-op without one.

## Approaches

### Approach A — least recommended: five new string options, each handed to a model, each running arbitrary code

`Options.Prompt`, `.PrePrompt`, `.PostPrompt`, `.OnErrorPrompt`, `.OnSuccessPrompt`, each sent to a model with a general-purpose agent loop that can do whatever it decides is needed.

Why not:

- **Four of the five are the same thing at different times.** Five independent fields means five code paths, five sets of semantics, and five places to fix a bug. Lifecycle hooks are a list of (phase, instruction), and modelling them as one list with a phase is strictly better — `prompt` is then just "the phase is `main`", which is also what makes "either prompt/pre/post could say to fix error thing" fall out naturally instead of needing to be special-cased.
- **An unbounded prePrompt is arbitrary code execution as a side door.** "make sure these dependencies exist where the job runs" resolved by a general agent means installing packages, which is the provisioning problem from #113 and needs its own confinement decisions. An exec option should not quietly be the more powerful interface.
- **It puts the model on the default path.** Every run pays a round trip even when the hooks do nothing surprising. `docs/consumer.md`'s rule — "never sample on a path that doesn't need it" — is violated by construction if hooks are evaluated eagerly.
- **Nothing is reproducible.** The same script plus the same prompts gives different behaviour run to run, which destroys the one property that makes `exec` worth having over a chat turn.

### Approach B — middle: one `hooks` list, deterministic hooks only

Add one field:

```jsonc
"options": {
  "hooks": [
    { "phase": "pre",     "script": "ensure-deps.ts" },
    { "phase": "post",    "script": "normalise.ts" },
    { "phase": "onError", "script": "cleanup.ts" }
  ]
}
```

Phases: `pre`, `main`, `post`, `onError`, `onSuccess`. Each hook is a script, run in the same content-addressed workdir with the same runtime and permissions, receiving a typed context (the run id, the result or the error plus its `diagnose.Diagnostic`, the artifact list). `post` transforms the result; `onError` sees the error first and may return a replacement result or re-raise — which differs from the shipped `script.onError`, where the error always propagates.

**The phase names and hook semantics are not this issue's to decide (#181 collision 2).** Four vocabularies exist or are proposed — the shipped `script.*` phases, #81's hook points, #82's runtime hooks and this list — and the one vocabulary is being decided in a decision record SURFACES is writing under `pkgs/mcpx/docs/decisions/`, carried by #81. The phases here are input to that record; this issue adopts what it decides.

This is genuinely useful on its own — `ScriptConfig.Prefix` proves the demand for "run this code around my code" and hooks generalise it to the other three edges — and it is the thing the prompt version needs underneath it anyway, because a prompt hook's output has to *become* something executable. It is also fully deterministic, cacheable, and testable.

What it does not give you is the actual ask: "hey i added a bunch of dependencies please make sure they exist where the job runs" is a sentence, not a script, and the whole point is not having to write the script.

### Approach C — recommended: one `hooks` list where a hook is *either* a script or a prompt, with a declared effect

Build B's structure, and let each entry be a script **or** a prompt:

```jsonc
"options": {
  "hooks": [
    { "phase": "pre",     "prompt": "I added @deps — make sure they exist where this runs",
                          "effect": "script", "model": "cheap" },
    { "phase": "post",    "prompt": "flatten the result to {id, title} and drop nulls",
                          "effect": "transform" },
    { "phase": "onError", "prompt": "if this is a rate limit, wait and say so; otherwise explain",
                          "effect": "advise" }
  ]
}
```

Four decisions make this safe and small:

**1. A hook declares its effect, and the effect bounds what it may do.**

| `effect` | what the hook's output may be | runs code? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `advise` | text, attached to the result or error | no |
| `transform` | a replacement for the result value only | no |
| `script` | TypeScript, diagnosed and typechecked, then run in the same sandbox | yes |
| `retry` | a decision: retry / retry-with-changes / give up | via the repair ladder |

`advise` is the default. This is the same dial as `repair.level` in #111 and should use the same vocabulary; a user who understands one understands the other. **#181 collision 3:** #111 carries that one dial vocabulary, via the SURFACES decision record under `pkgs/mcpx/docs/decisions/`; the `effect` values in this table are input to it, and #112 adopts what it decides rather than shipping its own. The ceiling a daemon puts on it is #185 (collision 5). A prompt hook whose effect is `script` is the only one that can execute anything, and it inherits `Options.Permissions` unchanged — a hook must never be able to do what the script it wraps could not.

**2. Template variables reuse the placeholder machinery that exists, including its safety property.** `@name` is already the spelling in recipes and launchers, and recipe values are **JSON-encoded, not text-substituted**, precisely so a placeholder cannot become an injection site. A prompt is text and the same discipline applies at a different layer: the substituted value must be delimited and marked as data, and a hook prompt must never be able to redefine the hook's own `effect`. Beyond user placeholders, offer a small set of built-ins the note is clearly asking for — `@result`, `@error`, `@diagnostic`, `@calls`, `@artifacts`, `@source` — so "onError gets provided above or below the error" is expressible as `"Here is what happened:\n@error\n@diagnostic\nWhat should I do?"` rather than being a positioning rule mcpx has to guess. **Position by template, not by convention**; when a prompt contains no built-in reference, mcpx appends the context after it, which is the sensible default the note describes.

**3. Hooks are declarable in config, not just per call.** `ScriptConfig.Prefix` and the shipped `script.before`/`onSuccess`/`onError`/`suffix` already layer across the config chain; `script.hooks` (or whatever collision 2's record names it) should layer the same way, so "always check dependencies before any run in this project" is written once. Per-call hooks append to config hooks rather than replacing them, with the same nearest-wins resolution `ResolveLines` already implements.

**4. Stop/resume is `internal/tasks`, not a new mechanism.** "for prompt overall to be stopped/resumed maybe" — a hook that needs a decision raises an elicitation through the existing broker (with a default and a deadline, as `elicit.Ask` enforces), and a run that must wait becomes a task with a handle, collectable from `/v1/tasks/{id}`. Both already exist and both already work for the recipe path. On `2026-07-28` this is also exactly MRTR: `resultType: "input_required"`, the client answers, the request is retried.

**Stream placement**, since the `Frame` order is a contract (`docs/exec.md:137`). **#181 collision 7:** #111 owns the rule every new frame kind follows (declared placement relative to `result`, listed in the documented order, asserted by a test comparing documented and emitted order); the `hook` frame is added under that rule and the placement below is input to it: a hook emits `log`/`emit`/`stdout` frames tagged with its phase and a `hook` frame recording phase, effect, model used, duration and whether it changed anything. `pre` frames come after `start`; `post`/`onSuccess` frames come after the `result` frame and before `end`; `onError` frames come after `error` and before `end`. The final `result` reflects a `transform` hook's output, with the original preserved in the `hook` frame — a caller must be able to see what mcpx changed.

**Cost and default posture.** Hooks are off unless declared. A prompt hook without an available model is a warning on the run, not a failure — the script still ran, and that is the honest degradation. `pre` hooks with `effect: script` should be cached by (prompt, placeholder values, catalogue fingerprint) so the same "ensure my dependencies" instruction resolves to the same generated script on every run instead of re-generating it; that caching is also what makes the generated script reviewable and promotable to a real hook script, which is how this feature should be expected to be *used* — prompt once, keep the script.

Recommended because the structure is one list rather than five fields, because effect-declaration is what keeps a convenience feature from being an execution back door, because everything it needs — placeholders, prefixes, tasks, elicitation, diagnostics, artifacts — already exists and this mostly wires them to four new points in time, and because the deterministic half (Approach B) is independently valuable and ships first.

## Open questions

- Does `onSuccess` earn its own phase when `post` exists? `post` running only on success and `onError` on failure covers it; a separate `onSuccess` is only distinct if `post` is meant to run on both. Pick one and document it — this is the note's ambiguity, not a design difficulty.
- Ordering when several hooks share a phase: declaration order across config layers, or an explicit `order`? Declaration order plus nearest-wins layering matches `ScriptPrefix`.
- Should a `transform` hook be allowed to change artifacts, or only the result value? Only the value is far simpler and probably enough.
- Timeout accounting: does a hook's time count against `Options.Timeout` or get its own budget? Its own, or a slow model silently eats the script's budget.
- Is there a case for hooks on a *tool call* rather than a run (`before every call to this server, ...`)? That is closer to a server-level middleware feature and may belong with tool views.
- Should a hook be able to abort the run before it starts (`pre` returning refuse)? Useful and cheap, but then a `pre` hook is a policy mechanism and needs the floor/ceiling clamping #185 owns.

## Ease · Impact · Related

**Ease** M (S for the deterministic half — much of it already ships as `script.*` launcher phases, so what remains is exposing them per call with a typed context; M with prompt hooks and effects; L if stop/resume gets its own machinery rather than reusing tasks) · **Impact** medium-high — it is what makes one script file portable across environments without the script knowing where it runs, which is the same goal #40 had for artifacts.

**Depends on / related**: #81 (owns the hook vocabulary via the SURFACES decision record — #181 collision 2), #111 (owns the autonomy dial and the frame-order rule — collisions 3 and 7), #185 (owns `ClampedBy` — collision 5), #82 (runtime hook registration, the fourth vocabulary), #40 (closed, fixed in #57: ExecOptions is the home; "not a new method, an option" is the governing precedent), #41 (closed, fixed in #58: placeholders, elicitation defaults/deadlines, diagnostics as hook context), #7 (launcher `@placeholder` spelling), #5 (config chain, for layered hooks), #79 (hook cost must not regress exec latency). Siblings: #110 (where a prompt hook's model comes from), #113 (the dependency-provisioning half of the `pre` example; also #103/#104 in #175).

Security/auth deferred; see tracker.

code.title: mcpx: checking, refusing and repairing a request — a graded ladder from deterministic diagnostics to rewrite-and-run
code.body:
Relocated from dezren39/nix#111 on 2026-10-28 (placement audit): mcpx's single source lives in developing-today/code (pkgs/mcpx); re-home tracked at #309. Original body below; issue references inside it are historical (dezren39/nix numbering).

Parent: #176

## Summary

Today a script that calls a tool wrongly fails at the wrong moment: the error arrives from a server, halfway through, after the side effects of every call before it. `--diagnose-preflight` (#41) fixed the statically-detectable half. This issue is the rest of it — a graded ladder of what mcpx does when a request is *probably* wrong, from "refuse it deterministically" through "ask the caller" to "rewrite it and run the rewrite", with the escalation policy as a setting rather than a hard-coded behaviour.

The unifying idea: **an execution outcome should be a structured verdict, not a boolean.** "It failed" loses the fact that eleven of twelve calls succeeded, which of them had side effects, what specifically was wrong with the twelfth, and what the minimal fix is. mcpx already computes most of those facts and throws them away.

## Original notes

> - mcp-owned opencode api support
>   - receive errors check io and elicit/prompt caller, or fix-retry, clean up return what worked with explanation of what happened, pass-through
>   - check inputs, reject any request with/without reason, prompt 'hey are you sure? you did this and that maybe doesnt do what you think', 'hey i mean this probably cant work because y', or it can look at a script and say 'oh, they used search instead of query, query is only thing that makes sense here and they used the args for query, i'll rewrite the script and run that instead (or offer alternative ask them), user can just tell it what to do and then mcpx does the ai part/script-selection, or write a lazy psuedocode script mixing 4 languages and calling packages from different ecosystems and it puts together best it can with some guidance/instruction/accuracy/precision/strictness either decline, propose script ask for approval, emit scriptfile and return fileid, decide to run first part first thats safer, implement a dry-run and try that, disregard users attempt and exec/make/suggest what they actually want.
>     - need ways for server and client both to control their section maybe need auth

## Current state (what mcpx does today, with file refs)

A surprising amount of the deterministic half already exists and is not yet connected.

| piece | where | state |
| --- | --- | --- |
| static scan of a script for tool calls | `internal/diagnose`, `internal/preflight` | works; `--diagnose-preflight` on by default for `run`/`exec` |
| schema history, so "when did this change" is answerable | `<state>/catalog-history.json`, `internal/diagnose` | works; appends every flattened-shape change per tool |
| a missing-required-argument diagnostic with a minimal fix | `internal/diagnose` | works — `demo.echo: the argument object is no longer optional: message is required` + `minimum: await demo.echo({ message: "" })` |
| **the upstream half** — catching a `-32602` from a live call and diagnosing it | `diagnose.CallError` (`internal/diagnose/diagnose.go:483` at 05c78b2) | **exists, tested, and at 05c78b2 nothing outside tests calls it.** Wiring it is #116, in flight with SURFACES; when it lands, rung 0 below is done and the structured diagnostic field it attaches is the one every rung here reads rather than redefines. `docs/consumer.md` §1: "the code path that would — the exec service catching a `-32602` from a tool call — is being rebuilt concurrently. The signature is deliberately a plain struct in, diagnostics out." Wiring it is one call. |
| destructive-call confirmation | `elicit.confirmDestructive` (`internal/settings/consumer.go:47`), `internal/elicit/policy.go` | works, off by default; fires on `destructiveHint: true`; an unanswered confirmation **refuses** the call |
| disambiguation elicitation | `elicit.disambiguate` | works, off by default; unanswered takes `elicit.disambiguateDefault: new` |
| `--typecheck` | `deno check`, Deno only | ~80ms repeat, ~400ms new program (#79 proposes making it default) |
| recipe matching + intent-to-script | `/v1/intent`, `internal/recipes` | works; generation off by default; generated script is diagnosed before it runs |
| structured exec output | `execsvc.Frame` (`internal/execsvc/execsvc.go:145`) | `start`, `log`, `emit`, `stdout`, `artifact`, `result`/`error`, `end` — a per-call record is **not** among them |
| artifacts | #40 | a script can emit a file and return an id rather than content |

Known limits the scanner already states, and which any repair feature inherits: it does not parse TypeScript, a dynamically assembled call is invisible to it, a spread in an argument object silences the missing-argument check entirely, and only configured namespaces are diagnosed. Those are correct failures — a diagnostic about a call nobody wrote is worse than none — and repair must fail the same way.

## Approaches

### Approach A — least recommended: send the error and the script to a model and run whatever comes back

The literal reading of "i'll rewrite the script and run that instead". One prompt, one retry loop, done.

Why not:

- **It runs with the user's credentials.** `docs/consumer.md`'s trust rule — return the script by default, run only on explicit request — exists for exactly this. A silent rewrite-and-rerun is the single highest-blast-radius thing in this whole theme.
- **Retry is not idempotent.** A script that failed at call 9 of 12 has already done 8 things. Re-running the whole script from the top repeats them. Nothing in mcpx currently knows which of those 8 were safe to repeat; `destructiveHint` is the only signal and it is optional and sparsely set.
- **It skips the free answer.** The most common failure is a schema change, and mcpx can already name it exactly, with the date, for nothing. A model rewording that is pure cost. `docs/consumer.md` §"Not built" says this directly: "the value is in the error being specific, not in a model rewording it."
- **It has no confidence signal.** "they used `search` instead of `query`" is a high-confidence, near-deterministic fix. "mixing 4 languages and calling packages from different ecosystems" is not. Treating both as one operation means either refusing the easy case or running the hard one.

### Approach B — middle: a deterministic repair ladder, no model

Everything the note asks for that needs no model at all, which is more than it looks:

1. **Wire `diagnose.CallError`** — this item is #116 (in flight), listed here because the ladder starts from it. The exec service catches `-32602` from a tool call and attaches the diagnostic to the failing call. This is the single highest-value item in the issue and it is one function call; it is listed first for that reason.
2. **Per-call records in the exec stream.** A new `Frame` type — `call` — carrying server, tool, arguments hash, duration, ok/error, and `destructiveHint`. That makes "clean up return what worked with explanation of what happened" mechanically possible: the caller receives *what succeeded*, in order, with the failure and its diagnostic attached to the one call that failed, rather than a string. **Owns #181 collision 7:** this issue extends the documented order in `docs/exec.md:137` ("The frame order, and why it is the order") first, and states the rule every new frame kind follows — a declared placement relative to `result`, listed in the documented order, and a test that compares the documented order with the order actually emitted. #112's `hook` frame is added under that rule, not beside it.
3. **Deterministic near-miss detection.** When a call fails with unknown-tool or unknown-argument, mcpx already has the catalogue and can compute the edit-distance-1/2 candidates: `search` → `query`, `olderThan` → `olderThanDays`. That is exactly the note's example, and it needs no model — it needs the same typo tolerance the search issue proposes, applied to error messages. When there is exactly one candidate within distance 1 and the supplied argument *names* match the candidate's schema, the fix is provably the intended one. **Correction (issues pass, 2026-09-30):** the note's own examples are not typos — `search`→`query` is edit distance 5 and `olderThan`→`olderThanDays` is 4, so no name threshold finds either. Two deterministic signals are needed: *closeness* for genuine typos, which is #186's shared matcher (#181 collision 6; one definition for search, diagnostics and the launcher), and *argument-shape fit* for substitutions — the supplied argument names satisfy exactly one other tool's schema in the namespace, or a supplied name is a prefix of exactly one declared parameter. The second is this issue's; the first it calls.
4. **Argument validation before the wire.** mcpx has every tool's input schema. Validating arguments against it locally turns a round trip and a server-side rejection into an instant, specific local error, and catches the extra-property and wrong-type cases the current preflight does not. (Note `2026-07-28` loosened `inputSchema` to any JSON Schema 2020-12 keywords, so the validator needs to be a real one, not a shape check.)
5. **Dry run.** `ExecOptions.dryRun`: run the script with every tool call intercepted, returning a schema-valid synthetic result and recording what *would* have been called. The static scanner cannot see dynamic calls; a dry run sees all of them, at the cost of the results being fake. This is the note's "implement a dry-run and try that", it is deterministic, and it is independently useful for the prompt-hooks and recipe features.
6. **Safe-prefix execution.** "decide to run first part first thats safer" — with `destructiveHint` and a read-only/idempotent annotation, mcpx can execute up to the first destructive call and stop for confirmation. `elicit.confirmDestructive` already does the per-call version; this is the batched one, and batching matters because four deadlines are four chances for a run to die half-configured (the same reasoning that made recipe placeholders one form).
7. **Refusal with a reason.** `internal/elicit` already distinguishes cancel from decline; errors should carry a machine-readable `reason` code alongside prose, so a caller can branch on it. "reject any request with/without reason" is a request for *structured* refusals.

All of this is testable, free, offline, and reusable by every other feature in the theme.

### Approach C — recommended: B first, then a strictly-graded model layer above it, with the grade as a setting

Build B. Then add the model-backed rungs, and make the thing that decides which rung applies a single explicit setting rather than a behaviour baked into each code path.

**The escalation ladder**, in order, each rung only reached when the one below produced nothing:

| rung | model? | what it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 deterministic diagnostic | no | today's schema-change and missing-argument messages |
| 1 deterministic near-miss | no | one candidate by #186's closeness or by argument-shape fit, argument names corroborate |
| 2 explain | yes | a sentence saying *why* this probably will not work, attached to the error; changes nothing |
| 3 warn / confirm | yes | "you did this and that, maybe doesn't do what you think" — raised through the **existing elicitation broker** with a default and a deadline, exactly as `elicit.Ask` already enforces |
| 4 propose | yes | emit a rewritten script as an **artifact** (#40) and return its id; the caller reviews and runs it |
| 5 repair-and-retry | yes | rewrite and re-run, only when the failure is provably side-effect-free or the caller opted in |
| 6 reinterpret | yes | "disregard users attempt and exec/make/suggest what they actually want" — this is `/v1/intent` with the failed attempt as context, not a new feature |

**One setting governs how far it goes**: `repair.level` (`off | explain | confirm | propose | retry | rewrite`), default `explain`, scoped per call so `ExecOptions` can lower it. The note's "some guidance/instruction/accuracy/precision/strictness" is asking for a dial; make it one dial with named stops, not five booleans. **Owns #181 collision 3:** this is one of three autonomy dials (with #112's hook `effect` and #113's `prompt.mode: plan`), and this issue carries the single vocabulary. The vocabulary itself is being decided in a decision record SURFACES is writing under `pkgs/mcpx/docs/decisions/` (not merged at 05c78b2; linked here when it is) — the stops above are this issue's input to it, not the decision. The ceiling that stops a caller raising the dial is #185.

**The delivery vehicle for rung 4 is already built.** A proposed script is an artifact: `artifact("repair.ts", src)` returns an id, the caller fetches it, nothing large enters anyone's context, and `POST /v1/recipes/{name}` already exists to save a successful one as a reusable recipe. "emit scriptfile and return fileid" is #40 plus #41 wired together, not new machinery.

**The pseudocode case is `/v1/intent` with a source, not a repair.** "write a lazy psuedocode script mixing 4 languages and calling packages from different ecosystems and it puts together best it can" is intent-to-script where the intent happens to be written as code. It should route to the same generator, with the pseudocode as the prompt, and inherit `prompt.mode: script` — return the script, do not run it. Worth noting what makes this tractable in mcpx specifically and not elsewhere: the *target* language is fixed (TypeScript against the generated client), the tool surface is known and typed, and `--typecheck` plus `internal/diagnose` can verify the output before a human sees it. Multi-ecosystem package resolution is a different and much harder problem — see the environment-provisioning half of the self-administration issue.

**On "receive errors check io".** Before any model is consulted, the deterministic check is whether the *transport* failed rather than the call: a dead server process, a broken pipe, an expired credential, a timeout. Those look like tool errors to a script and have completely different fixes. `internal/pool` and `/v1/health` know which; the diagnostic should say "the server exited" rather than diagnosing an argument that was fine. This is cheap and should come before rung 0.

**On "pass-through".** Every rung must be defeatable. A caller that wants the raw upstream error, unmodified, with no mcpx opinion attached, sets `repair.level: off` and gets exactly the bytes the server sent. This is not a nicety — an agent harness doing its own error handling is actively harmed by a rewritten error, and mcpx's value proposition is that it does not surprise you.

**On the nested bullet — "need ways for server and client both to control their section maybe need auth".** Security is out of scope, but the *non*-security half of this is a real and separable design question: **whose policy wins when the daemon and the caller disagree?** `internal/settings` already has scopes (`ScopeDaemon`, `ScopeCall`, `Hot`) and `elicit.confirmDestructive` is deliberately `ScopeDaemon` — `docs/consumer.md`: "Whether a destructive call is confirmed is not a question with two correct answers depending on which process asked." The right generalisation is that each repair setting declares a **floor and a ceiling**: the daemon sets the maximum autonomy it will ever exercise, a caller may lower it but never raise it above the daemon's ceiling, and the resolved value plus which layer set it is reported in the response. That is a settings-registry feature (a `ClampedBy` field), not an auth feature, and it is worth having independently of any credential work. **This paragraph is now input to #185**, which owns the mechanism (#181 collision 5); this issue, #112 and #113 consume it rather than each implementing a clamp.

Recommended because rung 0 and rung 1 answer the common cases for free, because every model-backed rung degrades to the rung below it on failure rather than to nothing, because "propose" rather than "retry" as the highest default preserves the trust rule that already exists, and because one named dial is a thing a user can reason about where five independent behaviours is not.

## Open questions

- Should `call` frames be on by default or behind a capability, the way artifacts are (`Options.Capabilities`)? Default-on is more useful; it changes the stream shape for existing consumers.
- Is there an idempotency signal better than `destructiveHint`? MCP tool annotations also carry `readOnlyHint` and `idempotentHint`; both are optional and sparsely set. A config-level per-tool override (like tags in the search issue) may be necessary for rung 5 to ever be safe.
- Dry run semantics: what does a synthetic result look like for a tool with no `outputSchema`? Probably refuse to dry-run those rather than invent a shape.
- Does repair need the *session's* history, or only the failing script? History makes rung 6 much better and is a large context and privacy increase.
- How does a repaired script relate to the original in the artifact store — a parent link, a diff, or an independent id?
- `2026-07-28` renumbers error codes (`-32020`..`-32099` reserved for the spec). Does the `-32602` catch need widening, and does resource-not-found's move from `-32002` to `-32602` change what a `-32602` means? Overlaps #77. #116 (in flight) has to take a position on this for rung 0 — which codes `CallError` reads as "the arguments were wrong" — and the ladder should inherit it rather than decide it again.

## Ease · Impact · Related

**Ease** L overall; the first two items (wire `diagnose.CallError` — now #116's, in flight — and add `call` frames) are **S** and should ship independently of everything else here · **Impact** high — this is the difference between "it failed" and "here is what worked, here is exactly what was wrong, here is the one-line fix".

**Depends on / related**: #116 (wires `diagnose.CallError` — rung 0; in flight), #186 (owns the near-miss matcher rung 1 calls — #181 collision 6), #185 (owns `ClampedBy` — collision 5), #41 (closed, fixed in #58: diagnose, `CallError`, recipes, intent — this is the direct continuation), #40 (closed, fixed in #57: artifacts as the vehicle for a proposed script; ExecOptions as the place `dryRun`/`repair` live), #79 (typecheck by default; repair depends on cheap validation), #78 (daemon state/cache correctness — the schema cache trap in `docs/consumer.md` silently disabled the destructive policy once already), #77 (error-code renumbering). Siblings: #110 (where rungs 2–6 get a model), #112 (`onErrorPrompt` is the user-supplied version of rung 2; adopts this issue's dial and frame rule — collisions 3 and 7), #113 (`prompt.mode: plan` adopts the dial), #109 (shares #186's matcher).

Security/auth deferred; see tracker.

code.title: mcpx: where the model comes from — a provider layer mcpx owns, model profiles, and life after MCP Sampling's deprecation
code.body:
Relocated from dezren39/nix#110 on 2026-10-28 (placement audit): mcpx's single source lives in developing-today/code (pkgs/mcpx); re-home tracked at #309. Original body below; issue references inside it are historical (dezren39/nix numbering).

Parent: #176

## Summary

mcpx has no model and deliberately never had one: `docs/consumer.md` records that "a configured provider with an API key, was not built and should not be. It is the one that makes mcpx an agent." Everything model-shaped in mcpx today borrows the caller's model through MCP sampling.

Two facts have changed since that was written, and together they invert the conclusion:

1. **MCP deprecated Sampling in `2026-07-28.**` The spec changelog's Deprecated section, item 1 (SEP-2577) deprecates Roots, Sampling and Logging, and names the migration explicitly: *"integrate directly with LLM provider APIs instead of Sampling."* Sampling is not the long-term channel; the spec says so.
2. **Nothing in the opencode line will ever send mcpx a sampling request.** `docs/opencode-plugin.md` §2.6: neither v1 nor v2 declares the `sampling` capability. v1 comments it out with issue links; v2 declares `roots` + `elicitation` only. The primary consumer of mcpx cannot answer the channel mcpx's only model path depends on.

So the question this issue settles is not "should mcpx sample?" — it is "where does mcpx's AI layer get a model, what does it expose, and how does it stay from becoming a second agent harness?"

## Original notes

> - mcp-owned opencode api support
>   - support multiple providers/models
>   - name priority sets of models as an 'agent'
>   - ? just embed opencode and call it? is there a golang or rust opencode? 
>   - proxy
>   - respond to elicit/prompt

## Current state (what mcpx does today, with file refs)

| capability | where | state |
| --- | --- | --- |
| sampling passthrough (upstream server → mcpx → caller) | `internal/elicit`, `docs/protocol.md` §4.1 | works; a decline becomes an error, since the spec has no decline result for sampling |
| sampling declared upstream | `docs/protocol.md:271`; `internal/mcpclient/modern.go:46-57` | `sampling` declared to servers only when a handler is installed — and the daemon always installs one (`internal/daemon/hooks.go:69` → `internal/pool/pool.go:393-397`), so in practice **every upstream server is told sampling works**, whether or not any caller can answer. `roots` is declared unconditionally (`modern.go:52`) and is deprecated by the same SEP. |
| sampling raised by mcpx itself | `/v1/intent`, `prompt.sample` (`internal/settings/consumer.go:105`) | exists, **off by default** (`never`) |
| the catalogue slice sent with a generation request | `prompt.catalogBudget` (`:119`), `prompt.maxTokens` (`:134`), `prompt.sampleTimeout` (`:127`) | bounded; sends the ranked slice and nothing else |
| generated script is validated before running | `internal/diagnose` preflight, `prompt.mode` (`:97`) default `script` | returns the script; runs only on explicit request |
| answering an elicitation as a client | `mcpx elicit`, `GET/POST /v1/elicit*`, the plugin | works; the broker is the store and the fallback |
| a model of mcpx's own | — | **none** |
| `logging` declared as a server | `internal/mcpserver/server.go:566` | **no longer declared** since #171 (mcpx sends no `notifications/message`); `logging/setLevel` still answers. `docs/protocol.md` §2.2 still shows it declared for three revisions — stale. |

`Server.execScript` running a recipe from the daemon is marked in `docs/consumer.md` as "a seam, not a design", pending `POST /v1/exec` — which now exists (`internal/api/ops_exec.go:12`). That seam should close as part of any work here; at 05c78b2 it still calls `internal/runner` directly (`internal/daemon/consumer.go:509-517`).

`docs/consumer.md:192-198` still says a configured provider "was not built and should not be. It is the one that makes mcpx an agent." SEP-2577 names exactly that as the migration from Sampling, so that sentence must change in the same change that lands whatever this issue decides — otherwise it is another #159-class contradiction.

(Checked at 05c78b2. The PROTOCOL work in flight — conformance against the official schemas and a modern-first era probe — touches `internal/mcpclient`, `internal/pool` and `docs/protocol.md`; the capability rows above may change when it lands. Nothing in the recommendation depends on them.)

## What "is there a golang or rust opencode" actually resolves to

Checked, because it decides the whole shape:

| candidate | language | what it is | usable as a library inside mcpx? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **sst/opencode** | TypeScript/Bun | the opencode mcpx already plugs into | No. It is an application, and embedding it means shipping Bun. |
| **charmbracelet/crush** | **Go**, ~28k stars | *literally the original Go opencode codebase*, renamed after the 2025 split (maintainers' own words in charmbracelet/crush#1097: "Crush is the continuation of the original OpenCode project… sst/opencode is a fork of that repo") | Practically no. It is a TUI application, not a library; its packages are internal-shaped; and the repo is **source-available, not OSI** (GitHub reports the licence as `NOASSERTION`), which is a distribution problem for a Nix-packaged binary. |
| **Google ADK for Go** | Go | `go get google.golang.org/adk` — first-party, model-agnostic, MCP + tool-calling + multi-agent | Yes, technically. Heavy. |
| **Microsoft Agent Framework for Go** | Go | first-party, public preview since July 2026 | Yes. Preview-grade; missing RAG/CodeAct/declarative agents. |
| **cloudwego/eino** | Go, ~12k stars | LangGraph-like graphs, typed `ChatModel`/`Tool`/`Retriever`, ReAct + DeepAgent, Apache-2.0 | Yes. The most capable OSS Go option. |
| **tmc/langchaingo** | Go, ~9k stars | broadest provider/vector-store surface, pre-1.0 (v0.1.14) | Yes, with API churn. |
| **firebase/genkit** (Go) | Go | 1.0 GA, flows + dev UI + built-in OpenTelemetry | Yes. |
| **openai/openai-go**, **anthropics/anthropic-sdk-go**, **googleapis/go-genai** | Go | plain provider clients, no agent loop | Yes, and this is the low-dependency option. |
| Rust | — | `rmcp` (official MCP SDK), `rig`; OpenAI's Codex CLI is Rust. No Rust opencode. | irrelevant — mcpx is Go |

Two conclusions worth stating plainly:

- **The answer to "is there a golang opencode" is yes, and it is Crush** — but it is an app under a source-available licence, not a library, so "just embed opencode and call it" is not available in the form the note imagines.
- **OpenAI and Anthropic still ship no first-party Go *agent* SDK** (Python/TS only, as of mid-2026). Their plain Go clients exist and are fine. So an mcpx AI layer built on provider clients plus a hand-written loop is not a second-class choice in Go; for a single model with a handful of tools, the loop is ~40 lines and owning it beats adopting a framework.

## Approaches

### Approach A — least recommended: embed or shell out to an agent application

Ship Crush (or opencode, or `claude -p`) as a subprocess and hand it the prompt. Superficially the cheapest thing: no provider plumbing, no loop, someone else's model config.

Why not:

- **Licence and packaging.** Crush is source-available (`NOASSERTION`); opencode means shipping Bun. mcpx's whole distribution story is one Go binary plus a Nix derivation, and #44 (closed, fixed in #53) spent real effort making the *plugin* binary-free. Adding a mandatory agent binary reverses that.
- **It is the harness, twice.** The agent app has its own config, its own model list, its own MCP client, its own permission model, its own sessions. mcpx would then have two of each, disagreeing. `docs/consumer.md`'s scope concern — "anything that makes mcpx call a model has to justify that it isn't rebuilding the harness" — is violated maximally here: you have not avoided rebuilding the harness, you have adopted a whole second one.
- **No structured control.** You cannot bound the token budget, pin a model per operation, or get a typed result. You get whatever the app printed.
- It does, however, have one genuine merit worth preserving as a *fallback*: for a user who already runs opencode, "use the model opencode is already configured with" is exactly right — which is what the v2 plugin's `ctx.generate.text` gives, without the subprocess. See C.

### Approach B — middle: a Go agent framework (eino / ADK-Go / Genkit) as mcpx's AI layer

Adopt one framework, get the ReAct loop, tool-calling, streaming, interrupt/resume and multi-agent orchestration for free, and map "an agent" (the note's named priority set of models) onto the framework's agent type.

Facts and opinions:

- **eino** is the strongest OSS option: Apache-2.0, typed components, real graph orchestration with branching and human-in-the-loop interrupt/resume — and interrupt/resume maps *exactly* onto mcpx's existing elicitation broker and `2026-07-28` MRTR input-required flow, which is a genuine architectural fit rather than a coincidence. **ADK-Go** and **Microsoft Agent Framework for Go** are first-party and better-supported bets but Gemini-first / Azure-first respectively, and the Go builds trail their Python siblings. **Genkit Go** is 1.0 GA and brings OpenTelemetry tracing — which mcpx would otherwise hand-roll onto `/v1/log` and `/v1/stats`.
- The real cost is **dependency weight and gravity**. A framework brings a provider registry, a message type, a streaming abstraction and a state model, and every one of them competes with something mcpx already has: `internal/tasks`, `internal/elicit`, `internal/logstore`, `internal/execsvc`'s `Frame` stream. The seams between "mcpx's stream" and "the framework's stream" are where this gets expensive.
- It also over-buys. mcpx's model jobs are all *small and one-shot*: expand a search query, generate a script from an intent, explain an error, propose a repair, draft an adapter spec. None of them is an agent loop. A graph framework for five one-shot completions is the wrong ratio.
- Worth revisiting if mcpx ever wants a genuinely agentic operation (the "install any language/tool/framework/library" case in #113 is the one candidate).

### Approach C — recommended: a thin provider interface mcpx owns, with sampling and the plugin as two of several backends

One internal package — call it `internal/model` — with one small interface, roughly:

```go
type Provider interface {
    Name() string
    Generate(ctx context.Context, req Request) (Response, error) // messages, maxTokens, stop, optional JSON schema
}
```

and several implementations, chosen by configuration:

| backend | when it is right | notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **sampling through the broker** (today's path) | an MCP client that declared `sampling` is driving | keep it; it is correct per the legacy spec and costs nothing. But it is **deprecated in 2026-07-28** and no opencode declares it, so it cannot be the only path. |
| **the opencode plugin answering sampling via `ctx.generate.text`** (opencode v2) | an opencode user, no API key configured | `docs/opencode-plugin.md` §2.5 — v2 plugins get one-shot completion; v1 has no route short of a full agent turn. This makes "use the model my harness already has" real, with no subprocess and no key. Depends on #47. |
| **a configured provider** (`openai-go`, `anthropic-sdk-go`, `go-genai`, or any OpenAI-compatible base URL) | CI, headless, a daemon on another machine, or anyone who just wants it to work | the thing `docs/consumer.md` refused. The 2026-07-28 changelog now names this as *the* migration from Sampling. Reading an existing `OPENAI_API_KEY`/`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`/`OPENAI_BASE_URL` from the environment means most users configure nothing. |
| **an OpenAI-compatible proxy endpoint** | a company gateway, LiteLLM, Ollama, LM Studio, opencode-zen | falls out of the previous row for free — it is a base URL — and is the honest reading of the note's `proxy` bullet, see below. |

**Everything goes through the settings registry, not new endpoints.** `internal/settings` already gives every setting a config key, an `MCPX_*` env var, a CLI flag, `/v1/settings` and an MCP tool, and `prompt.*` is already the precedent. Proposed:

| setting | meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `model.provider` | `auto \| sampling \| plugin \| openai \| anthropic \| google \| none`; `auto` prefers a live sampling-capable client, then the plugin, then a configured key, then fails cleanly |
| `model.baseURL`, `model.apiKeyEnv` | the proxy/compatible-endpoint case |
| `model.default` | the model id used when an operation names none |
| `model.agents.<name>` | **the "agent" concept: a named ordered list of models, tried in order** |
| `model.budget`, `model.timeout` | hard bounds, per the existing `prompt.maxTokens`/`prompt.sampleTimeout` shape |
| `<operation>.model` | per-operation override: `prompt.model`, `search.model`, `repair.model` — each can name a model id *or an agent name* |

**"Name priority sets of models as an 'agent'" is the best idea in this note and should be built literally.** It is a fallback chain plus a policy, and it solves four problems at once that are otherwise solved four times: rate-limit failover, cost tiering (try the cheap local model, escalate on refusal or low confidence), capability routing (this operation needs tool-calling/JSON mode, that one does not), and offline degradation. Define it as:

```jsonc
"model": {
  "agents": {
    "cheap":   { "models": ["ollama/qwen3:8b", "openai/gpt-5-mini"], "maxTokens": 2000 },
    "careful": { "models": ["anthropic/claude-opus-5", "openai/gpt-5"], "temperature": 0 }
  }
}
```

and let every operation take `model: "careful"` or `model: "openai/gpt-5"` interchangeably. Do **not** call it "agent" in the config schema — the word already means something else in every harness mcpx sits under, and mcpx is explicitly not one. `model.profiles` or `model.sets` says the same thing without the collision; keep "agent" as documentation prose if the user prefers it.

**On `proxy`**, the note's bullet has three plausible readings and they should not be conflated:

1. *mcpx points at an OpenAI-compatible proxy* — free, it is `model.baseURL`. Do this.
2. *mcpx **is** an OpenAI-compatible proxy* — it serves `/v1/chat/completions`, forwards to a real provider, and injects mcpx's tools. This is genuinely interesting: it would let any OpenAI-compatible client get mcpx's whole catalogue with no MCP support at all, reusing exactly the pattern `GET /v1/openapi.json` already establishes (one declaration, many surfaces). It is also the single largest scope increase in this issue and should be its own issue if wanted. Note the collision: mcpx's API prefix is already `/v1`, and `POST /v1/chat/completions` would sit inside the ops table's namespace.
3. *mcpx proxies model calls on behalf of scripts* — `await mcpx.model.generate(...)` inside an exec script, so a script can use a model without its own key. This is small, falls out of the `Provider` interface for nearly nothing, and is probably wanted. Put it behind the same off-by-default posture.

**On `respond to elicit/prompt`**, keep the existing direction rules from `docs/protocol.md` §3 and add exactly one thing: when an upstream server sends `sampling/createMessage` and *no* caller can answer, mcpx currently returns an error. With a configured provider it can answer itself — `sampling.answerLocally` (default off), bounded by `model.budget`. That is the case where mcpx-as-a-model genuinely earns its place: the alternative is a failed call. Symmetrically, mcpx may answer an upstream `elicitation/create` from a model only when the question is not a consent question; `internal/elicit/policy.go`'s existing routing rule — a lone boolean `confirm` goes to a **human**, because consent is not the agent's to give — must hold, and a model is even less entitled to give consent than an agent is.

Recommended because it is the smallest thing that removes the hard dependency on a deprecated protocol feature that mcpx's main consumer does not implement; because every existing path (sampling, the plugin) survives as a backend rather than being replaced; because it is all settings, so a user who wants none of it configures nothing and nothing changes; and because it does not make mcpx an agent — it gives mcpx one function, `Generate`, which is what all five of its model-shaped jobs actually need.

### The scope guard, restated

`docs/consumer.md`'s rule should be kept and made checkable: **no mcpx operation may call a model on a path where a deterministic answer exists.** Diagnostics before repair, recipe matching before generation, lexical search before query expansion. The provider layer is a capability, not a strategy; every caller of it should be reviewable as "what happens when this returns an error", and the answer should always be "the deterministic result, plus a sentence saying the model was unavailable."

## Open questions

- Is `model.provider: auto` too clever? An explicit default of `none` (nothing calls a model until you say so) matches `prompt.sample: never` and is more predictable; `auto` is friendlier. Probably `none` for the daemon default and `auto` documented as the recommended setting.
- Should the provider be resolved in the daemon or the CLI? `docs/consumer.md` records that the daemon had no access to settings until #41 folded `settings.Resolve` in; the provider must live daemon-side since `/v1/intent` and the exec service are the callers.
- Does a per-session model override make sense (`_meta["ai.opencode/sessionID"]` from #47 gives session attribution for free)?
- What is the model id namespace? `provider/model` (crush/opencode convention) is the obvious one and makes `model.profiles` entries self-describing.
- Should the seam (`Server.execScript` calling `internal/runner` directly) close onto `POST /v1/exec` as part of this, or separately? It is one function and it is marked.
- Reading `OPENAI_API_KEY` from the ambient environment by default: convenient, or a surprise? Probably opt-in via `model.apiKeyEnv` naming the variable rather than scanning for known ones.

## Ease · Impact · Related

**Ease** L (M for the `Provider` interface + one provider + settings; L including profiles, plugin backend and local sampling answers; XL if mcpx-as-an-OpenAI-proxy is in scope — it should not be, split it) · **Impact** high — every other issue in this theme depends on where the model comes from.

**Depends on / related**: #41 (closed, fixed in #58 and #61: sampling passthrough, `prompt.sample`, `/v1/intent` — this generalises them), #47 (opencode v2 plugin, `ctx.generate.text` backend), #40 (closed, fixed in #57: ExecOptions, the shape settings-not-endpoints follows), #77 (protocol follow-ups — Sampling's deprecation belongs there too), #5 (config chain), #159 (the `docs/consumer.md` provider sentence is an instance), #172 (every `model.*` setting goes through the one registry). Callers of this layer: #109 (query expansion), #111 (rungs 2–6), #112 (prompt hooks), #113 (operation routing), #114 (spec generation).
