code.title: mcpx: a harness-free plugin core, with adapters for codex, claude code, pi, manus
code.body:
Relocated from dezren39/nix#48 on 2026-10-28 (placement audit): mcpx's single source lives in developing-today/code (pkgs/mcpx); re-home tracked at #309. Original body below; issue references inside it are historical (dezren39/nix numbering).

Parent: #181

Backlog. The same plugin is wanted for codex, claude code, pi, manus and others. `pkgs/mcpx/docs/opencode-plugin.md` §5 separates what is general from what is opencode's.

**Shape:** a harness-free core that speaks the daemon's `/v1` API over a unix socket (discovery ladder, client, timing, exec), plus a thin adapter per harness. `plugin/opencode/mcpx/daemon.ts` is already nearly that core; once a second harness exists, move it to `plugin/core/`.

Checked at 05c78b2:

- `daemon.ts` says so itself: "Nothing here imports from opencode … `mcpx-session.ts` is opencode's adapter; this file is the part that ports" (`plugin/opencode/mcpx/daemon.ts:34-38`). It needs no binary: the ladder reads the daemon's info files and dials the socket, and spawns `mcpx --json status` only as rung 4, the last fallback (`plugin/opencode/README.md:83-110`; #53).
- **One runtime assumption to lift first:** the socket client dials through Bun's `fetch({ unix })` (`daemon.ts:335-352`). opencode runs plugins under Bun; a Node-hosted harness needs `node:http` with `socketPath` (or undici's unix dispatcher) behind the same interface.
- #171's guard (`TestThePluginReadsNoUndeclaredSetting`, `internal/settings/consumed_test.go:209-236`) scans all of `plugin/**/*.ts(x)`, so a `plugin/core/` or a second adapter is covered without changes; every variable a new adapter honours must be declared in `internal/settings/plugin.go`.

What an adapter must provide — only the first two are required, everything else degrades:
1. a directory (to resolve which daemon)
2. a session identifier (attribution, leasing, elicitation routing)
3. somewhere to put environment variables, or a way to wrap tool calls
4. a hook after a tool call (timings)
5. a way to show a line of text (ambiguity, warnings)
6. optionally: ask a question; run a model (to answer sampling)

Per harness, research which of these exist and how, before writing any code. Where a harness only supports MCP servers (no plugin API), mcpx-as-MCP-server is the adapter, and the session id should come from request `_meta` where the harness provides one.

No real choice on the shape (core + thin adapters, with mcpx-as-MCP-server as the adapter of last resort); the work is the per-harness research, and it should precede any move of files.

## Ease · Impact · Related

Related: #47 (opencode v2 is the first new adapter), #80 (a plugin's `/v1` back-channel is the same client), #84 (the Go `/v1` client is this core's twin).

code.title: mcpx: port the opencode plugin to opencode v2 (a rewrite, and several things get better)
code.body:
Relocated from dezren39/nix#47 on 2026-10-28 (placement audit): mcpx's single source lives in developing-today/code (pkgs/mcpx); re-home tracked at #309. Original body below; issue references inside it are historical (dezren39/nix numbering).

Parent: #181

Backlog. Findings: `pkgs/mcpx/docs/opencode-plugin.md` §2 and §4.

**v1 plugins do not load in opencode v2** — no shim, no fallback (`packages/core/src/plugin/module.ts:60-73`). v2 needs a rewrite against `{id, setup}`, not a port.

What changes, each better than the v1 equivalent:

| v1 today | v2 |
| --- | --- |
| `shell.env` per command (carries sessionID) | `shell.create.before` has **no sessionID** → use `PUT /api/experimental/session/:id/environment` once per session |
| `experimental.chat.system.transform` | `session.hook("context")` → `event.system` (or a budgeted catalog in `event.tools`, diffed between turns) |
| `tool` map, un-namespaced | `tool.transform(e => e.add(...))` with a namespace |
| `tool.execute.after` sees success only | union on `status` — record failures too |
| state file for the remembered daemon | `ctx.storage` |
| no way to answer MCP sampling | `ctx.generate.text` — the plugin can answer mcpx's sampling questions |
| `$` for the CLI | gone — and nothing is lost: since #53 (closes #44) the plugin reaches the daemon over the unix socket and spawns `mcpx --json status` only as rung 4, the last fallback (`plugin/opencode/README.md:83-110`, `plugin/opencode/mcpx/daemon.ts`); `backend: v1` never spawns and `bin: ""` forbids it. In v2, drop rung 4 or keep it through `node:child_process`, which `daemon.ts` already imports |
| subdirectory to hide helpers from the loader | unnecessary; only `default` is read |

Also new in v2 and worth using: `mcp.transform` (register a *filtered* server set per session), `permission.hook("evaluate")` (real, unlike v1's dead `permission.ask`), promise-based TUI `select()` for the daemon picker.

**Also:** opencode v2's MCP client sends `_meta["ai.opencode/sessionID"]` on tool calls (`packages/core/src/mcp/client.ts:278`). When opencode v2 talks to mcpx as an MCP server, mcpx should read that for session attribution and leasing — no environment injection needed at all on that path.

Depends on: #44 (closed, fixed in #53 — the binary-free core exists).

Since this was filed (checked at 05c78b2):

- **#171's guard covers a v2 port automatically.** `TestThePluginReadsNoUndeclaredSetting`
  (`internal/settings/consumed_test.go:209-236`) scans every `plugin/**/*.ts(x)` except tests
  (`pluginSources`, `:288-320`), so a v2 plugin anywhere under `plugin/` must honour only variables declared in
  `pluginSettings()` (`internal/settings/plugin.go:18`). #171 also wired `plugin.discoveryRetry` and declared
  `plugin.remember`/`plugin.annotate`; the v2 port keeps all three.
- **The dead `permission.ask` hook** is recorded among the "declared but did nothing" incidents
  (`docs/declared-but-unread.md:8-12`, #75's PR body); nothing in the v1 plugin is built on it
  (`docs/plugin-discovery.md:144-145`). v2's `permission.hook("evaluate")` is the real one.
- The opencode-side line references above (`packages/core/src/plugin/module.ts:60-73`,
  `packages/core/src/mcp/client.ts:278`) are against opencode's `v2` branch and were not re-checked in this pass.

No real choice: v1 plugins do not load in v2, so the only question is when. The table above is the design.

## Ease · Impact · Related

**Ease** L (a rewrite against `{id, setup}`, not a port) · **Impact** med-high — nil while v1 is what runs,
total once v2 is (the v1 plugin does not load at all).

Related: #48 (the harness-free core this adapter sits on), #80 and #82 (the extension side; the same `/v1`
back-channel), #87 (`ctx.storage` replaces the remembered-daemon file; its lifetime follows #87's rule).

Security/auth deferred; see tracker.

code.title: Event store: one table for every statistic, from any source
code.body:
Relocated from dezren39/nix#6 on 2026-10-28 (placement audit): mcpx's single source lives in developing-today/code (pkgs/mcpx); re-home tracked at #309. Original body below; issue references inside it are historical (dezren39/nix numbering).

Parent: #181

## Idea

Record everything mcpx and its harness learn as events in one table, so that
any statistic is a query rather than a new code path.

Today `mcpx stats` has seven dimensions and `mcpx stats --opencode` has six,
each a hand-written query against a differently-shaped source. Adding a source
— a REST API, a hosted mcpx, a second harness — means writing that set again.

## Shape

```sql
CREATE TABLE event (
  id         INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  ts_unix_ms INTEGER NOT NULL,
  kind_id    INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES kind(id),
  idset_id   INTEGER REFERENCES idset(id),   -- who/what this concerns
  source     TEXT NOT NULL,                  -- mcpx, opencode, rest, tui
  value      REAL,                           -- the number, when there is one
  data       TEXT                            -- the rest, as JSON
);
```

### Identifier sets

The repeated shape is "this event concerns session X, whose parent is Y, in
worktree Z". Those combinations recur constantly, so interning them is both a
large space saving and what makes `GROUP BY idset_id` mean something.

```sql
CREATE TABLE idset (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, fingerprint TEXT UNIQUE);
CREATE TABLE idset_member (idset_id INTEGER, key TEXT, value TEXT,
                           PRIMARY KEY (idset_id, key, value));
```

`MCPX_TRACE_IDS` already carries exactly this, as pairs, with variadic entries
for aliases. The set is the natural landing place for it.

### Kinds

A kind is a declared event type, so a writer cannot invent a field shape and a
reader cannot guess one.

```sql
CREATE TABLE kind (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  name TEXT UNIQUE,        -- mcp.call, harness.tool, session.start
  unit TEXT,               -- ms, tokens, usd, count
  schema TEXT              -- JSON Schema for `data`
);
```

## Open questions

- **Is the schema table worth it?** The variadic/required/optional machinery
  sketched in the original note is a type system. It may be more than this
  needs; JSON Schema on `data` gets most of the value for none of the design.
- **Retention.** Events are smaller than log lines but there are more of them.
  Probably the same age-and-count rotation, but per kind.
- **Does it replace `records`, or sit beside it?** Beside, initially. The log
  index answers "what happened"; the event store answers "how much, over
  time". Merging them means one of the two questions gets a worse answer.

## Gap semantics (owns #181 collision 13)

**Owns #181 collision 13:** what a consumer of a bounded event history is told when it misses events. The
live bus (`internal/events`) has this problem today and the store will inherit it; #81's hooks consume
whatever is decided here rather than inventing their own.

What exists at 05c78b2:

| way to miss events | what happens | where |
| --- | --- | --- |
| reconnect with a `since` older than the retained history | `gap=true`; `/v1/events` sends `event: gap` with `{since, latest}` in-band | `internal/events/events.go:185-187`, `internal/daemon/server.go:838-842` |
| a live subscriber that is not reading | its 256-slot channel fills, the event is dropped and `Dropped` is incremented -- **nothing outside `internal/events` reads `Dropped`**, so the gap is silent | `events.go:177`, `:224-231`, `:144-147` |
| a replay longer than the channel | `SubscribeFrom` replays under the bus lock into the same 256-slot channel before anyone drains it, so `?since=0` (or a `Last-Event-ID` more than 256 matching events back) keeps the oldest 256, **silently drops the rest**, then continues live | `events.go:176-199`; history is `events.history`, default 1024 (`internal/defaults/defaults.json:52`, declared at `internal/settings/wire.go:225`, wired at `server.go:165`) |

The third row is a defect in shipped code, not only a design question: `docs/story.md:2203-2214`
("Lossless reconnection": "`?since=0` replays everything retained") and the `New` comment
(`events.go:124-129`, "lets a reconnecting subscriber miss nothing") promise a reconnecting subscriber
misses nothing or is told so, and past 256 matching events it is neither. Found in the 2026-09-30 issues pass, not reproduced by running it.

**A -- raise the limits.** Bigger history, bigger channel. Cheap, and it moves the cliff rather than
removing it; memory grows with every subscriber and a hook pool that saturates still loses events silently.

**B -- back-pressure.** Let a hook subscriber block the publisher. Nothing is lost, and one slow hook stalls
every tool call, which is exactly what `Publish`'s "never blocks" rule (`events.go:203-206`) exists to
prevent. Not for a bus that sits on the call path.

**C -- recommended: one gap contract, three triggers.** Every consumer has a `seq` watermark. Whenever
delivery skips -- reconnect past history, live overflow, replay truncation -- the consumer receives the same
explicit marker the SSE path already sends for the first case (`gap {since, latest}`), and `Dropped` is
reported (in the marker and per subscription in `/v1/status`). A consumer that sees a gap resynchronises
from state instead of trusting the stream. Replay should drain history in order without the fixed-size
channel (or mark the truncation). For #81, a hook whose worker queue overflows is a consumer with a gap and
is told so the same way; "replay hooks over history" then works from the watermark. Recommended because it
is the only option where a consumer can always tell a complete stream from an incomplete one, and it reuses
a marker that already ships.

## Why it is filed rather than built

The value is entirely in having several sources to query uniformly, and there
are currently two. Building the general mechanism now means designing against
imagined sources, which is how a schema acquires fields nothing fills. Worth
doing when the third source exists and its shape is known.

The gap contract above is the exception: it is small, #81 depends on it, and one of its three cases is a
live defect, so it should not wait for the third source.

## Ease · Impact · Related

**Ease** S for the gap contract (collision 13); M-L for the store. **Impact** med-high for the gap contract
(every `/v1/events` consumer and every #81 hook depends on it); med for the store until a third source exists.

Related: #193 (the live bus already loses replayed events past 256 without a gap marker -- the first consumer of the gap contract), #81 (hooks consume the gap contract; the store is their history), #87 (expiry events belong here),
#86 (a browser `EventSource` is a reconnecting subscriber), #85 (a remote TUI lives on `/v1/events`).

Security/auth deferred; see tracker.

code.title: Proof-of-concept Android app + input interface extension (touch, mouse, hover) for relaying into live apps
code.body:
## Origin

Owner direction (Drew, 2026-10-28), added alongside the #795 phone-test plan (#1826): 'add another issue for designing and implementing a proof-of-concept Android app and extending the accepted interfaces.' The Android app is both a product-direction PoC and a native phone endpoint for the id connectivity stack — it relays the phone's input into one of the raw apps (e.g. a TUI app) running elsewhere, over a limited interface built from what the platforms can actually support.

## Design: extend the accepted input interfaces to cover

**Environments / devices:**
- Multi-touch touchscreens (Android)
- Mice (desktop/native)
- Mouse over (hover) on web
- Mouse over (hover) on TUI

**Events, as supported per environment:**
- mouse enter / mouse leave
- click
- right click
- (Android) press and long press — the platform's native equivalents where right click does not exist

**Platform realities the design must state plainly:**
- Web has no real right click unless the app takes over the context menu — with a Wasm build we might do exactly that; in general, web = no right click.
- Android has press / long press instead of right click; how the other options map onto Android gestures is an open design question to answer here, not assume.
- The relayed interface is deliberately LIMITED to the subset we can support end to end: minimally the ability to click things, and ideally drag and scroll. Extend from there once the subset is proven.

## Proof of concept

An Android app that connects (id connectivity) to a running app instance and relays its touch input — tap as click, plus drag/scroll if the subset allows — so the remote app is genuinely operable from the phone. This also gives the #795/#1826 line a native phone peer alongside the Wasm page.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A design (in `doc/` or on this issue) defining the input event model: the common core (press/click, drag, scroll, long press) plus per-environment extras (hover enter/leave on web + TUI, right click where the platform allows it, incl. the web/Wasm context-menu question answered explicitly).
- [ ] The accepted-interface definitions in the codebase are extended per that design (events named above), with unsupported-per-environment events refused explicitly rather than silently dropped.
- [ ] The PoC Android app builds, connects to a live app instance, and relays tap (+ drag/scroll if in the proven subset) well enough to click through a real screen — demonstrated and recorded (here or on #795).
- [ ] Gaps found (events a platform cannot produce, latency limits) are recorded on this issue.

code.title: P3.7 test access: #1831 Android phone peer + laptop VM NAT emulation
code.body:
## Origin

Owner ruling on #795 (Drew, 2026-10-28). The issue was blocked on 'owner provides two networks', framed as two home-style networks with a host on each. Drew's answer, in substance:

- He does not have a second computer on a second home network, and no VPC / paid networking will be set up for this — any server we run would be a plain host (e.g. plain OVH), not a VPC.
- He WILL run a test himself if it is runnable from a website on his phone (Wasm is fine), or from a mobile app.
- VMs on the laptop with an emulated NAT configuration are acceptable for the cells a phone cannot cover.
- His phone on carrier NAT is not a second home network — but per the #795 discussion it IS a legitimate test cell (see below).

## Plan

1. **Phone peer — #1831's Android app (OPEN, unstarted).** The real-network cell is measured by a *native* endpoint: the #1831 proof-of-concept Android app runs as an iroh peer on Drew's phone, on the carrier network, against the laptop peer at home. Carrier CGNAT × home NAT is a real, hard, and realistic cell — it is the pairing actual mobile users present — and it needs zero new hardware.
   - A browser/Wasm page **cannot** be the phone peer. Browsers have no UDP sockets, which iroh's holepunch and QAD probes require; `pkgs/id/crates/id-core/src/connectivity.rs` is native iroh (`iroh = "1"` at `pkgs/id/Cargo.toml:84`, `pkgs/id/crates/id-core/Cargo.toml:20`) and there is no wasm32 connectivity target. At most, a Wasm page is a **result viewer** for a run the native peers performed.
2. **Laptop VM NAT emulation — remaining cells (DONE).** A VM test config on the laptop places peers behind different emulated NAT types (full-cone / restricted / symmetric) to cover the home-NAT × home-NAT combinations no available hardware provides. Emulated results are recorded AS emulated — never presented as real-network measurements (the acceptance brief's 'not falsely passed' rule cuts both ways). Landed in #4984 (PR #5665, merged `a3eba8fb6649`); the nine ordered pairs were recorded on #795 on 2026-11-04.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] **Phone leg (OPEN — depends on #1831).** The #1831 Android app runs as a native iroh endpoint on Drew's phone over the carrier network and completes a holepunch + QAD check against the laptop peer at home; NAT types observed on both ends are recorded on #795. A Wasm page cannot satisfy this criterion — it can only display results of a run the native peers performed.
- [x] The VM emulation config exists, is reproducible from the repo, and runs the C2 matrix cells the phone pairing cannot cover; results recorded on #795 and labelled emulated. (Done: #4984 closed, PR #5665 merged `a3eba8fb6649`.)
- [x] #795's acceptance is updated to this plan (its 'two owner-provided networks' criterion is superseded by the owner's ruling above). Done 2026-11-08 — see #795; the superseded criterion and the answered escalation are reconciled there.

## Status (2026-11-08)

State correction only — no Android app, Wasm page, or connectivity code is built under this issue:

- AC1 now names #1831's Android app as the phone peer; the browser/Wasm peer page is dropped (a Wasm page may only view results).
- AC3 is done: #795's acceptance now carries the two-leg plan, the superseded 'two owner-provided networks' criterion is withdrawn, and its `user/escalated` / `queue/blocked` labels are cleared because the 2026-10-28 ruling answered that escalation.
- The phone-leg implementation remains on #1831; this issue is blocked on it.

code.title: Audit: socket activation as the default pattern for laptop services
code.body:
## Direction (Drew, 2026-10-28)

Reviewing the #437 decision, Drew's ruling: systemd socket activation — systemd holds the port across service restarts so connections queue instead of being refused — 'should be what we do for everything', and asked why it isn't already the pattern across the board.

## Verified current state (2026-10-28, flake at laptop ~/git/code)

Exactly ONE service does this today: OpenChamber (`systemd.user.sockets.openchamber`, `ListenStream 127.0.0.1:3000`, home/common/default.nix:999). A grep of the flake finds no other socket units, no `LISTEN_FDS` consumers, and no socket-proxyd anywhere. Everything else binds its own port and refuses connections while it restarts:

- PM stack: pm-aggregator (:4870), pm-projector (:7801) — plain systemd services.
- PM apps (Postgres, Kaneo, Grist, Pad) — Docker containers (compose today, oci-containers once #1762 lands); containers cannot inherit a systemd socket fd the same way.
- OpenCode server (laptop :13420 / tailnet serve :4096) — plain user service.
- OpenClaw gateway (:18789) — plain user service.
- cloudflared, id-mail services — to be inventoried.

## Honest constraint (why this is an audit, not a blanket flip)

Socket activation only works when the program can accept a socket handed to it by systemd (the `LISTEN_FDS` protocol — trivial shim for our own Node services, supported natively by many daemons) or when a proxy shim (systemd-socket-proxyd) in front is acceptable, which adds a hop and its own failure modes. Postgres and Docker containers are the known hard cases. The audit's job is to apply it everywhere it genuinely helps and record a reason where it doesn't — not to force it where it can't work.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] An inventory in this issue: every laptop service that listens on a port, with a per-service verdict — socket-activate (with the mechanism), or skip (with the concrete reason).
- [ ] Implementation issues filed for each 'socket-activate' verdict (the four `bin/` proxies already have theirs: #1821).
- [ ] Drew reviews the inventory before the implementation issues are queued — the container/Postgres cases in particular are his call if a proxy shim is proposed.

code.title: EPIC: Basement Talos/Cozystack cluster program
code.body:
Relocated from dezren39/nix#508 on 2026-10-28 - it was filed in the wrong repo; developing-today/code is its home. Original content follows, verbatim.

---

## EPIC: Basement Talos/Cozystack cluster program

Turn the basement fleet — ~12 Threadripper machines, 15–16 × 16 TB helium HDDs, ≥3 TB DDR4 ECC — into a **3–5 node Talos Linux cluster under Cozystack**, bootstrapped declaratively with TALM, plus the cheap-cloud program around it.

Source of truth: [idea register 2026-10-20](https://github.com/dezren39/hatch-personal/blob/main/workspace/goals/stand-up-lab-cluster-talm-talos-cozystack-postgres-rustfs/files/idea-register-2026-10-20.md) (goal `stand-up-lab-cluster-talm-talos-cozystack-postgres-rustfs`). Research baseline: `hidden_files/research-brief-2026-10-03.md` in the goal (talm v0.35.0, Talos v1.14.1, Cozystack v1.6.4, RustFS 1.0 GA, managed Postgres = CloudNativePG).

### Hard constraints (Drew, explicit)

- **No HashiCorp anything.** Nomad was the plan; the company was sold. All-in on Kubernetes.
- **Everything bootstrappable and declarative.** No undocumented hand-built state — that is why the machines have no OS right now. The fleet must be rebuildable from config in git.
- **Egress is the scarce resource**, not compute: one 2 Gbps symmetric fiber link behind very fast, very cheap local hardware.
- Cloud budget: Turso $5 / Cloudflare $5 Workers plans in play, free tiers preferred, $25–$30 possible later, **$75 out**.

### Day-one cluster services

Postgres (CloudNativePG via Cozystack) · Cloudflare tunnel · Tailscale · NATS · RustFS (S3, cold tiers on HDD pools) · FluxCD running the app directly · DRBD + LINSTOR replication.

### Child issues

- [ ] #1810 — Hardware inventory + hardware-stats gathering: pick the first 3–5 cluster machines (**starts here**: stats decide node order)
- [ ] #1811 — BMC/BIOS configuration audit + routine KVM screenshot verification system
- [ ] #1812 — TALM bootstrap: declarative per-node disk config for non-identical drives
- [ ] #1813 — Storage pools: RAID10 HDD tier for RustFS + striped/mirrored NVMe tiers with LINSTOR/DRBD
- [ ] #1814 — Egress strategy: 2 Gbps home fiber behind Cloudflare/Turso/Tailscale
- [ ] #1816 — OCI always-free maximization: account setup + automation
- [ ] #1815 — Research: boats.dev

### Suggested order

1. #1810 inventory (stats → node shortlist) and #1811 audit groundwork.
2. #1812 TALM proof-of-flow on the first nodes, with #1813 storage design feeding its per-node configs.
3. Cozystack + day-one services on the proven nodes.
4. #1814 egress design before anything user-facing; #1816 OCI in parallel (blocked only on Drew's email/card choice).

### Blockers / open questions for Drew (from the register)

- Basement power capacity + mess: full-fleet power-on is a long tail; 3–5 nodes first.
- Which app does FluxCD run first ("the ID app" — name/repo)?
- OCI account email/card; exact NIC spec + switch gear; boats.dev context; Turso account state.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Child issues #1810–#1814 (and any later children) are tracked from this epic with their states kept current.
- [ ] Node selection for the first 3–5 machines is made from #1810's hardware stats and recorded here.
- [ ] The cluster bootstrap is reproducible from config in git (TALM + Talos + Cozystack), with no HashiCorp tooling anywhere in the path.
- [ ] Day-one services from the register (Postgres/CloudNativePG, Cloudflare tunnel, Tailscale, NATS, RustFS, FluxCD, DRBD+LINSTOR) each have a child issue or a recorded deferral.

code.title: Storage pools: RAID10 HDD tier for RustFS + striped/mirrored NVMe tiers with LINSTOR/DRBD
code.body:
Relocated from dezren39/nix#504 on 2026-10-28 - it was filed in the wrong repo; developing-today/code is its home. Original content follows, verbatim.

---

## Problem

Design and validate the cluster's storage before the hardware is committed. Drew's sketch (from the register — to be validated, not assumed): three tiers across 3 hosts, replicated with DRBD + LINSTOR so that **data loss needs the same failure on 2 machines at once**.

Source: [idea register 2026-10-20](https://github.com/dezren39/hatch-personal/blob/main/workspace/goals/stand-up-lab-cluster-talm-talos-cozystack-postgres-rustfs/files/idea-register-2026-10-20.md) (goal `stand-up-lab-cluster-talm-talos-cozystack-postgres-rustfs`).

## Drew's sketch

- **HDD tier (cold-ish RustFS buckets):** 3 hosts × 4 × 16 TB helium WD drives in **RAID 10**. (15–16 drives exist in total.)
- **Fast NVMe tier:** all Samsung 990 Pro.
- **Mid NVMe tier:** 980s, smaller 990s, good consumer SSDs — stripe 3 (≈ 990-class aggregate performance) × mirror 2 = **6 drives ("RAID 100": 3 stripes, 2 mirrors)**, so two drives must die to take down a machine.
- Two named pools from earlier work: (1) 4 drives RAID 10; (2) 6 drives RAID 100 (3 stripes × 2 mirrors).
- Goal: 3–5 devices with near parity in disk size and capability.
- Consumers: RustFS (S3) on the HDD tier; Postgres (CloudNativePG) and general volumes on NVMe tiers; LINSTOR/DRBD for cross-machine block replication.

## Acceptance / first steps

- [ ] Map the validated hardware inventory (see inventory issue) onto the three tiers: exact drive counts per host, usable capacities per pool.
- [ ] Decide the layering: md RAID vs LINSTOR/DRBD-native striping/mirroring vs ZFS — and where each pool's redundancy actually lives (in-host vs cross-host), checking the "2 machines must fail" claim against the design.
- [ ] Benchmark the mid tier's 3-stripe claim against a single 990 Pro (does striping 980-class drives actually reach parity?).
- [ ] Define failure drills: pull a drive, pull a host; measure rebuild time/impact on 16 TB members.
- [ ] Emit the result as declarative per-node storage config feeding the TALM bootstrap issue.

## Open questions

- NIC throughput between core hosts (pending inventory) — caps DRBD replication and rebuild speeds.
- RustFS erasure coding across hosts vs RAID 10 under it: one redundancy layer or two?

## Acceptance criteria

- A storage design is recorded on this issue (or a linked design doc/PR) validating or revising the three-tier sketch (RAID10 HDD / fast NVMe / mid NVMe with DRBD + LINSTOR).
- The design states the replication/failure model: which single-machine failures are survived with no data loss.
- Drive counts are reconciled against the actual inventory (see #1810) before any purchase/commitment.
- Follow-up implementation issues are filed and linked for any build work.

code.title: BMC/BIOS configuration audit + routine KVM screenshot verification system
code.body:
Relocated from dezren39/nix#502 on 2026-10-28 - it was filed in the wrong repo; developing-today/code is its home. Original content follows, verbatim.

---

## Problem

The core machines share one motherboard/CPU spec and should be **setting-identical**, but BIOS and BMC ("ASM") firmware versions and settings have never been audited. Undocumented divergence is exactly the failure mode Drew wants eliminated: everything bootstrappable and declarative, nothing that "just existed forever".

Source: [idea register 2026-10-20](https://github.com/dezren39/hatch-personal/blob/main/workspace/goals/stand-up-lab-cluster-talm-talos-cozystack-postgres-rustfs/files/idea-register-2026-10-20.md) (goal `stand-up-lab-cluster-talm-talos-cozystack-postgres-rustfs`).

## What we want

A system that:

- knows every device's KVM/BMC IP address and can reach it programmatically;
- **screenshots and verifies every BIOS/BMC setting on a routine basis** (KVM-over-IP capture, or Redfish/IPMI reads where the platform exposes settings directly);
- diffs each machine against the golden config for the core spec and reports drift;
- emits the verified settings as a **reappliable config** (declarative file in git), so a board swap or reset is a re-apply, not archaeology — "make some config out of it and pray we never have to touch it."

## Acceptance / first steps

- [ ] From the hardware-inventory issue: the canonical list of BMC/KVM IPs and current BIOS + BMC firmware versions per machine.
- [ ] Pick the access method per platform (Redfish API preferred; scripted KVM screenshot + OCR/template-match as fallback) and prototype on one core machine.
- [ ] Define the golden settings profile for the core motherboard (every BIOS and BMC setting we care about) as a checked-in file.
- [ ] One-by-one audit of all core machines against the profile; fix or record every divergence.
- [ ] Schedule the routine re-verification (cron/CI-style job) and decide where drift reports land.

## Open questions

- Does the BMC expose BIOS settings via Redfish on this platform, or is screenshot verification the only path?
- Firmware update policy: converge all core machines to one BIOS/BMC version, or freeze at "verified identical settings" per version?

## Acceptance criteria

- A BMC/BIOS audit exists for the core machines: firmware versions and settings per machine, with divergences listed.
- A repeatable check (script or documented routine) can re-verify settings parity, including the KVM screenshot verification described in the body.
- Divergences found are either corrected or filed as follow-up issues and linked.

code.title: Hardware inventory + hardware-stats gathering: pick the first 3–5 cluster machines
code.body:
Relocated from dezren39/nix#501 on 2026-10-28 - it was filed in the wrong repo; developing-today/code is its home. Original content follows, verbatim.

---

## Problem

We have ~12 basement Threadripper machines and no per-machine records. We cannot choose the first 3–5 Talos/Cozystack cluster nodes — or keep them at parity — until we know exactly what each box contains. Drew's directive: gather all hardware stats **first**, so the cluster starts with the best / most-identical machines.

Source: [idea register 2026-10-20](https://github.com/dezren39/hatch-personal/blob/main/workspace/goals/stand-up-lab-cluster-talm-talos-cozystack-postgres-rustfs/files/idea-register-2026-10-20.md) (goal `stand-up-lab-cluster-talm-talos-cozystack-postgres-rustfs`).

## What we know

- Core machines are the same motherboard, same CPU, same specs **except SSDs**; ≥3 TB DDR4 server ECC RAM across the fleet.
- 15–16 × 16 TB helium WD server-pull HDDs; every machine has some NVMe boot drive (best: Samsung 990 Pro); fast NVMe tier is "all 990s", mid tier mixes 980s / smaller 990s / good consumer SSDs.
- Core machines have enterprise BMC/IPMI ("ASM") with KVM; NIC spec on core machines is unconfirmed ("at least 200 Gb ports" as dictated — exact spec TBD here).
- GPUs are not a resource (3× Intel B50, 1× RTX 2060, old display-only cards) — record them, don't plan around them.
- Blockers: basement power capacity and mess — full-fleet power-on is a long tail, so stats gathering must work machine-by-machine, including via BMC without a full boot where possible.

## Acceptance / first steps

- [ ] Define the per-machine record schema: motherboard, CPU, RAM (total + DIMM layout), every SSD/HDD (model, size, firmware, SMART/health, wear), NICs (model, speed, ports), BMC/KVM IP, BIOS version, BMC firmware version, PSU(s), GPU.
- [ ] Gather stats for all ~12 machines (BMC/Redfish/iKVM where possible; minimal boot media otherwise) and store the records in this repo (or the goal's files/) in a diffable text format.
- [ ] Produce a ranked shortlist of the first 3–5 cluster nodes: parity of disk size/capability first (3 hosts × 4× 16 TB for the HDD tier; matching NVMe tiers), then health.
- [ ] Pin down the exact NIC spec and the switch gear between core machines (feeds the LINSTOR/DRBD design issue).

## Open questions

- Exact NIC spec / switch hardware (register open question 5).
- Are all 15–16 HDDs healthy enough for RAID 10 pools, or are some spares-only?

## Acceptance criteria

- A per-machine hardware inventory exists (linked from this issue) for the ~12 basement machines: CPU, motherboard, RAM, and especially SSD/drive details per box.
- The first 3–5 cluster machines are picked from that inventory, with the parity reasoning recorded.
- The inventory is in a form that can be re-gathered/refreshed, not a one-off prose list.

code.title: pm stack: centralize all service data as shared tables in one database schema
code.body:
## Problem

Every PM-stack service keeps its own private data store today:

- aggregator: JSON files in ~/.local/state/pm-aggregator/ (actions, comments, registry, fleet feed, quota state, snapshots/)
- projector: its own SQLite file (~/.local/state/pm-projector/projector.db) — even though its design already namespaces its tables pmp_ precisely so they can live in a shared database (see pm-stack/projector/README.md: the registry fields are name-spaced so they can live in the fleet's existing database rather than requiring a dedicated one)
- Grist: its own document storage for the roadmap table and the registers
- Kaneo, Pad, ready-for-agent: their own stores again

Consequences: cross-service questions (links between projects, issues, roadmap rows; one event stream) need bespoke joins per pair; freshness depends on each service's own polling/restart behavior (see code#1288 for the Grist live-apply problem); backups and restarts are per-service crafts.

## Proposal

Move the stack's service data into ONE database with a shared schema of namespaced table groups:

- One database (libSQL/Turso-shaped, matching the projector's existing storage choice; local file on the laptop with the fleet's existing backup legs) as the single home.
- Table groups per service with clear prefixes (pmp_ projector/link registry, agg_ aggregator stores, plus shared entity tables for items, links, comments, events that more than one service uses).
- Shared entities (items, links, comments, events) are written once and read by every service — no private copies. The projector's disposable-projection principle is preserved: its tables rebuild from GitHub; the registry (link writes) is the only non-rebuildable part and gets the backup legs.
- Services pick up data changes live (subscription or short-interval change polling with lag surfaced per code#1734) instead of on restart — this issue provides the data layer code#1288 needs.
- The event log (code#1739) and roadmap file integration (code#1738) should be designed against this schema, not against per-service files.

## Acceptance

- An inventory + schema map: every current store (file, table, owner service, rebuildable or not) and its target table group.
- A migration plan per service, ordered so each step is independently shippable and reversible, with the aggregator's JSON stores and the projector DB as the first two moves.
- After migration: no service holds a private copy of items/links/comments; one backup target covers the stack's data; a data change made through one service is visible to the others without restarting any of them.

Raised by Drew 2026-10-28 (centralized management of all these services' data using shared tables in a db schema). Related: code#1288, code#1734, code#1738, code#1739, code#1199.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] An inventory + schema map exists: every current store (file, table, owner service, rebuildable or not) and its target table group.
- [x] A migration plan per service exists, ordered so each step is independently shippable and reversible, with the aggregator's JSON stores and the projector DB as the first two moves. (Plan: pm-stack/SHARED-SCHEMA-MIGRATION-PLAN.md, PR #4881, merged 612ac376.)
- [ ] After migration: no service holds a private copy of items/links/comments; one backup target covers the stack's data; a data change made through one service is visible to the others without restarting any of them.

code.title: power-guard: gate UPower's critical-power hybrid-sleep behind a sustained-reading confirmation (laptop slept 2h40m on a glitched battery reading, 2026-10-28)
code.body:
## Incident (2026-10-28, laptop amd-6)

The laptop was unreachable fleet-wide ~06:11–09:00 CDT. Journal evidence:

- `06:12:29 systemd-logind: hybrid-sleep requested from client PID 38231 ('upowerd') ... The system will hybrid sleep now!`
- `06:12:29 systemd[1]: Reached target Sleep` / `systemd-sleep: Performing sleep operation 'hybrid-sleep'` / kernel `PM: hibernation: hibernation entry`
- `08:53:10 systemd[1]: Stopped target Sleep` (resume)

UPower's critical-power action (`CriticalPowerAction=HybridSleep`, PercentageAction=2, PercentageCritical=5, TimeAction=120) fired on a reading that could not have been real: no low-battery warnings were logged beforehand, and minutes after resume the battery read **99%, Charging, AC online=1**. A real drain to 2% cannot recharge to 99% that fast. Most likely a glitched time-to-empty/percentage sample (the machine also carries several churning UCSI USB-C power-source entries). Cost: a ~2h40m fleet-wide laptop outage (46 queue items parked on the outage tracker).

UPower has no "wait and re-check" setting — it acts on a single sample. Drew's direction: keep sleep as the response to a *genuine* critical battery (this machine is normally on AC, but if it were on battery, sleep beats a hard power loss); a false sleep is worse than either.

## The guard (built + tested 2026-10-28)

A small poller that adds the missing confirmation step. Tested implementation already exists on the laptop at `~/tools/power-guard.py` (python3, no deps):

- Polls `/sys/class/power_supply` every 15s.
- While **discharging** and at/below 20% (UPower's PercentageLow) or a ≤900s time-to-empty, it holds a `systemd-inhibit --what=sleep --mode=block` lock, so UPower's sleep request cannot fire unconfirmed.
- Any recovery (AC back, status Charging/Full, charge above the low line) releases the lock and resets all timers — a glitch never survives minutes of continuous polling.
- Only a **sustained** critical state makes the guard release the lock and issue `systemctl hybrid-sleep` itself:
  - at/below 2% (UPower's PercentageAction): sustained **60s**
  - at/below 5% or ≤300s-to-empty: sustained **300s**
- On AC it can never fire.

Fake-battery test (fake sysfs tree, stubbed inhibitor + sleep command, compressed timers) — all assertions passed:

- engages the block when unplugged at 18%
- detects critical at 4%, does **not** fire inside the confirmation window
- AC returning mid-confirmation releases the block, no sleep
- sustained 2% fires exactly once, via the edge path

## Landing spec

1. Add a `power-guard` systemd service to the laptop's NixOS config (the `#amd` system in this repo's flake), beside `nixos/services/pm-stack/`: runs the script as root, `Restart=always`, starts at boot. Install the script content from the tested `~/tools/power-guard.py` on amd-6 (pin it into the repo; do not hand-copy at deploy time).
2. Leave UPower's config and thresholds unchanged — the guard gates the action, it does not replace UPower's detection.
3. After the switch, verify on the live machine: service active; `systemd-inhibit --list` shows the block only while discharging at/below the low line (test by a brief AC unplug above the critical line — expect block engaged, no sleep, release on replug).
4. Retire the hand test copy at `~/tools/power-guard.py` once the flake service is live (pointer comment is fine).

Drew approved the design + thresholds in chat 2026-10-28 09:13 CDT (5-minute confirmation, 1 minute at a true 2%).


## Acceptance criteria
- A `power-guard` systemd service exists in the laptop's NixOS config (the `#amd` system in this repo's flake), beside `nixos/services/pm-stack/`, running the guard script as root with `Restart=always`, starting at boot; the script content is pinned into the repo from the tested `~/tools/power-guard.py` on amd-6 (not hand-copied at deploy time).
- UPower's config and thresholds are unchanged — the guard gates the action, it does not replace UPower's detection.
- Live verification after the switch: the service is active; `systemd-inhibit --list` shows the sleep block only while discharging at/below the low line; a brief AC unplug above the critical line engages the block with no sleep, and replugging releases it.
- The hand test copy at `~/tools/power-guard.py` is retired once the flake service is live (a pointer comment is fine).


<!-- hands:v1 kind=physical action="Unplug the laptop AC adapter, confirm power-guard prevents hybrid-sleep on a glitch reading, then replug - or reply waive on this issue." -->

**Quantified trade:** in `specialist`, the tail seat **GPT-6.1 Sol #medium** now out-scores the head seat **Claude Sonnet 5.5 #high** on Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index **v5** (released 2026-10-27; AA's biggest overhaul since v4, 60% private/held-out evaluations):

| seat | AA v5 II | AA $/task | AA t/s | AA TTFT |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sonnet #high (specialist head, via antigravity-ls sonnet-plan) | 41 | $1.64 | 115 | 11.08s |
| Sol #medium (specialist tail, via openai sol-plan) | 46 | $0.36 | 59 | 3.62s |

Sol #medium is **+5 II**, **4.6× cheaper per AA task**, and **~3× lower TTFT** than the seat that currently fires first on every specialist dispatch. Under AA v4.3.2 the ordering was defensible (Sonnet #high 47 vs Sol #medium 48 — near-tied, Sonnet first on quality-first grounds); v5 widened the gap in Sol's favour while raising Sonnet's cost/task ($0.88 → $1.64).

**Cost-to-pool:** Sol burns the OpenAI final-reserve window; Sonnet burns the Antigravity window the summit Opus head also depends on. Promoting Sol spends the reserve earlier — that is the trade to test, not a free win.

**Caveats (why this is a hypothesis, not a config change):**

- Fleet measured n for both seats in the specialist role is ~0 (no route-pinned specialist sample); our own measurements win over AA when they exist.
- Per the flag protocol, this earns a config change only through the controlled-test mechanism (#1342) and the steward's PR path.

code.title: id(web): collab server stores and broadcasts steps it never validates — one bad step poisons the document's history and loops every client
code.body:
## Summary

The collab server accepts, stores, broadcasts and Acks `ProseMirror` steps without ever checking that they parse or apply — one invalid step poisons a document session for every current and future client.

In `pkgs/id/src/web/collab.rs` a step is an opaque blob end to end:

- `Step` is a flattened `serde_json::Value` (`collab.rs:164-169`) — there is no parse or validation constructor.
- `CollabMessage::decode` (`collab.rs:536-545`) accepts a Steps frame as `(u8, u64, Vec<serde_json::Value>, u64)`: any JSON values at all count as "steps".
- The Steps handler (`collab.rs:986-1052`) checks only that the frame's version equals the current version, then pushes every step into `doc.steps` (:1019-1024), bumps the version by `steps.len()` (:1028), broadcasts an `Update` to the other clients (:1032-1036) and Acks the sender (:1044-1052). It never applies the steps to a document and never asks whether they are well-formed.
- On join, the catch-up path (`collab.rs:787-810`) replays **all** stored steps to the new client, so a stored bad step is re-delivered forever, for the life of the `Document` (cleanup only runs an hour after the last client disconnects).

Auth is not a gate: a client that sends no AUTH frame in 5 seconds "proceeds as anonymous" (`collab.rs:694-755`) and can send Steps. A merely buggy or version-skewed client reaches the same place without malice — e.g. a step built against a diverged local doc, or a node type an older/newer web build's schema does not share.

## Evidence (verified on main `b2adaf47`, 2026-10-28)

`collab.rs` sha256 `55e04270…` and `collab.ts` sha256 `0fb75f70…`, identical in the sandbox and laptop clones. Two probes ON THE LAPTOP (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-28-laneA-collabsteps/`; sources + logs in the goal's `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-28-laneA-collabsteps/`):

Rust verbatim-decode probe (the exact encode/decode tuple shapes from `collab.rs:479-482` / `:536-545`):

```
CTRL one text step:       decode -> Ok(tag=1, version=3, steps=1, client_id=4242)
BOGUS stepType:           decode -> Ok(...)   {"stepType":"bogusType","from":1,"to":2}
RANGE replace to=999999:  decode -> Ok(...)
NON-OBJECT steps (42, null, "hi"): decode -> Ok(steps=3)
```

TS probe driving the real client receive path (`Step.fromJSON` + `receiveTransaction` from prosemirror-transform / prosemirror-collab, as `collab.ts:278-279` calls them; basic schema standing in for the mode-aware editor schema):

```
CTRL_valid:    fromJSON OK, apply ok, receiveTransaction OK ("hello world!")
BOGUS_type:    Step.fromJSON -> THROW "No step type bogusType defined"
RANGE_replace: Step.fromJSON OK, Step.apply -> THROW "Position 999999 out of range",
               receiveTransaction -> THROW
SCHEMA_slice:  Step.fromJSON -> THROW "Unknown node type: no_such_node"
```

The receiving client's only handling for that throw is `collab.ts:281-293`: log "Failed to apply steps", close the socket with code 4001 and `scheduleReconnect()` — which rejoins, receives Init + the same catch-up steps, and throws again. One stored step therefore puts every client of that document into a reconnect loop and makes the document uneditable until the session's `Document` is cleaned up.

## Why it matters

The server is the authority for the shared step history — clients trust its Update/catch-up stream to be applicable, because `receiveTransaction` cannot skip a step in the middle of the version sequence. Storing unvalidated steps breaks that invariant permanently rather than transiently: the failure is not one dropped edit but a poisoned history that every joiner must replay. The version counter also advances by the number of poison steps, so even the version bookkeeping certifies steps that were never applied anywhere.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A Steps frame containing a step that does not parse against the document's schema, or does not apply to the document at the frame's version, is refused (Error to the sender, no Ack): nothing is stored, the version does not advance, and nothing is broadcast.
- [ ] Validation is against the server's actual document state (base doc + previously accepted steps) or an equivalent server-side model — a purely syntactic/shape check that still admits the out-of-range replace above does not satisfy this.
- [ ] Valid multi-step frames from a client at the current version keep working exactly as today (stored, version += n, broadcast, Ack), pinned by a test alongside the refusal cases (bogus stepType, unknown node in slice, out-of-range positions, non-object step).
- [ ] A client that somehow still receives an unappliable step does not loop forever on the same history: e.g. the reconnect path distinguishes "catch-up itself is poisoned" and surfaces a terminal error for that document instead of rejoining indefinitely — or the server-side guarantee is documented as the sole line of defence with a test that a poisoned history cannot be created.
- [ ] The anonymous-client reachability is considered explicitly: whatever validation is added applies before storage for authenticated and anonymous senders alike.

code.title: stewardship: Muse subscription panel has no owning read lane — flagged-stale 90% figure survived 24h+ and closed the pool by rule
code.body:
## Bug: the Muse subscription panel has no owning read lane — a flagged-stale figure survived 24h+ and drove routing

**What happened (2026-10-27):** Drew's subscription changed Power → Maximum (usage reset to ~2%). For over a day, the fleet's compiled quota view kept quoting the 2026-10-26 12:21 CDT observation — "Power, 90% of weekly used" — and the ≥85% measurement gate treated the pool as closed. The main chat repeated the stale figure to Drew as current before he corrected it himself.

**The system KNEW and still failed:** stewardship cycles 67–70 each recorded, in writing, "Muse consumer panel 90% weekly at 2026-10-26 12:21 CDT — STALE past daily cadence (count as unmeasured)". The staleness was flagged four times and never repaired:

- The daily full console refresh that owns repairing stale pools was deferred cycle after cycle ("owed by the first cycle at/after 06:00 CDT"), and when a recovery cycle did run console reads (Command Code, Open Design), it attempted the Claude *provider* console, hit a sign-in wall, and recorded "unmeasured" — it never checked the subscription panel's actual automatic feed.
- That feed EXISTS: every sandbox boot's init END line in ~/logs/init.log captures the live panel verbatim (2026-10-27 captures: 04:13 "Maximum … 2%", 05:55 "2%", 08:12 "3%", 10:06 "4%", 12:14 "6%", 14:11 "7%"; live read 15:31: 8%, resets Nov 3 00:59 CST). Cycles 30/56/57 transcribed boot captures into the view on 2026-10-25/26 — proving the route — but no lane OWNS doing it, so it happens only when a cycle happens to.

**Meanwhile the pools WITH owning lanes stayed fresh:** Go (hourly watch, published every run), Meta API (console read 2026-10-27 00:03). The gap is specific to the subscription panel.

### Acceptance

1. One named lane (stewardship cycle or the boot-init verify step) transcribes the newest boot-capture panel (plan name, % used, reset) into quota-view.md + provider-quota-registry.md on a defined cadence — at minimum daily and on every boot where the panel changed.
2. A plan-NAME change in a capture (Power → Maximum) is treated as a material event: it invalidates the pool's prior figures everywhere they are quoted and is surfaced to the main chat the same cycle, not left for Drew to spot.
3. The compiled view may not present a figure flagged STALE in the cycle log as the pool's current state; stale pools render as "unmeasured (last read <date>)" in the summary rows too.
4. Regression case: this incident — decision/routing consumers (orchestrator measurement gate) must treat the panel pool by its transcribed capture age, the same as every other pool.

code.title: Repo-universe issue tracker: watch every repo we own or depend on, pull its issues into one tracked system
code.body:
## Problem

The fleet watches exactly four repos (developing-today/code, developing-today/opencode, developing-today/openchamber, dezren39/nix). The 2026-10-27 all-repos census (`hidden_files/git-cleanup-2026-10-27/all-repos-census.md` in the repo-health goal workspace) counted ~146 clones across the laptop and sandbox, plus dozens of upstream repos nested inside `/home/user/repo-archive` — and almost none of them are watched. Issues filed in Drew-owned side repos (dezren39/hatch, dezren39/hatch-personal, developing-today/hardware-doc, developing-today/opencode-auto-continue) and in upstream projects we depend on (the crosspoint-reader ecosystem, tanmatsu, M5GFX, LilyGO, and similar) are never seen, so problems surface late or never.

Filed at Drew's direction, 2026-10-27: "make a system for checking the extended universe of repos for issues to pull in and track/resolve."

## What to build (design first, then implementation issues)

1. **Universe inventory** — a maintained repo list, generated from the census scan plus GitHub enumeration of the developing-today org and the dezren39 account, classified per repo: owned / fork / upstream-dependency / archive-nested. The list itself is a versioned artifact a human can edit, not a hardcoded constant.
2. **Scheduled checker** — polls GitHub issues for every in-scope repo on a cadence, detecting new, changed, and closed issues since the last run. Read-only against GitHub; runs wherever the other read-only fleet checks run.
3. **Pull-in surface** — one place where pulled-in issues land with source repo + number links, deduped by (source repo, issue number) so re-runs never create duplicates. Open design question: mirrored tracking issues in this repo vs an index (e.g. Atlas) with references only — the design must pick one and say why.
4. **Track/resolve workflow** — pulled-in items enter the existing label/queue system: owned-repo issues route to triage like any other fleet issue; upstream issues get an explicit disposition — waiting-on-upstream, contribute-a-fix, or local workaround/pin — and a mirror resolves automatically when the source issue closes.

## Acceptance criteria

- The universe list exists as a maintained artifact covering, at minimum, every Drew-owned repo on GitHub plus the upstream repos named in the census, each with its class.
- The checker runs on a schedule and emits a delta report (new / changed / closed per repo) without human prompting.
- A test issue opened in a side repo (e.g. dezren39/hatch-personal) appears on the tracking surface within one check cycle.
- Running the checker twice in a row creates zero duplicate entries.
- Closing the source issue moves its tracked entry to resolved on the next cycle.
- The design names its scope limits explicitly: which classes of repo are checked for issues vs merely inventoried.

## Related

- Census: `all-repos-census.md` (repo-health goal workspace, 2026-10-27) — the inventory this builds on.
- dezren39/hatch-personal#1 — hardware docs into the Atlas search index (the search side of knowing the wider repo universe; this issue is the issue-tracking side).
- Epic #1233 (fleet reliability) — this extends the fleet's field of view beyond its four home repos.

code.title: feat(orchestrator): GitHub intake triage — every new issue + issue comment assessed, labeled, horizon-set, answered
code.body:
Gap named by Drew (2026-10-27): "does orchestrator or triage workflow receive every issue and issue comment and assess priority, add labels, leave a comment? what about comments in already open issues? can we add a priority or a time frame — from github or how?"

CURRENT STATE (verified from the job bodies 2026-10-27): no event-driven intake exists. Coverage is polling, split by role:
- The per-repo issue sweeps (every 2h, up to 5 items/run) FIX first and TRIAGE second — verify issues, comment findings, apply labels, close stale, re-prioritize the backlog file. New issues reach the backlog when a sweep's triage reaches them; comments on open issues are read when an issue is worked, not as an intake signal.
- The orchestrator (hourly) reconciles the org Project: issues labeled now/next/epic auto-add as Todo; Status syncs from signals. It does not read issue comments and does not write labels or issue comments (single-writer rule covers Project fields only).
- Drew's GitHub mentions/reviews surface only via the daily Gmail summary.

WORK — a real intake triage, owned by the orchestration pass (it already classifies everything else):
1. Each run, poll the four repos for issues created and issue comments posted since the last run (persist a watermark in orchestrator-state.json).
2. Every NEW issue gets assessed in that run: priority + Horizon (Project field write), labels applied (now/next + area), and a short triage comment on the issue itself: the assessment, the horizon, and what happens next (queued for a sweep / needs-orchestrator / needs-Drew with the one-line why, passing the triage gate).
3. Every new comment on an open issue gets read: Drew's comments are directives — route them to the owning lane (the working session, the sweep backlog, or the orchestrator's tiers) and reflect any priority/timeframe change he states (label + Horizon updates). Others' comments get assessed for state changes (fixed? blocked? new info?) and the item re-classified when they move it.
4. Authority to grant explicitly in the job body: the orchestrator may add labels and post triage comments on issues for intake purposes (Project single-writer rule unchanged).
Acceptance: a test issue + a test comment demonstrate end-to-end intake within one pass, with the triage comment, label, and Horizon visible on GitHub.


## Acceptance criteria

- An orchestrator pass polls all four repos for issues created and issue comments posted since the persisted watermark in `orchestrator-state.json`, and the watermark advances only after a successful pass.
- Every new issue is assessed in that same pass: priority label and Project Horizon set, intake labels applied (now/next + area as applicable), and a short triage comment posted on the issue stating the assessment, the horizon, and what happens next.
- Every new comment on an open issue is read and classified: Drew's comments are routed as directives to the owning lane with any stated priority/timeframe change reflected in labels + Horizon; other comments are assessed for state changes and the item re-classified when they move it.
- The orchestrator job body explicitly grants label + triage-comment authority for intake (Project single-writer rule unchanged).
- End-to-end proof: a test issue and a test comment each receive intake within one pass, with the triage comment, label, and Horizon visible on GitHub.

code.title: design(mcpx): resume upstream HTTP sessions after a cold restart — persist the resumable session state
code.body:
**Decision for Drew (one line):** Approve persisting mcpx upstream HTTP session state (session IDs + protocol state, never resolved header secrets) to the owner-only state dir so a cold restart resumes sessions instead of re-initialising every HTTP upstream — yes/no; the graceful-shutdown DELETE question in Phase 3 rides on the same decision.

Design doc: `files/designs/code-mcpx-cold-restart-session-resume.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace. Register: central potential-projects list, same workspace (`files/potential-projects.md`).

## Summary

A takeover preserves upstream HTTP sessions; a cold restart does not. `pkgs/mcpx/TODO.md` item 3: "The lease table is restored from `sessions.json`, but the upstream `Mcp-Session-Id` is kept only in memory and in the takeover handoff, so after a restart each HTTP upstream is initialised again." Roadmap: `planning/roadmaps/mcpx.md` → Next → "Resume upstream sessions after a cold restart" (status `idea`).

Costs per cold restart, per HTTP upstream: a fresh `initialize` handshake, silent loss of upstream per-session state, and one leaked upstream session (the dead daemon never sent DELETE; the new daemon doesn't know the ID — #260 fixed this leak for takeover only).

**Proposal:** persist the resumable half of each legacy streamable-HTTP upstream session in a new versioned state-dir file (same discipline as `internal/daemon/sessions.go`: atomic tmp+rename, `defaults.PrivateMode`, version envelope, ignore-on-mismatch), and let a cold-started daemon take the *existing* takeover restore path with the record standing in for the socket:

- Record per pool instance: instance key, URL, config fingerprint (hash over session-defining config fields + header/auth *names*, never values), `HTTPHandoff` minus Headers (`SessionID`, `Negotiated`), the full `mcpclient.Session` protocol state, `savedAt`.
- **No resolved header values on disk** — the codebase's rule is that handoff headers travel "over the takeover's unix socket only" (`internal/mcpclient/http.go`, `HTTPHandoff` comment). On restore, headers are re-derived from live config (`httpOptions()` + `resolveAuth()`), then the transport/client are seeded with the exact calls takeover makes: `ht.Resume(...)` and `mcpclient.Resume(...)` (`internal/pool/handoff.go:238,326`). No parallel resume implementation.
- Save on legacy session establishment and on session-ID change (`internal/mcpclient/http.go:156` is where IDs are adopted); save failure is logged, non-fatal — resume is an optimisation.
- Scope: legacy-era streamable HTTP only. Modern era (2026-07-28) has no sessions; legacy SSE holds its session in the GET stream (TODO item 2 already accepts re-init there).

Grounding: `internal/mcpclient/http.go` (sessionID/negotiated in memory only), `internal/mcpclient/handoff.go` (`SessionState()`, `Resume` — the no-handshake client already exists), `internal/pool/pool.go:704` (`dial()` seeds nothing today), `internal/daemon/sessions.go` (persistence precedent). Sibling of #1384 (stdio supervisor), which names cold-restart HTTP resume as an explicit non-goal — this design is that non-goal, designed separately. Alternatives (do nothing; fold into `sessions.json`; persist full handoff incl. headers; era-cache-only) and risks (stale-session resume, session IDs as bearer tokens on disk, write amplification, restore-path drift) are argued in the design doc.

## Phased breakdown

- **Phase 1 — persist and resume.** New state file + record type; fingerprint gate; restore via the takeover path. Defining test: session established → daemon SIGKILLed → restarted → first call succeeds, upstream saw no second `initialize`, request carried the original `Mcp-Session-Id`. Filed as a sub-issue of this issue.
- **Phase 2 — expiry fallback and record hygiene.** First request on a resumed session answered 404 (or 401/403 after credential rotation) → drop record, fresh `initialize`, retry once, transparently. Server removed from config → record deleted + best-effort upstream DELETE, or logged left-to-expire (the #260 degradation, made explicit). Coordinate with the roadmap's "Legacy client robustness" row (nix#200–#203) — this is only the resumed-session slice. Filed as a sub-issue of this issue.
- **Phase 3 — open questions, NOT filed.** Graceful-shutdown semantics (should a restart-intent stop skip the DELETE that `Close` → `closeSession` sends today?); record TTL; dashboard resumed-vs-fresh visibility; whether takeover should also write the record. The shutdown question is part of Drew's decision above.

---
agent-note:v1 — filed by the repo design architect (dedicated code job, pass 2, 2026-10-27). Design doc + register entry as linked above. `user/review` carries the one-line direction decision at the top; Phases 1–2 are filed as sub-issues with `queue/queued` + `task/triage` packets enqueued to repo-health-code-pilot; Phase 3 stays as questions in the design doc.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Drew's decision on persisting upstream HTTP session state (IDs + protocol state only, never resolved header secrets) is recorded on this issue.
- [ ] If approved: Phase 1 (#1415) and Phase 2 (#1416) land with their own acceptance criteria met, and the Phase 3 graceful-shutdown DELETE question is answered in the same decision thread.
- [ ] If declined: this issue and its phases are closed with the rationale recorded, and `pkgs/mcpx/TODO.md` item 3 is updated to match.

code.title: design(mcpx): a supervisor that owns each stdio child's pipes — replace the takeover handoff for stdio
code.body:
**Decision needed (one line):** Adopt the per-instance mcpx supervisor design — stdio children owned by a supervisor that outlives the daemon, Phases 2–3 make it the default — or keep investing in the takeover handoff instead?

<!-- decision above is why this carries user/review; the rest routes through normal fleet triage -->

## Summary

Replace the stdio half of mcpx's takeover handoff with **one supervisor per stdio instance**: a tiny process (the same mcpx binary re-executed as a hidden `mcpx supervise` subcommand) that spawns each stdio MCP server, owns its pipes for the child's whole life, and serves whichever daemon is currently attached over a unix socket in the state directory. A daemon upgrade then becomes a plain restart of the front end — the new daemon *attaches* to supervisors that are already running. No pipes move, no descriptors are passed, nothing is detached or restored.

This extends — does not duplicate — the repo's own design thread: `pkgs/mcpx/TODO.md` item 1 ("Replace the takeover handoff with a supervisor… The current handoff is a stopgap") and `planning/roadmaps/mcpx.md` → Next → "A supervisor that owns each stdio child's pipes" (status: `idea`, no issue until now). Full design doc: `files/designs/code-mcpx-stdio-supervisor.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace (registered in `files/potential-projects.md`).

## Current state (evidence)

- `pkgs/mcpx/internal/daemon/takeover.go` is 726 lines of framed handoff protocol (`hello`/`listener`/`state`/`pools`/`pipe`/`conn`/`end`/`ack`/`commit`), one fd per frame, a single commit point after which nothing can be put back.
- `pkgs/mcpx/internal/pool/handoff.go` (390 lines): pool `Detach` refuses while calls are in flight (`ErrBusy`), parks every other instance, carries stdio pipes beside the JSON as raw fds.
- `pkgs/mcpx/internal/mcpclient/stdio.go`: plain `os.Pipe()`s instead of `cmd.Std*Pipe` *so the ends can be passed to another process*; a `pending` buffer for a partial frame interrupted by handoff; a `detached` state while another process owns the pipes.
- Costs already on record: takeover is unsupported on darwin (#237); a takeover bug orphaned a removed server's upstream HTTP session (#260, closed).
- Cross-repo theme (`ROADMAP.md`): "Handing a running service to its successor."

## Proposal (point of view)

- **Per-instance, not per-daemon**: the failure unit stays one server instance; the supervisor protocol never multiplexes, so the one component that must stay trivial stays trivial.
- **Byte pump, not frame proxy, in v1**: framing stays in the daemon's existing `StdioTransport` reader (one home for the partial-frame logic). Child output produced while no daemon is attached goes to a bounded supervisor buffer; overflow keeps the tail and reports the dropped byte count on attach — loss visible, never silent.
- **Same binary re-exec** (pattern already used by `internal/cli/explore.go` and the takeover successor path), not a second artifact: mcpx ships as one Nix package.
- Alternatives that lose, with reasons, are in the design doc: keep improving the handoff; one supervisor for all children; delegate to systemd/launchd (portability — the #237 wound); separate supervisor binary.

## Phased breakdown

1. **Phase 1 — supervised transport behind a flag.** Hidden `mcpx supervise` subcommand; supervised `mcpclient` transport with the same interface; per-server opt-in flag, default off. Defining test: SIGKILL the daemon mid-session, start a new one — child PID unchanged, next call succeeds. *(Filed as a sub-issue of this design issue and enqueued for triage.)*
2. **Phase 2 — takeover becomes attach for supervised instances.** Successor attaches via state-dir scan; no `kindPipe`/`pools` frames for supervised instances; listeners/HTTP keep the existing handoff. E2E supervised variant of `internal/e2e/takeover_test.go` asserting no pipe frames + PID continuity. *(Not filed yet — its exact diff depends on Phase 1's socket protocol as built.)*
3. **Phase 3 — supervised by default + lifecycle hygiene.** Adopt-or-reap scan on daemon start, `mcpx restart` through the supervisor, protocol-version refusal surfaced in status, darwin build/test parity shrinking #237's skip list to the legacy handoff. *(Not filed yet — the default-flip is part of the decision above.)*

## Open questions (in the design doc, deliberately not filed as issues)

- Buffer bound/policy for unattached child output (tail-drop vs backpressure).
- Opportunistic supervisor refresh on binary upgrade vs protocol versioning alone.
- Supervisor socket authentication beyond state-dir 0600 precedent (`internal/daemon/sessions.go`).

## Non-goals

- Cold-restart resume of upstream HTTP sessions (`TODO.md` item 3) — a sibling design, separable, not bundled here.
- SSE upstream session mobility (`TODO.md` item 2); `ExecIdentity` semantics (`TODO.md` item 4) — unchanged.

## Related

- #237 (darwin takeover tests), #260 (closed; takeover orphan), #308/#309 (mcpx single-source), #1351 (design-architect job)
- Files: `pkgs/mcpx/TODO.md`, `planning/roadmaps/mcpx.md`, `pkgs/mcpx/internal/daemon/takeover.go`, `pkgs/mcpx/internal/pool/handoff.go`, `pkgs/mcpx/internal/mcpclient/stdio.go`

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The decision in the first line is recorded on this issue (adopt the per-instance supervisor, or keep investing in the takeover handoff), with the decider named.
- [ ] If adopted: implementation issues exist for each phase (supervisor subcommand + attach protocol; stdio instances migrated; takeover handoff retired for stdio), each with its own acceptance criteria, and this design issue links them.
- [ ] If not adopted: the rationale is recorded here and `pkgs/mcpx/TODO.md` item 1 / the roadmap entry are updated to match, so the design thread does not stay dangling.
- [ ] No code changes land under this design issue itself.

code.title: chore(fleet): scope tailnet policy for the laptop opencode serve endpoint (amd-6:443)
code.body:
From the #1363 close-out (2026-10-27): the laptop opencode background service is now published to the tailnet via Tailscale Serve (`https://amd-6.raptor-pumpkinseed.ts.net/` → 127.0.0.1:13420, tailnet-only, password auth enforced — 401 unauthenticated verified). The remaining hardening is policy-side:

- Today, any device the tailnet policy admits can attempt the endpoint; the opencode server password is the only gate. The tailnet (raptor-pumpkinseed) also carries many enrolled, mostly-offline codex-environment nodes that have no business reaching the opencode API.
- Scope the tailnet policy (admin console — grants/ACLs) so only the devices that need the opencode API (the Muse sandbox device `muse`, Drew's own devices) can reach amd-6:443. Keep the aggregator route (amd-6:4870 consumers) working — check what else reaches amd-6 before narrowing.

code.title: id(ci): nixos-playwright-e2e VM test fails on first curl — no server readiness wait (nightly 40457980141)
code.body:
## Finding (from #1075 slice 1, queue task 1256)

`nixos-playwright-e2e` fails on a readiness race in its own VM test script: the first probe is a single non-retried `curl` against a server that is not up yet.

**Evidence:** `id e2e nightly` run [40457980141](https://github.com/developing-today/code/actions/runs/40457980141) on `main` @ `dd4ee06e13393df7d6f2f0ccc72ffd2f5d36e865`, concluded failure 2026-10-27T07:51:41Z:

- ❌ `checks.x86_64-linux.nixos-playwright-e2e` — builder failed exit code 1. Traceback in `vm-test-run-id-playwright-e2e`:
  ```
  File "<string>", line 17, in <module>
    chromium_client.succeed("curl -sf http://chromium_server:4173/")
  RequestedAssertionFailed: command `curl -sf http://chromium_server:4173/` failed (exit code 7)
  ```
  Exit code 7 = connection refused. The failure fired ~53s after the VMs started (07:31:31Z → 07:32:24Z), while the server VMs were still booting / the app was still starting (pkarr/DNS publish noise in the same window). There is no `wait_for_open_port` / retry before the `succeed(...)` probe in the failing script path.
- This check never got to run any Playwright test in this nightly — the harness failed before the suite started, so the nightly currently gives no NixOS-Playwright signal at all.
- Not covered by #176 (that is the non-VM `test-e2e` derivation) or #896 (VM serve/e2e/integration; playwright-e2e was still running when it was summarised). No commit between `dd4ee06e` and current `main` (`6f4532ab`) touches the id nix tests.

## Acceptance criteria
- The playwright-e2e VM test waits for the server properly (e.g. `wait_for_open_port(4173)` / retried probe with a named timeout) before the first `curl` assertion.
- `nixos-playwright-e2e` reaches and runs its Playwright suite in a full `nix flake check` run; pass/fail is then about the tests, not harness readiness.
- Result recorded on #1075 (slice 1 follow-up).

Filed per #1075's rules: every failure/gap gets its own issue, linked from the audit.
