code.title: Program tending: scheduled care for roadmaps, epics, projects, and stalled PRs
code.body:
## Work (Drew, 2026-10-27)

The fleet monitor tends issues and queue state; nobody tends the
planning layer. Build `program-tending` (daily, all four repos,
≤~12 actions/run, everything logged):

- **Epics:** open `epic` issues — child progress, last activity,
  body-vs-reality. Silent 7+ days → status comment (last movement,
  next step, blockers); all children closed → completion comment
  proposing closure.
- **Roadmaps:** ROADMAP.md + planning/roadmaps vs landed work.
  Drift is fixed by PR (forward-looking rows only — never Done
  rows); ambiguous drift gets `meta/roadmap-drift` + a comment
  instead of a guess.
- **Projects:** board items whose status contradicts issue/PR
  reality get corrected where possible; unreadable board state is
  reported, never fabricated.
- **Stalled PRs:** open PRs with no activity in 48h+ (and no
  held/do-not-merge) get one check-in comment naming what they're
  waiting on + the next step; fleet-owned PRs that merely need
  shepherding get a `pr_shepherd` queue packet instead of only a
  comment. Drew's own feature PRs: comment at 7 days, never a
  packet.
- **Loose ends:** parent/epic notification when children close,
  duplicate cross-links, and the aging `user/review` list surfaced
  daily (his queue — reported, not re-decided).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Job live; first run's log shows actions (or verified
      no-actions) in all five sections.
- [ ] First roadmap-drift PR or `meta/roadmap-drift` application
      lands within the first three runs, or the run reports the
      roadmaps verified-clean with the checks named.
- [ ] A stalled PR receives a check-in inside the first two runs,
      or the run verifies none met the 48h rule.

Child of epic #1334. Filed by Muse (operator) 2026-10-27.

code.title: Controlled pool tests: A/B real task batches before any pool change lands
code.body:
## Work (Drew, 2026-10-27)

Pool changes proposed by pool-intelligence flags or the steward's
hunches don't land on vibes — they run a controlled test first. This
issue builds the standing mechanism:

- A test is a small batch of comparable real tasks (same kind/effort
  class, drawn from the live queues) run on the candidate
  configuration vs the incumbent, in the same window where possible.
  Minimum viable batch: 3 tasks per arm for a directional read, 6 for
  a config-change recommendation.
- Measured per arm: completion, wall-clock, tokens (context-inclusive
  input + output), stalls/nudges, rework within 48h (follow-up fixes
  on the same issues).
- The test harness is a documented procedure + a results template in
  the goal workspace; runs are dispatched through the normal queues
  with the route pinned by packet (the packet format already carries
  routing intent), so tests cost no special infrastructure.
- Verdicts are recorded on the flag's issue and in the interpretive
  model doc; a passed test hands the steward a PR-ready change, a
  failed one retires the flag with its numbers attached.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] Procedure + template exist in the goal workspace. — met by PR #13419 (procedure + template versioned in the repo under `doc/agents/` per the PR placement note; filled per-run records go to the goal workspace).
- [ ] First controlled test executed end-to-end (two arms, real
      tasks, verdict recorded) — candidate chosen from the first
      pool-intelligence flag or the #1191 routing trial's leftovers.
- [ ] #1191's trial results are folded in as the mechanism's first
      historical dataset rather than re-run.

Child of the pool & routing intelligence epic. Filed by Muse
(operator) 2026-10-27.

code.title: Meta-reviewer: grade the reviewers, score model/effort choices, and evolve the reviewer guidelines
code.body:
## Work (Drew, 2026-10-27)

A daily meta-reviewer job (`pool-meta-reviewer`) reviews the
reviewers — the quota steward, the lane shifts, the dispatcher, the
babysitter, the diff reviewers — and closes the learning loop:

- Audit the steward's change ledger: every change has an event,
  every event has a measured outcome, predictions vs actuals scored.
  Changes that didn't do what they claimed get named, with the
  evidence.
- Grade model/effort choices by outcome across the window: per pool
  and per effort level — completion rate, stall rate, rework
  (reopened issues, follow-up fixes), cost per merged PR, wall-clock
  per task. Answer, with data, the standing questions: when does
  model-up + effort-down beat model-down + effort-up? Where is max
  effort buying nothing (equal outcomes at high)? Where is a pool
  failing tasks a stronger pool would have finished?
- Update the **reviewer guidelines** (living doc in the goal
  workspace `files/`) from the evidence: routing defaults, effort
  assignment heuristics, nudge/steward thresholds. Guideline changes
  are dated, evidence-linked, and themselves reviewed next cycle —
  the guidelines carry a changelog the meta-reviewer appends to.
- Escalate to Drew only decisions that are genuinely his (new pool,
  new provider, spend-class change); everything inside the POOL MAP
  is the fleet's to tune and report.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Job live; first daily review produced with per-pool/per-effort
      outcome tables from real fleet data.
- [ ] Guidelines doc exists with its first evidence-based revision
      and changelog.
- [ ] At least one standing question (max-effort waste, model-up/
      effort-down crossover) answered with fleet numbers, or an
      explicit "insufficient data, collecting via <mechanism>".

Child of the pool & routing intelligence epic. Filed by Muse
(operator) 2026-10-27.

code.title: epic(fleet): pool & routing intelligence — lanes everywhere, live dispatch + babysitting, quota stewardship, reviewer oversight, AA + measured-speed model
code.body:
## Purpose

Drew (2026-10-27, with the Muse usage upgrade): the fleet has token
headroom now — spend it on throughput and on intelligence about the
fleet's own routing. This epic scales the lane pattern to every queue
and every producer, puts the OpenChamber dispatcher and babysitter
live, and builds the oversight stack that keeps the model pools
honest: a quota/config steward that makes bounded routing decisions
and logs every change, a meta-reviewer that grades the reviewers
and updates their guidelines, and a pool-intelligence function that
combines Artificial Analysis data with our own measured session
speeds to flag models to add or retire, with controlled tests.

## Scope (children)

- Lane scale-out: A/B shifts for the opencode, openchamber, and nix
  queues (implements #1130's pattern for all queues).
- Producer lanes: second offset lanes for the issue creator and the
  PR diff reviewer.
- Dispatcher v1 live (extends #1187): launches OpenCode/OpenChamber
  sessions for queued issues under admission control.
- Babysitter live (extends #1185): rounds over ALL OpenCode sessions
  on an interval, with verdicts, quota, and pool attribution.
- Quota & config steward: monitors every pool's quota, makes bounded
  ad-hoc routing decisions (config changes land ONLY via PR to the
  canonical repo config), and keeps an append-only change-event
  ledger with before/after quota snapshots and measured impact.
- Meta-reviewer: reviews the reviewers' (steward, lanes, dispatcher,
  babysitter) activity and outcomes; updates the reviewer guidelines
  from evidence — when model-up/effort-down wins, when max effort is
  waste, which pools earn their place.
- Pool intelligence: Artificial Analysis monitoring + our own
  measured session speed per provider/model/effort; an interpretive
  model combining AA scores with our history; add/retire flags with
  quantified tradeoffs (score vs speed vs cost per pool), validated
  by controlled tests before a change is recommended.

## Execution mode

Scheduled fleet (cron lanes + steward/reviewer/intelligence jobs
under the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal), reporting to the token /
fleet side chat. Config authority stays canonical: repo PRs only,
never hand-edited deployed files. Credentials by name only.

## Dependencies

- #1234 (OpenChamber dispatch + babysitter design/pilots) — this
  epic operationalizes it.
- #1271 (paired-client enrollment) gates remote babysitter/
  dispatcher reach; early runs measure around it from the laptop.
- #1272 (routing-policy alignment) feeds the steward's decision
  bounds; the steward starts conservative until it lands.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] All children filed, labelled, and linked as sub-issues.
- [ ] Every job named in the children exists as a live cron with a
      written instruction file, verified by cron list/status.
- [ ] The change-event ledger exists and every config change in the
      window has a matching event with before/after quota snapshots.
- [x] Roadmap rows added for this epic (child issue tracks it).

code.title: design(pm-stack): chaos/rotation drills — scheduled game-days (kill collector, age the feed, drop a service) verifying banners, watchdogs, and self-healing fire
code.body:
Part of epic #1184 (PM stack coherence — wave 2, 2026-10-26).

The PM stack's failure modes are silent by default: a dead collector, an aged feed, a rejected orchestration section, or a down service have all presented as "everything is fine" at least once (#1110 being the worked example). Health pages and watchdogs only help if they actually fire — and that is only ever tested by accident. Scheduled chaos/rotation drills make it deliberate: on a cadence, a drill injects one known fault (kill the fleet-feed collector, artificially age the feed, drop one component service, corrupt one feed section), then verifies the expected signals fire — the degraded banner on the affected pages, the watchdog entry in NEEDS ORCHESTRATOR, the health page state — and files the drill result automatically as an issue comment (or a new issue when a signal does NOT fire). Drills run against the deployed stack in a maintenance window, restore everything they touched, and never run two faults at once.

Acceptance:
- A documented drill schedule exists (at least collector-kill, feed-aging, and one service-drop), runnable on demand and on cadence.
- Each drill verifies named expected signals (banner / watchdog / health state) and records pass/fail per signal.
- A failed signal files an issue automatically under epic #1184 with the drill evidence attached; a passed drill posts its result to the tracking issue.
- Drills restore all touched state (verified by a post-drill health read) and are interlocked against overlapping with each other or with a real ongoing incident flag.

## Acceptance criteria

- A scheduled drill set exists (kill collector, age the feed, drop a service — at minimum these three) and each drill verifies the expected banner/watchdog/self-healing actually fires.
- A failed drill files an issue automatically under epic #1184 with the drill evidence attached; a passed drill posts its result to the tracking issue.
- Drills restore all touched state (verified by a post-drill health read) and are interlocked against overlapping each other or a real ongoing incident flag.

code.title: feat(aggregator): source-conflict inbox — one resolvable queue for Project-vs-derived and Kaneo-vs-GitHub disagreements, with per-class trust rulings
code.body:
Part of epic #1184 (PM stack coherence — wave 2, 2026-10-26).

The stack's sources disagree regularly — Project Status vs the aggregator's derived state, Kaneo card state vs GitHub issue state — and today each disagreement lives where it happens to render: a ⚠ badge on /projects, invisible everywhere else, with no way to resolve the class of problem, only the instance. A source-conflict inbox collects every live disagreement into one queue: each entry names the item, the two sources, both values, and how long they have disagreed. Drew (or the orchestrator, for classes Drew has ruled on) records a per-class ruling — "for Kaneo-vs-GitHub state, trust GitHub" — and the ruling applies to that class going forward, recorded as data (not code), until changed. Resolved classes stop generating inbox entries; a source that starts disagreeing in a new way creates a new class rather than re-opening an old ruling silently.

Acceptance:
- One page lists all current source disagreements across facets (not only /projects), each with item, sources, both values, and disagreement age.
- A per-class "trust source X" ruling can be recorded, is stored as data, and measurably suppresses that class's entries while applying the trusted value in renders.
- Rulings are listed and revocable in the same place; revoking re-surfaces the class's current disagreements.
- The inbox count appears in the stack health surface so a growing conflict backlog is itself visible; covered by tests with seeded disagreement fixtures.

## Acceptance criteria

- A source-conflict inbox exists: one resolvable queue collecting Project-vs-derived and Kaneo-vs-GitHub disagreements, grouped per conflict class.
- Each class can receive a trust ruling; renders then apply the trusted value consistently, and rulings are listed and revocable in the same place (revoking re-surfaces the class's current disagreements).
- The inbox count appears in the stack health surface; behaviour is covered by tests with seeded disagreement fixtures.

code.title: Home network: IPv6 uplink stalls on payload transfers (PMTUD/router/ISP)
code.body:
## Problem: home IPv6 uplink stalls on real transfers

Diagnosed 2026-10-26 during the OpenClaw install work on the amd laptop.

**Symptom:** IPv6 connections to Cloudflare-fronted hosts (e.g. registry.npmjs.org) stall at zero bytes on payload-sized responses, while IPv4 to the same hosts is healthy (~530 KB/s).

Evidence (on amd, home network):
- `curl -6` of a ~4 MB npm tarball: 0 bytes after ~22 s (hard stall, not slowness).
- `curl -4` of the same tarball: full download in ~8 s.
- Interactive tools with happy-eyeballs (curl default) mask the problem by falling back to IPv4; node/pnpm does not fall back the same way, so nix fixed-output fetches for npm/pnpm deps repeatedly stalled mid-build (notably the ~780-package summarize pnpm-deps FOD), while shell tests looked fine.

## Impact

- npm/pnpm fetches from Nix builds on home machines are unreliable/slow.
- Any IPv6-first client without robust fallback can hang on this network.

## Workaround in place

- IPv4 precedence via `networking.getaddrinfo` in the amd host config (precedence ::ffff:0:0/96 = 100), marked as temporary.
- Prefer-IPv4 choices in ad-hoc tooling until this is fixed.

## What "fixed" means

Find and repair the root cause on the home network. Suspects, in order:
1. PMTUD black hole on the IPv6 path (large packets dropped; small handshakes succeed — matches the 0-byte-after-connect shape).
2. Router/ONT IPv6 handling (prefix delegation, RA/MTU advertisement, firmware).
3. ISP IPv6 routing/peering toward Cloudflare.

Acceptance: `curl -6` sustains multi-MB downloads from registry.npmjs.org and other Cloudflare hosts at speeds comparable to IPv4, repeatedly; then the getaddrinfo IPv4-preference workaround comes back out.

<!-- hands:v1 kind=interactive-login action="In the Deco admin app during your planned router session, open the IPv6 WAN screen and post the WAN IPv6 and MTU details here." -->

code.title: design(aggregator): conversational layer — ask and act over PM data in plain language through the same audited action path
code.body:
Part of epic #1184 (PM stack coherence — ideal-system design series, 2026-10-26).

## Why
The dashboard answers fixed questions on fixed pages; anything else means Drew opens GitHub, Kaneo, and a chat and stitches the answer himself. An ideal aggregator has a conversational layer: 'what's blocked on me across all projects?', 'dispatch the next nix item', 'why is this epic stalled?' — answered from the canonical PM data, with actions executed through exactly the same mediated, confirmed, audited path as dashboard clicks (no side door).

## Design questions to answer
- Where does the conversation live (a dashboard surface, the existing Muse, or both) and what data/actions does it reach through the aggregator's API — never around it?
- Action safety: which actions may run from language directly, which need an explicit confirm step, and how is the confirmation rendered?
- Grounding: how are answers cited to items/pages so Drew can verify, and what does the layer say when data is stale or fixture-backed?
- Audit: every conversational action writes the same attributed record as a UI action (identity from the SSO design), visible in the activity river.
- Scope honesty: what question classes are out of scope v1 (free-form reporting, bulk edits) and how are they refused usefully?

## Acceptance
- Design note landed in repo `doc/` + implementation issues filed and linked as sub-issues of #1184; open questions needing Drew named explicitly in the design note.

## Acceptance criteria
- A design note is landed in the repo `doc/` answering the design questions above: where the conversation lives, the action-safety/confirm model, grounding/citation of answers (including what it says when data is stale or fixture-backed), and the audit record shape.
- Implementation issues are filed and linked as sub-issues of #1184.
- Open questions needing Drew are named explicitly in the design note.
- No conversational action path bypasses the aggregator's mediated, confirmed, audited action path.

code.title: design(pm-stack): one identity across the stack — SSO propagation from the public entry into every layer, roles replace asserted authorship
code.body:
Part of epic #1184 (PM stack coherence — ideal-system design series, 2026-10-26).

## Why
Today authorship on dashboard writes is caller-asserted (tracked in #941) and each layer (aggregator, Kaneo, Pad, Grist) has its own account story, so 'who did this' is unenforceable and per-person permissions don't exist. The ideal system has one identity: the Cloudflare Access identity at the public entry (#1182) propagates through every layer, and roles (owner / orchestrator / agent / read-only) are checked server-side on every write.

## Design questions to answer
- Identity propagation mechanism per layer: Access JWT validation in the aggregator, and what Kaneo/Pad/Grist can accept (header trust behind the entry point, native SSO, or API-token-per-role)?
- Role model: which roles exist, what each may do (comment kinds, triage actions, dispatches, admin), and where the role mapping lives?
- Agent identity: how do fleet agents authenticate as themselves (not as Drew), and how are their actions attributed in the audit trail?
- Migration: how do existing dashboard comments/registry records map to real identities, and what happens to anonymous reads?
- Break-glass: what still works when Access or the IdP is down, without reopening asserted authorship?

## Acceptance

code.title: Model data pipeline: workbook-free append-only event log + agent interpretation
code.body:
## What

Replace the Drive-workbook → Postgres import for model/benchmark data with a workbook-free, append-only event log in the muse-dev Supabase (alongside the existing `ainventory` schema), plus an agent interpretation pass whenever new data lands.

Full design: `~/workspace/goals/supabase-muse-dev-platform-backups/files/aa-event-log-design-2026-10-26.md` (Drew's brief, 2026-10-26).

## Core requirements

- **Append-only**: measurement and price data are INSERT-only event rows with full provenance (source kind: aa / modelsdev / firstparty / thirdparty / probe / provider-doc; source URL; source date; ingest timestamp). Never edit an existing measurement. "Current" is a view: newest per (model × effort × benchmark × benchmark version), so a model's history across weeks and benchmark versions stays comparable.
- **Notes as data**: dated notes/anecdotes attach to models and ingest batches, attributed by kind — first-party claims (e.g. vendor launch claims), third-party reports, agent observations. Multiple per model; never collapsed into a single summary.
- **Dimensional pricing**: price rows carry a context band (min/max tokens — Luna/Haiku charge differently ≤100k vs >100k) and a time window (flat / peak / off-peak with hours). Cost per task is computed per band and per window.
- **Provider pricing policy**: a versioned table recording, per provider (and model/family scope), whether that provider passes windowed pricing (DeepSeek peak/off-peak) through or charges flat — seat valuation depends on it.
- **Gather + interpret loop**: a scheduled gatherer pulls AA + models.dev + provider catalogs, diffs against the current views, inserts only new observations, and dispatches an agent to interpret each non-empty batch (batch note + follow-up research). New-model detection is part of the diff.

## Migration path

1. New tables/views land beside `ainventory` (archive stays readable).
2. Backfill current values from `ainventory` as first events (source kind `workbook-import`, dates preserved).
3. Explorer collector (fleet feed `aa` section) switches to the new views at parity.
4. Retire the workbook leg of `coding-plan-watch-daily` after a clean week.

## Open questions (from the design doc)

- AA structured access vs page scraping for the gatherer.
- DeepSeek peak/off-peak exact windows/multipliers (verify from the official pricing page — do not encode from memory), and which of our DeepSeek doors pass the window through vs charge flat.
- Context-band edges per provider stay in data, not code.

## Acceptance criteria

- Measurement and price data are INSERT-only event rows in muse-dev Supabase with full provenance (source kind, source URL, source date, ingest timestamp); no code path updates or deletes an existing measurement.
- A 'current' view returns the newest row per (model × effort × benchmark × benchmark version), and a model's history across weeks/benchmark versions remains queryable.
- Price rows carry a context band (min/max tokens) and a time window (flat / peak / off-peak with hours), and cost-per-task is computed per band and per window.
- A versioned provider-pricing-policy table records per provider (and model/family scope) whether windowed pricing is passed through or charged flat.
- The scheduled gatherer (AA + models.dev + provider catalogs) inserts only new observations, detects new models, and dispatches an agent interpretation pass for each non-empty batch (batch note + follow-up research filed).

code.title: epic(openchamber): session dispatch + babysitting — OpenChamber as the fleet's workhorse executor
code.body:
# Session dispatch + babysitting (OpenChamber program)

## Purpose
Move the fleet's larger code work off Claude cron shifts — whose every turn re-buys a large context — onto OpenChamber-hosted OpenCode sessions running on plan pools, watched by ONE babysitter worker instead of one worker per issue. Design record: `openchamber-dispatch-babysitter-design-2026-10-26.md` (keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace, files/).

## Scope
- **Locations abstraction:** a session executor is a location (kind: openchamber | opencode-server | openclaw | codex-aster) with an adapter + capacity, so more OpenChamber machines, an OpenClaw gateway, or a Codex `.aster` route plug in without changing the babysitter loop. First location: the laptop's OpenChamber.
- **Dispatcher with admission control:** hands queue tasks marked `executor: openchamber` to sessions only when a slot is free and the routed pool passes the quota measurement gate; otherwise hands the task back (parked `executor-saturated`, noted on the issue) — never a silent backlog.
- **One babysitter:** rounds over every bound session — progress verdicts, one stall nudge then escalation, quota walls as named parks, harvesting finished sessions into verified terminal queue states. Reports quota per pool and a routing ledger (pool used per session, escalations, burn per landed task).
- **Routing, Workhorse-first:** Fast / Workhorse (default) / Frontier tiers per the POOL MAP; Frontier only on evidence or for the design half of a split (Frontier plans, Workhorse/Fast implements).
- **OpenClaw long-term path:** babysitting-by-comment — the monitor's routine issue comment is the control channel; OpenClaw reports and obeys in-thread. Reached via pilot → mirror mode → handover (see the design record).

## Execution mode
Online. Builds land as fleet job bodies, helper tooling, and Supabase/queue conventions under the fleet goal; session work happens on the laptop location.

## Dependencies
- Babysitter v1 (#1185) depends on the session-API inventory pilot (#1188).
- Dispatch v1.1 (#1187) is blocked by #1185, #1188, and the quota-attribution pilot (#1189).
- Routing thresholds wait on the routing pilot (#1191); stall detection waits on the stall-taxonomy pilot (#1192); OpenClaw mirror mode waits on the comment-loop pilot (#1190).

## Acceptance
- The babysitter runs as one worker regardless of session count; every dispatched task ends in a verified terminal state or a named hand-back.
- A week of babysitter reports shows per pool: sessions run, landed rate, Frontier escalations with reasons, quota burn per landed task.
- OpenClaw comment-loop pilot produces a go/no-go for mirror mode with the comment format pinned if go.

Filed by Muse (operator) 2026-10-26 under Drew's direction (design + issues filed the same evening; this epic groups them for the roadmap and PM dashboard).

code.title: epic(fleet): queue fleet reliability — lane workers for every queue, certified shift reporting
code.body:
# Queue fleet reliability

## Purpose
The queue system that keeps the four repos healthy (Supabase `agent.tasks`, the repo-health queues, lane shifts, the fleet monitor) proved itself on 2026-10-26 — and showed exactly two reliability defects. This epic closes both, so the fleet runs for a week at a time without operator repairs.

## Scope
1. **Claim evaporation on the non-code queues.** The code queue runs two staggered lane shifts (~90-min budgets); opencode/openchamber/nix are worked by short-budget arrangements whose runs end mid-task, stranding claims. On 2026-10-26 the monitor repaired 10+ divergences and two tasks died in queue (repaired by operator cap raises + migration 0012's park/resume accounting fix). Child: #1130 — lane-style long-budget shifts for the non-code queues.
2. **Uncertified shift runs.** Five runs on 2026-10-26 ended with a tool result lost, unable to certify their own completion even when the work landed; the parent re-verified from GitHub/queue state by hand each time. Child: #1131 — certify completion from durable state, automatically.

Out of scope: producer jobs (new-issue-creator, pr-diff-review) and the Phase 3 sweep-producer expansion (paused by Drew 2026-10-26; separate decision).

## Execution mode
Online: cron job bodies, worker instructions, monitor duties, Supabase migrations. All changes follow the fleet's isolation rules (pilot functions only; global claim/fail untouched) and the no-uncommitted-code rule.

## Dependencies
Builds on migration 0012 (applied 2026-10-26: park/resume no longer consumes attempts). Measured by the queue-pilot interim check (2026-10-28) and the fleet monitor's hourly reports.

## Acceptance
- Zero dead-in-queue tasks across all four queues over a rolling 7 days.
- Every shift delivery is certified from queue/GitHub state; no delivery rests on a run's self-report alone.
- The monitor's evaporation-repair count trends to zero; operator cap raises are no longer a routine event.

code.title: Pilot: Workhorse-first vs Frontier-plan split on comparable effort/m tasks (routing evidence)
code.body:
## Pilot — routing policy evidence: Workhorse-first vs the split

Drew's routing rule (2026-10-26): prefer Workhorse over Frontier,
Frontier only when absolutely required, try Workhorse first — or split
(Frontier designs/plans, Workhorse or Fast implements). This pilot
produces the evidence to set the dispatcher's thresholds.

## Run

Pick 3 comparable `effort/m` implementation tasks (similar area, clear
acceptance, tests exist). Run:

- **A — Workhorse only** (DeepSeek Flash high or Luna Max).
- **B — Workhorse only**, second data point.
- **C — Split:** short Frontier session writes the design/plan on the
  issue; Workhorse session implements from it.

Record per run: landed or not (PR merged / task completed), iterations
to green, wall-clock, pool burn (per the quota attribution pilot's
method), and a one-line quality note from the reviewing pass.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A comparison table with the five measures above for A/B/C.
- [ ] A recommended default written as a rule the dispatcher can
      encode (e.g. "Workhorse first always; split when triage marks
      design-risk X; pure Frontier only on evidence Y").
- [ ] If Workhorse fails a run, the failure mode is named precisely
      (capability, context, tooling) — "needed Frontier" alone is not
      an acceptable conclusion.

code.title: OpenChamber dispatch v1.1: admission control, hand-backs, stall nudges, harvesting, Workhorse-first routing
code.body:
## What

v1.1 of the OpenChamber dispatch system (design:
`files/openchamber-dispatch-babysitter-design-2026-10-26.md`): turn
the report-only babysitter into the working dispatcher + babysitter.

## Scope

- **Dispatcher:** claims queue tasks whose packet carries
  `executor: openchamber` (larger code work: effort/m+l, session-shaped
  per triage), admits against (a) location capacity and (b) the POOL
  MAP measurement gate for the routed pool (fresh quota read; ≥85% of
  window = no new heavy work). Creates the session in a per-task
  worktree on branch `queue/<task-id>-<issue>-<slug>` and records the
  binding (session id, location, pool/route, started-at) on the task.
- **Hand-back:** no slot or no headroom → park the task with reason
  class `executor-saturated` and note it on the issue. Saturation is
  reported, never a silent backlog; a Claude lane can still claim the
  task if urgent.
- **Babysitter actions:** stall nudge (one message into a session idle
  >20 min while claiming work: checkpoint/continue/state blocker; max
  2, then escalate to the monitor tracker); wall handling (quota stop =
  park blocked with the wall named, never a PAYG fallback); harvesting
  (session done → verify against GitHub → complete/park/block the task
  with labels synced and an agent-note on the issue).
- **Routing policy as config:** Fast / Workhorse (default) / Frontier
  tiers per the design; escalation to Frontier requires recorded
  evidence (failed Workhorse attempt or design-shaped triage); the
  split pattern (Frontier plan → Workhorse/Fast implementation) is a
  first-class dispatch shape. Routing ledger entries land in the
  babysitter report.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A task marked `executor: openchamber` flows queue → session →
      PR → verified terminal queue state with no Claude lane involved.
- [ ] With the location at capacity, the next candidate is handed back
      (parked, `executor-saturated`, issue noted) within one round.
- [ ] A deliberately stalled session receives exactly one nudge, and a
      second stall escalates instead of nudging forever.
- [ ] Every Frontier session in a week of reports has a recorded
      escalation reason; Workhorse-first is the observed default.
- [ ] No dispatched task evaporates: every binding ends in a terminal
      state or a named hand-back (monitor Duty 1 stays clean).

Depends on: babysitter v1 (report-only) and the session-API + quota
attribution pilots. Filed by Muse (operator) 2026-10-26.

Stage-2 epic under #1047, per Drew's direction 2026-10-26 22:41 CDT. Design: quota-plane-design-2026-10-26.md (usage-billing-hub goal files), Stage 2. Parent context: epic #1047.

Direction, in Drew's terms: quotas and plan details gathered routinely at every regular interval (~15 minutes) by a process inside the PM stack; that data informs automated decisions the OpenCode pools make; Muse may change the plumbing so the stack reaches quota data directly — for browser-only dashboards, pull from a file or use the browser token directly against the undocumented API the dashboard page calls; all but two providers are reachable that way, and the two exceptions carry their own integration-plan issues (login -> capture token -> undocumented dashboard API); visibility stays fully current, with a pull on page load when data is older than ~1-5 minutes.

Priority order (children filed in this order; horizons on org Project #4):
1. P0 Gatherer service (15-min tick, quota-current)
2. P0 Token-adapter framework
3. P0 Exceptions audit — name the two
4. P1 OpenCode consumption contract
5. P1 Adapters: ClinePass / OpenCode Go / Claude / Command Code
6. P1 Exception integration: Meta
7. P1 Exception integration: Google/Antigravity
8. P1 Aggregator lazy refresh on page load
9. P1 Daily model + route audit (stewardship block LIVE 2026-10-26)
10. P2 Quota-plane visibility (gatherer health on /quota)
11. P2 Stage-3 design (predictive quota ops)

Acceptance for the epic: every held provider's quota arrives via the gatherer at 15-minute cadence (or its exception issue closes with the file-export fallback live); OpenCode placements consume the fresh data; /quota freshness is self-evident per provider.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Every held provider's quota arrives via the gatherer at ~15-minute cadence, or its exception issue closes with the file-export fallback live.
- [ ] OpenCode placements consume the fresh quota data.
- [ ] /quota freshness is self-evident per provider.

code.title: id: idea — native TUI client (ratatui) on the shell contract
code.body:
## Idea: native TUI client (ratatui)

From `pkgs/id/TODO.md`:

A high-performance TUI (ratatui or the best-performing Rust TUI stack) that works locally without a server, or connects to a local/remote server over iroh (not SSH). Custom efficient protocol: the server sends intents and bytes (e.g. 'draw this blob at 64x,16y at 256x256', kitty image protocol) instead of a raw terminal stream, with thought given to avoiding a second round trip for uncached blobs. Roughly three panels: room/object selector + search + pinned favourites | the interactive room/document or meta pages | a chatroom for the room/topic. code.title: impl(dns-registry): recurring DNS backup job, renewal/cost tracking, dashboard view of the domain register
code.body:
## Context

Drew's direction (2026-10-25): a standing registry of every domain/DNS name we own, a regular backup of the full DNS config for every zone, and one place to see which domain renews next, which are completely unused, and which are unused but earmarked for projects.

**First pass is DONE (2026-10-25)** — this issue covers only the recurring machinery that pass deliberately did not build.

- Register: `~/workspace/goals/stand-up-lab-cluster-talm-talos-cozystack-postgres-rustfs/files/dns-domain-register.md` — 41 domains (39 in the Porkbun account `developingtoday`, + drewrypope.com and boats.dev which are Porkbun-registered under a different account), sorted by next renewal, with registrar, DNS host, renewal date, auto-renew state, list renewal price, where-used evidence, plan/status, and a review flag per domain.
- Seed snapshot: `~/workspace/goals/stand-up-lab-cluster-talm-talos-cozystack-postgres-rustfs/hidden_files/dns-backup-2026-10-25/` — Cloudflare zone export (1 zone: security.cab, all 21 records), Porkbun account inventory (39 domains) + full TLD pricing table, public-DNS probe for all 41 domains, RDAP for the 2 outside-account domains. The snapshot README documents coverage and gaps precisely.

Headline facts from the first pass: all 39 account domains have auto-renew ON ($595.62/yr at list prices); next renewal is 1110x.de on 2027-02-09; only 3 of 41 domains show genuine use (security.cab, developing-today.com, drewrypope.com).

## To build

### 1. Scheduled DNS-config backup job
Recurring (suggest weekly) read-only export producing a dated snapshot in the seed's format, diffed against the previous snapshot, surfacing: record changes, new/removed domains, expiry-date changes, price changes. Sources: Cloudflare API (zones + records; tokens in Bitwarden as `cloudflare.api-token-day-to-day` / `cloudflare.api-token-account-wide`) and Porkbun API (`porkbun.api-key` / `porkbun.secret-key` in Bitwarden).

### 2. Renewal & cost tracking over time
Each cycle appends to the register (or a history file beside it): observation date, per-domain renewal date, per-TLD list renewal price. This is how prior-year costs accumulate — the first pass could only mark them "unknown" (no invoice source reachable). Alert when a domain enters its renewal window (suggest ≤45 days; with auto-renew universal, the alert is about upcoming spend, not lapse risk) and when a renewal price changes cycle-over-cycle. If an invoice-grade source becomes available (Porkbun billing history, Gmail receipts), record actual charged amounts alongside list prices.

### 3. Dashboard / aggregator view
A view of the register data showing Drew's three lists: **next renewal** (with date + price), **completely unused**, **unused but earmarked** — fed by a structured export (e.g. `register.json`) the backup job emits alongside the Markdown register, consumed by the PM aggregator (same pattern as the fleet feed / quota panel).

### 4. Gap-closers identified by the first pass
- **Porkbun API key is domain-restricted**: `dns/retrieve` succeeds only for security.cab and refuses the other 38 domains, so zone-file-grade exports don't exist yet for the Porkbun-hosted zones (first pass used a public-DNS probe instead). Extend the key's domain allowlist in the Porkbun control panel, or file an unrestricted key in Bitwarden (by name) and point the job at it.
- **Second Porkbun account**: drewrypope.com (expires 2028-06-14) and boats.dev (expires 2027-04-02) are Porkbun-registered but absent from the `developingtoday` API account — identify the account and bring both domains under the same inventory (auto-renew state and full exports are currently unknowable).
- **security.cab expiry discrepancy**: Porkbun account says expires 2027-02-24 (created 2018-02-24); registry RDAP said 2027-08-14. Resolve against the Porkbun control panel and correct whichever source is wrong.

## Acceptance

- Backup job runs on schedule and produces a diffed snapshot without human prompting.
- Register history shows ≥2 cycles of renewal/price observations appended automatically.
- Aggregator renders the three lists from the structured export.
- A test domain entering the renewal window produces the spend alert.

## Acceptance criteria

- A scheduled (weekly or better) read-only job exports the full DNS config for every owned zone/domain (Cloudflare + Porkbun) into a dated snapshot in the seed snapshot's format, using the Bitwarden-stored API credentials.
- Each snapshot is diffed against the previous one; record changes, new/removed domains, expiry-date changes, and price changes are surfaced in the run output.
- A renewal/cost history accumulates per domain (observation date, renewal date, list renewal price; actual charged amounts when an invoice-grade source is reachable).
- An alert fires when a domain enters the renewal window (≤45 days) or a renewal price changes cycle-over-cycle.
- A dashboard view shows the domain register sorted by next renewal, flagging unused and earmarked-but-unused domains.

code.title: id phase-3: P3.7 real-network holepunch and n0 QAD results — phone leg via #1831 + labelled VM emulation
code.body:
## Finding

P3.7 (real-network holepunch and n0 QAD tests on two networks, N29) was originally framed as owner-blocked on two owner-provided networks and was tracked only in plan/prose, not as a standalone issue.

**That blocker was withdrawn by Drew on 2026-10-28.** The plan is now a native phone peer over the carrier network against the laptop peer at home, plus a reproducible laptop VM NAT-emulation lab for the cells a phone cannot cover. The plan issue is #1826. This issue tracks running and recording those tests.

## Test-access plan (2026-10-28 owner ruling — supersedes the two-network blocker)

Drew does not have a second computer on a second home network and will not set one up. There is no VPC or paid networking — any server we run would be a plain host, not a VPC. He will run the phone leg himself. Laptop VMs with an emulated NAT configuration are acceptable for the cells a phone cannot cover. Carrier CGNAT × home NAT is a legitimate, realistic cell — it is the pairing actual mobile users present — and it is what the phone run measures honestly.

- **Phone leg — real network, OPEN.** The peer must be a native iroh endpoint. The tracked implementation is #1831's proof-of-concept Android app (`S3`). A browser/Wasm page **cannot** be an iroh peer: browsers have no UDP sockets, which are what iroh's holepunch and QAD probes need, and there is no wasm32 connectivity target. At most, a Wasm page can be a *result viewer* for a run the native peers performed.
- **Emulated leg — labelled emulated, ALREADY RECORDED.** The reproducible C2 NAT-emulation lab landed in #4984 (PR #5665, merged `a3eba8fb6649`). Its 2026-11-04 results are recorded on this issue as **Linux netfilter emulation**, never as real-network measurements.

Ruling comment: https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/795#issuecomment-6480740733.
The lane D escalation (queue task 2226) is answered by that ruling; there is **no pending Drew decision** here.

## Evidence

Historical context, kept for the record (pre-ruling):

- `doc/2026-10-11T11-08-42Z_design_remaining_work/plan-phases.md` §8 Phase 3, step P3.7: "Real-network holepunch and n0 QAD tests on two networks (N29)" — Blocked by "owner provides networks", tests "the C2 matrix on real networks (owner-blocked)".
- `doc/2026-10-12T08-58-59Z_phase_3_sync_relays/2026-10-12T08-58-59Z_phase_3_sync_relays.md` P3.7 row: status "owner-blocked", notes "needs two networks". Open questions: "Real-network numbers are not measured (P3.7)." End: "Not verified: ... real-network sync and relay numbers."
- `doc/2026-10-14T_platform_completion/acceptance-brief.md` line 75 (unchecked), grouped with P7.5.

## Why it matters

The C2 NAT/holepunch matrix and n0 QAD behaviour have been validated only on loopback so far. Real-network results (NAT type combinations, QAD relay ordering) are the connectivity claims the plan makes. The phone leg is the honest real-network measurement; the VM lab covers the remaining cells and is labelled emulated.

## What's needed

1. **Phone leg:** build and run #1831's Android app as the native phone peer, run the C2/N29 checks from Drew's phone over the carrier network against the laptop peer at home, and record the results (including observed NAT types on both ends) here.
2. **Emulated leg:** already done — keep the emulated results labelled as emulated, and do not re-run or re-record them as real-network numbers.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] **Phone leg (real network, OPEN — pending #1831).** The #1831 Android app runs as a native iroh peer on Drew's phone over the carrier network against the laptop peer at home, and completes a holepunch + QAD check; the observed NAT types on both ends are recorded on this issue. This is the remaining blocker for real-network results.
- [ ] **Emulated leg (ALREADY RECORDED — 2026-11-04).** The reproducible C2 NAT-emulation lab from #4984 (PR #5665) covers the C2 matrix cells the phone pairing cannot; its results are recorded on this issue and labelled emulated. Keep them labelled emulated, never as real-network measurements.
- [ ] The Phase 3 record's real-network numbers section is updated with a clear split between the phone-leg (real) results and the emulated VM results — OR this issue is closed as superseded by later connectivity work, with the superseding work linked.

**Superseded:** the former first criterion — "Two owner-provided networks are available and identified for the test run (this is the blocker)" — is withdrawn. It is not a prerequisite and must not gate this issue.

code.body:
Part of the fleet-wide OpenCode 2 migration tracked at https://github.com/developing-today/opencode/issues/374 (origin issue for the whole set).

Upstream migration guide: https://dev.opencode.ai/v2/docs/migrate-v1/

- Config files, agents, commands, and skills under `.opencode/` are intended to be compatible; some v1 fields are **accepted but ignored** by v2. Hard rejections get fixed (PR); accepted-but-ignored fields get listed here so we can decide whether to keep them while runtimes are still migrating or drop them.
- Note: `.opencode/cli.json` already targets the v2 CLI schema (`https://opencode.ai/v2/cli.json`), while `.opencode/tui.jsonc` still exists alongside it (v2 auto-migrates tui.json → cli.json).

## 2. Plugin ports — v1 plugin API → v2 plugin API

v1 plugins do not run in v2 (new plugin API). Ours, in order of how much we depend on them:

- **mcpx bridge + mcpx-session** — `.opencode/plugin/mcpx-session.ts` is the plugin entry (imports `tool` and `Plugin` from `@opencode-ai/plugin`; default export is `async ({ directory, worktree, project, client }, options) => …`), backed by the `.opencode/plugin/mcpx/` modules (daemon client, ops). First step: inventory the v1 hooks/lifecycle points and SDK calls these use, and diff them against the v2 plugin API in the migration guide; list anything with no v2 equivalent.
- **subtask2** — third-party npm plugin `@openspoon/subtask2@latest` in the config `plugin` array, configured by `.opencode/subtask2.jsonc`. First step: check whether subtask2 ships a v2-compatible release; if not, decide between a fork, vendoring, or replacing it.
- **The rest of the `plugin` array** is also v1-era npm plugins (opencode-working-memory, opencode-scheduler, opencode-pty, opencode-devcontainers, @openchamber/opencode-claude, @pieliesdie/opencode-antigravity-auth, and more). Each needs the same v2-compatibility check; the two items above are the ones we own or depend on most.
- `.opencode/package.json` pins `@opencode-ai/plugin` 1.18.19 — the plugin SDK bump belongs to this workstream.

Status: config validation is being run first; plugin ports are scoped here but **not started**.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Workstream 1 (config validation) is recorded as done: `.opencode/opencode.jsonc` loads clean under OpenCode v2 (validation comment, 2026-10-24); any accepted-but-ignored v1 fields are listed on this issue with a keep/drop decision each.
- [ ] The mcpx bridge + mcpx-session plugin has a v2 port, or a written gap list naming every v1 hook/SDK call with no v2 equivalent and the chosen workaround.
- [ ] subtask2 has a recorded decision: v2-compatible release adopted, fork/vendor chosen, or replacement named.
- [ ] Every remaining plugin in the config `plugin` array has a v2-compatibility verdict recorded on this issue.
- [ ] `.opencode/package.json` pins a v2-era `@opencode-ai/plugin` SDK and the repo's agents/commands/skills still load under the v2 CLI.

## What and why

Lazy open, idle eviction with checkpoint and a bounded memory budget per world, measured against 1,000 idle and 100 active (20 ev/s, p99 < 50 ms) targets with the F11.8 harness. Lazy open, eviction and per-guest memory caps exist, but nobody has measured the targets and a world's total memory is not bounded.

## Current status

**Partial.** Mechanisms exist from Phase 9/10: pkgs/id/src/world_hub.rs:7-15 (lazy single-flight open, session and open-world ceilings, idle eviction), and a per-guest linear memory cap of 16 MiB (pkgs/id/src/sandbox.rs:25-36). The per-world total memory budget with refusal tests landed in #4628. code.title: Seitan V2 (P6.1): check the Keybase server side, old-style invites, and a real accept before P6.3
code.body:
Phase 6, step P6.1 (Seitan V2) has an open item from the Keybase admin path. It is not blocked by it: the local rules (expiry, single use, revocation, freshness) are implemented and tested. This item must be settled before P6.3 and P6.4 (invite events and links) ship, and before the e2e invite and accept test.

Branch `p6-seitan` (not pushed), commit `3eafe3b3` (`pkgs/id/src/seitan/`).

## Verified by reading keybase/client (master, 2026-10-12)

- Accept message: `SigPayload` in `go/teams/seitan_v2.go` has the fields `stage`, `uid`, `eldest_seqno`, `ctime`, `invite_id`, `version`, in that order. Our `accept::message` matches.
- Encoding: `kbcrypto.CodecHandle()` sets only `WriteExt`. `keybase/go-codec` writes positive integers in their smallest form and strings as fixstr below 32 bytes, then str8. Our golden test assumes the same.
- Signature: `kbcrypto.NaclSigningKeyPrivate.Sign` is plain `ed25519.Sign` over the payload, with no domain prefix. Keybase verifies with `ed25519.Verify`. We verify strictly, which accepts a subset of what Keybase accepts. Honest signers are unaffected.
- `ctime` unit: V2 is milliseconds (`handler.go`, "For V2 this is ms since the epoch"). V1 and invite links are seconds.
- Admin V2 check: `verifySeitanSingleV2` (`go/teams/handler.go`) verifies the signature over the message rebuilt from the server-supplied `UnixCTime`. It has no freshness check on `ctime`.

## Not verified: what must be checked

1. **Server side (closed source).** The `team/seitan_v2` endpoint receives `sig`, `now`, and `invite_id`, and forwards `UnixCTime` to the admin's handler. The signature covers `ctime`, so the server cannot alter it without failing the check. Still unknown: what the server does with a withheld or replayed accept, and whether it keeps any state that the admin relies on. This cannot be checked from the client repo.
2. **Keybase's own V2 invites are old-style.** `Team.InviteSeitanV2` (`go/teams/teams.go`) creates an `SCTeamInvite` with only type, name, and ID. `IsNewStyleInvite` is `invite.MaxUses != nil` (`go/teams/chain.go`), so the admin path does not check expiry or a use count for these invites. `CanConsumeInvite` and `ConsumeInviteByID` (`go/teams/transactions.go`) check only the completed-invite marker within one transaction. Expiry and single use in our design are our rules, not Keybase's. Still to check: how a V2 invite stays single-use across transactions (the chain's stored state). Until that is settled, Keybase must not be cited as the reference for single use or expiry.
3. **No accept sample from a real client.** No Keybase test vector covers an accept or a signed accept. Capture one accept (`uid`, `eldest_seqno`, `ctime`, `invite_id`, and the signature) from a real Keybase client and check that `seitan::accept::verify` accepts its bytes. This is the only check of the accept bytes beyond the source reading.
4. **V3 (invite links).** The invite-link path (`verifySeitanSingleInvitelink`, seconds-based `ctime`, AKey) is out of scope for P6.1 and is not checked here.

## What the code assumes until these are checked

- The accept message is Keybase's field set and encoding, as read above.
- Expiry and single use are local rules, enforced by the admin's node on its own invite state, not by Keybase.
- The freshness window (N23) is a local rule, not part of the accept bytes.

Reference: the S9 spike `doc/2026-10-11T03-44-33Z_design_groups_events_delegation/spikes/s9-seitan/RESULTS.md`, and the phase record `doc/2026-10-12T19-11-31Z_phase_6_invites_pull_cli/`.

## Acceptance criteria

- A real Keybase client accept sample (uid, eldest_seqno, ctime, invite_id, signature) is captured and `seitan::accept::verify` is shown to accept its bytes (golden test added).
- The single-use question for old-style V2 invites across transactions is settled from keybase/client chain state, or Keybase is explicitly no longer cited as the reference for single use/expiry.
- The server-side unknowns (withheld/replayed accepts, server state) are documented as accepted unknowns with a stated rationale, since the closed-source endpoint cannot be checked from the client repo.
- This item is closed out before P6.3/P6.4 (invite events and links) ship, per the body's constraint.

code.title: Nix Playwright E2E suite fails after vendoring dependencies
code.body:
## Summary

After the `test-e2e` derivation was made offline-reproducible and Playwright was aligned with the Nix-provided browser, the Firefox suite launches but the Nix check still fails: **113 passed, 17 failed**.

Reproduced locally with:

`nix build ./pkgs/id#checks.x86_64-linux.test-e2e -L`

Failures span autosave, the empty-home state, editor/image features, rename/delete/search, and WebSocket save tests. Examples include:

- Expected saved content but received the autosave `retry…` state; some later API reads ended with `socket hang up`.
- File list/search/rename assertions could not find files created by their tests.
- `/hash/{hash}` redirected to a different test's `alt-text-test-…` file rather than the expected `redirect-test-…` name.

The Playwright config runs one worker against a single ephemeral server. Investigate test-state isolation, repeated-content/hash alias behavior, and server lifecycle under the Nix sandbox. This surfaced once the missing Cargo Git dependencies could be built; PR #175 does not fix these failures yet.

Related follow-up: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/175

opencode.title: fix(tui): truncated session.json is overwritten with in-memory pins on the next pin change — pinned sessions silently erased
opencode.body:
## Problem

The TUI session-pin store (`packages/tui/src/context/local.tsx`, `createSession()`) has the same corrupt-overwrite shape as #2778 / #2771: a present-but-unreadable `session.json` is silently replaced with in-memory state on the next pin change.

- Load (`local.tsx:535-548`): `readJson<unknown>(filePath).then(...).catch(() => {})` — any read/parse failure (truncated JSON, EACCES, etc.) is swallowed and the store stays at its empty default (`pinned: []`), then `ready` is set true.
- Save (`local.tsx:524-533`): `save()` unconditionally `writeJsonAtomic(filePath, { pinned: sessionStore.pinned })` once ready — including the `state.pending` flush and every `togglePin`/`prune`/`session.deleted` path.

So one bad byte in `<state>/session.json` erases every pinned session the next time the user pins/unpins anything (or a session is deleted): the write is built on the empty fallback, not on what the file holds.

This is distinct from #2778 (model.json favorites/recents) and PR #2781 (which hardens only `model-preference.ts` and `context/storage.tsx`): `local.tsx` session pin state is a third store with its own file (`<state>/session.json`) and is untouched by that PR.

## Repro (logic mirror of the exact load/save lines)

1. Write a truncated `<state>/session.json`: `{"pinned":["ses_aaa","ses_bbb"]`
2. Run the load shape: `JSON.parse` throws → `.catch(() => {})` → `pinned` stays `[]`
3. Run the save shape: `writeJsonAtomic(file, { pinned: [...[], "ses_new"] })`
4. File now holds `{"pinned":["ses_new"]}` — `ses_aaa`/`ses_bbb` silently wiped

Verified with node against the exact `readFileSync`/`JSON.parse`/catch/save sequence (before: truncated 31 bytes, after: `{"pinned":["ses_new"]}`, original IDs gone).

## Fix shape

Same `readForWrite` precedent as #2771 / #2781, scoped to this store:

- Add a strict read for the write path: `ENOENT` → `{ pinned: [] }` (first run, unchanged); unparseable/unreadable → refuse the write with an error naming the file.
- Keep the tolerant `readJson...catch(()=>{})` for load/display so the TUI never stops.
- Route `save()` (including the pending flush) through the strict read, or gate `save()` on a successful initial load flag — nothing is overwritten until the file is fixed or moved aside.

## Evidence

- `packages/tui/src/context/local.tsx:519` — `const filePath = path.join(paths.state, "session.json")`
- `packages/tui/src/context/local.tsx:524-533` — `save()` writes `{ pinned }` unconditionally once ready

opencode.title: fix(files): public-file cache hits ignore If-None-Match — a revalidating client gets 200 and the full body instead of 304
opencode.body:
## Evidence (source, services/files/src/index.ts)

- Lines 51–57: the cache lookup copies \`If-None-Match\`, \`If-Modified-Since\` and \`Range\` into a \`headers\` object and calls \`caches.default.match(new Request(cacheKey, { headers }))\`. Line 55 drops \`If-Modified-Since\` when \`If-None-Match\` is present, so the author expected the lookup to honour the validators.
- Lines 58–59: a hit returns the stored response (\`return cached\`) with no conditional evaluation. The 304 logic (lines 93–100) is only reached on a miss.
- The Cache API \`match()\` matches on URL and \`Vary\`; it does not evaluate request conditionals against the stored response, so those headers have no effect on the result. This is from the Cache API contract, not a workerd run.
- \`services/files/src/index.test.ts:38\` stubs \`caches.default.match\` to return \`undefined\`, so the hit path never runs in tests. The 304 test passes only because it skips the cache.

## Impact

For a cached public file (objects up to 512 MiB are cached, line 157), a client that revalidates with \`If-None-Match\` gets a 200 with the full body rather than a bodyless 304. Bytes are correct, but the bandwidth saving the 304 path exists for is lost on every hit.

Confidence: medium. Not reproduced under \`wrangler dev\`.

## Repro (to confirm before fixing)

1. \`GET /files/site/<key>\` once so the response is cached (complete 200s only, line 154).
2. \`GET /files/site/<key>\` with \`If-None-Match: <etag from step 1>\`.
3. Expected: 304, no body. Expected per the source: 200 with the full body.

## Fix shape

- On a cache hit, evaluate \`If-None-Match\` / \`If-Modified-Since\` against the cached response's \`ETag\` and \`Last-Modified\` and return 304 when they match, or skip the cache when a conditional header is present.
- Add a test that stubs \`caches.default.match\` to return a stored 200 and asserts a matching \`If-None-Match\` yields 304.

Related, not duplicated: #1646 (closed, Range handling in the same worker).

opencode.title: fix(tui): an unparseable model.json is overwritten with defaults on the next preference update — favorites and recent models silently erased
opencode.body:
## Problem

The TUI model-preference store treats an unreadable `model.json` as empty and then writes that empty state back over the file. A single malformed or truncated `model.json` (for example a hand edit with a syntax error, or an external tool that truncates the file) is silently replaced, erasing the user's favorites, variants and the rest of the recent list on the next preference update.

## Evidence

- `packages/tui/src/model-preference.ts:106-109`: `read()` is `readJson(filePath).then(decodeModelPreference).catch(() => decodeModelPreference(undefined))`. Any read or parse failure becomes the empty preference, not an error.
- `packages/tui/src/model-preference.ts:116-119`: `update()` runs under `Flock.withLock`, calls `read()`, then `writeJsonAtomic(filePath, { ...current, ...patch(...) })`. The write therefore always proceeds from the empty fallback.
- `packages/tui/src/util/persistence.ts:20-23`: `readJson` is a bare `JSON.parse(await readFile(...))`, so a syntax error throws and reaches the catch above.
- Reproduced against the real `createModelPreferenceRepository` (module and `persistence.ts` copied out of the repo with only the `Flock` import stubbed, bun run):
  - initial file: `{"recent":[{"providerID":"openai","modelID":"gpt-4"}],"favorite":[{"providerID":"openai","modelID":"gpt-4o"}]` (missing closing brace)
  - `addRecent({ providerID: "anthropic", modelID: "claude" })`
  - result on disk: `{"recent":[{"providerID":"anthropic","modelID":"claude"}],"favorite":[],"variant":{}}`. The `gpt-4` recent entry and the `gpt-4o` favorite are gone.
- The same shape exists in `packages/tui/src/context/storage.tsx:66-70` (`load()` returns `options.initial` on any `JSON.parse` error) and `storage.tsx:75-80` (`update()` writes the draft derived from that fallback under the lock). Covers every `storage.store(...)` key, for example session pins in `context/local.tsx`. Source-verified only; not reproduced.
- `packages/tui/test/model-preference.test.ts` covers concurrent updates and decoding of malformed fields, but has no case for an unparseable file followed by an update. Nothing pins the reset as intended.

## Why it matters

The fallback is meant to tolerate a missing file (first run), but it also covers a present-but-unparseable file. The user loses prompt-independent state (favorites, pinned variants, recent models) with no error, no backup and no log line, and the loss happens on an ordinary preference change. It is the TUI counterpart of the core route-overrides reset (#2771) and the JSONL read-as-empty defect (#2752); those cover other stores.

## Suggested fix

- Distinguish ENOENT (use the empty default) from parse or read failure. On parse failure, do not overwrite the file: either surface the error and leave the file untouched, or move the corrupt file aside (for example `model.json.corrupt-<ts>`) before writing the fresh default.
- Apply the same rule to `storage.tsx` `load()`, so a corrupt store is not rewritten from `options.initial` under the lock.

## Acceptance criteria

- A test that writes an unparseable `model.json`, calls `addRecent` / `saveVariant`, and asserts either the original bytes are preserved (or backed up) and an error is reported, not a silent overwrite.
- The same behavior is covered for a `storage.store` key with a corrupt file.
- A missing file still starts from the default with no warning.

Related: #2752 (JSONL read failures treated as empty), #2771 (route-overrides corrupt-store overwrite), #2528 (TUI concurrent rewrites).

opencode.title: fix(core): surface ambiguous outcomes when command recovery may replay side effects
opencode.body:
## Problem

Durable shell/command admission makes an admitted command recoverable, but command execution is explicitly at-least-once across a process crash. `packages/core/src/session/operation.ts:45-57` says a command whose execution is lost after delivery runs again; `:91-105` invokes the registered command and consumes its inbox row only in `ensuring` after execution settles. `packages/core/src/session/execution.ts:96-127` restarts pending operation rows during a later drain.

A crash after a command definition has performed a side effect but before `InboxDelivered` is projected leaves the row pending. Recovery then invokes that definition again. `packages/core/src/command.ts:22-26,84-91` permits registered definitions to run arbitrary Effects, so repeated file, external-service, or other side effects are possible. The current durable row does not distinguish never-started from started-with-unknown-outcome.

This is a follow-up to #2698 / PR #2760, which deliberately introduced durable admission and documented at-least-once recovery. It is not asking for exactly-once execution of arbitrary external effects; that cannot be guaranteed without cooperation from the effectful command.

## Acceptance criteria

- Persist enough operation lifecycle state to distinguish an admitted-but-never-started command from one whose execution started but has no durable terminal result.
- On recovery, do not silently rerun an operation with an ambiguous prior outcome. Surface an explicit interrupted/unknown result and an intentional retry path, or another design that prevents automatic duplicate side effects while preserving recoverability.
- Preserve automatic start of commands that were admitted but never started, and preserve normal success/failure behavior.
- Add crash-boundary tests covering recovery before start, after start with no side effect, and after a side effect but before terminal settlement; the post-side-effect case must not silently apply the effect twice.

## Evidence

- `packages/core/src/session/operation.ts:53-57,69-105` documents and implements at-least-once command recovery and consumes the row after execution settles.
- `packages/core/src/session/execution.ts:96-127` drains pending operation rows after a lost start/restart.
- `packages/core/src/command.ts:22-26,84-91` defines command handlers as arbitrary Effects.
- `packages/core/test/session-shell.test.ts` covers shell admission and execution, but there is no focused crash/replay test for command operations.

The behavior is explicitly documented, but the user-visible ambiguous-outcome and duplicate-side-effect tradeoff has no recovery affordance or focused regression coverage.

opencode.title: cli-rs: regenerated types require sections/models that leaner wire payloads omit — decide the tolerance policy
opencode.body:
Found during the #2733/#2738 landing (PR #2768), corroborated by Lane TO's independent verification recorded on #2733 (comment 7104002680).

The current-main regeneration makes two previously unmodelled payloads strict:

- `ConfigUpdatedData` was `crate::de::NotNull` (any non-null data); it is now a struct requiring `sections: Vec<String>`, matching packages/core's `UpdatedData = Schema.Struct({ sections: Array(String) })`. But the recorded F.7 parity fixture and the TS client's own `solid-refresh.test.ts` carry `config.updated` with `data: {}`, and TS core consumers guard with `Schema.is(UpdatedData)` rather than requiring the field.
- `ProviderInfoWithModels.models` is required (schema-required); provider payloads without `models` no longer decode.

PR #2768 adapts the in-repo fixtures to the current contract (empty `sections` / `models`), which is right for a client built against the current server. The open question this issue tracks: should the generated Rust types tolerate a payload from an older or leaner server that omits these now-required fields (for example, generator-emitted defaults for `sections`/`models`), or is strictness the intended posture — in which case the parity fixture's `data: {}` shape is simply a legacy recording?

Not blocking #2733/#2738: their acceptance (generate completes end to end; workspace suites at the pristine-main baseline) is met without a decision here.

opencode.title: Model routes: follow-ups after #2674, #2676 and #2679
opencode.body:
Follow-ups to the model-route work in #2674 (per-model default effort and lock, waits for pools of pools), #2676 (the last target is not cut off by the first-output wait) and #2679 (a pool turn moves on to the next member when a failure after output is not retried). Nothing here blocks them.

## 1. A granted retry after output can ask the same failed member again

On the #2679 branch, pool `recovery-three` = `broken`, `broken2`, `okay` (a mock whose `broken*` models stream text and then fail) received `broken`, `broken`, `broken2`, `okay`.

- The first failure after output was granted a retry (`attempts` 2). The turn continued through the existing `Continue` path, and re-selection picked `broken` again.
- The comment in `session/runner/step.ts` says re-selection "sees the target marked failed above", but here one failure evidently did not bench it. Not traced further.
- Options: send the granted continuation through the fallback chain too, so members are asked in order with no repeats; bench a member on its first failure after output; or document that `attempts` covers this case.

## 2. A plugin's `session.retry` hook can no longer stop a routed turn after output

Since #2679, while another member can take the turn, a hook that declines only stops the same member being asked again. Before output this was already the rule (#1014). If a plugin needs to end the turn, it would need an explicit "stop" decision. Only worth building if someone needs it.

## 3. `opencode run` exits 1 when a later member answered

When a reply in the turn failed and the next member then answered, the CLI prints both and exits 1. That happens on 2.0.30's existing continuation and on #2679 alike; a plain answer exits 0. Options: exit 0 when the turn's last reply succeeded, or document the meaning.

## 4. Test isolation: a `TMPDIR` under `HOME` breaks `location-layer.test.ts`

With `TMPDIR=~/.local/share/opencode/tmp`, which the OpenCode agent harness sets, `test/location-layer.test.ts` fails 4 of 28. One failure is "Expected to not contain: opencode-route": pools from outside the test show up. With `TMPDIR` unset, all 28 pass.

Adding `OPENCODE_CONFIG`, `OPENCODE_DB`, `XDG_CONFIG_DIRS`/`XDG_DATA_DIRS`, the `OPENCODE_EXPERIMENTAL*`/`OPENCODE_ENABLE*` flags or the `OPENCHAMBER_*` variables to a clean environment does not reproduce it; `TMPDIR` alone does. Likely cause, not traced: the test's temporary project sits under `HOME`, so config discovery walking up finds real config. "Core test environment > isolates global home and XDG roots" failed in the same full run and may be related.

## 5. Local test notes (unconfirmed in CI)

- On a loaded machine, `test/session-runner-recorded.test.ts` and `test/session-checkpoint-transport.test.ts` › "trigger recovers over SSE ... reconnect is rejected" time out at 5 s. They do so with main's sources in place of #2679, too.
- The full `bun test` in `packages/core` did not finish within 40 minutes there.
- Already tracked: client codegen (#2495).

opencode.title: feat(app): restore custom provider setup in V2
opencode.body:
## Problem

The Connect Provider flow still exposes **Custom Provider** and a form for an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, API key, models, and headers, but saving can never succeed in V2. `packages/app/src/providers/credentials/dialog.tsx` unconditionally throws `provider.custom.unavailable` from the save mutation (the adjacent TODO says config and arbitrary credential APIs are not yet exposed). The option remains discoverable in `packages/app/src/providers/connect/dialog.tsx`, so users can complete the form and only then learn that custom providers are unavailable.

## Expected behavior

Restore a supported V2 path for adding a custom OpenAI-compatible provider: validate the fields, persist its configuration and credentials through supported APIs, and make the configured provider available for connection/model selection after saving and reload. If the V2 APIs are not ready, the UI should not present this as a saveable setup flow.

## Acceptance criteria

- A user can complete the Custom Provider flow and save an OpenAI-compatible endpoint with its credentials, models, and optional headers using V2-supported APIs.
- The saved provider is available to connect/select and remains configured after reopening/reloading.
- Validation and persistence failures are surfaced without claiming success or losing the entered form state.
- Tests cover successful save/reload and API failure; unavailable V2 capability is handled without exposing a dead-end form.

## Scope and deduplication

This is provider onboarding/configuration and credential persistence in the V2 Connect Provider UI. It is distinct from #1708, which tracks protocol/tool-call support after a custom provider is configured, and from #374, the broad V1-to-V2 migration tracker. No matching issue or open PR was found in fresh all-state issue and open-PR searches. Filed under the OpenCode platform epic as required by #2319.
